maamme: The music was composed by Fredrik Pacius, a German immigrant, to the Swedish words of Johan Ludvig Runeberg. It is said that Pacius composed the tune in four days. The song was written for the 500th anniversary of Porvoo and was first performed on 13 May 1848.

The poem formed the prologue to the verse cycle The Tales of Ensign Stål (Fänrik Ståhls sägner), a classic example of Romantic nationalism. The Finnish text now in use is usually attributed to Paavo Cajander's 1889 translation of the cycle, but it in fact originates from the 1867 translation by Julius Krohn.

The song was popular throughout the 19th century but established its present position only after Pacius's death. There were attempts in the 1880s and the 1920s to replace it with a version in Finnish, but these ceased by the 1930s. Some Finns have proposed the Finlandia piece by Jean Sibelius as the anthem instead.

Finland has no law naming an official national anthem, unlike its coat of arms and flag, which are legally defined. The position of Maamme was established gradually by convention, and in use it fills the function of a national anthem: it is played during state visits and used to represent Finland at international sporting fixtures. It is customary to sing only the first and the last verse, unless the people gathered are a mix of Finnish and Swedish speakers. In that case three verses are sung: the first in Finnish, the first in Swedish and the last in Finnish.

The melody of Maamme is also used for two other anthems: the Estonian anthem Mu isamaa, mu õnn ja rõõm (My Fatherland, My Happiness and Joy) and the Livonian anthem Min izāmō (My Fatherland). Both borrow the tune that Pacius wrote for Runeberg's poem.
maan-jordan: Ma'an lies in southern Jordan, 218 kilometres south-west of Amman, at a height above 1,000 metres. The climate is a cold desert one, with hot summers, mild to cold winters and rainfall averaging only 44 millimetres a year. The modern city stands just north-west of the ancient town of the same name, which dates at least to the Nabatean period. It lies on the old King's Highway and on the modern Desert Highway, and it is the capital of the Ma'an Governorate.

Ma'an was founded, according to the account given for it, by the Minaeans, an ancient Arab people based in Yemen, between the 2nd and 4th century BCE, on a major trade route. Local tradition holds that it was named after Ma'an, the son of Lot. Under Byzantine rule it lay in the territory of the Arab Christian tribe of Banu Judham. Its governor in the early 7th century, Farwa ibn Amr al-Judhami, converted to Islam and was executed by crucifixion on the Byzantine emperor's order. The Muslim state in Medina then sent an army under Usama ibn Zayd to conquer the town.

The Hajj route to Mecca ran through Ma'an, and its economy depended on the pilgrim caravans. Its main trade partner was Gaza, and it sold livestock, above all camels and sheep, to pilgrims. Most residents were literate and many served as imams or advisers to the Bedouin, with whom the town had unusually good relations. The Ottomans annexed Transjordan in 1517 and in 1559 built a fort to protect the pilgrim road. In the late nineteenth century they tried several times to raise Ma'an's rank, but al-Karak was preferred as district capital. The railway station opened in 1902, connecting the city to Damascus and Medina.

In April 1918 the Arab Northern Army besieged the Ottoman garrison at the Battle of Maan, from 13 to 17 April. It failed to take the city but wrecked the Hejaz railway to the south. In 1920 the Hashemite emir Abdullah I arrived with several hundred fighters in an attempt to restore the Sharifian throne in Damascus after its overthrow by France. Ma'an was annexed to the Transjordanian state in 1925.

Ma'an is the seat of Al-Hussein Bin Talal University and of the Ma'an Development Area, a special economic zone whose industrial park began construction in 2008. A railway building at the station, used by Abdullah I as the seat of the first government, is now called the Ma'an Palace and appears on the reverse of the 5 dinar note. Most of the inhabitants are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school.
maasai-people: The Maasai are an Eastern Nilotic people whose language, Maa, belongs to the Nilo-Saharan family. They arrived in the African Great Lakes region by way of South Sudan. Like other groups in East Africa, they adopted customs and vocabulary from neighbouring Cushitic-speaking peoples, including the age-set system of social organisation and circumcision. Groups already settled in the region were forcibly displaced by the incoming Maasai, while other, mainly Southern Cushitic, groups were assimilated into Maasai society. They are pastoralists and have a reputation as fearsome warriors and cattle raiders.

The Maasai territory reached its largest size in the mid-19th century, covering almost the whole Great Rift Valley and adjacent lands from Mount Marsabit in the north to Dodoma in the south. Raiders used spears and shields but were most feared for their throwing clubs. In 1857, after depopulating what was called the Wakuafi wilderness in south-eastern Kenya, Maasai warriors threatened Mombasa.

The period of expansion was followed by the Emutai of 1883 to 1902, marked by epidemics of cattle pleuropneumonia, rinderpest and smallpox, and by drought. A German lieutenant estimated that 90 per cent of cattle died of rinderpest, and by one estimate two thirds of the Maasai themselves died. Later, Maasai in Tanganyika were displaced in the 1940s from fertile lands between Mount Meru and Mount Kilimanjaro. In 1951 British colonial policymakers removed all Maasai from the Serengeti National Park and moved them to the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. More land was taken for wildlife reserves and national parks in both Kenya and Tanzania, among them Amboseli, Maasai Mara and Lake Manyara.

There are twenty-two geographic sectors of the Maasai, called iloshon, each with its own customs, leadership and dialect. The Maasai are monotheistic and worship a single deity, Enkai, who has a benevolent aspect, Engai Narok, the Black God, and a vengeful one, Engai Na-nyokie, the Red God. The laibon is the central human figure of their religion, with roles that include healing, divination and prophecy. Many Maasai have also adopted Christianity or Islam.

Their way of life has centred on cattle, which are the main source of food, and a man's wealth is measured in cattle, wives and children. Warriors are the only members of the community who wear long hair, and at the Eunoto ceremony a warrior becomes a junior elder and has it shaved off. Boys are circumcised as a rite of passage, and girls undergo a female rite, a form of genital mutilation, which activists such as Agnes Pareyio campaign against.
maastricht: Maastricht lies on both sides of the Meuse, at the point where the river is joined by the Jeker, close to the border with Belgium. Mount Saint Peter is largely within the municipal borders, and the city belongs to the Meuse-Rhine Euroregion, which includes Aachen, Liège and Hasselt. Neanderthal remains have been found to the west of the city, and Celts lived here around 500 BCE at a spot where the Meuse was shallow and easy to cross. The Roman settlement, Trajectum ad Mosam, developed into a medieval centre of river trade and religion.

In the early Middle Ages Maastricht, with Aachen and Liège, formed part of the heartland of the Carolingian dynasty, and was an important centre of river trade and manufacturing; Merovingian coins minted there have been found throughout Europe. The Vikings plundered the town in 881, and in the tenth century it was briefly the capital of the duchy of Lower Lorraine. Its position at a major river crossing led to an array of fortifications from the sixteenth century, and the Spanish and Dutch garrisons shaped its economy. In 1579 the Spanish army under the Duke of Parma sacked the city.

For over fifty years the Spanish crown held the joint sovereignty that the dukes of Brabant had held before; in 1632 Prince Frederick Henry of Orange conquered the city, and the Dutch States General took the Spanish crown's place. A Spanish attempt to retake it in 1634 failed.

In 1815 Maastricht became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and the capital of the new province of Limburg. When the southern provinces seceded in 1830, the Dutch garrison stayed loyal to King William I, although most of the townspeople sided with the Belgian revolutionaries. The arbitration of 1831 gave the city to the Netherlands, but neither side accepted it until the Treaty of London of 1839. In this isolation Maastricht became an early industrial town. Traditional industries such as its potteries declined in the later twentieth century, and Maastricht University was founded in 1976.

Maastricht is the capital and largest city of the province of Limburg. European Councils were held there in 1981 and 1991, and the second led a year later to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which created the European Union and the euro. The city has 1,677 national heritage buildings, the second highest number in the Netherlands after Amsterdam, and its whole centre is a conservation area. The Bonnefanten Museum shows old masters and contemporary art.
maastricht-treaty: The treaty was negotiated against the end of the Cold War and the reunification of Germany, and had to reconcile member states seeking deeper integration with those wishing to keep national control. French President François Mitterrand had been forced to abandon his Socialist programme in 1983 because of speculation against the franc, and he was afterwards committed to drawing Germany into a currency partnership. When Chancellor Helmut Kohl asked for reunification in 1990, Mitterrand would accept it only if Germany agreed to give up the Deutsche Mark for a common currency.

The twelve members of the European Communities signed the treaty on 7 February 1992. It was signed in Maastricht because the Netherlands held the presidency of the Council during the six months of negotiation.

Title I established the European Union on the foundation of the three partly merged communities, the European Economic Community, the European Coal and Steel Community and Euratom. Its objectives were a citizenship of the Union, economic and monetary union ultimately with a single currency, and a common foreign and security policy. Title II renamed the European Economic Community the European Community and set a staged path to monetary union, with criteria for adopting the single currency and a future European Central Bank.

Every national of a member state became a citizen of the Union, with the right to vote and stand in local and European elections where they lived. The European Parliament gained co-decision on some legislation and the power to confirm the Council's nominations for the Commission. Foreign policy and justice and home affairs stayed intergovernmental, and the United Kingdom obtained opt-outs from the social protocol and the final stage of monetary union.

Ratification required referendums in Denmark, France and Ireland. Danish voters rejected the treaty on 2 June 1992 by 50.7 to 49.3 percent, but after concessions agreed at Edinburgh, including an exemption from the single currency like the British one, a second referendum on 18 May 1993 approved it with 56.7 percent. Ireland approved it on 18 June 1992 with 69.1 percent, and France narrowly in September 1992 with 50.8 percent. In Britain Prime Minister John Major overcame Conservative rebels only by tying ratification to a vote of confidence. The German Federal Constitutional Court ruled it compatible with the Basic Law on 12 October 1993.
macau: Macau lies on China's southern coast, 60 km west of Hong Kong, on the south shore of Zhongshan Island on the western side of the Pearl River estuary. It consists of the Macau Peninsula, Taipa, Coloane and the Cotai reclamation zone between them. The peninsula was originally a separate island with hilly terrain that became a tombolo as a sandbar formed, and natural sedimentation and land reclamation have enlarged it. The land area grew from 10.28 square kilometres in the late 19th century to 32.9 square kilometres in 2018.

During the Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE) the region came under Panyu County, Nanhai Commandery, and it is first known to have been settled in the Han dynasty. In 1152, under the Song, it fell under the new Xiangshan County. In 1277 about 50,000 refugees fleeing the Mongol conquest of China settled on the coast. The earliest written record of the name, A Ma Gang, is in a letter of 20 November 1555. It refers to the sea goddess Matsu, or A-Ma, whose temple the local people took the Portuguese to be asking about when they gave the name Ma Kok.

The explorer Jorge Álvares, the first European to reach China by sea, arrived in 1513. Portuguese merchants set up a trading post at Tamão, now Tuen Mun, but after their expulsion in 1521 the Ming and Portuguese navies clashed. Portugal lost two ships at the Battle of Tamão in 1521 and two more at the Battle of Sincouwaan; later defeats came at Shuangyu in 1548 and near Dongshan County in 1549. Merchants kept trying to settle on the Pearl River estuary and finally settled at Macau.

The Ming dynasty first leased the territory to Portugal as a trading post in 1557. Portugal paid an annual rent and administered it under Chinese sovereignty until 1887, when the Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking gave it perpetual colonial rights. Portuguese rule lasted until the handover to China in 1999. The Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration provided for economic and administrative continuity, and the Basic Law of Macao, under the principle of one country, two systems, serves as the regional constitution.

Macau is a special administrative region of China, with a population of about 720,000 and one of the highest densities in the world. Its economy rests largely on casino gaming and tourism. More than four centuries of Chinese and Portuguese contact have left a mixed culture, with Macanese people of mixed Portuguese ancestry, and a downtown that blends Portuguese, French, English, Italian and Chinese architecture. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
macbeth-king-of-scotland: Little is known of Macbeth's early life. He was the son of Findláech of Moray, who had been killed by Gille Coemgáin, and may have been a grandson of Malcolm II, presumably through the king's daughter Donada. His name, Mac Bethad, means son of life, and implies a righteous or religious man. When Cnut the Great came north in 1031 to accept the submission of Malcolm II, Macbeth also submitted to him.

He became Mormaer of Moray, a semi-autonomous province, in 1032, and was probably responsible for the death of Gille Coemgáin. He then married Gille Coemgáin's widow, Gruoch, who may herself have had a claim to the throne. They had no children together, and Macbeth accepted her son Lulach as his heir.

Duncan I was acclaimed king of Alba on 30 November 1034, apparently without opposition. In 1039 the Northumbrians attacked Strathclyde and a retaliatory raid by Duncan against Durham ended in disaster. The next year he led an army into Moray, apparently on a punitive expedition, and was killed in action at Bothnagowan, near Elgin, by the men of Moray led by Macbeth, probably on 14 August 1040. Macbeth became king and no resistance to his accession is known.

In 1045 Duncan's father Crínán of Dunkeld was killed in a battle between two Scottish armies, and Duncan's brother Maldred is believed to have died there too, fighting Macbeth in defence of Duncan's young son Máel Coluim, later Malcolm III. Marianus Scotus records that Macbeth made a pilgrimage to Rome in 1050 and gave money to the poor as if it were seed.

In 1052 he received Norman exiles from England at his court. In 1054 Siward, Earl of Northumbria, led a very large invasion of Scotland. The Annals of Ulster report 3,000 Scots and 1,500 English dead in the bloody battle at Dunsinane. Macbeth did not survive the English invasion for long: he was defeated and mortally wounded or killed by the future Malcolm III at Lumphanan in 1057. The Prophecy of Berchán says he died at Scone some days later. His stepson Lulach was installed as king but was soon killed by Malcolm.

Unlike later writers, no near-contemporary source calls Macbeth a tyrant. The Duan Albanach calls him Mac Bethad of fame, and the Prophecy of Berchán calls him the generous king of Fortriu. His life had moved far towards legend by the end of the 14th century, when John of Fordun and Andrew of Wyntoun wrote. William Shakespeare's tragedy, probably first performed in 1606 and based on Holinshed's Chronicles, is not historically accurate. A likely reason for its unflattering portrait is that James VI and I descended from Malcolm III, while Macbeth's line died out with Lulach.
maccabean-revolt: Alexander the Great's Macedonian forces conquered the Levant in 333 and 332 BCE. Judea passed to Ptolemaic Egypt in 302 and 301 BCE and was then conquered by the Seleucid Empire in campaigns between 235 and 198 BCE. Under both dynasties many Jews, especially in the upper class, learned Greek, and many adopted a Greek name beside a Hebrew one.

In 168 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes began a campaign of repression against the Jewish religion. His reasons are not entirely clear, but he seems to have mistaken a conflict within the Jewish priesthood for a full rebellion. Jewish practices were banned, Jerusalem was placed under direct Seleucid control and the Temple became the site of a mixed pagan and Jewish cult.

In 167 BCE a rural priest of the Hasmonean family, Mattathias of Modein, refused to sacrifice at a new altar there, killed a Jew who stepped forward to do so and the Greek officer sent to enforce it, and fled to the hills with his five sons. After his death his son Judas Maccabeus led a band that grew into an army. It raided the countryside, destroyed Greek altars and attacked Hellenized Jews.

In 164 BCE the rebels captured Jerusalem. The cleansing of the Temple and rededication of the altar on 25 Kislev is the origin of Hanukkah. Judas died in 160 BCE at the Battle of Elasa against the Seleucid general Bacchides. His brother Jonathan Apphus kept a rival government in the countryside, and Seleucid civil wars let him bargain: Alexander Balas made Jonathan high priest.

In 141 BCE Simon Thassi expelled the Greek garrison from the citadel in Jerusalem, and an alliance with the Roman Republic helped guarantee independence. When Antiochus VII besieged Jerusalem in 134 BCE, John Hyrcanus paid a ransom and the Seleucids left. After Antiochus VII died in 129 BCE the Hasmoneans paid no more tribute, and Hyrcanus's son Aristobulus I took the title of king.

The main sources, 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees, favour the Maccabees and present the war as a divinely sanctioned struggle. A later view, popularised by Elias Bickerman in 1937, holds that it was also a civil war between traditionalist Jews in the countryside and Hellenized Jews in the cities.
maccabees: Maccabee was a personal epithet of Judas Maccabeus, and the name is often used for the whole Hasmonean dynasty, though strictly it refers to Judas and his brothers, since later generations were not his direct descendants. One explanation derives it from the Aramaic maqqəḇa, the hammer, for his ferocity in battle. The traditional Jewish explanation reads it as an acronym of the verse of Exodus 15:11, the battle cry of the Maccabees.

In the 2nd century BCE Judea lay between the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Seleucid Empire and fell to the Seleucids around 197 BCE. Some Hellenizing Jews, mainly of the urban upper class, wished to adopt a Greek way of life. When Antiochus IV Epiphanes took power in 175 BCE the office of high priest became a matter of bribery between Jason and Menelaus, and in 168 BCE Antiochus pillaged the Temple. According to 1 Maccabees he then banned Jewish practices, including circumcision and the sabbath. Most modern scholars see a civil war between traditionalists and Hellenizers that Seleucid intervention turned into a revolt.

In the narrative of 1 Maccabees, Mattathias the Hasmonean, a rural priest from Modi'in, started the revolt by refusing to worship the Greek gods. He and his five sons fled to the wilderness of Judah. After he died in 166 BCE his son Judas led a guerrilla war, entered Jerusalem, ritually cleansed the Temple and restored traditional worship, an event marked at Hanukkah. Judas was killed in battle in 160 BCE and was succeeded as army commander by his brother Jonathan, who was already high priest.

Jonathan was assassinated in 142 BCE by Diodotus Tryphon, and the last remaining son of Mattathias, Simon, was recognised in 140 BCE by an assembly as high priest, military commander and ruler. Simon was murdered in 134 BCE by his son-in-law Ptolemy, and his son John Hyrcanus I succeeded him. Independent Hasmonean rule lasted until 63 BCE, when the Roman general Pompeius intervened in a Hasmonean civil war. The dynasty ended in 37 BCE when Herod the Great became king.

The story is told in the books of First and Second Maccabees. They are not part of the Tanakh but belong to the Septuagint, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches count them as deuterocanonical, while most Protestants regard them as apocryphal. The miracle of the oil lasting eight days is first described in the Talmud, about 600 years after the events. Christians also venerate the Holy Maccabean Martyrs, seven brothers, their mother and their teacher, who are not said to belong to the family; their feast day is 1 August.
macedonia-region: Macedonia is a geographical and historical region of the Balkan Peninsula in Southeast Europe. In the 19th century the name was revived for a region bounded by Mount Olympus, the Pindus range, the mountains Shar and Osogovo, the western Rhodopes, the lower course of the river Mesta and the Aegean Sea. The ancient kingdom of Macedonia, which gave the region its name, lay before the expansion of Philip II within the central and western parts of what is now Greek Macedonia.

The earliest known settlements, such as Nea Nikomedeia in Imathia, date back about 9,000 years. Rome ended Macedonian sovereignty in the 2nd century BCE: Philip V was defeated in the Second Macedonian War, and Perseus lost his kingdom in the Third. The land was divided into four districts and annexed as a Roman province in 146 BCE.

From the beginning of the 6th century Slavic tribes raided the Byzantine Balkan provinces, and great parts of Macedonia came to be controlled by Slavic-speaking communities, though Thessaloniki held out. The parts ruled by the First Bulgarian Empire in the 9th and 10th centuries were taken into the Byzantine Empire in 1018. After the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa in 1371 most of Macedonia accepted vassalage, and the Ottomans took Thessalonica in 1430. The region remained Ottoman for nearly 500 years and became multicultural, with Greeks, Bulgarians, Turks, Albanians, Jews and Aromanians among its peoples.

In the 19th century Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria contested the region, and the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization organised the Ilinden-Preobrazhenie Uprising in 1903. In the First Balkan War, begun in August 1912, Greek forces entered Thessalonica first. In the Second World War about 60,000 Jews from Thessaloniki were deported to extermination camps in occupied Poland.

The modern region at its maximum extent spans the largest part of Northern Greece, known as Greek Macedonia, all of North Macedonia, a large part of southwestern Bulgaria, known as Pirin Macedonia, and small parts of Albania, Serbia and Kosovo. Greek Macedonia's largest city, Thessaloniki, is the second largest in Greece.
macedonia-roman-province: After the Third Macedonian War Rome abolished the Macedonian monarchy and divided the country into four client republics, called merides, with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. They belonged to a federal league, the League of the Macedonians, and both the merides and the league continued as parts of the province. Its northern border notionally ran from Lissus on the Adriatic east to the Hebrus river, but was loosely defined: Cicero claimed that for the governors of Macedonia the borders were always those marked by swords and shields.

The Via Egnatia, begun by Gnaeus Egnatius, ran from Dyrrhachium on the Adriatic across the Pindus mountains and through Macedonia to Thessalonica and on to Cypsela on the Hebrus. This stretch was finished by 120 BCE. It followed an older route but was a more solid, level road, three to six metres wide, and its eastern end was later extended to Byzantium.

In the first decades the Romans fought nearly constant campaigns against the Dardani, the Thracians and above all the Scordisci, a Celtic people who first invaded in the Fourth Macedonian War. Two pretenders also tried to restore the kingdom. In 114 BCE Gaius Porcius Cato invaded the Scordisci but was defeated and nearly his whole army was killed. After the Mithridatic Wars the governors were consuls or proconsuls, often holding command for several years, and Gaius Scribonius Curio became the first Roman commander to lead an army to the Danube.

Macedonia was a main arena of the civil wars. Pompey and about two hundred senators withdrew to it in 49 BCE and set up a Senate in exile at Thessalonica. Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in August 48 BCE, and in 42 BCE Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi. Six Roman colonies were then founded for veterans, among them Cassandrea, Philippi, Dium and Pella.

Under Augustus the northern lands became the provinces of Moesia, Dalmatia and Pannonia, and the territories south of Thermopylae became Achaia. Macedonia lost much of its military role but stayed important for supplies and manpower. Greek remained the main language, with Latin used officially and in the colonies, and there were substantial Christian communities by the mid-first century CE. Around 293 CE Diocletian's reforms split the province into smaller units, including Macedonia Prima, governed from Thessalonica, and Macedonia Salutaris, with its capital at Stobi. The provincial system faded until the themes replaced it in the mid-seventh century.
macedonian-dynasty: The dynasty is named after its founder, Basil I the Macedonian, who came from the theme of Macedonia in the region of Thrace, and it followed the Amorian dynasty. Its ethnic origin is unknown and has been debated. During Basil's reign an elaborate genealogy was produced that claimed his ancestors were not mere peasants, as everyone believed, but descendants of the Arsacid kings of Armenia, of Alexander the Great and of Constantine the Great.

Some Persian writers, such as Hamza al-Isfahani and al-Tabari, called Basil a Saqlabi, a term usually denoting Slavs but which can mean the inhabitants of the region between Constantinople and Bulgaria. Claims have therefore been made for Armenian, Slavonic or mixed descent. The author of the only dedicated English biography of Basil concludes that his origins cannot be established with certainty, though he relied on the support of Armenians in prominent positions.

Basil I ruled from 867 to 886 and married Eudokia Ingerina, mistress of Michael III; he died in a hunting accident. His son Leo VI the Wise, possibly the natural son of Michael III, caused a church crisis by his fourth marriage, to Zoe Karbonopsina, who ruled as regent for their son Constantine VII from 914 to 919. Romanos I Lekapenos staged a coup in 919 and became senior emperor in 920, until he was deposed and exiled in 944. Constantine VII, born in the purple, ruled again from 945 to 959.

After Romanos II (959–963) came two successful generals: Nikephoros II Phokas (963–969), who was assassinated, and John I Tzimiskes (969–976), the regents for Basil II. Basil II, the Bulgar-slayer, reigned from 976 to 1025. His brother Constantine VIII followed as sole emperor until 1028, and then Constantine's daughter Zoe ruled until 1050 with a succession of husbands: Romanos III Argyros, who was murdered, Michael IV the Paphlagonian and Constantine IX Monomachos.

Michael V the Caulker, Zoe's adopted son, reigned in 1041–1042. Zoe's sister Theodora ruled jointly with her in 1042 and alone from 1055 to 1056. Michael VI, chosen by Theodora, was a non-dynastic ruler who was deposed and entered a monastery.

Under the dynasty the Byzantine state reached its largest extent since the early Muslim conquests, and the Macedonian Renaissance in letters and arts began. The dynasty's family ties reached beyond the empire: Basil's daughter Anna was betrothed to Louis the Blind, and Basil II's sister Anna Porphyrogeneta married Vladimir I of Kiev.
machado-de-assis: Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis was born on 21 June 1839 in Rio de Janeiro, then the capital of the Empire of Brazil. His father, Francisco José de Assis, was a wall painter and the son of freed slaves; his mother, Maria Leopoldina da Câmara Machado, was a Portuguese washerwoman from the Azores. He was born in a country house owned by a senator's widow, who protected his parents and became his godmother. His mother died when he was ten.

He barely studied in public schools and never attended university, learning French from an immigrant baker and Latin from a priest he met while serving at mass. His first poem, Ela, was published on 12 January 1855, when he was fifteen, and the next year he became a typographer's apprentice at the Imprensa Oficial.

In 1858 Francisco Otaviano hired him as a proofreader at the Correio Mercantil. The writer José de Alencar, a friend, taught him English, and he later learned German and, in old age, Greek. Emperor Dom Pedro II hired him as an assistant director of the Diário Oficial in 1867 and knighted him. He married the Portuguese Carolina Augusta Xavier de Novais on 12 November 1869; her family disapproved because he was of African descent, and the couple had no children. He rose through the bureaucracy, beginning in the Agriculture Department.

He published the poetry books Falenas in 1870 and Americanas in 1875, but their weak reception made him try other genres. His romantic novels, among them Helena and Iaiá Garcia, pleased the public but not the critics. Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas, in 1881, brought a sceptical and realistic tone and is widely considered a masterpiece. The overthrow of the monarchy on 15 November 1889 took him by surprise; he considered himself a liberal monarchist. Quincas Borba followed in 1891, Dom Casmurro in 1899, Esaú e Jacó in 1904 and Memorial de Aires in 1908. In 1893 he published the short story A Missa do Galo.

With fellow writers and intellectuals including Joaquim Nabuco, Machado helped found the Brazilian Academy of Letters in 1897 and was its president until his death. In 1905 he obtained a proper headquarters for it. His wife died on 20 October 1904, and he died on 29 September 1908.

Critics are divided about his writing. Abel Barros Baptista sees an anti-realist who attacks Realism, John Gledson a faithful description of Brazilian reality executed with daring technique, and Roberto Schwarz a prose that exposes the hypocrisies and dysfunction of 19th-century Brazil. His work has been adapted for television, theatre and cinema and translated into many languages, though his books have never sold widely in the English-speaking world.
machilipatnam: Machilipatnam lies on the south-eastern, or Coromandel, coast of India at the mouth of the River Krishna on the Bay of Bengal, about 60 kilometres from Vijayawada. In the 17th century it was known as Masulipatnam, Masulipatam, Masula and Bandar, the last from the Persian word for port. In ancient times it was also called Maesolia. It is the administrative headquarters of Krishna district.

The town has existed since at least the 3rd century BCE, the Satavahana period, when according to Ptolemy it was known as Maisolos. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea calls it Masalia. Sea trade flourished at the port, and the word muslin is derived from the name Maisolos. Muslin was a significant source of income and a favourite of Roman traders, and several Roman coins have been found in excavations of Buddhist towns near the town.

Machilipatnam served as the primary sea port of the Kingdom of Golkonda, an outlet for textiles produced in the Godavari Delta. It was a major source of income for the kingdom and contributed to its prosperity in the 1620s and 1630s. From the 16th century European traders settled there, and in the 17th century it was a major trading port for the Portuguese, British, Dutch and French. It was known for minting copper coins and for exporting diamonds and textiles. By the end of the 17th century the port had fallen into decline, which coincided with the Mughal conquest of Golkonda, though mismanagement before the conquest may also have been a factor.

Salabat Jung, the son of Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, owed his throne to the French East India Company and granted it in return the district of Kondavid, or Guntur, and soon afterwards the remainder of the Circars. The British captured the Circars from the French in 1759 and returned them to the Nizam, but the East India Company kept Masulipatnam, which it had taken in the Siege of Masulipatam. The town became the headquarters of Masulipatnam district, from which the Krishna district was formed in 1859 in Madras state. On 1 November 1864 a giant wave damaged the port, and the cyclone of that year is said to have killed at least 30,000 people.

Machilipatnam is known for its handloom industry and for Machilipatnam Kalamkari, hand-dyed block-painting on cloth, which is carried out at the nearby town of Pedana and has a geographical indication. Boat building and fishing are other local trades. The town has the ruined buildings built by the Europeans who settled there, and it is home to Shia Muslim imambargahs, some more than 600 years old, where Ashura is observed.
machu-picchu: Machu Picchu stands in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru, on a narrow saddle between two peaks, Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu, at about 2,430 metres. It lies some 80 kilometres north-west of Cusco and more than 1,000 metres lower than the Inca capital, so its climate was milder. The Urubamba River bends round the site on three sides, and cliffs drop 450 metres to the water. A study of 2021 suggests that its builders called it Huayna Picchu, or simply Picchu.

The dating is debated. Models based on John H. Rowe's reconstruction of the reign of Pachacuti put the start of building around 1450, while radiocarbon measurements on human remains, reported in a 2021 study led by Richard L. Burger, indicate occupation from about 1420 to 1530. Archaeologists generally hold that Pachacuti ordered the royal estate after conquering the middle and lower Urubamba, as part of a programme of royal estates along the river, though no contemporary written record confirms it.

The estate seems to have been a seasonal retreat. About 750 people are estimated to have lived there, most of them permanent support staff known as yanaconas, with religious specialists and temporary workers. The site was abandoned in the mid-16th century, around the time of the Spanish conquest, probably because Inca rule collapsed and disease followed European contact; smallpox may have killed most of its inhabitants before the conquistadors arrived.

The forest overgrew the ruins, and few outside the area knew of them. The Peruvian explorer Agustín Lizárraga reached the site in the early 20th century, but the American historian Hiram Bingham III brought it to international attention in 1911.

The citadel is built in the classical Inca style, with finely worked dry-stone walls. About 200 buildings stand on parallel terraces round a central square, divided into an agricultural sector and an urban sector with an upper and a lower town. Its main structures include the Temple of the Sun, the Temple of the Three Windows and the Intihuatana stone. Peru declared a Historic Sanctuary there in 1981, and UNESCO listed Machu Picchu as a World Heritage Site in 1983.
macon: Mâcon lies on the western bank of the river Saône, between Bresse to the east and the Beaujolais hills to the south, about 65 kilometres north of Lyon. It is the southernmost city of the department of Saône-et-Loire. The town controlled access to the present-day Lamartinien Valley, where the southern end of the Côte de Bourgogne joins the first foothills of the Beaujolais hills and opens the way to the plains of the Loire.

The settlement began as an oppidum and river port established by Celts from the Aedui, probably at the start of the 1st century BCE. Known as Matisco, it grew considerably under the Roman Empire, as the large hoard called the Mâcon Treasure shows: it was found in 1764, and its remains are in the British Museum. The town was fortified in the 4th century.

In the Middle Ages Mâcon was the administrative centre of a county belonging to the Duchy of Burgundy, at the end of the bridge over the Saône that led to Bresse, which belonged to the Duchy of Savoy. Its position made it a possible entrance into the kingdom for Swiss or German mercenaries during the French Wars of Religion. On 3 June 1564 Charles IX stopped there during his Royal Tour of France, and was welcomed by Queen Jeanne III of Navarre and 1,500 Huguenots.

In 1790 the Revolutionary government made Mâcon the chef-lieu of the new department of Saône-et-Loire. Austrian troops invaded in 1814 and captured the town again after the Hundred Days. In the Second World War it was the northernmost town of the unoccupied zone between Paris and Lyon; nearly eight hundred German soldiers settled there on 11 November 1942, and it was liberated on 4 September 1944.

Mâcon has about 35,000 residents. Its sights include the Cathedral of Saint-Vincent, the old Saint-Vincent in the town centre, the Hôtel de Senecé, which houses the Lamartine museum, and a town hall finished in 1751. Alphonse de Lamartine was born in the town on 21 October 1790. The vineyards around it, of about 5,000 hectares, grow mostly Chardonnay, and the best-known appellation of the Mâconnais is Pouilly-Fuissé. The Saône gives the town a river port.
madagascar: Madagascar covers 592,800 square kilometres and is the world's fourth-largest island and second-largest island country. It split from Africa around 180 million years ago and from the Indian subcontinent approximately 90 million years ago, so that its plants and animals evolved in relative isolation; over 90 per cent of its wildlife is endemic. A narrow, steep escarpment with tropical lowland forest runs along the east coast, and west of it lies a central plateau of terraced, rice-growing valleys between 750 and 1,500 metres high. The highest point is Maromokotro, at 2,876 metres.

Madagascar was first permanently settled during or before the mid-first millennium CE by Austronesian peoples, presumably arriving by outrigger canoe from present-day Indonesia, and scholars are cautious about dates earlier than 250 CE. The first settlers met giant lemurs, elephant birds and Malagasy hippopotamuses, which later became extinct through hunting and habitat destruction. Arab traders reached the island between the 7th and 9th centuries and brought Islam and the Arabic script, adapted as sorabe. Bantu-speaking migrants from south-eastern Africa arrived around the year 1000, and zebu cattle from South India were brought about then.

Until the late 18th century a fragmented set of shifting alliances ruled the island. King Andrianjaka founded Antananarivo as capital of the Imerina Kingdom around 1610 or 1625. From the early 19th century a series of Merina nobles united most of the island as the Kingdom of Madagascar. France's annexation ended the monarchy, and the country became independent in 1960.

Madagascar has had four republics and has been a constitutional democracy since 1992. A political crisis and coup in 2009 led to a long transition, and constitutional governance returned in January 2014. Malagasy and French are the official languages.

The Malagasy form over 90 per cent of the population, divided into 18 ethnic subgroups, of which the Merina of the highlands are the largest at about 26 per cent. The Malagasy language is of Malayo-Polynesian origin, closest to Ma'anyan of Borneo. The valiha, the most emblematic instrument, is a bamboo tube zither carried by early settlers from southern Borneo.
madame-de-pompadour: Jeanne Antoinette Poisson was the daughter of François Poisson, a steward to the Paris brothers who financed the French state. It was suspected that her biological father was a financier or the tax collector Charles François Paul Le Normant de Tournehem, who became her guardian and paid for an expensive education, with tutors including the dramatist Crébillon and the singer Jélyotte. At twenty she married his nephew Charles Guillaume Le Normant d'Étiolles. She attended Paris salons, held her own at Étiolles, and met Voltaire, Montesquieu and Helvétius there. In 1744 she contrived to be seen by Louis XV while he hunted, and at a masked ball at Versailles on 25 February 1745 he declared his interest in her.

By March 1745 she was the king's mistress. The king bought her the marquisate of Pompadour in June, and she was presented at court on 14 September. She won the favour of Queen Marie Leszczyńska, became a duchess in 1752 and lady-in-waiting to the queen in 1756. She acted in effect as a prime minister, handling appointments, favours and dismissals, and in 1755 the Austrian diplomat Kaunitz approached her during the talks leading to the Treaty of Versailles, which allied France with Austria. Later she brought the duc de Choiseul into office. France was diminished by the Seven Years' War, and she was widely blamed. Around 1750 her sexual relationship with the king ended, and she remained his confidante.

Libels called poissonnades, a pun on her name, attacked her. Historians stress that the Parc-aux-Cerfs, a house at Versailles where the king later met young women, was not the harem of legend, and that she only accepted it.

Pompadour was a major patron of architecture, painting and the decorative arts, supporting Boucher, Nattier and the engraver Jacques Guay, who taught her to engrave gems. In 1759 she bought the porcelain factory at Sèvres. She protected the physician and economist François Quesnay and defended the Encyclopédie of Diderot and d'Alembert against those who wished to suppress it. She made 52 prints after Guay's engraved stones and acted in plays at her private theatres. She died of tuberculosis on 15 April 1764, aged 42.
madara-rider: The Madara Rider is a large early medieval rock relief on the Madara Plateau east of Shumen in north-eastern Bulgaria. It is dated to the very late 7th or, more often, the very early 8th century, in the reign of the Bulgar khan Tervel. The relief shows a horseman, almost life-size, about 23 metres above the ground on an almost vertical cliff 100 metres high. He faces right and thrusts a spear into a lion lying at his horse's feet, while a dog runs after him on the left. Erosion and the poor condition of the monument have left his halo, his garments and the bird before his face barely recognisable. The relief was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

Its meaning and symbolism are uncertain, as are its masonry tradition and cultural source. The relief probably combines elements of Thracian cults and those of the newly arrived Bulgars. Its monumental size and many details, the stirrup, halo, skull-cup and bird among them, belong to Bulgar tradition, while the rightward direction and the lion are more typical of Thracian. Some early researchers took it for a Thracian horseman, a recurring figure of a deity in Paleo-Balkanic mythology, but this view was rejected because of differences in iconography. Others see a resemblance to Sasanian rock reliefs, or link the horseman to the Bulgar deity Tangra or to the Iranian deity Mithra. A simpler suggestion is that it represents Khan Tervel.

Three partly preserved texts in medieval Greek are carved in the rock around the rider. The oldest is by Tervel, so the relief is thought to date from his rule or soon after the Bulgars settled the region in 680–681. The others name Khan Krum and Khan Omurtag. The first mentions a treaty with the emperor Justinian, whom it calls the emperor with the cut-off nose.

In 1924–1935, some 250 metres north beneath the relief, excavators found the remains of a complex believed to have been a pagan shrine and a rectangular building, probably the ruler's dwelling, where he performed rituals to Tangra, together with a damaged inscription of Omurtag mentioning Tangra. The relief appeared on Bulgarian coins of 1 to 50 stotinki issued in 1999 and 2000.
madeira: Madeira lies in the North Atlantic, in the region of Macaronesia, just under 400 kilometres north of the Canary Islands, 520 kilometres west of Morocco and 805 kilometres south-west of mainland Portugal. The archipelago includes the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, administered together with the separate Savage Islands. The main island is mountainous, with Pico Ruivo reaching 1,862 metres. It is wet in the north-west and dry in the south-east. The Portuguese name means wood, after the forest that once covered the island; settlers burned much of it to clear land, though laurel forests survive on the northern slopes. From the 16th century the settlers built levadas, irrigation channels carrying water to the dry south.

Ancient authors and legend hint at earlier knowledge of the islands. Plutarch, in his life of Sertorius, reports sailors' tales of two Atlantic islands called the Isles of the Blessed, and archaeological evidence suggests the Vikings may have visited between 900 and 1030. A legend of the lovers Robert Machim and Anna d'Arfet, driven ashore in 1346, is said to have given Machico its name. Medieval atlases such as the Medici-Laurentian Atlas of 1351 show the islands. The uninhabited archipelago was claimed in 1419 by Portuguese sailors in the service of Prince Henry the Navigator and settled after 1420.

Sicilian advisers and Genoese capital transformed its sugar industry, with water-driven mills and the levadas, and by 1490 Madeira was the principal source of European sugar. The sugar was cultivated by enslaved labour. In the 18th century vineyards replaced the sugar plantations, in a wine trade dominated by English merchants, and British forces first occupied the island in 1801. On 3 December 1916 the German submarine SM U-38 sank three ships in Funchal harbour and bombarded the city. In April 1931 the garrison joined a military uprising against the National Dictatorship, crushed by mainland forces after seven days. After the 1974 Carnation Revolution a separatist front carried out about 200 bomb attacks before the 1976 Constitution granted Madeira its own administration and legislature.

Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal and an outermost region of the European Union. Its capital and largest city is Funchal, on the south coast of the main island, and about half the population lives there. The population was 251,060 in 2021, mostly descended from Portuguese settlers. Madeira wine, a fortified wine, goes back to the Age of Exploration, when the islands were a standard port of call for ships bound for the New World and the East Indies. Its laurel forest is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
madhab: The Arabic word madhhab means way to act. Early Islamic law grew out of administrative and community practice in the conquered territories, shaped by Islamic religious and ethical principles, and it developed in circles of learning where students gathered round a local master. In the 8th century the schools of fiqh were regional, and their jurists were loyal to the practice of their own community, whether Mecca, Kufa, Basra or Syria.

Joseph Schacht held that the real basis of doctrine in these ancient schools was the living tradition of the school, expressed in the consensus of its scholars, rather than reports of Muhammad's sayings.

The four main Sunni schools, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali, are named after classical jurists and emerged in the 9th and 10th centuries. By the 12th century almost all jurists aligned themselves with one of them, and the schools recognise each other's validity.

Each ranks its sources of law differently: the Maliki school, for example, gives weight to the practice of the people of Medina, and the Hanafi school to istihsan and custom. Each came to dominate in different regions: the Maliki in North and West Africa, the Hanafi in South and Central Asia, the Shafi'i in East Africa and Southeast Asia, and the Hanbali in central and northern Arabia.

Shia law followed theological lines and produced the Ja'fari school of the Twelver Shia, named after the sixth Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and the Ismaili and Zaydi schools. The Ibadi school, derived from the moderate wing of the Kharijite movement, is distinct from both and predominates in Oman. The Zahiri school survives with fewer followers, and the Jariri, Awza'i, Laythi and Thawri schools died out.

Why some schools survived is attributed to state support for particular scholars, success in debate and numbers of students. Historians differ on the sequence, but one account has the Jarirites excluded by dynasties and the Zahirites by the Mamluk Sultanate, which set up four independent judicial posts for the Maliki, Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools. The Ottoman Empire later reaffirmed the official status of the four in reaction to Shia Persia.

The schools were often in political and academic conflict, vying for the favour of rulers so that their representatives would be appointed to legislative and judicial posts. Ibn al-Nadim in the 10th century named eight groups, and by the 12th century the Jariri and Zahiri schools had been absorbed by the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools respectively.
madhvacharya: Madhvacharya was born at Pajaka near Udupi on the west coast of Karnataka, in a Shivalli Brahmin household, and was named Vāsudeva. His father's name is traditionally given as Naduillaya, while sources variously name his mother as Satyavati or Vedavati. The year of his birth is unclear: many sources date him to 1238–1317, and some to 1199–1278. As a teenager he took sannyasa, or renunciation, and received the name Pūrnaprajña. The name Ānanda Tīrtha was conferred when he became head of his monastery, and Madhva or Madhvacharya is the name most used today. Several hagiographies were written by his disciples, of which the most authentic is Narayana Panditacharya's Madhvavijaya, in sixteen cantos.

Thirty-seven Dvaita texts are attributed to him. They include thirteen commentaries on the principal Upanishads, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, a commentary on forty hymns of the Rigveda and the Bhagavata-tatparya-nirnaya on the Bhagavata Purana. His Anu-Vyakhyana, a supplement to his Brahma Sutras commentary, is regarded as his masterpiece. In several texts he proclaims himself the third incarnation of Vayu, the wind god, after Hanuman and Bhima, and he claimed that his commentary rested on his personal encounter with Vishnu. His disciples told of miracles, such as crossing the Ganga without wetting his clothes.

Madhva called his philosophy Tattvavada, arguments from a realist viewpoint. Reality is of two kinds, independent and dependent, and Vishnu, whom he also names Krishna, is the only independent reality. Individual souls and matter are dependent, and he describes a fivefold difference between God, souls and matter that is neither temporary nor merely practical. He accepted three means of knowledge: perception, inference and testimony. He held that knowledge alone does not liberate; liberation comes through devotion and the grace of God, and Vishnu can be reached only through Vayu. Each soul has real agency and free will, though it is influenced by its nature and past karma.

Madhva was a fierce critic of rival schools. He accused Shankara and the Advaitins of teaching Buddhism under the cover of Vedanta, and he wrote arguments against twenty-one ancient and medieval scholars to establish his own school. His reading of the saying Tat Tvam Asi stressed difference rather than identity. Dvaita became one of three influential Vedanta philosophies, with Advaita and Vishishtadvaita, and influenced Vaishnavism and the Bhakti movement. Kulandran and Kraemer judged his historical influence salutary but not extensive. His lineage of students produced scholars such as Jayatirtha, Vyasatirtha and Raghavendra Tirtha.
madhya-pradesh: Madhya Pradesh, whose name means Central Province, lies in the geographic heart of India. It borders Rajasthan to the northwest, Uttar Pradesh to the northeast, Chhattisgarh to the east, Maharashtra to the south and Gujarat to the west. The state straddles the Narmada River, which runs east and west between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges; these ranges and the river are the traditional boundary between the north and south of India. The Narmada is considered very sacred and is worshipped throughout the region, and the Tapti runs parallel to it. The highest point is Dhupgarh, at 1,350 m.

Isolated remains of Homo erectus found at Hathnora in the Narmada Valley suggest the area may have been inhabited in the Middle Pleistocene. Painted pottery of the later Mesolithic period has been found in the Bhimbetka rock shelters, and Chalcolithic sites of the Kayatha culture (2100-1800 BCE) and the Malwa culture (1700-1500 BCE) lie in the west. The region includes the area of the ancient Avanti Mahajanapada, whose capital Ujjain arose as a major city in the sixth century BCE.

Major dynasties of India ruled the region in later centuries, and the Maratha Empire dominated most of it in the 18th century. After the Third Anglo-Maratha War it was divided into several princely states under the British. After independence, the Central Provinces and Berar was renamed Madhya Pradesh, with Nagpur as its capital, and the Central India Agency became Madhya Bharat, with Gwalior as its capital. In 1956 these states were reorganised and combined with Vindhya Pradesh and Bhopal into the new Madhya Pradesh. The state was the largest in India by area until 2000, when its southeastern Chhattisgarh region became a separate state.

Bhopal is the capital, and other major cities include Indore, Gwalior, Jabalpur and Sagar. The state has over 72 million residents, and Hindi is its official language. Tribal groups such as the Gondi, Bhil, Baiga and Korku form a significant part of the population. UNESCO has declared three sites in the state World Heritage Sites: the Khajuraho Group of Monuments (1986), the Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka (2003). Buddhism and Jainism were once prominent here, especially on the central plateau near Raisen and Bhopal, and Malwa still has a significant Jain minority.
madikeri: Madikeri lies in the Western Ghats at an elevation of 1,170 metres and has a tropical highland climate. It is a popular hill station. The nearest large cities are Hassan, 110 kilometres to the north, Mysore, 120 kilometres to the east, and Mangalore, 138 kilometres to the north-west. Rainfall is heavy: the Madikeri hobli received 3,957 millimetres in 2022. The lowest temperature recorded is 4.5 degrees, and the monsoon makes the weather chilly from June.

The town was known as Muddu Raja Keri, meaning Mudduraja's town, after the Haleri king Mudduraja, who ruled Kodagu from 1633 to 1687. From 1834, under the British Raj, it was called Mercara, and the Government of Mysore later renamed it Madikeri. Its history is bound up with that of Kodagu. Kadambas ruled the northern part from the 2nd to the 6th century, Gangas the southern part from the 4th to the 11th, and then came the Cholas, the Hoysalas in the 12th century and the Vijayanagar kings in the 14th.

After Vijayanagar fell, local Kodava chieftains, the Palegars, ruled their own areas and appointed Veeraraju, founder of the Haleri dynasty, as ruler. His descendants ruled Kodagu from 1600 to 1834. Mudduraja, the third Haleri king, began levelling the land around Madikeri and built a fort in 1681, making the town the capital. The fort was first built of mud and was later replaced by Tipu Sultan. Kodagu became part of British India after 1834.

Madikeri is the headquarters of Kodagu district in Karnataka. Its attractions include Madikeri Fort, Raja's Seat, the Sri Omkareshwara Temple, the Gaddide, which is the tomb of the rajas, the General Thimmaiah War Museum and Abbey Falls. The census of 2011 counted 33,381 inhabitants. A national highway links it eastward to Mysore and Bengaluru and westward to Mangalore.
madrasa: Madrasa is the Arabic word for any educational institution, secular or religious, and means a place where learning and studying take place. In Arabic it can refer to a primary or secondary school as well as a university-level school. In English it usually refers to Islamic institutions of learning, and historians use it for a college where Islamic law was taught along with other subjects. In medieval usage the term was usually specific to higher learning, as opposed to elementary schools, which were known as kuttab, khalwa or maktab.

Tradition holds that the first madrasa education took place under Muhammad at the estate of Zayd ibn Arqam, and that after the Hijrah a school known as Suffa was set up beside the mosque at Medina. The formal madrasa developed in the late 11th century under the Abbasid caliphs, when the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk created a system of state madrasas, called the Nizamiyahs after him, in cities from Mesopotamia to Khorasan. Nizam al-Mulk was later murdered by the Assassins.

Madrasa-type institutions appear to have existed in Iran before him, but his period is considered by many to be the starting point for the spread of the formal madrasa across the Muslim world, adapted to all four Sunni legal schools and to Sufi orders. Part of the motive of Sunni rulers and elites in adopting it was a wish to counter the influence of Shi'ism by spreading Sunni teachings.

In its formative period the madrasa curriculum included only the religious sciences, and philosophy and the secular sciences were often excluded. The curriculum slowly diversified, and many later madrasas taught logic, mathematics and philosophy, and some history, ethics, medicine, astronomy and chemistry. The founder usually set the curriculum. Between 1155 and 1260 there were 75 madrasas in Cairo, 51 in Damascus and up to 44 in Aleppo.

Architecturally, the classical madrasa was centred on an interior courtyard with four iwans, vaulted chambers open on one side, arranged symmetrically around it. Practically none of the first Nizamiyah madrasas survives. Many Seljuk madrasas of Anatolia survive, often with an attached mausoleum, a minaret and an ornate entrance portal, and some courtyards were covered by a dome, as at the Karatay Madrasa in Konya, founded in 1279.

In the Maghreb madrasas flourished only in the 13th century under the Marinid and Hafsid dynasties, which followed the Almohad dynasty. The earliest Hafsid madrasa was founded in Tunis in 1252, and the first in Morocco was built in Fes in 1271. In the Ottoman Empire madrasas trained doctors, engineers, lawyers and religious officials, among other members of the governing elite, for nearly six centuries. Muhammad the Conqueror built eight higher madrasas for specialised studies and eight lower ones beside a mosque.
madrid: Madrid lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula on the southern Meseta Central, 60 kilometres south of the Guadarrama mountain range, at an average altitude of about 650 metres. It straddles the Jarama and Manzanares river sub-drainage basins, within the wider catchment of the Tagus. The oldest urban core stands on hills beside the left bank of the Manzanares. The city grew eastwards to the creek now followed by the Paseo de la Castellana and on to the Abroñigal Creek, and also by annexing neighbouring settlements.

The origin of the name is unknown. Theories include a Latin derivation from matrix, a Celtic form meaning 'ford', and an Arabic word for a water stream, majrā. All have difficulty explaining the phonetic change fully. Nicknames include Los Madriles and La Villa y Corte, 'the town and court'.

The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. Archaeological remains include a settlement of the Celtic Carpetani, Roman villas, a Visigoth basilica near the church of Santa María de la Almudena and three Visigoth necropolises. The first historical document of an established settlement dates from the Muslim period. In the second half of the 9th century the Umayyad emir Muhammad I built a fortress on a headland near the Manzanares, one of many on the border between Al-Andalus and the kingdoms of León and Castile, to protect Toledo from attack from the north.

After the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up in the early 11th century, Madrid became part of the Taifa of Toledo. In 1083 Alfonso VI of León and Castile seized it as an outpost against Toledo, which he took in 1085. Christians then occupied the centre of the town, while Muslims and Jews were displaced to the suburbs. Madrid remained a borderland for a time and suffered raids during the Almoravid period; its walls were destroyed in 1110. Philip II moved his court to Madrid in 1561 and transformed the town into a capital city.

Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain and of the autonomous community of Madrid, with about 3.4 million people in the city proper. Its landmarks include the Plaza Mayor, built in 1617 to 1619 and attributed to Juan Gómez de Mora, the Royal Palace, the Buen Retiro Park, founded in 1631, and the Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza museums along the Paseo del Prado, which form a UNESCO World Heritage site called the Golden Triangle of Art.
madriu-perafita-claror-valley: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley is a glacial valley in the south-east of Andorra, covering 42.47 km2, about 9 per cent of the country, and part of its second largest watershed basin. It has high pastures, craggy cliffs and steep wooded valleys, bounded by ridges to the south, east and west, the southern edge running along the border with Spain, and by an escarpment dropping to the Valira valley in the north. It is isolated from the rest of Andorra and can be reached only by tracks passable on foot. It is recognised as a haven for rare or endangered wildlife, and has recently been considered the spiritual heart of Andorra.

The dwellings, field terraces, tracks and remains of ironworking show how the natural resources of the high Pyrenees were used by the local people over many centuries, through changes in climate, prosperity and social structure. Two small settlements, Entremesaigües and Ramio, lie on the narrow valley floor; both were occupied all year until about the last fifty years. The twelve houses are built of local granite with schist roofs, each with a barn for grain and hay. The settlements are surrounded by terraced fields, once used for wheat and rye and now mostly for grazing, and the slopes held vines in the Middle Ages. The forests, owned communally, were managed to produce charcoal until the nineteenth century.

Iron was smelted from local ore on the banks of the Madriu River, in a Catalan forge of the kind typical of the Pyrenees, which was abandoned in 1790. The high pasture has been grazed in summer by sheep, cows and horses on land owned communally since the Middle Ages, and shepherds spent the summer in borders, small stone huts with turf roofs. Milk was made into cheese.

The valley became Andorra's first and only UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004, with a small extension in 2006. Tracks link it to Roussillon, Languedoc and Catalonia, and paved tracks connect it to the centre of Andorra. Many shepherds' huts, trackways and field walls have been restored, no access road is planned, and the land is intended for farming high-quality livestock and for limited tourism.
madura: Madura is an island off the north-eastern coast of Java, part of the province of East Java and separated from Java by the narrow Madura Strait. The island itself covers about 4,471 square kilometres; the administered area is about 5,408 square kilometres because it includes smaller islands, which belong to the easternmost regency, Sumenep. The island is relatively flat, and its limestone hills are lower and rounder than those of northern Java. It is warmer and drier than the Javanese mainland. It is named for Madurai, the home of the Hindu deity Azhagar.

In 1624 Sultan Agung of Mataram conquered Madura, and its government was brought under the Cakraningrats, a single princely line. The family often opposed Central Javanese rule. After the First Javanese War of Succession the Dutch gained control of the eastern half of Madura in 1705. In 1743 Pakubuwono II ceded full sovereignty over Madura to the Dutch, which Cakraningrat IV contested; he fled to Banjarmasin, was betrayed by the sultan there, and was captured and exiled to the Cape of Good Hope.

The Dutch kept Madura's four states, each with its own regent. The island was at first important as a source of colonial troops, and in the second half of the 19th century it became the main source of salt for Dutch-controlled territories in the archipelago. The Dutch gradually sidelined the Sultan and took over direct control of the whole island in the 1880s, governing it as the Madoera Residency. From 1948 to 1950, under the United States of Indonesia, it was a federative state called the State of Madura.

Madura has about four million inhabitants, most of them Madurese, who speak Madurese, an Austronesian language. The Madurese number around seven million, and many live elsewhere, especially in eastern Java. The soil is not fertile enough for major agriculture, and maize, cattle, small-scale fishing and tobacco and cloves for the kretek industry are mainstays, with salt exported since the Dutch era. The island is well known for karapan sapi, bull racing, in which a jockey rides a wooden sled pulled by two bulls over about 100 metres in ten to fifteen seconds. Its theatre includes masked topeng performances of the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and the Madurese are regarded as excellent sailors. The Suramadu Bridge to Surabaya opened in 2009.
madurai: Madurai stands on the flat, fertile plain of the river Vaigai, which runs through the city and divides it into two almost equal halves. The Sirumalai and Nagamalai hills lie to the north and west. A 2nd-century BCE Tamil-Brahmi inscription refers to the city as matiray, an Old Tamil word that Iravatham Mahadevan reads as meaning a walled city. Tradition holds that the site was once a forest of Kadamba trees, and the city has also been called Koodal and Thirualavai. Vaishnava texts call it the southern Mathura.

The recorded history of Madurai goes back to the 3rd century BCE. Megasthenes may have visited it as Methora, though some scholars believe he meant the northern city of Mathura. Sangam literature such as Maturaikkāñci records its importance as the capital of the Pandyan dynasty, and the third Tamil Sangam, an assembly of poets, is said to have been held there. The second book of the Tamil epic Silappatikaram is set in the city. Over the centuries it was ruled by the Pandyan Kingdom, the Chola Empire, the Madurai Sultanate, the Vijayanagar Empire, the Madurai Nayaks and the Carnatic kingdom.

The first Madurai Nayak king, Viswanatha Nayak (1529–64), redesigned the city according to the Shilpa Shastras. It is built around the Koodal Azhagar and Meenakshi temples, in concentric quadrangular streets named after Tamil months and their festivals, such as the Aadi, Chittirai and Masi streets.

In 1801 the East India Company took direct control of Madurai and annexed it to the Madras Presidency. In 1837 the British demolished the fortifications around the temple, drained the moat and used the debris to build new streets. The municipality was constituted on 1 November 1866. In 1921 Mahatma Gandhi first adopted the loincloth in Madurai, after seeing agricultural labourers wearing it. In 1939 the Madras Presidency passed the Temple Entry Authorization and Indemnity Act, and the temple entry movement was led at the Meenakshi temple by A. Vaidyanatha Iyer.

Madurai is the administrative headquarters of Madurai district in Tamil Nadu and is called the cultural capital of the state. It had a population of 1,470,755 in 2011, and Tamil is the main language. Its best-known monuments are the Koodal Azhagar temple, the Meenakshi Temple and the Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal. The surrounding land is farmed mainly for paddy, and the city is a centre of learning and of industries such as automobile and granite manufacturing.
maeotians: The name comes from the sea: Maeotian was at first a label for the tribes living around the Maeotis, above all on its eastern coast. In sources of the 4th century BCE it has three senses: a broad term for the peoples around the sea, the name of the coastal tribes later listed by Strabo, and, in the usage of the Bosporan chancery, the lesser tribes of the Kuban region as distinct from the Sindi.

Their language, and even its family, is uncertain; the place names of their country suggest that they were not of Iranian stock. The Cambridge Ancient History reports two main views, that they were of Cimmerian ancestry, akin to the Thracians, or that they were Caucasian natives under Iranian overlordship. Soviet scholars concluded that they were among the ancestors of the Circassian, or Adyghe, people.

Strabo names among them the Sindi, Dandarii, Toreatae, Agri, Arrechi, Tarpetes, Obidiaceni, Sittaceni and Dosci, and adds that there were many others. Which peoples counted as Maeotian was disputed already in antiquity: Hellanicus of Lesbos and Pseudo-Scylax set the Sindi apart, while Pseudo-Scymnus and Strabo include them. The Sindi are the best attested and were probably the dominant people of the region.

The Maeotians lived in earthworks and open settlements on the Taman Peninsula and along the middle Kuban. According to Strabo they were as warlike as their nomadic neighbours, paid tribute at times to the rulers of Tanais and at times to the Bosporans, and rose in revolt from time to time. In the Kuban region they lived under successive steppe overlords. The graves show it: the ruling Scythians, and in Sindica the Sindian elite, were buried in richly furnished kurgans, while the Maeotian population used poorly equipped flat cemeteries.

In the early 4th century BCE Maeotian tribes fought a major war against the Bosporan Kingdom and its Sindian subjects. When the Sindian king Hecataeus repudiated his Maeotian wife Tirgatao, she roused her people, the Ixomatae, and other tribes to a destructive war on both kingdoms, which ended only under Gorgippus through supplication and gifts.

After Leucon I annexed Sindica, probably in the 380s BCE, the tribes of the Kuban were brought into the Bosporan state by stages. Leucon ruled the Toretae, Dandarii and Psessi as king, and under Paerisades I the royal style became king of the Sindi and all the Maeotians. Under Aspurgus, in the early 1st century CE, the royal titles still listed the Sindi and Maeotians, now with the Tarpetes and the people of Tanais.
magadha: Magadha was a region and kingdom of ancient India in the eastern Ganges plain, one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas of the period of the second urbanisation. Before it expanded, its territory was bounded on the north, west and east by the Ganga, Son and Campa rivers, with the eastern spurs of the Vindhya mountains to the south, and corresponded to the modern Patna and Gaya districts of Bihar. Its first capital was Rajagriha, now Rajgir, and later Pataliputra, now Patna. A wider Greater Magadha, covering neighbouring parts of the eastern Gangetic plain, had a distinct culture.

The Atharvaveda, composed about 1200 to 900 BCE, lists the Magadhas among non-Vedic tribes outside the Kuru-Panchala cultural sphere, and according to the Puranas the Brihadratha dynasty was the first to rule. Information on early rulers is scarce; the main sources are the Buddhist Pali Canon, the Jain Agamas and the Puranas, all written long after the events. The Haryanka dynasty is said to have ruled for some 130 years, with dates that are uncertain and could be significantly later. Its notable kings, Bimbisara and his son Ajatashatru, appear in Buddhist and Jain literature as contemporaries of the Buddha and Mahavira. Magadha grew to include most of Bihar and Bengal by conquering the Vajjika League and Anga.

Mahapadma Nanda took the throne and founded the Nanda dynasty, which conquered much of north India from about 345 to about 322 BCE. Chandragupta Maurya overthrew it and founded the Maurya Empire, which lasted from about 322 to 185 BCE. The Shunga Empire and the Kanva dynasty followed, then rule from outside and later the Gupta Empire, from about 240 to about 579, centred in Magadha. The Later Guptas and the Maukharis ruled parts of the region afterwards, and from the 11th to the late 13th century Buddhist kings known as the Pithipatis called themselves Lords of Magadha.

Magadha was a centre of the sramana movements, which rejected Vedic authority and gave rise to Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivika. The Buddha lived much of his life in Magadha, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, and the first Buddhist council was held at Rajgriha. Early Magadhan kings supported Buddhism and Jainism. Its language, Magadhi Prakrit, later evolved into Magahi, Maithili and Bhojpuri, and the Pali language has traditionally been identified with Magadhi. Two UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the region: the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya and the Nalanda monastery.
magdalena-river: The Magdalena rises in the south of Colombia, in Huila Department, where the Cordillera Central and the Cordillera Oriental separate. It runs east and then north in a great valley between the two ranges, reaches the coastal plain at about nine degrees north, runs west for about 100 kilometres, and turns north again to enter the Caribbean at Barranquilla, in the zone called Bocas de Ceniza. Its length is 1,528 kilometres, and it is the largest river system of the northern Andes. It is navigable through much of its lower reaches, despite shifting sand bars at the mouth of its delta, as far as Honda, at the foot of its rapids.

Its basin covers 273,000 square kilometres, 24 percent of the area of Colombia, and 66 percent of the country's people live there. The valley was formed by tectonic depressions that filled with sediment from the Central Ranges in the Tertiary period. The river takes its name from Mary Magdalene.

Since pre-Columbian times the river has been a route into the interior of present-day Colombia and Ecuador. Carib-speaking peoples such as the Panche and the Yariguí went up its western bank, while the Muisca civilisation lived on the eastern side and called the river Yuma. Rodrigo de Bastidas discovered and named it on 1 April 1501. Spanish conquistadors used it in the 16th century to push into the mountainous interior, and during the colonial period it was the only transport link between Bogotá and the port of Cartagena de Indias, and so with Europe.

The Magdalena Campaign of Pierre Labatut and Simón Bolívar took place along the river. In 1825 the Congress of Colombia awarded Juan Bernardo Elbers a concession for steam navigation, but his company closed soon after. By 1845 steamboats ran regularly, and they continued until 1961, when the last steamers stopped. The first recorded European contact with the potato was in 1537 in the Magdalena Valley, and potatoes probably reached Europe by Spanish ship around 1570.

The valley crosses ecosystems from páramo at the headwaters through dry forest and rainforest to swamps and wetlands in the lower course. The basin, which includes the Cauca River, is very rich in fish, and about 55 percent of its species are endemic. The Magdalena Valley is also an important area for oil exploration. Gabriel García Márquez's novel The General in His Labyrinth is a fictionalised account of Bolívar's last voyage down the river.
magdeburg: Magdeburg stands on the Elbe river and is the capital of the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. It is first mentioned in a document as Magadoburg in the Capitulary of Diedenhofen issued by Charlemagne in 805, and the name probably comes from Old High German magado, big or mighty, and burg, fortress. The city marked its 1,200th anniversary in 2005.

King Henry the Fowler fortified the town in 919 against the Magyars and Slavs. In 929 King Otto I granted it to his English-born wife Edith as dower, and Otto himself was buried in the cathedral. The archbishops played a prominent part in the German colonisation of the Slavic lands east of the Elbe. In 1035 the city received a patent giving it the right to hold trade exhibitions, which formed the basis of the Magdeburg rights. In the thirteenth century Magdeburg joined the Hanseatic League. Fires in 1188 and 1207 destroyed much of it.

Martin Luther preached there in 1524, after which the city left Roman Catholicism, and Matthias Flacius and his companions wrote the Magdeburg Centuries there. The city withstood a siege by Albrecht von Wallenstein in 1629. In 1631 imperial troops under Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, stormed it, massacred the inhabitants and burned it, and only about 4,000 people remained after the war. Otto von Guericke, its mayor and a scientist, led the recovery. Under the Peace of Westphalia the city passed to Brandenburg-Prussia in 1680.

Magdeburg surrendered to French troops in 1806 and in 1815 became the capital of the Prussian Province of Saxony. A British air raid on 16 January 1945 destroyed much of the city centre. It belonged to East Germany from 1949 to 1990, and in 1990 became the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.
maghreb: The word maghrib is an Arabic term that the first Muslim Arab settlers gave in the 7th century to the recently conquered area west of the Umayyad capital of Damascus. It means both the western land and the place where the sun sets, in contrast to the Mashriq in the east. The Atlas Mountains and the Sahara isolate its northern parts from the rest of the continent, and these have long had commercial and cultural ties across the Mediterranean to Southern Europe and Western Asia.

The extent of the term has changed. Before the 20th century it most commonly meant Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia between the Mediterranean and the Atlas Mountains, often with eastern Libya and never with Mauritania. It has since widened to include Mauritania and the disputed territory of Western Sahara. During the era of al-Andalus its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were known to Europeans as the Moors.

The Berber people have inhabited western North Africa since at least 10,000 BCE. Trade with the Phoenicians dates back to the 1st millennium BCE, and tradition holds that they founded Carthage around 800 BCE. The region was somewhat unified under the kingdom of Numidia, then briefly under the Kingdom of Mauretania, and then under Roman rule. The Vandals invaded afterwards, and the Byzantine Empire briefly re-established a weak Roman rule.
