The Arabs reached the Maghreb in early Umayyad times. The founding of Kairouan in 667 gave Islam its first permanent foothold, Carthage fell in 698 and the rest of the region by 709. The Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid caliphates held power, but the longest-lasting rule was that of local dynasties such as the Idrisids, Almoravids, Almohads, Zirids and Marinids. Trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold, ivory and slaves was costly and dangerous but highly profitable. In the 19th and early 20th centuries France, Italy and Spain administered the region, and decolonization followed after the Second World War.

Jewish communities have a long presence there. The earliest documented one dates to the third century BCE, when Ptolemaic rulers of Egypt settled Jews in eastern Libya, and after the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492 many Sephardic Jews settled in North Africa. The region is primarily inhabited by peoples of Arab and Berber ancestry, and couscous was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020.
magna-carta: England was ruled by King John, the third of the Angevin kings. John and his predecessors had ruled by the principle of vis et voluntas, force and will, taking executive and sometimes arbitrary decisions, often on the basis that a king was above the law. Many contemporary writers believed that monarchs should rule in accordance with custom and law, with the counsel of the leading men of the realm, but there was no model for what should happen if a king refused to do so.

John had lost most of his ancestral lands in France to King Philip II in 1204 and spent years trying to regain them, raising heavy taxes on the barons to pay for a war that ended in costly failure in 1214. After the defeat of his allies at the Battle of Bouvines he had to sue for peace and pay compensation. Rebel barons in the north and east began to organise resistance.

The charter was first drafted by Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, and sealed by John at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. It promised the protection of church rights, protection for the barons from illegal imprisonment, swift and impartial justice and limits on feudal payments to the Crown, to be carried out through a council of 25 barons. Most of it governed the feudal rights of the Crown over the barons. Clauses 39 and 40 demanded due process in royal justice, which John had used to extort large sums.

At least thirteen copies were issued in 1215, and four survive: two at the British Library, one at Salisbury Cathedral and one at Lincoln Castle. There were no signatures, and the numbering of clauses used today was introduced by William Blackstone in 1759.

Neither side stood by its commitments, and Pope Innocent III annulled the charter, which led to the First Barons' War. After John's death the regency of his young son Henry III reissued it in 1216 without some of its more radical content, and again in 1217 as part of the peace agreed at Lambeth. Henry reissued it in 1225 in exchange for new taxes, and Edward I confirmed it in 1297 as part of England's statute law.

In the early 17th century lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke argued against the divine right of kings, claiming that an ancient English constitution had been restored by the charter. Victorian historians showed that the 1215 charter concerned the king and the barons, not ordinary subjects, and most historians now call its reading as a charter of universal rights a later myth. Only three clauses remain in force in England and Wales.
magna-graecia: The Greek expression Megale Hellas, later translated into Latin as Magna Graecia, is first attested in the historian Polybius, writing around 150 BCE, who ascribed it to Pythagoras and his school. Ancient authors used it for different parts of southern Italy, with or without Sicily. The sense that spread was the Greek cities of southern Italy along the coast between Cumae and Taras. The settlements lay in what are now Calabria, Apulia, Basilicata, Campania and, where Sicily is included, Sicily. Their inhabitants are called Italiotes and Siceliotes.

Greeks founded colonies because of famine and overcrowding, civil strife, a need for new ports and markets, and expulsion after wars. Unlike Roman colonies, they were not dependent on their mother cities but were independent city-states.

Greeks began to settle in southern Italy in the 8th century BCE. The first great wave, by Euboeans, went to the Gulf of Naples and the Strait of Messina; Pithecusae on Ischia is considered the oldest Greek settlement in Italy and Cumae the first on the mainland. A second wave of Achaeans, shortly before 720 BCE, settled the Ionian coast at Metapontion, Poseidonia, Sybaris and Kroton. Governments were typically aristocratic, though Syracuse had tyrants such as Dionysius.

By the 6th century BCE the Ionian cities were wealthy enough to fight one another. The Battle of the Sagra river set Locri Epizefiri against Kroton, Siris was destroyed by Sybaris and Metapontum, and Kroton destroyed Sybaris, which had an estimated population of 300,000 to 500,000 between 600 and 510 BCE. Pythagoras moved to Crotone and founded his school there in 530 BCE.

Neapolis was the first Greek city absorbed by the Roman Republic, in 327 BCE. Threatened by the Bruttii and Lucanians, other cities asked Rome for help, and it sent garrisons in the 280s BCE. Their independence ended when the Roman Republic annexed them during the Second Punic War, in 205 BCE.

Ruins of several cities remain, among them Syracuse, Agrigento, Taranto, Reggio Calabria and Crotone. The Valley of the Temples at Agrigento, with seven Doric temples, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, and Syracuse is also listed. Poseidonia and Elea are part of the Cilento World Heritage Site, listed in 1998. South Italian Greek pottery, especially of the 4th century BCE, is a notable legacy, and athletes of Crotone alone won 18 titles at the Olympic Games over 25 Olympiads. The Griko language, spoken by Griko communities in Calabria and Apulia, is the last living trace of the Greek presence.
magnentius: Magnus Magnentius was born in Samarobriva, now Amiens, in Gaul, purportedly the son of a British father and a Frankish mother, though some scholars suspect that these origins were exaggerated or invented by Constantinian propaganda. He served in the protectores, a bodyguard corps attached to the imperial court, and rose to command the Herculians and Jovians, two guard units. He was well liked by important court officials, notably Marcellinus, the comes rerum privatarum, who backed his bid for power against the emperor Constans, whom the ancient sources describe as unpopular.

At Augustodunum, now Autun, on 18 January 350 Magnentius stepped out of a dinner party and came back in a purple toga, and the guests hailed him Augustus. Constans, hunting near the Pyrenees away from his troops, was pursued and killed at Helena, near Perpignan. Magnentius quickly won the loyalty of Britannia, Gaul and Hispania, took Italy within a month and secured Africa, but Illyria came under Vetranio. Lacking any link to the dynasty of Constantine, he married Justina, possibly a great-granddaughter of Constantine, presented himself on coins as liberator of the Roman world, and for six months spoke of Constantius II as his senior. Libanius conceded that he governed in accordance with the laws.

Constantius, whose brother Constans he had killed, would not recognise him. In the early months of 351 Constantius offered him control of Gaul, which he refused. The armies met at the Battle of Mursa Major, a victory for Constantius at great cost and one of the largest battles ever fought among Romans, with low estimates of over 50,000 dead. Zosimus says Constantius feared Rome could no longer hold off barbarian invaders.

Magnentius withdrew across the Alps. In 352 his offers of peace, even to step down and take a soldier's post, were refused, and his legions along the Rhine began to defect. After a final defeat at the Battle of Mons Seleucus in July 353 he fled to Lugdunum, now Lyon, where on 10 August 353 most sources say he fell on his sword. His brother Decentius, whom he had made caesar to hold Gaul, hanged himself on hearing the news. Constantius then rooted out his followers, using the notary Paulus Catena, called Paul the Chain, for the purpose.

Almost all of Magnentius' acts were repealed, and the succeeding regime condemned his rule as an illegitimate barbarian usurpation, which is why historians call him a usurper. His religion is disputed: some see him as a nominal Christian, others point to his allowing night sacrifices, and his coinage includes a series bearing a Christogram.
magnetic-compass: Early references to lodestone and its attraction of iron come from several cultures. The Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus, in the 6th century BCE, was credited with discovering that a lodestone attracts iron, and the Sushruta Samhita, an ancient Indian medical text, describes using it to remove arrows from a body. The earliest Chinese literary reference to magnetism is in the 4th-century BCE Guiguzi, and the Lüshi Chunqiu of the 2nd century BCE states that the lodestone makes iron come to it. The Lunheng, composed between 20 and 100 CE, says that a lodestone attracts a needle.

The first devices to use these properties may date to Han China. In the 2nd century BCE Chinese geomancers were experimenting with a south-pointing spoon of lodestone for divination, which turns to a north–south axis on a smooth bronze plate, though archaeologists have not found a magnetite spoon in a Han tomb. Some historians believe that a compass using an iron fish floating in a vessel of oil was in use in southern India in the 4th century, while others think the evidence for compasses before the 11th century is very weak.

The first compasses used for navigation appeared in China by 1088, under the Song dynasty, as described by Shen Kuo. They were made of iron needles magnetised by striking them with a lodestone. The first use recorded in Western Europe dates to around 1190 and in the Islamic world to the 13th century. Such needles, set in a cork or a piece of wood and floated in a bowl of water, were universally used until the box-like compass with a dry pivoting needle appeared around 1300. The dry compass was supplanted in the early 20th century by the liquid-filled compass.

Compass cards were originally marked only with north or with the four cardinal points. These were later divided into 24 points in China and 32 in Europe, and in the modern era the 360-degree system took hold. Mariners also learned that a compass needle does not point exactly to true north: variation values for most of the oceans had been calculated and published by 1914. Iron in a ship causes further error, called deviation, and navigators made correction tables by comparing compass bearings with landmarks of known magnetic bearing.

A magnetic compass has a magnetised needle that aligns itself with the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field and so points approximately to the north magnetic pole. The needle turns on a low-friction pivot, in better compasses a jewel bearing. The angle between true north and magnetic north is called magnetic declination, and it varies widely from place to place and changes slowly over time. The compass is counted among the Four Great Inventions of China.
magnificat: The Magnificat is recorded only in Luke's Gospel, as one of four hymns, distilled from a collection of early Jewish-Christian canticles, that complement the theme of promise and fulfilment in Luke's infancy narrative. The others are Zechariah's Benedictus, the angels' Gloria in Excelsis Deo and Simeon's Nunc dimittis. They are patterned on the hymns of praise in Israel's Psalter and reflect pre-Christian Jewish hymnology. The oldest and likely original version was written in Koine Greek. Scholars discuss whether the historical Mary herself proclaimed it, though Luke portrays her as its singer. Adolf von Harnack argued in 1900 that Luke 1:46 should read And Elizabeth said, following several ancient readings.

The canticle echoes several biblical passages, above all the Song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:1 to 10. Its first stanza shows the Hebrew device of synonymous parallelism, in which my soul mirrors my spirit and of the Lord mirrors in God my Savior. The third stanza sets three contrasts: the proud are reversed by those of low estate, the mighty by those of low degree, and the rich by the hungry.

Its structure has four parts: Mary rejoices that she is to bear the promised Messiah (Luke 1:46 to 48); she glorifies God for his power, holiness and mercy (1:49 to 50); she looks forward to God transforming the world, bringing the proud low and feeding the hungry (1:51 to 53); and she exalts him for his faithfulness to his promise to Abraham (1:54 to 55).

The Magnificat is the most popular canticle, and is used in the liturgies of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Lutheran churches and the Anglican Communion. In the West it is most often sung or recited at the main evening service: Vespers in Catholic and Lutheran churches and Evening Prayer, or Evensong, in Anglicanism, where it is usually paired with the Nunc dimittis. Western tradition usually adds the doxology Gloria Patri, which is not part of the original text. In the Eastern Orthodox Church it is always sung at Matins, with a refrain sung after each verse. Lutherans commonly use it at the Feast of the Visitation on 2 July.

Many composers, beginning in the Renaissance, set it to music, among them Claudio Monteverdi in his Vespro della Beata Vergine of 1610, Johann Sebastian Bach in 1723, Vivaldi, Anton Bruckner and Arvo Pärt. Charles Villiers Stanford wrote a Magnificat in every major key.
magnitogorsk: Magnitogorsk lies in Chelyabinsk Oblast, on the eastern side of the southern Ural Mountains beside the Ural River. Its name means city of the magnetic mountain, after Mount Magnitnaya, a geological anomaly that once consisted almost completely of iron ore, around 55 to 60 percent iron. The city straddles von Strahlenberg's line, the boundary between Europe and Asia, and its official motto calls it the place where Europe and Asia meet. It is one of a small number of planned socialist realist settlements of the Soviet bloc, alongside Nowa Huta in Poland, Havířov in Czechoslovakia and Eisenhüttenstadt in the GDR.

A settlement was founded in 1743 as part of the Orenburg Line of forts built under Empress Elizabeth, and it had a small wooden chapel by 1747. Iron-ore mining dates from 1752, when two entrepreneurs named Tverdysh and Myasnikov, taking advantage of the fact that the mountain belonged to no one, petitioned the empress for it. The petition was accepted in 1759 and they began to produce ore.

In 1928 a Soviet delegation went to Cleveland, Ohio, to ask the American consulting firm Arthur G. McKee to plan a copy of the U.S. Steel mill at Gary, Indiana. The contract was enlarged four times, and the new plant eventually had a capacity of over four million tons a year. Many of the workers were former peasants with little industrial experience, so several hundred foreign specialists came to direct the work, including a team of architects headed by the German Ernst May. His plan for a linear city had to be altered because factory and housing construction had already begun. John Scott's book Behind the Urals documents the city's development in the 1930s. It received city status in 1931.

In 1937 foreigners were told to leave and the city was declared closed. Little reliable information survives from the closed period. In the Second World War it supplied much of the steel for the Soviet war effort, and its position east of the Urals kept it out of reach of the German army. The closed status was lifted under perestroika, and the steelworks later became a joint-stock company. With local ore depleted, raw materials are brought from northern Kazakhstan.

Magnitogorsk contains the largest iron and steel works in Russia, the Magnitogorsk Iron and Steel Works. It has the Magnitogorsk State Technical University and the Magnitogorsk State Conservatory, three theatres, and a monument called The First Tent to the first builders of the works. It is served by an airport and a railway.
magnus-barefoot: Magnus was born around the end of 1073 as the only son of King Olaf Kyrre. Most of what is known comes from Norse sagas and chronicles that began to appear in the twelfth century; the later sagas are the most detailed but are generally considered the least reliable, and since they chiefly describe warfare they may have made the image of kings like Magnus one-sided. Olaf died in September 1093 after a long period of peace, and Magnus was probably proclaimed king at the assembly of Viken. In the north his cousin Haakon Magnusson contested his claim, and the two ruled uneasily together until Haakon died in 1095.

Under Magnus, Norway came to resemble other European kingdoms more closely: royal rule became established, he consolidated power through a network of noblemen, and church organisation developed, though in practice he ruled the church. His main effort lay in the west. In 1098 he sailed into the Western Sea and reached Orkney with a large fleet, of which the sources give sizes from 60 to 160 ships. He raided Orkney, the Hebrides and Mann, secured Norwegian control by a treaty with the Scottish king and built forts and houses on Mann. Norwegian and Scottish historians generally believe his chief aim was to control the Norse communities around the Irish Sea.

After his return he campaigned in the Swedish provinces of Dalsland and Västergötland, claiming an ancient border at the Göta älv. The Danish king Eric Evergood arranged talks, and in 1101 Magnus made peace by agreeing to marry Margaret, daughter of King Inge Stenkilsson, and received Dalsland as her dowry.

In 1101 or 1102 Magnus again set out for Ireland. He allied with Muirchertach Ua Briain, king of Munster, whose daughter married Magnus's son Sigurd, and Muirchertach recognised his control of Dublin and Fingal. The next year Magnus was killed in an ambush by the Ulaid while obtaining food supplies, in unclear circumstances. He was the last Norwegian king to fall in battle abroad. His sons Sigurd, Eystein and Olaf succeeded him peacefully. His memory is stronger in Ireland and Scotland than in Norway, and he is the subject of Gaelic ballads as Manus Mór.
magnus-maximus: Magnus Maximus was born in Gallaecia, Hispania, on the estates of Count Theodosius the Elder, to whom he claimed to be related. In their youth he and the future emperor Theodosius I served together in the army of Theodosius the Elder in Britannia. He served under the Count in Africa in 373 and was assigned to Britain in 380, where he defeated an incursion of the Picts and Scots in 381. He gained the support of his soldiers and the admiration of the Romano-Britons he defended.

In the spring of 383 the discontented Roman army proclaimed Maximus emperor in place of Gratian, who was accused of favouring Alans in his bodyguard. He took at least part of the garrison of Britain to Gaul, and after skirmishing near Paris Gratian fled and was killed at Lyon on 25 August 383. An accord seems to have been reached in 384 in which Valentinian II and Theodosius I recognised Maximus as Augustus in the West, while he acknowledged Valentinian's rule of Italy, Africa and Illyricum. He ruled Britain, Gaul and Spain from Trier and ordered the execution of Priscillian and six companions for heresy, despite protests from Ambrose and Martin of Tours.

In 387 he invaded Italy and drove Valentinian II out of Mediolanum. Theodosius I, who had married Valentinian's sister Galla, invaded with Valentinian in 388, and Maximus was defeated at the Battle of Poetovio, retreated to Aquileia, surrendered and was executed. The Senate decreed damnatio memoriae against him, and his son Victor was executed at Trier.

In the view of some historians his death marked the end of direct imperial presence in northern Gaul and Britain. Gildas wrote that he took from Britain its troops, governors and the flower of its youth, and the ninth-century Historia Brittonum says he settled his British soldiers in Armorica, which modern historians think may reflect a real settlement in Brittany. In Welsh legend he is Macsen Wledig, who in The Dream of Macsen Wledig marries the Welsh princess Elen. The earliest Welsh genealogies make him founding father of the dynasties of Powys, Gwynedd and Gwent.
magnus-the-good: Magnus Olafsson was born around 1024, an illegitimate son of King Olaf Haraldsson, later Saint Olaf, and Alfhild, an English slave of Olaf's queen Astrid Olofsdotter. Born prematurely and weak, he was hastily baptised by the skald Sigvatr Þórðarson, who named him after Charlemagne. When Cnut the Great dethroned Olaf in 1028 the family fled through Sweden and the Baltic to Kievan Rus', where Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise sheltered them. In 1031 Magnus's uncle Harald Sigurdsson brought news of Olaf's death at the Battle of Stiklestad. The boy was educated in Old Russian and some Greek and trained as a warrior.

Cnut had appointed his first wife Ælfgifu and their son Svein as regents of Norway, but the Norwegians found their rule oppressive and drove them out before Cnut died in 1035. Einar Thambarskelfir and Kalf Arnesson went to Kievan Rus' to bring the boy back, and Magnus was established as king at the age of eleven. He first sought revenge on his father's enemies, but on Sigvatr's advice stopped, and so became known as the Good.

Harthacnut, king of Denmark, wanted the two kingdoms reunited, and Magnus began a campaign against Denmark around 1040, but nobles of both countries brought the kings together at the Göta älv, where they agreed that the first to die would be succeeded by the other. When Harthacnut died in England in 1042 Magnus also became king of Denmark, against the claim of Cnut's nephew Sweyn Estridsson. He destroyed Jomsborg, the headquarters of the Jomsvikings, and in 1043 decisively defeated an invasion by the Wends at the Battle of Lyrskov Heath, near Hedeby, with up to 15,000 killed. He also wrote to Edward, the new English king, that he meant to attack England, but never did so.

Harald Sigurdsson returned to Norway from the east and contested Magnus's rule there, allying himself with Sweyn, and in 1046 Magnus made him co-king of Norway. By late 1046 Magnus had driven Sweyn out of Denmark. He died suddenly in Denmark on 25 October 1047; accounts vary between an accident, such as falling overboard or from a horse, and disease. He is said to have named Sweyn his heir in Denmark and Harald in Norway, and he was buried with his father in the cathedral at Nidaros, now Trondheim.

His line ended with his death. In 1280 Eric II of Norway, descended through his mother from Magnus's legitimate sister Wulfhild, was crowned king. Heimskringla describes Magnus as a man of middle height, light-haired, well spoken and generous.
magway-region: Magway Region, formerly Magway Division, is a first-level administrative division of central Myanmar and the second largest of its seven regions, with an area of 44,820 square kilometres. It is bordered by Sagaing Region to the north, Mandalay Region to the east, Bago Region to the south and Rakhine State and Chin State to the west. The capital and second largest city is Magway, and the largest is Pakokku. At the 2014 census the region had 3,912,711 inhabitants, mostly Bamar, with the Chin as the largest minority; 98.8 per cent were Buddhists.

Fossils of early primates more than 40 million years old were excavated at Pondaung and Ponnya in Pakokku District. An ancient city of the Pyu, Peikthano-myo, about 2,000 years old, lies in Taungdwingyi Township. The region's older name was Minbu Region, or Minbu Province, established with three districts, Minbu, Thayet and Yenangyaung, and its capital was Yenangyaung. Late in the Konbaung era two forts, Fort Min Hla and Fort Kway Chaung, were built on opposite banks of the Irrawaddy to resist a British invasion.

After the military coup of 2 March 1962 under General Ne Win and the constitution of 1974, Minbu Region was renamed Magway Region and Yenangyaung District was abolished. Pakokku District was added, while Mindat District went to Chin State, and the capital moved from Yenangyaung to Magway. In 1996 Pakokku District was divided into Pakokku and Gangaw, giving five districts, with 25 townships.

The Irrawaddy is the main transport route, and most major towns, among them Magway, Pakokku, Minbu, Yenangyaung and Chauk, are river ports. Pakokku Bridge, the longest in the country, is part of the India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway. The principal product of the region is petroleum, and it yields most of Myanmar's oil and natural gas, from fields at Yenangyaung, Chauk and elsewhere, which has earned it the name oil pot of Myanmar. Sesame and groundnut are the major crops, and Pakokku is the largest rice market of Upper Myanmar. The Thihoshin Pagoda in Pakokku was built by King Alaungsithu.
mahabad: Mahabad lies south of Lake Urmia in a narrow valley 1,300 metres above sea level, and is the capital of Mahabad County in West Azerbaijan province. By road it is 122 kilometres from the provincial capital Urmia and 679 kilometres from Tehran. Most of its people are Kurds who follow Sunni Islam, and many also speak Persian and Azeri Turkic. Neo-Aramaic-speaking Jews once lived in the city as well. Because of its place in Kurdish nationalism, the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization treats it as the capital of Iranian Kurdistan.

The city's older name, Savojbolagh, is a Persian corruption of the Turkic soghuk bulak, meaning cold spring; the Kurdish form was Sablagh. It is first attested in the 16th century, in the Safavid era, when the Mukri Kurds took part in the wars between the Safavid dynasty and the Ottoman Empire and gained prominence. In the 17th century it became the seat of the Mukri principality. Many believe that Budaq Sultan Mukri, who built the congregational mosque, founded the present town. The name Mahabad came into use after the First World War, in the reign of Reza Shah, who ruled from 1925 to 1941.

Mahabad was the capital of the short-lived Republic of Mahabad, declared on 1 January 1946 under the Kurdish nationalist Qazi Muhammad. It had strong Soviet support, as the Soviet Union had occupied northern Iran during the Second World War, and it included the mainly Kurdish-speaking towns of Bukan, Piranshahr, Sardasht and Oshnavieh. After an agreement brokered by the United States, the Soviets agreed to leave Iran. The Shah's government then moved against the republic, and its leaders were arrested. Qazi Muhammad was hanged on 31 March 1947.

The 2016 census counted 168,393 people in the city. The Mahabad dialect is the literary standard of Kurdish in western Iran and is very close to the Sorani used in Iraqi Kurdistan. Several poets and writers came from the city, among them Hejar (Abdurrahman Sharafkandi), who wrote the first Kurdish-Kurdish-Persian dictionary in Iran, and Hemin, and both were given the title of Kurdistan's national poet under the republic. The translator Mohammad Ghazi, who rendered more than 70 literary works into Persian, was also from Mahabad.
mahabharata: Tradition ascribes the Mahabharata to the sage Vyasa, who is also a major figure in the epic and who described it as itihasa, history. Scholars regard the story of the scribe Ganesha writing down Vyasa's dictation as a later interpolation, and the Critical Edition does not include it. The epic began as an orally transmitted tale of charioteer bards. Unlike the Vedas, which had to be preserved letter-perfect, it was a popular work whose reciters conformed to changes in language and style, so its earliest surviving components are believed to be no older than the earliest external references to it, among them Panini's grammar of the 4th century BCE. The text probably reached its final form by the early Gupta period.

The core story is a dynastic struggle for the throne of Hastinapura, ruled by the Kuru clan, between two collateral branches, the Kauravas and the Pandavas. The eldest Kaurava, Duryodhana, is younger than the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, and both claim to be first in line. The Pandavas build the capital of Indraprastha, but Duryodhana's uncle Shakuni wins their wealth and kingdom from Yudhishthira with loaded dice. They spend thirteen years in exile, and when negotiations through Krishna fail, both sides summon vast armies to Kurukshetra.

The epic runs to over 100,000 shlokas, about 1.8 million words, roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined. It is divided into 18 parvas and holds many other stories, including those of Damayanti, Shakuntala and Savitri and Satyavan, as well as discussions of philosophy and of dharmayuddha, just war, which sets criteria such as proportionality, just means and fair treatment of captives and the wounded. Its best-known part, the Bhagavad Gita, is a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna.

Within the Indian tradition the Mahabharata is sometimes called the fifth Veda. Between 1919 and 1966 scholars at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune compared manuscripts from India and abroad and produced the Critical Edition, in 19 volumes on 13,000 pages, which is the text usually used in current studies. The epic was translated into Tamil and Javanese, where part of a Kawi prose version survives from the late 10th century. It inspired plays by Bhasa and many later works, and in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand villagers still perform the Pandav Lila, a ritual re-enactment of episodes from it. Swami Vivekananda, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Mahatma Gandhi, among others, drew on the text in the Indian independence movement.
mahajanga: Since the 10th century the ports of northern Madagascar, home to an Islamized population, had drawn merchants and migrants from East Africa, the Middle East and the Far East; by the late 15th century the Arab geographer Ibn Mājid identified at least a dozen of them. In the early eighteenth century Andriamandisoarivo, backed by an army of eight hundred men, founded a new Sakalava dynasty in the north called Volamena. He died at Bezavo around 1710. His kingdom held the established trading port of Mazalagem Nova and the new ports of Boina and Mahajanga.

An English captain described Mahajanga in 1764 as a bustling, cosmopolitan port, built after the Indian fashion, with many stone buildings and mosques, and with Muslim inhabitants from Surate, Johana, Mosembeck and the Commoro islands. The Sakalava rulers let Muslims practise their religion freely and in return imposed trading controls through a purser who traded in the king's name. Sakalava kings and queens also allowed European merchants to trade, and some incorporated Islamic beliefs into their divine kingship and had converted to Islam by the early nineteenth century.

In the 1780s, according to the French traveller Dumaine, about 200 Muslim traders from the Indian subcontinent had settled at Mahajanga at the mouth of the Betsiboka River, mostly Khojas, Ismailis and Da'udi Bohras, with some Hindus coming later. Their legal status was confused: they often declared themselves Malagasy subjects to avoid laws against slave-holding and stone houses that bound British subjects, and their dhows flew French flags. The 1911 census found 4,480 Indians in Madagascar. The word Mahajanga may have an Indic etymology. In 1977 the city saw ethnic unrest that forced the evacuation of the Comorian minority living there.

Mahajanga is a seaport on the north-west coast of Madagascar and the capital of the Boeny Region; the district, which is identical with the city, had 258,068 inhabitants in 2020. Only small ships can reach the wharf, and deeper ships anchor off and transfer cargo by barge. The city is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese and has a large Muslim population and a university. Its symbol is an African baobab near the coast, 21 metres round, said to be 700 to 800 years old; it was once used for important meetings and, in the nineteenth century, for executions. The climate is tropical savanna, with a wet season from November to mid-April.
mahalia-jackson: Mahalia Jackson was born Mahala Jackson on 26 October 1911 to Charity Clark and Johnny Jackson, a stevedore and weekend barber who lived elsewhere and never joined Charity as a parent. Both sets of her grandparents were born into slavery. She grew up in the leaky three-room house of her aunt Mahala, called Duke, in New Orleans, the thirteenth person living there.

In a very cold December around 1928 she arrived in Chicago. Her aunts took her to Greater Salem Baptist Church, where she felt at home at once. She sang Hand Me Down My Silver Trumpet, Gabriel, joined the choir, and became part of the Johnson Singers, Chicago's first black gospel group.

From about 1931 the Johnson Singers were asked to other church services and revivals, often by small storefront churches whose members were newly arrived migrants, one of whom called her a fresh wind from the down-home religion. The Great Depression drove church attendance, and larger churches gradually became more open to her style as they sought ways to attract members. In 1946 she appeared at the Golden Gate Ballroom in Harlem, where a scout for Apollo Records heard her.

Her first two Apollo releases sold poorly, and when the company asked her to record blues she refused. The song she had sung as a warm-up, Move On Up a Little Higher, was recorded in two parts, and the 1947 release sold two million copies and reached number two on the Billboard charts, both firsts for gospel music.

In 1954 she learned that Apollo's chief executive had withheld royalties and became the first gospel artist to sign with Columbia Records. When Mitch Miller asked her to record ballads and classical songs she again refused. She sang the national anthem at John F. Kennedy's Inaugural Ball in 1961, became the first gospel recording artist to tour Europe, and sang at the March on Washington in 1963. She was a loyal supporter of Martin Luther King Jr.

Completely self-taught, she never learned to read or write musical notation. She adapted the style of Bessie Smith to Protestant hymns and drew on Thomas Dorsey. Asked how she sang, she answered that she sang the way she felt, off-beat, on the beat, between beats. She sold an estimated 22 million records. The historian Robert Marovich identifies her success with Move On Up a Little Higher as the event that launched gospel from a niche movement in Chicago churches to a commercially viable nationwide genre, in the period called the Golden Age of Gospel, from 1945 to 1965. She died on 27 January 1972.
mahanadi: The name Mahanadi combines the Sanskrit words maha, great, and nadi, river. The river drains around 132,100 square kilometres of east-central India and flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha to the Bay of Bengal. Like many seasonal Indian rivers it is a combination of mountain streams, so its precise source cannot be pinpointed. Its farthest headwaters lie in forest south of Sihawa town in Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh, in hills that extend the Eastern Ghats.

It first flows north through Raipur district, then east after the Shivnath joins it, and enters Odisha after about half its length. Near Sambalpur it is dammed at Hirakud. It then forces its way through the Eastern Ghats by the 64-kilometre Satkosia Gorge and reaches the plain at Naraj, near Cuttack.

Cuttack and Sambalpur were prominent trading places in the ancient world, and Ptolemy refers to the river as the Manada. Before the Hirakud Dam the Mahanadi was navigable from its mouth up to Arrang, but barrages have ended that.

The river was notorious for devastating floods for much of recorded history and was called the sorrow of Orissa. It deposits more silt than any other river of the Indian subcontinent, and before the dam it was about a mile wide at Sambalpur. At its monsoon peak its discharge is almost as great as that of the much larger Ganges, but for most of the year it is a narrow channel between wide sand banks. The Hirakud Dam was the first major multipurpose river valley project after India's independence in 1947. It is the longest earthen dam in the world, measuring 26 kilometres including its dykes.

Just before Cuttack the river gives off a large distributary, the Kathjori, and the city stands on the spit between the two channels. The Mahanadi proper enters the sea by several channels near Paradeep. The combined delta of its distributaries and the Brahmani is one of the largest in India, and the valley is best known for its fertile soil and agriculture.
mahapadma-nanda: What is told of Mahapadma comes from the Puranas, which make him the first Nanda king and the son of Mahanandin, the last king of the preceding Shaishunaga line, by a Shudra woman. His name, also given as Mahapadma-pati, means lord of the great lotus. Other traditions about the founder of the dynasty do not use this name at all.

Buddhist texts call the first Nanda king Ugrasena and describe him as of unknown lineage. According to the Mahavamsa-tika he came from the frontier region, was captured by a gang of robbers and later became their leader. One theory holds that Ugrasena was probably another name for Mahapadma. Jain texts such as the Parishishtaparvan and the Avashyaka sutra say that the Nanda king was the son of a courtesan by a barber and that he succeeded Udayin, with Kalpaka, a Jain, as his chief minister.

The Puranas describe him as ekarat, sole sovereign, and as sarva-kshatrantaka, destroyer of all the Kshatriyas, the warriors and rulers. The lines he is said to have exterminated include the Maithalas, Kasheyas, Ikshvakus, Panchalas, Shurasenas, Kurus, Haihayas, Vitihotras, Kalingas and Ashmakas.

The length of his reign is uncertain. The Matsya Purana assigns him 88 years, the Vayu Purana only 28. Modern estimates of his coronation also differ: the Indologist F. E. Pargiter put it in 382 BCE, the historian R. K. Mukherjee in 364 BCE and the historian H. C. Raychaudhuri about 345 BCE, and the beginning of Nanda rule has been placed as early as the 5th century BCE.

According to the Puranas, eight sons of Mahapadma ruled in succession after him for twelve years in all; only one, Sukalpa, is named. The Buddhist texts instead make the next eight kings brothers of the first, give the dynasty 22 years in total and name the last of them as Dhana Nanda.

Greek and Roman writers call the Nanda king of the time of Alexander's invasion Agrammes, possibly a corruption of the Sanskrit Augraseniya, son or descendant of Ugrasena. They suggest that the founder was a barber who took the throne from the last king of the earlier dynasty. The Roman historian Curtius, of the 1st century CE, reports on the authority of Porus that this barber became the queen's lover, murdered the king, seized power while pretending to act as guardian of the princes and later killed them, and that the king reigning in Alexander's day was his son.
maharana-pratap: Pratap Singh was born in 1540, the year his father Udai Singh II took the throne of Mewar. His mother was Jaiwanta Bai, and his younger brothers included Shakti Singh, Vikram Singh and Jagmal Singh. After Udai Singh's death in 1572 his wife Rani Dheer Bai Bhatiyani wanted her son Jagmal to succeed, but senior courtiers preferred Pratap as the eldest son. He was crowned at Gogunda on the day of Holi as the 54th ruler of Mewar in the line of the Sisodia Rajputs. Jagmal swore revenge and went to join Akbar's armies at Ajmer.

The siege of Chittorgarh in 1567 and 1568 had cost Mewar its fertile eastern belt, but the wooded hills of the Aravalli range were still held by Pratap. Akbar wanted a stable route to Gujarat through Mewar and sent envoys, among them Man Singh I of Amber, Bhagwant Das and Todar Mal, asking Pratap to become a vassal. Pratap consistently refused, either with vague promises or by declining to meet them. Akbar's demands probably included attendance at court, tribute, allegiance or a marriage alliance, none of which he would accept.

On 18 June 1576 Pratap, with about 3,000 cavalry and 400 Bhil archers, met Man Singh, who commanded about 10,000 men, at Haldighati near Gogunda. After more than three hours Pratap was wounded and the day was lost, but he escaped to the hills and the Mughals did not capture him or his family. Akbar himself campaigned against him in September 1576, and Gogunda, Udaipur and Kumbhalgarh came under Mughal control. Shahbaz Khan Kamboh's later invasions weakened Pratap further and forced him to take refuge in the hills, where he fought as a guerrilla.

Mughal pressure eased after 1579 because of rebellions in Bengal and Bihar. A Mughal expedition under Jagannath Kachhwaha in 1584 was driven back, and in 1585 Akbar moved to Lahore for twelve years. Pratap recovered thirty-six outposts, including Udaipur, Gogunda and Mandal, and by his death he had regained a large part of Mewar. He could not retake Chittor itself. His court at Chavand sheltered poets and artists, and the Chavand school of art developed there.

Pratap reportedly died of injuries from a hunting accident at Chavand on 19 January 1597, aged 56, and his eldest son Amar Singh I succeeded him. He is a folk hero in Rajasthan and across India. The historian Satish Chandra wrote that his defiance of the Mughal empire, almost alone and unaided by the other Rajput states, was a saga of Rajput valour, and that his guerrilla methods were later elaborated by Malik Ambar and by Shivaji.
maharashtra: Maharashtra covers 307,713 square kilometres of the western peninsular region of India and occupies a substantial part of the Deccan Plateau. It has a coastline of 840 kilometres on the Arabian Sea. The dominant feature is the plateau, separated from the narrow Konkan coastal plains by the Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri Range, which run parallel to the coast and average 1,200 metres in height. The Satpura Hills form its northern border. The Godavari and Krishna are its two major rivers. Its main regions are North Maharashtra, Konkan, Marathwada, Vidarbha and Desh, or Western Maharashtra.

The region has a history of many thousands of years. Late Harappan or Chalcolithic sites of the Jorwe culture, c. 1300 to 700 BCE, have been found throughout the state, the largest at Daimabad, which had a mud fortification and an elliptical temple with fire pits. In the Late Harappan period many people migrated from Gujarat to northern Maharashtra. Among the dynasties that ruled the region were the Asmakas, the Mauryas, the Western Satraps, the Abhiras, the Vakatakas, the Chalukyas, the Western Chalukyas, the Khaljis, the Tughlaqs, the Bahamanis and the Mughals, besides the Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas and Seuna Yadavas.

In the early 19th century the region was divided between the Peshwa's dominions in the Maratha Confederacy and the Nizamate of Hyderabad. The British East India Company then defeated the Marathas and brought most of present-day Maharashtra under its control, directly and through many princely states, and from 1858 the British crown took over. The region was divided among the Bombay Presidency, the Central Provinces, Berar and princely states including Hyderabad. After independence in 1947 the Bombay Presidency became Bombay State, which gained Berar, the Deccan states and the Gujarat states between 1950 and 1956. The United Maharashtra Movement campaigned for a separate state for Marathi speakers, and on 1 May 1960 Bombay State was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat.

Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra, with Nagpur as its winter capital, and the state has 36 districts in six divisions. Marathi, written in the Devanagari script, is the official language and is spoken by about 69 per cent of the people. Its earliest literature is the Dnyaneshwari, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita by the 13th-century Bhakti saint Dnyaneshwar. Seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the state, among them the Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta Caves and the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus.
mahatma-gandhi: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula and then part of a small princely state. His father Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi was the dewan, or chief minister, of Porbandar and later of Rajkot. A family friend advised that he study law in London, and to win his mother's consent he vowed to abstain from meat, alcohol and women. The elders of the Modh Bania community excommunicated him from his caste, but he sailed on 4 September 1888 and was called to the bar at 22.

After two uncertain years in India, Gandhi went to South Africa in April 1893 to represent an Indian merchant in a lawsuit, and stayed for 21 years. He faced discrimination at once: he was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave the first-class compartment. He had thought of himself as a Briton first and an Indian second, but the prejudice he saw made him question his people's standing in the British Empire. There he first used nonviolent resistance, in a campaign for civil rights.

Gandhi returned to India in 1915 at the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale. He took leadership of the Indian National Congress in 1920 and formulated satyagraha as a political movement in a Resolution on Non-cooperation that September. Congress declared the independence of India on 26 January 1930, and that year he led the 400 km Dandi Salt March against the British salt tax. In 1942 he demanded immediate independence, and the British imprisoned him and tens of thousands of Congress leaders. He was imprisoned many times in both South Africa and India.

The Muslim League moved, against Gandhi's strong opposition, to demand a separate Muslim state. In August 1947 the British partitioned the land, and India and Pakistan each became independent on terms Gandhi disapproved. Religious violence followed, especially in Punjab and Bengal. He visited the affected areas and undertook several hunger strikes to stop the violence.

On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who opposed Gandhi's advocacy of nonviolence and his friendship with Indian Muslims, shot him three times in the chest in the garden of Birla House in Delhi on his way to a prayer meeting. Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India, Gandhi Jayanti, and is marked worldwide as the International Day of Nonviolence. He is regarded as the Father of the Nation in India and was often called Bapu. His pamphlet Hind Swaraj of 1909 became the intellectual blueprint of the independence movement. Writers differ on him, some presenting a paragon of ethical living and others a more complex, contradictory and changing figure.
mahavira: Historical information about Mahavira is scarce, and traditional accounts vary by sect, but scholars do not dispute that he lived in ancient India. Both Jain sects agree that he was born in 599 BCE. The Śvetāmbaras say that he died in 527 BCE and the Digambaras in 510 BCE. Historians place him in the 6th or 5th century BCE, reviving and reforming an earlier community that was probably led by Parshvanatha, whom Jains consider his predecessor.

According to the Kalpa Sūtra and the Uttarapurana, he was born at Kundagrama in the Kingdom of the Videhas, in present-day Bihar, though its exact location is disputed. His father was King Siddhartha of the Nāya tribe and his mother Queen Trishala of the Licchavi republic. His parents were lay followers of Parshvanatha. The Digambaras hold that he refused to marry, while the Śvetāmbaras say that he married Yashoda and had a daughter.

At about thirty, or twenty-eight according to some accounts, Mahavira abandoned royal life and became an ascetic. He undertook severe fasts, meditated under the Ashoka tree and discarded his clothes. The Ācārāṅga Sūtra describes his hardships and self-mortification in graphic terms. After about twelve and a half years of penance he is said to have attained Kevala Jnana, or omniscience, under a Sāla tree on the bank of the river Rijuvalika.

He then preached for thirty years. Jain texts name eleven Brahmanas as his first disciples, the Ganadharas, led by Indrabhuti Gautama. According to the Kalpa Sūtra his followers numbered 14,000 monks and 36,000 nuns, with 159,000 male and 318,000 female lay followers. Tradition names Srenika and Kunika of the Haryanka dynasty, popularly known as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, and Chetaka of Videha among his royal followers. He died at Pawapuri in present-day Bihar, now a pilgrimage site, and Jains commemorate the night of his nirvana as Diwali.

Mahavira taught that the observance of five vows is necessary for liberation: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity and non-attachment. Non-violence was already an established rule among the followers of Parshvanatha. He also taught Anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sided reality. Moriz Winternitz notes that his teaching contains a very elaborate belief in the soul, unlike that of the Buddhists.

Gautama Swami compiled his teachings as the Jain Agamas, which monks passed on orally. According to Jain tradition they were gradually lost after about 300 BCE, when a severe famine in Magadha dispersed the monks. In the early centuries of the common era the surviving teachings were written on palm-leaf manuscripts, and the Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions each hold their own incomplete and somewhat different versions.
mahayana-buddhism: Mahāyāna, Sanskrit for Great Vehicle, is a broad group of Buddhist traditions, texts, philosophies and practices that developed in ancient India from about the 1st century BCE. Its origins are still not completely understood, and there are many competing theories. The earliest textual evidence comes from sutras originating around the beginning of the common era. According to Jan Nattier, the term was at first an honorary synonym for Bodhisattvayāna, the vehicle of a bodhisattva who seeks buddhahood for the benefit of all beings, and in the earliest sources it meant the rigorous emulation of the path of Gautama Buddha. The movement remained quite small until it grew strongly in the 5th century, when manuscripts and inscriptions begin to show popular and some royal support.

Mahāyāna accepts the main scriptures and teachings of early Buddhism but also recognises sutras that Theravāda does not accept as canonical, such as the Lotus Sutra and the Vajra-cutter Sutra. These emphasise the ideal of the bodhisattva, who vows to attain buddhahood to save all living beings, an attitude called bodhicitta. Mahāyānists hold that the bodhisattva path is superior to the path of those seeking only their own release from suffering, which they call a lesser aspiration. Its teachings include the Perfection of Wisdom, Buddha-nature and skilful means, the idea that the Buddha adapts his teaching to each hearer. Its cosmology includes buddhas such as Amitābha and Vairocana, and philosophical schools such as Madhyamaka and its theory of emptiness.

Mahāyāna texts and philosophy reached Central Asia and China along trade routes such as the Silk Road. Translators from Central Asia, among them Lokakṣema, Dharmarakṣa, Kumārajīva and Dharmakṣema, were central to this transmission, and Dunhuang was an important place of study. In India the great scholastic centres of Nalanda and Vikramashila thrived between the 7th and 12th centuries. From the Gupta period a new tantric movement grew within it, called Vajrayāna, which dominated Indian Buddhism in the Pala era. Mahāyāna traditions such as Zen, Pure Land and Tiantai are the main forms of Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, and tantric forms are dominant in Tibet, Mongolia and Bhutan.
mahdi: The Arabic word al-Mahdī means the guided one. It comes from the root h-d-y, which indicates divine guidance, but the word does not occur in the Quran. From the beginning of Islam it was an honorific without messianic meaning, applied to Muhammad, to Abraham, to al-Husayn and to some Umayyad caliphs. During the Second Muslim Civil War (680 to 692) it came to mean a ruler who would restore Islam and justice after oppression. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who claimed the caliphate against the Umayyads, presented himself in this role, and a hadith was circulated in which Muhammad foretells a just ruler.

Some historians suggest that southern Arabian tribes settled in Syria in the mid-7th century introduced the term. The idea is also linked to the Christian Second Coming, the Jewish Mashiach ben David and the Zoroastrian Saoshyant; Islamic scholars reject a Zoroastrian influence and defend the traditions. They appear in Sunan Abi Dawud and Sunan al-Tirmidhi but not in the early works of al-Bukhari and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj.

The Mahdi is the Islamic messianic figure expected to appear before the end of time, alongside Jesus, to restore justice and defeat tyranny. In Sunni Islam he is a descendant of Muhammad through Fatima who has not yet appeared and is not identified with any historical person. In Twelver Shia Islam he is the twelfth and last Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, born in 869, who entered occultation and remains alive until his return. Shia writers often call him al-Qa'im, he who will rise.

Traditions about the occultation of a future imam circulated for about a century before the death of the eleventh Imam in 260 AH (874 CE). Sects now extinct, such as the Kaysanites, who said Ibn al-Hanafiyya was hiding near Medina, used them, and the Twelver doctrine took shape in the first half of the tenth century in the works of al-Qummi, al-Kulayni and Ibn Babawayh.

Belief in the Mahdi has had a central place in Islamic theology, devotional literature and popular piety for over a millennium, and it has influenced many religious, political and messianic movements. There have been a vast number of Mahdi claimants. Many Muslims hold that the Mahdi appears occasionally to pious individuals, and every year millions celebrate Mid-Sha'ban, the birth of Muhammad al-Mahdi.
mahdia: Mahdia is a Tunisian coastal city, south of Monastir and south-east of Sousse, and the capital of Mahdia Governorate. Its old part corresponds to the Roman city called Aphrodisium and later Africa, or Cape Africa. A bishopric called Africa is supposed to have been established when the city was held by the Kingdom of Sicily, within the Kingdom of Africa from 1147 to 1160, and Pope Eugene III consecrated a bishop for it in 1148. A ship carrying Greek art treasures, dated to about 80 BCE and found sunk off the shore, is known as the Mahdia shipwreck.

The Fatimid caliph Abdallah al-Mahdi founded the city and made it the capital of Ifriqiya. Since the new Fatimid Caliphate was a Shi'a regime backed by a Berber Kutama army, he may have wished to put distance between his power base and Kairouan, a mainly Sunni city and the traditional capital. Construction began in 916, and the city was inaugurated on 20 February 921. It had heavy walls, the Fatimid palaces, an artificial harbour and the Great Mosque of Mahdia. Most of the Fatimid city has not survived, but the mosque is among the best-preserved Fatimid monuments in the Maghreb, though much of it was rebuilt by archaeologists in the 1960s.

The Zirid dynasty, successors of the Fatimids in the Maghreb, moved their capital to Mahdia in 1057. In 1087 ships from Genoa and Pisa raided it and burned the Muslim fleet in the harbour, which helped Christians take control of the western Mediterranean and supply the First Crusade by sea. The city fell to the Norman conquest in 1148 and came under Almohad rule in 1160. The role of capital passed to Tunis in the 12th century. In 1390 a French army besieged Mahdia in the Barbary Crusade and failed to take it.

The Spaniards captured the city in 1550. Charles V offered it to the Order of Saint John, who refused as too costly, and he ordered the Viceroy of Sicily, Juan de Vega, to dismantle it. The Ottomans then reoccupied it, but it lived only by fishing and oil-works and lost its commercial importance. It remained under Turkish rule until the 19th century.

The city, with 76,513 inhabitants, is a provincial centre north of Sfax and is known for fish processing and weaving. Its railway station is the southern terminus of the Sahel Metro line from Sousse and Monastir. The Great Mosque and fragments of mosaic pavements from the Fatimid palaces are what remain of its early history.
mahdist-war: After Muhammad Ali's invasion of 1820 to 1821, Sudan was governed as part of the Ottoman-Egyptian state, known locally as the Turkiyah. Large sections of the population suffered heavy taxation, forced labour and coercion, and many people left the Nile Valley for Kordofan and Darfur. The slave trade remained a major part of the economy. Egypt's debts under Isma'il Pasha led to his forced abdication in 1879. In 1873 Isma'il had appointed Charles George Gordon governor of the Equatorial Provinces, and Gordon tried to suppress the slave trade, but resigned in 1880. Resentment of Turco-Egyptian rule grew among merchants, tribal leaders and religious figures, and the British government refused to assume direct responsibility.

In the 1870s the cleric Muhammad Ahmad preached renewal of the faith and proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the promised redeemer. In August 1881 two Egyptian companies sent to arrest him fired on each other in the dark and were destroyed in turn at the Battle of Aba. He retreated to Kordofan and declared a jihad, calling his followers the Ansar. On 7 June 1882 his army surprised an Egyptian force of 4,000 under Yusef Pasha and destroyed it. In November 1883 the Mahdi, with about 40,000 men, defeated the army of the retired colonel William Hicks at the Battle of Shaykan, and only about 500 Egyptians survived.

Britain then decided that Egypt should evacuate Sudan and sent Gordon, who reached Khartoum on 18 February 1884. He grew reluctant to leave while any who wished to go had not been able to, and it is debated whether he deliberately stayed too long. The telegraph lines were cut on 15 March. A relief column of 9,000 under Sir Garnet Wolseley won at Abu Klea and Abu Kru in January 1885, but Khartoum fell on 26 January 1885, after a siege of 313 days, and Gordon and the garrison were killed. Muhammad Ahmad died on 22 June 1885 and was succeeded by the Khalifa Abdallahi ibn Muhammad.

The Mahdist state fought Ethiopia in the 1880s and Italian troops in the 1890s. In 1898 Herbert Kitchener led an Anglo-Egyptian force of 8,200 British soldiers and 17,600 Egyptian and Sudanese soldiers up the Nile with railways and gunboats. After the Battle of Atbara in April the force reached Omdurman, the Mahdist capital, on 2 September, where the Mahdist army of more than 60,000 attacked and was cut down by machine guns and rifles. Organised resistance ended the next year, and Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, a condominium in which Britain held de facto control, was created in 1899.
mahe-india: Mahé, also known as Mayyazhi, is a municipality and small town in the Mahe district of the Puducherry Union Territory. It lies at the mouth of the Mahe River and is surrounded by the State of Kerala: the district of Kannur encloses it on three sides and Kozhikode district on one. The name derives from Mayyazhi, the Malayalam name of the local river and region. French documents of the early 1720s spell it Mayé, and the spelling Mahe became the norm only in the early 19th century, so the belief that the town was named for Bertrand François Mahé de La Bourdonnais is incorrect.

Before European trading companies arrived, the area belonged to Kolathu Nadu. The French East India Company built a fort here under an accord made between André Mollandin and Raja Vazhunnavar of Vatakara. In 1741 La Bourdonnais retook the town after a short occupation by the Marathas. The British captured it in 1761 and handed it to the Rajah of Kadathanadu, and restored it to the French by the 1763 Treaty of Paris. It was lost again in the Anglo-French war of 1779 and returned in 1785.

A British force under James Hartley captured Mahe in 1793, and it was restored to the French in 1816 under the 1814 Treaty of Paris. For the long period that followed it was a small French colony, an enclave within British India. Hyder Ali of Mysore had earlier given Naluthara to the French in appreciation of their help in war. After Indian independence in 1947 Gandhians such as I. K. Kumaran led the movement for union with India. On 21 October 1948 the French flag was removed from the municipal building and the Indian flag raised, but a French navy ship arrived on 26 October and French control returned. The struggle ended with the town's union with India in 1954.

Mahe is one of the four districts of the Union Territory of Puducherry and has one representative in its Legislative Assembly. The 2011 census counted 41,816 people, mostly Malayalis, of whom 66.8 per cent were Hindu and 30.7 per cent Muslim. Malayalam is the main language, and fewer than 100 people speak French. French influence survives mainly in buildings, among them St. Teresa's Shrine, built in 1736, the Government House, the Mahe Lighthouse and a statue of Marianne commemorating the French Revolution.
mahikeng: Mahikeng, in the classic Setswana language, means place of rocks, or place among rocks, and refers to volcanic rocks that gave temporary shelter to Stone Age people hunting animals that came to drink at the Molopo River. The town lies close to South Africa's border with Botswana, built on open veld at about 1,500 metres by the banks of the Upper Molopo, 1,400 km northeast of Cape Town and 260 km west of Johannesburg. It was long written Mafeking by British settlers, a spelling still used for the siege of 1899–1900, and it later became Mafikeng, the form in common speech.

The town began as Molema's town. In 1857 Molema Tawana led an advance guard of the Barolong to scout the Molopo River and settled there, while the main body under his brother Montshiwa followed. Montshiwa felt unsafe because of the nearby Boers of the Transvaal and moved to Moshaneng, but Molema stayed and used diplomacy to keep the Boers from settling near the town. Montshiwa returned in 1876. Molema was a firm believer in Western education and opened a school for the Barolong; he died in 1882.

In 1882 the Boers set up the Republic of Stellaland and the State of Goshen in Bechuanaland. Tswana chiefs sought British protection, and a force of 4,000 troops under Major General Charles Warren dissolved the two states in a campaign of 1884–1885. Bechuanaland was proclaimed a British protectorate with Mafeking as its capital, though the protectorate was later divided and Mafeking lay south of its boundary, in British Bechuanaland, later passed to the Cape Colony. It remained the protectorate's administrative capital until Gaborone was established in 1965.

When the Second Boer War broke out in 1899 the Boers besieged the town. The siege lasted 217 days, from October 1899 to May 1900, and made Robert Baden-Powell a national hero; the use of adolescent boys as military auxiliaries helped lay the groundwork for the Scouting movement. British losses were 212 killed, soldiers and civilians, and more than 600 wounded, and Boer losses were significantly higher. In 1900 the British also built a concentration camp there for Boer women and children. A local referendum took the town into the Bantustan of Bophuthatswana in 1980.

After the end of apartheid in 1994 Bophuthatswana was reincorporated into South Africa, and the merged Mafikeng and Mmabatho became the capital of the new North-West Province. The provincial legislature stands in the New Parliament Building in Mmabatho. The North-West University has a campus there, and the town has a museum, a railway station and the Mafikeng Game Reserve on its edge.
mahmud-ii: Mahmud II was born on 20 July 1785, the youngest son of Sultan Abdul Hamid I and his consort Nakşidil Kadın. According to tradition he was confined in the Kafes after his father's death. In 1808 his half-brother Mustafa IV ordered his execution along with that of the deposed Sultan Selim III. Selim was killed, but Mahmud was kept hidden by his mother and placed on the throne after rebels deposed Mustafa IV. Their leader, Alemdar Mustafa Pasha, became his vizier and resumed reforms, but he was killed in a rebellion that year and Mahmud temporarily abandoned reform.

The Russo-Turkish War of 1806 to 1812 ended in the Treaty of Bucharest, by which the empire ceded the eastern half of Moldavia to Russia, which renamed it Bessarabia. His governor of Egypt, Muhammad Ali, reconquered the Hejaz, taking Medina in 1812 and Mecca in 1813. A Greek rebellion began in 1821, and after the combined British, French and Russian navies defeated the Ottoman fleet at Navarino in 1827 the empire had to recognise Greece in July 1832. France began the conquest of Ottoman Algeria in 1830.

In June 1826 he carried out the Auspicious Incident. When the Janissaries demonstrated against his proposed military reforms, he had their barracks fired upon, and many were executed or exiled. This allowed a European-style conscript army. With it he subdued the derebeys and ayans, hereditary local chiefs who had become petty princes, until only Cyprus kept such power. He closed the Court of Confiscations and forbade governors to execute anyone without a sentence signed by a judge.

Mahmud reformed the bureaucracy, raised salaries to end bribery, and in 1831 founded the first Ottoman Turkish newspaper, the official gazette Takvim-i Vekayi. In 1838 he established the Supreme Council of Judicial Ordinances and in 1839 a Council of Ministers. He died of tuberculosis on 1 July 1839 and was succeeded by his son Abdülmecid I, who announced the Tanzimat. He is often called the Peter the Great of Turkey, and the abolition of the Janissaries removed a major obstacle to later reforms, although his reign also brought military defeats and loss of territory.
mahmud-of-ghazni: Mahmud was born in Ghazni, in the region of Zabulistan, on 2 October 971. His father, Sabuktigin, was a Karluk Turkic slave who founded the Ghaznavid dynasty in 977, ruling as a subordinate of the Samanids. His mother was a local woman of possible Iranian descent. As a young man he served his father against the Hindu Shahi ruler Jayapala and in the capture of Khorasan in 994, and received the title Saifu'd-Dawlah, Sword of the State.

Sabuktigin died in August 997 and was succeeded by Mahmud's brother Ismail, for reasons that are uncertain. Mahmud revolted and defeated Ismail at the battle of Ghazni, taking the throne at the age of 27.

In 999 Mahmud took Khorasan from the Samanids, defeating their army near Merv on 16 May, and the Oxus was fixed as the border with the Kara-Khanids. In 1002 he ended the Saffarid dynasty by deposing Khalaf ibn Ahmad in Sistan. He defeated the Kara-Khanids at the Battle of Katar on 5 January 1008, and in 1017 he conquered Khwarazm and captured Gurganj. In 1029 and 1030 his forces took Ray and Isfahan.

In the Indian subcontinent he defeated Jayapala at Peshawar on 28 November 1001 and later fought Jayapala's son Anandapala. He took Multan in 1006, where the Ismailis were massacred. His coinage from Lahore called him the breaker of idols, and he presented his wars as the defence of the Sunni Abbasid caliphate against Shia rivals.

Mahmud contracted malaria on his last Indian campaign in 1027, which led to tuberculosis. He returned to Ghazni about 22 April 1030 and died on 30 April. His sultanate was served by departments of finance, war, correspondence, intelligence and household, with a postal service that carried news to the ruler. Dawlatshah reckoned that he had 400 poets at court, and Ghazni drew al-Biruni and Ferdowsi. Many Indian Muslim scholars regard him as a founder of Muslim rule in the subcontinent's interior.
mahon: Mahón stands on the eastern coast of Menorca. Its harbour is one of the longest natural harbours in the world, 5 kilometres long and up to 900 metres wide, deep and mostly clear because it is so enclosed. It was one of the most strategically important harbours of the western Mediterranean.

The name is attributed to the Carthaginian general Mago Barca, brother of Hannibal, who is thought to have taken refuge there in 205 BCE. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the island became part of the Eastern Roman Empire. It suffered raids from Vikings and Arabs until the Caliphate of Córdoba conquered it in 903. Alfonso III of Aragon took Mahón from the Moors in 1287 and made it part of the Kingdom of Majorca, and the harbour was refortified. In 1535 Ottoman forces under Hayreddin Barbarossa attacked Mahón and carried 600 captives to Algiers as slaves.

A British and Dutch force captured Menorca in 1708, in the War of the Spanish Succession, and the Treaty of Utrecht confirmed British possession in 1713. The capital moved from Ciutadella to Mahón, which housed the governor, the best known being General Richard Kane. A Royal Navy dockyard was set up on the north side of the harbour in 1715 and served as the principal Mediterranean base for much of the century.

France took the island in 1756, returned it in 1763, and Spain regained it in 1782, confirmed in 1783. Britain retook it in 1798, and under the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 it passed to Spain. In the Spanish Civil War the island stayed loyal to the Republic until the Nationalists captured it in 1939.

Mahón, officially Maó in Catalan, is the capital and second largest city of Menorca and the seat of the Island Council of Menorca. Mahón cheese takes its name from the city, and in Spanish mahón is also the word for nankeen cloth. Buildings of the British dockyard from the 1760s survive on the island of Illa Pinto, and the ruins of the Royal Naval Hospital, founded in 1711, stand on Illa del Rei.
maiduguri: Maiduguri lies along the seasonal Ngadda River, which disappears into the Firki swamps in the country around Lake Chad. The climate is hot and semi-arid, and the colonial administration made tree planting a priority, so that large trees along the main roads give shelter from the sun. The region had been home to the Kanem-Bornu Empire for centuries.

The city consists of two parts: Yerwa to the west and Old Maiduguri to the east. Yerwa was founded in 1907 by Abubakar Garbai of Borno as the capital of the kingdom of Bornu, replacing Kukawa as the capital of the Kanuri people. The site had been a small village called Kalwa. In 1908 the British chose Old Maiduguri, in place of Mafoni, as their military headquarters, and in the same year it became the seat of the British Resident Commissioner for British Bornu. In 1957 the name Yerwa was officially given to the urban centre and Maiduguri to the surrounding rural area. When the railway was extended to the city in 1964, it began to rise as a major commercial centre of the region.

Maiduguri has also been known as a centre of Islamic scholarship in West Africa. Since the mid-1960s it has seen riots between religious groups, in 1982 and 2001 among others. In 2002 the cleric Mohammed Yusuf founded the group later known as Boko Haram there, with a mosque and a madrasa that drew children from poor Muslim families in Nigeria and neighbouring countries. In 1975 the University of Maiduguri was founded.

Maiduguri is the capital and largest city of Borno State and is one of the local government areas of the traditional Borno Emirate. Its residents are mostly Muslim and include Kanuri, Hausa, Shuwa, Bura, Marghi and Fulani, with a considerable Christian population and people from southern Nigerian states such as the Igbo, Ijaw and Yoruba. A railway line links it with Port Harcourt, Enugu, Kafanchan and Bauchi, and it has an international airport. It is the principal trading hub of north-eastern Nigeria, with an economy based mainly on services and trade, and has three large markets, among them the Monday Market. The city is also home to the El-Kanemi Warriors football club and to Kyarimi Park, the oldest and largest zoo in Nigeria.
maimonides: Moses ben Maimon, known in Hebrew by the acronym Rambam, was born in Córdoba under the Almoravid dynasty, at the end of the Golden Age of Jewish culture in Spain. His father, Maimon ben Joseph, was a dayyan, or rabbinic judge, and taught him Torah. At an early age he took an interest in contemporary science and philosophy, reading ancient Greek philosophy through Arabic translations.

The Almohads conquered Córdoba in 1148 and abolished the protected status of non-Muslims in some territories. Jewish and Christian communities faced a choice between conversion, martyrdom and exile. Many Jews were forced to convert and had to wear identifying clothing, because the authorities suspected false conversions. Maimonides' family chose exile. For ten years he moved about southern Spain and North Africa before settling in Fez, and he wrote his commentary on the Mishnah in 1166-1168.

Around 1171 Maimonides was appointed nagid, or head, of the Egyptian Jewish community; Shelomo Dov Goitein believes his leadership during the ransoming of Crusader captives led to the appointment. He was replaced by Sar Shalom ben Moses in 1173, excommunicated him and quarrelled with him for years, and was appointed nagid again in 1195. After the family's funds were lost in a business venture, he took up medicine, which he had studied in Spain and in Fez. He became court physician to Qadi al-Fadil, the chief secretary to Sultan Saladin, then to Saladin himself, and he remained a physician to the Ayyubid dynasty after Saladin's death.

He died in Fustat on 12 December 1204. Medieval sources beginning with al-Qifti say he was buried near the Sea of Galilee, though there is no contemporary evidence that his body was moved from Egypt. A tomb in Tiberias is a pilgrimage site and bears the inscription 'From Moses to Moses arose none like Moses.'

The Mishneh Torah is a code of Jewish law in fourteen books that gathers the binding laws of the Talmud and the positions of the Geonim. It is still regarded as one of the chief authoritative codifications of Jewish law and is closely studied in yeshivot. In his Mishnah commentary he set out thirteen principles of faith, which he saw as the required beliefs of Judaism. His Guide for the Perplexed sought to reconcile Aristotelianism and science with the Torah, and French rabbis banned it and burnt copies in Montpellier.

He also wrote on medicine, including a Guide to Good Health composed in Arabic for Sultan al-Afdal, son of Saladin, who suffered from depression. Translated into Latin, it was printed in Florence in 1477. His writings influenced the Scholastic philosophers Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus.
mainz: Mainz lies on the left bank of the Rhine at the northern end of the Upper Rhine Plain, opposite the mouth of the Main. Its name does not come from the river but is a simplification of Mogontiacum, a name that appears to be Celtic, probably linked to the Gallic god Mogons whom Roman soldiers had adopted. The city is in one of Germany's important wine regions.

The Roman general Nero Claudius Drusus founded the stronghold of Mogontiacum, perhaps as early as 13 or 12 BCE, on the northern frontier of the empire, and it became the capital of the province of Germania Superior. The Emperor Julian liberated the city in 357, and in 451 Attila's Huns sacked it. The Franks settled there from 459.

In the early Middle Ages Mainz played a significant part in the Christianisation of the German and Slavic peoples. Its first archbishop, Boniface, was killed in 754 while trying to convert the Frisians. The archbishopric was established in 781, when Boniface's successor Lullus received the pallium from Pope Adrian I, and the archbishops held high office in the Holy Roman Empire as archchancellors. A Jewish community existed from the 10th century and was known for its teaching, notably that of Rabbi Gershom ben Judah (960–1040). From the 12th century Mainz belonged to the ShUM cities with Speyer and Worms.

French revolutionary troops occupied the city in 1792, and on 18 March 1793 the Jacobins of Mainz proclaimed a Republic of Mainz under Georg Forster. After an 18-week siege the French surrendered to the Prussians on 23 July 1793. In 1816 Mainz became the capital of Rhenish Hesse, and until 1866 it was the chief fortress of the German Confederation against France.

Mainz is the capital and largest city of Rhineland-Palatinate, with about 223,000 inhabitants. It is the birthplace of Johannes Gutenberg, and its cathedral, one of the three Rhenish Imperial Cathedrals, is over a thousand years old. Roman remains include Jupiter's column, and the ShUM sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
maison-carree: The Maison carrée, French for square house, is an ancient Roman temple in Nîmes in southern France and one of the best-preserved Roman temples to survive in the territory of the former Roman Empire. It is a mid-sized Augustan provincial temple of the imperial cult, a caesareum. The temple dominated the forum of the Roman city. It stands on a podium 2.85 m high and measures 26.42 m by 13.54 m, a rectangle almost twice as long as it is wide. Its deep portico, almost a third of the building's length, emphasises the temple front and distinguishes the layout from Greek temples.

The temple was dedicated or rededicated to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, grandsons and adopted heirs of Augustus who both died young. The dedicatory inscription was removed in medieval times, but a local scholar, Jean-François Séguier, reconstructed it in 1758 from the order and number of the holes in the frieze and architrave to which bronze letters had been fixed. In his reconstruction it reads: to Gaius Caesar, son of Augustus, consul; to Lucius Caesar, son of Augustus, consul designate; to the princes of youth.

The temple is similar to the Tuscan-style Roman temple described by the contemporary writer Vitruvius, though it uses the Corinthian order. It is hexastyle, with six Corinthian columns under the pediment at each end, and pseudoperipteral, with twenty engaged columns along the walls of the cella. A large door leads to the small windowless interior, which has no ancient decoration. The carving is not as precise as that of the Parthenon.

Until the nineteenth century the temple formed part of a larger complex of adjoining buildings, which were demolished when it housed, from 1821 to 1907, what is now the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nîmes. The present door dates from 1824, and a restoration between 1988 and 1992 re-roofed it and cleared the square, revealing the outlines of the forum. Thomas Jefferson had a stucco model made of the temple in 1785 while minister to France, and it inspired the Virginia State Capitol he designed, as well as the Église de la Madeleine in Paris and St Marcellinus Church in Rogalin, Poland. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in September 2023.
maitreya: Maitreya, in Pali Metteyya, is regarded in all schools of Buddhism as the future Buddha of this world and the direct successor of Gautama Buddha. His name comes from the Sanskrit maitrī, meaning loving-kindness, and is related to the Indo-Iranian name Mitra. In Tibetan Buddhism he is called the Lord of Love. Tradition counts him as the fifth and final Buddha of the present eon. He is expected to appear in an age of decline, when the teachings of Gautama have been forgotten, and to re-establish the dharma, 5,670,000,000 years from now.
