Meanwhile he lives as a bodhisattva in the Tushita heaven, where Gautama also lived before his birth.

The Cakkavatti Sutta says that Maitreya will be born in the city of Ketumatī, when humans live for eighty thousand years, to the chief priest Brahmayu and his wife Brahmavati. He will live as a householder, have a son, then renounce the world and attain Buddhahood, and the wheel-turning emperor Sankha will give away his palace and follow him. Jan Nattier distinguishes four kinds of Maitreya myth: meeting him in this life, meeting him in a later life, seeing him in a vision of his court, and rebirth in his Tushita palace.

Mahayana Buddhists hold that Maitreya revealed five scriptures to the Indian master Asanga in the 4th century, texts important to the Yogacara tradition. Chinese Buddhists regard the monk Budai, traditionally dated to the tenth century, as an emanation of Maitreya, which gave rise to the image of the Laughing Buddha.

Maitreya devotion in China goes back at least to Dao'an in the 4th century and was popular under the Northern Wei. Masters such as Xuanzang, Wonhyo and Yijing hoped to be reborn in his Inner Court. In Japan the Hossō school treats him as its founder.

The prophecy was also used by secret societies and rebels. Three people declared themselves incarnations of Maitreya under the Sui dynasty in failed attempts to overthrow it, and in 515 the monk Faqing proclaimed himself the New Buddha and raised an army against the Northern Wei. The White Lotus Society, whose roots go back to the 12th century, and later Chinese salvationist religions made Maitreya a saviour sent by the Eternal Venerable Mother.
maize: Maize, Zea mays, is a tall annual grass with a single stem, ranging in height from 1.2 to 4 m. The tassel at the top bears the male flowers, and a female inflorescence lower down develops into an ear wrapped in husks. The grains are usually yellow or white in modern varieties but can be orange, red, brown, blue, purple or black. Maize relies on humans for its propagation, since its kernels, unlike those of its wild ancestor teosinte, do not fall off the cob on their own.

The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the botanist Nikolai Vavilov in 1931 and by George Beadle in 1932. In 2004 John Doebley identified Balsas teosinte, native to the Balsas River valley in Mexico's south-western highlands, as the wild relative most similar to maize. All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700-year-old layer in a cave near Iguala, Guerrero, and maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8,000 years ago.
The Olmec and Maya cultivated it in numerous varieties and processed it by nixtamalization, and by 3,000 years ago it was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language and myths.

The niacin in maize is not available without nixtamalization, the alkali treatment, and the Maya made nixtamal meal into porridges and tamales. After 1492 explorers and traders carried maize to Europe. Spanish settlers preferred wheat bread, and maize flour could not replace wheat in communion bread, since only wheat was believed able to undergo transubstantiation. Maize was nevertheless grown in Spain within a few decades of Columbus's voyages, and by the 18th century it was the chief food of the southern French and Italian peasantry, especially as polenta.
majapahit-empire: Majapahit, also called Wilwatikta, was a Javanese Hindu-Buddhist empire based on the island of Java. The name means bitter maja, after the fruit of a tree; the 16th-century chronicle Pararaton says that workers clearing the forest of Trik for Raden Wijaya found maja trees and ate their bitter fruit. Before it, the kingdom of Singhasari had become the most powerful polity of the region after the Pamalayu campaign against the Melayu Kingdom in Sumatra. Its king Kertanagara refused tribute to Kublai Khan and sent a Yuan envoy back to China with his face mutilated. In response the khan sent a punitive expedition of 30,000 soldiers and 1,000 ships to Java in 1293, and Majapahit rose to power in the aftermath of the Mongol invasion.

After the reign of King Jayanegara, his stepmother Gayatri Rajapatni, who had become a Buddhist nun, appointed her daughter Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi queen. In 1336 the queen made Gajah Mada her prime minister, and at his inauguration he swore the Palapa oath, vowing to take no rest until he had united the archipelago under Majapahit. Under Tribhuwana and her son Hayam Wuruk, in the mid-14th century, conquests extended Majapahit's authority through Southeast Asia. The Nagarakretagama, written in 1365, describes an empire of 98 tributaries stretching from Sumatra to New Guinea, although historians still debate how far its influence reached and the nature of its relations with its overseas vassals.

After Hayam Wuruk died in 1389, a dispute over the succession began. His nephew and son-in-law Prince Vikramavardhana succeeded him, but Bhre Wirabhumi, a son by a concubine, also claimed the throne, and this led to the Regreg Civil War of 1405 to 1406. The war weakened control over the vassal states and the empire slowly declined, until it collapsed in 1527 when the Sultanate of Demak invaded. Its fall saw the rise of Islamic kingdoms in Java.

The capital Trowulan was known for its annual festivities. On the first day of the month of Caitra, in March or April, representatives of all the territories that paid tax or tribute came to court. The realm was divided into the palace and its vicinity, the parts of east Java and Bali administered directly by royal officials, and outer dependencies with considerable internal autonomy. Buddhism, Shaivism and Vaishnavism were all practised, and the king was regarded as the incarnation of the three; there were certainly Muslim courtiers by this period.

Poets wrote kakawin in Old Javanese, among them Prapanca's Nagarakretagama and Tantular's Sutasoma. The ruins of the capital lie around Trowulan, which Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles described in the 19th century, and aerial and satellite images have shown a wide network of canals. Chinese accounts, such as the 1451 work of Zheng He's translator Ma Huan, also describe Majapahit.
majdanek-concentration-camp: The camp stood on the outskirts of Lublin, next to the Lublin Ghetto of Majdan Tatarski, from which local residents gave it the nickname Majdanek, "little Majdan", in 1941. Nazi documents first described it as a prisoner-of-war camp of the Waffen-SS. On 9 April 1943 the Reich Security Main Office renamed it Konzentrationslager Lublin, but the Polish name remained the more common one. It covered about 2.7 square kilometres, with some 227 structures, three gas chambers and two wooden gallows.

Heinrich Himmler ordered the camp after a visit to Lublin on 17 to 20 July 1941. It was planned for 25,000 prisoners of war, a figure raised several times as Soviet prisoners were taken, to 250,000 by March 1942. Building began on 1 October 1941 with 150 Jewish forced labourers, later joined by 2,000 Red Army prisoners who slept in the open. By mid-November only 500 of them were alive, and a typhus epidemic had killed all the slave labourers by January 1942.

Around March 1942 the camp was refurbished as a killing centre within Operation Reinhard, the plan to murder the Jews of the occupied Polish territory. Prisoners were killed with Zyklon B and by shooting squads of Trawniki men. Until June 1942 the dead were buried in mass graves; afterwards they were burned, and the graves were later opened by prisoners of Sonderkommando 1005. On 3 November 1943, the first day of Aktion Erntefest, 18,400 Jews were shot at the main camp. Estimates of the total dead have ranged from 360,000, given in 1948, to the figure of 78,000 reached in research published in 2005.

The Red Army reached the camp on 24 July 1944. The Germans had evacuated it in haste and partly destroyed the crematoria, but most of it stood. The Soviet NKVD then held soldiers of the Polish Home Army there. A museum was founded on the grounds in autumn 1944, the site became a monument of martyrdom by a decree of the Polish Parliament in 1947, and in 1965 it became a national museum.

A mound holding some 1,300 cubic metres of soil mixed with ashes and bone fragments was raised in 1947. A large monument designed by Wiktor Tołkin was built in July 1969, with a gate at the entrance and a mausoleum for the ashes. The camp now occupies about half its original area and lies within the boundaries of Lublin, with houses overlooking it. The Majdanek State Museum also runs branches at Sobibór and Bełżec.
majeerteen: The Majeerteen, also known as Mohammed Harti, belong to the Harti branch of the Darod. They traditionally inhabit the Bari, Nugaal and Mudug regions, from Bosaso to Garacad, between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and are most numerous in the regional capitals of Bosaso, Garowe and Galkacyo. Migrations that began in the 19th century took some to Kismayo in the south, and some live in the Dollo Zone of the Somali Region of Ethiopia. Historically the clan formed part of a coastal trading network around the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.

The first recorded mention of the clan in English is by Henry Salt, who described them as living on the coast of Hafun under a Sultan Hassan. Salt relates that the Imam of Muscat had sent gifts and asked leave to build a small fort there, and that both the request and the gifts were refused. In the 19th century Majeerteen merchants were active across the Red Sea. One of them, Ahmed Muhammad, was granted the island of Baka by the Damoheita Afar, and his family ruled it as sultans into the period of Italian rule in Eritrea.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the 15th or 16th century and rose to prominence in the 19th under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. It was nearly destroyed by his struggle with his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid, who was forced into exile in Yemen, returned with a band of Hadhrami musketeers, overpowered the local Hawiye clans and founded the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

Kenadid signed a protectorate treaty with Italy, and Boqor Osman followed in late 1889. Each hoped to use Italian support against the other and to avoid direct occupation. When Kenadid refused to let British troops land in his territory to fight the Dervish forces of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, the Italians exiled him to Aden and then to Eritrea. After two years of resistance by Boqor Osman and Majeerteen rebels, which Italian forces put down with long coastal bombardments of towns and naval blockades, the territory came under the full authority of Rome by late 1927.

Osman Yusuf Kenadid, a son of the first sultan of Hobyo, devised the Osmanya script for the Somali language in the 1920s. Members of the clan held many government posts in the 1960s and 1970s, among them Abdirashid Shermarke, the first prime minister and second president of Somalia. In the 1980s and 1990s the Somali Salvation Democratic Front was a predominantly Majeerteen political group.
makarios-iii: Makarios III was born Michael Christodoulou Mouskos on 13 August 1913 in Panayia village in the Paphos District of Cyprus, then a British protectorate. At thirteen he entered Kykkos Monastery as a novice. He finished secondary school at the Pancyprian Gymnasium in Nicosia in 1936 and studied theology and law at the University of Athens, graduating in 1942. A World Council of Churches scholarship took him to Boston University. In 1948, still a student there, he was elected Bishop of Kition against his will and took the name Makarios, meaning happy or blessed. Like many Greek Cypriot public figures he supported enosis, union with Greece.

Elected Archbishop on 18 September 1950, aged 37, Makarios became both head of the Church and Ethnarch, the de facto national leader of Cypriots. He argued for enosis and encouraged Greece to take the question to the United Nations in 1954. His relation to the insurgent organisation EOKA, led by George Grivas, is unclear and disputed, and he later denied any involvement in its violence. In March 1956 British Special Branch officers seized him at Nicosia airport and exiled him to the Seychelles. Released after a year but barred from Cyprus, he worked from Athens. Greece gradually dropped enosis for independence, and after the Zurich Agreement of 1958 he agreed, at first reluctantly, to the terms for independence.

He returned to Cyprus on 1 March 1959 and won the presidential election on 13 December 1959 with two-thirds of the vote against Ioannis Clerides. Taking office on 16 August 1960 with Fazıl Küçük as vice-president, he followed non-alignment and attended the first Non-Aligned Movement summit at Belgrade in 1961. In November 1963 he proposed thirteen constitutional amendments to ease the ethnic restrictions on public office. Many Turkish Cypriots saw a threat to their protections, most in public office resigned, and intercommunal violence broke out again by the end of 1963. UN peacekeepers arrived in 1964. In the 1968 election he won about 96 per cent of the votes.

During the early 1970s the Greek junta backed Grivas and his EOKA B, and in July 1974 Makarios demanded that Greek officers leave the island. On 15 July Dimitrios Ioannidis organised a coup in Nicosia; Makarios escaped to Paphos and was taken off by a British helicopter, and Nikos Sampson was installed as president. Turkey invaded on 20 July and captured roughly 36 per cent of the island, where the unrecognised state of Northern Cyprus was later established. Makarios returned in December 1974. He died of a heart attack on 3 August 1977 and is buried on Mount Throni, near Kykkos Monastery. An estimated 250,000 people filed past his coffin.
makhachkala: Makhachkala stands on the Caspian Sea and has been a major Russian seaport and a transport hub. Its historic predecessors were the towns of Tarki and Anji, or Anji-kala, which according to some sources date back to Khazar times; some chronicles suggest Anji-kala was the name of a citadel of the Khazar capital Semender. Anji was a port town in Kumykia and part of the possessions of the Tarki state, known as the Kumyk capital from the 8th century. Among the Kumyks the place was still called Anzhi-Qala, the Pearl Fortress, after the Russian town was founded.

Dagestan was long contested. Muslim armies arrived under the Umayyad Caliph Hisham, the Khazars captured Derbent in 796, and the region later fell under Seljuk, Mongol, Timurid, Safavid and, between 1578 and 1606, Ottoman influence. From the 17th century Iranians, Russians and Ottomans struggled for it. In the 1840s, after the Russian Empire seized the Kumyk plateau, the fort of Petrovskoye was founded at Anji-kala, named for Tsar Peter the Great, who had waged war in the region in 1722. The fortress received town status in 1857 and was renamed Petrovsk-Port. A railway linked it to Vladikavkaz and Baku in 1894.

During the Russian Civil War two British Royal Air Force squadrons were based at Petrovsk in 1919 and bombed Bolshevik forces. The Red Army took the city in March 1920. On 14 May 1921 it was renamed Makhachkala, after the Dagestani revolutionary Magomed-Ali Makhach Dakhadaev, and became the capital of the new Dagestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. An earthquake on 14 May 1970 did major damage.

Makhachkala is the capital of the Republic of Dagestan and has 623,254 residents. It is ethnically very diverse: the Avar, Kumyk, Dargin, Lezgin and Lak nations each make up a substantial part of the population, with Russians a minority. Oil refining, mechanical engineering and textiles are the main industries, and the city is a centre of education, research and the regional press. Its commercial port handles oil, grain, timber and other cargo, and it is linked by rail to the North Caucasus network.
mala-strana: Malá Strana means the Little Side, and the district is also called the Lesser Town, the Lesser Quarter or the Lesser Side. It lies on the left bank of the Vltava on the slopes just below Prague Castle, and is joined by the Charles Bridge to the larger districts of the right bank. In the Middle Ages it was a dominant centre of Prague's ethnic German citizens, and from the 16th century also of Italian ones. It housed many noble palaces, while the towns of the right bank were more bourgeois and more Czech.

King Ottokar II of Bohemia founded Malá Strana in 1257 as a royal town with many privileges, joining several settlements beneath the castle into one administrative unit. Its original residents were expelled and mostly German craftsmen and merchants were invited in. It was first called the New Town beneath Prague Castle, but after Charles IV founded the New Town of Prague in 1348 it was renamed the Lesser Town of Prague, and the unofficial name Little Quarter came into use in the 17th century. In the second half of the 14th century Charles IV extended it and built a new defensive wall, the Hunger Wall.

The Hussites burned the Lesser Town down in 1419 and 1420. In 1541 a fire that killed fifty people again damaged it severely, and it was rebuilt in the Renaissance style with many noble palaces. Baroque architecture, brought in after that fire, came to dominate. The market place, now Lesser Town Square, was the centre of the town, divided into an upper and a lower part by the Church of St Nicholas.

The largest Baroque building in the district is the Wallenstein Palace, built for Albrecht von Wallenstein, general-in-chief of Emperor Ferdinand II, with five courtyards and a garden laid out as a French park. St Nicholas, the finest church, is a masterpiece of Christoph Dientzenhofer and his son Kilian Ignaz. The Church of Our Lady Victorious holds the statue of the Holy Infant Jesus of Prague, which has drawn Catholic pilgrims for years. In 1989 thousands of East German refugees gathered at the West German embassy in the Lobkowicz Palace. The novelist Jan Neruda was born and lived in the district and wrote about it, and Nerudova Street is named after him.
malacca: Malacca faces the Strait of Malacca on the south-western coast of the Malay Peninsula, in a low, flat landscape in which 98 percent of the land lies below 150 metres. The Malacca River drains most of its catchment. Its position at a narrow point of the strait gave it a port accessible in all seasons, and it lay on the maritime routes between China, India, the Middle East, Africa and Europe.

Before a sultan arrived, the area was a fishing village. Malay tradition says Parameswara, also called Iskandar Shah, founded the settlement after fleeing a Majapahit invasion of Singapura, and that the name comes from a Malacca tree under which he sheltered when a mouse deer pushed a hunting dog into a river. With the Orang Laut, the "sea people", he required passing ships to call and built warehouses and trading facilities. In 1403 the first official Chinese envoy, Admiral Yin Qing, arrived, and in 1405 Zheng He brought a stone tablet and an imperial order raising the port to the status of a country. Ming protection shielded it from Siam and Majapahit, and China made it a base for its voyages into the Indian Ocean.

On 24 August 1511 the Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque, who had sailed from Goa with about 1,200 men, conquered the city. Trade then spread among rival ports such as Aceh and Johor, and the Jesuit Francis Xavier visited in 1545, 1546 and 1549. The Dutch East India Company, allied with the Johor Sultanate, captured Malacca on 14 January 1641 after a long siege and held it until the late 18th century. It passed to the British under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 in exchange for Bencoolen, joined the Straits Settlements with Singapore and Penang, and was occupied by Japan from 1942 to 1945.

Malacca is a state of Malaysia, which it joined on 16 September 1963, after Malayan independence on 31 August 1957. Its capital, Malacca City, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with George Town in 2008. The state has about one million people, among them Malays, Chinese, Indians, Peranakan Chinese, Kristang, Chitty and Temuan. Surviving buildings from the Dutch period include the Stadthuys.
malang: Malang, historically known as Tumapel, lies in the south of Java at about 506 metres above sea level, which gives it a mild climate. In the Pleistocene the area was a deep basin ringed by volcanoes, uninhabited because of the lava flows, which filled in the rainy season to form an ancient swamp and lakes. The origin of the name is uncertain. One theory derives it from Malangkuçeçwara, a temple of tradition whose name is read as God has destroyed the false and enforced the right. The name Malang first appears in the Pamotoh or Ukirnegara Inscription of 1198, found in 1975.

The Dinoyo inscription of 760 is the main early document for the area. It was long taken as showing that the Hindu kingdom of King Gajayana, called Kanjuruhan, began government in Malang in the 8th century, and it gives the date as 28 November 760. A newer inscription found in 1986 has not yet been deciphered. The city was later the capital of Singhasari, in 1222.

Under the Dutch, Malang was modernised, and its climate and nearness to the port of Surabaya made it popular with Europeans. The railway reached it in 1879, which encouraged industry, and on 1 April 1914 it became a gemeente, a municipality. The Imperial Japanese Army occupied it on 7 March 1942, and the Dutch troop headquarters on Jalan Semeru became a Japanese security building. Malang joined the Republic of Indonesia on 21 September 1945, and re-entered it on 2 March 1947 after Dutch reoccupation.

Malang is a landlocked city and the second most populous in East Java, with about 3.1 million people in the Malang Valley. Most residents are Javanese, with Madurese and Chinese minorities. Dutch Gothic buildings such as the Kayutangan church and Ijen Cathedral survive, and the Tugu Malang monument stands in the round Alun-alun. Brawijaya University and Malang State University make it known as an educational city, and the Malang Tempo Doeloe Festival preserves its cultural heritage.
malatya: Malatya lies in Eastern Anatolia, and its name is thought to come from the Hittite word melid or milit, "honey". Over time it has been called Malidiya in Hittite, Meliddu in Akkadian, Meliṭeia in Urartian and Melitene in Roman times. The ruins of ancient Melitene lie around Arslantepe in the Battalgazi district. The historical city stayed at Battalgazi, once called Old Malatya, until the 19th century, when it gradually moved to its present site.

Arslantepe has been inhabited for nearly 6,000 years, since the development of agriculture. In the Bronze Age it became the administrative centre of a larger region in the kingdom of Isuwa, and it was heavily fortified. The Hittites conquered it in the 14th century BCE. After the end of the Hittite Empire it became the centre of the Neo-Hittite state of Kammanu, which kept Hittite traditions and styles; archaeologists found a palace within the walls with monumental stone lions and a statue of the ruler. Kammanu was a vassal of Urartu between 804 and 743 BCE. The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I made the kingdom of Malidiya pay tribute, and Sargon II sacked the city in 712 BCE.

Under Roman rule the settlement was refounded in 72 CE on a different site as Melitene, the base of the Legio XII Fulminata, which controlled access to southern Armenia and the upper Tigris. Trajan probably gave it city status in the early second century.

In 392 Theodosius I made it the capital of Second Armenia, and the emperors Anastasius and Justinian built its walls in the sixth century. The Sassanids sacked it in 575. It was captured by Arab forces, and in the ninth century the emir Umar al-Aqta made it a major opponent of the Byzantine Empire until he was killed at the Battle of Lalakaon in 863. John Kourkouas took it for the Byzantines in May 934. Its merchants grew very wealthy, but the Seljuks attacked and devastated the city in 1058, and many people were killed or sold into slavery. The Danishmends took it in 1101.

Malatya is the capital of Malatya Province in Eastern Anatolia and a regional centre of industry, education and agriculture. It is one of the most prominent apricot-growing areas in the world and is nicknamed the Land of Apricots. The French archaeologist Louis Delaporte began excavating Arslantepe in the 1930s, and an Italian team has worked at the site since 1961.
malawi: Malawi is a landlocked country in Southeast Africa, bordered by Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique. The Great Rift Valley runs through it from north to south, and Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, makes up over three-quarters of its eastern boundary. The lake is about 587 kilometres long and 84 kilometres wide, and the Shire River flows from its southern end to join the Zambezi in Mozambique. South of the lake lie the Shire Highlands, where the Zomba and Mulanje peaks rise. The altitude moderates what would otherwise be an equatorial climate, with rains between November and April.

The name Malawi means 'flames' in Chichewa and Chitumbuka and was chosen by the first president, Hastings Banda, after independence in 1964. It comes from the Maravi, a Bantu ethnic group that emigrated from the southern Congo around 1400.

Before the arrival of Bantu peoples from the north around the 10th century CE, the area had a small population of hunter-gatherers, known in oral tradition as Akafula or BaTwa, who were gradually overtaken by agrarian Bantu peoples. By the 16th century the Bantu groups had established kingdoms such as the Maravi Empire, which reached from north of Nkhotakota to the Zambezi River, and the Nkhamanga. In the 17th century, with the area mostly united under one ruler, people began trading and making alliances with Portuguese traders and soldiers. By the 18th century the empire had broken up.

The Indian Ocean slave trade reached its height in the mid-19th century, when about 20,000 people a year are believed to have been enslaved and taken from Nkhotakota to Kilwa. David Livingstone reached Lake Malawi in 1859 and identified the Shire Highlands as suitable for European settlement.

Anglican and Presbyterian missions followed Livingstone's visit in the 1860s and 1870s, the African Lakes Company was established in 1878, and a British consul took up residence at Blantyre in 1883. To prevent Portuguese occupation, the British government sent Harry Johnston as consul to make treaties with local rulers. In 1891 the area became the British Central African Protectorate, renamed Nyasaland in 1907. Nyasaland became independent under Hastings Banda in 1964.

Malawi is the Republic of Malawi, with its capital and largest city at Lilongwe and its commercial centre at Blantyre. English is the official language, and Chichewa, Chitumbuka and Chiyao are major regional languages. Lake Malawi National Park, listed in 1984, and the Chongoni Rock Art Area, listed in 2006, are its two UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
malay-language: Historical linguists agree that the Malayic homeland was probably in western Borneo. A form called Proto-Malayic was spoken there by at least 1000 BCE and is argued to be the ancestor of all later Malayic languages. Its own ancestor, Proto-Malayo-Polynesian, began to break up by at least 2000 BCE, possibly through the southward expansion of Austronesian peoples from Taiwan.

Old Malay, believed to be the ancestor of Classical Malay, was influenced by Sanskrit. The earliest known stone inscription in Old Malay, the Kedukan Bukit inscription, was found on Sumatra near Palembang and is dated 1 May 683, written in the Pallava variety of the Grantha alphabet. Srivijaya, a maritime empire based on Sumatra from the 7th to the 11th centuries, spread Old Malay through the Malay Peninsula and Archipelago, where it served as the lingua franca of traders in ports and marketplaces.

The Terengganu Inscription Stone, dated approximately to 1303 CE and written in Jawi script, is considered the earliest evidence of Classical Malay. Its ruler urges his subjects to uphold Islam and sets out ten basic laws. Classical Malay came into wide use as a lingua franca under the Malacca Sultanate (1402 to 1511), a hub of trade and Islamic learning. Islamic literature brought a large infusion of Arabic vocabulary, alongside continued influence from Sanskrit and Tamil.

After the Portuguese captured Malacca in 1511 the court re-established itself as the Johor Sultanate and kept Classical Malay as its literary and administrative language, while literary centres dispersed to Aceh, Java, Makassar, the Moluccas and Champa. In the 19th century the Dutch and British, divided by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, both used Malay as a tool of centralisation and modernisation.

Before Arabic script arrived, Malay was written in the Pallava, Kawi and Rencong scripts. From the era of the Kingdom of Pasai and the golden age of Malacca, Jawi gradually replaced them. From the 17th century, under Dutch and British influence, the Latin script Rumi gradually replaced Jawi.

Malay is an Austronesian pluricentric macrolanguage, native to several islands of Maritime Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. It is an official language of Brunei, Malaysia and Singapore, where its standard form is Standard Malay, and Indonesian, an autonomous standard, is the official language of Indonesia. It is spoken as a first language by about 80 million people and as a first or second language by close to 300 million. Latin script is official in Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and Jawi is co-official with it in Brunei and Malaysia.
malay-peninsula: The peninsula runs approximately north to south, and at its end, Tanjung Piai, lies the southernmost point of the Asian continental mainland. It contains Peninsular Malaysia, Southern Thailand and the southernmost tip of Myanmar, at Kawthaung. Singapore, an island country, has historical and cultural ties with the region. The Titiwangsa Mountains, part of the Tenasserim Hills system, form the backbone of the peninsula. The Kra Isthmus is its narrowest point, the Strait of Malacca separates it from the Indonesian island of Sumatra, and the Straits of Johor separate its south coast from Singapore.

Ancient and medieval sources name the peninsula in various ways. Some scholars think that Malayadvipa, mentioned in the ancient Indian text the Vayu Purana, may refer to it. An inscription on the south wall of the Brihadeeswarar Temple records Malaiur, a kingdom with a strong mountain for its rampart. Ptolemy's Geographia names a region of the Golden Chersonese as Maleu-kolon, and the Tabula Rogeriana of Muhammad al-Idrisi shows a long island called Malai. Chinese chronicles of the Yuan dynasty mention Ma-li-yu-er, a nation threatened by the southward expansion of the Sukhothai Kingdom under King Ram Khamhaeng, and Marco Polo refers to Malauir.

The Malay term Tanah Melayu, meaning the Malay land, appears in texts from the early 17th century, notably the Hikayat Hang Tuah, where it refers to the area under the dominion of the Malacca Sultanate. The Negarakertagama, written in 1365, calls the area Hujung Medini. The Portuguese apothecary Tomé Pires, who stayed in Malacca from 1512 to 1515, used the form Terra de Tana Malaio for south-eastern Sumatra, where the deposed sultan Mahmud Shah established his exiled government.

In the early 20th century, during the rise of Malay nationalism, Tanah Melayu was used for the idea of uniting all the Malay states of the peninsula under one nation. The ambition was largely realised in 1948 with the formation of the Federation of Malaya.

The peninsula is covered with tropical moist broadleaf forests, with dipterocarp trees in the lowlands and evergreen trees on the mountains. Its fauna includes the Asian elephant, tiger, sun bear and Malayan tapir. The Kangar-Pattani floristic boundary crosses it in southern Thailand and the far north of Malaysia, marking the boundary between the biogeographic region of Indochina to the north and Sundaland and Malesia to the south. Extensive mangroves line both coasts.
malayalam-language: The origin of Malayalam is disputed. The mainstream view holds that it descends from a western coastal dialect of early Middle Tamil, which began to separate in the 8th century and became distinct between the 9th and 13th centuries. The Western Ghats isolate the Malabar Coast, and Sanskrit and Prakrit influence from the Nambudiri Brahmins helped the dialect to diverge. A second view, generally rejected by historical linguists, holds that Tamil and Malayalam developed separately from a common ancestor. Some scholars treat the Quilon Syrian copper plates of 849 or 850 CE as the oldest inscription in Old Malayalam, though others regard the language of such inscriptions as a variety of Tamil. The Malayalam calendar dates from 825 CE.

Malayalam is the majority language of Kerala and an official language in Kerala, Lakshadweep and Mahé in Puducherry. At the census of 2011 there were 32,413,213 speakers in Kerala. Its word order is subject-object-verb, and verbs are conjugated for tense, mood and aspect but not for person, gender or number. It has borrowed most from Sanskrit and later English, and also from Arabic, Dutch, Persian, Portuguese and Syriac. Besides its own script it has been written in others: Suriyani Malayalam, in a Syriac script, was used by the Saint Thomas Christians until the 20th century, and Arabi Malayalam, in an Arabic script, until the early 20th century.

Folk songs, the oldest literary form, were oral. The Ramacharitam, of the late 12th or early 13th century, is the oldest extant work distinct from the Tamil tradition. Middle Malayalam was shaped by Manipravalam, a blend of Tamil and Sanskrit whose name means ruby-coral. Cherusseri Namboothiri's Krishnagatha, written for the court of Udaya Varman Kolathiri in the 15th century, appears to be the first work in the present-day language. In the 16th century Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan wrote the Adhyathmaramayanam Kilippattu. The first travelogue in any Indian language is the Malayalam Varthamanappusthakam, by Paremmakkal Thoma Kathanar in 1785. Later writers include Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai, M. T. Vasudevan Nair, Vaikom Muhammed Basheer and Arundhati Roy.
malbork: Malbork lies on the Nogat river in the region of Powiśle, in the Pomeranian Voivodeship of northern Poland. The river and the flat terrain allowed barges to reach the town a hundred kilometres from the sea. The town grew around the fortress Ordensburg Marienburg, founded in 1274 on the east bank of the Nogat by the Teutonic Knights. Both castle and town were named for their patron saint, the Virgin Mary, and are called Marienburg in German and Malbork in Polish.

Under the Teutonic Order the town collected tolls on river traffic and the Order held a monopoly on the amber trade. The town later joined the Hanseatic League. After the Battle of Grunwald the Order was greatly weakened, and the Teutonic Knights burned the town in 1410 before the Polish and Lithuanian siege of the castle, which failed. In the Thirteen Years' War the Order pawned the castle to its soldiers from Bohemia, who sold it in 1457 to King Casimir IV of Poland. The town resisted for three more years under Mayor Bartholomäus Blume, who was hanged and quartered when it fell.

From 1457 to 1772 the castle was one of the royal residences of Poland, and from 1568 it housed the Polish Admiralty. In 1710, during the Great Northern War, half the population died of cholera. The First Partition of Poland brought the town to Prussia in 1772. Near the end of the Second World War the town was declared a fortress and almost completely destroyed in fighting between German forces and the Red Army, which lasted until 9 March 1945. In June 1945 it was handed to Polish authorities and renamed Malbork, and the remaining German population was expelled.

Malbork Castle was built over nearly 230 years and is in fact three castles combined in one. It is the world's largest brick castle and Europe's largest Gothic fortress. More than half of it was destroyed in the war, and restoration has been ongoing since. The castle and its museum are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Other sights include the Gothic church of St John the Baptist, the Gothic town hall and parts of the medieval town walls.
malbork-castle: The Teutonic Order had been founded in 1191 in Acre, and after that stronghold fell to the Muslims in 1291 it moved its headquarters to Venice before arriving in Prussia. The castle was built after the conquest of Old Prussia, and its main purpose was to strengthen the Order's control after it suppressed the Great Prussian Uprising of the Baltic tribes in 1274. Work lasted until around 1300 under Commander Heinrich von Wilnowe, and it was named Marienburg for Mary, patron saint of the Order. The castle stands on the south-eastern bank of the Nogat.

The castle grew in importance after the conquest of Gdańsk and Eastern Pomerania in 1308, when the Order's administrative centre moved there from Elbing. Grand Master Siegfried von Feuchtwangen, who came from Venice, undertook the next phase of building and in 1309 relocated his headquarters to Marienburg. The complex has three separate castles, the High, Middle and Lower, divided by dry moats and towers, on a site of nearly 21 hectares, and once housed about 3,000 brothers in arms. The Order collected river tolls, held a monopoly on the amber trade, and the town's membership in the Hanseatic League brought Hanseatic meetings there. Most historians accept the years from 1274 to 1406 as the construction period.

After the defeat at Grunwald in the summer of 1410, Heinrich von Plauen led the defence in a siege during which the town outside was razed. By 1456, in the Thirteen Years' War, the Order was in severe financial distress. Its Bohemian mercenaries, long unpaid, agreed to sell the castle, and in 1457 King Casimir IV Jagiellon entered it in triumph. For over 300 years the castle served as a Polish royal residence, home to the Polish Admiralty from 1568, a royal mint from 1584 and the Commonwealth's largest arsenal. Swedish forces occupied it in 1626 and 1629 and again from 1656 to 1660.

After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the castle became a Prussian barracks and poorhouse, and in 1794 the architect David Gilly surveyed it. His son Friedrich Gilly's engravings, published from 1799 to 1803, led the Prussian public to rediscover it, and after the Napoleonic Wars it became a symbol of Prussian history. Restoration began in 1816 under Theodor von Schön. In the early 1930s the Nazis used it as a pilgrimage destination, and fighting with the Red Army in early 1945 destroyed more than half of it. Restoration has been ongoing since 1962, and UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in December 1997.
malcolm-ii-of-scotland: Máel Coluim mac Cinaeda, anglicised Malcolm II, was a son of King Kenneth II and a grandson of Malcolm I. The Prophecy of Berchán says his mother was a woman of Leinster. Succession among Scottish kings of the time often involved murder, and Malcolm killed Kenneth III in 1005 in a battle at Monzievaird in Strathearn. The Irish annals call him ard rí Alban, high king of Scotland, though the geographical area of modern Scotland also held a king of Strathclyde in the south-west, Norse–Gaels kings on the western coast and the Hebrides, and the kings or mormaers of Moray, his nearest and most dangerous rivals.

The first reliable report of the reign is an attack in 1006 on the lands of the Northumbrian rulers of Bamburgh, perhaps the customary raid of a new king, which included a siege of Durham. According to the Annals of Ulster it ended in a heavy defeat by Uhtred of Bamburgh. A second war, probably in 1018, went better. At the Battle of Carham, by the River Tweed, the Scots under Malcolm and the men of Strathclyde under their king, Owain Foel, were victorious. A twelfth-century tract claims that Eadwulf Cudel, Uhtred's brother, then surrendered Lothian to Malcolm.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports that Cnut the Great led an army into Scotland on his return from a pilgrimage to Rome. It dates this to 1031, though there are reasons to place it in 1027. The Burgundian chronicler Rodulfus Glaber describes Malcolm as powerful in resources and arms and very Christian, and says the two made peace. Cnut came away with a promise of peace and friendship, and the Chronicle remarks that Malcolm kept to the submission only a little while.

Malcolm had no surviving sons. He arranged marriages for his daughters with the regional dynasties that might otherwise have rivalled him. Bethóc married Crínán of Dunkeld, and a daughter named Donada is said by later writers to have married Finlay of Moray, father of Macbeth.

Marianus Scotus gives the date of Malcolm's death as 25 November 1034, and the king lists place it at Glamis Castle. The Annals of Tigernach call him the honour of all the west of Europe, while later accounts say he was killed fighting bandits. His grandson Duncan I succeeded him as his chosen heir and reigned for five years and nine months. Tradition from the time of John of Fordun, if not earlier, called a Pictish stone at Glamis King Malcolm's grave stone.
malcolm-iii-of-scotland: Malcolm was the son of Duncan I, who became king in late 1034 and was killed in battle in Moray on 15 August 1040 by a force under Macbeth. Malcolm and his brother Donald were probably children. Later tradition says they were sent away for safety, Malcolm to England, but neither the place of exile nor the fact of it is certain; Orkney, Ireland and Strathclyde have also been suggested. Later tradition, attested by the fifteenth century, made his mother the daughter of the miller of Forteviot.

Chroniclers report that Malcolm killed Macbeth at Lumphanan in Aberdeenshire on 15 August 1057. Macbeth's stepson Lulach was crowned at Scone, probably on 8 September 1057, and was killed by Malcolm "by treachery" near Huntly on 23 April 1058.

Malcolm's kingdom did not cover all of modern Scotland: many islands and the land north of the River Oykel were Scandinavian, and south of the Firth of Forth lay independent or semi-independent realms. In 1061 the Scots plundered Lindisfarne. In 1068 Malcolm gave asylum to English exiles fleeing William of Normandy, among them Edgar Ætheling and his sisters Margaret and Cristina. By the end of 1070 he had married Margaret, later Saint Margaret. Their sons were given English royal names, including Edward and Edmund, and also Alexander and David, the later kings Alexander I and David I.

In 1072 William came north, and at Abernethy Malcolm became his man, as the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle puts it, and handed over his eldest son Duncan as a hostage. Raids into Northumbria followed. In 1080 William's son Robert Curthose marched north and Malcolm again made peace. In 1091 Malcolm besieged Newcastle, then withdrew before William Rufus's army and again acknowledged English overlordship. A tradition in the Orkneyinga saga gives him an earlier marriage to Ingibiorg, widow of Thorfinn Sigurdsson.

In August 1093 Malcolm travelled to Gloucester, but William Rufus refused to negotiate and insisted that English barons decide the dispute. Malcolm returned north and invaded Northumbria, a ravaging seen as harsh even by the standards of the time. On 13 November 1093 Robert de Mowbray's forces confronted him on his march north, and Robert's steward Morel of Bamburgh killed him. His son Edward was mortally wounded, and Margaret is said to have died soon after hearing the news.

His brother Donald III succeeded him. His body was buried at Tynemouth Priory and later moved north, probably to Dunfermline Abbey. In 1250, after Margaret was canonised, both were reburied beside the altar there. Malcolm secured the line that ruled Scotland until the late thirteenth century, and he is a major character in Shakespeare's Macbeth.
malcolm-x: Malcolm X was born on 19 May 1925 in Omaha, Nebraska, the fourth of seven children of Louise Little, born in Grenada, and the Reverend Earl Little, a Baptist minister. Both parents admired the Pan-African activist Marcus Garvey and led the local branch of his Universal Negro Improvement Association, and they taught their children self-reliance and black pride. In 1946 he was sentenced to eight to ten years in prison for larceny and burglary. There he met a fellow convict, John Bembry, who gave him a voracious appetite for reading, and joined the Nation of Islam, taking the name Malcolm X in place of what he called the white slavemaster name of Little.

After his parole in August 1952 Malcolm X rose quickly in the Nation. He took charge of Temple Number 7 in Harlem in 1954 and became its public face for twelve years, preaching black empowerment and the separation of Black and white Americans, and criticising Martin Luther King Jr. and the mainstream civil rights movement for its emphasis on non-violence and integration. The Federal Bureau of Investigation began watching him in 1953. He is credited with helping the Nation grow from about 1,200 members in the early 1950s to an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 by the early 1960s.

On 8 March 1964 he announced that he was leaving the Nation. He founded Muslim Mosque, Inc., a religious organisation, and the Organization of Afro-American Unity, a secular group advocating Pan-Africanism. In April 1964 he made the Hajj to Mecca, and he then toured Africa.

Throughout 1964 Malcolm X received death threats as his conflict with the Nation intensified. On 21 February 1965 he was shot as he prepared to address the Organization of Afro-American Unity at the Audubon Ballroom in Manhattan. Three Nation of Islam members were convicted, and in 2021 two of the convictions were vacated. Whether others conceived or aided the killing has been debated since.

Apart from his autobiography, written with Alex Haley and published posthumously in 1965, Malcolm X left no published writings, and his philosophy is known from his speeches and interviews. His ideas were an important influence on the Black power movement.
malebo-pool: Malebo Pool is a broad, lake-like widening of the lower Congo River, about 35 km long and 23 km wide, covering about 500 square kilometres. It is shallow, mostly 3 to 10 metres deep, and seasonal floods can change its level by up to 3 metres. M'Bamou Island, the largest of its islands, lies at its centre.

The pool is the boundary between the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with Brazzaville on its northern shore and Kinshasa on its southern one. Malebo is the plural of lilebo, the Lingala word for the Borassus palm. The pool was renamed Stanley Pool in 1887 after Henry Morton Stanley and took its present name in January 1972. Upstream the pool marks the start of the navigable Congo toward Kisangani, and downstream the river drops about 300 metres through the Livingstone Falls to the port of Matadi.

The older names include Ntamo, Nkuna and Mpumbu. Olfert Dapper described Pombo as a province under the Makoko, ruler of the Téké, and Jan Vansina reads the name as the northern shore of the pool, the political centre of the Téké kingdom. It is also understood to mean large market. From the sixteenth century the pool was a transshipment point on a trade axis along the Congo. The western zone, from the coast to the pool, relied on overland routes, while the eastern zone upriver produced pottery, salt, ivory, rubber and copal.

The Bobangi moved from the Ubangi to the pool between the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, drawn by its trade, and traded ivory and enslaved people for guns and textiles. Slave exports continued until about 1850 to 1860. In the 1870s they brought 5,000 to 6,000 elephant tusks to the pool, and the river-trade language Lingala spread from their commerce. In 1881 Stanley founded the post of Léopoldville and launched the steamboat L'En Avant. By 1894 forty-three steamers worked the basin, and in 1907 the port handled 16,205 tons of traffic and employed 1,462 workers, 112 of them Europeans.

The pool has a dry season of about three months, from June to August. Palm and papyrus swamps fringe its margins, and the water hyacinth Eichhornia crassipes, an invasive plant, forms dense mats that drift along the channel and displace native vegetation.
mali: Mali is a landlocked country of 1,240,192 square kilometres in West Africa, the eighth largest in Africa. Its northern borders reach deep into the Sahara Desert, and most of the country lies in the southern Sahara, while southern Mali, where the majority of inhabitants live, is in the Sudanian savanna. The Niger and Senegal rivers run through the south. Late April to early October is the rainy season there, and flooding of the Niger is common, creating the Inner Niger Delta. The Adrar des Ifoghas massif lies in the northeast, and gold, uranium, phosphates, salt and limestone are among its natural resources.

Rock art in the Sahara suggests that northern Mali has been inhabited since about 10,000 BCE, when the Sahara was fertile. Early ceramics from Ounjougou, dating to about 9,400 BCE, are believed to show an independent invention of pottery. Farming took place by 5000 BCE and iron was used by around 500 BCE. In the first millennium BCE Mandé peoples related to the Soninke created early towns along the middle Niger, among them Dia, from around 900 BCE, and Djenné-Djenno, which lasted from around 300 BCE to 900 CE.

Mali was part of three successive West African empires that controlled this trade: the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire. At its peak in 1300 the Mali Empire was the wealthiest country in Africa, and Mansa Musa is believed to have been one of the wealthiest individuals in history. Medieval Mali was a centre of Islam, culture and knowledge, and Timbuktu became a notable place of education.

The Songhai Empire absorbed the Mali Empire in 1468, and a Saadian army defeated the Songhai in 1591. In the late 19th century France seized control during the Scramble for Africa and made it part of French Sudan. It became independent in 1960, first in a brief federation with Senegal, and then as the Republic of Mali.

Bamako is the capital and largest city. The name Mali comes from the Mali Empire and originally meant hippopotamus, the clan symbol of the Keita dynasty. Most people live in the south, and the Bambara are the largest ethnic group, with the Fulani, Senufo, Malinke, Soninke, Dogon, Songhai and Tuareg among others. Malian musical tradition derives from the griots, the Keepers of Memories, and literary tradition is passed mainly by word of mouth, with jalis reciting histories and stories known by heart.
mali-empire: The empire began as a small Mandinka kingdom at the upper reaches of the Niger River, in the Manding region, which developed in the eleventh and twelfth centuries as the Ghana Empire declined. From at least the beginning of the eleventh century Mandinka kings ruled from the city-state of Ka-ba, today Kangaba, in the name of Ghana. When Ghana's control ended in the twelfth century, the province split into twelve kingdoms.

Sundiata Keita, a warrior-prince of the Keita dynasty, led the combined armies of Mema, Wagadou and the Mandinka city-states against the Sosso king Soumaoro Kanté. They defeated the Sosso army at the Battle of Kirina in about 1235, and Sundiata was declared mansa over the twelve kingdoms. The Kouroukan Fouga, an assembly of clan delegates, set out the empire's constitution. History before the thirteenth century is unclear, since Arab chroniclers and oral traditionalists give conflicting accounts.

After Sundiata's death in about 1255, rulers took the title mansa. In 1285 Sakura, a former slave of the imperial family who had become a general, carried out a coup, and the Keita line returned after his death. Mansa Musa took the throne in about 1312 and made his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324-1326, where his gifts and spending of gold caused significant inflation in Egypt. Ibn Battuta visited the empire in 1352, in the reign of Suleyman, who had deposed his nephew Maghan I in 1341. Suleyman's death ended the Golden Age and began a slow decline.

In 1433-1434 Mali lost Timbuktu to the Tuareg, and the Songhai Empire took Mema in 1465 and Timbuktu in 1468. The Mossi conquered Macina in 1477. Mali was still a sizeable state in the fifteenth century and in the early sixteenth, when Leo Africanus described it, but neighbours cut away at its borders from 1507. In 1599 Mansa Mahmud IV tried to take Djenne after the Moroccan conquest of Songhai and was defeated by Moroccan forces with firearms. He died around 1610, after which no single Keita ruled Manden, and the Keitas became provincial chiefs at Kangaba.

The empire was a loose structure of provinces and vassal states, and the farther from the capital, the weaker the mansa's direct power. Its wealth came from taxing the gold, copper and salt that entered its borders, rather than from direct rule of the gold-producing regions. Most people were farmers. Historians disagree about the site of the capital, placing it at Niani in Guinea, elsewhere on the Niger or even on the upper Gambia. Its spread of language, laws and customs, notably through Dyula traders, left political institutions with Malian structures and terms in West Africa into the colonial period and beyond.
mali-federation: After the May 1958 crisis the colonies of French West Africa were offered a choice between immediate independence and membership of a reorganised French Community, and only Guinea chose independence. In late November 1958 French Sudan, Senegal, Upper Volta and Dahomey declared their intention to form a federation. A congress at Bamako from 28 to 30 December, with Modibo Keïta as its president, produced the name Mali Federation, largely through Léopold Sédar Senghor. Pressure from France and the Ivory Coast kept Upper Volta and Dahomey from ratifying the constitution, so only French Sudan and Senegal remained.

The federation was to rest on parity: a federal assembly of 20 members from each colony, six ministers, three from each, and a single party. Until a president was elected, Keïta was premier and Mamadou Dia of Senegal vice-premier in charge of the armed forces. France, which had resisted the federation, supported it once both countries agreed to remain in the French Community and keep French military bases.

Tensions grew over the powers of a federal executive: French Sudan wanted a single strong executive, Senegal wanted to keep parity. Senghor and Keïta also had different visions, Keïta claiming later that he pursued socialism and Senghor a bourgeois agenda. The crisis came in August 1960, as a federal president was to be elected. On 19 August Keïta dismissed Dia as defence minister, declared a state of emergency and mobilised the army. Senghor and Dia had the army demobilised and called out the gendarmerie, which surrounded Keïta's house and the government offices. Senegal declared its independence from the federation at a midnight session on 20 August. Little violence occurred, and the Sudanese officials were sent back to Bamako on a sealed train.

On 22 September 1960 Keïta's party renamed the Sudanese Republic Mali and broke its ties with the French Community. Both countries were admitted to the United Nations later that month. Senghor was president of Senegal from 1960 to 1980 and Keïta of Mali from 1960 to 1968. Keïta refused diplomatic relations with Senegal for many years, and Senghor became wary of unification efforts. The railway between the two countries reopened on 22 June 1963, when the two leaders embraced at the border.
malik-shah-i: Malik-Shah was born on 16 August 1055 and spent his youth in Isfahan. In 1064 he joined his father Alp Arslan's campaign in the Caucasus with the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, and in 1066 he was named heir at a ceremony near Merv and given Isfahan as a fief. In 1072 Alp Arslan was fatally wounded on a campaign in Transoxiana against the Karakhanids, and Malik-Shah was declared sultan.

His uncle Qavurt claimed the throne as the elder brother. Malik-Shah replied that a brother does not inherit when there is a son. In 1073 they fought the three-day Battle of Kerj Abu Dulaf near Hamadan, where Malik-Shah's army of ghulams and Kurdish and Arab contingents defeated Qavurt's Turkmens, although the Turks in his own army mutinied. Qavurt was captured and later strangled with a bowstring.

Nizam al-Mulk held near absolute power under the nominal sultan. Malik-Shah repelled the Karakhanids in 1073, and campaigns in 1087 and 1089 took Bukhara and Samarkand and brought Transoxiana up to the borders of China under Seljuk rule. In the Caucasus, George II of Georgia submitted as a vassal in Isfahan in 1088 after campaigns in 1075 and 1078 and 1079. In 1086 the army took Aleppo, Antioch, Edessa and Harran in northern Syria. In 1092 Seljuk armies took Yemen and Aden.

Revolts in the family marked the reign. His brother Tekish rebelled in Khorasan in 1081 and again in 1086, when he was captured and blinded, and another brother, Toghan-Shah, rebelled at Herat and was imprisoned. Isfahan became the chief residence, and he built mosques there and the Isfahan Observatory, whose work led to the Jalali Calendar. Omar Khayyam's poetry belongs to his reign.

In 1092 Nizam al-Mulk was assassinated near Sihna by a man disguised as a Sufi. One theory blames the Assassins; another suggests Malik-Shah had tired of his overmighty vizier. Malik-Shah then went to Baghdad and sought to depose the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadi.

He died on 19 November 1092 while hunting, probably poisoned, by the caliph or by supporters of Nizam al-Mulk according to one view. He was buried in a madrasa in Isfahan. The empire then fell into chaos as rival successors and governors divided it and fought one another. The success of the First Crusade is attributed at least in part to the political confusion that followed his death.
maliki-school: The Maliki school was founded in the 8th century by Malik ibn Anas, who lived from about 711 to 795 and was a native of Medina. Malik taught al-Shafi'i, who in turn taught Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he was himself a student of Ja'far al-Sadiq, as was Abu Hanifah. In the Muslim east the school faced competition from the Shafi'i, Hanbali and Zahiri schools, and it was the Hanafi school that earned official favour from the Abbasids. The Malikis had more success in Africa, and for a time in Spain and Sicily.

Unlike the Ahl al-Hadith and the Ahl al-Ra'y, the Maliki school takes a position known as Ahl al-A'mal: it treats the Sunnah as sourced chiefly from the practice of the people of Medina and the living tradition of the community. Its sources are ranked: the Quran, mass-transmitted traditions of Muhammad, the customs of Medina, single-chain hadith, the consensus and opinions of the Companions, analogy, public benefit and finally common opinion.

The school rests on the Muwatta of Malik, which records the practice of Medina beside the hadith, and on the Mudawwana, compiled from the notes of Malik's student Ibn Qasim and the questions of Sahnun. It is closest to the Hanafi school, but it gives analogy less weight and uses public benefit and common opinion where the Quran and the mass-transmitted traditions give no guidance.

Under the Umayyads and their remnants in al-Andalus, the Maliki school was promoted as the official code of law, and its judges were expected in return to legitimise the rulers. The Almoravids continued this dominance, but they gave way to the predominantly Zahiri Almohads, under whom the Malikis lost official favour. After the loss of the Iberian Peninsula the school kept its hold across North and West Africa. Although it was at first hostile to some mystical practices, many Maliki scholars later learned from Sufi practice. Notable figures include Sahnun, Averroes, Ibn Khaldun and, in the 19th century, Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate.
mallorca: Mallorca takes its name from the Latin insula maior, the larger island, which became Maiorca in Medieval Latin in contrast with Menorca, the smaller one. Geologically it extends the fold mountains of the Betic Cordillera of Andalusia. It has two mountain ranges, the Serra de Tramuntana in the north-west and the Serres de Llevant in the east, and the highest peak, Puig Major, rises to about 1,445 metres.

Humans first colonised the Balearic Islands around 2500–2300 BCE, from the Iberian Peninsula or southern France, among people associated with the Bell Beaker culture. Their arrival caused the rapid extinction of the three land mammals native to Mallorca. The islanders built prehistoric settlements called talaiots and raised Bronze Age megaliths as part of their Talaiotic culture. The Phoenicians arrived around the eighth century BCE, and the island came under the control of Carthage; after the Second Punic War the Romans took over.

In 534 the Eastern Roman Empire recaptured the island from the Vandals. From 707 Muslim raiders from North Africa attacked repeatedly, and the islanders asked Charlemagne for help. In 902 Issam al-Khawlani conquered the Balearic Islands, which became part of the Emirate of Córdoba. Palma was reshaped and expanded as Medina Mayurqa, and the Muslims improved agriculture with irrigation.

James I of Aragon took the island in 1229. Barbary corsairs attacked the islands so often that the people built coastal watchtowers and fortified churches. In the Spanish Civil War the island, a Nationalist stronghold, was the target of a Republican landing on 16 August 1936; Nationalist air power, supplied largely by Fascist Italy, forced the Republicans to leave by 12 September.

Mallorca is the largest of Spain's Balearic Islands, with its capital at Palma, which is also the capital of the autonomous community. Catalan and Spanish are the two official languages. The Cultural Landscape of the Serra de Tramuntana was registered as a World Heritage Site in 2011. The Majorcan cartographic school, which flourished in the 13th to 15th centuries, developed the normal portolan chart.
malmedy: Malmedy is a city and municipality of Wallonia in the province of Liège. It lies on the Warche river, whose regular floods are said to have given the town its name, from the Latin phrase A malo mundarum, meaning "purifying from evil". The municipality has three districts: Malmedy, Bellevaux-Ligneuville and Bévercé, which includes the hamlets of Baugnez and Xhoffraix. A portion of the Spa-Francorchamps motor-racing circuit lies within it, although most of the circuit is in neighbouring Stavelot.

Saint Remacle, abbot of Solignac Abbey in France, founded the town in 648 with a Benedictine monastery. From then until 1794 its history is that of the Princely Abbey of Stavelot-Malmedy, a clerical microstate ruled by a prince-abbot. The two towns formed one principality for 1,146 years under seventy-seven successive prince-abbots, but a rivalry grew between them, because Remacle chose Stavelot as the main city. From the 16th century cloth, leather and gunpowder industries appeared, and in the 17th century the principality became the most important tannery centre in Europe. Papermaking was the main industry and brought the town considerable wealth.

France annexed the principality in 1795, and Malmedy became a lower prefecture in the département of the Ourthe. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna joined the Romance and Walloon town to Prussia. Its people kept the right to use French, even in the town council, until the German Empire was founded after the Franco-German War of 1870. Under Chancellor Bismarck a policy of Germanisation banned French lessons in schools and forbade priests to preach in French. Malmedy was annexed to Belgium after the First World War under the Treaty of Versailles, after a plebiscite in which pro-German voters had to register their names; it was formally annexed in 1920 and joined the province of Liège in 1925.

Between 1940 and 1945 Malmedy was again part of Germany. In the Battle of the Bulge in 1944 the area saw the Malmedy massacre, in which SS troops under Joachim Peiper killed 84 American prisoners of war. On 21 December 1944 German forces under Otto Skorzeny attacked the town, then held by American troops, and were repelled. On 23, 24 and 25 December United States aircraft bombed it repeatedly in friendly-fire incidents that killed about 200 civilians.

The town has about 12,000 inhabitants, roughly 95 per cent of them French speakers, with a German-speaking minority that has language facilities. Walloon, the historical language, is spoken mostly by older people but survives in the songs of the Cwarmê, the carnival held from Shrove Friday to Shrove Tuesday, in which the Haguète and the Long-Né are among the traditional costumes.
malta: Malta is an archipelago in the central Mediterranean, about 80 kilometres from southern Italy across the Malta Channel. Only Malta, Gozo and Comino have permanent residents, and Comino is practically uninhabited. The islands lie on a shallow shelf that was once part of a land bridge between Sicily and North Africa, and the archipelago sits on the African tectonic plate. The terrain is coarse and hilly, with many harbours along an indented coastline. The highest point, Ta' Dmejrek near Dingli, is 253 metres high, and Malta has no rivers or lakes.

The earliest reliable evidence of habitation dates to 6500 BCE, when Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, probably from Sicily, arrived. Neolithic farmers from Sicily are thought to have followed by around 5400 BCE. Around 3500 BCE the islanders built the Ġgantija temples on Gozo, among the oldest free-standing structures in the world, and other early temples include those at Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra. After 2500 BCE Malta was depopulated until a new people arrived who cremated their dead and built small dolmens as tombs; they probably differed from the temple builders.

Phoenician traders colonised the islands around 1000 BCE, with their seat of government at Mdina and their main port at Cospicua on the Grand Harbour, which they called Maleth. Carthage controlled the islands after the fall of Phoenicia. It is unsure whether Roman rule began after the first or second Punic War, but Rome held Malta after the second, when it was surrendered by Hamilcar, a son of Gisco, to the consul Titus Sempronius Longus. The Arabs, Normans and Aragonese ruled in the Middle Ages, and the Knights Hospitaller, French and British in the modern era.

Malta became a British crown colony in the early 19th century and served as headquarters of the British Mediterranean Fleet. It was besieged by the Axis powers in the Second World War. Independence came in 1964, and the current parliamentary republic was established in 1974. Malta joined the European Union in 2004 and the eurozone on 1 January 2008.

The two official languages are Maltese, a Semitic language with close ties to Arabic and Sicilian, and English. Catholicism is the state religion, though the constitution guarantees freedom of religion. The 2025 census counted 588,254 people.
maltese-language: Maltese is a Central Semitic language derived from late medieval Sicilian Arabic. The pioneering Maltese linguists Giovanni Pietro Francesco Agius de Soldanis and Mikiel Anton Vassalli both hypothesised that it came from the Punic language, a view that later scholars did not accept. The language is generally traced to the arrival, early in the 11th century, of settlers from neighbouring Sicily, where Siculo-Arabic was spoken.

The Norman conquest of 1091, followed by the expulsion of the Muslims, complete by 1249, permanently isolated the vernacular from its Arabic source and created the conditions for its evolution into a distinct language. In Sicily, Siculo-Arabic became extinct and was replaced by Sicilian, but in Malta the vernacular continued to develop alongside Italian. The first written reference to it is in a will of 1436, where it is called lingua maltensi, and the oldest known document in Maltese is the 15th-century poem Il-Kantilena by Pietru Caxaro.

Maltese is spoken by the Maltese people and is a national language of Malta. It is the only standardised Semitic language written exclusively in the Latin script. The core vocabulary, including the most common words and the function words, is Semitic, and the Arabic base makes up around one third of the vocabulary. About half of the vocabulary comes from standard Italian and Sicilian, and English words make up between 6 and 20 per cent. The rural dialects keep archaic features and use more Semitic roots and broken plurals than Standard Maltese. The modern spelling system was introduced in 1924.

Under the Knights Hospitaller both French and Italian were used for official documents, and in the British colonial period English was encouraged through education, with Italian as the next most important language. Hieronymus Megiser, who visited Malta in 1588 and 1589, included a list of Maltese words in two works, and Agius de Soldanis produced the first systematic lexicon and grammar and proposed a standard orthography. Late in the 18th century and through the 19th, Vassalli and others made a concerted effort to standardise the written language. Maltese was recognised as an official language, alongside English, in 1934. Its use declined under British administration relative to English, and after independence language reforms increased its use.
maluku-islands: The Maluku Islands cover about 850,000 km2, 90 per cent of it sea, and number an estimated 1027 islands. The two largest, Halmahera and Seram, are sparsely populated, while the most developed, Ambon and Ternate, are small. Most of the islands are forested and mountainous, and several, such as Ternate, are volcanoes rising from the sea; there have been over 70 serious eruptions in the last 500 years. All but the Aru group lie in Wallacea, between Weber's Line and Lydekker's Line, so their fauna is more Australasian than Asian.

Australo-Melanesians were the first people on the islands, at least 40,000 years ago, and Austronesian speakers arrived around 2000 BCE. Arab merchants began to arrive in the fourteenth century, bringing Islam, which took hold especially in the trading centres. The earliest recorded word identifiable with Maluku, Maloko, appears in the Old Javanese Nagarakertagama of 1365.

The Portuguese conquered Malacca in August 1511 and soon sent ships to the Spice Islands. Francisco Serrão, shipwrecked at Hitu on Ambon in 1512, allied himself with the ruler of Ternate and built a fortress there. From 1546 Portuguese missionary work under Francis Xavier created large Christian communities. The Dutch arrived in 1599, and in 1605 the Dutch East India Company, allied with the Sultan of Ternate, conquered Ambon and Tidore and expelled the Portuguese. It then monopolised the production and trade of spices by a ruthless policy, including the genocidal conquest of the nutmeg-producing Banda Islands in 1621, the elimination of the English on Ambon in 1623 and the subordination of Ternate and Tidore in the 1650s.

The Nuku Rebellion, led by a Tidore prince, spread across much of Maluku and Papua in 1780-1810. British forces held the islands in 1796-1801 and again in 1810-1817, and uprooted many spice trees for planting elsewhere in the British Empire. After Indonesian independence a Republic of South Maluku was declared in 1950 and was put down by the Indonesian army.

Since 1999 the islands have formed two Indonesian provinces: Maluku, with its capital at Ambon, and North Maluku, with its capital at Sofifi on Halmahera. Their combined population in 2020 was 3,131,860. Over 130 languages were once spoken, and many speakers have moved to the creoles of Ternate and Ambon. Cloves and nutmeg are still grown, alongside cocoa, coffee and fruit, and fishing is a large industry.
mamai: Mamai belonged to the Turco-Mongol Kiyat clan, which claimed descent from an older brother of Genghis Khan's father Yesugei Baghatur. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan and his son Jochi in the male line, he never took the title of khan. His birth is dated only to the mid-to-late 1320s, and his father is named as Alash Beg, possibly Ali Beg. Members of the clan had served the Golden Horde from the time of Batu Khan, and some governed the Crimea and the eastern lands of the Horde. Mamai became an emir under Jani Beg, who reigned from 1342 to 1357, and under Berdi Beg he was named chief emir and married the khan's daughter.

After Berdi Beg's death in August 1359 Mamai lost his place at court. From 1361 he acted as kingmaker, promoting khans of his own choosing from a base in the Crimea and the western Horde. He installed his first khan, Abdallah, at Sarai in 1362, but rivals from the line of Jochi's son Shiban expelled him within the year. Over the next decade Mamai took the capital and lost it again several times. In 1362 a Lithuanian victory at the Battle of Blue Waters cost him Podolia. He lowered the tribute of the Venetians at Tana, was received with honour in Genoese Caffa in 1374, and restored friendly relations with Mamluk Egypt.

Mamai's dealings with the Russian princes were opportunistic. He played Dmitrij of Moscow against Mihail of Tver' for the grand princedom of Vladimir, and each had to bring gifts. After 1374 Dmitrij refused tribute. Mamai defeated the men of Nižnij Novgorod at the P'jana river and burned their city in 1377. In 1378 a Mongol army he sent against Rjazan' was beaten by Dmitrij at the Voža river on 11 August. Mamai then demanded submission and higher tribute for his new khan, Tūlāk. Dmitrij refused, and on 8 September 1380 the Russian forces attacked Mamai's army at Kulikovo Field, near the Don, and routed it.

Tokhtamysh, a descendant of Jochi's son Tuqa-Timur, had meanwhile taken Sarai and gained the Horde's allegiance. Mamai met him on the Kalka River without a legitimate khan to put forward. Many of his commanders deserted to Tokhtamysh with their troops, and Mamai fled, losing his harem and much of his property. The Genoese of Caffa refused to admit him, as did the governor and people of Solkhat. At the end of 1380 or the beginning of 1381 agents of Tokhtamysh caught up with him outside Solkhat and killed him, though Tokhtamysh ordered an honourable burial. His death opened the way for Tokhtamysh's attempt to reunite the Golden Horde. The Princes Glinski, later prominent in Lithuania, were said to descend from his son Mansur Kiyat.
mamallapuram: Mamallapuram lies on the Coromandel Coast of the Bay of Bengal, about 60 kilometres south of Chennai. Its ancient name was Thirukadalmallai. The earliest mention is in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, by an unknown Greek navigator, and Ptolemy calls the place Malange. Mariners have known it since at least the time of Marco Polo as the Seven Pagodas, after shrines on the shore, of which only the Shore Temple survives.

A Neolithic burial urn, cairn circles and burial jars of the 1st century BCE have been found nearby. Chinese coins and Roman coins of Theodosius I from the 4th century CE show that the port was an active hub of trade in the late classical period. The Pallava kings ruled it from Kanchipuram, their capital from the 3rd to the 9th century CE, and used the port to launch trade and diplomatic missions to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

The town was named after the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, also known as Mamalla, who reigned from 630 to 670 CE and is said to have founded it in the 7th century. A group of royal monuments, many carved from the living rock, was built largely under him and his successor Rajasimhavarman, and they show the shift from rock-cut to structural architecture. The present town plan was established under the British Raj in 1827.

The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with some 40 ancient monuments. They include the ratha temples, monolithic processional chariots built between 630 and 668 CE, among them the Pancha Rathas, each carved from a single stone. There are over ten rock-cut cave temples of the 7th century and the giant open-air rock relief known as the Descent of the Ganges or Arjuna's Penance, one of the largest in the world. The Shore Temple, of dressed stone and dedicated to Shiva, was built about half a century after the rock-cut works.
mamluk: The Arabic word mamluk means one who is owned. Mamluks were non-Arab and ethnically diverse enslaved mercenaries, slave-soldiers and freed slaves given military and administrative duties in the Muslim world. At first they were mostly Turks from the Eurasian Steppe, and the institution later took in Circassians, Mongols, Georgians, Armenians, Russians and Balkan peoples such as Albanians and Greeks. David Ayalon called the creation of this warrior class the Mamluk or Ghulam phenomenon. It lasted nearly a thousand years, from the 9th century to the early 19th. Historians agree that a large slave military class developed in the 9th-century Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad, under the caliph al-Muʿtaṣim.

From the 900s to the 1200s Egypt was controlled by foreign dynasties, among them the Ikhshidids, Fatimids and Ayyubids, who used thousands of mamluk soldiers and some of whom took high office. In 1249 the Seventh Crusade under Louis IX of France landed in Egypt. After the sultan as-Salih Ayyub died, his widow Shajar al-Durr took control with Mamluk support, and the Bahri commander Baibars defeated Louis's troops. Louis was captured in March 1250. After the assassination of Aybak, Shajar al-Durr's husband, Qutuz took power and founded the Mamluk Sultanate and the Bahri dynasty.

In 1260 the Mamluk army under Qutuz ambushed a reduced Ilkhanate force at the Battle of Ain Jalut and routed it. With the capture of Ruad in 1302 the Sultanate formally expelled the last Crusaders from the Levant. In 1382 the Burji dynasty began when Barquq was proclaimed sultan, and by then most Mamluks were Circassians. The Mamluk Sultanate lasted from 1250 to 1517. In 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte's army defeated a Mamluk army at the Battle of the Pyramids.

Under the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo, Mamluks were bought as young males and raised in the barracks of the Citadel of Cairo. Because they had no social ties or political affiliations and went through austere military training, they were trusted to be loyal to their rulers. After training they were freed but stayed attached to the patron who had bought them, whose reputation in turn depended on his recruits. Their status was above that of ordinary slaves, who could not carry weapons.

Georgian mamluks in Egypt kept their native language and sent gifts to relatives. The practice ended in Egypt after 1 March 1811, when Muhammad Ali invited the leading Mamluks to his palace and his forces killed almost all of the 600 to 700 who came, in the Massacre of the Citadel.
mamluk-dynasty-delhi: Historians use the name for three dynasties of Mamluk origin that ruled the Ghurid territories in India and then the Sultanate of Delhi: the Qutbi dynasty (1206–1211), the first Ilbari or Shamsi dynasty (1211–1266) and the second Ilbari dynasty (1266–1290). Mamluks were soldiers of slave origin who had converted to Islam. They became a powerful military class in several Muslim societies, in Egypt, the Levant, Iraq and India.

Qutb al-Din Aibak served as a Ghurid administrator from 1192 to 1206 and led forays into the Gangetic plain.
