When Muhammad of Ghor, Sultan of the Ghurid Empire, was assassinated in 1206 without male heirs, the empire split into minor sultanates under his former Mamluk generals: Taj-ud-Din Yildoz held Ghazni, Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khilji took Bengal and Nasir-ud-Din Qabacha became sultan of Multan. Aibak became sultan of Delhi.

Aibak made Lahore his capital and began the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar. He died in 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing polo. Forty nobles known as the Chihalgani then conspired against his successor Aram Shah and invited Shams-ud-din Iltutmish, governor of Badaun, to replace him. Iltutmish defeated Aram in 1211, moved the capital to Delhi, defeated Qabacha and Yildoz, and incorporated Bengal in 1227. He kept India clear of the Mongol invasions that followed Genghis Khan's defeat of the Khwarazmshah Jalal-ud-din Mangabarni at the Battle of the Indus in 1221.

After Iltutmish died in 1236 a series of weak rulers followed. Rukn-ud-din Feroze reigned seven months, with his mother Shah Turkan running the government, and both were killed by the Chihalgani on 9 November 1236. Razia al-Din, the first female Muslim ruler in India, reigned until 1240; nobles resented her, and she was defeated and killed on 14 October 1240. Muiz-ud-din Bahram was put to death in 1242 while the Mongols sacked Lahore. Ala-ud-din Masud was a puppet of the Chihalgani until 1246, when Nasiruddin Mahmud replaced him; his Deputy Sultan, Ghiyath-ud-din Balban, handled state affairs.

Balban ruled from 1266 to 1287. He consolidated royal authority, eliminated rival members of the Chihalgani and used news-writers and spies to curb insubordination. The court chronicler Ziauddin Barani records that his expeditions in Mewat and Katehr involved large-scale executions and the demolition of forts. Balban repelled many Mongol invasions and lost his son Prince Muhammad at the Battle of Beas River. His grandson Muiz-ud-din Qaiqabad ruled from 1287 until his murder in 1290, and the dynasty ended with the rise of the Khalji dynasty. Iltutmish's Hauz-i-Shamsi reservoir and Sultan Ghari, the first Islamic mausoleum in Delhi, survive from the period.
mamluk-sultanate: A mamluk was a freed slave soldier, trained in martial arts, court etiquette and Islamic sciences and expected to stay loyal to his former master. Mamluks had served in Syria and Egypt since at least the 9th century, and under the Ayyubids, beginning with Saladin, they were the backbone of Egypt's army. Most were Kipchak Turks from Central Asia. In 1249 Louis IX of France captured Damietta in the Seventh Crusade, and the Ayyubid sultan al-Salih died. His son Turanshah promoted his own entourage at the expense of his father's mamluks, and on 2 May 1250 disgruntled emirs of that corps assassinated him at Fariskur, which established the sultanate.

Under Sultan Qutuz and Baybars the Mamluks routed the Mongols in 1260, halting their southward expansion, and took the Ayyubids' Syrian principalities. Baybars re-established an Abbasid caliph in Cairo, though with a ceremonial role. By the end of the 13th century Baybars, Qalawun and al-Ashraf Khalil had conquered the Crusader states and expanded into Makuria, Cyrenaica, the Hejaz and southern Anatolia. Historians call the period to 1382 Bahri and that from 1382 to 1517 Burji or Circassian. Stability and prosperity marked the third reign of al-Nasir Muhammad (1310–1341).

Foreign invasions, tribal rebellions and natural disasters then eroded Mamluk authority, and the state fell into financial distress. Sultan Barsbay monopolised trade with Europe and forced Cyprus to submit in 1426. The last effective sultan, Qansuh al-Ghuri, was killed in battle against the Ottoman sultan Selim I in 1516, and Selim conquered Egypt in 1517, ending Mamluk rule.

The sultan was the supreme authority and delegated power to provincial governors, mamluk emirs called nuwwab al-saltana. The Mamluks left the Ayyubid administrative, legal and economic systems largely unchanged, but their state was unitary, with Cairo holding absolute paramountcy over Syria. Entry into the military hierarchy was essentially restricted to mamluks, and revenue came largely from the iqta', a right to collect revenue from a fixed territory, granted to emirs to provision their soldiers.

The economy was mainly agrarian, but Egypt and Syria also stood at the centre of trade between Europe and the Indian Ocean. Cairo reached the peak of its size and wealth before the modern period. Mamluk enamelled glass, inlaid metalwork and illuminated Qur'an manuscripts were prized around the Mediterranean, and Mamluk architecture still makes up much of historic Cairo.
mammad-amin-rasulzade: Mahammad Amin Rasulzade was born on 31 January 1884 in Novkhany, near Baku, and studied at the Russian-Muslim Secondary School and the Technical College in Baku. While a student he created the Muslim Youth Organisation Musavat, the first secret organisation in Azerbaijan's modern history. From 1903 he wrote for opposition newspapers, and in 1904 he founded Hummet, the first Muslim social-democratic organisation, editing its papers Takamul and Yoldash. He took an active part in the First Russian Revolution of 1905 to 1907.

Persecuted by the tsarist authorities, he fled in 1909 to Iran, where he edited the newspaper Iran-e Azad, helped found the Democrat Party of Persia and published Iran-e Now. After Russian troops entered Iran in 1911 he went to Istanbul and founded the journal Türk Yurdu. Under the Amnesty Act of 1913 he returned to Baku and joined the Musavat party, which had been established in 1911 and which he soon led. After the February Revolution it became a leading party of the Caucasian Muslims.

On 28 May 1918 the Azerbaijani National Council, headed by Rasulzade, declared an independent Azerbaijan Republic. His phrase, The flag once raised shall never fall, became the motto of the independence movement. He also initiated the founding of Baku State University in 1919, with funds from the oil magnate Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev, and taught Ottoman literature there. After the republic collapsed in April 1920 he went into hiding in the village of Lahıc to direct resistance to Sovietization. He was arrested in August 1920, but was released, said to be because he had once hidden Joseph Stalin from the police, and was transferred to Russia.

Rasulzade escaped to Finland in 1922 and lived the rest of his life in exile, first in Turkey, where he edited the magazine Yeni Kafkasya from 1923 to 1927. He was expelled from Turkey in 1931 and later went to Poland. In 1942 the leadership of Nazi Germany approached him, and in May 1942 he sought an alliance to restore Azerbaijan's independence, demanding a commitment to the restoration of the Transcaucasian states, which the Reich evaded. He returned to Ankara in 1947. He died in 1955 and was buried in the Cebeci Asri cemetery in Ankara.
Baku State University was named in his honour, and he appeared on the Azerbaijani 1000 manat banknote of 1993 to 2006. A high school in Ankara also bears his name.
manado: Manado lies on the Bay of Manado, surrounded by mountains, with a tropical rainforest climate and no real dry season. The name comes from the Sangir word manaro, meaning on the far coast or in the distance, and first referred to the farther of two islands seen from the mainland. When the settlement there moved to the mainland the name came with it, and the island became Manado Tua. A world map by the French cartographer Nicolas Desliens, which shows the island as Manarow, mentions it first.

Before Europeans arrived, the area was ruled by the Sultan of Ternate, who collected tribute and introduced Islam. The Portuguese made the sultan their vassal and set up a trading post at Wenang. The Spanish took the Portuguese fortress at Amurang in the 1550s with native allies and built a fort at Manado, and one of the first Indo-Eurasian communities of the archipelago developed there in the 16th century. The first King of Manado, Muntu Untu, in 1630, was the son of a Spanish mestizo. Spain later renounced its Minahasa possessions to the Portuguese for 350,000 ducats, and the Minahasa, allied with the Dutch, expelled the last Portuguese.

The Dutch East India Company built Fort Amsterdam in 1658, and missionaries spread Christianity there; the first church, the Oude Kerk, still stands as Gereja Sentrum. HMS Dover captured Manado in June 1810, and in 1830 the Dutch exiled the Javanese prince Diponegoro there. The Japanese captured it in January 1942, and Allied bombing badly damaged it. In 1958 the rebel movement Permesta moved its headquarters to Manado; the central government bombed the city in February and invaded in June. In 1962 it was declared capital of North Sulawesi.

Manado is the second largest city of Sulawesi after Makassar. Most residents belong to the Minahasa people, and the main language is Manado Malay, a Malay-based creole. Christianity is the majority religion, and the city holds a large Christmas celebration each year. The Ban Hin Kiong Temple, founded in 1819, is the oldest temple in the city, and Bunaken National Park lies offshore.
managua: Managua stands on the southern shore of Lake Managua, also called Lake Xolotlán, in western Nicaragua, with a tropical wet and dry climate and two seasons: a rainy season from mid-May to mid-November and a dry one for the rest of the year. The lake has been polluted by the dumping of chemicals and waste water since 1927, and a waste-water treatment plant at Las Mercedes, funded by the German government, was inaugurated in 2009. The name may come from the Nahuatl mana-ahuac, 'adjacent to the water', or from a word in the Mangue language meaning 'place of the big man' or 'chief'.

The area was inhabited by Paleo-Indians as far back as 12,000 BCE. The footprints of Acahualinca, fossilised in volcanic ash along the shore, are 2,100 years old. Founded as a pre-Columbian fishing town, the settlement was incorporated in 1819 as Leal Villa de Santiago de Managua. Efforts to make it the capital began in 1824, after the Central American nations attained independence from Spain, and Nicaragua became an independent nation in 1838. Its position between the rival cities of León and Granada made it a logical compromise, and it was officially selected as the national capital in 1852. Between 1842 and 1930 it expanded and urbanised rapidly.

A disastrous earthquake in 1931 destroyed much of the city and killed between 1,000 and 2,450 people, and a large fire in 1936 destroyed much of what was left. Under the rule of Anastasio Somoza García and his family, from 1936 to 1979, the city was rebuilt and grew rapidly, with new government buildings, industry and universities. The earthquake of 1972 destroyed 90 percent of the city. Among the few buildings to survive were the National Palace, the Rubén Darío National Theatre and, though heavily damaged, the Old Cathedral, built from 1928 to 1938 as the first cathedral in the Western Hemisphere made entirely of concrete on a metal frame. The New Cathedral, designed by Ricardo Legorreta, was inaugurated in 1993 to replace it.

Managua is the capital and largest city of Nicaragua, with an estimated population of 1,063,815 in 2023, and the main economic, political and cultural hub of the country. Most of its universities are there, among them the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua, established in 1812 at León. The Plaza de la Revolución, on the shore of the lake, holds its historic centre, the Old Cathedral, the National Palace of Culture, which houses the National Museum, and the Rubén Darío National Theatre. The Museum of Acahualinca preserves the ancient footprints. The city's patron saint, Santo Domingo de Guzmán, is honoured each August in a festival in which his statue is carried across the city.
manama: Manama lies in the north-eastern corner of Bahrain on a small peninsula along the Persian Gulf. The land is flat and arid, with extremely hot summers and mild winters, and reclaimed land has extended the coastline in recent decades. Its coastal position made it a port and trading point of the Gulf. Historically the city was confined to what is now the Manama Souq and the Manama Fort to its south, and it has since grown to take in suburban developments and older neighbouring villages.

There is evidence of human settlement on Bahrain's northern coastline from the Bronze Age. The Dilmun civilisation inhabited the area in 3000 BCE as a trading hub between Mesopotamia, Magan and the Indus Valley Civilisation, and about 100,000 Dilmun burial mounds have been found across the north and centre of the country. The name Manamah is first recorded around 730 AH, about 1330 CE, during a visit by Turan Shah of Hurmuz to the island. Manama remained a small trading port until the Portuguese took control in the early 1500s, and in 1602 the Safavid Persians expelled them. The Safavids sidelined Manama and made the nearby town of Bilad Al Qadeem the provincial capital, while the islands' pearl exports grew.

The twin towns of Manama and Muharraq appear to have been founded together in the 1800s. Muharraq, with its more defensible position, was the capital of Bahrain until 1923, while Manama became the mercantile capital and the gateway to the main island. After the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 the British Raj used Manama as a base for the Mesopotamian campaign, and a municipal government was established there in 1919. In the 1920s the British pressed administrative reforms, including a reorganised customs office in 1923, civil courts, and in 1926 the appointment of Charles Belgrave as financial adviser. Manama was declared the capital when Bahrain became independent in 1971.

Manama is the capital and largest city of Bahrain, and its population has long been cosmopolitan: in 1904 it was estimated at 25,000, half of them foreigners from Basra, Najd, al-Hasa, Iran, India and Europe. Shia and Sunni Islam have coexisted there for centuries, each represented by distinct ethnic groups. Oil wealth spurred growth in the 20th century, and diversification from the 1990s made the city a financial hub of the Persian Gulf and a centre of Islamic banking. Bab Al Bahrain and the adjacent souq are among its notable cultural sites, and the city centre is the main location of Muharram processions in the country.
manas-river: The Manas, known in Bhutan as the Drangme Chhu, is the largest of Bhutan's four major river systems. It drains 41,350 square kilometres of eastern Bhutan and northeast India through three main branches, the Drangme Chhu, the Mangde Chhu and the Bumthang or Chamkhar Chhu. Part of its main stem rises in southern Tibet at about 4,500 metres and enters India in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh before crossing into Bhutan near Trashigang. The Lhobrak or Kuri Chhu, its main central tributary, is the only one that rises north of the Great Himalayas.

In Bhutan the river runs southwest through V-shaped gorges between two ranges of the Lower Himalayas. In the foothills the valley widens into swamps and marshes. The Aie River joins it in Assam, and it then meanders for about 75 kilometres to the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa. It is the largest tributary on the Brahmaputra's north bank and contributes 5.48 per cent of its average volume. From May to October the southwest monsoon brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain to the southern part of the basin; the flow in the monsoon is said to be as much as 20 times that of the dry season.

The core of the present Manas Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam was designated a sanctuary in 1928 and declared a tiger reserve in 1978; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1985. A dam proposed in the 1970s would have sent a canal 100 kilometres long through the tiger reserve to the Sankosh River. India's Ministry of Environment and Forests objected, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO supported the objection, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi discontinued the project. Two dams proposed on the Bhutanese side were dropped in 1986. In February 1989 members of the All Bodo Students Union entered the park and killed several wardens and guards.

The lowlands north of the confluence, the Duars, are very fertile and have been made into tea estates and paddy fields. Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, raised to a national park in 1993, is 92 per cent forested, and five thousand people live in villages inside it. The two reserves shelter the Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, greater one-horned rhinoceros, wild water buffalo, pygmy hog, hispid hare and golden langur, and the Ganges river dolphin lives in the river.
manasseh-of-judah: Manasseh was the fourteenth king of the Kingdom of Judah and the oldest of the sons of Hezekiah and Hephzibah. According to the books of Kings and Chronicles he became king at the age of 12 and reigned for 55 years, the longest reign in the history of Judah. He was the first king of Judah who was not a contemporary of the northern kingdom of Israel, which the Assyrians had destroyed around 720 BCE, deporting much of its population. He married Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah, and their son Amon succeeded him.

Manasseh is named in Assyrian records as a loyal vassal of Sennacherib's son Esarhaddon, among twenty-two kings required to provide materials for his building projects. Esarhaddon's son Ashurbanipal also names him among the vassals who assisted a campaign against Egypt. These records agree with archaeological evidence of demographic trends and settlement patterns that suggest a period of stability in Judah. The archaeologists Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman credit Manasseh with reviving the rural economy, with an export trade in olive oil and forts protecting the trade routes, though they argue that trade also deepened the gap between rich and poor.

The books of Kings condemn his religious policy. They say he reversed his father Hezekiah's centralising reforms, re-established local shrines, restored the worship of Baal and Asherah, sponsored an Assyrian astral cult and took part in the cult of Moloch. They also report a persecution of the prophets, and later tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two on his orders. Chronicles adds that he was taken in chains to the Assyrian king in Babylon, then restored, repented and removed the foreign idols. Arnold J. Toynbee thought him nearer to a pious conservative defending his ancestors' faith.

Manasseh was buried not in the City of David among his ancestors but in the garden of Uzza, the garden of his own house. Jeremiah 15:4 links the coming destruction of Judah to the evil done by Manasseh. Finkelstein and Silberman suggest that the writer or editor of 2 Kings reworked the traditions about him to present his outward-looking involvement in trade as apostasy. The Prayer of Manasseh, a penitential prayer attributed to him, appears in some Christian Bibles but is regarded as apocryphal by Jews, Catholics and Protestants. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's 1 Meqabyan cites him as an example of an ungodly king.
manbij: Manbij lies in the north-east of Aleppo Governorate in northern Syria, 30 kilometres west of the Euphrates. Coins struck there before Alexander's conquest give its Aramean name as Manbug, meaning Site of the Spring; the Assyrians knew it as Nappigu or Nanpigi, and the Greeks hellenized it as Bambyce. As the centre of worship of the Syrian goddess Atargatis it became Hieropolis, City of the Sanctuary, and then Hierapolis, the Holy City. The cult was described in De Dea Syria, traditionally attributed to Lucian of Samosata, which tells of a sacred tank of fish, a temple served by some three hundred priests and a lake where votaries swam out to decorate an altar.

The city was part of the kingdom of Bit Adini and was annexed by the Assyrians in 856 BCE; Shalmaneser III renamed it Lita-Ashur and built a palace there, and Tiglath-Pileser III reconquered it in 738 BCE. At the end of the Achaemenid Empire it seems to have been the centre of a dynasty of Aramean priest-kings. Under the Seleucids it was the chief station on their main road between Antioch and Seleucia on the Tigris. Crassus sacked the temple in 53 BCE on his way to meet the Parthians. In the third century it was the capital of the province of Euphratensis, and Khosrau I held it to ransom after Justinian I failed to defend it.

Harun al-Rashid restored Manbij at the end of the 8th century as capital of the frontier province of al-Awasim. Salih ibn Mirdas took it about 1022 and made it a foundation of the Mirdasid emirate. In 1068 the Byzantine emperor Romanos Diogenes captured it, killed its inhabitants and plundered the countryside. The Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I took it in 1086, and in 1124 Belek Ghazi was killed by an arrow during his siege. The Crusaders never captured it. Nur ad-Din took it by 1152, Saladin conquered it in 1175, and in 1260 the Mongols under Hulagu destroyed Ayyubid Manbij.

Almost all the ancient remains, including the temple of Atargatis, its sacred lake, colonnades, Roman baths and theatres, Byzantine churches and medieval madrasas, have been destroyed, and the sacred lake has become a football field. The Ottoman government resettled the area with Circassian refugees from the Russo-Turkish War in 1878, and in 1915 Armenian refugees were brought to a camp there. The 2004 census gave a population of nearly 100,000, largely Arab with Kurdish, Turkmen, Circassian and Chechen minorities. Manbij changed hands several times in the Syrian civil war, from 2012 onwards.
manchukuo: Manchuria, now Northeast China, was historically the homeland of the Manchu people, but by the twentieth century Han Chinese were by far its largest group. The Qing dynasty fell in the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 and the last emperor Puyi abdicated at the age of six. In the Warlord Era Marshal Zhang Zuolin established himself in Manchuria with Japanese backing, and the Japanese Kwantung Army had him assassinated in 1928, expecting anarchy that would justify seizing the region. The plot failed because his son Zhang Xueliang succeeded him without incident.

Japan invaded and occupied Manchuria in 1931 after the Mukden incident. A puppet government was set up the following year, with Puyi as nominal regent. Manchukuo was proclaimed a monarchy on 1 March 1934, with Puyi as emperor.

The State Council was the centre of power. Each of its ministers was assisted by a Japanese vice-minister, and the commander-in-chief of the Kwantung Army served as Japanese ambassador with the ability to veto the emperor's decisions. Chinese advisers gradually resigned or were dismissed. The Legislative Council was largely ceremonial, and the only authorised party was the government-sponsored Concordia Association. Manchukuo received only limited diplomatic recognition, mainly from states aligned with the Axis powers.

More than a million Japanese settled there by 1945, many of them land-poor farmers resettled by Japan. Under the vice-minister Nobusuke Kishi and the Manchurian Industrial Development Company heavy industry expanded, using the forced labour of local people. Manchukuo was the base for Japan's invasion of the rest of China, beginning with the Marco Polo Bridge incident of 1937.

On 8 August 1945 the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchukuo. Its imperial army, on paper 200,000 strong, performed poorly, and whole units surrendered without firing a shot. Puyi abdicated on 17 August. The Soviets captured him and later extradited him to China, where he was imprisoned on war crimes charges after the Communist Party came to power in 1949. The government was formally dissolved after Japan's surrender in September 1945, and the territory was transferred to Chinese administration the following year.
manchuria: Manchuria is most often associated with the three Chinese provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning. Its extent varies with the definition: the Qing region also included land now in the Russian Far East, and the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo added Chengde and parts of Inner Mongolia. The seasons are extreme, from humid heat in summer to dry Arctic cold in winter.

The name Manchuria is an exonym of Japanese origin, from Manshu, used by Japanese cartographers from the late eighteenth century. In Qing times the region was called the Three Eastern Provinces or Guandong, 'east of the pass'. In China the term is now deprecated because of its association with Japanese imperialism, and the area is called the Northeast.

Many peoples rose to power here, among them the Sushen, Donghu, Xianbei, Wuhuan, Mohe, Khitan and Jurchens, and the Koreanic kingdoms of Gojoseon, Buyeo and Goguryeo held large parts of it. The Qin, Han, Cao Wei, Western Jin and Tang dynasties controlled parts, and the First Turkic Khaganate and Eastern Turkic Khaganate held parts of the north-west. The Khitan Liao dynasty (916-1125) was the first state to control all of Manchuria.

The Qing forbade Han Chinese from settling in the region in 1668, and in 1681 built the Willow Palisade to mark the limit of settlement, but Han farmers kept arriving. The Qianlong Emperor allowed refugees from famine in the north to move in, and by 1800, according to one observer, Han Chinese made up 80 to 90 per cent of the population of garrisons and towns. The Treaty of Aigun in 1858 and the Treaty of Peking in 1860 ceded the lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri to Russia, and the Qing lost access to the Sea of Japan.

Russia built the Chinese Eastern Railway from 1896. After the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905, Japan took over its southern branch as the South Manchurian Railway, and in 1915 it forced China to cede economic privileges there. Manchuria supplied Japan with coal and other raw materials. Under the People's Republic it became a centre of heavy industry, with the Daqing oil field developed from the 1960s.

Manchuria is home to Manchus, Mongols, Koreans, Han Chinese, Nanai, Nivkhs and Ulchs, though the Han are now the large majority. Of the old Qing region, the parts north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri remain in Russia; a boundary dispute over islands in the Amur was settled by agreements of 2004 and 2008.
manchus: The Manchus are a Tungusic East Asian ethnic group native to Manchuria, the region that takes its name from them. Their name, manju in Manchu, was adopted as the official name of the people by Emperor Hong Taiji in 1635, replacing the earlier name Jurchen. The Qing dynasty's own record derived it from Mañjuśrī.

The Manchus are said to descend from the Jurchens who founded the Jin dynasty, although historians dispute this. The Jianzhou Jurchens, from whom they came, originated in part from the Huligai, whom the Liao dynasty classed as separate from the Jurchens of the Jin. When Nurhaci reorganised the Jurchens into the Eight Banners, many Manchu clans were artificially created from unrelated people, who took a place name as their clan name.

The Manchus founded the Later Jin dynasty (1616 to 1636) and the Qing dynasty (1636 to 1912). After 1644 the majority of the people living in the inner city of Beijing were Manchu and Mongol bannermen, and Han Chinese were not allowed to enter it until after the Hundred Days' Reform. Manchu and bannermen were declared legally equivalent in the 17th century, so banner membership was never genetically uniform, and Manchu identity was traditionally patrilineal. Many Manchu bannermen in Beijing supported the Boxers in the Boxer Rebellion and sustained heavy casualties.

The Manchus were sedentary agriculturalists who lived in permanent villages and practised hunting and mounted archery. Hong Taiji said that riding and archery were the most important martial arts of the country, and the results of yearly tests could affect Manchu rank in the nobility. Manchu men traditionally shave the front of the head and wear the hair at the back in a single braid, the queue, which the Qing made compulsory for Han men under pain of execution for treason.

Nurhaci ordered the scholars G'ag'ai and Erdeni to make a Manchu script from the Mongolian script, and Dahai later added dots and circles to complete it. Fluency among the bannermen declined from the early 18th century. Manchus were Buddhists with shamanist influences, and after the conquest of China adopted Confucianism, though shamanic traditions persisted. Their most important piece of literature is the Tale of the Nisan Shaman.
mandalay: Mandalay lies on the east bank of the Irrawaddy River, 631 km north of Yangon, in the central Dry Zone, at about 80 metres above sea level. It stands on the Sagaing Fault, the boundary between the India and Sunda plates. An earthquake on 23 March 1839, of an estimated magnitude of 8.2, destroyed the former capital Ava and did great damage in nearby cities, and a quake of magnitude 7 in 1956 did most harm at Sagaing. The city takes its name from Mandalay Hill, probably from a Pali word, perhaps mandala, a circular plain.

King Mindon founded the royal city on 13 February 1857 at the foot of Mandalay Hill, ostensibly to fulfil a prophecy that a great city of Buddhism would be founded on that spot at the 2,400th jubilee of Buddhism. Its official name was Yadanarbon, from the Pali Ratanapura, meaning City of Gems. It was the last royal capital before the British annexation of 1885, after which commercial and political importance moved to Yangon. The British looted the palace, and part of the treasure went on display in the Victoria and Albert Museum until it was returned in 1964. A railway reached Mandalay in 1889, but its first college was founded only in 1925.

The city was extensively destroyed in the Japanese conquest of Burma in the Second World War, and most of the palace was burnt, a replica standing there now. After independence in 1948 Mandalay remained the main cultural, educational and economic centre of Upper Burma. Fires in the 1980s cleared large areas, and from the 1990s a large migration of Han Chinese, mostly from Yunnan, changed the ethnic makeup of the city and its commerce. Its population doubled from about 500,000 in 1980 to one million in 2008.

Mandalay is the second-largest city of Myanmar, with 1,225,553 inhabitants in 2014, and the economic centre of Upper Myanmar. It is regarded as the centre of Burmese culture and Buddhism, with numerous monasteries and more than 700 pagodas. At the Kuthodaw Pagoda at the foot of Mandalay Hill, 729 stone slabs carry the whole Pali Canon, each in its own white stupa. Traditional industries include silk weaving, jade cutting, stone and wood carving, and the making of bronze and marble Buddha images.
mandarin-chinese: The hundreds of modern local varieties of Chinese developed from regional variants of Old Chinese and Middle Chinese. Besides Mandarin, six other major groups are traditionally recognised: Wu, Gan, Xiang, Min, Hakka and Yue. Mandarin originated in North China, and its spread is attributed to the greater ease of travel on the North China Plain compared with the mountainous south.

After the fall of the Northern Song in 1126, and under the Jin and the Yuan dynasties in northern China, a common form of speech developed from the dialects of the North China Plain around the capital, called Old Mandarin. New genres of vernacular literature were written in it. The Zhongyuan Yinyun, a rime dictionary of 1324, records many features of modern Mandarin, such as the disappearance of final plosives.

Mandarin is the largest branch of the Sinitic languages. Mandarin varieties are natively spoken by 71 per cent of all Chinese speakers, over an area stretching from Yunnan in the southwest to Xinjiang in the northwest and Heilongjiang in the northeast. Many varieties are not mutually intelligible with the Beijing dialect. Most have four lexical tones, and many keep retroflex initial consonants, which southern varieties have lost. Chinese languages are strongly analytic, relying on word order and particles rather than inflection.

The English word mandarin originally meant an official of the Ming and Qing empires. These officials, whose native varieties were often mutually unintelligible, ran the empire in a koiné based on northern varieties called Guānhuà, the language of the officials; Jesuit missionaries who learned it in the 16th century called it Mandarin. Until the early 20th century formal writing was in Literary Chinese, but a literature in written vernacular Chinese had grown up from at least the Yuan dynasty, with Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber.

After the Republic's founding, intellectuals of the New Culture Movement, among them Hu Shih and Chen Duxiu, campaigned to replace Literary Chinese with it. The National Language Unification Commission settled on the Beijing dialect as the national standard in 1932, and the People's Republic, founded in 1949, kept it as pǔtōnghuà. Singapore's Speak Mandarin Campaign began in 1979.
mandate-of-heaven: In the doctrine, Heaven (Tian) bestows its mandate on a virtuous ruler, the Son of Heaven (Tianzi), who rules all under heaven (Tianxia). It does not require noble birth: the Han and Ming dynasties were founded by men of common origins, who were seen as successful because they had gained the mandate. Keeping it depended on the just and able performance of the ruler and his heirs.

The Zhou were the first to use the concept to explain their right to rule. They held that the Shang came to power because the Xia had lost their mandate, and that the Shang ruling house had become morally corrupt. Early records such as the Da Yu ding inscription speak of 'the great command in the sky'. Heaven's authority was held to pass through the founder, King Wen, to his heirs.

In the Eastern Zhou the kings lost real power but not their divine legitimacy, while inscriptions show that the rulers of the state of Qin held privately that their ancestors had received the mandate. Qin's own surviving material never mentions it. Han writers painted the Qin as tyrannical and so as having lost the mandate, and Liu Bang, who came from outside the aristocracy, was credited with a magical birth and later a divine ancestry.

In 220 CE the last Han emperor abdicated to Cao Pi, and the court prognosticator Xu Zhi listed signs showing that Wei should succeed the Han. To justify their own succession the Song had the scholar Xue Juzheng argue that the mandate had passed through each of the Five Dynasties. The Qing, a Manchu dynasty, argued that peasant rebels led by Li Zicheng had overthrown the Ming and that they themselves had won the mandate by defeating those rebels and restoring stability.

Mencius held that the people are of supreme importance and the ruler last, so the mandate gave no unconditional right to rule. Han Feizi rejected the idea of a just rebellion entirely. The right of rebellion was never written into law, and rebellion was always punished. Because the winner decided who held the mandate, some Chinese scholars regard it as victor's justice, and accounts of a dynasty's fall must be read with caution.

The idea spread to other East Asian countries. The Joseon dynasty made it an enduring state ideology, and in Vietnam it gave the emperor the right to rule on his competence rather than his lineage. Japan's Taihō Code of 703 adapted Tang government but omitted it.
manduria: Manduria stands in the province of Taranto in Apulia, about 35 kilometres east of the city of Taranto. Its name is thought to derive from a Proto-Indo-European stem meaning foal, which would make it Messapic in origin and related to the Illyrian theonym Iuppiter Menzanas and the Albanian word for foal. Plutarch also refers to it as Mandonion. The ancient town lay close to the modern one, and considerable remains of its defences can still be seen: a double line of walls of rectangular stone blocks laid without mortar, with a broad ditch in front.

In antiquity Manduria was an important stronghold of the Messapii against Taras. Archidamus III, king of Sparta, was killed beneath its walls in 338 BCE while leading the army of Taras. The town revolted to Hannibal but was taken by the Romans in 209 BCE.

Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History, describes a well in which the water level never changed however much was drawn, with an almond tree growing from the middle of the shaft. The Saracens destroyed the town in the 10th century. Its people rebuilt on the site of the present town, which they called Casalnuovo, and in 1700 they took back the ancient name of Manduria. Tombs with gold ornaments were found in 1886.

The well, called the Fonte Pliniano, can still be seen as Pliny described it and is the symbol of the city. Other sights include the medieval Chiesa Madre, renovated in the 16th century, the Church of the Holy Trinity of the 11th or 12th century, with three Renaissance portals and a 15th-century bell tower, the medieval Jewish quarter and a castle that was the seat of the Imperiali princes from 1719. The Church of San Pietro Mandurino was probably a Hellenistic hall tomb adapted as a church in the 8th or 9th century. The local Primitivo di Manduria wine is made from the Primitivo grape alone.
manetho: Little is certain about the life of Manetho. His name is a Greek form of an Egyptian name, and scholars have no agreement on the original: it may invoke Thoth or Neith, or be an occupational name meaning shepherd or groom. He came from Sebennytos and was probably a priest of the sun god Ra at Heliopolis, and an authority on the temple cult of Serapis.

He worked at the beginning of the Hellenistic order in Egypt, when Ptolemy I Soter founded the Ptolemaic Kingdom in 305 BCE. Manetho wrote under Ptolemy I or Ptolemy II Philadelphus to preserve the history of his homeland and, since he wrote in Greek, for its new foreign rulers. Ancient writers grouped him with the Mesopotamian writer Berossus, and both used king-lists as the framework of their histories.

Eight works have been attributed to Manetho, but modern scholars agree only that he wrote the Aegyptiaca. This was a chronological history in three scrolls, perhaps written in answer to Herodotus. It ran from a mythical age of divine rulers through the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt by Menes and thirty or thirty-one dynasties to the establishment of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in 305 BCE, and treated periods of stability against internal strife and foreign rule by the Hyksos, Kushites and Achaemenids.

Manetho coined the word dynasty, but he meant groups of rulers separated by a break, of place or of descent, not simply a line of blood relatives. His division of the rulers into thirty or thirty-one dynasties remains the chronological framework of Egyptology. Because he wrote in Greek, his history stayed readable after the last hieroglyphic text of 394 CE. His own writings are lost, and the fragments survive through later authors including Josephus, Africanus, Eusebius and Syncellus.

In the account preserved by Josephus, Manetho described the departure of the Israelites as the expulsion of a colony of lepers and ritually polluted people, led by the renegade priest Osarseph whom he identified with Moses. Scholars read this as an answer to the anti-Egyptian side of the Exodus story.
manfred-king-of-sicily: Manfred was born in 1232 at Venosa, a natural son of Emperor Frederick II, who seems to have regarded him as legitimate and named him Prince of Taranto in his will. He studied in Paris and Bologna and shared his father's love of poetry and science. After Frederick's death in 1250 he acted as regent of Sicily while his half-brother Conrad IV was in Germany. When Conrad came to southern Italy in 1252 he stripped Manfred of his fiefs except Taranto. Conrad died of malaria in May 1254, and Manfred took the regency for the infant Conradin.

Pope Innocent IV excommunicated him in July 1254. Manfred submitted in September and accepted the title of papal vicar, but he fled to the Saracens at Lucera, and with their help defeated the papal army at Foggia on 2 December 1254. By 1257 he had crushed another papal army and put down the rebellions.

On 10 August 1258, on a rumour that Conradin was dead, Manfred was crowned king of Sicily at Palermo. The pope declared the coronation void, but Manfred named vicars in Tuscany, Spoleto, the Marche, Romagna and Lombardy. After Montaperti he was recognised as protector of Tuscany by the citizens of Florence, and in 1262 his daughter Constance married the future Peter III of Aragon. He also took Helena Angelina Doukaina, daughter of the ruler of Epirus, as his second wife.

Pope Urban IV excommunicated him and in 1263 gave the investiture of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, a brother of Louis IX of France. Charles entered Italy in late 1265 with an army of some 30,000 and was crowned in Rome in January 1266. The armies met at the Battle of Benevento on 26 February 1266. Manfred refused to flee, rushed into the midst of his enemies and was killed.

Manfred was buried on the battlefield under a heap of stones, but with the pope's consent his remains were dug up and interred on the bank of the Garigliano, outside the territory of Naples and the Papal States. Charles imprisoned Helena, who died in 1271, and kept her sons in chains for decades. Peter III eventually became king of Sicily in 1282 after the Sicilian Vespers. Manfred founded the modern city of Manfredonia between 1256 and 1263, and in the Divine Comedy Dante meets him outside the gates of Purgatory.
mangalore: Mangaluru lies on the western coast of India in Dakshina Kannada district, between the Laccadive Sea and the Western Ghats. The Gurupura flows around its north and the Netravati around its south, and the two rivers form an estuary in the south-west of the city before reaching the sea. The landscape is one of rolling hills, coconut palms and hard laterite soil. It has a tropical monsoon climate, and about 95 percent of the year's rain falls between May and September. The name comes from the goddess Mangaladevi, whose temple stands at Bolar; local legend tells of a princess from Malabar who became a disciple of Matsyendranath and was renamed Mangaladevi.

Foreign writers mention the coast from early times. In the first century CE Pliny the Elder named a place called Nitrias, where pirates made landing undesirable, and in the second century Ptolemy named Nitra, probably the area of the Netravati River. In the sixth century the Greek monk Cosmas Indicopleustes listed Mangarouth, the port of Mangaluru, among the five pepper markets that exported pepper. The city was ruled by several powers, among them the Mauryan empire, the Kadambas, the Alupas, the Vijayanagara Empire and the Keladi Nayaks.

European influence began in 1498, when Vasco da Gama landed at the nearby St Mary's Islands. The Portuguese were friendly with Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara and sought to destroy the Arab and Mappila coastal trade. In 1524 Vasco da Gama ordered the rivers blockaded after hearing that Muslim merchants of Kozhikode had agents at Mangaluru and Basrur, and in 1526 the Portuguese under the viceroy Lopo Vaz de Sampaio took the city, and the coastal trade passed into their hands. The city was later contested between the British and the Mysore rulers Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, and the British annexed it in 1799. It stayed in the Madras Presidency until 1947 and joined Mysore State, now Karnataka, in 1956.

A municipal council was set up on 23 May 1866 under the Madras Town Improvement Act. Italian Jesuits who arrived in 1878 played an important part in education, health and social welfare. The railway reached the city in 1907, and by the early 20th century it was a major source of educated workers for Bombay, Bengaluru and the Middle East.

Mangaluru is the administrative headquarters of Dakshina Kannada district, and its urban area held 619,664 people at the 2011 census. A new port was built in 1968. Tulu, Konkani, Kannada and Beary are all spoken there, and Tulu is the most widespread first language. Hindus form the largest religious community, with large Christian and Muslim communities; the Masjid Zeenath Baksh is among the oldest mosques in the Indian subcontinent.
manghud: The Manghud belonged to the Urud-Manghud federation of the Mongolian plateau, and ancient sources derive them from the Kiyat Mongols. The Persian historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who chronicled the Mongols, claimed that many old Mongol clans, the Manghud among them, were founded by members of the Borjigin.

Some Manghud warriors supported Genghis Khan, while a body of them resisted his rise to power. As the Mongol Empire expanded, the Manghud were carried westward with many other Mongol tribes. The clan name was also used for Mongol vanguard troops, though sources differ widely on the military units called mangudai.

In the Golden Horde the Manghud supported Nogai, who died in 1299, and formed a horde of their own, semi-independent of the khans at Sarai. After Nogai's death most of their warriors entered the service of Tokhta Khan. Edigu, who lived from 1352 to 1419 and was the son of the noble Kutlukiya, led the eastern begs and by the end of the 14th century dominated the Golden Horde.

The Nogais guarded the northern borders of the Astrakhan and Crimean khanates and by organised raids into the northern steppes prevented Russian and Lithuanian settlement. Many entered the service of the Crimean khan and contributed to the formation of the Crimean Tatars. About 1630 the Kalmyks, migrating from southern Siberia to the lower Volga, drove the Nogais out; they fled to the plains of the northern Caucasus and to the Crimea, and a small part joined the Kazakh Khanate.

Other Manghits had been settled by Genghis Khan around the city of Qarshi, which remained their base under the Khanate of Bukhara. Their power there grew in the early 18th century through the office of ataliq to the khan. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son killed. The family ruled behind the scenes until the 1780s, when the emir Shah Murad declared himself ruler openly. Not being descendants of Genghis Khan, the Manghits took the Islamic title of emir, not khan, and based their legitimacy on Islam.

The last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, was ousted by the Soviet Red Army in September 1920 and fled to Afghanistan. Whether his dynasty was of Mongol or of plain Uzbek origin is disputed. The Nogai and Karakalpak peoples are counted among the descendants of the Manghud, and Manghits are found among the Tatars of Russia, the Bashkirs and the Kazakhs, as well as among the Khalkha Mongols of Mongolia.
manhattan: Manhattan is the geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City and is coextensive with New York County. It lies almost entirely on Manhattan Island, bounded by the Hudson River to the west and the East River to the east, while the Harlem River divides it from the Bronx. The island is 13.4 miles long and 2.3 miles wide at its widest point, near 14th Street, and is loosely divided into Lower Manhattan, Midtown and Upper Manhattan. Its bedrock of Inwood marble, Fordham gneiss and Manhattan schist is well suited to the foundations of skyscrapers.

Manhattan was part of Lenapehoking, the territory of the Munsee, Lenape and Wappinger peoples. Their main trail, from what is now Inwood to Battery Park, later became Broadway. Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing for Francis I of France, became the first documented European to visit the area, in April 1524. Dutch colonists set up a trading post on the island in 1624, named New Amsterdam in 1626. The English took the territory in 1664 and renamed it New York for the Duke of York.

Manhattan was at the heart of the New York Campaign in the American Revolutionary War, and the Continental Army abandoned it after the Battle of Fort Washington on 16 November 1776. British occupation lasted until 25 November 1783. New York was the capital of the United States from 1785 until 1790, and by 1810 it was the most populous city in the country. The Commissioners' Plan of 1811 laid out the grid, and the Erie Canal opened in 1825. The subway opened in 1904, and Manhattan became a borough in the consolidation of 1898.

Manhattan had 1,694,250 residents at the 2020 census, in a land area of about 22.7 square miles. It is the economic and administrative centre of New York City, with City Hall, Wall Street, the New York Stock Exchange and the headquarters of the United Nations in Turtle Bay. Central Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1850s, covers 840 acres. The Statue of Liberty is part of the borough, and its landmarks include the Empire State Building, Grand Central Terminal and Times Square.
manhattan-project: The discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in 1938, and its theoretical explanation by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, made a uranium bomb theoretically possible, and there were fears that Germany would build one first. In August 1939 Leo Szilard and Eugene Wigner drafted a letter, signed by Albert Einstein and delivered to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, that warned of "extremely powerful bombs of a new type".

In Britain, Otto Robert Frisch and Rudolf Peierls calculated in 1939 that the critical mass of uranium-235 was within an order of magnitude of 10 kilograms, and their March 1940 memorandum began the British project, Tube Alloys. The United States committee meeting of 18 December 1941 met just after the attack on Pearl Harbor, and work went ahead on several methods of isotope separation and on reactors.

In June 1942 Colonel James C. Marshall began to head the Army's part from a temporary headquarters at 270 Broadway in Manhattan, which gave the Manhattan District its name. Major General Leslie Groves then took over the project, which employed nearly 130,000 people at its peak and cost nearly 2 billion dollars. Enriched uranium was produced at the Clinton Engineer Works at Oak Ridge in Tennessee, on land acquired by eminent domain that affected about 1,000 families. Plutonium came from the world's first industrial-scale reactors at Hanford in Washington. J. Robert Oppenheimer directed the Los Alamos Laboratory in New Mexico, which designed two weapons: the uranium gun-type Little Boy and the plutonium implosion bomb Fat Man.

The key raw material was uranium. In 1940 there were four known major deposits, in Colorado, northern Canada, Joachimsthal and the Belgian Congo, and Kenneth Nichols negotiated the purchase of 1,200 short tons of ore from the Congo stored on Staten Island.

Canada supplied uranium and heavy water. The Fat Man design was at first a low-priority fallback, but in 1944 it was confirmed that Hanford plutonium was unsuitable for a gun-type bomb. The first nuclear device was detonated at the Trinity test in New Mexico on 16 July 1945.

The project delivered the bombs used in the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Through Operation Alsos its personnel also gathered intelligence on the German nuclear programme, and Soviet spies penetrated the project despite its emphasis on secrecy. After the war it tested weapons at Bikini Atoll in Operation Crossroads, helped to create the network of national laboratories and laid the foundations of the nuclear navy. It kept control of American atomic weapons research and production until the United States Atomic Energy Commission was formed in January 1947.
manichaeism: Mani was born in 216 CE in or near Ctesiphon, then in the Parthian Empire. According to the Cologne Mani-Codex, his parents belonged to the Jewish Christian Gnostic sect of the Elcesaites. His writings say he received revelations at the ages of 12 and 24, and that he grew dissatisfied with the Elcesaites. He saw his teaching as completing the partial truths of earlier faiths, among them Zoroastrian, Buddhist, Jewish and Christian traditions, and he wrote seven works, six in Syriac and one, the Shabuhragan, in Middle Persian. He presented that book to the Sasanian emperor Shapur I, who tolerated the spread of the religion but is not known to have followed it.

Manichaeism teaches a dualism in which a spiritual world of light stands against a material world of darkness. In its account the Father of Greatness ruled the World of Light and the King of Darkness the World of Darkness. When Darkness attacked, the Father of Greatness sent Original Man to fight it. Humanity, the world and the soul came from this battle, and light is gradually drawn out of matter and returned to the divine. Followers held that Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus had brought true teachings later corrupted, and that Mani was the final prophet.

Its sacramental rites included prayers, almsgiving, fasting and, most centrally, the daily ritual meal of the elect. Communal life centred on confession and the singing of hymns. As the religion spread east, translators often replaced the names of its deities with those of Zoroastrian figures, so that the Father of Greatness could be rendered as Zurwān.

Manichaeism spread quickly through Aramaic-speaking lands, the Mediterranean and the Middle East. It reached Rome in about 280, and persecution followed. The Sasanian emperor Bahram II had the apostle Mar Sisin killed in 291, and Roman rulers legislated against the religion under Diocletian, later in 372 under Valentinian I and Valens, and in 382 under Theodosius I. It had largely vanished from the Roman West by the end of the sixth century.

In the east it lasted longer. It reached Tang China in the seventh century and was the official religion of the Uyghur Khaganate until the khaganate collapsed in 840. The Tang court then banned it, but it revived under the Yuan dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries before being absorbed into Buddhism and Taoism. The temple of Cao'an in Jinjiang, Fujian, survives. Most of Mani's writings were lost, and manuscripts found at Turpan and Dunhuang in the early 20th century now supply original texts.
manila: Manila lies on the eastern shore of Manila Bay, on the western coast of the island of Luzon, 1,300 kilometres from mainland Asia. The protected harbour is regarded as the finest in Asia. The Pasig River flows through the middle of the city and divides it into northern and southern sections. Almost all of the city sits on prehistoric alluvial deposits built by the Pasig and on land reclaimed from the bay. The name derives from Maynilà, commonly interpreted as the place where indigo plants are abundant, from the Sanskrit nīla; it was probably given for the plants growing around the settlement, since indigo extraction became important in the area only in the 18th century.

The earliest evidence of human life near Manila is the Angono Petroglyphs, dated to around 3000 BCE. By 1258 a fortified Tagalog polity called Maynila existed on the site, and with Tondo it traded with the Song and Yuan dynasties of China. In 1365 both Brunei and Manila were conquered by the Majapahit Empire, which named Manila Selurong in Sanskrit texts.

On 24 June 1571, after Rajah Sulayman, the polity's last indigenous ruler, was defeated at the Battle of Bangkusay, the Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi began building the walled fortification of Intramuros. Manila became the capital of the captaincy general of the Spanish East Indies, administered for the Spanish crown from Mexico City in the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Its commercial networks were the first to extend across the Pacific Ocean and connect Asia with the Spanish Americas through the galleon trade.

Under American occupation Manila became the first chartered city in the country, by Philippine Commission Act No. 183 of 31 July 1901, and in 1905 Daniel Burnham was commissioned to design the new capital on the principles of the City Beautiful movement. During the Second World War it was razed by Japanese forces and by American shelling. It became autonomous with the Revised Charter of 18 June 1949, and most historical buildings were reconstructed, though many in Intramuros were damaged beyond repair.

Manila is the capital of the Philippines and its second most populous city after Quezon City, with 1,902,590 people in the 2024 census. It has 16 administrative districts, and the name is also used for Metro Manila, the capital region. The National Museum Complex in Rizal Park holds Juan Luna's painting Spoliarium, and the historic Walled City of Intramuros is administered by a national agency, the Intramuros Administration.
manisa: Manisa lies about 40 kilometres north-east of İzmir, with its historic quarter on the forested slopes of Mount Sipylus beside the Çaybaşı Stream. Near it are the rock called Niobe's Weeping Rock and an ancient bridge, the Red Bridge. The Gediz plain, formed by river deposits, stretches out below. Ancient writers called the city Magnesia ad Sipylum to tell it from Magnesia on the Maeander. Pliny the Elder says a notable city called Tantalis, the city of Tantalus, once stood on the same spot, and its ruins were still visible in his time.

The Cybele monument at Akpınar, on the northern flank of Mount Sipylus, is among the evidence of Hittite influence in the region of the Luwian kingdom of Arzawa. Figures of tradition such as Tantalus, Pelops and Niobe are tied to the mountain. In the early seventh century BCE the Lydians under the Mermnad dynasty ruled much of Anatolia from Sardis, 62 kilometres inland.

Under Roman rule the city became important after the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE, was nearly destroyed by an earthquake in the reign of Tiberius, and was restored by him. The Seljuks took it in 1076, and the Byzantine Empire recovered it after the Battle of Dorylaeum in 1097. During the Empire of Nicea, from 1204 to 1261, it held the imperial mint and treasury and was in effect the capital.

Turkish raids in the late 13th and early 14th centuries drove most inhabitants away after a failed campaign in 1302 by Michael IX. In 1313 Manisa fell to the Beylik of Saruhan, whose founder reigned until 1346, and the Ottomans absorbed it in 1410, after an interval following the Battle of Ankara. In a practice begun by Murad II in 1437, fifteen members of the Ottoman dynasty, among them Mehmed II and Süleyman I, governed the Saruhan district in seventeen near-continuous periods until 1595. The princes there gained experience of government, and the city is still known as the city of shahzades. A severe earthquake in 1595 dealt a heavy blow to its prosperity.

Manisa was one of the first Ottoman cities served by a railway, the Smyrna Cassaba line, which reached Kasaba in 1866. The Greek army occupied it on 26 May 1919 and left on 8 September 1922; most of the city was burned as the army retreated. Manisa was rebuilt, and its name replaced Saruhan for the province and the city in 1927.
manitoba: Manitoba lies at the longitudinal centre of Canada, bordered by Nunavut and the Northwest Territories to the north, Hudson Bay to the northeast, Ontario to the east, North Dakota and Minnesota to the south and Saskatchewan to the west. Its landscape runs from arctic tundra and the Hudson Bay coast in the north to boreal forest, large freshwater lakes and prairie in the centre and south. It lies at the centre of the Hudson Bay drainage basin, where much of the water drains into Lake Winnipeg and then north down the Nelson River. Most of the inhabited south developed in the bed of the prehistoric Glacial Lake Agassiz, and the Red River Valley is flat and fertile.

First Nations peoples settled the area about 10,000 years ago, shortly after the last ice age glaciers retreated. The Ojibwe, Cree, Dene, Sioux, Mandan and Assiniboine founded settlements, and the first farming was along the Red River, where corn and other seed crops were planted before contact with Europeans. English and French fur traders arrived in the early 17th century. England secured the region in 1670 as Rupert's Land under the Hudson's Bay Company, and the early economy centred on the trade of beaver pelts and other furs. Lord Selkirk brought the first agricultural settlers in 1811, and a Red River Colony of Indigenous and Métis people grew up.

Deep disagreements over self-determination during the transfer of Rupert's Land to Canada in 1869 led to armed resistance under the Métis leader Louis Riel, who established a provisional government. Its assembly sent three delegates to Ottawa, and the negotiations produced the Manitoba Act, introduced by Prime Minister Sir John A. Macdonald, which made Manitoba the fifth province of Canada in 1870. The name was chosen by Thomas Spence, and Riel preferred it to the alternative Assiniboia. Riel fled into exile, and the Canadian government blocked the Métis' attempts to obtain the land promised to them. Facing racism from a flood of settlers from Ontario, many Métis moved to what became Saskatchewan and Alberta.

By 1911 Winnipeg was the third largest city in Canada. Nellie McClung led the campaign for women's votes, and on 28 January 1916 Manitoba became the first province to allow women to vote in provincial elections, two years before Canada did so nationally.

Manitoba is a province of Canada with Winnipeg as its capital and largest city, home to nearly two thirds of the provincial population in its metropolitan region. English and French are both official languages of its legislature and courts under the Manitoba Act, a status the Supreme Court of Canada upheld in 1985. The population was 1,342,153 at the 2021 census. The Winnipeg-based Royal Winnipeg Ballet, granted its royal title in 1953, is Canada's oldest ballet company.
manmohan-singh: Manmohan Singh was born on 26 September 1932 in Gah, in Punjab, British India, into a Punjabi Sikh family of dried fruit traders. His mother died when he was very young, and his paternal grandmother, Jamna Devi, raised him. He was first educated at a local gurdwara and a government primary school in Urdu, then at the Khalsa School in Peshawar after the family moved there. After the Partition of India his family migrated to Haldwani and in 1948 to Amritsar. He took his bachelor's and master's degrees in economics at Panjab University in 1952 and 1954, completed the Economics Tripos at the University of Cambridge in 1957 and earned a doctorate at Oxford. He married Gursharan Kaur in 1958, and they had three daughters.

Singh taught economics at Panjab University and the Delhi School of Economics, and worked for the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development from 1966 to 1969. He served the Government of India as chief economic adviser from 1972, as secretary in the Finance Ministry from 1976, as governor of the Reserve Bank of India from 1982 to 1985, and as deputy chairman of the Planning Commission from 1985 to 1987. From 1987 to 1990 he was secretary general of the South Commission in Geneva.

In June 1991 Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao chose him as finance minister. India's foreign reserves then barely covered two weeks of imports. Despite resistance within the party, Singh and Rao removed the licensing system known as the licence raj, reduced state control and import taxes, eased foreign direct investment and began the privatisation of public companies. Singh sat in the Rajya Sabha from 1991 and was leader of the opposition there from 1998 to 2004.

After the 2004 general election Sonia Gandhi, chairperson of the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance, named Singh, a technocrat who had never won a direct popular election, as its candidate for prime minister. He took the oath on 22 May 2004. His first ministry passed laws and launched schemes including the Rural Employment Guarantee scheme and the Right to Information Act. In 2008 the Left Front withdrew its support over a civil nuclear agreement with the United States. After the 2009 election he was sworn in again on 22 May 2009, the first prime minister since Jawaharlal Nehru to win re-election after a full five-year term. His premiership ended on 17 May 2014.

Singh remained a member of the Rajya Sabha until April 2024. He died in New Delhi on 26 December 2024, aged 92, and received a state funeral on 28 December. He was the first Sikh prime minister of India. His colleague P. Chidambaram compared his part in the reforms of 1991 to that of Deng Xiaoping in China.
mannheim: Mannheim stands at the confluence of the Upper Rhine and the Neckar, in the Electoral Palatinate region of north-western Baden-Württemberg, on the Upper Rhine Plain. It forms a continuous urban zone with Ludwigshafen am Rhein across the river. The city centre is unusual for Germany: its streets are laid out in a grid, earning the nickname Quadratestadt, and most of the blocks are named by a letter and a number rather than by street names. The practice is centuries old and comes from the original use of the centre as a fort, whose internal system was kept when the streets became public.

A brick kiln of 74 CE to the early second century shows Roman settlement. The name was first recorded as Mannenheim in 766, in a twelfth-century copy of a Lorsch Abbey codex, and the place remained a village throughout the Middle Ages. In 1606 Frederick IV, Elector Palatine began building the fortress of Friedrichsburg and the adjacent city centre with its grid, and on 24 January 1607 he gave Mannheim the status of a city. Tilly's forces mostly levelled it around 1622 in the Thirty Years' War, and after rebuilding it was badly damaged by the French army in 1689. The National Theatre, founded in 1779, is called the oldest stage in Germany, and Friedrich Schiller's Die Räuber premiered there in 1782.

The city became known for inventions. Karl Drais built the first two-wheeled draisine in 1817, and Karl Benz drove the first automobile on the streets of Mannheim in 1886; in August 1888 his wife Bertha Benz made the first road trip by automobile, to Pforzheim and back. The Lanz Bulldog tractor followed in 1921, and Benz and Cie. built the first compact diesel-powered car in 1923. Mannheim became a Großstadt in 1896, and the Schütte-Lanz company, founded in 1909, built 22 airships. In the Second World War air raids destroyed the city centre and killed thousands of civilians, while 2,262 of the city's Jews were sent to concentration camps. The palace and water tower were rebuilt, and the University of Mannheim was established in 1967.

Mannheim is the second-largest city of Baden-Württemberg after Stuttgart, with a population of over 315,000, and the cultural and economic centre of the Rhine-Neckar region. It is a major railway junction and river port. Mannheim Palace, the former home of the Prince-elector of the Electoral Palatinate, now houses the University of Mannheim, and the Mannheim Water Tower, completed in 1886, is the civic symbol. The city has been a UNESCO City of Music since 2014.
manorialism: Manorialism grew out of the rural economy of the later Roman Empire, in which labour was the key factor of production. Successive administrations tried to stabilise the economy by fixing the social structure in place, and the coloni, the cultivators of the land, were not to leave the land they were attached to. Laws of Constantine I around 325 reinforced their semi-servile status. As Germanic kingdoms replaced Roman authority in the fifth century, Roman landlords were often simply replaced by Germanic ones with little change to the underlying situation. Self-sufficiency in the countryside received a boost in the eighth century, when normal trade in the Mediterranean was disrupted.

A manor was a local jurisdiction held by a lord, the seigneur, usually in return for undertakings to a higher lord. Bishops, abbots and military orders could be lords too. A manor held up to three classes of land: the demesne, directly controlled by the lord; dependent holdings of serfs or villeins, who supplied labour or part of their output; and free peasant land owing a fixed money rent. The lord also took charges for the use of his mill, bakery or wine-press, for hunting and feeding pigs in his woodland, and payments at each change of tenant.

Villeins were not slaves: they had legal rights under local custom and could go to court. Their holdings became in practice hereditary, and from the 13th century labour on the demesne was increasingly commuted into money payments. The demesne usually made up roughly a third of the arable area, and manors varied greatly from place to place.

Manorialism faded away slowly, together with its most vivid feature in the landscape, the open field system. It outlasted serfdom, since it continued with freehold labourers. According to Andrew Jones it also outlasted feudalism because it could maintain a warrior just as well as a capitalist landlord. The last feudal dues in France were abolished in the French Revolution, and in parts of eastern Germany the Rittergut manors of the Junkers remained until World War II.
mansa-musa: Musa was the ninth mansa of the Mali Empire. His birth date is unknown, but he appears to have been a young man in 1324. Accounts of his parentage differ: Djibril Tamsir Niane names his father as Faga Leye, a descendant of a brother of Sunjata, while Francois-Xavier Fauvelle has proposed that he was a grandson of Sunjata through his daughter.

By his own account, his predecessor led an expedition to explore the Atlantic and appointed Musa deputy, and when the mansa did not return Musa was crowned. Some modern historians suspect he deposed his predecessor and invented the story. Most of what is known comes from Arabic writers, especially Al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun.

Musa's wealth came mainly from taxing the salt trade from the north and from gold mined in Bambuk and Bure to the south. His early reign was spent in conflict with neighbouring non-Muslim societies. The empire reached its territorial peak under him, and Gao and Timbuktu came under Mali.

He made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and 1325, leaving his son Muhammad to rule. Arabic chroniclers give widely varying figures for his caravan and its gold, and modern historians treat them as rhetorical rather than statistical. He stayed about three months in Cairo, where his gifts are said to have lowered the value of gold, although Warren Schultz argues the fall was normal. The return journey cost many lives, and he borrowed from Cairo merchants. He persuaded the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili and Maliki jurists to come to Mali, and Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning.

The date of his death is uncertain: Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths suggest 1332, while a later report points to 1337, which Nehemia Levtzion thought most likely. Musa is commonly seen as Mali's golden age, though this may reflect that his reign is the best recorded in Arabic sources. In Mandé oral tradition he is less prominent than earlier rulers, and some jeliw criticise him for wasting Mali's wealth. European maps from the Catalan Atlas of 1375 onward show a wealthy West African ruler inspired by his pilgrimage.
manta-ecuador: Manta, also known as San Pablo de Manta, is the head of the Manta Canton and the largest and most populated city of Manabí Province. It lies on the Pacific coast and has the largest seaport in Ecuador. Despite its position on the equator, the Humboldt Current gives it an arid climate. The city is cloudy and hot most of the year, and rainfall is erratic and largely confined to the months between January and April, occurring mainly during El Niño events, when the Humboldt Current weakens.

Manta has existed since Pre-Columbian times, when it was a trading post for the Manta, also known as the Manteños. The Central Bank Museum in the city holds an important collection of Pre-Columbian craft.

In 1735 Charles Marie de La Condamine, leading the French mission to measure the location of the equator, arrived in Ecuador through the port of Manta, and from there began his journey inland to Quito. Nearby Montecristi, founded in the early 17th century, has colonial architecture and is known for its wickerwork weaving; the original Panama hats were historically produced in Ecuador, and are made at Montecristi.

Between 1999 and 2009 the Manta Air Base, also called the Eloy Alfaro Air Base, was used by U.S. air forces to support anti-narcotics operations and surveillance flights against Colombian drug trafficking cartels. The Ecuadorian government did not renew the lease.

The 2022 census gave the city a population of 258,697. Its main economic activity is tuna fishing and canning, with processed tuna exported abroad, alongside vegetable oil and other chemical products. Manta has an international airport, several universities, including the Universidad Laica Eloy Alfaro, and an international film festival.
manuel-azana: Manuel Azaña Díaz was born on 10 January 1880 into a wealthy family and was orphaned young. He took a doctorate at the Universidad Complutense in 1900, worked from 1909 in the Directorate of the Registries and practised as a civil law notary. He joined the Reformist Republican Party in 1914, wrote for newspapers and was secretary of the Ateneo de Madrid from 1913 to 1920. He published a manifesto against the dictator Primo de Rivera and Alfonso XIII in 1924, and in 1930 signed the Pact of San Sebastián, which united the republican and regionalist parties.

After the Second Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931 Azaña became Minister of War and then, in October, prime minister, leading a coalition of left-wing parties and the Socialists. His government expanded public education, passed labour laws, reduced the size of the army and abolished Church-operated schools and charities. An agrarian law, passed late in 1932, was little carried out: only 12,000 families received land in the first two years. Alcalá-Zamora ordered his resignation on 8 September 1933, and the right won the election that November.

Azaña founded the Republican Left in 1934 and helped build the Popular Front, which won the election of 16 February 1936. He became prime minister again on 19 February and was elected President of the Republic on 7 April 1936. On 17 July a military rising began the Spanish Civil War. From October 1936 he never lived in Madrid again, and on 5 February 1939 he crossed into France on foot.

Azaña resigned as president on 3 March 1939 rather than return to Madrid, a decision that Nationalist and Republican commentators alike condemned as desertion. After the German invasion of France the Mexican government gave him citizenship and the rank of honorary ambassador, so that he could not be arrested. He died at Montauban on 3 November 1940, and the flag of Mexico covered his coffin. His diaries are a main source for the Republican government in the war, and his speech of 18 July 1938 asked for peace, pity and pardon. Piers Brendon calls him a brilliant speaker but a clumsy actor in politics, and he has become a hero of the left in Spain.
manuel-belgrano: Manuel Belgrano was born in Buenos Aires on 3 June 1770, the fourth child of the Italian merchant Domingo Belgrano y Peri. As a criollo he ranked below the peninsulares. He studied at the San Carlos school, then in Spain, where he chose law rather than commerce. A papal dispensation let him read forbidden authors such as Montesquieu and Rousseau. He returned in 1794 as perpetual secretary of the Commerce Consulate of Buenos Aires and held the post until 1810. Unable to change the economic system, he put his effort into education, advocating schools of agriculture and commerce and free primary schools for poor children.

Belgrano first took part in fighting during the first British invasion of the River Plate, when his untrained men scattered after a single cannon shot. After Ferdinand VII was deposed, he led the Carlotist movement, which sought to put the king's sister Carlota Joaquina, then in Rio de Janeiro, in his place.

He took part in the plot against the viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros in May 1810 and was elected to the Primera Junta. As the junta's delegate he led the campaign to Paraguay, where Bernardo de Velasco beat him at Paraguarí and Tacuarí.

He designed the flag while fortifying Rosario. The First Triumvirate did not approve it, and Belgrano learned this only weeks later, at Jujuy. Facing royalist armies from Upper Peru, he ordered the Jujuy Exodus, which moved the province's whole population to San Miguel de Tucumán. His counter-offensive won the Battle of Tucumán and then a full victory over Pío Tristán at Salta.

Defeats at Vilcapugio and Ayohuma ended his incursion into Upper Peru, and José de San Martín replaced him. Belgrano then went to Europe with Bernardino Rivadavia to seek support, and on his return took part in the Congress of Tucumán, which declared independence in 1816. He backed the Inca plan for a constitutional monarchy under an Inca descendant, which delegates from Buenos Aires strongly rejected.

Belgrano took command of the Army of the North again, but his troops mutinied in January 1820. Gravely ill, he was briefly imprisoned in Tucumán during a coup and was released when it ended. He died of dropsy on 20 June 1820, reportedly saying, Oh, my homeland. His flag was approved by the Congress of Tucumán as the national flag. Argentines regard him as one of the main Founding Fathers, and National Flag Day is held on 20 June in memory of his death.

A bronze equestrian statue stands in the Plaza de Mayo, and a mausoleum by Ettore Ximenes, completed in 1903, holds his ashes at the Santo Domingo Convent. He remained a monarchist, favouring a constitutional monarchy on the British pattern, and he translated George Washington's Farewell Address into Spanish.
manuel-i-komnenos: Manuel was born on 28 November 1118 in the Purple Chamber of the Great Palace of Constantinople, and was therefore called Porphyrogenitus, born in the purple. He was the eighth child and fourth son of the emperor John II Komnenos and Irene of Hungary. He was trained as a soldier and accompanied his father on campaigns against the Anatolian Turks. In 1143 John lay dying from a hunting accident and chose Manuel over his elder surviving brother Isaac, citing Manuel's courage and readiness to take advice. After John died on 8 April 1143 the armies acclaimed Manuel, and he was crowned in Constantinople in mid-August 1143 after John Axouch had arrested Isaac.

Manuel pursued an energetic foreign policy meant to restore the empire as the great power of the Mediterranean. In 1146 he led a punitive expedition against Masud, Sultan of Rûm. In 1147 the Second Crusade crossed his lands, with clashes between Byzantines and Germans, and Roger II of Sicily captured Corfu. Manuel allied with Conrad III of Germany and the Venetians and recovered Corfu in 1149. After Conrad died in 1152 no agreement could be reached with Frederick Barbarossa, and Manuel turned to the Papacy, the Normans, Hungary and the crusader states.

In 1167 an army under Andronikos Kontostephanos won a decisive victory at Sirmium, and the peace that followed gave the empire Syrmia, Bosnia and Dalmatia, so that by 1168 nearly the whole eastern Adriatic coast was in his hands. He established a protectorate over the crusader states, and in autumn 1169 sent a large fleet and army to join King Amalric I of Jerusalem in an invasion of Egypt.

Manuel's last years were marked by the defeat at Myriokephalon, which resulted largely from his attacking a well-defended Seljuk position. He then made an advantageous peace with Kilij Arslan II, but Myriokephalon proved the empire's last unsuccessful effort to recover the interior of Anatolia. He died on 24 September 1180, and his son Alexios II Komnenos succeeded him.
