In 54 BCE Brutus served as triumvir monetalis and issued denarii with the portraits of two ancestors honoured as defenders of liberty, Lucius Junius Brutus and Gaius Servilius Ahala. In 52 he wrote a pamphlet opposing demands that Pompey be made dictator.

When Caesar's Civil War began in January 49 BCE, Brutus sided with Pompey, his father's killer, perhaps because his closest allies, among them Cato and Cicero, also did. After Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus on 9 August 48 BCE, Brutus wrote to Caesar, who welcomed him into his camp. Caesar later made him governor of Cisalpine Gaul and praetor urbanus for 44.

By autumn 45 BCE public opinion of Caesar was souring, and ancient authors report graffiti recalling Lucius Junius Brutus and taunts that Marcus was failing his ancestors. In February 44 Caesar accepted the title dictator perpetuo. Brutus took a leading part in the assassination on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BCE. Cicero brokered a settlement with an amnesty for the assassins and ratification of Caesar's acts for two years.

Brutus and Cassius left Rome in April 44 BCE and went east. After Octavian had a law passed retroactively making the conspirators murderers, a second civil war followed. At the two battles of Philippi in October 42 BCE the Caesarians decisively defeated their armies, and Brutus took his own life.

His name has become a byword for betrayal, and Dante placed him in the lowest circle of Hell. Others have praised him as a committed republican who fought for freedom against tyranny. Historians hold no consensus on his actions, and Ronald Syme observed that to judge Brutus because he failed is simply to judge from the results.
marcus-licinius-crassus: Crassus belonged to the gens Licinia, an old and highly respected plebeian family, and was the second of three sons of the senator Publius Licinius Crassus. His father and younger brother were killed, or took their own lives, in Rome in the winter of 87 to 86 BCE when hunted down by supporters of Gaius Marius. Plutarch says his wealth was acquired rather than inherited and that he was raised in modest circumstances. He fled to Hispania, where he raised 2,500 men, and later joined Sulla. At the Battle of the Colline Gate he commanded the right flank, whose success helped Sulla win the battle.

Crassus rebuilt his family's wealth by buying the seized property of Sulla's victims at discounted auctions. Pliny the Elder put his wealth at about 200 million sesterces. Plutarch says that he bought burnt and collapsing houses cheaply and rebuilt them with slave labour.

As praetor in 73 BCE he was sent by the Senate against Spartacus after several legions had been defeated. When part of his army fled, he revived decimation, the execution of one man in ten, chosen by lot. In the battle at the Silarius river he won a decisive victory, and Spartacus is believed to have been killed. Crassus ordered the six thousand captured slaves crucified along the Via Appia. He and Pompey were consuls in 70 BCE and were not friendly in office.

In 65 BCE Crassus was censor and acted as Julius Caesar's patron. Caesar's mediation between Crassus and Pompey led to the First Triumvirate in 60 BCE. After the Luca Conference in 56 BCE, a law assigned Syria to Crassus.

As governor of Syria, Crassus crossed the Euphrates to attack Parthia, seeking riches and a victory to match those of Pompey and Caesar. At the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE, Parthian horse archers defeated his heavy infantry. His son Publius died in the battle, and a fight broke out at a parley with the Parthian general Surena, in which Crassus was killed. A later story says the Parthians poured molten gold into his mouth to mock his greed. His death permanently unravelled the alliance between Caesar and Pompey, and within four years Caesar crossed the Rubicon.
marcus-vipsanius-agrippa: Agrippa came from a plebeian family of uncertain origin in the Italian countryside, humbler than the great aristocratic houses though wealthy by ordinary standards. Pliny the Elder derived his cognomen from a breech birth and said he was lame as a child. He was the same age as Octavian, the future Augustus, and the two were educated together. In 45 BCE Julius Caesar sent them to study at Apollonia on the Illyrian coast, where news of Caesar's assassination reached them in March 44 BCE. Agrippa and Quintus Salvidienus Rufus advised Octavian to march on Rome with the troops from Macedonia, but Octavian sailed to Italy with a small retinue.

Agrippa helped Octavian raise troops, probably fought at Philippi in 42 BCE and took a major part in the Perusine War. As urban praetor in 40 BCE he defended Italy against Sextus Pompeius and retook Sipontum from Antony. As governor of Transalpine Gaul he put down an Aquitanian rising in 38 BCE and crossed the Rhine. He was consul for 37 BCE, far below the usual minimum age of 43, to prepare the war against Sextus Pompeius, building the harbour of Portus Julius and larger ships with an improved grappling hook. In 36 BCE he won the battles of Mylae and Naulochus and received a naval crown decorated with ships' beaks.

As aedile in 33 BCE he repaired streets and aqueducts, cleaned the Cloaca Maxima and built baths and gardens. At Actium on 2 September 31 BCE the victory is held to have been mainly his, and he built the first Pantheon to mark it. After 23 BCE his powers grew to include proconsular authority and, in 18 BCE, the powers of a tribune; in 21 BCE he married Augustus's daughter Julia the Elder. In 19 BCE he put down a rising of the Cantabrians in Hispania, and from 17 BCE he governed the east a second time.

Agrippa began the conquest of the upper Danube region, which became the province of Pannonia in 13 BCE, and died in Campania in 12 BCE, aged fifty or fifty-one. Augustus gave him a lavish funeral, mourned for over a month and placed his remains in his own mausoleum. Agrippa also wrote on geography; under his supervision Caesar's plan for a survey of the empire was carried out, and a circular chart was set up in the colonnade built by his sister Polla. He was the maternal grandfather of Caligula and the maternal great-grandfather of Nero.
mardin: Mardin lies near the Syrian border on a rocky hill near the Tigris River. The old city is built mostly on the southern slope of a long hill topped by a rocky ridge, and the slope descends towards the Mesopotamian plain. The historic citadel occupies the top of the ridge. Houses have several levels and terraces to suit the sloping site, which gives the old city its stepped appearance, and most buildings are of beige limestone quarried locally.

A legal document of the Neo-Assyrian period mentions a road to Mardiānê, commonly identified with Mardin. In the Roman period the city was known as Marida, from a Syriac word meaning fortress. The Byzantine city was captured in 640 by the Muslim commander Iyad ibn Ghanm, and control then passed between the Hamdanids, the Marwanids, the Uqaylids and, from 1085, the Great Seljuks.

From 1103 Mardin was the capital of one of the two main branches of the Artuqid dynasty, an Oghuz Turkish family, under whom many of its mosques and madrasas were built. The last Artuqid ruler, al-Salih, yielded the city to Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu in 1408–9. The Aq Qoyunlu held it for the rest of the 15th century, and the Safavid ruler Ismail I captured it in 1507. The Ottomans forced its surrender in late 1516 or early 1517.

Mardin kept large Syriac and Armenian populations and was a centre of several churches. On the eve of the First World War it had over 12,000 Syriacs and over 7,500 Armenians. In the war it was one of the sites of the Syriac and Armenian genocides. In 1923 it became the capital of a province of the same name.

Mardin is known for the Artuqid architecture of its old city. Its landmarks include the Great Mosque of Mardin, the Sultan İsa Medrese of 1385 and Mardin Castle. The Syriac Orthodox Saffron Monastery stands about 5 kilometres to the south-east. In February 2000 the Turkish Ministry of Culture placed the city and its surrounding landscape on the country's Tentative List for UNESCO World Heritage nomination. The population is a mix of Kurds, Arabs, Mhallami and Assyrians.
marduk: Marduk, written in cuneiform dAMAR.UTU, from the Sumerian for calf of the sun, was a god of ancient Mesopotamia and patron deity of Babylon, where he was worshipped in the Esagila temple. He and Babylon were unimportant in the 3rd millennium BCE, and the earliest mention is a fragmentary inscription in which an unnamed ruler of a city probably to be read as Babylon built a temple for him. His original role is unknown; one scholar suggests a minor underworld god.

Under the First Dynasty of Babylon, in the reign of Sumu-la-El, Marduk appears in oaths and year names. Sanctuaries to him began to appear in other cities from the reign of Hammurabi. In the Kassite period names containing his name passed 10 per cent and his temple at Nippur was well established, though Enlil still headed the list of gods with Anu and Ea.

Marduk came to be worshipped as a god of creation, justice, water, agriculture, magic and medicine. His symbol was the spade, he was associated with the dragon-like Mušḫuššu, and by the 1st millennium BCE he was linked with the planet Jupiter. He was the son of Ea and was identified with Asalluhi, who appears with Ea in incantations, and with Enlil, so that he was often called the Enlil of the gods. He was commonly called Bēl, lord. Under Nebuchadnezzar I in the 2nd millennium BCE he was enshrined as leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon.

The Enūma Eliš, the Babylonian epic of creation, tells how Marduk, born to Ea and Damkina, defeats Tiamat, fashions the world from her corpse with Babylon at its centre, becomes king of the gods and receives fifty names, fifty being the number of Enlil. A ritual tablet says the epic was recited, and perhaps reenacted, at the Akitu festival. Other texts show his anger and mercy: in Ludlul bēl nēmeqi, called the Babylonian Job, a sufferer blames Marduk's anger for his illness and praises his mercy once healed.

In the Epic of Erra, by contrast, Marduk leaves his seat in the Esagila and the world falls into instability. In the Assyrian Marduk Ordeal Text he is held captive and subjected to a river ordeal, though the text is not simply hostile to him. In Neo-Assyrian Assyria only Shamash was invoked more often than Marduk in incantation-prayers.
margaret-i-of-denmark: Margaret was born in March 1353 at Søborg Castle, the sixth and youngest child of Valdemar IV of Denmark and Queen Helvig. In 1359, aged six, she was engaged to the 18-year-old Haakon VI, youngest son of King Magnus IV and VII of Sweden and Norway. The match served her father's wish to regain Scania, which had been mortgaged to Sweden since 1332, and it was dissolved and revived amid the wars of those years. The wedding took place in Copenhagen on 9 April 1363, when she was ten.

After her father's death in 1375, Margaret secured the election of the infant Olaf as king of Denmark, over the claims of her sister Ingeborg's husband Henry III, Duke of Mecklenburg, and their son Albert. Olaf succeeded Haakon in Norway and died in 1387, aged 16. Margaret was then chosen regent of Denmark and Norway. She had already recovered Schleswig from the Holstein-Rendsburg counts through the Compact of Nyborg of 1386, which left the Danish crown with most of the advantages.

Swedish nobles in revolt against King Albert of Mecklenburg offered her the regency of Sweden. In March 1388, at Dalaborg Castle, they elected her Sovereign Lady and Ruler. Albert returned with mercenaries, and on 24 February 1389 his forces were beaten near Falköping, at either Aasle or Falan, even though Margaret's Mecklenburger commander Henrik Parow was killed.

Albert was released under the Compact of Lindholm of 1395 on a promise to pay 60,000 marks, and the Hanseatic League handed Stockholm to Margaret in September 1398. She adopted her great-nephew Bogislav, who took the name Erik of Pomerania, and on 17 June 1397 he was crowned in Kalmar as king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, while she remained the effective ruler.

Margaret took back crown lands from nobles and the church, replaced worthless copper tokens with silver coin and kept out of the war between France and England. She bought Gotland from Albert of Mecklenburg and the Livonian Order and regained much of Schleswig by purchase.

In 1412 she went to war with Holstein to recover the rest, and she fell ill on board her ship in Flensburg Harbour and died on the night of 28 October. Her sarcophagus, made by Johannes Junge in 1423, stands behind the high altar of Roskilde Cathedral. Historians have seen her as an idealist, a nationalist or a calculating pursuer of dynastic power, while few dispute her political skill.
margaret-maid-of-norway: Margaret was born at Tønsberg in Norway between March and 9 April 1283, the only child of King Eric II of Norway and Margaret, daughter of Alexander III of Scotland, who died apparently from complications of childbirth. The infant was kept in Bergen in the custody of Narve, Bishop of Bergen.

Alexander III's last surviving son died on 28 January 1284, and on 5 February the king had his earls, barons and clan chiefs swear at Scone to accept Margaret as his heir. Alexander set out on horseback in stormy weather on the evening of 18 March 1286 and was found dead with a broken neck the next day, and his posthumous child by Yolanda of Dreux was stillborn in November.

After Alexander's death, Scottish magnates chose six guardians to govern the country. Robert Bruce, 5th Lord of Annandale, and John Balliol, Lord of Galloway, were in dispute, and Bruce raised a rebellion with his son, the Earl of Carrick, which was defeated in early 1287. Because the situation was precarious, Eric was reluctant to send his three-year-old daughter to Scotland.

In 1289 he and Edward I of England negotiated her marriage to Edward of Caernarfon, and the Treaty of Salisbury of 6 November 1289 asked Edward to act for his grandniece. The Treaty of Birgham, agreed on 18 July 1290, provided that Scotland would remain fully independent despite the union and that Margaret alone would be inaugurated at Scone.

Margaret sailed from Bergen in late summer 1290 on her father's ship, with Bishop Narve in her entourage. She fell ill, and the ship put in at Orkney about 23 September. She suffered for up to a week, from food poisoning or, less likely, motion sickness, and died between 26 and 29 September 1290 in the arms of Bishop Narve. Her coffin was taken to Bergen, where Eric had it opened to confirm her identity.

Margaret was the last legitimate descendant of William the Lion, and thirteen men claimed the succession, chiefly Bruce and Balliol. In 1301 a German woman impersonated her and was burned at the stake. Historians disagree whether she was a queen. She was never inaugurated, and Scots called her their lady far more often than their queen. Her biographer Archie Duncan argues that she was never queen of Scots, while Norman H. Reid holds that she was accepted as queen, though her reign never started. Modern writers nearly always call her queen, and reference books give 19 March 1286 as the start of her reign.
margaret-of-anjou: Margaret was born on 23 March 1430 at Pont-à-Mousson in Lorraine, the second daughter of René of Anjou, titular king of Naples, Sicily and Jerusalem, and Isabella, Duchess of Lorraine. Several women of her family exercised power as regents, among them her mother and her grandmother Yolande of Aragon, which may have shaped her later actions.

In 1444 she was betrothed by proxy to Henry VI of England, in a marriage negotiated principally by William de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk, as part of peace efforts near the end of the Hundred Years' War. She married Henry at Titchfield Abbey on 23 April 1445 and was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 30 May. The loss of Maine to Anjou, negotiated soon afterwards, was deeply unpopular.

Henry's mental condition was unstable when they married, and by the birth of their only son, Edward of Westminster, on 13 October 1453, he had suffered a complete breakdown. Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, was Lord Protector in 1453 and 1454. In May 1455 Margaret and Henry called a Great Council that excluded the Yorkists, and York marched south to meet the Lancastrian army, which was crushed at the First Battle of St Albans on 22 May. Historians differ on when her enmity with York began. Helen Maurer places it in 1455, while Paul Murray Kendall held that it came earlier.

Margaret's commander Henry Beaufort, 3rd Duke of Somerset, won the Battle of Wakefield on 30 December 1460, where York was killed. She won the Second Battle of St Albans on 17 February 1461. The Lancastrians lost at Towton on 29 March 1461, and Edward, York's son, deposed Henry and took the throne as Edward IV. Margaret fled to Scotland and then France, where, at the instigation of her cousin Louis XI, she accepted an alliance with Warwick, sealed by the marriage of her son to Warwick's daughter Anne Neville.

Warwick was defeated and killed at the Battle of Barnet on 14 April 1471. At the Battle of Tewkesbury on 4 May, Margaret led her own army to defeat, and her seventeen-year-old son was killed. It is not known whether he died in the fighting or was executed afterwards by the Duke of Clarence. She was taken captive and in 1475 was ransomed by Louis XI. She lived in France for seven years as a poor relation of the king, and died on 25 August 1482 at the castle of Dampierre-sur-Loire, aged 52.
She obtained a licence on 30 March 1448 to found Queens' College, Cambridge, and many of her letters survive. William Shakespeare made her a major character in his first group of history plays.
margaret-of-austria-duchess-of-savoy: Margaret was born in Brussels on 10 January 1480, the daughter of Maximilian of Austria and Mary of Burgundy. Her mother died in 1482, and the Treaty of Arras that year promised her in marriage to the Dauphin Charles of France, and she was raised at the French court as a future queen. In 1497 she married John, Prince of Asturias, in Burgos Cathedral, but he died of fever six months later, and she gave birth to a stillborn daughter in 1498.

In 1501 she married Philibert II, Duke of Savoy. When she came to Savoy the government was in the hands of his illegitimate brother René, and she fought to strip him of his powers until he was declared a traitor and took refuge in France. She then took hold of the government herself. Philibert died in 1504.

In 1507 her father Maximilian I named her governor of the Low Countries and guardian of her nephew Charles. She governed from Mechelen until 1515 and again from 1519 until her death, for Maximilian and then for Charles V. In 1508 she helped form the League of Cambrai, which turned French attention to northern Italy. She struggled with Charles of Egmont of Guelders and in 1513 had to recognise him as duke. She restored the Intercursus Magnus trade agreement with England, which favoured Flemish textiles, and in 1524 signed a grain agreement with Frederick I of Denmark. Her rule was relatively peaceful apart from the early Reformation: Jan van Essen and Hendrik Vos were burnt in Brussels in 1523.
Her court at Mechelen was visited by Erasmus, Adrian of Utrecht and Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, who dedicated a work on the female sex to her, and from 1513 to 1514 Anne Boleyn was in her household.

Margaret commissioned manuscripts from the Ghent-Bruges school and had the Sforza Hours finished by her court artist Gerard Horenbout. Her collection passed to Charles V and Mary of Hungary and later to Philip II of Spain. On 15 November 1530 she stepped on broken glass, gangrene set in and her leg was amputated. She died soon after midnight on 1 December, having named Charles her heir. She was buried beside Philibert at the Royal Monastery of Brou, under a tomb by Conrat Meit, and Mary of Hungary succeeded her as governor.
margaret-thatcher: Margaret Hilda Roberts was born on 13 October 1925 in Grantham, Lincolnshire. Her father, Alfred Roberts, owned a tobacconist's and a grocery shop, served as an alderman and was a Methodist local preacher; he brought her up as a strict Wesleyan Methodist. She won a scholarship to Kesteven and Grantham Girls' School and entered Somerville College, Oxford, in October 1943 to study chemistry.

In 1950 and 1951 she was the Conservative candidate for the Labour seat of Dartford, losing both times. She married Denis Thatcher in December 1951 and qualified as a barrister in 1953. She was elected Member of Parliament for Finchley in 1959. Edward Heath appointed her Secretary of State for Education and Science in 1970, and in 1975 she defeated him in the Conservative Party leadership election, becoming the first woman to lead a major British political party.

Thatcher became prime minister on 4 May 1979. Her economic policies emphasised individual liberty, the privatisation of state-owned companies and reducing the power of trade unions. Her popularity waned during the recession and rising unemployment, but victory in the Falklands War in 1982 brought a resurgence of support and a landslide victory in 1983. In 1984 she survived the Provisional IRA's bombing of a Brighton hotel, and she achieved a political victory against the National Union of Mineworkers in the strike of 1984–85. In 1986 she oversaw the deregulation of financial markets known as the Big Bang.

She won a third term in 1987. Her support for the Community Charge, also called the poll tax, was widely unpopular, and her increasingly Eurosceptic views were not shared by others in her cabinet. After a challenge to her leadership she resigned in 1990 and was succeeded by John Major.

Thatcher retired from the House of Commons in 1992 and became Baroness Thatcher with a life peerage. She died of a stroke at the Ritz Hotel, London, on 8 April 2013, aged 87. Thatcherism was a systematic overhaul of the post-war consensus on Keynesianism, the welfare state, nationalised industry and high taxes. During her tenure the number of adults owning shares rose from 7 per cent to 25 per cent, and more than a million families bought their council houses. She remains a polarising figure, and the legacy of the shift towards neoliberal policies is still debated.
margaret-tudor: Margaret was born on 29 November 1489 at the Palace of Westminster, the second child and first daughter of Henry VII and Elizabeth of York. Her siblings included Arthur, Prince of Wales, the future Henry VIII, and Mary, who briefly became Queen of France. The Treaty of Perpetual Peace of 24 January 1502 was the first peace between England and Scotland in over 170 years, and the marriage treaty concluded the same day was meant to guarantee it. The marriage was completed by proxy at Richmond Palace on 15 January 1503, and Margaret left for Scotland that summer, crossing the border at Berwick upon Tweed on 1 August.

After James IV died at Flodden in 1513, a parliament at Stirling confirmed Margaret as regent. She was the sister of an enemy king, and a pro-French party urged that John Stewart, Duke of Albany, born and raised in France, replace her. By July 1514 she had reconciled the contending parties, and Scotland and France concluded peace with England. But on 6 August 1514 she secretly married Archibald Douglas, 6th Earl of Angus, which alienated other noble houses, and by the terms of her husband's will she had forfeited the regency. Albany was installed in 1515 and gained custody of her two sons. Pregnant by Angus, she escaped to England, where Henry VIII received her well, and returned in 1517.

Her marriage to Angus declined. In 1524 she took advantage of Albany's absence in France to bring the twelve-year-old James V from Stirling to Edinburgh, and Parliament declared the regency over. She was recognised in November as the king's chief councillor. When Angus arrived in Edinburgh with armed men she had cannon fired on him. In March 1527 Pope Clement VII granted her divorce, and on 3 March 1528 she married Henry Stewart, whom James V made Lord Methven. In June 1528 James freed himself from Angus. Margaret helped bring about the Anglo-Scottish peace agreement of May 1534.

Margaret died at Methven Castle on 18 October 1541, aged 51, after what was reported as palsy, possibly resulting from a stroke. She was buried at the Charterhouse in Perth. Through her first marriage she was the grandmother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and through her second, of Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley. Her descendants brought the House of Stuart to the thrones of England and Ireland, culminating in the Union of the Crowns under her great-grandson James VI and I in 1603.
margarita-island: Margarita Island lies in the Caribbean Sea off the north-west coast of Venezuela. It is in fact two islands, Paraguachoa in the east and Macanao in the west, joined by La Restinga, a sandy tombolo that encloses a lagoon. Together they are 78 kilometres long and up to 20 kilometres wide. With the islands of Coche and Cubagua the island forms the state of Nueva Esparta, whose capital, La Asunción, lies on it. Macanao has a mountain range along its length, and Paraguachoa one running north to south.

Christopher Columbus was the first European to reach the island, in 1498. Its native people were the Waikeri. The coast was rich in pearls, which accounted for almost a third of all tribute from the Western Hemisphere to the Spanish Crown. The island became the centre of the Spanish colonial Margarita Province, established in 1525, and was fortified against pirate attacks. In 1561 the conquistador Lope de Aguirre seized it and killed the governor Juan Villadrando. After the French buccaneer Marquis de Maintenon attacked in early 1676, the Santa Rosa de la Eminencia castle was built.

The island gained independence from the Spanish in 1814, after the collapse of the First Republic of Venezuela, and became the first permanently free territory in Venezuela. In that year Luisa Cáceres de Arismendi was held in the Fortress of Santa Rosa to put pressure on her husband Juan Bautista Arismendi, who was fighting for independence. In 1815 General Pablo Morillo landed with 18 warships and 42 cargo ships to put down revolts. In 1816 Simón Bolívar was confirmed there as Commander-in-Chief of the Second Republic of Venezuela, and from the island began a nine-year campaign to free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from the Spanish Crown.

La Asunción, the state capital, is overlooked by the Santa Rosa de la Eminencia castle, and Pampatar holds the San Carlos de Borromeo Fortress, built in the late 17th century. Porlamar is the largest city. The island became a duty-free port in 1974, and tourism has been its main industry. The Tetas de María Guevara, two small hills, lie in the Laguna de La Restinga National Park, declared in 1974.
maria-carolina-of-austria: Maria Carolina was born on 13 August 1752 at Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the thirteenth child of Empress Maria Theresa and Holy Roman Emperor Francis I. She was known in the family as Charlotte and was the daughter who most resembled her mother in her strong-willed character. She grew up close to her youngest sister, Maria Antonia, with whom she shared a governess.

Her marriage came about because two elder sisters, each engaged to Ferdinand IV of Naples, died of smallpox. Charles III of Spain, Ferdinand's father, wanted to keep the Austro-Spanish alliance and asked for a replacement. Maria Carolina was married by proxy on 7 April 1768 and entered the kingdom on 12 May. She bore eighteen children between 1772 and 1793, of whom seven reached adulthood.

After the birth of an heir in 1775 she joined the Privy Council. A quarrel over Freemasonry, which she favoured, led to the dismissal of the minister Bernardo Tanucci in October 1776 and ended Spanish influence in Naples. Together with Sir John Acton she enlarged the navy, opening four marine colleges and commissioning 150 ships. She patronised Angelica Kauffman and Jacob Philipp Hackert, and in 1784 founded the San Leucio silk-weaving colony.

The French Revolution changed her course. Alarmed for her sister Marie Antoinette, she abandoned enlightened absolutism, divided Naples into twelve police wards and created a secret police. After Marie Antoinette's execution in October 1793 she banned the works of Gaetano Filangieri and Giuseppe Maria Galanti and allied Naples with Britain against France. A failed attack on the Roman Republic forced the royal family to flee to Sicily in January 1799, and the Parthenopean Republic lasted six months before royal forces retook Naples.

The court returned to Naples in 1802 after Maria Carolina's two years in Vienna. French forces under Napoleon's brother Joseph Bonaparte drove the family back to Sicily in February 1806. In 1813 her husband appointed their son Francis regent, which ended her political influence, and she was made to leave for Vienna.

She reached Vienna in January 1814 and negotiated with Prince Metternich for the restoration of her husband. She died on 8 September 1814 of a stroke, a year before his return, and was buried in the Imperial Crypt. She was the last surviving child of Maria Theresa.
maria-ii-of-portugal: Maria da Glória was born on 4 April 1819 in the Palace of São Cristóvão in Rio de Janeiro, the eldest daughter of Pedro, later Pedro I of Brazil, and of Maria Leopoldina, daughter of Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor. She is the only European monarch to have been born outside Europe. The death of her grandfather João VI in March 1826 caused a succession crisis, since Pedro had proclaimed Brazilian independence in 1822 and his younger brother Miguel had been exiled to Austria after rebellions. Pedro renounced the Portuguese throne in favour of the seven-year-old Maria, who was to marry Miguel, accept the liberal constitution and act as regent until she came of age.

Maria stayed in Brazil during her first reign, with her aunt Isabel Maria as regent until Miguel returned in early 1828. A few months after his arrival he deposed Maria, proclaimed himself king on 11 July 1828 and abrogated the constitution, which began the Liberal Wars. Maria arrived in Gibraltar on 3 September 1828 to learn of the coup. She went to London, where the Wellington and Peel ministry backed Miguel, and returned to Brazil in October 1829.

In 1831 Pedro abdicated the Brazilian crown and came to Europe, taking the title Duke of Braganza and acting as regent in her name. He left Maria in Paris to finish her education, sailed to the Azores in March 1832 and landed at Matosinhos on 8 July. After the Siege of Porto, his forces entered Lisbon on 24 July 1833. Maria reached Lisbon for the first time in September 1833. Miguel abdicated in 1834, and Maria was restored as undisputed queen at fifteen.

Her second reign was marked by turmoil. She married Auguste, Duke of Leuchtenberg, in January 1835, and he died two months later. In April 1836 she married Prince Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, who became King Fernando II. The September Revolution of 1836 led to the Constitution of 1838, Costa Cabral restored the Charter of 1826 in 1842, and the Maria da Fonte revolt of 1846 led to the Patuleia civil war, which ended in June 1847.

Maria faced difficult pregnancies from the age of eighteen, and doctors warned her of the risks. She is said to have replied that if she died she would die at her post. She died on 15 November 1853, aged 34, in labour with the stillborn Infante Eugénio, her eleventh child. Her eldest son succeeded as Pedro V. She is remembered as the Educator, for policies aimed at raising the level of education, and as the Good Mother.
maria-montessori: Maria Tecla Artemisia Montessori was born on 31 August 1870 in Chiaravalle, in the province of Ancona. Her father, Alessandro Montessori, was an official of the Ministry of Finance working in the local state tobacco factory; her mother, Renilde Stoppani, was well educated for the time and a niece of the geologist Antonio Stoppani. The family moved to Rome in 1875.

She first enrolled at an all-boys technical school, hoping to become an engineer, then entered medical school at the Sapienza University of Rome as one of the first women to study medicine in Italy, and graduated with honours in 1896. From 1896 to 1901 she researched children then described as phrenasthenic, in modern terms children with some form of cognitive delay or disability, and became an advocate for women's rights and for the education of children with learning difficulties.

In 1902 Montessori enrolled in the philosophy course at the University of Rome, which then included much of what is now psychology, and did anthropological research with Italian schoolchildren. She lectured at the university's Pedagogic School until 1908. In 1906 she was invited to oversee the care of children of working parents in a new apartment building for low-income families in the San Lorenzo district of Rome.

The first Casa dei Bambini opened on 6 January 1907 with 50 or 60 children aged between two or three and six or seven. Montessori observed while the building porter's daughter did the daily teaching. By the end of 1911 Montessori education had been adopted in public schools in Italy and Switzerland, and by 1912 schools had opened in Paris and many other Western European cities. In 1916 she moved to Barcelona and for twenty years taught training courses across Europe. In 1946 she returned to Amsterdam, and she died of a cerebral haemorrhage on 6 May 1952 in Noordwijk aan Zee.

Montessori drew on Jean Marc Gaspard Itard, Édouard Séguin, Friedrich Fröbel and Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi. Her method rests on observing children free to act in an environment prepared to meet their needs. She concluded that their spontaneous activity revealed an internal programme of development and that the educator's role was to remove obstacles to it. She described four planes of development, from birth to six, six to twelve, twelve to eighteen and eighteen to twenty-four, and developed methods and materials for the first two. Her major books include The Montessori Method, in English in 1912.

The name Montessori is not trademarked, so a range of practices exists under it. Common elements are mixed-age classrooms, free choice of activity, long uninterrupted work periods and specially trained teachers.
maria-theresa: Maria Theresa was born in Vienna on 13 May 1717, the eldest surviving child of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI and Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Her father, the only surviving male of the House of Habsburg, had hoped for a son, and her birth was a disappointment to him. He spent his reign securing the Pragmatic Sanction through international diplomacy and, against the advice of Prince Eugene of Savoy, neglected the army and treasury. She married Francis Stephen of Lorraine, whom she had become close to as a girl, and bore sixteen children between 1737 and 1756.

Charles VI died on 20 October 1740, leaving a bankrupt state and an army of about 108,000 instead of the full 160,000. Saxony, Prussia, Bavaria and France repudiated the sanction, and Frederick II of Prussia invaded and took Silesia, beginning the War of the Austrian Succession. She won the support of the Hungarians, defended most of her lands and lost Silesia and a few minor territories in Italy. Her attempt to recover Silesia in the Seven Years' War, which began with Frederick's invasion of Saxony in 1756, failed. Before it, Wenzel Anton of Kaunitz-Rietberg arranged the First Treaty of Versailles of 1 May 1756 with France.

She ruled as an autocratic sovereign, with her husband and her son Joseph as co-rulers in Austria and Bohemia. Friedrich Wilhelm von Haugwitz created a standing army of 108,000 men, taxed the nobility, who had never before paid taxes, and in 1749 headed a new central Directory; Hungary and several other lands were left almost untouched. Gerard van Swieten reformed medicine, a criminal code of 1769 allowed torture, and the Theresianum, founded in 1746, and a military academy of 1751 trained officials and officers. She was a devout Catholic who rejected religious toleration, exiled Protestants to Transylvania, regarded Jews as dangerous to the state and censored books.

Francis died on 18 August 1765, and Maria Theresa dressed in mourning for the rest of her life. She died on 29 November 1780, and Joseph issued a Patent of Toleration soon after. Her reforms made the empire a modern state of international standing, and her reign is seen as the start of enlightened absolutism in Austria, although historians such as Vocelka judge her reforms more absolutist and centralist than enlightened. A bronze monument to her stands at Maria-Theresien-Platz in Vienna, built in 1888.
marian-anderson: Marian Anderson was born in Philadelphia on 27 February 1897 to John Berkley Anderson, who sold ice and coal at the Reading Terminal, and Annie Delilah Rucker. Her mother had worked as a teacher in Virginia but could not teach in Philadelphia, under a law applied only to Black teachers, and earned her living caring for small children. Marian was the eldest of three children, and her sisters Alyse and Ethel also became singers. Ethel's son James Anderson DePreist became a noted conductor.

Anderson's first break came in 1925, when she won a competition sponsored by the New York Philharmonic and sang with the orchestra on 26 August. Racial prejudice kept her career from gaining momentum, though she made her first Carnegie Hall appearance in 1928. A Rosenwald Fellowship of 1,500 dollars paid for study in Berlin, followed by a successful European tour. In Scandinavia in 1930 she met the pianist Kosti Vehanen, who became her accompanist, and the composer Jean Sibelius, who for many years altered and composed songs for her. Sol Hurok became her manager in 1934. She gave about seventy recitals a year in the United States, yet some hotels and restaurants turned her away; Albert Einstein hosted her several times, first in 1937.

In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused her Constitution Hall in Washington under a white performers-only policy. With the help of Eleanor Roosevelt and President Franklin D. Roosevelt she sang on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, before an integrated crowd of more than 75,000 and a radio audience in the millions. She sang at Constitution Hall in 1943 at the DAR's invitation.

On 7 January 1955 she became the first Black American singer at the Metropolitan Opera, as Ulrica in Verdi's Un ballo in maschera. In 1957 she sang at Dwight D. Eisenhower's inauguration and toured India and the Far East, and she was later a delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Committee. She sang at the March on Washington in 1963 and retired from singing in 1965. Honours included the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1963, the Congressional Gold Medal in 1977 and Kennedy Center Honors in 1978.
mariana-islands: The Mariana Islands form a crescent of fifteen mostly dormant volcanic summits in the north-western Pacific, between the 12th and 21st parallels north and along the 145th meridian east. They lie south-south-east of Japan and east of the Philippines, in the northern part of Micronesia. A northern group of ten volcanic islands, all uninhabited, is separated from a southern group of five coral limestone islands: Rota, Guam, Aguijan, Tinian and Saipan. The islands rise from the Izu–Bonin–Mariana arc, where the Pacific Plate dives under the Mariana plate, and the Mariana Trench just east of them is named after them.

Migrants from the Philippines first settled the Marianas around 1500 to 1400 BCE, in the first ocean-crossing voyage of the Austronesian peoples into Remote Oceania, and the Chamorro language is closest to the Philippine languages. From about 900 to 1700 CE the Latte period brought rapid change. Its mark is the megalithic latte stones, pillars capped with a stone that kept rodents from climbing, which supported wooden houses. Rice agriculture, unique in the pre-contact Pacific, was introduced then.

The first Europeans, on the expedition of Ferdinand Magellan, saw the islands on 6 March 1521. Antonio Pigafetta wrote that the inhabitants stole a skiff from the flagship, and the Spanish burned houses and killed seven men in return, so naming the islands the Islands of the Thieves. Spain claimed them formally in 1667, and in 1668 it began a colony and named them Las Marianas after Queen Mariana of Austria. Settlement began on 14 June 1668, and Guam became a stop for the Manila galleons. The Chamorros were estimated at 50,000 in 1668, but diseases brought by the galleons killed many, and a century later only 1,800 natives remained, most of the population being of mixed Spanish and Chamorro descent.

Spain ceded Guam to the United States in 1898 after the Spanish–American War. It sold the Northern Marianas to Germany in 1899, and Japan seized them in the First World War and held them under a League of Nations mandate. In 1944 the United States captured the chain. Saipan and Tinian then became bases for B-29 bombers, and the Enola Gay and Bockscar flew from Tinian's North Field in August 1945. Afterwards the Northern Marianas came under American trusteeship, separate from Guam.
marib: Marib lies in the region of the Sarawat Mountains, about 120 kilometres east of Sanaa. It is the capital of Marib Governorate. The ancient city, known as Mirwah, is one of the most important places for Arabian archaeology. In 2023 UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List as one of the Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba, Marib. The modern town stands about 3.5 kilometres north of the centre of the ancient city.

The Sabaean kingdom was based around Marib, with territory in northern Yemen, and its kings made the city their capital. Some scholars believe Saba to be the Sheba of biblical fame. The Sabaean kings built great irrigation works such as the Marib Dam, whose ruins are still visible and which supported a flourishing culture for more than a thousand years. They also built castles and temples in the area, most notably the temples of Almaqah at Awwam and Barran. Saba was known for dealing in the frankincense and myrrh trade.

In 25 BCE Aelius Gallus led a Roman expedition to Marib and laid siege to the city. He suffered heavy losses and was forced to retreat to Egypt. The site of the ancient city was largely abandoned during the 20th century. A small village remains, but the multi-storey mud-brick buildings of the historic city are mostly in ruins.

After floods ravaged the country in 1982, the president of the U.A.E., Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, financed the building of the present Marib Dam in 1984. He was reportedly descended from people who migrated from the Marib area to what is now the U.A.E. A refinery opened in Marib in 1986, and an oil pipeline runs from the town to Ra's Isa.
Marib has a hot desert climate. It had 16,794 inhabitants in 2005. Its ancient ruins, above all the dam and the temples at Awwam and Barran, are the chief survivals of the Sabaean past.
maribor: Maribor is the largest city of the traditional region of Lower Styria and the economic, administrative, educational and cultural centre of eastern Slovenia. The Drava River divides it, and two hills, Calvary Hill and Pyramid Hill, rise among vineyards. Settlement in the area goes back to the fifth millennium BCE, and in Roman times it lay in the province of Noricum on the border with Pannonia.

A castle was built on Pyramid Hill to guard the Frankish Empire against Hungarian raids, and it was first mentioned on 20 October 1164 as Castrum Marchburch. The settlement below it received town privileges in 1254 and grew rapidly after Rudolf I of Habsburg defeated King Otakar II of Bohemia in 1278. Jews are first mentioned in 1277 and had their own quarter and synagogue; Maximilian I ordered them out in 1496. Matthias Corvinus besieged the town in 1480 and 1481 without success, and in 1532 a large Ottoman army under Suleiman attacked it and was repulsed. Fires and plague in the seventeenth century cost the town 35 per cent of its population.

The Southern Railway reached it in 1846, and in 1859 Bishop Anton Martin Slomšek moved the seat of the diocese to Maribor. In 1900 the city was 82.3 per cent German-speaking, though most of the surrounding land was Slovene. In November 1918 Rudolf Maister organised Slovene units that took control of the city from those who wished it to join German Austria. On 27 January 1919 Slovene troops fired on a German crowd, killing nine; who gave the order has never been established. The Treaty of Saint-Germain of 10 September 1919 recognised the city as part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Nazi Germany annexed Lower Styria in 1941 and expelled many Slovenes, and the Jews of Maribor were deported. Allied bombing in the closing years of the war devastated some 47 per cent of the city area. After the war it became an industrial centre of Slovenia and Yugoslavia, and in 1991 it became part of independent Slovenia.

Maribor Cathedral dates from the thirteenth century and the Maribor Synagogue from the fourteenth, which is described as the second oldest synagogue in Europe. The Lent Festival is held every June, and the house at Lent grows the grapevine Žametovka, over 400 years old, recorded in 2004 as the world's oldest. The University of Maribor was established in 1975. Maribor was a European Capital of Culture in 2012.
marie-adelaide-grand-duchess-of-luxembou: Marie-Adélaïde was born on 14 June 1894 at Berg Castle, the eldest child of Grand Duke William IV and Infanta Marie Anne of Portugal. Her father had six daughters and no sons, and because Luxembourg followed Salic law he proclaimed her heir presumptive on 10 July 1907 to avert a succession crisis. When he died on 25 February 1912 she became the first reigning Grand Duchess of Luxembourg at the age of 17. Her mother served as regent until her eighteenth birthday on 18 June 1912, when the President of the Chamber, Auguste Laval, swore her in.

The constitution gave the monarch extensive political powers, and unlike her father and grandfather she took an active part in politics. A devout Catholic with very conservative views, she refused on the day of her accession to sign a law reducing the role of priests in education, and in 1915 she hesitated before appointing two mayors known for their anticlerical views. In late 1915 she dissolved the Chamber of Deputies to end a deadlock, with elections on 23 December. The act was permitted by the constitution but unconventional, and socialists and liberals resented it as resembling a coup d'état.

When Germany violated Luxembourg's neutrality at the outbreak of the First World War, she and her government protested formally but did not oppose the occupation further, which spared the country fighting and left its state intact. The Grand Duchess and her family worked for the Red Cross and cared for German and French soldiers. Her critics pointed to her German blood, her sister's betrothal to a German prince and her reception of the Kaiser. After the war the French government declared that it considered her government gravely compromised.

In January 1919 voices in parliament demanded her abdication, and Belgium sought to annex Luxembourg. On 9 January a group of Socialist and Liberal deputies proclaimed a republic after losing a vote to abolish the monarchy, and unrest followed in the streets. On 14 January 1919, on the advice of the Prime Minister, she abdicated in favour of her younger sister Charlotte, who saved the monarchy in a national referendum later that year. The constitution was revised and the monarch lost much of the political power the earlier text had given.

Marie-Adélaïde entered a Carmelite convent in Modena in 1920 and later joined the Little Sisters of the Poor in Rome, but poor health forced her to leave. She died of influenza at Schloss Hohenburg in Bavaria on 24 January 1924, aged 29, and in 1947 her body was interred in the Grand Ducal Crypt in Luxembourg City.
marie-antoinette: Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna was born on 2 November 1755 at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna, the fifteenth child and youngest daughter of Empress Maria Theresa and Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor. After the Seven Years' War, Maria Theresa ended her long hostility with Louis XV of France. Both wished to check the ambitions of Prussia and Great Britain, and they sealed the alliance with a marriage: on 7 February 1770 Louis XV formally asked for her hand for his grandson and heir, the Dauphin. When Louis XV died on 10 May 1774, the dauphin became Louis XVI and she became queen consort. Two weeks later the king gave her the Petit Trianon, a small château at Versailles.

As queen she became a target of those who opposed the policies of Louis XVI and of the monarchy in general. Libelles accused her of extravagance, promiscuity and sympathy for Austria. In 1785 members of her court defrauded jewellers in the Affair of the Diamond Necklace; she was falsely accused, but her reputation suffered. She was later called Madame Déficit, as the financial crisis was blamed on her spending and her opposition to reforms proposed by Turgot and Necker. In July 1789 she urged Necker's dismissal, and Paris rose to storm the Bastille.

In June 1791 the royal family tried to flee to Montmédy, the Flight to Varennes, which failed through poor execution. France declared war on Austria on 20 April 1792, and the queen was seen as an enemy. The attack on the Tuileries on 10 August 1792 forced the family to take refuge at the Legislative Assembly, and they were imprisoned in the Temple. The monarchy was abolished on 21 September, and Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793.

Marie Antoinette was moved to the Conciergerie, and a plot to free her failed in late August. Her trial before the Revolutionary Tribunal began on 14 October 1793; she and her lawyers had less than a day to prepare. The charges included sending millions of livres to Austria and incest, an accusation made by her son Louis-Charles under pressure from Jacques Hébert. She was convicted of high treason and guillotined on 16 October 1793. Her remains were exhumed in 1815, during the Bourbon Restoration, and buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. For many revolutionaries she symbolised the faults of the old regime.
marie-de-france: Almost nothing is known of Marie's life. Her name comes from a line of one of her works, Marie ai num, si sui de France, meaning My name is Marie, and I am from France, and the French scholar Claude Fauchet first called her Marie de France in 1581. Proposed identities include Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, the abbesses of Shaftesbury, Reading and Barking, Marie I of Boulogne and Marie de Meulan.

She was probably born in France but spent much of her adult life in England, where many manuscripts of her works were found. She was highly educated, wrote in an Old French with Anglo-Norman elements, and knew Latin, Middle English and possibly Breton, so she was probably of aristocratic birth or belonged to a religious house.

Scholars date her works between about 1160 and 1215. She was almost certainly known at the court of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine. The English poet Denis Piramus mentions the lais of a Marie, popular in aristocratic circles, in his Life of Saint Edmund the King of about 1180.

The Lais are dedicated to a noble king, usually taken to be Henry II or his eldest son Henry the Young King, and the Fables to a Count William, who may be William of Mandeville, William Marshall or William Longsword. Besides the Lais and the 102 Fables she wrote the Espurgatoire seint Patriz, a retelling of the legend of the Purgatory of St Patrick from a Latin text, and has been tentatively named as author of a saint's life, the Life of Saint Audrey.

The Lais are twelve narrative poems in eight-syllable verse, from 118 lines in Chevrefoil to 1,184 in Eliduc. Marie says she heard their stories from Breton minstrels, and she may have been the first to give the lai a narrative form. Most concern love entangled in triangles of loss and adventure, with intrusions from the fairy world, as in Bisclavret, whose hero is a werewolf, and Lanval, in which a fairy woman takes her lover to Avalon.

Over half involve adultery, and heroines are often shut in by jealous husbands. Only five manuscripts hold some or all of the Lais, but 25 hold the Fables, whose epilogue says they were translated from an English version by Alfred the Great. Fable 51 is an early version of the Reynard tales and inspired Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale, and in the late 14th century Thomas Chestre based his Middle English Sir Launfal on Lanval.
marie-louise-duchess-of-parma: Marie Louise was born at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna on 12 December 1791, the eldest child of Archduke Francis, who became Holy Roman Emperor the next year. She was brought up to detest France and the Revolution, influenced by her grandmother Maria Carolina, whose sister Marie Antoinette had died in it. The imperial family had to leave Vienna in 1805 and again in 1809. She learned English, French, Italian, Latin and Spanish, and her parents allowed her almost no contact with men.

After the Treaty of Schönbrunn in October 1809 Napoleon wanted an heir and a bride from a leading dynasty. His wish to marry a sister of Tsar Alexander I alarmed Austria, and at the urging of Prince Metternich a match with Marie Louise was proposed. Asked for her consent, she answered that she wished only what her duty commanded. They married by proxy on 11 March 1810 and in a civil ceremony on 1 April, and she became Empress of the French. Reserved in public, she never interfered in politics. On 20 March 1811 she bore a son, the King of Rome, later Napoleon II.

She served as regent when Napoleon was away, though he took all decisions. She left Paris on 29 March 1814, and after his abdication returned to Vienna with her son. The Treaty of Fontainebleau and the Congress of Vienna gave her the duchies of Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla for her lifetime only, since the Allies did not want a descendant of Napoleon to hold them by right.

Marie Louise entered Parma on 18 April 1816 with Count Adam Albert von Neipperg, an Austrian officer she had met in 1814, who became her chamberlain and lover and ran daily government on instructions from Metternich. After Napoleon died on 5 May 1821 she married Neipperg, who died in 1829. In 1831 an uprising inspired by the Carbonari forced her out of the city for a time, and Austrian troops crushed it. She then married Charles-René de Bombelles, who reformed the duchy's finances, on 17 February 1834. Her son died of tuberculosis in 1832. She died of pleurisy on 17 December 1847 and was buried in Vienna; Parma then passed to the Bourbons.
mariehamn: Mariehamn lies on the main island of Åland and borders Jomala to the north and west and Lemland to the east. It stands on a peninsula with two main harbours, west and east, both ice-free for most of the year and with minimal tidal variation. The Baltic Sea moderates the climate, giving mild winters and cool summers, and summers are cooler than in most of Sweden and Finland.

The town was founded on 21 February 1861 on land that belonged to the village of Övernäs in Jomala, and named after the Russian empress Maria Alexandrovna, so that the name means 'Marie's Port'. It grew from a planned layout that remains largely intact. One of its oldest streets, Södragatan, has preserved nineteenth-century wooden houses.

In the late nineteenth century shipping became central to the local economy, and shipowners and shipyards settled in the town. After the First World War Mariehamn became known for its Grain Fleet. The shipowner Gustaf Erikson (1872-1947) operated sailing ships from the town.

Mariehamn is the capital of Åland, an autonomous region of Finland, and the seat of its government and parliament. It has about 40 per cent of the region's population, and most residents have Swedish as their native language. Several buildings, among them the church of Mariehamn (1927), the Åland Maritime College (1927) and the town hall (1939), were designed by the Finnish architect Lars Sonck. The four-masted barque Pommern, now part of the Åland Maritime Museum, is moored in the Western Harbour, which has ferry connections to Sweden, Estonia and mainland Finland.
marija-gimbutas: Marija Birutė Alseikaitė was born in Vilnius to Veronika Janulaitytė-Alseikienė and Danielius Alseika, members of the Lithuanian intelligentsia. Her mother held a doctorate in ophthalmology from Berlin and her father a medical degree from Dorpat. Her parents were connoisseurs of Lithuanian folk art and received writers and scholars, among them Jonas Basanavičius, whose collected folklore remained important to her. The family settled in Kaunas in 1931, and after her father's sudden death five years later she resolved to become a scholar. From 1936 she joined ethnographic expeditions to record folklore and studied Lithuanian beliefs and rituals of death.

She studied linguistics at Vytautas Magnus University from 1938, then archaeology, ethnology and folklore at the University of Vilnius, where she took her master's degree in 1942. In 1941 she married the architect Jurgis Gimbutas. With a young daughter she fled the advancing Soviet army to areas held by Germany, and in 1946 she received a doctorate from the University of Tübingen for a study of prehistoric burial rites in Lithuania.

In the 1950s the family moved to the United States. She worked at Harvard, becoming a Fellow of the Peabody Museum in 1955, and then moved to UCLA, where she was Professor of European Archaeology and Indo-European Studies and became Curator of Old World Archaeology in 1965.

In 1956 she proposed the Kurgan hypothesis, which joined the archaeology of burial mounds to linguistics to explain the origin and migrations of the Proto-Indo-European speakers. Between 1967 and 1980 she directed excavations of Neolithic sites in southeastern Europe, including Anzabegovo in North Macedonia and Sitagroi and Achilleion in Greece. Her Bronze Age Cultures of Central and Eastern Europe appeared in 1965.

Her last three English-language books, The Goddesses and Gods of Old Europe (1974), The Language of the Goddess (1989) and The Civilization of the Goddess (1991), described a goddess-centred, peaceful Old Europe that she held was overturned by patriarchal Kurgan warriors. Joseph Campbell admired the work, and the ecofeminist Charlene Spretnak later argued that a backlash against it had been organised.

Many archaeologists rejected it: Bernard Wailes judged her knowledgeable but weak in critical analysis, and David W. Anthony, who praised her view of the Indo-European homeland, noted that Europe had hillforts and weapons long before the Kurgan peoples. Three genetic studies of 2015 were taken to support the Kurgan theory. She died in Los Angeles in 1994.
marinid-dynasty: The Marinids were a faction of the Zenata Berber tribal confederation. The Banu Marin were nomads from the Zab, a region around Biskra in present-day Algeria, who were pushed out after Arab Bedouins arrived in North Africa. They entered what is now Morocco in force by the beginning of the 13th century. They first submitted to the Almohads. Their leader Mahyu contributed to the Almohad victory at the Battle of Alarcos in 1195, though he died of his wounds, and his son Abd al-Haqq was the effective founder of the dynasty.

After the Almohad defeat at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa on 16 July 1212, the state was weakened. From 1213 or 1214 the Marinids began to tax farming communities in the north-east of today's Morocco, and from 1215 fighting with the Almohads broke out regularly.

Early rulers governed as emirs, first at Taza, then at Fez from 1244. Abu Yusuf Ya'qub captured Marrakesh in 1269, ending Almohad rule, and the later rulers were sultans of Fez and Morocco. The Marinids supported the Emirate of Granada against Castile, and after Granada ceded Algeciras they tried to control the traffic of the Strait of Gibraltar. By 1294 they had occupied Rota, Tarifa and Gibraltar. In the mid-14th century, under Abu al-Hasan and his son Abu Inan, they briefly held sway over most of the Maghreb, including large parts of modern Algeria and Tunisia. They were defeated at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340, and the Castilian capture of Algeciras in 1344 expelled them for good from the Iberian Peninsula.

After the death of Abu Inan Faris in 1358, real power lay with viziers while sultans succeeded one another quickly. In 1359 Hintata tribesmen from the High Atlas occupied Marrakesh and governed it independently until 1526. From the early 15th century the related Wattasid dynasty competed with the Marinids, whose last sultan, Abd al-Haqq II, reigned until 1465.

The Marinids largely continued Almohad structures, ruling a tribal state with little civil administration beyond the capital and relying on family members as governors. Their army was drawn from loyal tribes, other Zenata tribes, Arab tribes such as the Banu Hilal and Banu Ma'qil, and Christian mercenaries who served as the sultan's bodyguard. They made Fez their capital and restored Maliki Sunni Islam as the official religion. The Marinids built madrasas across the country, and the Qarawiyyin of Fez reached its height of prestige. They were the first to use zellij tilework extensively.
mario-soares: Mário Soares was born in Lisbon on 7 December 1924, the son of João Lopes Soares, founder of the Colégio Moderno and a republican activist who had once been a priest. He studied there, where for a short time Álvaro Cunhal, later the leader of Portuguese Communism and one of his chief rivals, taught him geography.

At university he joined the Portuguese Communist Party and led its youth section, which he left in 1951. The political police, PIDE, first arrested him in 1946. His arrests ended his career as a lecturer in history and philosophy, so he studied law and became a lawyer who defended political prisoners of the dictatorship founded by António de Oliveira Salazar.

In 1958 he supported General Humberto Delgado's presidential campaign and later became his family's lawyer after Delgado's murder in 1965. In April 1964 he helped found the Acção Socialista Portuguesa in Geneva. Arrested again in March 1968, he was banished to São Tomé and Príncipe, but he was released within eight months after Marcello Caetano replaced Salazar. Exiled in 1970, he taught in France, and in 1973 the Portuguese Socialist Action became the Socialist Party, founded in Bad Münstereifel under the umbrella of Willy Brandt's SPD, with Soares as secretary-general.

After the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 he returned and became minister for overseas negotiations in the provisional government, meeting Samora Machel of Frelimo about Mozambique's independence. He opposed an attempt by the Communist Party and radical officers to extend their control, which ended with the dismissal of Vasco Gonçalves in September 1975 and a failed far-left coup in November.

After the 1976 Constitution the Socialists won a plurality in the Assembly of the Republic and Soares formed a minority government, resigning in 1978 after an unpopular austerity policy. He returned as prime minister after the 1983 elections, and his main achievement was negotiating Portugal's entry into the European Economic Community.

In 1986 Soares was elected president, defeating Diogo Freitas do Amaral by little more than two per cent, and he was re-elected in 1991 with almost 70 per cent of the vote. He devised the Presidência Aberta, tours of the country each addressing a particular issue.

After leaving office in 1996 he sat in the European Parliament from 1999 to 2004. He died on 7 January 2017, aged 92, and was given a state funeral, the first in Portugal since that of President Óscar Carmona in 1951. He is considered the father of Portuguese democracy.
mario-vargas-llosa: Mario Vargas Llosa was born to a middle-class family on 28 March 1936 in the southern Peruvian city of Arequipa. He was the only child of Ernesto Vargas Maldonado, a radio operator in an aviation company, and Dora Llosa Ureta, the daughter of an old criollo family. His parents separated a few months before his birth. His first literary influences were relatively obscure Peruvian writers such as Martín Adán, Carlos Oquendo de Amat and César Moro, from whom he sought new narrative structures to describe urban Peru.

His first novel, The Time of the Hero (1963), is set among cadets in a Lima military school and draws on his own experiences at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy. It won the Premio de la Crítica Española, and its sharp criticism of the Peruvian military led several generals to attack it. The Green House (1965) and Conversation in The Cathedral (1969), a two-volume novel based on the dictatorship of President Manuel A. Odría, followed. In 1971 he published a study of Gabriel García Márquez, his doctoral thesis for the Complutense University of Madrid; the two writers' friendship ended in 1976, when Vargas Llosa struck García Márquez at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City.

The War of the End of the World (1981) was his first historical novel, recreating the 19th-century War of Canudos in Brazil. He initially supported Fidel Castro's Cuban government, but broke with it over the imprisonment of the poet Heberto Padilla in 1971 and afterwards identified as a liberal. In 1983 he served on the commission investigating the Uchuraccay massacre, whose conclusions drew intense criticism from anthropologists. In 1987 he became a leader of the centre-right Movimiento Libertad, and in 1990 he ran for the presidency of Peru for the FREDEMO coalition, losing to Alberto Fujimori.

From the 1990s he lived mainly in Madrid and acquired Spanish citizenship in 1993. He received the Rómulo Gallegos Prize in 1967, the Prince of Asturias Award in 1986, the Miguel de Cervantes Prize in 1994 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010. King Juan Carlos I made him Marquess of Vargas Llosa in 2011, and in 2021 he was elected to the Académie Française.

Vargas Llosa died in Lima on 13 April 2025, aged 89, surrounded by his family. His main theme was the individual's struggle for freedom within an oppressive reality, and he often challenged the inadequacies of society through his fiction. Scholars read his early novels as modernist and later ones such as Captain Pantoja and the Special Service as postmodernist and comic. He is counted among the major Latin American writers alongside Octavio Paz, Julio Cortázar, Jorge Luis Borges and Gabriel García Márquez.
maritsa: The Maritsa rises at the Marichini Lakes in the Rila Mountains of western Bulgaria and flows east-southeast between the Balkan and Rhodope Mountains, past Plovdiv and Dimitrovgrad to Edirne in Turkey. East of Svilengrad it forms the border between Bulgaria and Greece, and below Edirne, where it receives its two chief tributaries, the Tundzha and the Arda, it turns south and divides Greece on the west bank from Turkey on the east.

It enters the Aegean near Enez in a delta. Its basin covers about 53,000 square kilometres, two thirds of it in Bulgaria, and holds most of the historical region of Thrace. The river cannot be navigated; it is used for hydroelectric power and irrigation, and its upper valley is a principal east-west route in Bulgaria.

The earliest recorded name is the Greek Euros, used by the poet Alcman in the 7th or 6th century BCE. In Thracian the name became Ebros, which gave the Greek Hebros and the Latin Hebrus. The modern name Maritsa may derive from the name of a mountain near the river's mouth in antiquity. Proto-Indo-European roots meaning wide have been proposed for the ancient name, as has a Thracian word meaning splasher.

In 1371 the river gave its name to the Battle of Maritsa, also called the battle of Chernomen, in which Ottoman forces defeated the Serbian rulers Vukašin Mrnjavčević and Jovan Uglješa, both of whom died. After 1923 the lower river became the modern border between Greece and Turkey.

The lower course, where the river forms the Greek-Turkish border, floods for about four months in a typical year, and the low lands beside it suffer losses to farming and roads. The river lends its name to the Maritsa motorway in Bulgaria and to Shumi Maritsa, which was the Bulgarian national anthem from 1886 to 1947 and whose words picture the river running bloody after fighting. Since Greece joined the European Union in 1981 the river has been part of the Union's external boundary.
mark-antony: Marcus Antonius was born in Rome on 14 January 83 BCE into the plebeian gens Antonia. His family claimed descent from Anton, a son of Heracles, and he harnessed lions to his chariot and put a lion on many of his coins in memory of it. His father was Marcus Antonius Creticus, and his grandfather, the noted orator Marcus Antonius, was murdered in the purges of Gaius Marius in 87-86 BCE. His mother, Julia, was a third cousin of Julius Caesar. In 57 BCE he joined the staff of Aulus Gabinius, Proconsul of Syria, as cavalry commander, and won his first distinctions in Judea at Alexandrium and Machaerus.

Publius Clodius Pulcher secured Antony a place on Caesar's staff in 54 BCE. After a year in Gaul he was elected quaestor for 52 BCE, and he returned to command Caesar's cavalry at the Battle of Alesia against Vercingetorix. In the winter before the civil war he proposed that Caesar keep only two of his eight legions, a concession that Pompey found satisfactory but Cato and Lentulus refused; Antony then fled Rome for Caesar's camp. Caesar made him master of horse and left him to govern Italy. They were reconciled by 44 BCE, when Antony was elected consul alongside Caesar.

After Caesar's assassination Antony joined Lepidus and Octavian in the Second Triumvirate, and in 42 BCE they defeated Brutus and Cassius at the Battle of Philippi. Antony took the eastern provinces. He spent the winter in Athens, where he presented himself as a friend of Greek culture and was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries, and at Ephesus he was worshipped as Dionysus born anew. He married Octavia, Octavian's sister, in 40 BCE, but lived with Cleopatra VII, who bore him three children. Lepidus was expelled in 36 BCE, and the two remaining triumvirs split in 33 BCE.

In 31 BCE the Roman republic declared war on Cleopatra and proclaimed Antony a traitor, and Octavian's forces defeated him at Actium. Octavian invaded Egypt with Agrippa in August 30 BCE. Antony stabbed himself, mistakenly believing that Cleopatra had already died, and according to Plutarch he died in her arms at her tomb. She killed herself in mid-August. Octavian had Caesarion and Antony's son Antyllus put to death, but spared Antony's other children. His honours were revoked and his statues removed, though he was not subject to a complete damnatio memoriae. Octavian, known as Augustus from 27 BCE, became the uncontested ruler of Rome. Through his daughters by Octavia, Antony was ancestor of the emperors Caligula, Claudius and Nero.
mark-the-evangelist: Mark the Evangelist is also known as John Mark, and an unbroken tradition, according to William Lane, identifies him with John Mark and with the cousin of Barnabas. Hippolytus of Rome, in On the Seventy Apostles, instead distinguishes three figures: Mark the Evangelist, John Mark and Mark the cousin of Barnabas. All three, he says, were among the Seventy Disciples whom Jesus sent out to Judea.

Coptic tradition holds that Mark was born in Cyrene, in the Pentapolis of North Africa, and that his house hosted the disciples after the death of Jesus. Other denominations do not share the belief that he was a Roman African from ancient Libya.

According to Eusebius of Caesarea, Peter met Mark on his journey through Asia Minor and took him as companion and interpreter. Mark wrote down Peter's sermons, and so composed the Gospel according to Mark. The Acts of the Apostles says that after the Council of Jerusalem Mark went to Cyprus with Barnabas.

Tradition holds that Mark then travelled to Alexandria and founded the church there, from which the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Greek Orthodox Church of Alexandria and the Coptic Catholic Church all trace their origins. He is honoured as its first bishop and as the founder of Christianity in Africa. Eusebius says that Anianus succeeded him as bishop in the eighth year of Nero, probably because Mark's death was near.

Scholars are divided over the gospel's authorship. It does not name its author, as was common among ancient biographies. The earliest evidence for Mark's authorship comes from Papias, c. 60 – c. 130, whose information modern scholars find hard to interpret. Most scholars favour Rome as the place of composition.

Later Coptic tradition says that Mark was martyred in 68. According to this tradition, the pagans of Alexandria resented his efforts to turn the city away from its traditional gods, put a rope around his neck and dragged him through the streets until he died.

His feast is kept on 25 April by the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, and also by the Church of England. The Coptic Orthodox Church keeps it on Parmouti 30, which falls on the same date in the Julian calendar. In art Mark is shown writing or holding his gospel, and his symbol is the winged lion. Major shrines include the Basilica di San Marco in Venice and Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral in Alexandria.
mark-twain: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born on 30 November 1835 in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children of Jane Lampton, a native of Kentucky, and John Marshall Clemens, a lawyer from Virginia. Only three of his siblings lived beyond childhood. When he was four the family moved to Hannibal, Missouri, a port town on the Mississippi River that inspired the fictional St. Petersburg of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. Slavery was legal in Missouri at the time and became a theme in those books.

Twain became a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi, which gave him the material for Life on the Mississippi (1883). He then went west to join Orion in Nevada, joked about his failure at mining, and turned to journalism for the Virginia City Territorial Enterprise. A humorous story about a jumping frog of Calaveras County, published in 1865 and based on a tale he heard at the Angels Hotel in Angels Camp, California, brought him international attention. He became a much sought-after speaker.

His novels include The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), and he wrote The Gilded Age (1873) with Charles Dudley Warner. He began with light humorous verse and became a chronicler of the vanities, hypocrisies and murderous acts of mankind. In Huckleberry Finn he combined humor, narrative and social criticism, and he helped create a distinctive American literature built on American themes and language. The book has been repeatedly restricted in American high schools, not least for its frequent use of a racial slur.

His pen name, he said, came from the riverboatman's cry of mark twain, meaning that the water was two fathoms deep. He also said he took it from Captain Isaiah Sellers, who signed river news with it for the New Orleans Picayune. Some have doubted this story. His views became more radical with age, and he supported the labor movement, among others the Knights of Labor. He died of a heart attack on 21 April 1910, the day after Halley's Comet was closest to the Sun, as he had predicted.
maroons: Maroon was an English term for Africans in the Americas and the islands of the Indian Ocean who escaped from slavery, through flight or manumission, and lived in independent settlements. They were called cimarrones in Spanish America. The word entered English around the 1590s, from the French marron and probably the American Spanish cimarrón, first used in Hispaniola of feral cattle, then of Indian slaves who escaped to the hills, and by the early 1530s of enslaved Africans who did the same. As early as 1512 enslaved Africans escaped from Spanish captors and joined Indigenous peoples or lived on their own. The earliest Maroon communities formed in what is now the Dominican Republic after the first slave rebellion on 26 December 1522.

Colonial authorities tried to eradicate the Maroons, who hid in remote bush, caves and mountains and defended themselves by guerrilla warfare, sometimes allying with enemies of a colony. They farmed and hunted, and raided plantations to burn crops, steal livestock and invite others to join them. On small islands Maroons lost ground as planters took more land, and only on larger islands could organised communities thrive.

In Brazil, the quilombo of Palmares, established around 1600 near Recife, had at its height more than 30,000 free people and was ruled by King Zumbi. It withstood Dutch expeditions and on average one Portuguese expedition nearly every year between 1672 and 1694, when the Portuguese conquered it. In Panama, Bayano led a rebellion in 1552, and the Spanish offered his followers freedom on condition that they admit no newcomers and return runaways. After the Second Maroon War in Jamaica, nearly 600 Maroons were deported in 1796 to Nova Scotia and in 1800 to Sierra Leone.

Maroon cultures varied widely with history, geography, the African origins of their members and contact with Indigenous peoples. Some developed creole languages from European and African tongues, such as Saramaccan in Suriname, and some mixed with Indigenous peoples, as with the Garifuna, descended from Maroon communities on Saint Vincent and deported to Honduras in 1797. The Ndyuka treaty remains important in defining the territorial rights of the Maroons of Suriname, and in the Jamaican town of Accompong a festival on 6 January commemorates the peace treaty with the British.
marquesas-islands: The Marquesas Islands, known in Marquesan as Te Henua ʻEnana or Te Fenua ʻEnata, "the land of men", are among the most remote islands in the world. They lie about 1,370 kilometres north-east of Tahiti and about 4,800 kilometres south-west of Mexico. Most are volcanic, created by the Marquesas hotspot, and the highest point is Mount Oave on Ua Pou, at 1,230 metres. A northern group is centred on Nuku Hiva, and a southern group on Hiva ʻOa. Rainfall is greater on the northern and eastern windward coasts, and droughts, which seem to be linked with El Niño, are frequent and sometimes last several years.

The first settlers were Polynesians from West Polynesia, descendants of the Lapita culture. Early radiocarbon dates suggested arrival before 100 CE or about 600 CE, but a 2010 study with higher-precision methods found that eastern Polynesia was settled much later, in two waves. The first reached the Society Islands, and the second, between about 1190 and 1290 CE, spread to the Marquesas. Such rapid settlement is thought to explain the close uniformity of East Polynesian culture, biology and language.

The abundant natural resources long supported a large population, which lived by fishing, collecting shellfish, hunting birds and gardening. Breadfruit was the staple, and at least 32 other introduced crops were grown. Basalt from the quarry island of Eiao was carried by sailing canoe for more than 2,500 kilometres, to supply adze heads to Moʻorea, Mangareva, Tubuai, Rarotonga and Tabuaeran.
