The first Europeans to arrive may have been the crew of the Spanish ship San Lesmes, which vanished in a storm in June 1526. Álvaro de Mendaña reached the islands on 21 July 1595 and named them after his patron García Hurtado de Mendoza, Marquis of Cañete, Viceroy of Peru. He visited Fatu Hiva and Tahuata before sailing to the Solomon Islands. The first missionaries, William Pascoe Crook and John Harris of the London Missionary Society, arrived in 1797; Harris left after a few months, and Crook stayed until 1799.

The Marquesas form one of the five administrative divisions of French Polynesia, with its capital at Taioha'e on Nuku Hiva. French and Tahitian are the official languages, and the Marquesan languages remain widely spoken. The islands had 9,346 inhabitants at the 2017 census, and most are Catholic. In 2024 UNESCO listed the islands as a World Heritage Site under the name Te Henua Enata.
marquis-de-lafayette: Lafayette was born on 6 September 1757 at the Château de Chavaniac in the province of Auvergne, into a wealthy land-owning family with a martial tradition, and was commissioned an officer at age 13. After the marriage contract of 1773 he lived with his young wife in his father-in-law's house in Versailles. The Continental Congress lacked funds for his voyage, so he bought the ship Victoire with his own money. The French Crown disapproved, and he landed near Georgetown, South Carolina, on 13 June 1777. He offered to serve without pay, and Congress commissioned him a major general on 31 July 1777.

Lafayette first saw combat at the Battle of Brandywine on 11 September 1777, where he was shot in the leg but rallied troops during the retreat. In May 1778 he escaped a British attempt to trap him at Barren Hill. He returned to France in 1779 to seek more support, and spent eight days under house arrest for disobeying the king. Back in America in 1780, he evaded Lord Cornwallis in Virginia in 1781 with small squads that gave the impression his force was larger than it was.

In France he sat in the Assembly of Notables in 1787 and was elected to the Estates General in 1789. On 15 July 1789 he became commander of the Parisian National Guard and proposed the blue, white and red cockade, which began the French tricolour. He was blamed for the royal family's flight to Varennes in June 1791. On 17 July 1791 his troops fired on a crowd at the Champ de Mars, killing an unknown number of people. Radical factions ordered his arrest in August 1792.

Napoleon restored his citizenship in 1800, and Lafayette refused the offices he offered. After the Bourbon Restoration he opposed the narrow franchise and sat in the Chamber of Deputies from 1827. He broke with Louis-Philippe when the king backtracked on reforms. He died on 20 May 1834 and is buried in Picpus Cemetery in Paris, under soil from Bunker Hill.

Lafayette believed in a constitutional monarchy and opposed slavery, proposing that enslaved people work as free tenants. In the United States his image rested on his fighting without pay for a country not his own, and Samuel Adams praised him for it.
mars-mythology: In ancient Roman religion Mars was the god of war and also an agricultural guardian, a combination characteristic of early Rome. He was usually held to be the son of Jupiter and Juno, though in Ovid's version Juno bore him alone, after the goddess Flora touched her belly with a magic flower. His consort was Nerio, whose name means valour, and Venus was joined to him as a complementary pair in the public banquet of 217 BCE. The Latin name gave English "martial" and names such as Marcus.

Unlike the Greek Ares, who is often treated with contempt in Greek literature, Mars represented military power as a way to secure peace. Roman writers took over the myths of Ares and retold them under his name. His sacred animals were the wolf and the woodpecker. Mars may have begun as a god of the wild, and the Arval Brothers invoked him as ferus, "savage". By the third century CE soldiers of the legions worshipped him above all.

His main priest was the Flamen Martialis, and twelve patrician youths, the Salii, danced in armour through the city in March. Most festivals fell in March, the month named after him, and in October, which began and ended the seasons of campaigning and farming. They included the Equirria horse races on 27 February and 14 March, his birthday on 1 March, and the Mamuralia, a new year rite in which Mamurius Veturius was driven out. On 15 October the October Horse was sacrificed, Rome's only known horse sacrifice. The usual offering was a bull, and the suovetaurilia of pig, ram and bull was offered to Mars Pater.

His earliest centre was the Altar of Mars in the Campus Martius, which Romans thought Numa Pompilius had set up. Newly elected censors placed their chairs beside it, and after the census the citizens were purified there. A spear kept in the Regia was said to tremble before danger to the state, as it did before the assassination of Julius Caesar.

Mars took many titles. Mars Gradivus, "the Strider", was invoked by soldiers swearing oaths, and Mars Quirinus protected the citizens. Augustus created the cult of Mars Ultor, "the Avenger", after the defeat of Caesar's assassins at Philippi in 42 BCE and the return of the standards lost at Carrhae, and built a temple to him in his new forum. The 4th-century historian Ammianus Marcellinus treats Mars as still a living cult in his day. In 363 the emperor Julian sacrificed ten bulls to Mars Ultor before the siege of Ctesiphon; the tenth broke free, and the omens were bad.
mars-orbiter-mission: The first public acknowledgement of an uncrewed Mars mission came in November 2008, from the then ISRO chairman G. Madhavan Nair. The concept grew from a feasibility study made in 2010 by the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, after the launch of the lunar satellite Chandrayaan-1 in 2008. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh approved the project on 3 August 2012. The mission was meant as a technology demonstrator, to develop the means of designing, planning, managing and operating an interplanetary mission, and its secondary aim was to study Mars's surface features, mineralogy and atmosphere with five indigenous instruments. ISRO chose its Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle after the larger rocket failed twice in 2010.

The probe lifted off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota on 5 November 2013. Because the rocket could not send it directly to Mars, the spacecraft spent about a month in Earth orbit and used its own thrusters in a series of perigee burns. On 30 November 2013 a 23-minute engine firing sent it on a trajectory toward Mars, and it travelled some 780,000,000 kilometres in a 298-day transit. On 24 September 2014 it entered a highly elliptical Martian orbit, with a period of about 73 hours, as planned.

The orbiter returned the first global view of Mars on 28 September 2014. On 7 October 2014 ISRO moved it behind Mars for the passage of comet Siding Spring on 19 October. Its instruments reported argon in the Martian exosphere and mapped surface reflectance, and in 2015 its radio signals, passing through the solar corona, helped scientists study the Sun. It also provided the first views of the far side of Deimos.

The mission made India the first Asian nation to reach Martian orbit and ISRO the fourth space agency to do so, after the Soviet programme, NASA and the European Space Agency. The mission team won the National Space Society's 2015 Space Pioneer Award, and an illustration of the spacecraft appears on the reverse of India's 2,000 rupee note. In April 2022 the orbiter entered a seven-hour eclipse it was not designed to survive. On 2 October 2022 it was reported to have lost communications irrecoverably, and the next day ISRO declared it dead. A follow-up mission, Mangalyaan-2, is planned with a larger scientific payload.
marshall-islands: The Marshall Islands lie west of the International Date Line and north of the equator, about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, on the tops of ancient submerged volcanoes. The country consists of 29 atolls and five individual islands, and the atolls and islands form two roughly parallel chains running northwest to southeast, Ratak (sunrise) and Ralik (sunset). They cover about 1,900,000 square kilometres of ocean but only about 180 square kilometres of land, at an average height of 2.1 metres above sea level. The largest atoll by land area is Kwajalein, which surrounds a lagoon of about 1,700 square kilometres. Twenty-four of the atolls and islands are inhabited.

Austronesian settlers, possibly from the Solomon Islands, brought coconuts, giant swamp taro, breadfruit and domesticated chickens. Radiocarbon dates suggest Bikini Atoll may have been inhabited by 1200 BCE, though the samples are doubtful, and excavations on Majuro and Kwajalein show habitation around the 1st century CE. The wetter southern atolls probably held denser populations.

The first Europeans were the Spanish crew of Alonso de Salazar, who reached Taongi in 1526. European charts later named the group for the British captain John Marshall, who explored the region in 1788. American Protestant missionaries and Western traders arrived from the 1850s, and German copra traders dominated the economy in the 1870s and 1880s. After the First World War the islands became the Japanese South Seas Mandate. Under United States administration, 67 nuclear tests were conducted at Bikini and Enewetak between 1946 and 1958. In 1979 the United States recognised the Marshallese constitution and its president, Amata Kabua.

The capital and largest city is Majuro, where about half of the population lives; the 2021 census counted 42,418 residents. Marshallese and English are the official languages. The country is a presidential parliamentary republic in free association with the United States, with a legislature called the Nitijela and an advisory Council of Iroij of twelve paramount chiefs. Land is the main measure of a family's wealth and is inherited through the maternal line. Some 96.2 per cent of people identified with a Christian denomination at the 2021 census, the largest being the United Church of Christ - Congregational in the Marshall Islands.
marshall-mcluhan: Herbert Marshall McLuhan was born on 21 July 1911 in Edmonton, Alberta. His mother, Elsie Naomi Hall, was a Baptist school teacher who later became an actress, and his father, Herbert Ernest McLuhan, a Methodist, ran a real-estate business. The family moved to Winnipeg in 1915. McLuhan studied at the University of Manitoba, where he took a Bachelor of Arts in 1933 and a Master of Arts in English in 1934, and then went to Trinity Hall, Cambridge. His reading of G. K. Chesterton led him to convert to Catholicism in 1937.

McLuhan took a teaching post at the University of Wisconsin–Madison for the academic year 1936–1937 and then taught English at Saint Louis University from 1937 to 1944, with a return to Cambridge in 1939–1940. There he befriended and tutored Walter J. Ong. He moved to the University of Toronto in 1946 and stayed there for the rest of his life. In the early 1950s he began the Communication and Culture seminars, funded by the Ford Foundation, and with Edmund Carpenter he produced the journal Explorations. To keep him from moving elsewhere, the university created the Centre for Culture and Technology in 1963. McLuhan suffered a stroke in September 1979 that affected his speech, and he died in his sleep on 31 December 1980.

His first book, The Mechanical Bride (1951), studied advertising and popular culture. The Gutenberg Galaxy (1962) examined how alphabetic writing, the printing press and electronic media affect cognitive organisation and, through it, social organisation. In Understanding Media (1964) he put forward the aphorism the medium is the message, which calls attention to the effects that communications media have apart from their content, and he used the term global village. The Medium Is the Massage (1967), designed with Quentin Fiore, sold nearly a million copies.

In the posthumous Laws of Media (1988) he summarised his ideas in a tetrad of four questions: what a medium enhances, what it makes obsolete, what it retrieves that had been obsolete earlier, and what it flips into when pushed to extremes. His reputation was at its height in the late 1960s and declined in the early 1970s.
marshall-plan: By the end of the Second World War much of Europe was devastated. Bombing had damaged most major cities and industrial plants, trade flows were disrupted, and millions of refugees lived in temporary camps on aid from the United States. Food shortages were severe, especially in the harsh winter of 1946 to 1947. In 1947 agricultural production stood at 83% of the 1938 level, industrial production at 88% and exports at 59%, although the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and France had by the end of that year restored production to pre-war levels.

In 1947 the Moscow conference of the foreign ministers failed after six weeks of talks with the Soviets on rebuilding Germany, and the United States concluded that a solution could not wait. Secretary of State George C. Marshall gave an address at Harvard University on 5 June 1947 offering American aid to promote European recovery. The plan was largely the creation of State Department officials, especially William L. Clayton and George F. Kennan, and had bipartisan support in Washington, where Republicans controlled Congress and Harry S. Truman was president.

After Marshall's speech, British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin and French Foreign Minister Georges Bidault quickly arranged a European response, which led to the Committee of European Economic Co-operation. The offer included the Soviet Union, but Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov left Paris rejecting the plan, and the Soviet Union also blocked its Eastern Bloc neighbours, including Romania and Poland, from taking part. The USSR devised its own programme, the Molotov Plan.

The plan was enacted in 1948 and operated for four years from 3 April 1948. The United States transferred 13.3 billion dollars to participating countries, roughly on a per capita basis, with more for the major industrial powers. The United Kingdom received about 26% of the total, France 18% and West Germany 11%. Allied countries received somewhat more per person than former Axis or neutral ones.

The goals of the United States were to rebuild war-torn regions, remove trade barriers, modernise industry, improve prosperity and prevent the spread of communism. The plan encouraged the economic integration of Europe and the adoption of modern business procedures. How far it caused the rapid recovery is debated: aid amounted to about 3% of the recipients' combined national income between 1948 and 1951. Yugoslavia, after breaking with Stalin in 1948, later received American aid that was not part of the plan. The phrase "a Marshall Plan" is still used for any large rescue programme.
marsilio-ficino: Marsilio Ficino was born at Figline Valdarno on 19 October 1433. His father, Diotifeci d'Agnolo, was a physician under the patronage of Cosimo de' Medici, who took the young man into his household and remained his lifelong patron. Ficino became tutor to Cosimo's grandson Lorenzo de' Medici, and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was another of his students. In 1459 he became a pupil of John Argyropoulos, who was lecturing on Greek language and literature at Florence. Trained as a physician, he became a priest in 1473. A later account by the historian Cesare Baronio says that he and his friend Michele Mercati were first Epicureans before turning to Platonism.

The sessions of the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1438–1445 had brought Cosimo's circle into contact with the Neoplatonist George Gemistos Plethon. When Cosimo decided to refound Plato's Academy at Florence, he chose Ficino as its head, and in 1462 supplied him with Greek manuscripts of Plato. Ficino translated the whole corpus into Latin, finishing a draft of the dialogues in 1468–69 and publishing it in 1484. He also translated the collection later called the Hermetica and writings of Neoplatonists including Porphyry, Iamblichus and Plotinus. His students included Niccolò Valori and Francesco Cattani da Diacceto, whom he regarded as his successor as head of the Academy.

In 1474 he completed the Platonic Theology, a treatise on the immortality of the soul, and On the Christian Religion, a history of religions and defence of Christianity. In 1489 he was accused of heresy before Pope Innocent VIII, partly because of his interest in astrology, and was acquitted. His letters from 1474 to 1494 survive.

Ficino wrote Of Love, a commentary on Plato's Symposium, in 1484, and coined the term Platonic love, which first appears in a letter of 1476. His letters to his friend Giovanni Cavalcanti and the treatise helped spread the notion in western Europe. His Three Books on Life of 1489 gives medical and astrological advice for health and vigour and presents the world as ensouled and linked to the human soul. He also wrote treatises on medicine, among them advice on treating plague, and they influenced Renaissance physicians such as Paracelsus.

Behind his work lay a tendency to seek concord between Platonism and Christianity. In his commentary on Plotinus he reinterpreted the more pagan Neoplatonic doctrines, such as the transmigration of the soul, as moral allegories. In 1494 he revised his position on astrology as allegorical rather than dogmatic. Ficino died on 1 October 1499 at Careggi, and in 1521 a bust by Andrea Ferrucci was set up in his memory in the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore.
marsilius-of-padua: Marsilius was born in Padua, near Venice, around 1275, with the family name Mainardi or Mainardini. He was trained in medicine, probably at the University of Padua, and practised a variety of professions. He later went to the University of Paris, where he became a devoted admirer of Aristotle, whom he called the divine philosopher. He served as rector of the University of Paris approximately in 1312 and 1313, and probably taught there before and after his term.

Marsilius wrote Defensor pacis in 1324, during a power struggle between Pope John XXII and Louis of Bavaria, the elected candidate for Holy Roman Emperor. In 1323 Louis had sent an army to Italy to protect Milan against the Kingdom of Naples, a strong ally of the pope; John excommunicated him and demanded that he give up his claim to the imperial crown. Marsilius argued from reason and from authority that the empire was independent of the papacy and that the powers claimed by the popes were empty. Much of the work is theology: relying on Scripture, he sought to show that Jesus claimed no temporal power and that the church should be subordinate to the state in both secular and spiritual matters.

Its political philosophy is what it is remembered for. Marsilius agreed with Aristotle that government serves the natural human desire for a sufficient life, but went beyond him in embracing a republicanism in which the people are the only legitimate source of authority. The people should elect, correct and if necessary depose their rulers, and democracy, he argued, tends to produce the wisest laws. He held that scripture stands above the church and that the papacy was created by human arrangement. Pope John XXII declared a number of his views heretical in 1327. In the later Defensor minor he took up ecclesiastical jurisdiction, indulgences, excommunication and marriage.

Marsilius and John of Jandun, sometimes credited as a co-author, left France for Louis's court in Bavaria, where Louis protected them together with Michael of Cesena and William of Ockham. In 1326 Marsilius went with Louis to Italy. Louis was crowned King of Italy in Milan in 1327 and entered Rome in January 1328, where he was crowned emperor and declared John XXII deposed for heresy. Marsilius was appointed archbishop of Milan as recompense for his services. He died in Munich around 1342, still unreconciled to the Church. Some scholars see Defensor pacis as the most revolutionary political treatise of the later Middle Ages, and he is sometimes seen as a forerunner of the Reformation.
marthas-vineyard: Martha's Vineyard lies just south of Cape Cod and has a land area of about 96 square miles (250 km2). It includes the peninsula of Chappaquiddick Island and forms the bulk of Dukes County, Massachusetts, together with the Elizabeth Islands and Nomans Land. In the Massachusett language its Wampanoag name Noepe means land amid the streams. Another native name, Capawock, appears in the 1691 Massachusetts Charter as Cappawock.

The English name probably honours Martha Golding, the mother-in-law of the explorer Bartholomew Gosnold, who partly funded his 1602 expedition to Cape Cod. The name first belonged to a smaller island to the south and later moved to this one. For a time the island was also called Martin's Vineyard, possibly after John Martin, a captain in the party.

About 3,000 Wampanoag lived on the island in 1642; by 1764 the number had fallen to 313. English settlement began when Thomas Mayhew of Watertown bought Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and the Elizabeth Islands. His son, also Thomas Mayhew, founded the first settlement in 1642 at Great Harbor, later Edgartown, and built a relationship with the Wampanoag neighbour Hiacoomes, whose family converted to Christianity. The Mayhews respected Wampanoag land rights, and the island's band did not join the uprising of King Philip's War.

In 1665 the Mayhew lands were included in a grant to the Duke of York, and a settlement of 1671 placed them under the Province of New York. Enslaved people were bought, sold and probated on the island, though Samuel Sewall publicly opposed slavery in 1700. Whaling brought prosperity in the nineteenth century and had almost collapsed by 1870, when petroleum offered cheaper lamp oil. After the Old Colony railroad reached Woods Hole in 1872, summer residences began to appear.

The island was the last refuge of the heath hen, whose last known bird died in 1932. It also had an unusually high rate of hereditary deafness, and by the late nineteenth century about one person in 155 was born deaf. Sign language was widely used among hearing and deaf residents alike. The linguist William Labov studied the island's dialect in 1963.

The island is divided into six towns, each governed by selectmen and town meetings, and all belong to the Martha's Vineyard Commission, which regulates island-wide building and environmental matters. A substantial Wampanoag population remains, mainly in the town of Aquinnah. The island is reached by ferry, chiefly from Woods Hole, and is a summer resort.
martin-bucer: Martin Bucer was born on 11 November 1491 in Sélestat, a free imperial city of Alsace. His father and grandfather, both called Claus Butzer, were coopers. After the Latin school of Sélestat he joined the Dominican Order as a novice in 1507, and he later claimed that his grandfather had forced him into it. He was ordained deacon in 1510 and by 1515 was studying theology at the Dominican monastery in Heidelberg. In January 1517 he enrolled at the University of Heidelberg, where humanism influenced him. In 1518 he was influenced by Martin Luther and had his monastic vows annulled, and he then worked for the Reformation with the support of Franz von Sickingen.

His efforts at Wissembourg led to his excommunication, and he arrived in Strasbourg without means in 1523. The council was under the influence of Matthew Zell. On 24 August 1523 the largest guild appointed Bucer pastor of St Aurelia's Church, and the council accepted his application for citizenship a month later. He joined Zell, Wolfgang Capito and Caspar Hedio. From 1524 he tried to mediate between Luther and Huldrych Zwingli on the Eucharist. In 1530 he wrote the Tetrapolitan Confession, adopted by Strasbourg, Konstanz, Memmingen and Lindau. Strasbourg suspended the mass on 20 February 1529.

By 1534 he was a leading figure in the German Reformation and sought agreement between Wittenberg, the south German cities and Switzerland, with talks with Philipp Melanchthon at Kassel in December 1534. In 1538 Philip of Hesse commissioned him to draw up a policy on the Jews, and Bucer recommended stricter limits than Philip's draft; the ordinance of 1539 was a compromise, and many Jews left Hesse. From 1542 he led church reform at Bonn for the archbishop-elector Hermann von Wied of Cologne.

After the Schmalkaldic War Strasbourg surrendered to the imperial army on 21 March 1547, and the Protestants retreated within the Empire. Charles V sought the endorsement of a leading reformer for the Augsburg Interim, which imposed Catholic rites throughout the Empire, and chose Bucer. In 1549 he accepted Thomas Cranmer's invitation to England, arriving in London on 25 April, and became Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge. He influenced the Edwardine Ordinals and the second revision of the Book of Common Prayer. He died in Cambridge on 28 February 1551, aged 59. His ministry did not lead to a new denomination, but many Protestant denominations claim him, and he is remembered as an early pioneer of ecumenism.
martin-luther: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 to Hans Luder and his wife Margarethe in Eisleben. In 1484 the family moved to Mansfeld, where his father leased copper mines and smelters and later became a town councillor. Hans was determined that his eldest son should become a lawyer. Luther entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and received his master's degree in 1505, but dropped out of law almost at once. According to one story, a lightning bolt struck near him during a thunderstorm on 2 July 1505, and he cried out, "Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!" He entered St Augustine's Monastery in Erfurt on 17 July 1505, to his father's fury.

As an Augustinian friar Luther devoted himself to fasting, prayer and confession, and described this period as one of deep spiritual despair. He was ordained on 3 April 1507, began teaching theology at the University of Wittenberg in 1508 and received his Doctor of Theology on 19 October 1512, succeeding Johann von Staupitz as chair of theology.

From 1510 to 1520 he lectured on the Psalms, Hebrews, Romans and Galatians, and became convinced that the Church was corrupt. The most important doctrine for him was justification by faith alone through God's grace, which he held to be entirely God's work. He taught that the Bible is the only source of divinely revealed knowledge of the Gospel, which challenged the authority of the pope and bishops. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in January 1521, and that year Emperor Charles V condemned him as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms.

At Luther's death in 1546 his excommunication was still in effect. He made effective use of the printing press and wrote in German to reach a broader audience; between 1500 and 1530 his works made up one fifth of all materials printed in Germany. His German Bible of 1534 fostered a standard version of the German language, and his marriage to Katharina von Bora, a former nun, set a model for clerical marriage.

Luther expressed staunchly antisemitic views, calling for the expulsion of Jews and the burning of synagogues. According to the prevailing opinion among historians, his anti-Jewish rhetoric contributed significantly to the development of antisemitism in Germany, and Nazi propaganda cited it.
martin-luther-king-jr: Martin Luther King Jr. was born Michael King Jr. on 15 January 1929 in Atlanta, the second of three children of Michael King and Alberta King. His maternal grandfather, Adam Daniel Williams, was a minister who became pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church. King enrolled at Crozer Theological Seminary in Pennsylvania, where he was elected president of the student body, and later studied at Boston University. He married Coretta Scott on 18 June 1953.

King oversaw the 1955 Montgomery bus boycott, was the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, helped organise the 1963 protests in Birmingham, Alabama, and was one of the leaders of the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave the I Have a Dream speech. On 14 October 1964 he became the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. The FBI director J. Edgar Hoover ordered surveillance of him, and a 1975 congressional investigation found that from December 1963 until his death he was the target of an intensive campaign to neutralise him.

In March 1968 King went to Memphis, Tennessee, to support striking black sanitation workers, and on 3 April gave the address I've Been to the Mountaintop. He was assassinated on 4 April 1968. James Earl Ray was convicted of the killing, though conspiracy theories persist, and King's death led to riots in American cities. Martin Luther King Jr. Day was first observed as a federal holiday in 1986.
martin-of-aragon: Martin was born in 1356, in either Girona or Perpignan, both then in the Principality of Catalonia. He was the second son of King Peter IV of Aragon and Eleanor of Sicily, a princess of the Sicilian branch of the House of Aragon. As a younger prince he received the County of Besalú, and on 13 June 1372 he married María López de Luna, daughter and heiress of the Count of Luna.

In 1380 his father appointed him lord and regent of Sicily, whose queen, Maria of Sicily, was still a minor. His son Martin the Younger married her in 1391 and was crowned king of Sicily beside her. The Sicilians, led by the Alagona family, rebelled in 1392, partly because the marriage had been conducted by the Antipope Clement VII. Martin led an expedition that took Trapani and Palermo, but the opposition held out until 1398.

In 1396 Martin succeeded his elder brother John I, who had died without a son. Unrest in Sicily kept him there, and his wife claimed the throne on his behalf until he arrived in 1397. His right was contested by Count Matthew of Foix on behalf of his wife Joanna, John's elder daughter, and Martin defeated an invasion by the count's troops. After Joanna's death her sister Yolande of Aragon continued the claim. Martin launched crusades against the Moors of North Africa in 1398 and 1399.

In Sardinia the principality of Arborea had driven the Aragonese back under Eleanor of Arborea. Martin sent his son to reconquer the island, and Martin the Younger won the Battle of Sanluri in 1409 and subdued many Sardinian nobles, though he died soon afterwards of malaria. The father then became king of Sicily as Martin II. He supported the Avignon line of popes, and in 1403 his troops freed the Aragonese Pope Benedict XIII from his rivals.

Martin died on 31 May 1410 in the monastery of Valldonzella outside Barcelona. The cause is unclear: plague, uremic coma linked to his severe obesity, or poison, a claim supported only by one Renaissance chronicler. A story that he died laughing at a jester's joke lacks historical evidence. Asked whether the throne should go to the most legitimate claimant, he is said to have answered only "Hoc" (Yes), and he named no heir.

His second marriage, to Margaret of Prades in September 1409, produced no children. His illegitimate grandson Frederick, Count of Luna, could not be confirmed as heir in time. The two-year interregnum brought forward at least five contenders, among them Frederick and James II of Urgell. The Compromise of Caspe, on 28 June 1412, chose Martin's nephew Ferdinand, infante of Castile, and so began the House of Trastámara.
martin-of-tours: Martin was born in Savaria in the Diocese of Pannonia, now Szombathely in Hungary. His father was a tribune in the Roman army, who was given veteran status and land at Ticinum, now Pavia, in northern Italy, where Martin grew up. At the age of ten he attended a Christian church against his parents' wishes and became a catechumen. He served in the Roman cavalry in Gaul, and his contemporary biographer Sulpicius Severus tells how at the gates of Amiens he cut his military cloak in half to share it with a beggar. That night he dreamed of Jesus wearing the half he had given, and he was baptised at 18.

Martin left military service before 361 and became a disciple of Hilary of Poitiers, whose Nicene orthodoxy he shared in opposition to the Arianism of the imperial court. In Illyricum he took the Nicene side with so much zeal that he was publicly whipped and made to leave. He established the monastery at Ligugé.

In 371 he succeeded Litorius as the third bishop of Tours. According to one tradition he hid in a barn full of geese to avoid it, but their cackling gave him away. He ordered the destruction of pagan temples, altars and sculptures. In 385 Magnus Maximus ordered the beheading of the ascetic Priscillian and his followers. Martin, though strongly opposed to their teaching, had travelled to the imperial court at Trier to reject Bishop Ithacius's principle of putting heretics to death and the emperor's intrusion into such matters, as Ambrose of Milan also did. Maximus granted him a promise to spare Priscillian, then broke it.

Martin died at Candes-Saint-Martin in 397. People of Poitou and of Tours quarrelled over his burial, and residents of Tours carried the body by boat down the Loire to their city. His shrine became one of the most prominent establishments in medieval France. Charlemagne made his adviser Alcuin abbot, and the scriptorium at Tours developed Carolingian minuscule. The abbey was ransacked by Vikings in 853 and 903.

The half of the cloak he kept became a relic of the Merovingian kings, first attested in the royal treasury in 679, and was carried into battle and used for oaths. He is the patron of beggars, tailors, vintners and geese, and of cities such as Szombathely and Utrecht, and is usually shown on horseback dividing his cloak.
martin-slovakia: Martin lies in northern Slovakia on the Turiec river, in the Turiec Basin just south of the confluence of the Turiec with the Váh, between the Malá Fatra and Veľká Fatra mountains. It stands at an altitude of 402 metres. The nearest major cities are Žilina, 30 kilometres to the north-west, and Banská Bystrica, 60 kilometres to the south-east, and it is the centre of the Turiec region. Its older names were Turčiansky Svätý Martin in Slovak, Turócszentmárton in Hungarian and Turz-Sankt Martin in German.

From the second half of the 10th century until 1918 the area belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary. The first written reference to Martin dates from 1284, under the name Vila Sancti Martini. The 15th century was turbulent: the Hussites attacked in 1433 and burned the town, and ten years later an earthquake destroyed it again. Martin slowly declined from a royal town to a privileged one under the direct influence of the Révay family. In the 18th century it became the centre of Turóc county.

In the 19th century Martin became the foremost Slovak cultural centre. Several cultural institutions, among them the Slovak Matica and the Slovak National Museum, were founded there, and most of the political activity that led to Slovak national emancipation in the 19th and early 20th centuries was organised in or from the town. It was also industrialised then: its first printing works opened in 1869 and the furniture factory Tatra nábytok in 1890. The town lost some of its importance after Pressburg, today's Bratislava, became the capital of Slovakia in 1919.

Martin is the seat of the Slovak National Library and of Matica slovenská, and on 24 August 1994 the National Council of the Slovak Republic declared it the centre of national culture of the Slovaks. Its oldest building is a Romanesque church of Saint Martin of Tours, dating from the 13th century. The Slovak National Museum keeps its ethnographic collection there, and an open-air museum in the suburbs shows the traditional rural architecture of the Turiec region. The Slovak National Cemetery serves as the Slovak hall of fame and was inspired by the Panthéon in Paris. The Slovak Chamber Theatre, founded in 1944, was the second professional theatre company in Slovakia, and the Jessenius Faculty of Medicine is one of the country's three medical schools.
martos: Martos is a city and municipality in the province of Jaén in Andalusia. The housing lies at the foot of the Peña de Martos, a rock of 1,003 metres on the western side of the Sierra Sur de Jaén, a subrange of the Baetic System in the south of the Iberian Peninsula. Its economy has long rested on agriculture, above all the cultivation of the olive tree, and olive groves cover some 22,000 hectares, about 85 percent of the municipal area. The town has been nicknamed the Cradle of the Olive Grove.

The city has been linked to the Roman settlement of Colonia Augusta Gemella. Around 250 CE a bishopric was established in what is now Martos under the name Tucci, on territory taken from the suppressed Diocese of Iliturgi, as a suffragan of the archdiocese of Sevilla. In 350 it lost territory to the new Diocese of Cástulo and regained it when that see was suppressed about 400. In 715 the see was itself suppressed to found the Diocese of Beaza. The recorded bishops include Rogato, in office from about 675 to 688, and Teudisclo from about 693.

From the 8th century the Moors ruled the city under various Islamic states for over 500 years. In 1225 Ferdinand III of Castile and León received it from al-Bayyasi, in exchange for helping al-Bayyasi in his war against the Almohads in Andalusia, and incorporated it into his kingdom. During the Middle Ages it became a strategic place, and numerous fortifications were built to strengthen its defences.

At the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th, Martos went through a period of economic and urban growth, reflected in its architecture, thanks largely to the industrial production of olive oil. It became one of the most prosperous cities of eastern Andalusia. The population grew strongly in the first half of the 20th century, peaking at over 30,000 in the 1950s, and then fell as work was scarce and many people left for Madrid, Barcelona and the Spanish Levante.

Martos has a population of about 24,000, the fifth largest municipality of its province. It is also an industrial centre of inland Andalusia. The population rises unofficially in winter, when migrant workers come for the olive harvest.
martti-ahtisaari: Martti Ahtisaari was born in Viipuri (now Vyborg, Russia) on 23 June 1937. His father, Oiva, a non-commissioned officer in the supply troops, was at the front during the Continuation War, and his mother, Tyyne, took him to Kuopio in 1940, where he spent most of his childhood. The family moved to Oulu in 1952, and he graduated from high school in 1956 and qualified as a primary-school teacher in 1959. In 1960 he became director of a physical education boarding school in Karachi, Pakistan. In 1965 he joined the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, where he helped set up its International Development Assistance Office.

His diplomatic career began in 1973 as Finland's ambassador to Tanzania, Zambia, Somalia and Mozambique. In 1977 the United Nations recalled him to succeed Seán MacBride as Commissioner for Namibia. In April 1989 he went to Namibia as UN Special Representative to head the United Nations Transition Assistance Group. When SWAPO fighters crossed from Angola, he approved the deployment of South African troops to restore order, and in the fighting that followed at least 375 SWAPO insurgents were killed; some observers thought he had made too many concessions to the South Africans. After the independence elections he and his wife were made honorary Namibian citizens in 1992.

He was a UN under-secretary-general from 1987 to 1991, Secretary of State at Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs from 1991, and in 1992-1993 chaired the working group on Bosnia and Herzegovina at the Conference on Yugoslavia. Elected in the first direct presidential election, he beat Elisabeth Rehn in the second round and was sworn in on 1 March 1994. He supported Finland's entry into the European Union, approved by 57 per cent in a 1994 referendum, and in 1999 negotiated with Viktor Chernomyrdin to end the fighting in Kosovo with Slobodan Milošević. He did not stand for re-election, and Tarja Halonen succeeded him on 1 March 2000. He was the last strong president before the 2000 constitution reduced the office's powers.

He became chairman of the International Crisis Group in 2000 and founded the Crisis Management Initiative. In November 2005 UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed him Special Envoy for the Kosovo status process, which ended in 2007 and was followed by Kosovo's declaration of independence in February 2008. On 10 October 2008 he was announced as winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to resolve international conflicts over more than three decades. He died in Helsinki on 16 October 2023, aged 86, after an illness announced in 2021, and was buried at Hietaniemi Cemetery after a state funeral.
marwan-ii: Marwan ibn Muhammad belonged to the Marwanid house of the Umayyad Caliphate. He was the son of Muhammad ibn Marwan, a grandson of the caliph Marwan I and a nephew of the caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. Historical tradition places his birth around 695. Political opponents used his mother's lineage against him during the civil wars of the Third Fitna: hostile accounts claimed she was a non-Arab concubine of Kurdish origin who was already pregnant when Muhammad acquired her.

In 732-733 Caliph Hisham appointed Marwan governor of Armenia. In 735-736 he invaded Georgia, devastated it, took three fortresses of the Alans and made peace with Tumanshah; further raids in 739-740 brought tribute. For several years he supervised campaigns against the Byzantines and the Khazars on the northwestern frontiers. When a plot against al-Walid II took shape, he wrote from Armenia urging his relatives to preserve the unity of the Umayyad house, but he was ignored, and Yazid III deposed al-Walid. Yazid then made him governor of Upper Mesopotamia, where he lived at Harran.

Marwan at first opposed Yazid III and then gave him allegiance. When Yazid died early, Marwan ignored the successor Yazid had named, Ibrahim ibn al-Walid, and became caliph. Ibrahim received assurances of personal safety and accompanied him to Hisham's residence at Rusafah. Marwan named his sons Ubaydallah and Abdullah as heirs. Anti-Umayyad feeling was strong, especially in Iran and Iraq, and his reign was almost entirely devoted to holding the empire together.

He took Emesa (Homs) after a ten-month siege and fought a Kharijite rebellion led by al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Shaybani, which took Kufa; Marwan besieged the rebels at Mosul for six months before driving them out. In Khurasan the governor Nasr ibn Sayyar faced rivals while Abbasid envoys arrived, and during Ramadan of 747 the Abbasids unfurled the standards of their revolt. Nasr died at Rayy on 9 November 748. Marwan's campaign in Egypt in 749 against the Bashmuric Revolt failed.

Marwan suffered a decisive defeat by Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah on the Great Zab, at the Battle of the Zab, where over 300 members of the Umayyad family died. He fled through Damascus, Jordan and Palestine to Egypt, where he was caught and killed on 6 August 750. His sons escaped to what is now Eritrea, and Abdallah died fighting there.

His death ended Umayyad fortunes in the East and was followed by a mass killing of Umayyads by the Abbasids. Almost the entire dynasty was killed, except the prince Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, who escaped to Spain and founded an Umayyad dynasty there.
marxism-leninism: Marxism–Leninism drew on Bolshevism, Leninism and classical Marxism. It began as the practical politics of the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, which Vladimir Lenin turned into a vanguard of professional revolutionaries who chose leaders and policy by democratic centralism. The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution of 1917 and fought the White Movement in the Russian Civil War. In the 1917 election to the Constituent Assembly they won 23.3 percent of the vote against 37.6 for the Socialist Revolutionary Party, and the assembly was dissolved in January 1918.

After Lenin's death on 21 January 1924, Joseph Stalin and his supporters gained control of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, and Marxism–Leninism became a distinct movement. It rejected the view of Western Marxists that world revolution was needed first, in favour of socialism in one country. By the late 1920s Stalin had established ideological orthodoxy in the party and the Communist International.

Marxism–Leninism holds that a two-stage communist revolution must replace capitalism. A vanguard party, organised through democratic centralism, seizes power on behalf of the proletariat and establishes a one-party state, which controls the means of production and suppresses opposition to pave the way for a classless and stateless society. Its worldview is atheist, and it supports universal welfare, with healthcare and education provided by the state. Its approach to international relations rests on Lenin's essay Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism of 1917.

From 1928 Stalin's five-year plans brought rapid industrialisation, concentrated on heavy industry, and the collectivisation of agriculture, which stood at 23.6 percent in 1930 and 98.0 percent in 1941. After Stalin's death it was revised into Titoism, Guevarism, Ho Chi Minh Thought, Hoxhaism and Maoism.

Marxism–Leninism was the state ideology of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, and of the Communist International. The union Solidarity, formed in Poland in 1980, was the first trade union in the Warsaw Pact not controlled by a Marxist–Leninist party, and the Eastern European governments and the Soviet Union fell by 1991.

Critics from across the political spectrum have attacked it, above all in its Stalinist and Maoist forms. Historians such as Silvio Pons and David Martin Walker connect killings and repression of dissidents and social classes, as in the Red Terror and the Great Purge in the Soviet Union, partly to the ideology, while others offer different explanations. Rosa Luxemburg rejected the vanguard idea, and some left-wing critics see it as state capitalism.
mary-i-of-england: Mary was born on 18 February 1516 at the Palace of Placentia in Greenwich, the only child of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon to survive infancy. She could read and write Latin by the age of nine. In 1525 Henry sent her to preside over the Council of Wales and the Marches from Ludlow Castle. The annulment of her parents' marriage in 1533 declared her illegitimate and barred her from the succession, and after Anne Boleyn's fall in 1536 she was bullied into signing a document accepting Henry as head of the Church, her parents' marriage as unlawful and her own illegitimacy. The Third Succession Act of 1543 restored her place in the line.

Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, having excluded Mary and Elizabeth from the succession in favour of Lady Jane Grey at the urging of John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland. Mary fled to East Anglia, where Catholic supporters and Northumberland's enemies lived, and wrote to the privy council from Kenninghall on 9 July to order her own proclamation. Lady Jane was deposed, and Mary was crowned by Stephen Gardiner at Westminster Abbey on 1 October 1553. Northumberland was the only conspirator of rank executed at once.

A parliamentary delegation asked her to choose an English husband, but she chose Philip, son of her cousin Charles V, and they married in July 1554. Her first Parliament declared her parents' marriage valid and abolished Edward's religious laws, and the church returned to Roman jurisdiction. The Heresy Acts were revived in January 1555, and more than 280 religious dissenters were burned at the stake, among them Protestant churchmen such as Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, John Hooper and John Rogers. Queen's and King's Counties were founded in Ireland. In 1554 and again in 1557 she believed herself pregnant, but no child was born.

Weak and ill from May 1558, Mary died on 17 November 1558, aged 42, at St James's Palace, during an influenza epidemic, and was succeeded by Elizabeth I. She was buried in Westminster Abbey on 14 December in a tomb she later shared with Elizabeth. She was the first woman to successfully claim the throne of England. Protestant writers have often condemned her reign, and John Foxe's Actes and Monuments (1563) helped shape the picture of a bloodthirsty tyrant. By the seventeenth century the persecutions had given her the name Bloody Mary.
mary-ii-of-england: Mary was born on 30 April 1662 at St James's Palace in London, the daughter of James, Duke of York, and his first wife, Anne Hyde. Her uncle Charles II had no legitimate children, so for most of her childhood she was second in line to the throne. Although her father converted to Roman Catholicism, she and her sister Anne were brought up as Anglicans on the command of Charles II.

At the age of 15 she was betrothed to her first cousin William of Orange, the Protestant Stadtholder of Holland, and they married at St James's Palace on 4 November 1677. When her father told her of the match, she wept all that afternoon and all the following day. She had no surviving children, and her childlessness caused her deep unhappiness.

James II's attempt to grant religious freedom by royal decree, and the birth of his Catholic son in June 1688, led seven English nobles to invite William to England. Mary stayed in the Netherlands while William landed on 5 November 1688. On 13 February 1689 Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary as joint sovereigns, with the exercise of royal power to rest with William. They were crowned at Westminster Abbey on 11 April 1689.

While William was campaigning abroad, usually from spring to autumn, Mary governed with the advice of a nine-member Cabinet Council. When he was in England she kept out of politics. She nevertheless proved firm, ordering the arrest of her uncle Henry Hyde, 2nd Earl of Clarendon, for plotting to restore James. In January 1692 John Churchill, 1st Earl of Marlborough, was dismissed on similar charges, and the affair ended with her final quarrel with Anne. Mary was devout, and the composer Henry Purcell wrote birthday odes for her.

Mary contracted smallpox in late 1694 and died at Kensington Palace shortly after midnight on 28 December, aged 32. She was buried at Westminster Abbey on 5 March, in the first royal funeral attended by all the members of both Houses of Parliament. William was devastated.

Mary endowed the College of William and Mary in Virginia in 1693 and helped to found the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich. Jacobites portrayed her as a daughter who had destroyed her father for gain, while the assessment that came down to posterity was of a dutiful wife who took power reluctantly, used it ably when needed and deferred it to her husband.
mary-mother-of-jesus: Mary was a first-century Jewish woman of Nazareth, the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus. The canonical Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles are the primary sources, and they give limited information because they focus on the teaching of Jesus and his apostles. They are generally dated to about 66–110 CE, and their historical reliability is debated. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke describe Mary as a virgin chosen by God to conceive Jesus through the Holy Spirit. After the birth in Bethlehem, she and Joseph raised him in Nazareth in Galilee, and she was in Jerusalem at his crucifixion.

Apocryphal texts add details, such as the Gospel of James, which names her parents as Joachim and Anne and says she was given to the Temple in Jerusalem at the age of three. Scholars generally consider such texts mainly unreliable. In the 2nd century the pagan philosopher Celsus claimed that Jesus was the illegitimate son of a Roman soldier named Panthera, and the Church Father Origen dismissed this as a fabrication.

The Bible does not describe the end of Mary's life. Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and some Oriental Orthodox and Protestant traditions hold that her body was raised into heaven at its close, which Western Christianity calls the Assumption and Eastern Christianity the Dormition of the Mother of God. The Catholic Church also holds the dogma of her Immaculate Conception.

Mary has been venerated since early Christianity. Eastern and Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches hold that she is the Mother of God, while many Protestants pay far less attention to her. Devotion takes the form of prayers and hymns, feast days, the veneration of images and relics, churches and pilgrimages. In Islam, where she is called Maryam, she has the highest position among women, and a chapter of the Quran is named for her. She is also revered in the Druze and Bahá'í faiths. In Western art she is traditionally painted in blue, a custom that goes back to the Byzantine Empire.
mary-of-burgundy: Mary was born on 13 February 1457 in Brussels, at the ducal Palace of Coudenberg, to Charles the Bold, then Count of Charolais, and Isabella of Bourbon. When her grandfather Philip the Good died in 1467 and her father took control of the Burgundian State, Mary became his heir presumptive. He held the Duchy of Burgundy, the Free County of Burgundy and most of the Low Countries, so many princes sought her hand. Louis XI wanted her for his son Charles VIII, who was thirteen years younger, and Edward IV of England prevented a match with George Plantagenet, Duke of Clarence.

Charles was killed at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477, and Mary, aged 19, claimed the whole inheritance, which included Limburg, Brabant, Luxembourg, Namur, Holland and Hainaut. Louis XI seized the Duchy of Burgundy, Franche-Comté, Picardy and Artois. When he took Arras, the people refused to submit without her approval, and he had eighteen burgesses beheaded for trying to see her. The dispute led to the War of the Burgundian Succession.

At Ghent on 10 February 1477 she signed the Great Privilege, a charter by which Flanders, Brabant, Hainaut and Holland recovered the local rights the dukes had abolished, and she undertook not to declare war, make peace or raise taxes without consent. On 19 August 1477 she married Archduke Maximilian of Austria, son of the emperor Frederick III. He came without money or army, but his prestige and military competence strengthened her position. The state had lost a quarter of its tax revenue, and Mary pawned heirlooms to pay for the armies. Her marriage began the long rivalry between France and the Habsburgs.

In 1482 Mary was hunting with falcons near Wijnendale Castle when her horse tripped and fell on her, breaking her back. She died on 27 March from internal injuries, after making a detailed will, and was buried in the Church of Our Lady in Bruges. She was pregnant. Her children were Philip the Handsome, Margaret of Austria and Franz, who died in infancy.

By the Treaty of Arras of 1482 Franche-Comté and Artois passed for a time to France, and the Treaty of Senlis of 1493 recovered them. Her son Philip I the Handsome inherited her domains and claims under the guardianship of his father. In the 19th century she became a national symbol of Belgium.
mary-of-guise: Mary of Guise was born on 22 November 1515 at Bar-le-Duc, Lorraine, the eldest of twelve children of Claude, Duke of Guise, and Antoinette of Bourbon. Her siblings included François, Duke of Guise, and Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine. She grew up partly in the convent of the Poor Clares at Pont-à-Mousson and reached a height of 5 feet 11 inches (1.80 metres). On 4 August 1534 she married Louis II d'Orléans, Duke of Longueville, Grand Chamberlain of France, and had two sons, of whom Francis survived. Louis died on 9 June 1537, leaving her a widow at 21.

Both Henry VIII of England and James V of Scotland sought her hand. After persuasion from Francis I of France she agreed to marry James, and they wed in person on 18 June 1538 at St Andrews Cathedral. She was crowned at Holyrood Abbey on 22 February 1540. Both her sons by James died in April 1541, and when James V died in December 1542 their daughter Mary became Queen of Scots at six days old. James Hamilton, 2nd Earl of Arran, became regent, and Henry VIII's wish to marry the infant to his son Edward led to the Rough Wooing and an English invasion.

With the Treaty of Haddington in 1548 the child queen was betrothed to the Dauphin Francis and sent to France. Mary of Guise stayed in Scotland, and in July 1548 she came to watch the siege of Haddington and came within range of the English guns, which killed sixteen of her entourage. She replaced Arran as regent on 12 April 1554. Her regency aimed to protect her daughter's dynastic interests, maintain the Franco-Scottish alliance and restore the power of the Scottish crown. She was tolerant of the reform movement and sought accommodation with Protestants.

The marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots, to the dauphin on 24 April 1558 and the accession of Elizabeth I in England in November 1558 raised the stakes. Henry II of France died in July 1559. French troops were stationed at Leith, and the Lords of the Congregation complained of Frenchmen holding Scottish posts. After an English assault on Leith was repulsed, Mary fell seriously ill in Edinburgh Castle, made her will on 8 June and died of dropsy on 11 June 1560.

Apart from John Knox, historians have generally judged her favourably. Rosalind K. Marshall describes her as charming, highly intelligent and hard-working, and says she fought a long and in the end hopeless struggle to keep Scotland a pro-French, Roman Catholic nation for her daughter, never merely a pawn of the French king.
mary-shelley: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in Somers Town, London, on 30 August 1797, the child of the philosopher William Godwin and the women's rights advocate Mary Wollstonecraft, who died of puerperal fever eleven days after the birth. Godwin brought her up with her older half-sister, Fanny Imlay, gave her a rich informal education and encouraged her in his own anarchist political theories. When she was four, he married a neighbour, Mary Jane Clairmont, with whom Mary had a troubled relationship.

In 1814 she began a romance with Percy Bysshe Shelley, a follower of her father who was already married. With her stepsister Claire Clairmont they left for France and travelled through Europe. After their return they faced ostracism, constant debt and the death of their daughter. Percy's wife Harriet was found drowned in December 1816, and Mary and Percy married on 30 December.

In May 1816 the couple and Claire Clairmont went to Geneva to spend the summer with Lord Byron, who rented the Villa Diodati with his physician John William Polidori. There Mary conceived the idea for Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, published in 1818. How far Percy contributed to it is argued: James Rieger saw him as editor or minor collaborator, while Anne K. Mellor held that he only made technical corrections.

The Shelleys left Britain for Italy in 1818. Two of their children died there, and Percy Florence was born on 12 November 1819. In 1822 Percy drowned when his boat sank in a storm near Viareggio, and a year later she returned to England as a professional author. Her novels include Valperga, The Last Man (1826), Lodore and Falkner, and she wrote biographies for Dionysius Lardner's Cabinet Cyclopaedia between 1832 and 1839. She published Percy's Posthumous Poems in 1824 and a new edition of his poetry in 1839.

The last decade of her life was dogged by illness, most likely caused by the brain tumour that killed her at the age of 53, on 1 February 1851. Until the 1970s she was known mainly for Frankenstein and her efforts to publish her husband's works. Recent scholarship finds in her other writing a political radical who argued that cooperation and sympathy, as practised by women in the family, were the ways to reform society.
mary-wollstonecraft: Mary Wollstonecraft was born on 27 April 1759 in Spitalfields, London, the second of the seven children of Elizabeth Dixon and Edward John Wollstonecraft. The family had a comfortable income in her childhood, but her father gradually squandered it on speculative projects, and the family moved often. He was apparently a violent man who beat his wife in drunken rages, and as a teenager Wollstonecraft lay outside her mother's bedroom door to protect her. She played a similar maternal role for her sisters Everina and Eliza. In 1784 she arranged for Eliza, probably suffering from postpartum depression, to leave her husband and infant, a decision that brought her sister social condemnation and poverty.

After Blood's death in 1785, Wollstonecraft's friends helped her to a post as governess to the daughters of the Anglo-Irish Kingsborough family in Ireland. Her early writings concern education, among them Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (1787), the children's book Original Stories from Real Life (1788) and the anthology The Female Reader. She also translated children's works. Her first novel, Mary: A Fiction, appeared in 1788, and her unfinished Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman was published after her death in 1798. Both novels criticise marriage and its effects on women.

A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790) answered Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, attacking aristocracy and advocating republicanism. It was the first reply in what became known as the Revolution Controversy. Wollstonecraft left for Paris in December 1792, shortly before Louis XVI was guillotined, and associated mostly with the moderate Girondins. There she fell in love with the American adventurer Gilbert Imlay, and their daughter Fanny was born. She was disillusioned by what she saw, writing that the new government remained venal and brutal. She wrote An Historical and Moral View of the French Revolution (1794).

Imlay rejected her when she returned to London in April 1795, and she attempted suicide twice. She travelled to Scandinavia on his business and recounted the journey in Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796). She later married the philosopher William Godwin.

Wollstonecraft gave birth to her second daughter, Mary, on 30 August 1797 and died of septicaemia on 10 September, at the age of 38. The daughter became the author of Frankenstein. Godwin's Memoirs of 1798 revealed her love affairs, illegitimate children and suicide attempts, and the Romantic poet Robert Southey accused him of stripping his dead wife naked. Her reputation lay in tatters for nearly a century, and novelists such as Maria Edgeworth pilloried her in their characters. With the feminist movement at the turn of the twentieth century her advocacy of women's equality was increasingly recognised.
maryland: Maryland borders Virginia to the south, West Virginia to the west, Pennsylvania to the north and Delaware to the east, as well as the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Washington, D.C. to the southwest. With an area of 12,407 square miles (32,130 km2) it is the ninth-smallest state by land area. The western portion contains stretches of the Appalachian Mountains, the centre is mainly Piedmont, and the east takes in a large part of the Chesapeake Bay, which nearly bisects the state.

The variety of its landscape, from sandy dunes in the east to marshes near the bay, oak forests in the Piedmont and pine groves in the mountains, has earned it the nickname America in Miniature. Its history as a border state has left it with traits of both North and South.

Present-day Maryland was inhabited by Native peoples, mostly Algonquian, including the Piscataway, the Nanticoke and the Susquehannock. George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore, sought a charter from King Charles I for the territory between Massachusetts and Virginia. After he died in April 1632, the charter was granted to his son Cecilius Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, on 20 June 1632. The colony was named in honour of Henrietta Maria of France, wife of Charles I.

The land was first settled in 1634, primarily to provide a religious haven for Catholics persecuted in England. Religious strife was common in the early years, and Catholics remained a minority, though in greater numbers than in any other English colony. The original capital was St. Mary's City on the north shore of the Potomac River. The economy was plantation-based and centred on tobacco, and demand for cheap labour led to the importation of many indentured servants and enslaved Africans.

Maryland's current boundaries took form in 1760, after the settlement of a long-running border dispute with Pennsylvania. Georgetown, Maryland, and other land from Montgomery and Prince George's counties was ceded to the federal government in 1790 to form Washington, D.C. Although Maryland was a slave state, it remained in the Union during the American Civil War, in part because Abraham Lincoln left the National Guard there.

The capital is Annapolis and the most populous city is Baltimore. The 2020 census counted 6,185,278 residents. Its nearness to Washington, D.C. shapes its economy, which includes defense, biotechnology and higher education, and the state hosts some of the highest numbers of historic landmarks per capita.
masaccio: Masaccio was born Tommaso di Ser Giovanni di Simone Cassai on 21 December 1401 at Castel San Giovanni di Altura, now San Giovanni Valdarno in Tuscany. His father was a notary, who died in 1406, and his mother the daughter of an innkeeper. The name Masaccio is a humorous form of Maso, short for Tommaso, meaning clumsy or messy Tom, and may have been coined to tell him apart from his collaborator Masolino.

There is no evidence of his training. He is first documented in Florence on 7 January 1422, when he joined the painters' guild as an independent master. His first attributed works are the San Giovenale Triptych of 1422 and the Virgin and Child with Saint Anne of about 1424, painted with the older Masolino da Panicale.

In 1424 Felice Brancacci commissioned Masaccio and Masolino to paint frescoes in the Brancacci Chapel in Santa Maria del Carmine, Florence, and work began around 1425. Most scenes show the life of Saint Peter, with the temptation and expulsion of Adam and Eve at the entrance. Masolino left for Hungary in September 1425, and Masaccio left the cycle unfinished in 1426 and returned in 1427. Filippino Lippi completed it in the 1480s. The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden influenced Michelangelo, and in The Tribute Money the shadows of the figures fall away from the chapel window as if it lit them.

Around 1427 he painted the Holy Trinity for Santa Maria Novella in Florence, considered by many his masterwork and the earliest surviving painting to use systematic linear perspective, possibly devised with the help of Brunelleschi. A skeleton below the figures bears the inscription: I once was what now you are, and what I am you shall yet be.

Masaccio died in 1428 at the age of 26, and little is known of the circumstances. A legend says a jealous rival painter poisoned him. Filippo Brunelleschi said on hearing the news: We have suffered a great loss. Only four frescoes undoubtedly by his hand survive. He is considered to have begun the Early Italian Renaissance in painting by moving away from the ornament of International Gothic towards naturalism, perspective and chiaroscuro. Vasari wrote that the most distinguished painters from his time on studied the Brancacci Chapel, among them Michelangelo.
masada: Masada, Hebrew for fortress, is a mountain-top fortress complex in the Judaean Desert, overlooking the western shore of the Dead Sea in southeastern Israel, 20 km east of modern Arad. It stands on a natural plateau rising over 400 metres above the surrounding terrain. The flat top measures about 550 by 270 metres and ends in cliffs, so the natural approaches are very difficult. Herod built a casemate wall 4 metres high and 1,300 metres long around it, with towers, and three narrow, winding paths led up to fortified gates.

Almost all historical information about Masada comes from the Jewish Roman historian Josephus. The most significant remains date to the reign of Herod the Great, king of Judaea under Roman administration from about 37 to 4 BCE, who made it a fortified desert refuge. He built storerooms, an advanced water system, bathhouses and two elaborate palaces, among the finest examples of Herodian architecture.

In 66 CE the Sicarii, a Jewish rebel group, took the fortress from its Roman garrison by a ruse. After the fall of Jerusalem it was the last stronghold. The Roman governor Lucius Flavius Silva laid siege with the Tenth Legion, building a circumvallation wall and a massive ramp against the western face. According to Josephus, when the Romans entered in 73 or 74 CE, the defenders, 960 men, women and children, had killed themselves after speeches by their leader Eleazar ben Ya'ir; two women and five children survived. Archaeology does not match him exactly: he mentions one palace where excavation found two, and counts 960 dead where the remains of at most 28 people have been found. Some scholars reject the mass suicide altogether.

Excavations led by Yigael Yadin in 1963–1965 found the palaces, storerooms, ritual baths, a synagogue and scroll fragments of Deuteronomy and Ezekiel, and a Byzantine church. The Roman ramp, circumvallation wall and eight siege camps are among the best preserved Roman siege works, and for them Masada was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. In the 20th century the siege became a central symbol of heroism in Israeli national identity. The site lies in the Masada National Park, reached by a steep trail or a cable car, and a museum in memory of Yadin opened there in 2007.
mascara-algeria: Mascara lies in north-western Algeria. Relizane is 65 kilometres to the north-east, Sidi Bel Abbès 90 kilometres to the south-west, Oran 105 kilometres to the north-west and Saïda 80 kilometres to the south. The name is said to derive from an older form, either Oum El Asker, meaning the mother of soldiers, or Mo'asker, meaning the place where soldiers gather. Locally it is pronounced Mʿaskar. The town has an older Muslim part and a newer French one, and large parts of it lie inside the ruins of its ancient ramparts.

Mascara is said to have been founded in the 10th century by the Banu Ifran. In 1701, under the Regency of Algiers, a military garrison was built in the town, and the Ottomans and the Algerians settled many Muslims with Andalucian origins there. In 1708 the tribes of Mascara, led by the bey Mustapha Ben Youcef, captured Oran and expelled the Spaniards while Spain was occupied with the War of the Spanish Succession. Spain regained Oran in 1732.

In 1790 famine and sickness had worsened the Spanish position in Oran, and the bey of Mascara appeared before the town with 30,000 men. The Spanish commander held out until the Spanish government, having made terms with the bey of Algiers, was allowed to withdraw with its guns and ammunition. The bey Mohammed took possession of Oran in March 1792 and made it his residence in place of Mascara.

In 1832 Abd al-Qadir made Mascara his headquarters, and he is the best-known figure of the town. The French destroyed it in 1835 and established full control over it in 1841. An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 on 18 August 1994 killed 171 people there.

Mascara is the capital of Mascara Province and an administrative, commercial and market centre. Its trade has centred on leather goods, grain and olive oil, and the region is especially known for its wine. The 2008 estimate gave it 150,000 inhabitants. It has road and rail links with other Algerian towns.
maseru: Maseru lies in north-western Lesotho, directly on the border with South Africa, which is marked by the Mohokare, or Caledon, River. A border post at the Maseru Bridge connects the two countries, and the nearest town on the South African side is Ladybrand. The city sits in a shallow valley at the foot of the Hlabeng-Sa-Likhama, foothills of the Maloti Mountains, at about 1,600 metres above sea level. It has a subtropical highland climate with warm, rainy summers and cool to chilly, dry winters. The name is a Sesotho word meaning red sandstones.

The British founded Maseru as a small police camp in 1869, after the end of the Free State–Basotho Wars, when Basutoland became a British protectorate. It stands at the edge of the conquered territories relinquished to the Orange Free State under the peace terms, 24 kilometres west of King Moshoeshoe I's stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, the previous de facto capital. A busy market town soon grew around the camp.

Maseru served as the administrative capital from 1869 to 1871, before administration passed to the Cape Colony. During Cape rule from 1871 to 1884 Basutoland was treated like forcibly annexed territory, which led to the Gun War of 1881 and the burning of many buildings in Maseru. In 1884 Basutoland was restored to the status of a Crown colony and Maseru became the capital again. It stayed small under British rule, which took little interest in developing it. After independence in 1966 its area grew about sevenfold, from around 20 to 138 square kilometres, as nearby villages were incorporated, and its population grew by around 7% a year for several decades. Riots after the 1998 parliamentary elections damaged much of the city.

Maseru is the capital and largest city of Lesotho and of Maseru District, and the 2016 census counted 330,760 people, about one seventh of the country's population. Traditional thatched mud-brick rondavels have largely given way to modern buildings. Colonial-era buildings include the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Our Lady of Victories and the Anglican St. John's Church, and the city also has the Royal Palace, the Parliament building and the State House. Kingsway, which joins the Royal Palace and the airport, was the first paved road in Lesotho. The national stadium, Setsoto Stadium, is in the city.
mashhad: Mashhad lies in north-eastern Iran, about 740 kilometres east of Tehran and about 250 km from Ashgabat in Turkmenistan. It stands in the valley of the Kashafrud River, between the Binalood and Hezar Masjed mountain ranges, with hot summers, cold winters and about 250 millimetres of precipitation a year.

By the 9th century Mashhad was a small village known as Sanabad, lying with Tus on the ancient Silk Road towards Merv. It outgrew the surrounding villages and took its present name, meaning place of martyrdom, from the shrine of the eighth Shia Imam, Ali al-Rida, who is buried there; the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid is buried in the same shrine. In 1389 Miran Shah, a son of Timur, stormed Tus after a siege of several months and massacred 10,000 of its inhabitants; those who escaped settled near the shrine, Tus was abandoned, and Mashhad became the capital of the district.

In the 16th century the town suffered from the raids of the Uzbeks, who took it in 1507 and again entered it in 1544, plundering and killing. Shah Abbas I did not retake it until 1598. He is said to have walked from Isfahan to Mashhad, and in the Safavid period the city gained further religious recognition. Between 1736 and 1796 it was the capital of Afsharid Iran, founded by Nader Shah, whose tomb is in the city. In 1796 Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar conquered Khorasan.

Mashhad is the capital of Razavi Khorasan province. The Imam Reza shrine draws millions of pilgrims each year, and several theological schools are associated with it. The shrine's administration, the Astan Quds Razavi, owns much of the city's real estate. The poet Ferdowsi, author of the Shahnameh, was born in nearby Tus, and many institutions in Mashhad bear his name.
masinissa: Masinissa, whose name appears on his tomb as MSNSN, was the son of Gaia, chieftain of the Numidian Massylii, and was brought up in Carthage, his father's ally. Much of what is known of him comes from Livy and, to a lesser extent, Cicero's Scipio's Dream. At the start of the Second Punic War he fought for Carthage against Syphax, king of the western Masaesyli, who had allied with Rome, and won a decisive victory. He was betrothed to the daughter of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco, then commanded Numidian cavalry in Spain, where he was placed in charge of all Carthaginian horse and fought a guerrilla campaign against Scipio Africanus in 208 and 207.

When Gaia died in 206 BCE, Masinissa quarrelled with Oezalces, his father's brother, over the inheritance, and Syphax took much of eastern Numidia. Concluding that Rome was winning the war, Masinissa defected and promised to help Scipio invade Africa. Hasdrubal turned to Syphax, who married his daughter Sophonisba. Masinissa fought at the Battle of the Great Plains and Bagbrades in 203, and with Gaius Laelius pursued Syphax to Cirta, where he was captured. Masinissa married Sophonisba, but Scipio demanded that she be shown in a Roman triumph, and Masinissa sent her poison, with which she killed herself.

At the Battle of Zama he commanded the cavalry on Scipio's right wing, 6,000 Numidian and 3,000 Roman, and his return against the rear of the Carthaginian lines decided the battle. He received Syphax's kingdom and ruled both the Massylii and the Masaesyli. With Cirta as his capital he sought to build a unified state from semi-nomadic tribes, introduced Carthaginian farming methods and settled many Numidians as peasants. Major towns included Capsa, Thugga, Bulla Regia and Hippo Regius.

The peace treaty of 201 forbade Carthage to make war without Roman permission, which let Masinissa encroach on its territory. He defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Oroscopa in 151 BCE. Carthage's retaliation against Numidian raids, in defiance of the treaty, led to the Third Punic War. He died early in 148 BCE, aged over 90, apparently still leading his armies, without a breach in his alliance with Rome.

Polybius called him the best man of all the kings of his time and credited him with showing that Numidia could produce cultivated fruits; it later became known as the breadbasket of Rome. Delos honoured him in 179 BCE with a golden crown and a statue after a gift of grain. Micipsa succeeded him, and his descendants included Juba I and Juba II. Many Berbers regard him as an icon and forefather.
masjed-soleyman: Masjed Soleyman is the capital of Masjed Soleyman County in Khuzestan province. It is home to a large population of the Haft-lang branch of the Bakhtiari, a semi-nomadic people whose livelihood depended on herds of sheep, cattle and horses. The four main divisions of the Haft Lang are the Duraki, Babadi, Bakhtiarwand and Dinaruni. The city is counted among the ancient cities of the Elam civilisation, said to have been called Assak and renamed Parsomash by the early Achaemenids, and in 1955 Roman Ghirshman, who thought Parsomash might have been the oldest capital of the Achaemenid Empire, found evidence of human habitation some 10,000 years old in a nearby cave.

Ruins in the area include an ancient fire-temple known locally as Sar-masjid and the remains of an Achaemenid palace. The city stayed important under the Seleucids and Parthians, and in the Sasanian era canals and weir-bridges allowed tobacco and cereals to be grown. After the Muslim conquest many ancient structures were demolished and the region remained relatively obscure until the Qajar period, when it became a centre of the tar trade.

The Bakhtiari played a large part in Iran's Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1907.
