A Bakhtiari tribal coalition led by Ali-Gholi Khan, Sardar Asaad II, and his brother Najaf Qoli Khan marched up to the gates of Tehran in 1909 and deposed Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar. Reza Shah, who ruled from 1925 to 1941, later made the destruction of Bakhtiari influence his mission, and the oil on their territory gave him a further motive to curb the tribe's autonomy.

In 1901 Mozaffar al-Din Shah signed a sixty-year concession giving the millionaire William Knox D'Arcy exclusive rights to prospect for petroleum over about three quarters of Persia. A drilling team under George B. Reynolds struck oil near the present Iran-Iraq border in 1904, but the venture strained D'Arcy's funds, and in 1905 the British Admiralty steered him to the Burmah Oil Company, which financed a Concession Syndicate. Drilling moved to Masjed Soleyman, where Reynolds met hostile tribes and paid them fees and promised them a share of profits to protect the concession.

At 4 a.m. on 26 May 1908 a fifty-foot gusher of petroleum shot up from the first rig. The syndicate was renamed the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in 1909, later British Petroleum, and by 1911 a pipeline ran from the field to a refinery at Abadan.
masjid-al-haram: The Masjid al-Haram, 'the Sacred Mosque', encloses the Kaaba in Mecca and is among the pilgrimage sites of the hajj. It is also the main site of the umrah, the lesser pilgrimage that can be made at any time of the year, and the rites of both include circling the Kaaba. Within the mosque stand the Black Stone, the Zamzam Well, the Maqam Ibrahim and the hills of Safa and Marwa, where pilgrims perform the sa'i in memory of Hajar's search for water for her son Ismail.

Islamic tradition holds that Abraham and his son Ismail raised the foundations of the Kaaba, and that the Black Stone was brought to Abraham by an angel. After Muhammad's return to Mecca in 630 CE he and a number of his companions broke the idols in and around the Kaaba. The caliph Umar enlarged the mosque in 637 CE, and Uthman added covered porticoes. In 682 Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr enlarged it again, and after the Umayyads retook Mecca in 692 Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan ordered the first major renovation, which raised the outer walls. Before then the mosque was a small open area with the Kaaba at its centre.

The Abbasid caliphs al-Mansur, al-Mahdi and al-Hadi enlarged it between 754 and 786 to 28,000 m2, and it kept this form until Ottoman times. A fire in 1400 damaged its colonnades and wooden roofs, and Mamluk sultans paid for rebuilding. In 1570 Sultan Selim II commissioned the architect Mimar Sinan to replace the flat roof with domes, and the columns of that work are among the oldest surviving parts of the building. Murad IV had it renovated in 1629 after floods.

The first Saudi renovation ran from 1955 to 1976, added four minarets, brought the Mas'a gallery inside the mosque and demolished many Ottoman features. On 20 November 1979 insurgents who called for the overthrow of the Saudi dynasty seized the mosque and took hostages. Hundreds were killed in the siege that followed, and the events shocked the Islamic world, in which violence is strictly forbidden within the mosque. King Fahd's expansion between 1986 and 1994 added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area.

The mosque is under the control of the King of Saudi Arabia, who holds the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. The Kaaba is the qibla, the direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide, and its fabric covering, the kiswah, is replaced every year in a formal ceremony. The hajj is one of the Pillars of Islam, required of every Muslim who is able to make it.
masovia: Masovia lies on the North European Plain, roughly between Łódź and Białystok, on both sides of the Vistula and its confluence with the Narew and the Bug. The landscape is flat, in contrast to Lesser Poland, with no lakes, in contrast to Greater Poland, and forests, mainly coniferous, cover about a fifth of the region, among them the Kampinos Forest. The region developed a distinct sub-culture of folk songs, architecture, dress and traditions.

The region at first covered only the right bank of the Vistula near Płock, which was one of the seats of the first Piast rulers and in 1037 to 1047 the capital of an independent Mazovian state under Masław. Between 1079 and 1138 Płock was in practice the capital of Poland. Masovia was incorporated into the Polish state in the second half of the tenth century under Mieszko I. After the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth the Duchy of Mazovia was established in 1138, governed by a separate branch of the Piast dynasty. To protect its northern part, Conrad I of Mazovia called in the Teutonic Knights in 1226 and gave them the Chełmno Land as a fief.

Masovia became a fief of the Polish crown in 1351, and western Masovia, and in 1526 to 1529 the main part, with its capital at Warsaw, were incorporated into the Polish state. During the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth over 20 per cent of the population were petty nobility. The Union of Lublin of 1569 made Masovia the central region of the Commonwealth, with Warsaw as the seat of the sejm, and in 1596 King Sigismund III Vasa moved the capital from Kraków to Warsaw.

Prussia annexed western Masovia in 1793 and the rest two years later, and the region joined the Congress Kingdom of Poland in 1815, where it saw the November and January uprisings against Russian rule. Poland won the Battle of Warsaw against Soviet Russia in 1920. During the Second World War the region suffered massacres, the Warsaw Ghetto, and the deaths of some 200,000 inhabitants in the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. Warsaw's Old Town, almost entirely demolished in the war, was restored and designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980. The present Mazovian Voivodeship was created in 1999, and its borders do not exactly follow historical Masovia.
massawa: Massawa lies on the Red Sea at the northern end of the Gulf of Zula, beside the Dahlak Archipelago. The historical city stands on the islands of Basé, with the old centre, and Taulud, joined to each other and to the mainland by causeways. It seems to have emerged as a port between the 8th and 10th centuries, after the decline of Adulis, about 50 kilometres to the south.

With the rise of the Sultanate of Dahlak in the 11th century, Massawa became the main link between the Muslim-dominated coast and the Christian highlands. From the 14th century highland rulers took more interest in it. Emperor Zara Yaqob appears to have reached it in the mid-15th century, and both Massawa and Dahlak were pillaged by the Abyssinians in 1464/65. The Portuguese gained a foothold at Massawa and Arkiko in 1513 as a port from which to reach allied Ethiopia against the Ottomans.

The Ottomans captured Massawa in 1557 and tried to make it the capital of Habesh Eyalet, though they did not conquer the rest of Eritrea. In May 1865 the port passed to the Khedive of Egypt with Ottoman consent, and the governor Werner Munzinger rebuilt it, with a customs house, a school, a hospital and causeways.

The Italians took the port in February 1885, with British agreement, and it was their colonial capital until Governor Ferdinando Martini moved to Asmara in 1897. They built a railway to Asmara and an Asmara-Massawa cableway, 75 kilometres long, which was the longest ropeway conveyor in the world at the time. A great earthquake in 1921 destroyed most of the city, and later buildings were of reinforced concrete.

Massawa was besieged unsuccessfully by the Eritrean Liberation Front in 1977–78 and was captured by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front in February 1990, in an attack by land and sea known as Operation Fenkil. Most of the city was destroyed in the shelling and bombing that followed. Eritrea's independence in 1991 left Ethiopia landlocked.

The old town keeps coral-stone houses, the Sheikh Hanafi Mosque of the 15th century, and the Imperial Palace built in 1872 to 1874 for Munzinger. A naval base, dhow docks, a railway station and an airport serve the city, and ferries run to the Dahlak Islands.
massif-central: The Massif Central is an old massif formed during the Variscan orogeny and made up mostly of granitic and metamorphic rocks. It covers about 15 per cent of mainland France and is separated from the Alps by the deep cleft of the Rhône.

Uplift in the Paleogene, as the Alps and the Pyrenees rose, lifted its eastern and southern parts, so that the highlands of the south and east, including the Cévennes, look down on the Rhône valley and the plains of Languedoc, while Limousin in the north-west is lower. Mont Lozère, at 1,699 metres, is the highest non-volcanic summit. The region was a barrier to transport within France until the A75 motorway opened it.

The massif is volcanic, though activity has subsided in the last 10,000 years. It holds about 450 extinct volcanoes, among them the stratovolcanoes of Cantal and the Monts Dore, where the Puy de Sancy reaches 1,886 metres, and the volcanic plateaus of Aubrac and Cézallier. The Chaîne des Puys near Clermont-Ferrand, less than 160 square kilometres, has 115 small monogenic cones, with the Puy de Dôme at 1,464 metres. In the south the Causses are raised limestone plateaus cut by deep canyons, of which the Gorges du Tarn are the best known.

Twenty departments are generally counted as part of the massif, in the regions of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, Nouvelle-Aquitaine and Occitania. Its largest cities are Clermont-Ferrand, Limoges and Saint-Étienne. Industry is little developed except locally, with metallurgy at Saint-Étienne, tyres at Clermont-Ferrand, where Michelin has its headquarters, and aeronautics at Figeac. Cattle are raised in the west for meat and milk, including Cantal cheese, and sheep on the southern limestone plateaus for Roquefort cheese, while the Limagne plain grows cereals. The volcanoes of the Chaîne des Puys and the region of the Causses and Cévennes have UNESCO heritage status, and the Millau Viaduct stands on the A75.
matadi: Matadi lies on the left bank of the Congo River, 148 kilometres from its mouth and about 8 kilometres below the last navigable point before the rapids that make the river impassable for a long stretch upstream. It is close to the border with Angola. Its name means stone in the Kikongo language, and the town is built on steep hills; a local saying holds that to live in Matadi one must know the verbs to go up, to go down and to sweat.

Upstream is a series of caves called the rock of Diogo Cão, after graffiti the Portuguese explorer carved there in 1485 to mark the limit of his travels up the river. The climate is a relatively dry tropical savanna, with a long dry season from June to September.

Matadi stands near the site of the state of Vungu, first mentioned in 1535 and said to have been destroyed in 1624. The town was founded by Sir Henry Morton Stanley in 1879. It was strategically important as the last navigable port going upstream and became the furthest inland port in the Congo Free State. The Matadi–Kinshasa Railway, built between 1890 and 1898, made it possible to carry goods from deeper within the Congo to the port, which grew into an important trading centre. Portuguese and French West African commercial interests influenced its architecture and urban design, which borrowed from neighbouring Angola and Congo-Brazzaville.

Matadi is the chief seaport of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and capital of the province of Kongo Central. It is divided into three communes, Matadi, Mvuzi and Nzanza. The railway to Kinshasa is 366 kilometres long, and a monument to its builders stands on a nearby hill. The Matadi Bridge, a suspension bridge 722 metres long built in 1983, carries the road from Kinshasa to the coast and is the only bridge over the main stem of the Congo River. The chief exports are coffee and timber.
matanzas: Matanzas lies on all three sides of the Bay of Matanzas on the north shore of Cuba, 102 kilometres east of Havana. Three rivers, the Yumurí, the San Juan and the Canimar, flow into the bay within the city limits. Seventeen bridges cross them, which gave the city the name City of Bridges and the comparison with Venice. It was also called the Athens of Cuba for its poets.

A royal decree of 25 September 1690 ordered the bay and port to be settled by 30 families from the Canary Islands, and the city was founded on 12 October 1693 as San Carlos y San Severino de Matanzas. The name means massacre and is said to refer to a slaughter in 1510, when 30 Spanish soldiers crossing a river in boats handled by native fishermen drowned in their armour after the fishermen capsized the boats.

Matanzas was one of the regions where sugar plantations developed most intensively, and enslaved people were imported in large numbers, especially in the first half of the nineteenth century. There were 1,900 enslaved people in 1792, about 30 per cent of the population; 10,773 in 1817, nearly half; and 53,331 in 1841, or 62.7 per cent. The area saw several slave insurrections and plots, among them the Escalera conspiracy, discovered in late 1843. On 25 April 1898 American warships bombarded the city in the first action of the Spanish–American War.

Matanzas is the capital of the province of Matanzas. It is known as the birthplace of the music and dance traditions danzón and rumba. Its landmarks include the Sauto Theatre, opened in 1863 and a National Monument of Cuba, the cathedral of San Carlos de Borromeo, the aqueduct of 1870 and the nearby Bellamar caves.
mathura: Mathura is the administrative headquarters of Mathura district in Uttar Pradesh, about 15 kilometres from the town of Vrindavan. In ancient times it was an economic hub at the junction of important caravan routes, where the northern trade route of the Indo-Gangetic Plain met the routes to Malwa and the west coast. It lies at the centre of the cultural region of Braj. It is one of the Sapta Puri, the seven cities Hindus consider holy, and part of the Krishna circuit.

Tradition holds that Mathura was founded by Shatrughna after he killed Lavanasura, son of Madhu of the Yadu tribe. The forested place was called Madhuvan, then Madhupura, and later Mathura. Hindus believe that Krishna, of the Yadu dynasty, was born there, and that the Kesava Deo Temple was built on the site of his birthplace, a prison. The city was the capital of the kingdom of Surasena, ruled by Kamsa, Krishna's maternal uncle.

Excavations show a village growing into an important city during the Vedic age, beginning with the Painted Grey Ware culture of 1100 to 500 BCE. The Krishna Janmasthan site yielded pottery of the sixth century BCE and the remains of a large Buddhist complex, including a monastery called Yasha Vihara of the Gupta period, as well as Jain sculptures of the same era. Mathura was later ruled by the Maurya empire, and Megasthenes in the early third century BCE mentions it as a great city.

Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it in 1018, and the historian al-Utbi describes its stone wall and the thousand houses with attached temples. In 1724 Raja Jai Singh visited Mathura and married his daughter there on Janmashtami.

Mathura is regarded as the heart of Braj Bhoomi, the land of Krishna. The Krishna Janmasthan Temple Complex stands around what is considered his birthplace, and Vishram Ghat on the Yamuna is said to be where Krishna rested after killing Kamsa. Krishna Janmashtami is observed there every year, and the city shares Braj cuisine with Vrindavan.
matilda-i-countess-of-boulogne: Matilda was born between 1102 and 1110, the only known child of Count Eustace III of Boulogne and Mary of Scotland, and was heir to the counties of Boulogne and Lens and to estates in England. Her aunt Matilda of Scotland was queen of England, and through her mother she descended from the Anglo-Saxon kings. Around 1125 Count Eustace and King Henry I arranged her marriage to Henry's nephew Stephen of Blois. Eustace then gave up his titles and died as a monk, and Matilda became countess of Boulogne in her own right. Her inheritance included Boulogne and Wissant, the main ports on the shortest crossing to England, and the couple governed their lands together, though she took charge of the daily administration.

Henry I died on 1 December 1135, and Stephen was crowned king on 22 December, with Matilda crowned queen in Westminster Abbey on 22 March 1136. The civil war known as the Anarchy began in 1138, when Earl Robert of Gloucester rebelled for his half-sister Empress Matilda. The queen laid siege to Dover with a large army by land and her Boulogne allies by sea, and took the surrender of the rebel Walkelin Maminot. With a papal legate she brokered the Treaty of Durham with her uncle David I of Scotland, signed on 9 April 1139, and she arranged the marriage of her son Eustace to Constance, sister of King Louis VII of France.

After Stephen was captured at the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141, Matilda led the royalist cause from Kent. On 24 June 1141 the citizens of London, pressed by her and angered by the empress's harsh rule, drove the empress out and opened the gates to the queen's troops. In September the queen and William of Ypres besieged the empress's army at Winchester and routed it on 14 September, capturing Robert of Gloucester. She then exchanged him for her husband.

Matilda patronised the reformed religious orders. She founded the abbeys of Coggeshall, Faversham and Lillechurch, Cressing Temple, Temple Cowley and the hospital of St Katharine's by the Tower. She and Stephen worked to secure the succession of their son Eustace. She died on 3 May 1152, and after her death Stephen recognised the empress's son Henry as his heir, which ended the Anarchy. Historians credit her courage and determination with Stephen's continued hold on the throne.
matilda-of-flanders: Matilda was born into the House of Flanders, the daughter of Baldwin V of Flanders and Adela of France. She was descended from Charlemagne and from Alfred the Great, and her uncle was King Henry I of France, William's suzerain. She was of grander birth than William, who was illegitimate.

William began to negotiate with Baldwin as early as 1047. Both had reasons to want the match: Baldwin was in conflict with the Holy Roman Emperor Henry III and needed support, and the marriage would settle border disputes between Flanders and Normandy. Pope Leo IX banned it in 1049 at the Council of Reims on grounds of consanguinity, since the two were fourth cousins. The couple nevertheless married in about 1051 or 1052. Lanfranc, prior of Bec Abbey, went to Rome for William, and Pope Nicholas II granted a dispensation in 1059.

The marriage was by all accounts happy and fruitful. Matilda bore William at least nine children, four sons and at least five daughters, among them the future kings William II and Henry I of England. The daughters learned to read Latin at the Abbey of Sainte-Trinité in Caen, and the sons were tutored by Lanfranc.

When William set out to conquer England, Matilda was appointed regent of Normandy and guided the duchy without major unrest. She served as regent six times between 1066 and 1076. She first travelled to England in April 1068 and was crowned queen on 11 May 1068 in Westminster Abbey, at Pentecost, in a ceremony presided over by the archbishop of York. Three new phrases in the rite declared that she was placed by God, shared in royal power and blessed her people. Historians no longer believe that she had a hand in the Bayeux Tapestry, which seems to have been commissioned by William's half-brother Odo, Bishop of Bayeux.

Matilda fell ill in the summer of 1083 and died on 2 November 1083, with William present at her final confession. He swore to give up hunting in his grief and died four years later. She was buried at the Abbaye aux Dames in Caen, where a black slab with her epitaph marks the grave. Her skeleton was examined in 1959, and her height was found to be about 152 centimetres, a normal height for the time.
matilda-of-tuscany: Matilda of Canossa, called la Gran Contessa, was born around 1046, the youngest of three children of Boniface and Beatrice of Lorraine, who had married in June 1037. Beatrice was the niece and foster daughter of Empress Gisela of Swabia. Around 1055 Matilda was betrothed to her stepbrother Godfrey the Hunchback, and by 1069 she is clearly recorded as his wife. She bore a daughter in 1071 who died within weeks. She then repudiated her husband, a decision that ensured her independence. Her mother Beatrice trained her for rule by holding court with her and encouraging her to issue charters as countess and duchess.

After her mother's death Matilda took over her inheritance, though under Salic and Lombard law Emperor Henry IV would have been the legal heir. She made Canossa Castle, in the Apennines south-west of Reggio Emilia, the centre of domains that included present-day Lombardy, Emilia, Romagna and Tuscany. Pope Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV in 1076, and in January 1077 Henry made his penitential walk before Canossa Castle and was received back into the Church. From 1080, when conflict with Henry resumed, Matilda put all her military and material resources at the service of the papacy. Her court sheltered many refugees and became a cultural centre.

Between 1081 and 1098 the disputes with Henry put her rule in crisis. A coalition with the southern German dukes brought a turning point, and when Henry withdrew north of the Alps in 1097 she regained many lost domains from autumn 1098. Childless, she adopted Guido Guerra of the Guidi family around 1099 and, in November 1102, renewed a donation of her property to the Apostolic See. She directed her last gifts to Polirone Abbey, where she chose to be buried. According to Donizo, Henry V crowned her Imperial Vicar and Vice-Queen of Italy at Bianello Castle in May 1111.

Matilda died on 24 July 1115, and the House of Canossa became extinct. Popes and emperors fought over the Terre Matildiche, as her domains were called, well into the thirteenth century. The struggle between regnum and sacerdotium changed the Italian cities permanently, giving them room to escape foreign rule and develop as communes. Donizo's chronicle, called the Vita Mathildis, written between 1111 and 1115, is the main source for her life. Pope Urban VIII had her body moved to Rome in 1630, where she was the first woman buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. The Istituto Superiore di Studi Matildici, founded in Italy in 1977, studies the Canossa family.
matsu-islands: The Matsu Islands lie in the East China Sea alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. They form Lienchiang County, the smallest county in the Taiwan Area by area and population. The five major islands are Nangan, Dongju, Xiju, Beigan and Dongyin; Dongyin is the northernmost and Dongju the southernmost. Dongyin is slightly over 10 nautical miles (19 kilometres) from the mainland. The islands are mainly granite and diabase, the soil is not ideal for farming, and the highest point, on Beigan, is 298 metres. The climate is subtropical maritime, foggy in spring and summer.

Chinese from Fukien and Chekiang began migrating to the islands during the Yuan dynasty; most of the people of Matsu came from Houguan, today Changle in Fujian. Net fishing laid the base for the settlement at Fuao. Some crewmen of Zheng He stayed on the islands for a time during the Ming dynasty. In the early Qing dynasty pirates gathered there and the residents left temporarily. Unlike Taiwan and Penghu, the islands were not ceded to Japan by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895. In 1912 the British established the Dongyong Lighthouse on Dongyin Island.

The historical Lienchiang County lay partly on the mainland. After the Chinese Civil War it was effectively divided in 1949: the mainland portion came under the People's Republic of China, while the offshore islands stayed under the Republic of China, so that the county is the only former geographical unit of its name now divided between two administrations. Large numbers of soldiers were stationed there after 1949 and during the First and Second Taiwan Strait Crisis in 1954 and 1958 respectively, and the population reached a peak of 17,088 in 1971. It then fell as young people left for lack of work. County magistrates were appointed until 1993.

The islands are administered as Lienchiang County with Nangan Township as the county seat; it has no city or urban township. The native speech is the Matsu dialect, a subdialect of the Fuzhou dialect. The islands are named after the sea goddess Mazu, and the Matsu Nangan Tianhou Temple holds the sarcophagus of Lin Moniang. Tourism, military sites such as the granite tunnels, and the Matsu Distillery are central to the economy. Since 1990 a bird sanctuary has protected the Chinese crested tern, found nesting there in 2000.
matsue: Matsue lies at the northernmost point of Shimane Prefecture, on the banks of the Ohashi River, which connects Lake Shinji and Lake Nakaumi. It stands in the ancient province of Izumo, and archaeological sites of the Yayoi, Kofun and Nara periods lie within its borders. In the Sengoku period the area was the stronghold of the Amago clan.

The castle town was established by Horio Yoshiharu, who built Matsue Castle and planned the town around it over five years, from 1607 to 1611. After the Horio line ended with a childless heir, Izumo passed to the Kyōgoku, and Kyōgoku Tadataka received it in 1634. He too died childless.

The domain then went to the Matsudaira clan. Matsudaira Naomasa, a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, had made a name at the Battle of Osaka at the age of 14, and he became ruler of Izumo in 1638. His heirs held Izumo for ten generations until the end of the Edo period. The best known after Naomasa is the seventh daimyō, Matsudaira Harusato, known as Fumai, who set the clan's finances in order, planted mulberry bushes and promoted foods such as shijimi clams. He was an enthusiast of the tea ceremony, and the sweets for which Matsue is known, especially wakakusa, are credited to his influence. The city itself was founded on 1 April 1889.

Matsue is the capital of Shimane Prefecture. Its castle is one of the twelve original castles that survive in Japan. Lafcadio Hearn taught in the city from 1890 to 1891, and a memorial museum is dedicated to him. At the Sada Shrine the Sada Shin Noh, a sacred dance of purification, was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2011.
matsuo-basho: Matsuo Bashō was born Matsuo Kinsaku in 1644 near Ueno, in Iga Province. The Matsuo family was of samurai descent, and his father was probably a musokunin, one of a class of landowning peasants with certain samurai privileges. In his late teens he became a servant, in a humble capacity, to Tōdō Yoshitada, with whom he shared a love of haikai no renga, a form of collaborative poetry. A sequence opened with a verse of 5-7-5 mora called a hokku, later renamed haiku when it stood alone.

Yoshitada's sudden death in 1666 ended Bashō's peaceful life, and he is believed to have given up any chance of samurai status. By 1680 he taught twenty disciples in Edo, and that winter he moved to Fukagawa, where his disciples built him a hut and planted a banana tree, bashō in Japanese, which gave him his pen name.

In 1684 he left Edo on the first of four major journeys, travelling alone on routes regarded as dangerous. His poems grew less introspective, and in early 1686 he composed the hokku about an ancient pond and a frog jumping in, which was at once widely praised.

On 16 May 1689 he left Edo with his student Kawai Sora for the Northern Provinces of Honshū, a journey of 600 ri, about 2,400 km, that became his masterwork Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North. He edited it for three years, and the first edition appeared posthumously in 1702. It was an immediate commercial success and other itinerant poets followed his route. Bashō himself believed his best work lay in leading and joining renku.

In 1693 he adopted karumi, or lightness, a semi-Buddhist philosophy of greeting the mundane world instead of separating from it. In the summer of 1694 he left Edo for the last time and in Osaka fell ill with a stomach complaint, dying peacefully on 28 November 1694 among his disciples. In 1793 the Shinto bureaucracy deified him, so that for a time criticising his poetry was blasphemous. Masaoka Shiki challenged this orthodoxy in the late 19th century, yet also made Bashō accessible in English and coined the term haiku.
mattavilasa-prahasana: The play opens with two drunken Kapalikas, the mendicant Satyasoma and his partner Devasoma, stumbling from tavern to tavern in search of more liquor. The Kapalikas are presented as followers of a heretical Saivite sect whose rites included drinking, wild dancing and singing, and ritual intercourse. Asking for alms, Satyasoma finds that his skull-bowl is gone. It is not at the tavern they last visited, and he suspects that either a dog or a Buddhist monk has taken it.

A Buddhist monk named Nagasena then enters, and Satyasoma accuses him of the theft. He charges the monk with stealing, lying and desiring liquor, meat and women although his religion forbids them, and accuses Buddhism itself of stealing ideas from the Mahabharata and the Vedanta. The monk denies everything and the quarrel becomes a brawl, which a Pasupata acquaintance of Satyasoma tries to mediate. In despair the monk hands over his own begging bowl. At last a Madman comes on stage carrying the real skull-bowl, which he has recovered from a dog; it is returned to its owner and all leave on friendly terms.

The play was written during a strong revival of Hinduism in southern India, which Mahendravarman I supported; he had temples cut into the rock, most of them dedicated to Siva. It is widely held to be a satire on sects that seemed degenerate or peculiar in his day. The Kapalikas stood for Tantrism, in which enlightenment was sought through unorthodox rituals involving liquor and ritual intercourse; the monk, in turn, wonders why Buddhism forbids liquor and women, and both Kapalikas call the Jains heretics.

The text also gives a view of life in seventh-century Kanchipuram, with references to the sound of drums, flower shops, festive taverns, temple towers and courts whose officials were sometimes bribed. English translations include those of Michael Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat, of 1981, and David Lorenzen, of 2001. A dance-theatre adaptation directed by Stella Uppal-Subbiah, which gave prominence to bharatanatyam, toured the United Kingdom in 2003 and 2004.
matteo-maria-boiardo: Boiardo was born at or near Scandiano, in the present province of Reggio Emilia, the son of Giovanni di Feltrino and Lucia Strozzi. His mother was the sister of the humanist poet Tito Vespasiano Strozzi, and his grandfather Feltrino had been made Count of Scandiano by Niccolò III d'Este. The family moved to Ferrara, where he grew up until his father died in 1451. He entered the University of Ferrara early, learned Greek and Latin and was admitted doctor in philosophy and in law.

When his grandfather died in 1460, Matteo Maria and his cousin Giovanni inherited the fief of Scandiano. Joint administration led to family feuds, and in 1474 he narrowly escaped poisoning, instigated by his aunt Taddea Pio, Giovanni's mother. The lands were then divided and Boiardo became Lord of Scandiano.

Boiardo enjoyed the favour of Borso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, who sent him to meet Frederick III in 1469 and took him in his train to visit Pope Paul II in 1471. In 1473 he joined the escort that brought Eleonora of Aragon to Ferrara to meet her husband Ercole. In 1476 he returned to Ferrara as Duke Ercole's companion, and in 1478 he married Taddea dei Gonzaga of Novellara, with whom he had six children.

In 1481 he became governor of Reggio, an office he held with success until his death, except for a brief interval when he was governor of Modena. The war between Ferrara and Venice and his concern for Scandiano made him give up the post for a time. In 1487 Ercole appointed him ducal emissary for Reggio. His administrative letters from that office form the largest part of his surviving correspondence.

Boiardo wrote Latin works for the Este, the Carmina de laudibus Estensium and the Pastoralia, dating from 1463–4, and his Amorum libri tres, 180 sonnets, canzoni and madrigals in the Petrarchan manner, followed the course of his love for Antonia Caprara. Around 1476 he began Orlando Innamorato. It is the first chivalric poem to fuse the Carolingian and Arthurian cycles deliberately, and it makes Orlando, hero of the Song of Roland, a lover. Love is its main theme, beside arms, magic, honour and adventure. The poem was left unfinished and drew sequels, above all Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso.

Taste later turned against it, and Francesco Berni's recasting in Tuscan of 1542 replaced the original for centuries. Anthony Panizzi's edition of 1830 restored the text. Boiardo died at Reggio in December 1494, the same year as Poliziano and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.
matteo-ricci: Matteo Ricci was born on 6 October 1552 in Macerata. He studied law in Rome for two years and entered the Society of Jesus at the Roman College in April 1571, where he also studied mathematics, cosmology and astronomy under Christopher Clavius. He sailed from Lisbon in March 1578 and reached Goa that September, and in 1582 he was summoned to Macau.

In 1583 Ricci and Michele Ruggieri settled at Zhaoqing at the invitation of the governor Wang Pan. He stayed until 1589, when a new viceroy expelled him. In 1584 he composed a first European-style world map in Chinese, and the two men are thought to have compiled the first Portuguese-Chinese dictionary. He reached Nanjing and Nanchang in 1595, and in August 1597 his superior Alessandro Valignano appointed him head of the China mission. He first reached Beijing on 7 September 1598 but could not enter the palace.

In 1601 the Wanli Emperor invited him to the court in recognition of his scientific skill, chiefly his predictions of solar eclipses. He had free access to the Forbidden City but never met the emperor, who gave him a stipend. He founded the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, the oldest Catholic church in Beijing, and converted a number of officials, the most prominent being the agronomist Xu Guangqi.

Ricci adopted the dress of the Confucian literati and argued that Chinese people had always believed in God and that Christianity completed their faith. He used the term Tiānzhǔ, Lord of Heaven, for God, and took an accommodating view of rites such as ancestor worship, which Dominican and Franciscan missionaries later challenged in the Chinese rites controversy. His book The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven argued that Confucianism and Christianity were not opposed, and his Chinese Euclid appeared in 1607.

Ricci died in Beijing on 11 May 1610. Ming law required foreigners who died in China to be buried in Macau, but Diego de Pantoja pleaded for a plot, and the Wanli Emperor granted one at a Buddhist temple. His journals were edited by Nicolas Trigault and published in 1615.
matterhorn: The Matterhorn is a large, near-symmetrical pyramid in the Pennine Alps, whose summit is 4,478 metres above sea level. It has four faces, roughly facing the four cardinal points, separated by the Hörnli, Furggen, Zmutt and Leone ridges. Three faces are on the Swiss side and one on the Italian side. It overlooks the town of Zermatt to the northeast and Breuil-Cervinia to the south. The nearby Theodul Pass has been a trade route since Roman times. The name comes from the German Matte, meadow, and Horn. Early maps of 1545 and 1548 labelled the mountain Mons Silvius. In August 1792 Horace-Bénédict de Saussure made the first measurement of its height, using a sextant and a chain spread on the Theodul glacier.

The Matterhorn was one of the last main Alpine peaks to be climbed, less because of its technical difficulty than because of the fear it inspired in early mountaineers. The first serious attempts were from the Italian side, led by Jean-Antoine Carrel and his uncle Jean-Jacques Carrel, who tried in 1857 and 1858. Edward Whymper, an English artist and engraver hired to sketch the mountains around Zermatt, first saw it in the summer of 1860 and made his first attempt in August 1861.

Whymper and his party left Zermatt on 13 July 1865, and made the first ascent by the Hörnli ridge. Whymper found it much easier than the Italian ridge. During the descent a sudden fall killed four of the seven climbers, a disaster that marked the end of the golden age of alpinism. Two days after the first ascent Jean-Antoine Carrel set out to prove that the Italian side could be climbed, with Amé Gorret, Jean-Baptiste Bich and Jean-Augustin Meynet.

Lucy Walker became the first woman to reach the summit on 22 August 1871. A party of three English mountaineers made the first ascent without guides on 23 July 1876. The north face was not climbed until 1931, and the west face, the highest of the four, was completely climbed only in 1962.

Mountaineers try to climb the Matterhorn every year, most of them from the Hörnli Hut by the northeast Hörnli ridge. It is estimated that over 500 people had died on it by the late 1980s. The mountain is mainly composed of gneiss, which belonged to the African plate before the Alpine orogeny. It has become an emblem of Switzerland and of the Alps, and has been part of the Swiss Federal Inventory of Natural Monuments since 1983.
matthew-c-perry: Matthew Calbraith Perry was born on 10 April 1794 in Newport, Rhode Island, a son of Navy Captain Christopher Raymond Perry and Sarah Wallace Perry. His brother was Oliver Hazard Perry. He received a midshipman's warrant in 1809, at about fifteen, and served aboard USS President during the War of 1812, where a bursting cannon killed and wounded several men, Perry among the wounded.

After the war he served in the Mediterranean, in the Second Barbary War under Commodore William Bainbridge, and off West Africa and in the West Indies against piracy and the slave trade. On 25 March 1822 he sailed the schooner USS Shark to Key West and planted the American flag there.

Perry took a close interest in naval education and in the steam engine. He oversaw the building of the Navy's second steam frigate, USS Fulton, organised America's first corps of naval engineers and ran the first U.S. naval gunnery school from 1839 to 1841. He was called the Father of the Steam Navy. In 1841 he received the title of commodore, which, as the Navy had no rank above captain until 1857, carried considerable weight. In the Mexican–American War he captured Frontera and Tuxpan and led a landing force of 1,173 men against San Juan Bautista in June 1847.

In 1852 President Millard Fillmore sent him to open Japanese ports to American trade, by gunboat diplomacy if necessary. Whaling, trade with China, the search for coaling stations and the return of shipwrecked sailors were among the motives. Perry reached Uraga on 8 July 1853, refused to go to Nagasaki and delivered a letter for the Japanese ruler at Kurihama on 14 July. He returned on 13 February 1854 with ten ships and 1,600 men, landed at Kanagawa on 8 March, and signed the Convention of Kanagawa on 31 March. Afterwards he visited Hakodate and Shimoda, the two ports it opened.

Back in the United States, Congress voted him a reward of $20,000, and he published an account of the expedition in three volumes. His health failed in his last years, with arthritis, gout and cirrhosis of the liver, and he is known to have been an alcoholic. He died in New York City on 4 March 1858 of rheumatic fever that had spread to the heart, and was later reburied in Newport.

Japanese woodblock portraits showed him with blue eyeballs, a sign of the threatening in Japanese culture, and sometimes as a tengu. Over 90 per cent of Japanese schoolchildren can identify him. A monument at Yokosuka marks his landing place, and his diplomatic gifts from Japan are in the Smithsonian Institution.
matthias-corvinus: Matthias was born in Kolozsvár, now Cluj-Napoca in Romania, on 23 February 1443, the second son of John Hunyadi and Elizabeth Szilágyi. Scholars such as Gregory of Sanok and John Vitéz frequented the Hunyadi court, and under their influence he became an enthusiastic supporter of Renaissance humanism. In 1457 King Ladislaus the Posthumous had him imprisoned with his older brother Ladislaus Hunyadi, who was executed. The king then died unexpectedly, and Matthias's uncle Michael Szilágyi arrived at the Diet with 15,000 troops. The nobles, gathered on the frozen Danube, proclaimed the 14-year-old Matthias king on 24 January 1458.

Matthias took effective control of government within two weeks. He fought the Czech mercenaries who dominated Upper Hungary and Emperor Frederick III, who claimed Hungary for himself; a treaty of 1463 returned the Holy Crown, and Matthias was crowned on 29 March 1464. In 1468 he declared war on the Hussite King George of Bohemia and conquered Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia. The Catholic Estates proclaimed him King of Bohemia on 3 May 1469, but the Hussite lords elected Vladislaus Jagiellon. A treaty of 1478 confirmed the division of the Bohemian lands between them, and between 1482 and 1487 Matthias occupied Lower Austria.

He kept taxes at extraordinary levels, which provoked a rebellion in Transylvania in 1467. He maintained one of the earliest professional standing armies in medieval Europe, the Black Army, united the highest courts into one supreme court and promoted men for their abilities rather than their rank.

Matthias was the first non-Italian monarch to promote the Renaissance style in his realm, and his marriage to Beatrice of Naples strengthened Italian influence. From about 1479 his builders enlarged the castle of Buda and rebuilt the palace at Visegrád, and artists such as Andrea Mantegna and Filippino Lippi worked for him. His royal library, the Bibliotheca Corviniana, begun around 1465 under the librarian Martius Galeotti, was one of the largest collections of books in Europe. His nickname comes from the Latin corvus, raven, an emblem on the family coat of arms.

After his death on 6 April 1490 his conquests were lost within months, and Vladislaus Jagiellon was elected king on condition that he abolish Matthias's innovations, above all the extraordinary tax. Matthias remains a popular hero of Hungarian and Slovak folk tales as Matthias the Just.
matthias-holy-roman-emperor: Matthias was born in Vienna on 24 February 1557, the third son of Maximilian II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Maria of Spain. His brothers included Rudolf, later Emperor Rudolf II, Ernest, Maximilian, Albert and Wenceslaus. Almost nothing is known of his upbringing, though one of his teachers was the writer and historian Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq. When their father died the family's estates passed to Rudolf as the eldest, and the other sons received cash pensions and church or state appointments. Matthias married Archduchess Anna of Tyrol, and the marriage produced no surviving children.

In 1578 the States-General of the rebellious Netherlands provinces invited Matthias to be Governor-General, an arrangement made with Philippe III de Croÿ, Duke of Aarschot, and other moderates against the will of Philip II of Spain. Philip never recognised it. Matthias set down rules for religious peace in most of the United Provinces, and his work is noted in Article 13 of the 1579 Union of Utrecht, which made freedom of religion a local matter. He stayed as titular governor until 1581, when the rebels deposed Philip II.

Back in Austria from 1583, he failed in several attempts to become a bishop, and only after his brother Ernest took the Netherlands governorship in 1593 did he secure the government of Austria. There he faced Protestant estates defending their religious rights, heavy taxes and troops raised for the Long Turkish War. Peasants rose in Lower and Upper Austria in 1595 and 1597, and he forced them to submit with mercenary troops. He then followed a strict Counter-Reformation course, with Melchior Klesl as his chancellor.

From 1599 Matthias urged the childless Rudolf II in vain to arrange his succession. In 1606 the archdukes declared Rudolf insane and named Matthias head of the family. That year Matthias ended the conflict in Hungary by granting religious freedom there and guaranteeing Transylvania the right to elect its own princes. In April 1608 he marched on Prague, and the treaty of June 1608 left Rudolf Bohemia, Silesia and Lusatia while Matthias received Hungary, Austria and Moravia.

Matthias was crowned King of Bohemia on 23 May 1611 and, after Rudolf's death on 20 January 1612, was elected emperor. His rule was dominated by Klesl, who sought a compromise between Catholic and Protestant states. More intransigent Habsburgs, led by Archduke Maximilian, wanted the succession for Archduke Ferdinand, later Emperor Ferdinand II, who was elected King of Bohemia in June 1617. The Bohemian Protestant revolt led Matthias to imprison Klesl, but old and ailing he could not stop Maximilian's faction. He died of natural causes on 20 March 1619.
matyas-rakosi: Mátyás Rákosi, born Rosenfeld on 9 March 1892 in Ada, then in the Kingdom of Hungary, was the fourth son of a grocer, József Rosenfeld, and Cecília Léderer. His father, a supporter of the Party of Independence and '48, changed the family name to Rákosi in 1903. A diligent student, Rákosi finished school in Szeged in 1910, studied external trade, and won scholarships to Hamburg in 1912 and London in 1913. He joined the Hungarian Social Democratic Party in 1910.

After the First World War he joined the communist movement of Béla Kun. During the 133-day Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919 he was a people's commissar and took part in its military campaigns against Czechoslovakia and Romania. He fled on 2 August 1919 and worked in the Soviet Union for the Communist International. Arrested in 1924 after trying to return to Hungary, he spent more than fifteen years in prison before being allowed to leave for the Soviet Union in 1940.

Returning in 1945 as the Red Army drove the German forces out, Rákosi became General Secretary of the Hungarian Communist Party and deputy prime minister. The party was beaten in the free election by the Independent Smallholders' Party, but Moscow insisted that the Communists hold key posts. From 1947 they pressed the other parties to exclude those unwilling to cooperate, on grounds that they were fascists or sympathisers. The phrase salami tactics was later attached to Rákosi, though no verified source for it has been found. In 1948 the Social Democrats were forced to merge into the Hungarian Working People's Party, and in 1949 Hungary was proclaimed a people's republic.

His government was loyal to the Soviet Union and built a personality cult modelled on Stalin's. Hundreds of thousands were imprisoned and thousands died. Show trials claimed victims including his former lieutenant László Rajk. After Stalin's death in 1953 Imre Nagy became prime minister at Moscow's wish, but Rákosi used his post as First Secretary to block reform and secured Nagy's removal in 1955. Khrushchev's secret speech of February 1956 fatally weakened him, and he resigned in July 1956.

Rákosi left for the Soviet Union, and the Hungarian Revolution broke out about three months later. János Kádár, who came to power after its suppression, refused to let him return. He lived in Tokmok, Arzamas and finally Gorky. Offered return in 1970 on condition that he stay out of politics, he refused, and he died in Gorky on 5 February 1971. His ashes were secretly returned to Budapest, where the gravestone bears only his initials. He is generally seen in Hungary as a symbol of tyranny and oppression.
mau-mau-rebellion: Land was the first British interest in Kenya, which had some of the richest agricultural soils in the world, in districts where Europeans could live permanently. Kenya was claimed as a protectorate by a proclamation of 1 July 1895 and declared a colony in 1920. Kikuyu squatters formed most of the labour on settler farms, and from 1918 a series of Resident Native Labourers Ordinances curtailed their rights. The Ordinance of 1939 removed their remaining tenancy rights and let settlers demand 270 days' labour a year.

Political organisation grew in step. The Kenya African Study Union was founded on 1 October 1944 and became the Kenya African Union in 1946. Many organisers were ex-soldiers who had fought for Britain in Ceylon, Somalia and Burma, and who returned to find that they were unpaid and unrecognised, while British counterparts received medals and land.

The Kenya Land and Freedom Army, called Mau Mau by others, was made up mainly of Kikuyu, Meru and Embu fighters. The origin of the name is uncertain. The British and much international opinion saw it as a savage tribal cult. On 20 October 1952 Governor Evelyn Baring declared a State of Emergency, and Operation Jock Scott arrested Jomo Kenyatta and about 180 other identified leaders. Hundreds, then thousands, of adherents fled to the forests of the Aberdares and around Mount Kenya, where they formed platoons. In May 1953 General George Erskine was sent to restore order.

The British screened suspects in camps, the system known as the Pipeline, which developed into what has been described as a British gulag. Villagisation concentrated rural people in fortified villages, and the Swynnerton Plan created larger family holdings. The capture of Field Marshal Dedan Kimathi on 21 October 1956 signalled the defeat of Mau Mau and essentially ended the military campaign. Suppression cost Britain £55 million and at least 11,000 deaths, including 1,090 executions by hanging, with some estimates far higher. The war also set rebels against African loyalists within the Kikuyu community.

In June 1956 a land reform enlarged Kikuyu holdings and the ban on Africans growing coffee was relaxed. Direct election of African members to the Legislative Assembly followed, and a conference at Lancaster House in January 1960 accepted majority rule. Historians disagree on how far the rebellion hastened independence: a common view holds that continued colonial rule would have needed more force than the British public would tolerate, while others stress the growth of nationalism.

Mau Mau remained banned until September 2003. On 6 June 2013 the British government announced a settlement with 5,228 claimants, worth £19.9 million, and support for a memorial in Nairobi, while denying liability. Its place in Kenyan memory has been contested since independence.
maubeuge: Maubeuge is a commune in the Nord department of northern France. It lies on both banks of the Sambre, which is canalised at this point, 36 km east of Valenciennes and about 9 km from the Belgian border. Its Latin name was Malbodium, from the Old Frankish Malboden, meaning assizes of Boden. Because of its position near the border, the railway station has lines towards Mons and Charleroi in Belgium.

The town owes its origin to Maubeuge Abbey, a double monastery for men and women founded in the 7th century, whose founder's relics are kept in the church. The area later belonged to the territory of Hainaut. As part of the Spanish Netherlands the town changed hands several times before it was ceded to France in the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678. Louis XIV had it extensively fortified as part of Vauban's pré carré, a plan that protected the northern border of France with a double line of fortresses.

In 1793 Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld besieged Maubeuge, and the siege was lifted by the victory of Wattignies, which a monument in the town commemorates. An attempt on the town in 1814 failed, but it capitulated after vigorous resistance during the Hundred Days. After the War of 1870 a new fortress was built, later modernised and enlarged, with an entrenched camp of 18 miles in perimeter. Its forts were besieged by the German Empire in World War I. In World War II bombardments in May 1940 destroyed 90 per cent of the town centre, and fighting occurred again around its outskirts in early September 1944, involving units of the U.S. 1st Infantry Division.

The town was rebuilt after the war, and the new Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1970. Maubeuge has foundries, forges and blast furnaces, together with manufacture of machine tools and porcelain. It was the early home of the cyclist Maurice Garin, winner of the first Tour de France in 1903, who began his career with the local cycling club in 1892.
maui: Maui is the second-largest island in the Hawaiian archipelago, with an area of 1,883 square kilometres. Once part of Maui Nui, it is dominated by two volcanic features, Haleakalā in the southeast and the West Maui Mountains in the northwest, joined by an isthmus about six miles wide that gives the island its nickname, the Valley Isle. Like the other Hawaiian Islands it was formed by volcanism associated with the Hawaii hotspot, and is a volcanic doublet, made of two shield volcanoes that overlapped. In Native Hawaiian tradition the navigator Hawaiʻiloa named the island after his son, who was himself named for the demigod Māui; its earlier name was ʻIhikapalaumaewa.

Polynesians from Tahiti were the original inhabitants, and they introduced the kapu system, a strict social order that affected all aspects of life and became the core of Hawaiian culture. The island's central position gave it a pivotal role in Hawaiian history. In 1790 Kamehameha I, king of Hawaiʻi island, invaded Maui and fought the inconclusive Battle of Kepaniwai. He returned to Hawaiʻi to fight a rival and subdued Maui a few years later.

James Cook sighted Maui on 26 November 1778 but found no suitable landing, and the first European ashore was the Comte de Lapérouse, on 29 May 1786 at what became La Perouse Bay. Traders, whalers, loggers of sandalwood and missionaries followed. The missionaries, who began arriving from New England in 1823, settled at Lahaina, then the Hawaiian capital. They devised the Hawaiian alphabet to translate a Bible, ran a printing press in Lahaina and began recording history that had been passed down orally. They opened the Lahainaluna Mission School in 1831, which still exists.

During the height of the whaling era, from 1843 to 1860, Lahaina was a major centre: in one season over 400 ships visited, with up to 100 anchored at once. Whaling declined steeply at the end of the 19th century as petroleum replaced whale oil. Maui was part of the Hawaiian Kingdom, the Republic of Hawaii, the Hawaiian territory and then the state of Hawaii, and during the Second World War, in 1943–1944, over 100,000 soldiers were based there.

Tourism is the island's major industry, and agriculture has long included sugar and pineapple. Sugar production ended in 2016. Haleakalā National Park, Hāna and the Hāna Highway, and ʻĪao Valley are among its principal sights. The summit of Haleakalā has an observatory, the first astronomical facility in Hawaii. In August 2023 wildfires destroyed much of the town of Lahaina.
maurice-emperor: Maurice was born in Arabissus in Cappadocia in 539, the son of a man named Paul, and contemporary sources call him a native Greek speaker. He came to Constantinople as a notary and served the commander of the imperial bodyguard, Tiberius, and when Tiberius was named Caesar in 574 Maurice succeeded him in that command. In late 577, with no military experience, he was made commander-in-chief in the east and fought the war against Sasanian Persia. He failed to reach Ctesiphon in 581 and quarrelled with the Ghassanid ruler al-Mundhir III, whom he accused of treason, a charge modern historians dismiss.

The dying Tiberius II named Maurice his heir and son-in-law, and Maurice was crowned on 13 August 582. He inherited a bankrupt empire at war with Persia, paying the Avars 80,000 gold solidi a year, while the Slavs ravaged the Balkans. In 590 the Persian king Hormizd IV was overthrown and his son Khosrow II fled to Constantinople. Although the Senate advised against it, Maurice helped him regain his throne, and in 591 the combined forces defeated the rebel Bahram Chobin. Khosrow ceded western Armenia, and the empire no longer paid tribute to Persia.

From 591 Maurice turned to the Balkans, retaking Singidunum in 592 and crossing the Danube, the first Roman emperor to do so in over two centuries. In the west he created the Exarchate of Italy in 584, against the Lombards, and the Exarchate of Africa in 591. His fiscal measures were unpopular: in 588 he cut army pay by a quarter, and the troops on the Persian front mutinied, and about 599 he refused to pay a small ransom for 12,000 soldiers held by the Avars, who killed them.

In autumn 602 Maurice ordered the army to winter beyond the Danube, and the exhausted troops mutinied and proclaimed an officer named Phocas. Maurice left Constantinople by ship on 22 November, Phocas was crowned on 23 November, and Maurice was captured and murdered at Chalcedon on 27 November 602 after watching five of his sons executed. Khosrow II used the murder as a pretext for a war of twenty-six years that devastated both empires before the Arab conquests. The Strategikon, a manual of war, is traditionally attributed to Maurice, though some historians now think it the work of his brother or another general.
maurice-prince-of-orange: Maurice was born on 14 November 1567 at the castle of Dillenburg, the son of William the Silent and Anna of Saxony, and was named after his maternal grandfather, the Elector Maurice of Saxony. He was raised in Dillenburg by his uncle Johan of Nassau and studied with his cousin Willem Lodewijk at Heidelberg and then at Leiden, where he met Simon Stevin. The States of Holland and Zeeland paid for his studies. When his father was murdered in Delft in 1584 he was sixteen. The monarchs of England and France had refused sovereignty over the Dutch provinces, which left him the only acceptable candidate for his father's office.

Maurice became stadtholder of Holland and Zeeland in 1585, of Guelders, Overijssel and Utrecht in 1590 and of Groningen and Drenthe in 1620. In 1587 he was appointed captain-general of the army, bypassing the Earl of Leicester. With Willem Lodewijk he reorganised the Dutch States Army, and paid close attention to Stevin's siege theories. In the period known as the Ten Glory Years, 1588 to 1598, he took Breda in 1590, Zutphen and Knodsenburg in 1591, Steenwijk and Coevorden in 1592, Geertruidenberg in 1593 and Groningen in 1594, and in 1597 a further series of towns. These victories rounded out the borders of the Dutch Republic.

At Turnhout in 1597 and Nieuwpoort in 1600 he won pitched battles through cooperation between the arms, with cavalry playing a major part. Drill and exercise, for him, were the fundamental postulates of tactics; volley fire was first used in European combat at Nieuwpoort. Historians note his preference for sieges, and Spanish forces under Ambrogio Spinola defeated him at Mülheim in October 1605.

Maurice began as the protégé of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, but they quarrelled over the Twelve Years' Truce of 1609 to 1621, which Oldenbarnevelt signed against his advice, and over religion, Maurice backing the Gomarists and Oldenbarnevelt the Remonstrants. Maurice had him arrested and tried, and he was beheaded in 1619 for high treason despite requests for mercy. In 1618 Maurice succeeded his half-brother Philip William as Prince of Orange.

War with Spain resumed in 1621. Maurice died at The Hague on 23 April 1625, with the Spanish siege of Breda still under way, and Justin of Nassau surrendered the town in June. He had no legitimate children and was succeeded by his half-brother Frederick Henry. His reforms were applied later by pupils such as Marshal Turenne and Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden. The island of Mauritius was named in his honour by Wybrant Warwijck in 1598.
mauricio-funes: Carlos Mauricio Funes Cartagena was born in San Salvador on 18 October 1959. He finished secondary school at the Jesuit-run Externado San José and took a degree in mass media at the Central American University. He began as a news reporter for Channel 10 in February 1986 and moved to Channel 12 the next year, where he became news director and hosted The Daily Interview. In 1991 he interviewed the FMLN guerrilla leader Schafik Hándal, and Channel 12 lost advertisers as a result. In 1994 he was one of four winners of the Maria Moors Cabot Prize from Columbia University. He worked as a CNN en Español correspondent from 1997 to 2005.

Funes sought the FMLN's nomination for the 2004 election but senior leaders opposed him as not a historic member, and Hándal vetoed his candidacy. For 2009 the party's reformist wing proposed him, on condition that the former guerrilla leader Salvador Sánchez Cerén be his running mate. He became the first non-guerrilla to be the FMLN's presidential candidate. He campaigned on combating tax evasion and creating jobs, modelled his campaign on Barack Obama's, and promised to keep the dollar as currency. He won with 1,354,000 votes, 51.32 per cent, against Rodrigo Ávila of ARENA, and was inaugurated on 1 June 2009 in the first peaceful transfer of power since the civil war ended. His first act was to restore diplomatic relations with Cuba.

His government abolished public health care fees, gave schoolchildren free shoes, meals and uniforms, introduced cash transfers and pensions for the elderly, and raised teachers' salaries. In November 2009 Hurricane Ida buried the community of Verapaz in San Vicente. He was criticised for lacking a plan against rising crime and ordered the army to cooperate with the police. On 16 January 2010 he apologised in the name of the state for atrocities of the civil war, including the 1981 El Mozote massacre, and on 24 March 2010 for the assassination of Archbishop Óscar Romero. In October 2010 he apologised to Indigenous Salvadorans, calling La Matanza of 1932 a genocide.

After leaving office in 2014 Funes faced allegations of criminal conduct, and from 2016 he lived in exile in Nicaragua, which granted him asylum and later citizenship. He died in a hospital in Managua on 21 January 2025, aged 65, and was buried in Nicaragua.
mauritania: Mauritania lies in the western region of Africa and is generally flat, its 1,030,000 square kilometres forming vast, arid plains broken by occasional ridges and clifflike outcroppings. It borders the Atlantic Ocean, Senegal, Mali, Algeria and Western Sahara, and is considered part of both the Sahel and the Maghreb. Approximately three-quarters of the country is desert or semidesert, and the desert has been expanding since the mid-1960s after extended, severe drought. The highest of its sandstone plateaus, the Adrar Plateau, reaches 500 metres, and the concentric Guelb er Richat is a prominent feature of the north-central region.

The name comes from Mauretania, the Latin name of an ancient Berber kingdom and later Roman province that lay considerably farther north, along the western Mediterranean coast of Africa. The territories do not overlap. Arab geographers more commonly called the land Bilad Chinqit, the land of Chinguetti. The French officially used the term Mauritanie occidentale in 1899, on a proposal by the colonial administrator Xavier Coppolani.

The ancient tribes of Mauritania were the Niger-Congo and Bafour peoples. The Bafour were among the first Saharan peoples to abandon a nomadic lifestyle for agriculture, and migrated southward as the Sahara dried. They were displaced by Berbers who arrived between the 3rd and 7th centuries. The Umayyads were the first Arab Muslims to enter the region, establishing themselves by the end of the 7th century. In the 11th century several Berber confederations in the desert joined to form the Almoravid movement, which built an empire stretching from the Sahara to the Iberian Peninsula.

From 1644 to 1674 the indigenous peoples made a final, unsuccessful effort to repel the Maqil Arabs, led by the Beni Hassan tribe, in the Char Bouba War. The descendants of the Beni Hassan warriors became the upper stratum of Moorish society, and Hassaniya, a bedouin Arabic dialect named for them, became the dominant language of the largely nomadic population. In the early 20th century France colonised the country as part of French West Africa. It became independent in 1960.

Mauritania is the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. Its capital and largest city is Nouakchott, on the Atlantic coast, and its population is about 5 million. Arabic is the official language, with Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof as national languages, and Islam is the state religion. Its manuscript libraries at Chinguetti hold thousands of medieval manuscripts, and it has a long oral tradition of poetry.
mauritius: The main island lies 1,100 nautical miles (2,000 km) off the southeast coast of Africa, between latitudes 19°58.8'S and 20°31.7'S. It is 65 km long and 45 km wide. It is geologically young, created by volcanic activity some 8 million years ago, and with Réunion, Rodrigues and Saint Brandon it forms part of the Mascarene Islands, which are no longer volcanically active. White sandy beaches surround it, and lagoons are protected by a coral reef. The country also includes Rodrigues, Agaléga and St. Brandon. The main island was the only known home of the dodo, which became extinct soon after human settlement.

The island was uninhabited when first visited. Some historians have speculated from the Cantino planisphere of 1502, where it appears as Dina Arobi, that Arab sailors reached it around 975. Portuguese sailors visited in 1507, and Diogo Fernandes Pereira is the first European known to have landed; the Portuguese did not stay. A Dutch squadron under Admiral Wybrand Van Warwyck landed at Grand Port in 1598 and named the island after Prince Maurice of Nassau. The Dutch inhabited it from 1638, exploiting ebony trees and introducing sugar cane, domestic animals and deer.

French colonisation began in 1715, and the island was renamed Isle de France. In 1810 the United Kingdom seized it, and France ceded Mauritius and its dependencies in the Treaty of Paris. The British colony included Rodrigues, Agaléga, St. Brandon, the Chagos Archipelago and, until 1906, the Seychelles. Mauritius became the British Empire's main sugar-producing colony and stayed a plantation colony dominated by sugar until independence in 1968. The country became a republic in 1992.

In 1965, three years before independence, the United Kingdom split the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius to form the British Indian Ocean Territory, established on 8 November 1965. The local population was forcibly expelled, and the main island, Diego Garcia, was leased to the United States for a military base.

Mauritius is a parliamentary republic with a unicameral National Assembly, and its capital and largest city is Port Louis. Its people are diverse in ethnicity, culture, language and faith, drawn from Indian, African, Chinese and European, mostly French, origins. It is the only country in Africa where Hinduism is the most practised religion. Its architecture combines Dutch, French and British styles with influences from India and East Africa.
maurya-empire: The Maurya Empire had its power base in Magadha. Its origins are shrouded in legend. Greek sources refer to confrontations between the Greeks and Chandragupta Maurya, whom they call Sandrokottos, but say almost nothing of his conquest of the Nanda Empire, while Indian sources narrate only that conquest. Buddhist texts place him in the Moriya clan, and Jain texts call him the son of an imperial superintendent of peacocks.

Through military conquests and diplomatic treaties Chandragupta extended his rule as far west as Afghanistan below the Hindu Kush and as far south as the northern Deccan. Beyond the Magadha core, the technology and infrastructure of the time limited how deeply his rule could penetrate society.

Chandragupta was succeeded by Bindusara, and then by Ashoka, his grandson. Ashoka crushed revolts in Ujjain and Taxila as a prince. His conquest of Kalinga in 262–261 BCE became the pivotal event of his life: an estimated 100,000 soldiers and civilians were killed, and many more were affected by the destruction. Ashoka felt remorse, embraced Buddhism and renounced war. He sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, north-western India and Central Asia and propagated his own dhamma in edicts, most commonly set up along well-travelled roads.

Ashoka was followed for fifty years by weaker emperors. None of his sons took the throne: Mahinda became a Buddhist monk and Kunala was blinded. Dasharatha, Ashoka's grandson, lost many territories, some later retaken by Samprati. The last Mauryan ruler, Brihadratha, was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga during a military parade, and the Shunga Empire arose.

Ashoka's empire consisted of five parts. Magadha, with the capital at Pataliputra, was ruled directly. Four provinces, with capitals at Tosali, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri and Taxila, were governed by princes. Historians now often see the empire as a network of core regions and trade routes rather than a solid territory. The major rock edicts are found in the frontier provinces and are absent in large parts of the supposed territory, including Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

Megasthenes credited the empire with an army of 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 8,000 chariots and 9,000 war elephants. Roads such as the winter road Uttarapath, linking eastern Afghanistan to Pataliputra, promoted trade, and silver and copper coins were widely used. The population is estimated at between 15 and 30 million. The empire favoured Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivikism over Brahmanism.
mausolus: Mausolus was the eldest son of Hecatomnus, a native Carian who became satrap of Caria around 395 to 392 BCE, shortly after Tissaphernes died. The two may have shared rule in the early 370s BCE. Mausolus ruled alongside his wife and sister Artemisia, known as Artemisia II. Because they had no children, and incest of this kind was otherwise unknown in Caria, their marriage is thought to have been entirely symbolic. Only Mausolus was ever called satrap, but Artemisia clearly held some political authority as joint dynast.

Mausolus took part in the Revolt of the Satraps, in which many western satraps rebelled against Artaxerxes II, mostly in the 360s BCE. He mainly acted on the king's side: with Autophradates of Lydia he led the siege of Adramyttium in 366 BCE at the king's request, though Greek sources say he briefly rebelled. He was not punished and was rewarded with the governance of Lycia, where independent Lycian coinage ceased and his own coins circulated. He also supported the rebels against Athens in the Social War of 357 to 355 BCE, extending his authority among the neighbouring Greek islands. Rhodes came to be ruled by an oligarchy backed by a Carian garrison.

Greek writers portray him as a despot. The Economics attributed to Aristotle tells of schemes to raise money, such as telling the people of Mylasa that the Persian king was about to attack their unwalled city and then keeping the funds they gave for walls. Inscriptions record that he punished nobles who conspired against him, and he survived an assassination attempt at the festival at Labraunda in 355/4 BCE. Early in his reign he moved the capital from Mylasa to Halicarnassus, which he rebuilt on a new grid and enlarged by moving people from nearby Carian villages. It gained a theatre, an agora and harbour fortifications. He also rebuilt the sanctuaries at Amyzon, Labraunda and Sinuri.

Mausolus died shortly after the attempt at Labraunda. His remains were placed in the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, which tradition says Artemisia ordered built and which was finished only after her death; construction probably began in his lifetime. Its designers included the architects Satyrus and Pythis and the sculptors Scopas of Paros, Leochares, Bryaxis and Timotheus. Antipater of Sidon listed it among the Seven Wonders, and the word mausoleum came to mean any grand tomb. Artemisia held a funeral with games at which Theodectes of Phaselis won the verse contest with a tragedy called Mausolus. Most of the surviving sculpture is in the British Museum. His brother Idrieus probably succeeded him as satrap.
mawlid: The term Mawlid comes from the Arabic root walad, meaning to give birth. It is a generic word for any birthday, but usually refers to the observance of the birthday of Muhammad, also called Mawlid al-Nabi and, in some regions, Milad. It also names the text composed for and recited at the celebration. Most Sunni Muslims hold that Muhammad was born on 12 Rabi I, while many Twelver Shia assert 17 Rabi I, although prominent Shia scholars such as al-Kulayni and Ibn Babawayh have affirmed the 12th. Others contend that the date of his birth is not definitively recorded. Ibn Khallikan records the date as the first proven disagreement about the celebration.

Early observance of Muhammad's birth as a holy day was usually arranged privately, and some of the Tabi'un held sessions in which poetry and songs in his honour were recited. The early celebrations included Sufi elements, with animal sacrifices, torchlight processions, public sermons and a feast, and the ruler played a key role. In 1207 the Turkic general Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri, brother-in-law of Saladin, held a public festival of the Mawlid in Erbil, which included the slaughter of thousands of animals for a banquet said to have cost 300,000 dirhams. The festival then spread across the Muslim world, and the Ottomans declared the day an official holiday in 1588, known as Mevlid Kandil.

Celebrants hold gatherings called mahfils, in which religious poetry in praise of Muhammad is recited, followed by a feast. Other customs are voluntary fasting, prayer and dhikr. Sufi orders often organise large street processions, decorate homes and mosques and distribute food and charity, and scholars and poets recite the Qaṣīda al-Burda by the 13th-century poet Busiri. In Turkey the best known of the many mawlid poems is the Mawlid of Süleyman Çelebi. The word is also used in places such as Egypt for the birthday celebrations of Sufi saints.

The Hanafi, Maliki and Shafi'i schools of Sunni Islam generally approve of the Mawlid, as do the Shia. Jurists justified it as a way of giving thanks for the gift of Muhammad, and the scholars Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali and Ibn Hajar al-Asqalini wrote in this vein, Ibn Hajar allowing any form of celebration that is neutral under Shari'a. Early fatwas criticised hosts for taking contributions from guests. Salafism regards the celebration as a reprehensible innovation, bid'a, and prohibits it, while Deobandi jurists treat it as a matter of scholarly disagreement. It is a national holiday in most Muslim-majority countries.
mawtini: "Mawṭinī", Arabic for 'My Homeland', is an Arabic national poem by the Palestinian poet Ibrahim Tuqan, written around 1934 and composed as a song by the Lebanese musician Mohammed Flayfel. It became a popular patriotic song among Arab people. For much of the 20th century it served as an unofficial anthem of Palestinians and of other peoples of the Middle East, and it was Palestine's de facto national anthem from its beginning until 1996, when "Fidā'ī" officially replaced it. Many Arab artists have re-sung the anthem with new arrangements, among them Elissa, Christina Sawaya and Faia Younan, in a video clip that depicted the Syrian civil war.

The song has been described as a reflection of the shared experiences and struggles of Arab peoples. Its lyrics express a deep love for the homeland, a commitment to its liberation and a vision of a united and free nation. It is regarded as a symbol of resistance and of the collective longing for liberation in periods of occupation and oppression, conveying sorrow, anger and hope and a sense of renewal and solidarity among those who have endured similar adversities. This message resonates widely across the Arab world, reflecting shared struggles for independence, identity and sovereignty.

Many Palestinians still identify strongly with the song alongside "Fidā'ī" and consider it a sort of unofficial second national anthem of their country. In 2004 it was adopted as the national anthem of Iraq on the order of the Coalition Provisional Authority chief Paul Bremer. It replaced an earlier anthem also called "Mawṭinī", an unrelated instrumental piece without lyrics composed by Lewis Zanbaka, which Iraq had used in the late 1950s and early 1960s and had brought back temporarily after the fall of the Ba'athist regime in 2003. That piece had itself replaced "Arḍulfurātayni", in use since 1981 and associated with Saddam Hussein's regime.
max-frisch: Max Rudolf Frisch was born in Zurich on 15 May 1911, the second son of the architect Franz Bruno Frisch and Karolina Bettina Frisch, née Wildermuth. The family lived modestly, and their finances worsened after the father lost his job during the First World War. At school Frisch began writing drama but failed to get it performed and destroyed his early works. His father died in March 1932, and he took up journalism for the Neue Zürcher Zeitung to support his mother. A journey through eastern and southeastern Europe in 1933 led to his first novel, Jürg Reinhart, in 1934.

In 1936 Frisch enrolled at the ETH Zurich to study architecture, supported by a stipend from his friend Werner Coninx. His second novel, An Answer from the Silence (1937), won the 1938 Conrad Ferdinand Meyer Prize, though he burned the manuscript and later refused to include it in a collected edition. In 1942 he came first among 65 entrants in a competition to design the Freibad Letzigraben.

From 1944 Kurt Hirschfeld, director of the Zürich Playhouse, encouraged him to write for the theatre, and his first play, Santa Cruz, was performed in 1946. The Fire Raisers, about a man who shelters vagrants who then burn down his house, made him a dramatist of international standing; Swiss audiences took it as a warning against Communism, and Frisch felt misunderstood. His novels Stiller (1954) and Homo Faber (1957) brought a wider readership.

Frisch's work centres on identity, individuality, responsibility, morality and political commitment, and his post-war writing makes frequent use of irony. A recurring idea, set out in the Diary 1946–1949, applies the biblical ban on graven images to human relations: people reduce one another to fixed images, a sin against both self and other unless love lets each change. The diary became one of his characteristic forms, and the narrator of Stiller cries out that he has no language for his reality.

He received the Georg Büchner Prize in 1958, the Jerusalem Prize in 1965 and the Neustadt International Prize for Literature in 1986. Stiller and Gantenbein were widely taken up as models for treating identity through narrative structure. Frisch died on 4 April 1991; his estate is administered by the Max Frisch Foundation, whose archive is kept at the ETH Zurich.
max-weber: Maximilian Carl Emil Weber was born on 21 April 1864 in Erfurt and raised in Charlottenburg, the oldest of eight children. His father, Max Weber Sr., was a lawyer, civil servant and National Liberal parliamentarian, and the family's salon welcomed scholars such as the historian Theodor Mommsen. His mother, Helene Fallenstein, was a devout Calvinist and philanthropist.
