He studied law and history in Berlin, Göttingen and Heidelberg, took his doctorate in law in 1889 and his habilitation in 1891, and in 1893 married his second cousin Marianne Schnitger, a feminist activist and author.

Weber taught in Berlin, Freiburg and Heidelberg. In 1897 he suffered a breakdown after his father died following an argument, and he ceased teaching and travelled for several years. From 1904 he was an associate editor of the Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, in which he published The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.

He first supported Germany's war effort in 1914 but became a prominent critic of expansionism and of the Kaiser's war policies, and he called for democratisation. After the war he co-founded the German Democratic Party, advised on the drafting of the Weimar Constitution, and taught in Vienna and Munich, where he gave the lectures Science as a Vocation and Politics as a Vocation. He died of pneumonia on 14 June 1920, possibly as a result of the Spanish flu.

A central concern was rationalisation and disenchantment. In The Protestant Ethic he argued that Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, tied piety to a worldly calling and so encouraged rational economic gain. He later studied the religions of China, India and ancient Judaism. He defined the state by its monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a given area, and divided legitimate authority into traditional, charismatic and rational-legal forms.

Methodologically he placed social action at the centre of sociology, sought to understand it through interpretation, and used ideal types as models to compare with reality. Economy and Society was left unfinished. He is now regarded alongside Karl Marx and Émile Durkheim as a founding figure of sociology.
maxim-gun: Hiram Maxim's first British patents for the gun were granted in June and July 1883, and a prototype was shown to invited guests in October 1884. That November he founded the Maxim Gun Company in London with financing from Albert Vickers. The company later joined the Swedish firm Nordenfelt as Maxim Nordenfelt Guns and Ammunition Company, and was finally absorbed into Vickers, leading to the Vickers machine gun.

The gun was recoil-operated: energy from the recoil acting on the breech block ejected each spent cartridge and loaded the next. Maxim's earliest designs used a rotating cam to reverse the block, later simplified to a toggle lock. This made it far more efficient than earlier hand-cranked rapid-firing guns such as the Gatling gun of 1861. Trials showed that it could fire 600 rounds a minute, equal to 60 riflemen of the time.

The Maxim was water cooled, which let it keep up its rate of fire far longer than air-cooled guns but made it heavier and less flexible. A lone soldier could fire it, but it was usually worked by a team of four to six, who reloaded, spotted targets and carried ammunition and water. Moving or mounting it took several men. An air-cooled Extra Light version of 1895 was the lightest machine gun in the world, but it overheated quickly and only 135 were built.

A prototype went with Henry Morton Stanley's Emin Pasha Relief Expedition of 1886 to 1890, more as a publicity stunt than a military contribution, and it was used mainly to frighten off attackers. The first unit in the world to receive the gun was Hermann Wissmann's force, sent in 1888 to suppress the Abushiri revolt. At the Battle of the Shangani on 25 October 1893, in the First Matabele War, 700 soldiers with five Maxims fought off 5,000 Matabele warriors. Historian Martin Gilbert called it the weapon most associated with imperial conquest.

Governments were at first reluctant to adopt it, as soldiers distrusted machine guns that jammed. The British Army ordered 120 in October 1888 under Sir Garnet Wolseley, and Russia, Switzerland, the United States and many others followed. Popular myth has embellished its destructive power in colonial warfare; modern accounts suggest that it was effective in pitched battles such as Omdurman, but that much of its significance lay in its psychological impact. Its descendants include the Vickers, the German MG 08 and the Russian Pulemyot Maxim, which served in both world wars.
maximian: Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus was born around 250 near Sirmium in the province of Pannonia, into a family of shopkeepers. He joined the army and served with Diocletian under the emperors Aurelian and Probus. Probably in July 285, at Mediolanum, Diocletian appointed him Caesar. Historians suggest that Diocletian, who thought himself a mediocre general, wanted a lieutenant to do most of his fighting.

Maximian made his residence at Trier but spent most of his time on campaign. In late 285 he suppressed the Bagaudae, rebels in Gaul. He took the title of Augustus on 1 April 286, in the traditional dating, when the crisis with Carausius had broken out. Carausius, whom he had set to clear the Channel of pirates, rebelled in 286 and took Britain and part of Gaul with him. Maximian campaigned instead against the tribes of the Rhine, and in 288 he and Diocletian laid waste to Alamannic territory, burning crops. His own invasion fleet against Carausius failed in 289 or 290, perhaps lost to storms.

The rebel regime was ended in 296 by his subordinate Constantius. Maximian meanwhile held the Rhine frontier and then led an army through Spain to fight Berber raiders in Mauretania. At Diocletian's insistence he abdicated on 1 May 305 and retired to southern Italy.

Late in 306 Maximian took the title of Augustus again to support his son Maxentius, who had been declared emperor in Rome. In April 307 he tried to depose his son and fled to Constantine at Trier. At the Conference of Carnuntum in November 308 Diocletian and Galerius forced him to renounce his claim once more. In 310, while Constantine was campaigning against the Franks, Maximian announced at Arles that Constantine was dead and took the purple. Most of the army stayed loyal, and Constantine captured him at Marseille. Maximian hanged himself in July 310, on Constantine's urging. His image was first purged and, after Maxentius's defeat, restored, and he was deified.
maximilian-i-elector-of-bavaria: Maximilian was born in Munich on 17 April 1573, the eldest son of William V, Duke of Bavaria, and Renata of Lorraine to survive infancy. He was educated by the Jesuits and began to take part in government by about 1591 to 1594, as his father's difficulties in ruling grew. In 1595 he married his cousin Elisabeth Renata, daughter of Charles III, Duke of Lorraine, and he became Duke of Bavaria on his father's abdication in 1597. Frail in health, he had high ambitions for himself and his duchy. Although a rigid adherent of the Catholic faith, he was not always subservient to the church.

Maximilian took no part in German politics until 1607, when he was charged with executing the imperial ban against the Protestant free city of Donauwörth. His troops occupied it in December 1607 and restored Catholic supremacy. Alarmed Protestant princes formed the Protestant Union, which was answered in 1609 by the Catholic League, in whose formation he took an important part. His policy was defensive, and he refused to let the League become a tool of the Habsburgs.

In October 1619 he agreed a treaty with Emperor Ferdinand II, and on 8 November 1620 his troops under Count Tilly defeated Frederick, King of Bohemia, at the Battle of White Mountain. In February 1623 he was invested with the electoral dignity, and the Upper Palatinate came to him.

The war later turned against Bavaria. Early in 1632 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden marched into the electorate and occupied Munich, and the Swedes and their French allies ravaged it. In March 1647 Maximilian concluded the Truce of Ulm with France and Sweden but then disregarded it at the entreaty of Ferdinand III. His forces were defeated at Zusmarshausen in May 1648. By the Peace of Westphalia he kept the electoral dignity, now hereditary, and the Upper Palatinate, but gave up the Lower Palatinate to Charles Louis, Frederick V's son.

At home he restored the state finances, reorganised the administration and army, introduced mercantilist measures and issued a new body of law, the Codex Maximilianeus. He enlarged the Munich Residenz and commissioned four hunt paintings from Peter Paul Rubens.

After the death of Elisabeth Renata, who left no children, Maximilian married his niece Maria Anna of Austria on 15 July 1635, hoping for an heir. Two sons followed, and Ferdinand Maria succeeded him. He died at Ingolstadt on 27 September 1651 and was buried in St Michael's Church, Munich. In 1839 King Ludwig I of Bavaria erected a statue in his memory in Munich.
maximilian-i-holy-roman-emperor: Maximilian was born at Wiener Neustadt on 22 March 1459, the only surviving son of Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor, and Eleanor of Portugal. In his infancy he and his parents were besieged in Vienna by Albert of Austria. Charles the Bold of Burgundy died at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477, and his daughter Mary of Burgundy claimed his lands while Louis XI of France seized the Duchy of Burgundy by force. Mary agreed to marry Maximilian on 19 August 1477, and he took over the defence of her lands without help from the Empire. He defeated the French at the Battle of Guinegate on 7 August 1479.

Maximilian was elected King of the Romans at Frankfurt on 16 February 1486 and crowned at Aachen on 9 April, and he ruled jointly with his father until Frederick's death in 1493. He was never crowned by the Pope because the Venetians blocked the way to Rome, so in 1508 he proclaimed himself elected emperor at Trento, and Pope Julius II later recognised it. This broke the tradition of papal coronation.

He was open to reform. At the Reichstag of 1495 at Worms the Reichskammergericht was introduced as a court largely independent of the emperor, with a new tax, the Gemeine Pfennig. His campaigns in Italy against the French went badly, since the forces he could pay for were too small. He depended on loans from Upper German banking families, notably the Fugger and Welser families, and about 70 percent of his income went to war. His son Philip the Handsome married the future queen Joanna of Castile in 1496, which prepared the Habsburg succession in Spain. Maximilian lost family lands in Switzerland to the Swiss Confederacy.

Maximilian fell from his horse in 1501 and injured his leg, which pained him for the rest of his life, and from 1514 he travelled everywhere with his coffin. He died on 12 January 1519. In German tradition he is the last knight, a title from a poem by Anastasius Grün, and scholars still debate whether he was the last knight or the first Renaissance prince. Through an unprecedented programme of images, with the help of scholars and artists, he built a royal image of himself that historians call unmatched. Historians of the late nineteenth century such as Leopold von Ranke blamed him for putting his dynasty before Germany, while the work of Hermann Wiesflecker has led to a more favourable view.
maximilian-i-joseph-of-bavaria: Maximilian was born on 27 May 1756 at Schwetzingen, the son of Count Palatine Frederick Michael of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld. After his father's death in 1767 he was educated under the supervision of his uncle, Duke Christian IV of Zweibrücken. He became Count of Rappoltstein in 1776 and in 1777 took service as a colonel in the French Royal Army, rising rapidly to major-general and serving at Strasbourg from 1782 to 1789. At the outbreak of the French Revolution he moved to the Austrian service and fought in the opening campaigns of the French Revolutionary War. He succeeded his brother Charles II as Duke of Zweibrücken on 1 April 1795, though France had entirely occupied the duchy.

On 16 February 1799 Maximilian became Elector of Bavaria, as Maximilian IV Joseph, on the extinction of the Palatinate-Sulzbach line. He found the army in abject condition and made rebuilding it a priority. In his new ministry the most powerful influence was Count Max Josef von Montgelas, whose policies were enlightened and French. Agriculture and commerce were fostered, a new criminal code was drawn up, taxes were equalised without regard to traditional privileges, and a number of religious houses were suppressed and their revenues used for education. He moved the University of Ingolstadt to Landshut in 1800. Secularisation of 1802 and 1803 nationalised cultural assets of the Church, and Protestants were emancipated.

His foreign policy was dictated by dynastic and Bavarian considerations. Until 1813 he was the most faithful of Napoleon's German allies, a tie strengthened by the marriage of his eldest daughter to Eugène de Beauharnais. The Treaty of Pressburg of 26 December 1805 gave him the royal title and territory in Swabia and Franconia, and he took the title of king on 1 January 1806. After 1809 he received Tyrol and Innviertel from Austria. By the Treaty of Ried on 8 October 1813 he joined the Allies on condition that his kingdom's integrity was guaranteed, and declared war on France on 14 October.

In 1814 Bavaria returned Tyrol to Austria in exchange for Würzburg, and at the Congress of Vienna Maximilian ceded Salzburg and other districts in return for the western Palatinate. He opposed any reorganisation of Germany that endangered Bavarian independence, which contributed to the loose structure of the German Confederation. After Montgelas fell in 1817, he granted a constitution on 26 May 1818, partly to give unity to his varied territories. He founded the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1808 and ordered the National Theatre built in 1810. Maximilian died at Nymphenburg Palace on 13 October 1825 and was succeeded by his son Ludwig I.
maximilian-i-of-mexico: Maximilian was born on 6 July 1832 at the Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the son of Archduke Franz Karl and Princess Sophie of Bavaria. Not destined to rule, he trained in the small Imperial Austrian Navy, which his brother Franz Joseph helped to fund, and in 1856 he met and then married Charlotte of Belgium. On 28 February 1857 Franz Joseph named him viceroy of Lombardy-Venetia. His authority did not fully extend over the Austrian garrison, which opposed liberal reforms, and when Franz Joseph refused his request for wider powers, he was left with a limited role while tensions with Piedmont rose. He was dismissed in 1859.

Mexican conservatives, beaten in the civil war of 1858 to 1861, sought outside allies. After the government of Benito Juárez suspended payment of foreign debts in 1861, France began military operations in 1862, was repulsed at Puebla on 5 May 1862, and took the capital in June 1863. Maximilian, approached by Mexican monarchists, accepted the crown on 10 April 1864 after a referendum in Mexico that was not genuine, with a pledge of French military support.

His hold was shaky from the start. Instead of reversing the liberal reforms of the Constitution of 1857, as his conservative backers expected, he supported them and declared an amnesty for liberals. The United States, which saw the French intervention as a breach of the Monroe Doctrine, never recognised the empire, and after its Civil War ended in 1865 it aided Juárez with loans and volunteers. French armies withdrew in 1866 on the orders of Napoleon III.

Maximilian was captured at Querétaro. His trial opened on 13 June 1867, and after one day he was found guilty of conspiracy and sentenced to death. Victor Hugo and Giuseppe Garibaldi were among those who asked for mercy, but Juárez refused, to show that Mexico would not tolerate further foreign invasions. Maximilian was shot on 19 June 1867 with his generals Miguel Miramón and Tomás Mejía. His death ended monarchism as a major force in Mexico. Édouard Manet painted the execution three times, and recent writing treats Maximilian less as a villain and more as a liberal in the line of Juárez and Porfirio Díaz.
maximilian-ii-emanuel-elector-of-bavaria: Maximilian II Emanuel was born in Munich on 11 July 1662, the son of Ferdinand Maria, Elector of Bavaria, and Princess Henriette Adelaide of Savoy. He inherited the electorate while still a minor in 1679 and remained under the regency of his uncle Maximilian Philipp until 1680. By 1683 he had begun a military career, fighting in the defence of Vienna against the Ottoman attempt to push further into Europe. On 15 July 1685 he married Maria Antonia, daughter of Emperor Leopold I, an unhappy marriage that nonetheless produced an heir for both Bavaria and the Spanish monarchy.

His fame was assured in 1688 when he led the capture of Belgrade from the Turks, with the support of Serbian insurgents under Jovan Monasterlija. In the War of the Grand Alliance he fought on the Habsburgs' side on the Rhine frontier and was made governor of the Spanish Netherlands in late 1691. His son Joseph Ferdinand, born in October 1692, was named heir to the Spanish crown but died in 1699. In 1695 French troops besieged and bombarded Brussels, and the resulting fire was the most destructive event in the city's history.

In the War of the Spanish Succession he sided with France. After the defeat at Blenheim in 1704 the Bavarian court went to the Spanish Netherlands, his sons were held for years in Austria, and Bavaria was partitioned between Austria and the Elector Palatine, whose harsh administration provoked a serious peasant uprising. After the Battle of Ramillies on 23 May 1706 he found refuge at Versailles. The Treaty of Rastatt in 1714 compelled Austria to restore him fully, including the Upper Palatinate.

Back in Bavaria Max Emanuel turned to building to make up for the failure of his political ambitions, and was bitter that others were raised to royal rank. In 1717 he sent troops against the Turks again, and in 1724 he united the Wittelsbach lines, which with his son Clemens August of Cologne and the electors Palatine and of Trier commanded four votes in an imperial election. He died of a stroke in 1726 and is buried in the crypt of the Theatinerkirche in Munich.

A patron of the arts, he bought Dutch and Flemish paintings as governor, and his return in 1715 marked the beginning of Bavarian Rococo. The Nymphenburg Palace was enlarged, the new Schleissheim Palace was completed in 1726, and Joseph Effner built the hunting lodge of Fürstenried. His son Charles Albert later became Holy Roman Emperor.
maximilian-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Maximilian was born in Vienna on 31 July 1527, the eldest son of the Habsburg king Ferdinand I and nephew of Emperor Charles V. He was educated mainly in Italy by humanist scholars, learned something of Lutheran teaching in his youth and corresponded early with the Protestant prince Augustus of Saxony. On 13 September 1548 he married his cousin Maria of Spain, and the marriage produced sixteen children, of whom nine lived to adulthood.

In Vienna he grew close to the court preacher Sebastian Pfauser, which alarmed his father. After several refusals he agreed in 1560 to Pfauser's banishment and attended Catholic Mass again, though his views were tinged with Lutheranism to the end of his life.

Maximilian was crowned King of Bohemia in 1562, elected King of the Romans on 24 November 1562 and crowned King of Hungary and Croatia in 1563. He succeeded Ferdinand as emperor on 25 July 1564. He granted religious liberty to the Lutheran nobles and knights in Austria and refused to publish the decrees of the Council of Trent, but he would not meet the demands of the Lutheran princes at the Diet of Augsburg in 1566. His reign saw the high point of Protestantism in Austria and Bohemia, which he did not try to suppress.

War with the Ottomans resumed in 1566, and they took Szigetvár while their sultan died during the siege. The Treaty of Adrianople of 1568 required Maximilian to recognise Ottoman suzerainty over Transylvania, Wallachia and Moldavia. In 1576 part of the Polish and Lithuanian magnates elected him king of Poland against Stephen Báthory, but he was not widely accepted there.

Maximilian died at Regensburg on 12 October 1576 while preparing to invade Poland, and on his deathbed he refused the last sacraments. He is buried in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. His eldest surviving son Rudolf succeeded him. His court was a centre of humanist scholarship where Catholic and Protestant scholars worked together, including the botanist Carolus Clusius, and his library under Hugo Blotius became the nucleus of the Austrian National Library. Paula Sutter Fichtner holds that he failed in his three main aims, while Peter Marshall argues that his tolerance and patronage kept a precarious peace.
maximilian-ii-of-bavaria: Maximilian was born in Munich on 28 November 1811, the eldest child of Crown Prince Ludwig, later King Ludwig I, and Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen, and was named after his grandfather, King Maximilian I. He studied at Göttingen and Berlin and travelled in Germany, Italy and Greece. His father brought him into the council of state in 1836. He showed a studious disposition and once said that, had he not been born a prince, he would have chosen to be a professor. At the chateau of Hohenschwangau near Füssen, which he had rebuilt, he gathered artists and scholars around him. In 1842 he married the Prussian princess Marie Friederike Franziska Hedwig, and they had two sons, Ludwig II and Otto.

Ludwig I's abdication on 20 March 1848 called him suddenly to the throne, and his choice of ministers promised a liberal regime. An uprising in the Bavarian Palatinate in 1849 was put down with the help of the Prussian army. From 1850 his government leaned towards absolute monarchy, though he steered between classical liberalism, Prussian-inspired Pan-Germanism and the Ultramontanes. He attended the Frankfurt Assembly but opposed its plans, refused to recognise its imperial constitution and helped Austria restore the federal diet.

In 1850 Austria, Bavaria and their allies moved troops towards Hesse-Kassel, and Prussia backed down in the Punctation of Olmütz, which strengthened the alliance of Bavaria with Austria. He nonetheless tried to keep Bavaria independent by playing the two powers against each other. In 1863 he supported Austria's reform plan at the Frankfurt Fürstentag.

He invited scholars such as Geibel, Liebig, Heyse and Sybel to Munich whatever their religion, which angered conservative Catholics and Protestants. He also financed studies of the art, costumes, dialects and customs of the Bavarian peasantry, with the help of his secretary Franz Xaver von Schönwerth, to support a separate Bavarian identity against Pan-Germanism. He consulted ministers and experts before deciding, which caused delays, as did his frequent journeys to Italy and Greece.

Constant ill health often kept him abroad or in the countryside. After a brief illness he died in Munich on 10 March 1864 and was buried in the Theatinerkirche. His son Ludwig II succeeded him. He commissioned Maximilianstrasse and the Bavarian National Museum in Munich and founded the Maximilian Order for Science and Art in 1853. Hans Christian Andersen, who visited him, described him as young and highly amiable.
maximilien-robespierre: Robespierre was baptised on 6 May 1758 in Arras, in Artois, the eldest of four children of François Maximilien Barthélémy de Robespierre, a lawyer, and Jacqueline Marguerite Carrault, the daughter of a brewer. After three years of law studies he graduated in July 1780 with a special prize for academic achievement and conduct. Admitted to the bar, he was appointed one of the five judges of the local criminal court in March 1782, but soon resigned, uncomfortable at passing capital sentences because he opposed the death penalty.

In the Estates General he gave his first speech on 6 June 1789, attacking the hierarchy of the church. In 1790 he demanded that all Frenchmen be admissible to public positions without distinction other than virtue and talent, and on 31 March was elected president of the Jacobin Club. In 1791 he gave 328 speeches and argued that all citizens, not only those with the vote, should be allowed to serve in the National Guard. He warned the Jacobins against war with Austria, saying on 2 January 1792 that no one loves armed missionaries.

He was elected to the National Convention in September 1792, where the Jacobins sat on the high benches known as the Mountain, and he worked to bring about the execution of Louis XVI, who was guillotined on 21 January 1793.

On 27 July 1793 Robespierre joined the Committee of Public Safety, at a time when France faced rebellion in the Vendée and in Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux and hostility across Europe. In a report of 5 February 1794 he argued that in revolution the springs of popular government were virtue and terror together. Danton and Desmoulins were tried in April 1794. The Law of 22 Prairial, passed on 10 June, denied accused persons counsel and left the revolutionary tribunals only two verdicts, acquittal or death; within three days 156 people were sent to the guillotine. On 6 and 7 May 1794 he had announced the recognition of God and the immortality of the soul and the festivals of the Supreme Being.

On 9 Thermidor, almost thirty-five deputies, most of them from the Mountain, spoke against Robespierre, and his voice was shouted down. He was arrested with around 90 others, among them Louis Antoine de Saint-Just, Georges Couthon and his brother Augustin. On 28 July 1794 he and twenty-one others were condemned under the Law of 22 Prairial without a hearing and guillotined. The Thermidorians held him the most culpable for the bloodshed, and Lazare Carnot called him a hypocrite. His views and policies remain controversial: he is remembered for his campaigns for the voting rights of all men and against the Atlantic slave trade, and for his part in the repression of the Revolution's opponents.
maximinus-thrax: Maximinus, whose Latin name was Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, was born in about 173, a date inferred from later sources that give his age at death as 65. Herodian, the only contemporary source, calls him Thraco-Roman. The Historia Augusta, a notoriously unreliable work, says he was born in Thrace or Moesia to a Gothic father and an Alanic mother, a claim many scholars reject as anachronistic; his ancestry remains an open question. He was a provincial of low birth whom the Senate regarded as a barbarian. He joined the army under Septimius Severus and rose to command the Legio IV Italica, whose Pannonian recruits were angered by Severus Alexander's payments to the Alemanni and his avoidance of war.

In 235 the army killed Severus Alexander and his mother at Moguntiacum, modern Mainz, and elected Maximinus emperor. The Praetorian Guard acclaimed him and the Senate grudgingly confirmed the choice. He was the first emperor from neither the senatorial nor the equestrian class. He removed Alexander's close advisers, put down two plots, and defeated the Alemanni in a swamp in the Agri Decumates, taking the title Germanicus Maximus. He wintered at Sirmium and fought the Dacians and Sarmatians in 235–236. He doubled the soldiers' pay. This and almost continuous warfare required higher taxes, and tax collectors resorted to violent methods and illegal confiscations, which alienated the governing class.

In early 238 landowners in the province of Africa revolted and proclaimed the governor, Gordian I, and his son Gordian II co-emperors, and the Senate backed them. Capelianus, governor of Numidia, defeated them; Gordian II died in the fighting and Gordian I hanged himself. The Senate then chose Pupienus and Balbinus as co-emperors, and under pressure from the Roman crowd made Gordian I's grandson, Gordian III, caesar.

Maximinus marched on Rome, but Aquileia closed its gates against him. His troops starved and grew disaffected during the siege, and in about May or June 238 soldiers of the Legio II Parthica assassinated him and his son. He never visited Rome as emperor. His accession is commonly seen as the beginning of the Crisis of the Third Century, a period of instability and civil war that lasted until 284.
may-coup-poland: Józef Piłsudski had largely controlled the politics of the re-established Polish state but lost that advantage after the failed Kiev offensive of spring 1920, while keeping the esteem of parts of the armed forces. In November 1925 the cabinet of Władysław Grabski gave way to that of Aleksander Skrzyński, backed by the National Democrats and the Polish Socialist Party; when the socialists withdrew, it fell in turn and was replaced by a government under Wincenty Witos, formed by the Polish People's Party "Piast" and the Christian Union of National Unity. It had even less popular support than its predecessors.

Piłsudski regarded the constant shifts of power in the Sejm, the Polish parliament, as chaotic and damaging. He also saw threats to Poland's independence in the Locarno Treaties of 1925, by which the western but not the eastern borders of Germany were guaranteed, and in the Treaty of Berlin concluded by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1926.

On 10 May 1926, the day the Witos government was formed, Piłsudski told the newspaper Kurier Poranny that he was ready to fight the evil of sejmocracy, a contemptuous word for rule by parliament, and promised a sanation, or restoration to health, of political life. The edition was confiscated. In the night of 11–12 May units of the Warsaw garrison marched to Rembertów and pledged him their support; on 12 May they moved on Warsaw and took the bridges over the Vistula River.

At about 17:00 Piłsudski met President Stanisław Wojciechowski on the Poniatowski Bridge. He demanded the resignation of the cabinet; the president demanded that his forces capitulate. Fighting began at about 19:00. On 14 May the Polish Socialist Party declared for the rebels and called a general strike, and striking railwaymen kept government reinforcements from reaching Warsaw. To prevent a nationwide civil war, Wojciechowski and Witos resigned. In all 215 soldiers and 164 civilians were killed and some 900 people wounded.

Kazimierz Bartel formed a new government with Piłsudski as minister of military affairs. On 31 May the National Assembly nominated Piłsudski as president, but he declined, and Ignacy Mościcki took the office. Piłsudski held the posts of defence minister and inspector general of the armed forces in every government until his death, and headed two of them himself, in 1926–1928 and 1930. In 1935 his supporters replaced the democratic March Constitution with the April Constitution, which provided for a strong presidency but came too late for him to assume it.
maya-script: The script was used mainly in the Classic period to write Classic Maya, a literary form of the extinct Chʼoltiʼ language, on stelae and monuments. After the Classic Maya collapse its use declined and disappeared in the central and southern lowlands. In the Postclassic period it continued in northern Yucatán to write Yucatec Maya, in the surviving codices such as the Dresde, Madrid and Paris. Not every Mayan language used it: the Quichean languages, such as Kʼicheʼ and Kaqchikel, used the Mixteca-Puebla style of central Mexico.

It was a logosyllabic system. A glyph could stand for a word or morpheme or for a syllable. Syllabic glyphs often came from logograms for one-syllable words, so that the sign for a fish fin, read kah, came to stand for the syllable ka. The word bʼalam, jaguar, could be written with one logogram, with syllabic additions, or wholly in syllables as bʼa-la-ma. Texts were arranged in blocks, usually in columns two blocks wide.

The earliest inscriptions identifiably Maya date to the 3rd century BCE, at late Preclassic sites such as Chakjobon and San Bartolo. It was once thought that the Maya took writing from the Olmec or Epi-Olmec culture, but murals excavated in 2005 pushed the origin back by several centuries, and it now seems possible that the Maya invented writing in Mesoamerica. Knowledge of the script was kept to the elite.

Bishop Diego de Landa ordered Maya books collected and destroyed, and many codices were lost. He also recorded a so-called alphabet of Maya signs, which was long dismissed as nonsense but eventually became a key resource in decipherment. Knowledge of the script was lost, probably by the end of the 16th century.

Nineteenth-century and early twentieth-century scholars decoded the numbers and passages on astronomy and the calendar. In 1952 Yuri Knorozov argued that Landa's signs were syllabic, and J. Eric S. Thompson was among the last major opponents of this approach. In 1959 Tatiana Proskouriakoff showed that the dates on the monuments at Piedras Negras recorded the lives of individuals, so that the inscriptions were dynastic histories. In December 1973 a working group at Palenque, including Linda Schele, Floyd Lounsbury and Peter Mathews, reconstructed most of the dynastic list of Palenque in one afternoon.
Since the early 1980s scholars have shown that most of the remaining signs form a syllabary, and the exhibition The Blood of Kings in 1986 brought the results to a wide audience.
mayenne: The department lies in the Pays de la Loire region and has no sea coast, though Mont Saint-Michel Bay is about thirty kilometres to the north-west. It is roughly rectangular, 90 km long and 77 km wide, with an area of about 5,175 km2. The Manche, Orne, Sarthe, Maine-et-Loire and Ille-et-Vilaine departments surround it. The river Mayenne flows through its centre from north to south, passing the towns of Mayenne, Laval and Château-Gontier, and then joins the Sarthe to form the Maine, which flows into the Loire.

Mayenne is one of the original 83 departments, created on 4 March 1790 by the National Constituent Assembly during the early stages of the French Revolution. The new departments were meant to be uniform in administration and roughly equal in size and population. The old province of Maine was divided in two: Upper Maine, centred on Le Mans, became Sarthe, and Lower Maine, centred on Laval, became Mayenne. Anjou was too large for a single department and was cut down to form Maine-et-Loire, with Mayenne receiving Château-Gontier and Craon.

The border between Mayenne and Maine-et-Loire followed the southern limit of flax cultivation, since flax was a feature of the local economy. The northern two thirds of the department therefore correspond to western Maine, and the southern third to the northern part of Anjou. The department is also coextensive with the Roman Catholic Diocese of Laval.

The north of the department lies on the Armorican Massif, where the Mont des Avaloirs, at 417 m, is the highest point. The rest is largely flat, with some hilly areas and steep-sided valleys. Laval is the prefecture and largest town, and the department is divided into three arrondissements: Mayenne, Laval and Château-Gontier. It had 305,468 inhabitants in 2023, who are called Mayennais.

About 80 per cent of the land is farmed, and livestock rearing, above all of cattle, horses and pigs, predominates. Apple orchards supply a traditional cider industry. Iron and coal have been mined, and quarries yield marble, slate, limestone and flint. Industries include linen, paper and hemp, office furniture at Château-Gontier, and dairy products and electronics at Laval.
mayflower: The Mayflower was an English square-rigged merchant ship of about 180 tons, roughly 110 feet long and 25 feet in the beam, active from before 1609 until 1622. Her passengers included Separatists from a congregation of about 400 English Protestants who had gone to Leiden in 1608 to worship outside the Church of England, which they judged beyond reform. Others on board were hired hands, servants and farmers recruited by London merchants. The congregation's leader John Robinson stayed in Leiden with those who could not go.

The plan was for the small Speedwell to carry the Leiden group to England and for the Mayflower to take most passengers and supplies across the Atlantic. The Mayflower left London in mid-July 1620 with about 65 passengers and waited at Southampton. Speedwell sprang leaks three times, forcing the ships back to Dartmouth and then to Plymouth in England, and was abandoned, with 20 of her passengers crowded onto the Mayflower.

The ship sailed on 26 September 1620 with 102 passengers and a crew of about 30. The living area was about 20 by 80 feet with a ceiling of about five feet. Western gales slowed the crossing to more than two months. The ship sighted Cape Cod on 19 November 1620, in the old-style calendar, and anchored in what is now Provincetown Harbor on 21 November.

Before landing, the male Pilgrims and the other passengers, whom the Pilgrims called strangers, signed the Mayflower Compact, which set up a rudimentary government. The first winter at Plymouth was severe, with frozen ground, no shelter prepared and illness, and about half the crew died. William Bradford wrote that some who died took the origin of their death on an early exploring trip. The ship sailed for London on 15 April 1621, in the old-style calendar.

No record of the ship survives after 1624, when she was appraised at Rotherhithe at 128 pounds, eight shillings and fourpence. Charles Edward Banks held that she was broken up, and timbers bought from a Rotherhithe shipbreaker's yard in 1624 were used by Thomas Russell to build the Mayflower Barn at Jordans in Buckinghamshire, though this is not certain.

Bradford's journal and letters are the main source for the voyage and for Plymouth Colony. The harvest feast of 1621, attended by 90 Wampanoag people, is regarded as the origin of the American Thanksgiving. Richard Bevan calls the crossing the most culturally important of the voyages to the American colonies between 1620 and 1640.
mayor-of-the-palace: The mayor of the palace, in Latin maior palatii or maior domus, was in origin the manager of the Frankish king's household. He directed the operation of the whole court and stood at the head of the Merovingian administrative ladder. The king appointed him from among the magnates, the most powerful families. Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy each had their own mayor.

Burgundy lost its separate mayor in 626. Chlothar II, who ruled the whole Frankish kingdom, had ordered the execution of Warnachar, the mayor of Burgundy, and the Burgundian magnates then declared that they wanted no mayor of their own. This marks the effective end of the Burgundian court and the start of a Neustrian-Burgundian political alliance against Austrasian influence.

In the second half of the seventh century the office became the power behind the throne. The mayor made the decisions that affected the kingdom, while the kings were reduced to ceremonial duties and became little more than figureheads, known as rois fainéants, the do-nothing kings.

The Austrasian magnates revolted, and at the Battle of Tertry in 687 their leader Pepin of Herstal defeated Neustria and became its mayor of the palace. He took the title Duke of the Franks to mark his wider rule. His son Charles Martel, mayor in both Austrasia and Neustria, ruled without any king during the last four years of his life, from 737 to 741. Charles's sons Carloman and Pepin the Short raised another Merovingian king, Childeric III, but Pepin deposed him in 751 and was crowned king in his place.

The office shows how real power passed from a royal house to its chief servants. Neustria's mayors included Erchinoald, Ebroin and Grimoald II; Charles Martel held the post there from 718 and Pepin the Short from 741 or 742 until he became king.
mazandaran: Mazandaran lies on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea, in the Central Alborz mountains and the Hyrcanian forests. Its landscape runs from sandy beaches and plains to the snowcapped Alborz, which includes Mount Damavand. The name is Avestan and is understood as "the gate of the giants" or "the valley of the giants". In the 10th-century Persian epic the Shahnameh it names a land of daevas and sorcerers that is difficult to conquer, and the epic also places the capital of the king Fereydun at Tamishe near Amol, in the land known as Tabarestan.

Human habitation in the area goes back at least 75,000 years. Caves at Belt and Hotu near Behshahr show people there about 9,000 years ago, and excavations at Gohar Tape in Rostamkola show that the area was urbanised more than 5,000 years ago. Before Iranian-speakers arrived, the native people were subsistence hunters and cattle herders. The Amard lived in the mountains bordering the Caspian, including the area of present-day Amol, and the Tapuri, a tribe among the Medes, are mentioned by Ptolemy and Arrian.

After the Umayyad Caliphate replaced the Sasanian Empire in the early seventh century, Tabaristan stayed independent of it. Zoroastrian houses such as the Bavand and the Karen fought an effective guerrilla war against the Umayyads. A short-lived Alid Shiite state collapsed before the Ziyarid princes took over. Later local dynasties fell into three groups: families of pre-Islamic origin, the Alid sayyids, and families of secondary importance.

After the Safavid period the Qajar leader Agha Mohammad Khan campaigned south from Mazandaran and had incorporated it into his realm by 1782. On 21 March 1782 he proclaimed Sari his imperial capital. Local wars in the following years led Fath Ali Shah to move the capital from Sari to Tehran.

Mazandaran is one of the 31 provinces of Iran, with its capital at Sari, and covers 24,842 square kilometres. The population is overwhelmingly Mazandarani, with minorities that include Gilaks, Azerbaijanis, Kurds and Georgians. Rice is present in almost every meal, and the coast is rich in seafood. The Trans-Iranian Railway, built between 1927 and 1938 under Reza Shah, links Tehran to the Caspian Sea. The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was concluded in 1971 in the city of Ramsar in the province.
mbabane: Mbabane lies on the Mbabane River and its tributary the Polinjane River in the Mdzimba Mountains, at an average elevation of 1,243 metres. It is in the Hhohho Region, of which it is also the capital. Because of its altitude it has a moderate subtropical highland climate: snow is rare, having fallen only three times since 1900, and the city averages only four days of frost a year. Most of the rain falls in summer. The city takes its name from a chief, Mbabane Kunene, who lived in the area when British settlers arrived.

The town stands at the spot where the route from the Transvaal to Mozambique crossed the Mbabane River. It grew after the administrative centre of the country was moved from Bremersdorp, now called Manzini, in January 1902, and Great Britain declared it the capital of the new Protectorate of Swaziland that year. At that time it consisted of a few shops, churches and schools founded by white settlers, and Swazi Africans were not allowed to live in the town but had to reside in nearby rural districts. By the 1930s it had electricity, running water, a telephone connection and a hospital.

Before World War II most Swazis lived in rural districts and worked outside the country, so there was little growth in the town. After the war, the creation of trade schools in the city, the arrival of the Goba railway connecting Maputo to the mines in South Africa and Lesotho, and foreign investment, particularly in the sugar industry, contributed to its growth. In the years following independence government buildings were built in Mbabane, among them the British Consulate.

Mbabane is the most populous city of Eswatini, previously called Swaziland, with an estimated population of 94,874 in 2010. It is one of the two capitals, the executive capital, alongside Lobamba. The main language is siSwati, and English is widely spoken. Tin and iron were mined nearby, and the city is a commercial and financial hub for the surrounding region and a centre of the country's tourism. It is home to Waterford-Kamhlaba United World College of Southern Africa and one of the three campuses of the University of Eswatini.
mbanza-kongo: Mbanza Kongo lies close to Angola's border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on top of a flat-topped mountain sometimes called Mongo a Kaila, the mountain of division, because recent legends hold that the king created the clans of the kingdom there and sent them out. The Luezi River runs in the valley to the south. The city stood at a junction of major trade routes, and the Portuguese who first reached it in 1491 travelled ten days to get there from the mouth of the Congo River.

The city, formerly called Nkumba a Ngudi, Mongo wa Kaila and Kongo dia Ngunga, was founded by the first manikongo, Lukeni. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo from before the Portuguese arrived in 1483 until the kingdom's abolition in 1915, apart from a period of abandonment during the civil wars of the seventeenth century. When the Portuguese came it was already a large town, perhaps the largest in sub-equatorial Africa, and a Portuguese ambassador's letter to Lisbon compared the area within its inner walls with the town of Évora. The earliest documented kings called it the city of Congo; the name São Salvador first appears in the letters of Álvaro I of Kongo, who reigned from 1568 to 1587.

By the 1550s a community of Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries lived there, and they plotted with others to overthrow the manikongo Diogo I Nkumbi a Mpudi. In 1568 Jagas invaded and sacked the city, driving out Álvaro I, who regained it with Portuguese military help but had to yield Luanda, source of the nzimbu currency. Under Afonso II stone buildings, including a palace and churches, were added. An ecclesiastical statement of the 1620s reporting 4,500 baptisms is consistent with a population of around 130,000 in the city and its parish, of whom perhaps 30,000 to 45,000 lived in the city on the mountain. It had some twelve churches and a two-storey royal palace.

Several sackings during the civil wars that followed the Battle of Mbwila in 1665 ended with its abandonment in 1678. Followers of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita reoccupied it in 1705, and King Pedro IV of Kongo restored it as capital in 1709. It was never depopulated again.

Mbanza Kongo is the capital of Zaire Province in north-western Angola. Its ruins of the Cathedral of the Holy Saviour of Congo, said to date from 1491, are claimed by many Angolans as the oldest church in sub-Saharan Africa. Other sites include the Jalankuwo, the manikongo's judgement tree, and the sunguilu, where tradition says the king's body was washed before burial. The Royal Museum holds artefacts of the old kingdom. The city was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.
mbarara: Mbarara is a city in the Western Region of Uganda, about 270 km by road south-west of Kampala, at an average elevation of about 1,147 metres. It is a transport hub on the road west from Masaka to Kabale, near Lake Mburo National Park. The name comes from a colonial mispronunciation of Emburara, a tall grass that once covered the whole area. The climate is tropical savanna, with the most rainy days in October and the fewest in July.

The census of 2002 put the population of the town at 69,400, and the census of August 2014 at 195,013. From about 2000 modern buildings, including malls, hotels and new hospitals, went up, and the town became the main commercial centre of most of the south-western districts of Uganda and the site of the district headquarters. Mbarara hosted the annual general meeting of the Uganda Local Governments Association in 2004. The cabinet granted it city status in May 2019, which began on 1 July 2020, and the city is divided into six divisions.

Mbarara University of Science and Technology was founded in 1989, and the city also has the regional referral hospital, which is also the teaching hospital of the university's school of medicine, and several other universities and schools. Its water has come from the River Rwizi, which cannot meet the needs of a growing population, and plans were made to draw water from the Kagera River. A northern bypass of 14 kilometres takes long-distance trucks bound for Rwanda, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo off the city streets.
mccarthyism: Anti-communist measures in the United States predated Senator Joseph McCarthy. The Smith Act of 1940 made it an offence to advocate overthrowing the government by force. The House Committee on Un-American Activities, formed in 1938 and first known as the Dies Committee, turned to communism early, and its investigation of the espionage charges against Alger Hiss in 1948 convinced many of the usefulness of congressional committees. Truman's Executive Order 9835 of 21 March 1947 required loyalty screening of federal employees, probably in part a response to the Republican sweep of the 1946 elections.

McCarthy's own part began publicly on 9 February 1950, when he told a Republican women's club in Wheeling, West Virginia, that he held a list of known communists working in the State Department. The speech brought a flood of press attention.

Loyalty review boards and committees operated in federal, state and local governments and in private agencies. Between 1949 and 1954 Congress carried out 109 investigations through HUAC, the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee and the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. After Eisenhower took office in 1953 he strengthened the loyalty programme and narrowed the avenues of appeal. In 1954 J. Robert Oppenheimer lost his security clearance after a four-week hearing.

On 25 November 1947 the heads of the major film studios issued the Waldorf Statement, announcing the dismissal of the Hollywood Ten and marking the start of the Hollywood blacklist, which employers never publicly admitted. By 1952 several states had banned communists from public employment and required loyalty oaths. The number imprisoned is in the hundreds, and some ten or twelve thousand lost their jobs. Suspected homosexuality was also a common ground for targeting, and over 5,000 federal workers were fired in what many call the lavender scare.

Support came from the American Legion, militantly anti-communist women's groups and a wider coalition opposed to internationalism and New Deal welfare programmes. Critics included Truman, who in vetoing the McCarran Internal Security Act of 1950 wrote that in a free country men are punished for crimes, never for opinions. On 2 December 1954 the Senate voted 67 to 22 to condemn McCarthy. John Henry Faulk, dismissed by CBS Radio after being marked unfit by the private firm AWARE, won his suit against it in 1962.

Under Chief Justice Earl Warren the Supreme Court issued rulings that helped end the era. Declassified Soviet archives and the Venona decryptions later showed substantial Soviet espionage in the 1940s and that Moscow funded and influenced the Communist Party USA. Some historians, including Ellen Schrecker, hold that Hooverism, after FBI head J. Edgar Hoover, describes the phenomenon better than McCarthyism.
measles: Measles is a vaccine-preventable infectious disease caused by the measles virus, an RNA virus closely related to rinderpest, which affects cattle, and to canine distemper. Symptoms usually appear 10 to 12 days after exposure and last 7 to 10 days. They begin with fever, often above 40 °C (104 °F), cough, a runny nose and inflamed eyes, followed by a rash that starts on the face and spreads to the rest of the body.

The disease spreads through the air in the coughs and sneezes of infected people. Common complications include diarrhoea in 8 per cent of cases, middle ear infection in 7 per cent and pneumonia in 6 per cent, in part because measles weakens the immune system. Immunity is lifelong once acquired, through vaccination or after recovery.

Measles is of zoonotic origin: it evolved from rinderpest. Genomic analysis indicates that it arose as a human disease between 900 and 2,400 years ago. The Antonine Plague of 165 to 180 CE has been suggested as measles, but its cause is unknown and smallpox is thought more likely.

The first systematic description of measles as distinct from smallpox and chickenpox is credited to the Persian physician Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (860 to 932), who wrote The Book of Smallpox and Measles. Between 1100 and 1200 CE the virus is thought to have diverged completely from rinderpest. This fits the observation that measles needs a susceptible population of over 500,000 to sustain an epidemic, a size reached in historic times with the growth of medieval European cities.

Before vaccination, measles was endemic in every part of the world. In 1954 John Enders and Thomas C. Peebles isolated the virus from a 13-year-old boy in the United States, David Edmonston. Enders grew the Edmonston strain in human kidney tissue, then in amniotic membrane and finally in chick embryo culture, producing over three years a virus that gave immunity without causing disease, a process called attenuation.

At Merck, Maurice Hilleman attenuated the strain further, and the first successful measles vaccine became widely available in the United States in 1963. Measles vaccine was later combined with those for mumps and rubella as the MMR vaccine, licensed in the United States in 1971.
meaux: Meaux is a commune on the river Marne in the Seine-et-Marne department of Île-de-France, about 41 kilometres east-northeast of the centre of Paris. Its inhabitants are called Meldois. Both names come from the Meldi, the Latin name of the Gaulish tribe that occupied this part of the Marne valley.

The historic buildings stand mainly in the old city inside its old defensive walls, of which a segment from the Gallo-Roman period survives. A meander of the Marne divides the old city into the Cathedral Quarter and the Market Quarter. The Cathedral Quarter holds Meaux Cathedral, the episcopal palace and its gardens, which outline the shape of a bishop's mitre, and the archaeological remains of the sanctuary of La Bauve.

The Siege of Meaux took place from October 1421 to May 1422 during the Hundred Years' War, when the English under Henry V besieged the town. Its defence was led by the Bastard of Vaurus, who was known for his savagery. Mining and bombardment brought down the walls, and it is estimated that one sixteenth of the besiegers died of dysentery and smallpox. The town surrendered on 9 March 1422 and the garrison the next day.

The house of Etienne Mangin at 73 Rue du Marché is described on a plaque as the site of the first Reformed Church of France. Fourteen members of the congregation were burned there on 8 October 1546 by decree of the Parliament in Paris. Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet was bishop of Meaux from 1681 to 1704 and is called the eagle of Meaux. Philippe de Vitry, composer and author of the Ars Nova Notandi treatise, was bishop from 1351. In the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914 the German advance was halted at the gates of Meaux.

Meaux is a subprefecture of Seine-et-Marne. It is known for Brie de Meaux, a variety of Brie cheese, and for Meaux mustard, whose recipe has been a label owned by the Pommery company since the 18th century. Its museums include the Musée Bossuet in the episcopal palace and the Musée de la Grande Guerre du pays de Meaux, which stands beside the American monument La Liberté éplorée, erected in 1932.
mecca: Mecca, officially Makkah al-Mukarramah, lies in the Hejaz region of western Arabia, about 70 kilometres inland from Jeddah, in a narrow valley 277 metres above sea level. The city centres on the Masjid al-Haram, the Great Mosque, which contains the Kaaba. Muslims believe the Kaaba was built by Abraham and Ishmael. It is the direction of prayer (qibla) for all Muslims. The mosque is also the site of the Zamzam Well and of two rites of the Hajj and the Umrah, the circumambulation of the Kaaba (tawaf) and the walk between Safa and Marwa.

The early history of Mecca is poorly documented. The city lies in the interior of western Arabia, where few textual or archaeological sources survive, in contrast to Yemen and the Syro-Palestinian frontier. One study, by Majied Robinson, based on early Islamic genealogical records, estimates the population at the time of Muhammad at about 550, while Muslim scholars using traditional sources may place it as high as 10,000. One proposed etymology links the name to an Old South Arabian root meaning temple.

Muslim rulers from in and around the region long tried to control the city. The first printing press came to Mecca in 1885 with the Ottoman governor Osman Nuri Pasha. The city was last conquered in 1925, in the Saudi conquest of the Hejaz by Ibn Saud and his allies. Non-Muslims are forbidden to enter. The first recorded outsider to do so was Ludovico di Varthema of Bologna in 1503; Guru Nanak is said to have visited in December 1518, and Richard Francis Burton entered in 1853 disguised as a Qadiriyya Sufi from Afghanistan.

Mecca is the capital of Mecca Province in Saudi Arabia, and its metropolitan population was 2.4 million in 2022. Pilgrims on the Hajj, observed in the twelfth Hijri month of Dhū al-Ḥijjah as an obligation on Muslims once in their lives, more than triple that number each year. Mecca's economy depends heavily on pilgrimage. In the 20th century it expanded greatly, and several historical structures, among them the Ajyad Fortress, were demolished, in part for the enlargement of the Masjid al-Haram.
mecklenburg-vorpommern: The state covers 23,300 km2, the sixth largest German state by area. Its Baltic coastline of about 2,000 km has peninsulas, lagoons and islands, among them Germany's two biggest, Rügen and Usedom. In the south lies the Mecklenburg Lake District, where Lake Müritz is the largest lake in Germany. The name Vorpommern comes from West Slavic po more, land at the sea, with the German prefix vor- meaning the nearer part of Pomerania.

Human settlement began after the Ice Age, about 10,000 BCE. Germanic peoples recorded there about two thousand years ago mostly left during the Migration Period, and from the sixth century Polabian Slavs settled the area: the Obotrites in Mecklenburg, the Veleti and Rani in Pomerania. Vikings and Slavs set up trading posts along the coast, such as Reric, Ralswiek and Menzlin. In the late 12th century Henry the Lion, Duke of the Saxons, conquered the Obotrites and Christianized them, and German settlers followed in the Ostsiedlung. Mecklenburg became a duchy of the Holy Roman Empire in 1348 and its two grand duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz were created in 1815.

The Duchy of Pomerania was a vassal state of Poland from 1121 to 1138, and its dukes were later vassals of Saxony, the Holy Roman Empire and Denmark before staying with the Empire from 1227. Western Pomerania was under Swedish rule from the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 until 1815 and then became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania, remaining so until 1945.

The Soviet military administration created the Province of Mecklenburg and West Pomerania on 9 July 1945, by order of Marshal Georgy Zhukov. Expellees from the former eastern territories of Germany raised the population by 40%, and in 1949 they made up 43.3% of it. The state's name was shortened to Land Mecklenburg in 1947, and it became a constituent state of the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of Rostock, Schwerin and Neubrandenburg. At reunification in 1990 the state was re-established along its postwar boundaries under the name Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

Schwerin is the state capital, and Rostock, with about 205,000 inhabitants, is the largest city. The University of Rostock, founded in 1419, and the University of Greifswald, founded in 1456, are among the oldest in Europe. The old Hanseatic towns of Stralsund and Wismar are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and red Brick Gothic churches and houses are a feature of many towns.
medea: Médéa, in Arabic al-Madiya, is the capital of Médéa Province. The hills around it are covered with vineyards, orchards and farms that yield abundant grain. The town has a French character, with a rectangular plan, red tile-roofed buildings and public gardens. Its chief products have been wines, irrigation equipment and handicrafts.

The name goes back to a Roman city called ad Medix or Media, Latin for halfway. It stood equidistant from two rest houses on the road linking Caesarea, now Cherchell, to the colony of Auzia in Mauretania Caesariensis.

In Roman times a settlement called Lamdia stood at Médéa and was the seat of a Christian bishopric of Mauretania Caesariensis. Only one bishop is known, the Donatist Felix, who attended the Conference of Carthage in 411; the town then had no Catholic bishop. Lamdia survives as a titular bishopric. After the defeat of the Berbers in the 11th century, Arab tribes of Hilal and Sulaym descent were settled in the region and mixed with the local Berbers, Arabicizing them.

The Beylik of Titteri was established in 1548, with Médéa as its capital and a bey, a deputy of the Dey of Algiers, in residence. The last bey, Mostefa Boumezrag, ran it from 1819 to 1830, when the French arrived. After the Treaty of Tafna in 1837 Médéa became one of the capitals of the part of Algeria ruled by Abdelkader El Djezairi, but the French occupied it when they took possession of the whole country. Until 1962 it was a garrison town of the French army.

In the nearby village of Tibhirine stands the Abbey of Our Lady of Atlas, home from 1935 to 1996 to a Trappist community. Most of its monks were abducted by the Armed Islamic Group on 27 March 1997; the group announced their deaths two months later. The monastery buildings were afterwards given to the Chemin Neuf Community, a Catholic community from Lyon.
medellin: Medellín lies in the Aburrá Valley, a central region of the Andes in northwestern South America, at an elevation of about 1,500 m. The Medellín River, also called the Porce, flows northward through the valley. Because of its altitude the climate is milder than at other places at the same latitude, with an average temperature of 22 °C that varies little through the year, and the city is known as the City of the Eternal Spring.

In August 1541 Marshal Jorge Robledo saw what he took to be a valley, and Jerónimo Luis Tejelo reached the plain of the Aburrá Valley on the night of 23 August. The Spaniards called it the Valley of Saint Bartholomew, but the name soon gave way to the native name Aburrá, Painters, for the textile decorations of the local rulers. The valley lay between the gold mines northeast of Antioquia and the first provincial capital, Santa Fe de Antioquia, and supplied food to the mines.

In 1616 Francisco de Herrera Campuzano set up a small indigenous village, San Lorenzo de Aburrá, in what is now El Poblado. On 2 November 1675 the queen consort Mariana of Austria founded the Town of Our Lady of Candelaria of Medellín in the Aná region, now the city centre. In 1826 Gran Colombia's National Congress named the city capital of the Department of Antioquia. During the 19th century it was a commercial centre, first exporting gold, then coffee.

In the first half of the 20th century the population grew sixfold, from 59,815 in 1905 to 358,189 in 1951. The Coltejer textile company was founded in 1907 by Alejandro Echavarría. After the murder of the presidential candidate Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948, political violence spread in the countryside, farmers fled to the cities and the valley slopes filled with slums. The city later built the Medellín Metro.

Medellín is the capital of Antioquia and the second-largest city in Colombia after Bogotá, with 2,427,129 people at the 2018 census. The University of Antioquia, the National University of Colombia's Medellín branch and the Pontifical Bolivarian University have long been its academic centres. Little colonial architecture remains; the Candelaria Church and the Church of the Veracruz survive, much altered. The Museum of Antioquia holds works of Fernando Botero.
media-atropatene: Atropatene, also called Atropatia or Atropatian Media, was an ancient Iranian kingdom, established about 323 BCE by the Persian satrap Atropates and centred mostly on the region of Azerbaijan in north-western Iran. Its Old Persian name, Ātṛpātakāna, is the direct ancestor of the name of the historic Azerbaijan region. According to Strabo, Media was divided into two parts: Greater Media, with Ecbatana as its metropolis, and Atropatian Media, which took its name from the commander Atropates, who prevented this part from becoming subject to the Macedonians. Medieval Arab geographers instead derived the name from Adorbador, a priest whose name means guardian of the fire. Its main hub was Ganzak, near Lake Urmia, which presumably served as the capital of Atropates and his successors.

Atropates fought alongside the Achaemenid army at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE, then declared loyalty to Alexander the Great, who appointed him governor of Media in 328 to 327 BCE. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the satrapy was divided: Media Magna went to Peithon, one of Alexander's bodyguards, and the smaller northern region became Media Atropatene under Atropates, who had by then become father-in-law of the regent Perdiccas. It became an independent kingdom. In 223 BCE Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire attacked it and won, and its king Artabazanes accepted Seleucid ascendancy while keeping internal independence.

Later, Atropatene allied with Parthia against Rome. In 36 BCE the Roman general Antony besieged the city of Fraaspa and withdrew after a long blockade, losing about thirty-five thousand soldiers. The dynasty Atropates founded ruled for several centuries, first independently and then as vassals of the Arsacids, until it was supplanted by a line of the Arsacids in the early 1st century CE. After Pharasmanes II of Iberia devastated the region in 134 to 135 CE, the people of Atropatene allied themselves with the Persian Sasanian prince Ardashir I against the Parthian Artabanus IV. In 226 the region submitted with little resistance to Ardashir I and became a province governed by a marzban.

Atropatene was the only Iranian region to remain under Zoroastrian authority from the Achaemenids to the Arab conquest without interruption, apart from Alexander's brief rule. Under the Atropatids the region gained a dominant place in Zoroastrianism, which continued into the Sasanian period, and it served as a stronghold of Iranian culture. Local claims also placed the birthplace of Zoroaster in Atropatene rather than in the east.
medina: Medina lies in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia. Its built-up area is surrounded by the Hejaz Mountains, empty valleys, agricultural land and old dormant volcanoes. Before Islam it was called Yathrib, a name attested in an inscription of the Babylonian king Nabonidus of the 6th century BCE and used in the Qur'an. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad later renamed it Taybah or Tabah, and it came to be called Madinat an-Nabi, "City of the Prophet", and al-Madinah al-Munawwarah, "the Enlightened City", shortened to Madinah.

The city has been inhabited for about 1,500 years before the Hijrah, or about the 9th century BCE. By the fourth century Arab tribes were encroaching from Yemen, and around the time of Muhammad three prominent Jewish tribes lived there: the Banu Qaynuqa, the Banu Qurayza and the Banu Nadir.

Toward the end of the 5th century the Jewish rulers lost control of the city to the two Arab tribes, the 'Aws and Khazraj. In 622 Muhammad and an estimated 70 Meccan Muhajirun left Mecca over a few months for sanctuary in Yathrib. The longstanding enmity between the 'Aws and Khazraj was dampened as many of them and some local Jews embraced Islam, and Muhammad was agreed on as leader of the city. It served as the base of the early Muslim community, and a larger part of the Qur'an was revealed in Medina than in Mecca.

Later the city passed to the Umayyads, whose governors dug the spring called 'Ayn az-Zarqa'a and built irrigation ducts and dams, leading to an agricultural boom. It was held by the Mamluks of Egypt from 1254 to 1517 and then by the Ottomans, after Selim I conquered Mamluk Egypt.

In 1532 Suleiman built a fortress around it, and the Ottoman sultans repeatedly redesigned the Prophet's Mosque. The Sharif of Mecca, Husayn ibn Ali, attacked Medina on 6 June 1916, during the First World War, and the siege that followed brought food shortages, disease and mass emigration. The governor Fakhri Pasha held out until his own men arrested him and the Sharifate took the city on 10 January 1919. The Saudi forces conquered it on 5 December 1925.

Medina is the second holiest city in Islam after Mecca and the capital of Medina Province, with 1,477,023 inhabitants. Al-Masjid al-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque, was built by Muhammad in 622 and is the burial site of the prophet. The Quba Mosque is the oldest in Islam. The city also holds Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the Baqi' cemetery, Mount Uhud, site of the Battle of Uhud, and the King Fahd Glorious Qur'an Printing Complex.
medina-del-campo: Medina del Campo lies on the banks of the Zapardiel river, in the central part of the Douro basin. Initially a Berber settlement, it was repopulated after 1085. It was founded on the hill called La Mota in the 11th century, on the site of the castle, and in the Middle Ages that hill was the town centre. The hill holds remains of a stronghold, a medieval village and a Celtic walled settlement of the 4th century BCE. The walls date from the 11th century and were enlarged three times as the population grew.

By the 12th century the walled town was a major population centre of the Kingdom of Castile and drew large trading operations. Its free fairs flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries and supported banking and the trade in wool, textiles and books. In the 16th century the fair became the most important of the great Castilian fairs, with Villalón and Medina de Rioseco, and drew merchants chiefly Castilian, Portuguese, Italian and Flemish.

In 1489 the Treaty of Medina del Campo united Spain and England in a trade agreement meant to last 96 years, with reduced tariffs, the recognition of France as a common enemy and the marriage of Catherine of Aragon to Prince Arthur. During the Revolt of the Comuneros the town housed the royal artillery, and a royalist attempt to seize the guns ended in the burning of the town. Its Jewish community ended with the expulsion of 1492. From the 17th to the 19th century the town declined, and it grew again after the first railway train arrived on 3 September 1860.

The Castle of La Mota, built between the 12th and 15th centuries, served as a royal prison, and Cesare Borgia was among its prisoners. The Royal Palace, begun in the 14th century, is where Isabel la Católica, Queen of Castile, made her will and died on 26 November 1504. The Hospital of Simón Ruiz and the Palacio de Dueñas date from the 16th century, built by merchant bankers who prospered by the fair, and a Museum of the Fairs records the market.
medinaceli: Medinaceli stands on a hilltop at about 1210 metres above sea level, at the confluence of the rivers Jalón and Arbujuelo, and looks over the Jalón valley. The municipality includes other villages, among them Torralba del Moral, and two motorways, the A-15 and the A-2, meet within its bounds. Its name comes from the Arabic madinat Salim, City of Salim, which goes back to the Banu Salim, a lineage of the Berber Masmuda.

Before the Islamic period the site was a Celtiberian town known as Occilis or Okilis. Under Islamic rule it held the status of a madina, a city. The Berber Banu Salim settled in the area, and although they lost favour and were routed in 920, the town kept its strategic importance for the Cordobese authorities. It served as a powerbase for military operations in the north, including the campaign against the Christian settlements of the upper Duero and the suppression of the revolt of the Banu Tujib. In 946 Medinaceli became the head of the Middle March, the frontier district in this region.

The town has a Roman arch built between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE, the only three-gated Roman arch in Spain, which is used as a symbol of Spain's historic sites across the country. The castle was the residence of the Dukes of Medinaceli until the Ducal Palace took over that purpose. Other buildings include the Colegiata de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, whose abbots disputed with the bishops of Sigüenza to defend the city's rights, and the 16th-century Convent of Saint Elizabeth beside the church of San Martín. The beaterio of San Román is in ruins and may once have been a synagogue. A stone gate is one of the few remains of the old city walls dating from the Islamic period.
mediterranean: The Mediterranean Sea is an intercontinental sea between Europe, Asia and Africa, almost completely enclosed by land. It connects to the Atlantic Ocean by the Strait of Gibraltar, only 14 km wide, to the Black Sea by the Bosporus, and to the Red Sea by the Suez Canal. It covers about 2,500,000 km2 and has fifteen marginal seas, among them the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Marmara. Its average depth is 1,500 m, and the deepest point, 5,109 m, lies in the Calypso Deep in the Ionian Sea. The Nile is the longest river to end in it. Sicily and Sardinia are its two largest islands.

Geological evidence indicates that around 5.9 million years ago the sea was cut off from the Atlantic and was partly or completely dried up over some 600,000 years, in the Messinian salinity crisis. It was refilled about 5.3 million years ago by the Zanclean flood, in less than two years according to scientists' estimates.

The Levant, in the eastern Mediterranean, was among the first regions in the world with permanent human habitation, as early as 12,000 BCE. The earliest advanced civilisations on the sea were the Egyptians and the Minoans, who traded extensively with each other. Around 1200 BCE the Bronze Age Collapse destroyed many cities and trade routes in the east. The Greek city-states and the Phoenicians later colonised its coastlines extensively. Darius I of Persia, who conquered Egypt, built a canal linking the Red Sea to the Nile and so to the Mediterranean, wide enough for two triremes to pass and needing four days to traverse.

After the Punic Wars of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE the Roman Republic defeated the Carthaginians and became the preeminent power in the western Mediterranean. Once Augustus founded the Roman Empire, the Romans called it Mare Nostrum, Our Sea. For the next 400 years the empire controlled the sea and virtually all its coasts from Gibraltar to the Levant, which earned it the nickname Roman Lake. Rome is the only state to have ever controlled all of its coasts.

The Romans also called the sea Mare Magnum and Mare Internum. The name Mare Mediterraneum, meaning in the middle of land, is first attested in the 6th century in the work of Isidore of Seville. Arabic writers called it the Sea of the Romans, and the Ancient Egyptians called it Wadj-wr, great green. The countries on its shores include Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt and Morocco, and Cyprus and Malta are island countries within it. Its mild winters and warm summers give their name to the Mediterranean climate type.
medjerda: The Medjerda, the classical Bagradas, is also known as the Wadi Majardah or Mejerda. It originates in the Tell Atlas, part of the Atlas Mountains, in north-eastern Algeria, then flows east into Tunisia and enters the Gulf of Utica of the Mediterranean. The river is dammed in several places and is a major supplier of water to the country's wheat crops. Its water has been used for irrigation and has served the towns and farms along its banks.
The Gulf of Utica was formed by the postglacial rise of the sea about 6,000 years ago. Over time, deposits from the river gradually filled up the northern part of the gulf.

The Medjerda has long been Tunisia's crucial waterway, supplying fresh water to its population centres and agriculture along its banks. As a strategic resource it was fought over and settled many times by the Carthaginians, Romans, Vandals, Byzantines, Arabs and Ottomans. Several major cities were founded on or near it, among them Utica, Carthage and eventually Tunis.

The sequence of changes in historical times has been inferred from ancient documents and archaeological evidence, with aerial and satellite photographs used to study how the landscape evolved over the past 3,000 years. The southern part of the gulf was filled up in late ancient times, and the sea withdrew gradually from the northern part during the Middle Ages and modern times. The ports of Utica and Ghar el-Melh, once called Rusucmona or Porto Farina, were eventually closed by the silting of their harbours. The Ghar el Melh lagoon is the last vestige of the old gulf.

With a length of about 450 km, the Medjerda is the longest river of Tunisia. After the last great flood, in 1973, it shifted its course once more, and it now flows through a canal originally dug to carry off flood overflow.
meenakshi-temple: Tamil texts imply that a temple existed in Madurai by the mid-6th century, and the town of Koodal, as Madurai was called, is described as a temple town from which every street radiated. The temple is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, Shiva temples praised in the Tevaram hymns composed by the Nayanars between the 6th and 11th centuries. Most surviving inscriptions are dated after the 12th century, so the early structures are known chiefly from the Pandya period of the 12th to 13th centuries.

After the death of Maravarman Kulasekhara I in 1310, his sons fought over the Pandya throne while the Khalji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate raided the south. Records say that Malik Kafur looted and destroyed Hindu temples, the Meenakshi temple among them, and carried gold and jewellery to Delhi in 1311. The Vijayanagara Empire took Madurai in 1378, and Kumara Kampana is said to have rebuilt the temple, fortified it with walls and restored the hidden idols.

The temple stands on the southern bank of the Vaigai River and is dedicated to Meenakshi, a form of Parvati, and her consort Sundareswarar, a form of Shiva. Meenakshi means fish-eyed in Tamil. According to the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, she appeared from a sacrificial fire as the daughter of King Malayadhwaja Pandya, ruled as his successor and took her true form when she met Shiva. Her shrine stands at the centre of the inner enclosure, to the right of Sundareswarar's, and pilgrims visit it first.

The complex covers 5.7 hectares inside concentric walled enclosures. It has 14 gopurams, the towers over its gateways, of which the tallest, the southern tower built in the 16th century, rises to 52 metres. The thousand-pillared hall holds 985 carved pillars, and the sacred tank is called the Golden Lotus Pond. The streets around the temple are named after months of the Tamil calendar, because processions began from the spots matching each month.

The temple has long been a centre of Tamil literature. The poet Kumaraguruparar wrote the Meenakshi Pillaitamil in praise of the goddess in the 17th century, and Shyama Shastri composed nine Telugu songs for her, the Navaratnamalika. Its yearly wedding festival, the Meenakshi thirukalyanam, lasts 15 days in the month of Chithirai and is the most attended of the temple's monthly festivals.

Dalits were barred from entering the temple until the early 20th century. On 8 July 1939 a group led by A. Vaidyanatha Iyer and Kakkan entered it, an event that preceded legislation of the Madras Presidency later that year.
