The Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of the Government of Tamil Nadu manages the temple, and the state's emblem is based on its west gopuram.
meersburg: Meersburg stands on the northern shore of Lake Constance in Baden-Württemberg. It is known for its medieval town, which is divided into a lower town, the Unterstadt, and an upper town, the Oberstadt. Two stairways and a steep street, the Steigstrasse, link them. Half-timbered houses survive, together with two medieval town gates that are the remains of the fortification. The vineyards on the northern bank of the lake are well known in Germany, and the rosé Weissherbst is a local specialty.

The name means castle on the sea, and refers to a castle that, according to a tradition recorded in 1548, was built here in 630 by the Merovingian king Dagobert I. The Old Castle is held to be one of the oldest surviving castles in Germany. The town gained the status of a free city in 1299, although it nominally remained under the Bishop of Constance. In 1803 it was annexed to the Electorate of Baden. After World War II it lay in the French military occupation area of Germany.
The New Castle was built in the 18th century as the residence of the bishop of Constance. After the Secularization of 1803 it was put to various uses, and it is now a museum.

The poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff lived her last years at the Old Castle, from 1841 to 1848, and also owned the small vine-covered villa known as the Fürstenhäusle. Franz Anton Mesmer, the 18th-century physician from whose name the verb to mesmerize derives, died in Meersburg in 1815 and is buried by the old wall of the graveyard. Other residents were the Austro-Hungarian novelist Fritz Mauthner, who died there in 1923, and the antiquary Joseph Maria Christoph von Lassberg, who lived at the Old Castle from 1838.
meerut: Meerut lies in the Doab, the fertile land between the Ganges and the Yamuna, and is the administrative headquarters of the Meerut district, which covers 2,522 square kilometres, more than Delhi. The climate is monsoon-influenced and humid subtropical, with very hot summers.

The name is believed to have evolved from Mayarashtra, the capital of a mythological kingdom ruled by Mayasura, an architect and the father of Mandodari, wife of Ravana. Another tradition says King Yudhishthira granted the land to Mayasura in recognition of his skill as a builder.

Excavations of 1950 to 1952 at Vidura-ka-Tila, a group of mounds about 37 kilometres north-east of the city, concluded that the district holds the remains of Hastinapur, the capital of the Kauravas and Pandavas of the Mahabharata. In the eleventh century Har Dat, the Dor Raja of Bulandshahr, built a fort south-west of the city, and Mahmud of Ghazni defeated him in 1018. The local Hindu raja soon regained the city, and Qutb-ud-din Aybak captured it in 1193.

In 1803 Daulat Rao Scindia of the Marathas ceded the territory to the British East India Company. Its cantonment, near Delhi in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, became one of the largest in India, and Meerut was made the district headquarters in 1818. The rebellion of 1857 began in the Kali Paltan in the cantonment. The railway from Delhi was built in 1864. Meerut was one of the first places in northern India where publishing was established, and a major centre of commercial publishing in the 1860s and 1870s.

Meerut is known for sports goods, musical instruments, handloom work and its scissors, and is an education centre of western Uttar Pradesh. The Nauchandi Mela, a fair that began in 1672, is held each year two weeks after Holi. Nearby Hastinapur holds Jain temples and is regarded by Jains as one of their holiest places.
megali-idea: The expression first appeared in the debates between Prime Minister Ioannis Kolettis and King Otto that preceded the constitution of 1844, but the hope behind it was older. Greeks had long looked for liberation from Ottoman rule and a restoration of the Byzantine Empire; folklore told that the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, had been turned to marble and lay beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople awaiting the call to reconquer the city. The state created in 1830 was designed by the Great Powers, and most ethnic Greeks still lived outside it, within the Ottoman Empire.

The new state was imagined as the Greece of Two Continents and Five Seas, reaching from the Ionian Sea to Anatolia and the Black Sea and from Thrace, Macedonia and Epirus to Crete and Cyprus. When the Danish prince Wilhelm Georg was elected king in 1863 he was styled King of the Hellenes rather than King of Greece, implying a king of all Greeks wherever they lived.

The Ionian Islands were acquired in 1864. In 1897, with violence growing in Crete, a Greek force of 1,500 men under Colonel Timoleon Vassos landed at Kolymbari on 1 February and proclaimed the island's union with Greece. Irregulars then raided Turkish outposts in Thessaly without orders, and the Ottoman Empire declared war. The Greek army fell back, an armistice was signed in May, and Greece lost small border territories and paid reparations; Crete became an autonomous state with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner.

Eleftherios Venizelos, a Cretan who became prime minister after the Goudi coup of 1909, was a major proponent of the idea, and under him Greek territory doubled in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13. Greece joined the Allies in 1917 and afterwards gained a protectorate over Smyrna and its hinterland, where a referendum was to follow five years of Greek administration, and a frontier in Thrace a few miles from the walls of Constantinople.

Turkish revolutionaries defeated the Greek army and expelled the Greeks from Anatolia. By the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece ceded Eastern Thrace, Imbros, Tenedos and Smyrna. During the conflict 151,892 Greeks had already fled Asia Minor; the treaty moved 1,104,216 Greeks from Turkey, while 380,000 Turks left Greece. The League of Nations arranged a loan of 150 million francs to help settle the refugees. In 1930 Venizelos paid an official visit to Turkey, where he proposed Mustafa Kemal for the Nobel Peace Prize. The Dodecanese were acquired after the Second World War, in 1947.
megasthenes: Little is known about Megasthenes as a person. He spent time at the court of Sibyrtius, satrap of Arachosia under Antigonus I and then Seleucus I. Arrian writes that Megasthenes lived with Sibyrtius and often spoke of visiting Sandracottus, the king of the Indians, that is Chandragupta Maurya. He served as ambassador of the Seleucid king Seleucus I Nicator at Chandragupta's court in Pataliputra, modern Patna.

The date of the journey is uncertain. Seleucus reigned from 305 to 281 BCE, which gives the loose range within which the mission might have begun. Scholars dispute when he visited India and how long he stayed: A. B. Bosworth argued for a date before Seleucus, while Stoneman and others argue for a date after the Mauryan-Seleucid settlement of about 303 BCE. He appears to have passed through the Punjab, since he gives a detailed account of its rivers, and then travelled to Pataliputra along the Yamuna and the Ganga. It is not certain which other parts of India he saw. Later Greek envoys are known: Deimachus went to Bindusara and Dionysius to Ashoka.
Megasthenes described India in his book Indica, the first written description of India by a person from the Western world. The work is lost and survives in part through quotations by later authors.

Ancient opinion was divided. Arrian was the only ancient writer to speak favourably of him, and Diodorus quotes him while omitting some parts. Eratosthenes accused him of falsehood, though he borrowed much of his content on India from him.

Strabo called him a liar for fabulous stories and wrote that no faith whatever could be placed in Deimachus and Megasthenes. Pliny the Elder criticised his description of the fabulous races of India and his account of Herakles and Dionysus. Modern scholars such as E. A. Schwanbeck and B. C. J. Timmer have found him a generally reliable source of Indian history. Truesdell Sparhawk Brown is more critical, noting that he saw only a small part of India and relied on others, but his work remained the principal source for later writers.
meghalaya: Meghalaya is one of the Seven Sister States of north-eastern India. It covers about 22,429 square kilometres and borders Bangladesh to the south and west and Assam to the north and east. The state is mountainous, with valleys and highland plateaus, and rests mainly on Archean rock that holds deposits of coal, limestone, uranium and sillimanite. Its name means the abode of clouds, from the Sanskrit megha and alaya, and was given by Shiba P. Chatterjee, a geography professor at the University of Calcutta.

The southern Khasi Hills record an average of 12,000 mm of rain a year, and about 70 per cent of the state is forested. Some of the forest survives as sacred groves, small pockets of ancient forest kept by communities for centuries for religious reasons and reserved for ritual. British authorities nicknamed the region the Scotland of the East.

People have lived in Meghalaya since the Neolithic period. Neolithic sites have been found in the high Khasi Hills and the Garo Hills, where shifting cultivation known as jhum is still practised. The limited archaeology suggests ancient settlement, and Ian Glover has proposed that north-eastern India was the most favourable single area for the origin of domesticated rice. Folk tradition ties jhum to rice: one legend has the god of wind shake seeds from a celestial tree, which a bird sowed.

Khasis, Jaintias and Garos each kept traditional political institutions that, according to the account, have existed for hundreds of years and worked at village, clan and state level. Meghalaya itself was formed on 21 January 1972 by carving the united Khasi Hills and Jaintia Hills and the Garo Hills out of Assam. Its Autonomous District Councils exist under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which was added on the recommendation of a subcommittee led by Gopinath Bordoloi.

Shillong is the capital. The Khasis are the largest group in the population, followed by the Garos and the Jaintias, who follow a matrilineal system in which descent and inheritance pass through women, and the youngest daughter inherits the property and cares for aged parents. About 75 per cent of people are Christian. Meghalaya has 12 districts and a Legislative Assembly of 60 members.

Living root bridges, made by training the aerial roots of the rubber tree Ficus elastica, are found in the south, built by both Khasis and Jaintias. In July 2018 the International Commission on Stratigraphy named the Meghalayan age, the latest stage of the Holocene, after a stalagmite in Mawmluh cave that records a climate event around 2250 BCE.
mehmed-ii: Mehmed II was born on 30 March 1432 in Edirne, then the Ottoman capital, the son of Sultan Murad II and Hüma Hatun, a slave of uncertain origin. At eleven he was sent to Amasya with two advisers to govern and gain experience, as Ottoman princes did, and Murad sent teachers to instruct him. Akshamsaddin stressed to him the duty of overthrowing the Byzantine Empire by taking Constantinople. He was sultan from August 1444 to September 1446 and again from February 1451.

After his return in 1451 Mehmed strengthened the navy and built the fortress of Rumelihisarı on the European shore of the Bosphorus, which gave him control of the strait. When a Venetian vessel ignored the signals to stop, it was sunk, the surviving sailors were beheaded and its captain impaled. He took Constantinople in 1453, aged 21, and claimed the title caesar of Rome, which the Patriarchate of Constantinople soon recognised but most European monarchs rejected. He ordered Hagia Sophia protected and turned it into a mosque.

His later campaigns brought Serbia under Ottoman rule by 1459 or 1460, the Morea in 1460, Trebizond in 1461 and Bosnia in 1463. The Ottoman-Venetian War lasted from 1463 to 1479. In 1475 an Ottoman army was defeated by Stephen the Great at the Battle of Vaslui. Mehmed did not subdue Albania until 1478, ten years after Skanderbeg's death. At home he centralised government, drawing officials largely from the devşirme, and legalised fratricide, so that a sultan who took the throne might execute his brothers. He brought Italian artists and Greek scholars to his court, and wrote poetry under the name Avni.

Mehmed fell ill at Maltepe, near Istanbul, in 1481 and died on 3 May 1481 aged forty-nine. He was buried near the Fatih Mosque complex. The historian Colin Heywood finds substantial circumstantial evidence that he was poisoned, possibly at the behest of his son and successor Bayezid. News of his death was greeted with rejoicing in Europe. He is regarded as a hero in modern Turkey, and Istanbul's Fatih district and the Fatih Mosque bear his name.
mehmed-iii: Mehmed was born at Manisa Palace on 26 May 1566 and was the great-grandson of Suleiman I. His mother, Safiye, was an Albanian from the Dukagjin Highlands. When he heard of the birth, Suleiman named him Mehmed in honour of his own great-grandfather, Mehmed the Conqueror. Suleiman died in September 1566 during the Siege of Szigetvár, and in December 1574 Mehmed's father became Murad III. Mehmed spent most of his childhood and youth in Manisa, and his circumcision ceremony was held on 29 May 1582. Murad III died in January 1595, when Mehmed was 28.

Mehmed III was an idle ruler who left government to his mother. His first major problem was the rivalry between two viziers, Serdar Ferhad Pasha and Koca Sinan Pasha, which led to disturbances by janissaries. On 7 July 1595 he dismissed Ferhad Pasha as Grand Vizier for his failure in Wallachia and replaced him with Sinan. Safiye controlled appointments and dismissals, and her personal purse was three times that of the sultan. In 1600 Mehmed insisted she leave the palace, but after five weeks pressure from the court forced him to cancel her exile.

The Long Turkish War brought a defeat at Nikopol in 1599 by Wallachian forces under Michael the Brave. In 1600 Tiryaki Hasan Pasha captured Nagykanizsa after a 40-day siege. In Anatolia, Karayazıcı Abdülhalim, a former Ottoman official, captured Urfa in 1600 and declared himself sultan, beginning the Jelali revolts. In 1599 Elizabeth I of England sent gifts that included a jewel-studded clockwork organ and a ceremonial coach. England sought an alliance against the Spanish, but it was never concluded.

Safiye helped bring about the execution of Mehmed's son Mahmud in 1603, after she intercepted a message in which a religious seer predicted that Mehmed would die within six months and be succeeded by his son. Mehmed died on 22 December 1603, aged 37. One source gives the cause as distress at Mahmud's death, and another a plague or a stroke. He was buried in the Hagia Sophia. Safiye lost all her power and was exiled to the Old Palace by his successor, Ahmed I.
mehmed-iv: Mehmed IV was born at Topkapı Palace in Constantinople on 2 January 1642, the son of Sultan Ibrahim and Turhan Sultan, a concubine of Russian origin. Soon after his birth his parents quarrelled, and Ibrahim, enraged, flung the infant into a cistern; harem servants rescued him, but he kept a scar on his head for life. He came to the throne in 1648 at the age of six after his father was overthrown in a coup. His grandmother Kösem Sultan, the regent, was suspected of plotting to replace him with his half-brother Suleiman, and in September 1651 Mehmed signed her death warrant.

The early years brought palace intrigues, uprisings in Anatolia, the defeat of the Ottoman navy by the Venetians outside the Dardanelles and food riots. His mother then gave Köprülü Mehmed Pasha full executive powers as Grand Vizier, and he took office on 14 September 1656. The Köprülü era was an exceptionally stable period. Köprülü Mehmed and his son Fazıl Ahmed regained the Aegean islands from Venice, and Crete in the Cretan War of 1645–1669, and campaigned in Transylvania and Poland. When Mehmed accepted the vassalage of Petro Doroshenko, Ottoman rule extended into Podolia. Mehmed loved hunting from a young age, and it earned him the name Avcı, the Hunter. Contemporaries called him pious and gazi, a holy warrior.

The grand vizier Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa supported the Hungarian uprising of Imre Thököly in 1683 and besieged Vienna. On 12 September 1683 the Ottomans suffered a rout at the Battle of Vienna, in a flank attack by Polish cavalry under King John III Sobieski and the Imperial army. This began the Great Turkish War, in which the Holy League drove the Ottomans back toward the Balkans.

After the Second Battle of Mohács in 1687 the army mutinied. On 8 November 1687 it was decided to depose Mehmed and enthrone his brother Suleiman II. Mehmed was imprisoned in Topkapı Palace but allowed to leave it from time to time, and he died at Edirne Palace in 1693.
meiji-constitution: Before 1889 Japan had in practice no written constitution. The old ritsuryo system, whose last code, the Yoro Code of 752, was in theory still in force, had become an empty formality by the Heian period. The Charter Oath of 6 April 1868 called for deliberative assemblies without giving details. The conservative Meiji oligarchy favoured a gradual approach, while the Freedom and People's Rights Movement demanded an elected assembly and a constitution at once.

On 21 October 1881 Itō Hirobumi was appointed to chair a bureau studying constitutional government, and in 1882 he led a mission abroad. The United States Constitution was rejected as too liberal and the French and Spanish models as tending to despotism. The German Empire, above all Prussia, interested the mission most. The draft committee, advised by the German legal scholars Rudolf von Gneist and Lorenz von Stein, worked in secret from 1886 to 1888. Emperor Meiji promulgated the text on 11 February 1889, and it came into force on 29 November 1890, the day the first Imperial Diet convened.

The constitution had 76 articles in seven chapters, about 2,500 words. Sovereignty lay in the emperor through his divine ancestry. Article 1 spoke of a line of emperors unbroken for ages eternal, and Article 3 called the emperor sacred and inviolable. He commanded the army and navy, declared war and made treaties, and Ministers of State answered to him, not to the Diet.

The Diet had two houses: a House of Peers of imperial family members, hereditary peers and appointees, and an elected House of Representatives. Only men paying at least 15 yen in property taxes could vote, about 1.1 percent of the population. The Diet could initiate laws and had to approve the budget. Subjects had rights such as freedom of movement, religion and speech, but each was limited by law. The army and navy ministers had to be serving officers, which gave the military a veto over any cabinet.

The document set up the first parliamentary government in Asia. Its provisions were contradictory about whether the constitution or the emperor was supreme, and leaders and parties argued over whether it could serve authoritarian or liberal ends. Universal male suffrage came with the General Election Law of 1925. The constitution was never amended. After Japan's surrender the postwar constitution was enacted as an amendment under Article 73, to preserve legal continuity, and it took effect on 3 May 1947.
meiji-era: Prince Mutsuhito succeeded his father, Emperor Kōmei, on 3 February 1867 at the age of fourteen, as the 122nd emperor. The shogunate was under pressure to modernise, and a call arose for the restoration of governing power to the emperor. On 9 November 1867 the shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu offered his resignation, and the new government was formed on 3 January 1868. The fall of Edo in the summer of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and brought the Meiji era. Its first reform was the Charter Oath of 1868, which called among other things for a deliberative assembly and for all classes to unite in carrying out the affairs of state.

The leaders set out to catch up with the West through state-led industrialisation. The government built railways, began land reform and set up a Western-based education system, sending thousands of students abroad and hiring more than 3,000 foreign experts. The Iwakura Mission toured Europe and the United States in 1871. Land and tax laws of 1871 to 1873 legalised private ownership and replaced taxes in kind with cash. Military reform brought a small standing army, a large reserve and compulsory militia service for all men.

A new peerage, the Kazoku, with five ranks from prince to baron, was created for about five hundred court nobles, former daimyo and loyal samurai. Itagaki Taisuke led the Freedom and People's Rights Movement for representative government, and helped found the Liberal Party in 1881. In 1885 the essayist Fukuzawa Yukichi argued that Japan should orient itself on the civilised countries of the West.

Rapid change had opponents. Disaffected former samurai rebelled in the 1870s, the best known being Saigō Takamori in the Satsuma Rebellion, although other former samurai, such as Itō Hirobumi and Itagaki Taisuke, served the government. Fukuzawa's essay may also have laid intellectual foundations for later Japanese colonialism in the region.

The government promoted Japanese art abroad at world's fairs, beginning with Vienna in 1873. The years 1890 to 1910 are called the golden age of Japanese cloisonné enamel, and Shibata Zeshin renewed lacquerwork. The emperor promoted Western dress, which became common in public, while the kimono returned in bolder styles in the 1890s. The era ended on 30 July 1912, and the Taishō era followed.
meiji-restoration: In the Edo period Japan was ruled through a hierarchy of inherited rank, with the emperor and court at the top, then the shōgun and the daimyō, then the samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Since 1633 the shogunate had enforced a policy of national isolation, sakoku, with limited trade through the Dutch at Dejima. Famine and unrest in the 1830s and 1840s, and the failure of the Tenpō Reforms, exposed a deep divide between shogunate and daimyō. The arrival of the Perry Expedition and the unequal treaties that followed brought the shōgun's ability to protect Japanese sovereignty into question, and many lower-ranking samurai became shishi, men of spirit, committed to the slogan sonnō jōi, revere the emperor and expel the barbarian.

After setbacks in 1863 and 1864 the domains organised into an anti-Tokugawa alliance led by Satsuma and Chōshū. On 8 November 1867 the fifteenth shōgun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, returned power to the Imperial Court, and he resigned the title on 19 November. Iwakura Tomomi, Saigō Takamori and Ōkubo Toshimichi then planned a coup within the divided court to strip the Tokugawa house of its lands.

In the early hours of 3 January 1868 domain troops seized the Imperial Palace, and Emperor Meiji announced the restoration of the Imperial House's political functions. Tokugawa forces were beaten at the Battle of Toba–Fushimi on 27 January. Resistance continued in the Boshin War and the short-lived Republic of Ezo. The Charter Oath of 6 April 1868 set out the new government's aims, among them the adoption of Western technology.

The lands of the shōgun became prefectures, and the abolition of the domains followed between 1868 and 1873. In 1876 the conversion of samurai stipends into government bonds became compulsory. A standard language based on Tokyo speech was promoted in schools and government. Industrialisation under the slogan Enrich the country, strengthen the military made Japan a military power by 1895. The changes provoked the Saga Rebellion and the Satsuma Rebellion, and the Meiji Constitution of 1889 remained in force until the Allied occupation after World War II.
meiningen: Meiningen lies in the valley of the Werra between the Thuringian Forest and the Rhön Mountains, 80 kilometres south of Erfurt and 104 kilometres north of Würzburg. It grew from a settlement of the Frankish period, at an intersection of two trade routes and a ford near the Werra.

Meiningen was first mentioned in 982. Emperor Henry II gave it in 1008 to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Würzburg, to which it belonged for 534 years, and the bishops built a moated castle there in the 11th century. It was first called a town in 1230 and was granted wide autonomy in 1344. A fire in 1380 destroyed about a quarter of the town, and two fires at the end of the 15th century destroyed almost all of it. In 1542 it passed to the House of Henneberg in an exchange with the Prince-Bishop of Würzburg, and in 1583 to the Wettin family.

Fustian and linen weaving brought an economic boom that raised the population to about 5,000. The Thirty Years' War ended it: Croatian troops plundered the town in 1634 and Swedish troops besieged it in 1641, and thousands of inhabitants died or were expelled. From 1680 to 1918 Meiningen was the capital of the Duchy of Saxe-Meiningen. Schloss Elisabethenburg was built in 1682–92, and a court orchestra existed by 1690. A fire in September 1874 destroyed a third of the town, which was rebuilt in the Neoclassical style.

Georg II, Duke of Saxe-Meiningen, born in 1826, was a great patron of theatre, and his company, the Meininger, toured Germany and Europe and won international celebrity. In October 1880 the court orchestra began its most successful period under Hans von Bülow, with Johannes Brahms collaborating.

Meiningen is the capital of the district of Schmalkalden-Meiningen and the cultural, judicial and financial centre of southern Thuringia. It has a state theatre, and Schloss Elisabethenburg houses museums and the state archives.
meisenheim: Meisenheim lies in the valley of the River Glan at the northern edge of the North Palatine Uplands, in the Bad Kreuznach district of Rhineland-Palatinate. Its municipal area measures 1,324 hectares. The outlying homesteads of Hof Wieseck, Keddarterhof and Röther Hof belong to it. In 1896 it was joined to the railway network by the Lauter Valley Railway, which was absorbed in 1904 into the Glantalbahn.

Meisenheim is believed to have arisen in the 7th century, and its name is often derived from a hypothetical founder, Meiso. Its first documentary mention is of 1154. A document of 891 that is sometimes cited as the earliest is a forgery. In the 12th century it became the main seat of the Counts of Veldenz, and King Ludwig IV granted it town rights in 1315.

The counts built a castle on what is now Schlossplatz. Of it only two later buildings survive: the Magdalenenbau, today called the Herzog-Wolfgang-Haus, and the Schlosskirche, begun in 1479. Both were built after the Counts of Veldenz died out in 1444 and the county passed to the Dukes of Palatinate-Zweibrücken, who at first kept their seat at Meisenheim but soon moved it to Zweibrücken.

From 1538 to 1571 Duke Wolfgang of Zweibrücken kept a mint in the town, with one interruption, before it moved to Bergzabern. Its double thalers, thalers and half thalers are among the finest coins of Palatinate-Zweibrücken. A Jewish community may have existed from the Middle Ages, but the first Jew named in the records, a Jud Moses, appears in 1551. The Jews were expelled in 1569, and after the Thirty Years' War two families were allowed to settle. The outlaw Schinderhannes, Johannes Bückler, committed one of his early burglaries in the town in early 1797.

The Old Town is the only one in the area with continuous development since the 14th century, uninterrupted by war, fire or other destruction. It keeps parts of its town wall, the Untertor gate, the town hall of 1517 and many noble houses, among them the Boos von Waldeckscher Hof, built about 1400. The late Gothic Schlosskirche was built from 1479 to 1504 to the designs of Philipp von Gmünd, and the Catholic parish church of Saint Anthony of Padua is a Baroque building of 1685 to 1688. The town is a state-recognized recreational resort.
meissen: Meissen, in German Meißen, lies on both banks of the River Elbe in the Free State of Saxony, about 25 kilometres north-west of Dresden, and has about 30,000 inhabitants. Its Upper Sorbian name is Mišno. In Germany the spelling Meissen is the registered trademark of the State Porcelain Manufactory, while Meißen refers to the city itself.

The town grew out of the Polabian Slavic settlement of Meisa, inhabited by the Glomacze, a Sorbian tribe. King Henry the Fowler destroyed their fortress of Gana, and later founded the fortress of Misnia, around which the German town developed. Emperor Otto I founded the Margraviate of Meissen in 965 as a frontier march, and the bishopric dates from 968. It was suppressed in 1581, after accepting the Reformation in 1559, and re-created in 1921.

Bolesław I the Brave of Poland briefly seized Meissen in 1002, and the House of Wettin received the margraviate in 1089. A small force under Orda Khan attacked the town in the Mongol raid of 1241, and much of it was destroyed. It received town rights in 1332, and construction of the cathedral began in 1260 on the hill of the Albrechtsburg castle. Meissen became the capital of the Electorate of Saxony in 1423, and the seat moved to Dresden in 1464.

Meissen porcelain was the first high-quality porcelain made outside the Orient, using local deposits of kaolin. By decree of King Augustus II the Strong the factory was established in the Albrechtsburg, and in 1861 production moved to the Triebisch valley, where it remains. The Albrechtsburg, built between 1472 and 1525, is regarded as the first castle used as a royal residence in the German language area. The Gothic cathedral holds a chapel among the notable burial places of the Wettin family, and wine is grown on the slopes of the Elbe valley.
meknes: Meknes is one of the four imperial cities of Morocco. It takes its name from the Miknasa, a Berber tribe whose name derives from a root meaning to fight. The Miknasa settled the region around the 10th century and founded small unfortified villages. After conquering the area in the 11th century the Almoravids built a fortified settlement just south of them, called Tagrart, which formed the beginnings of the old medina. The Nejjarine Mosque and the Grand Mosque date from the Almoravid period.

Under the Alaouite sultan Moulay Rashid, Fes was the capital, and his brother Moulay Isma'il governed Meknes. When Rashid died in 1672, Isma'il became sultan and chose Meknes as his capital. He had had to fight to reconquer Fes and Marrakesh from his nephew Ahmad al-Mahriz, and the ulema of Fes disapproved of his ways, including his use of slaves. Meknes, further west, also seemed more defensible than Fes against Ottoman attacks from Algeria.

His palace complex was built over his entire reign, from 1672 to 1727, on the site of the medieval kasbah, and covers an area about four times larger than the old city. It had several autonomous palaces, gardens, a water system of wells, norias, canals and underground pipes, and monumental granaries said to hold supplies for a siege of ten years. After his death Morocco fell into relative anarchy as his sons competed for power, and Meknes lost its status as capital and was damaged by the earthquake of 1755.

The main monuments stand in the old medina and in the vast former kasbah of Moulay Isma'il to the south. Bab Mansur al-'Alj, the ceremonial entrance to the kasbah, was finished in 1732 by his son Moulay Abdallah. It is named after its designer, Mansour al-'Alj, a former Christian slave who converted to Islam, and is decorated with carved brick and coloured zellij tilework. In front of it lies Place el-Hedim, whose name means rubble and recalls the demolitions Isma'il carried out while building his palaces.

After French rule began in 1912 a new city was built on the plateau opposite the old one, and the capital moved from Fes to Rabat. The Dar Jamaï Museum, in a palace of 1882, is the best-known museum, and the Roman ruins of Volubilis lie about half an hour to the north.
mekong-delta: The Mekong Delta, also called the South-western Region, lies in southwestern Vietnam, where the Mekong River empties into the sea through a network of distributaries. It covers over 40,500 square kilometres, and the area under water varies with the season. The region lies immediately west of Ho Chi Minh City and stretches roughly in a triangle from Mỹ Tho in the east to Châu Đốc and Hà Tiên in the northwest and down to Cà Mau at the southern tip of Vietnam, including the island of Phú Quốc.

It is dominated by flat flood plains. The soil of the lower delta is sediment deposited by the Mekong and its tributaries over thousands of years, and over the last six thousand years the delta has pushed about 200 kilometres seaward.

The delta was probably inhabited long before history, and settlement may reach back to the 4th century BCE. Archaeological finds at Óc Eo and other sites show that it was an important part of the Funan civilisation, with trading ports and canals from the first century CE. Angkor Borei, occupied between 400 BCE and 500 CE, had maritime trade networks across Southeast Asia and with India and may have been Funan's capital. Khmer inscriptions appear in the Chenla period. In the early 15th century Champa made several incursions, and the declining Kingdom of Cambodia asked Ming China for intervention in 1408 and 1414.

Vietnamese acquisition came in two phases. In 1621 Lord Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên married his daughter to the Cambodian king Chey Chettha II in exchange for a Vietnamese trade port at Prei Nokor, now Ho Chi Minh City, and tax exemptions for Vietnamese settlers. The Nguyễn lords later intervened repeatedly in Cambodia, invited Chinese refugees to settle at Mỹ Tho and Biên Hoà, and after fully subduing Champa in 1697 annexed Prei Nokor, renaming it Gia Định.

After a war with Cambodia in 1754 and a ceasefire in 1756 Cambodia ceded Gò Công and Tân An. By 1757 the whole delta, including Cape Cà Mau, was under Vietnamese control. In the 1860s the French established the colony of Cochinchina there.

The inhabitants are mostly ethnic Vietnamese; the delta has the largest Khmer population outside Cambodia, along with Hoa (ethnic Chinese) and Cham communities. It is Vietnam's most productive region for agriculture and aquaculture, with rice grown on much of the land, and Cần Thơ is its economic centre. The delta is rich in wildlife, and its low-lying coast is vulnerable to rising seas and to coastal erosion.
mekong-river: The Mekong is about 4,909 kilometres long and drains some 795,000 square kilometres. It rises as the Za Qu on the Tibetan Plateau and soon becomes the Lancang River, named in Chinese from the Lao kingdom Lan Xang. It flows through Tibet and Yunnan, then along the borders of Myanmar and Laos to the Golden Triangle, where the Ruak River joins it. Downstream it crosses Laos, Thailand and Cambodia and reaches the South China Sea through a complex delta in Vietnam.

Thai and Lao speakers called it Mae Nam Khong, from an old word for river borrowed from Austroasiatic languages. The historian William Dalrymple suggests that the name Mekong derives from the Khmer phrase Me Kongkia, in its Indic values Ma Ganga, meaning mother river, in reference to the Ganges.

Rapids, waterfalls and extreme seasonal variation in flow make the river hard to navigate, so it has divided the peoples near it rather than united them. The earliest recorded civilisation was the Indianised Khmer culture of Funan in the Mekong delta, in the 1st century CE. Excavations at Oc Eo, near modern An Giang, have found coins from as far away as the Roman Empire. Funan was succeeded around the 5th century by the Khmer state of Chenla, and the Khmer Empire of Angkor was the last great Indianised state of the region. From about the time of its fall the Mekong was the front line between the emerging states of Siam and Tonkin, with Laos and Cambodia torn between their influence.

The first European to reach the river was the Portuguese António de Faria in 1540, and a European map of 1563 depicts it, though little was known upstream of the delta. Gerrit van Wuysthoff led an expedition up the river as far as Vientiane in 1641-42. The French captured Saigon in 1861 and established a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863.

The river remains a trade route between Tibet and Southeast Asia, and traditional trade in small boats between riverside communities continues. Its basin holds one of the richest concentrations of plant and animal life in the world, including the Mekong giant catfish. The section of the river in the deep gorges of Yunnan lies within the Three Parallel Rivers of Yunnan Protected Areas, a World Heritage Site, and the Tonle Sap lake in Cambodia is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.
melbourne: Melbourne occupies much of the northern and eastern coastlines of Port Phillip Bay, in the southeastern part of mainland Australia. The Boonwurrung and Woiwurrung languages call the area Narrm or Naarm; in Boonwurrung, Naarm means the Bay. The city is named after William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne, who was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom when it was founded in 1835. At its centre is the Hoddle Grid, a grid of streets measuring about 1.61 by 0.80 kilometres, whose southern edge fronts onto the Yarra River.

Aboriginal Australians have lived in the Melbourne area for at least 40,000 years. When British colonists arrived in the 19th century, up to 20,000 Kulin people from three language groups, the Wurundjeri, Bunurong and Wathaurong, lived there. The area was an important meeting place for the clans of the Kulin nation alliance and a vital source of food and water. A short-lived British penal settlement was founded at Port Phillip in 1803, then part of the Colony of New South Wales. Melbourne itself was founded in 1835 with the arrival of free settlers from Van Diemen's Land, now Tasmania, and was incorporated as a Crown settlement in 1837.

Queen Victoria declared it a city in 1847, and in 1851 it became the capital of the newly separated Colony of Victoria. The Victorian gold rush of the 1850s began a long boom which, by the late 1880s, had made it one of the largest and wealthiest cities in Australia and the world. After the federation of Australia in 1901 it was the interim seat of government until Canberra became the permanent capital in 1927. In 1956 it hosted the Summer Olympics, the first Olympic Games held outside Europe and the United States.

Melbourne is the capital of the state of Victoria and the second most populous city in Australia, with more than five million people. It is known for the Victorian architecture left by the gold rush and the land boom of the 1880s; the Royal Exhibition Building, completed in 1880, is World Heritage listed. Little survives from before the gold rush, St James Old Cathedral (1839) and St Francis' Church (1845) being among the few examples in the city centre.

The city gave rise to Australian rules football, Australian impressionism and Australian cinema. The Melbourne Cup horse race, first held in 1861, was declared a public holiday for all Melburnians in 1873. The University of Melbourne is the second-oldest university in Australia.
meles-zenawi: Meles Zenawi was born Legesse Zenawi Asres on 9 May 1955 in Adwa, in northern Ethiopia, the third of six children of Zenawi Asres, a Tigrayan from Adwa, and Alemash Ghebreluel, an Eritrean from Adi Quala. He won a full scholarship to General Wingate High School in Addis Ababa and finished in 1972 with honours. He took the name Meles in honour of Meles Tekle, a fellow Tigrayan university student executed by the Derg government in 1975. In that year he left Haile Selassie I University to join the Tigray People's Liberation Front, or TPLF.

The TPLF was one of the armed groups fighting the Derg, the military junta that governed Ethiopia from 1974 to 1991. Meles was elected to the leadership committee in 1979 and became chairman of the TPLF's executive committee in 1983. He also led the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front, the EPRDF, formed in 1988. After the EPRDF won the civil war in 1991 he became president of the Transitional Government. Eritreans voted for independence in a referendum on 24 May 1993.

A new constitution approved in 1994 provided for a parliamentary system. The EPRDF won the 1995 elections, and Meles was sworn in as prime minister when the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia was inaugurated on 21 August 1995. His governments introduced ethnic federalism and encouraged privatisation, reversing the Derg's communist policy. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a war over a territorial dispute from 1998 to 2000, and the EPRDF won the elections of 2000, 2005 and 2010.

Meles married Azeb Mesfin, a former TPLF fighter, and had three children. He chaired the Organization of African Unity from June 1995 to June 1996. In July 2012 his absence from African Union meetings raised questions about his health, and he died on 20 August 2012 of an infection in Belgium.

Views of his rule differ. Supporters point to school expansion, in which enrolment rose from 27 per cent of children in 1991, and to years of rapid economic growth. Many human rights groups and analysts describe his government as authoritarian. His principles and policies of ethnic federalism are called Zenawism and are studied by scholars. The Meles Zenawi Foundation was established in 2013 to honour his legacy.
melfi: Melfi stands on a hill at the foot of Mount Vulture in the province of Potenza in Basilicata, roughly midway between Naples and Bari, next to the borders of Campania and Apulia. Daunians and Lucanians lived there, and under the Romans it fell within the territory of the colony of Venusia, founded in 291 BCE.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Melfi was a strategic point between lands held by the Byzantines and by the Lombards. It was assigned to the Norman leader William I of Hauteville, and the Hauteville family began from here their conquest of southern Italy, which led in the early 12th century to the Kingdom of Sicily. In 1059 Melfi became the capital of the Duchy of Apulia, and papal councils met there in that year and in 1089 and 1109. In 1231 Emperor Frederick II promulgated the Constitutions of Melfi, creating a bureaucracy of paid officials who imposed a tax system on resentful feudal lords.

Later Melfi shared the decline of the Kingdom of Naples. In March 1528 the French army under Odet de Foix besieged it and killed about 3.000 people, women and children included, and Charles V then gave Andrea Doria the title of Prince of Melfi. In 1799 Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo's forces arrived on 29 May, and he prevented a sack. After unification the peasant army of Carmine Crocco occupied the town on 15 April 1861. Antifascists such as Manlio Rossi-Doria were exiled there, and the 1930 earthquake devastated it.

The castle was probably built new by the Normans in the 11th century. Since 1976 it has housed the Museo Nazionale Archeologico Melfese, whose best-known piece is the sarcophagus of Rapolla, an imperial sculpture of the 2nd century CE found in 1856. The cathedral dates from the 11th century and keeps its Norman bell tower, and the town runs along the Norman walls, whose Venosina gate dates from the early 13th century. The rock church of Santa Margherita is dug out of volcanic tufa.
melilla: Melilla lies in northwest Africa on the shores of the Alboran Sea, on the eastern side of the peninsula of Cape Tres Forcas, at the foot of Mount Gurugú and around the mouth of the intermittent stream called the Río de Oro. The city is arranged in a wide semicircle around the beach and the port. Its urban nucleus was originally a fortress, Melilla la Vieja, built on a peninsular mound about 30 m high. The Moroccan settlement of Beni Ansar lies immediately to the south.

Melilla was a Phoenician and later Punic trading establishment under the name Rusadir, taken from the Phoenician name of the nearby Cape Three Forks. After Carthage's defeat in the Punic Wars it fell under the Roman client state of Mauretania, and it was later part of the province of Mauretania Tingitana. It was made a Roman colony in 46 CE.

In the 15th century the city declined, like most Mediterranean cities of the Kingdom of Fez, as Atlantic ports eclipsed them. After the Catholic Monarchs conquered the Kingdom of Granada in 1492, their secretary Hernando de Zafra gathered information on the North African coast, and he reported that in 1494 the locals had expelled the authority of the Sultan of Fez and offered to pledge loyalty. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 placed Melilla within the sphere of Castile, but the conquest waited. It was seized by Christians in 1497 and was a condominium of the House of Medina Sidonia and the Crown of Castile until 1556.

For much of the early modern period the fortress of Melilla la Vieja remained a military garrison with a small civilian population. The current limits of Spanish territory around it were fixed by treaties with Morocco in 1859, 1860, 1861 and 1894, and the area between the old fortress and the outer forts was settled by mainland Spaniards, Sephardi Jews and Riffians.

Melilla became an autonomous city in 1995, having until then been a municipality of Málaga. Spanish is the official language and Tarifit, the Berber language of the Rif, is also spoken. The Chapel of Santiago, with a dome of the mid-16th century, is a rare example of Gothic architecture in Africa, and the architect Enrique Nieto left the city the second largest concentration of Modernista works in Spain after Barcelona.
melisende-queen-of-jerusalem: Melisende was the eldest daughter of Baldwin II, then Frankish count of Edessa, and Morphia of Melitene, an Armenian noblewoman of the Greek Orthodox faith. She and her sisters grew up speaking Armenian and probably Greek, and became proficient in French. When Baldwin I of Jerusalem died in 1118, her father was elected to succeed him, and the family joined him in Jerusalem in late 1119. Melisende remained unmarried for an unusually long time, since her father may still have hoped for a son. After Morphia died, probably in 1126 or 1127, Baldwin named Melisende his heir, and in 1129 she married Fulk V of Anjou.

Baldwin II died on 21 August 1131, having commended the kingdom to Melisende, Fulk and their infant son Baldwin, and the patriarch crowned Fulk and Melisende on 14 September. For the first five years Fulk did not associate her with his public acts, against both their marriage contract and her father's will. In 1134 noblemen led by Count Hugh II of Jaffa revolted against Fulk. After their reconciliation, Fulk never again issued a charter for the kingdom without her consent. The Melisende Psalter, a luxurious prayer book, is believed to have been commissioned by Fulk for her around 1135.

Fulk died on 10 November 1143 after a fall from his horse. Melisende took full charge of the government and was crowned again on Christmas 1143 together with her son Baldwin III, then thirteen. She appointed her cousin Manasses of Hierges constable, to command the army in her name. After the fall of Edessa in 1144 she urged intervention from Europe, which led to the Second Crusade. Her relations with Baldwin broke down as she refused to give him real authority. Baldwin invaded her share of the divided kingdom and besieged her in the Tower of David, and she agreed to retire to Nablus.

After her fall Melisende still advised her son and in 1157 took a military initiative while he was in Antioch, when the cave-fortress of el-Hablis was recovered from the Muslims at her insistence. She died in 1161 after an illness, possibly a stroke. William of Tyre, who took her side, praised her wisdom, but two disasters, the fall of Edessa and the failure to take Damascus in 1148, came in her reign, though her personal blame is arguable. The historian Folda calls her the foremost patron of art in the twelfth-century Kingdom of Jerusalem.
melissus-of-samos: Melissus was the third and last member of the Eleatic school, after Parmenides and Zeno. Little is known of his life. He may have been born around 500 BCE, and the date of his death is unknown. What is known comes mostly from a short passage in Plutarch's Life of Pericles, which describes him as commander of the Samian fleet in the Samian War, who defeated the Athenian fleet in 440 BCE. Plutarch also reports that Aristotle said Melissus had beaten Pericles in an earlier battle. He was reputed to be a pupil of Parmenides and the teacher of Leucippus, claims that should be treated with scepticism.

Melissus wrote a treatise, later titled On Nature, in prose rather than in verse like Parmenides. Much of it survives through Simplicius, who quoted it in his commentaries on Aristotle's Physics and On the Heavens, and most fragments are collected in Diels and Kranz. Like Parmenides, he held that what exists is one, ungenerated, indestructible, indivisible, changeless and motionless. He differed in two respects. Parmenides held that Being is limited, while Melissus held it to be wholly unlimited, and where Parmenides placed Being in a timeless present, Melissus made it eternal.

His argument for eternity runs that whatever comes to be must have a beginning, and whatever has a beginning must end. Since the One did not come to be, it has neither beginning nor end. Modern commentators find this reasoning faulty.

His case for the oneness of what exists is regarded as his best: if what exists were more than one, the boundaries between things would limit it, but it is unlimited. He also argued that it cannot change, since change would make it different and so no longer whole, and that it is full and therefore cannot move, because to be empty would be to be nothing. He claimed too that the One has no body, since a body has limits and the One has none.

His version of Eleatic philosophy was the chief source for its presentation in Plato and Aristotle. Aristotle called it a bit crude and said it made invalid arguments from false assumptions. Aristocles of Messene thought several arguments absurd. Modern scholars judge him more kindly, as an inventive philosopher who offered clear, direct arguments and made original contributions to Eleaticism.
melk: Melk lies in Lower Austria next to the Wachau valley on the Danube. The town is first mentioned as Medilica in 831 in a donation of Louis the German, its name coming from a Slavic word for border. In 976 the area was given to Leopold I, Margrave of Austria, to serve as a buffer between the Magyars to the east and Bavaria to the west. A mention in 996 of an area known as Ostarrîchi is the origin of the German word Österreich.

The bluff that carries the abbey held a Babenberg castle until Leopold II gave the site to Benedictine monks from nearby Lambach in 1089. Melk received market rights in 1227 and became a municipality in 1898. The Danube reached 15.8 metres above its usual level in 1501, and the Schiffsmeisterhaus bears marks of high water on its facade. During the Holocaust a subcamp of Mauthausen concentration camp operated at Melk. Its former crematorium is now a museum, and the rest of the camp became part of the Birago barracks of the Austrian Army.

Melk is best known for its massive baroque Benedictine monastery, Melk Abbey, but the town itself holds architecture of many centuries in a small area. The Rathaus on the Rathausplatz was built in 1575, and the Kolomanbrunnen fountain in the square is a gift from the abbey. The Lebzelterhaus dates from 1657, and the Haus am Stein, built in the 15th century, is the oldest building in town. The Old Post Office was built in 1792. The Gothic parish church holds a Kalvarienberg sculpture group, and the Wiener Tor stood until 1874. About five kilometres to the south stands the Renaissance castle Schallaburg. Melk appears in fiction as the home of Adso, the co-protagonist of Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose.
memory-of-the-world-programme: UNESCO began the programme in 1992 to preserve and promote documentary heritage, among them manuscripts, maps, rock inscriptions, court documents and diplomatic exchanges, judged to be of such global significance that they transcend the boundaries of time and culture. The programme seeks to safeguard documentary heritage against collective amnesia, neglect, decay and deliberate destruction. Its International Advisory Committee met in an interim capacity from 1993 and created the International Register at its second meeting in 1995. The first inscriptions followed in 1997, after the statutes that made the committee permanent took effect.

Any organisation or individual may propose an item through a UNESCO Member State's National Commission, and two proposals per state are considered in each nomination cycle, with no limit on joint proposals. Items are recommended by the International Advisory Committee, whose 14 members are appointed by UNESCO's Director-General, and endorsed by the Director-General, using the criteria of world significance and outstanding universal value. The register includes manuscripts, oral traditions, audio-visual materials and library and archive holdings, among them recordings of folk music, landmark films and the lifetime works of writers and composers. The committee has subsidiary bodies for the register, preservation, and education and research. National and regional committees are autonomous and made up of local heritage professionals.

National and regional committees keep their own registers for heritage of national or regional importance, such as those of Australia, Canada, Ghana, Mexico and New Zealand, and there are regional registers for Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Africa. The Jikji Prize, established in 2004 with the South Korean government to mark the 2001 inscription of Korea's Jikji, honours institutions that preserve and open documentary heritage; its first recipient, in 2005, was the Czech National Library. The audiovisual concern goes back to UNESCO's 1980 Recommendation for the Safeguarding and Preservation of Moving Images. In 1995 UNESCO published its first Memory of the World list, on national cinematic heritage.
memphis-egypt: Memphis stood on the west bank of the Nile, about 20 kilometres south of Cairo, at the mouth of the Delta, where it marked the boundary between Upper and Lower Egypt. It was the capital of the first nome of Lower Egypt, and its Egyptian name was Inebu-hedj, "the white walls". The principal port, Peru-nefer, held many workshops and warehouses that distributed food and goods through the kingdom. The great temple of Ptah, Hut-ka-Ptah, "Enclosure of the ka of Ptah", gave its name, in Manetho's Greek rendering, to Egypt itself.

According to Manetho, writing in the early third century BCE, King Menes, the first to unite the Two Lands, founded the city by diverting the Nile with dikes. Herodotus tells a similar story and says the Persians later kept the dams in repair. Some Egyptologists identified Menes with Narmer, shown on the Narmer Palette, but a 2012 inscription showing the predynastic king Iry-Hor visiting Memphis suggests that Narmer cannot have been its founder.

The city was capital through the Early Dynastic Period and the Old Kingdom, for more than six consecutive dynasties, and its prestige peaked under the Sixth Dynasty. Its main worship focused on the Memphis triad of Ptah, his consort Sekhmet and their son Nefertem. Djoser's complex at Saqqara, of the Third Dynasty, served as the royal necropolis.

At the start of the Middle Kingdom the court moved to Thebes, but Memphis remained perhaps the most important commercial and artistic centre. Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV of the Eighteenth Dynasty favoured it, and its port became the gateway for trade with Byblos and the Levant. In the Late Period it was often the scene of struggles against Kushite, Assyrian and Persian occupiers, and the Kushite ruler Piankhi captured it and restored its temples. In 332 BCE Alexander the Great was crowned king in the Temple of Ptah. After his death in 323 BCE, Ptolemy I brought his body to Memphis, and Ptolemy II later moved the sarcophagus to Alexandria.

The decline came with the rise of coastal Alexandria, which took away Memphis's economic importance. Its religious role faded after the Edict of Thessalonica of 380 CE made Nicene Christianity the sole religion of the Roman Empire. By the Middle Ages nearby Cairo had become the major political and economic centre.

The footprint of the ancient city is uninhabited, and the nearest settlement is the village of Mit Rahina. Memphis and its necropolis, together with the pyramid fields stretching more than 30 kilometres along the desert plateau to the west, including the Pyramids of Giza, are a World Heritage Site. The ruins are open to the public as an open-air museum, and an alabaster sphinx stands beside the Temple of Ptah.
mencius: Mencius was born Meng Ke in the state of Zou, in what is now Zoucheng, Shandong. His father, Meng Ji, died when he was very young, and his mother, Meng Mu, is often held up as an exemplary woman in Chinese culture. Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women gives four stories about her. In the best known she moved house three times, from beside a cemetery to beside a market and finally to beside a school, because her son imitated what he saw around him. He is supposed to have been a pupil of Zisi, the grandson of Confucius.

Mencius lived in the Warring States period. According to legend he travelled throughout China for forty years, as Confucius had, offering advice to rulers on reform. He served as an official and scholar at the Jixia Academy in the state of Qi from 319 to 312 BCE, and took three years' leave from his duties for Qi to mourn his mother. Ying Shao's Fengsu Tongyi records that King Hui of Liang appointed him a high official after the capital of Wei was moved to Daliang. Disappointed that he could not bring about change, he retired from public life. He was buried in the Cemetery of Mencius, 12 km north-east of Zoucheng, where a stele carried by a stone tortoise stands before his grave.

His conversations with rulers form the Mencius, later canonised as a Confucian classic and grouped by Zhu Xi (1130-1200) among the Four Books at the core of orthodox Neo-Confucian thought. Mencius held that human nature is righteous and humane and that society causes bad character. He gave the example of onlookers who feel alarm at a child falling into a well, and argued that feelings of compassion, shame, deference and right and wrong are the beginnings of humanity, righteousness, propriety and wisdom. These can grow or fail, so education in a favourable environment matters. In this he differed from Xunzi, who thought human nature evil.

In politics he stressed the importance of ordinary people. A ruler who ignores their needs and rules harshly is no longer a true ruler, and Mencius said of the overthrow of King Zhou of Shang, 'I have merely heard of killing a villain Zhou, but I have not heard of murdering him as the ruler.' He favoured low taxes and free trade. Neo-Confucians of the Song dynasty took his reading of Confucianism as the orthodox one. François Noël published a full edition in Latin at Prague in 1711.
mendelian-inheritance: Gregor Johann Mendel, a nineteenth-century Moravian monk, formulated his ideas from simple hybridisation experiments with pea plants in the garden of his monastery. Between 1856 and 1863 he cultivated and tested some 28,000 plants. He presented a two-part paper, Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden, to the Brünn Natural History Society on 8 February and 8 March 1865, and it was published in 1866. His method contributed to his success: he started only with plants shown to be true-breeding, measured discrete characters such as the colour, shape and position of seeds, expressed his results numerically and analysed them statistically, followed several successive generations, and used test crosses to reveal recessive characters.

Mendel found that when he crossed purebred white-flowered and purple-flowered peas, every plant of the first generation was purple, so he called purple dominant. Allowing those plants to self-fertilise gave both colours in the next generation in a ratio of 3 to 1. He conceived of heredity units he called factors, now called genes, which exist in alternative forms now called alleles; an organism inherits two, one from each parent.

Three principles became known as laws. Dominance and uniformity: the offspring of two purebred parents differing in one character all show the dominant trait. Segregation: the two alleles separate when gametes are formed, giving a 1:2:1 ratio of genotypes. Independent assortment: alleles for separate traits pass independently, and in dihybrid crosses Mendel found 9:3:3:1 ratios.

Mendel himself warned that care was needed in extending his patterns to other organisms or traits. Many traits are non-Mendelian: many genes have more than two alleles, and some traits, such as height, depend on many genes. Incomplete dominance, in which hybrids look intermediate, appears in four o'clock plants, studied first by Carl Correns.

Mendel's results were at first largely ignored, and even he thought they applied only to some species or traits. Nineteenth-century biologists attached importance to the apparent blending of inherited traits. In 1900 Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak and Hugo de Vries are credited with rediscovering his work, though the order and nature of the rediscovery is debated. William Bateson promoted it vigorously in Europe and coined the terms genetics and allele. Critics objected that it implied discontinuous heredity. Work by Ronald Fisher showed that several Mendelian factors could produce the continuous variation seen, making the theory compatible with natural selection. Thomas Hunt Morgan integrated it with the chromosome theory in 1915 to create classical genetics.
mendoza-argentina: Mendoza lies in the northern-central part of its province, in a region of foothills and high plains on the eastern side of the Andes. The road between Buenos Aires and Santiago, Ruta Nacional 7, runs through it, and the city is a frequent stopover for climbers on their way to Aconcagua. Before the 1560s the area was populated by the Huarpes and Puelches. The Huarpes devised a system of irrigation that the Spanish later developed, and its trenches, the acequias, still run along the city's streets.

On 2 March 1561 Pedro del Castillo founded the city and named it Ciudad de Mendoza del Nuevo Valle de La Rioja, after the governor of Chile, García Hurtado de Mendoza. Fewer than 80 Spanish settlers are estimated to have lived in the area before 1600. Prosperity later increased through the use of indigenous and slave labour and the Jesuit presence in the region. In 1776 the city was transferred from the Captaincy General of Chile, and agricultural production grew, with more trade with Buenos Aires, after nearby rivers were tapped for irrigation in 1788.

The state of Cuyo was created in 1813 with José de San Martín as governor. From Mendoza, San Martín and other Argentine and Chilean patriots organised the army with which they won the independence of Chile and Peru.

A severe earthquake in 1861 killed at least 5,000 people. The city was rebuilt with large squares and with wider streets and sidewalks than any other city in Argentina, so as to better withstand seismic activity. The layout of the modern city was established in 1863, with a central main square surrounded by four smaller plazas.

Mendoza is the capital of Mendoza Province. The surrounding region is the largest wine-producing area in South America, and olive oil is the other main local industry. Suburbs such as Godoy Cruz, Guaymallén, Las Heras and Luján de Cuyo have grown far faster than the city proper, and together they make up most of a metropolitan area of over a million people. The Museo del Área Fundacional on Pedro del Castillo Square and the Museo Nacional del Vino, in nearby Maipú, record its history.
menelaus: Menelaus was a descendant of Pelops, son of Tantalus, and the younger brother of Agamemnon. In the usual version, followed by Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, the two were sons of Atreus, king of Mycenae, and Aerope. Later sources say that Atreus feuded with his brother Thyestes over the throne of Mycenae, and that Thyestes took it after his son Aegisthus murdered Atreus. Menelaus and Agamemnon went into exile and returned with the help of King Tyndareus of Sparta to drive Thyestes away. Agamemnon took the throne of Mycenae.

When Tyndareus's stepdaughter Helen came to be married, many kings and princes sought her hand. On the advice of Odysseus, all the suitors swore to defend the chosen husband in any quarrel, and straws were drawn. Menelaus won and became ruler of Sparta with Helen. A supposed palace has been found at Pellana in Laconia, though other archaeologists think it too far from other Mycenaean centres to have been his capital.

Paris, the Trojan prince, ran off to Troy with Helen. Invoking the oath, Menelaus and Agamemnon raised a fleet of a thousand ships. In Book 3 of the Iliad Menelaus beats Paris in a duel, but Aphrodite carries Paris away. In Book 4 Pandarus wounds Menelaus with an arrow, though Athena protects him from death, and in Book 17 he recovers the corpse of Patroclus. According to Hyginus he was one of the Greeks hidden in the Trojan Horse, and at the sack he killed Deiphobus. Ancient versions tell how he raised his sword against Helen and then spared her.

According to Book 4 of the Odyssey Menelaus's fleet was blown by storms to Crete and Egypt, where he forced Proteus to reveal the way home, and he reached Sparta eight years after leaving Troy. In Herodotus's account Helen never went to Troy but spent the war in Egypt. In the Odyssey the couple live in harmony at Sparta, though some scholars detect underlying conflict.

Menelaus and Helen were worshipped at the Menelaion in Therapne, and only Pausanias says they were buried there. In the Odyssey it was ordained that Menelaus would not die but go to Elysium, and in Euripides's Helen he spends his afterlife on the Isle of the Blessed. He appears in Greek vase painting from the 6th to the 4th century BCE and in 5th-century tragedies by Sophocles and Euripides.
menelik-ii: Menelik was born in 1844 at Ankober in the Kingdom of Shewa and baptised Sahle Maryam. He was the son of Haile Melekot, Negus of Shewa, of the Shewan branch of the Solomonic dynasty. His grandfather Sahle Selassie named him after Menelik I, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba in tradition. After his father's death in 1855 Emperor Tewodros II imprisoned him at the fortress of Magdala, though he later said Tewodros had treated him like a son. In 1865, as the emperor's power declined, he escaped and returned to Shewa, and in August 1866 he proclaimed himself Negus there.

As king of Shewa he submitted to Emperor Yohannes IV in 1878. Confined to Shewa, he turned south and conquered lands inhabited by Oromo, Wolayta and Gurage peoples, drawing revenue from ivory, coffee, gold and the slave trade. He bought arms through direct European diplomacy with advisers such as the Swiss engineer Alfred Ilg, defeated Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam at the Battle of Embabo in 1882 and took Harar in 1887. When Yohannes was killed fighting the Mahdists in March 1889, Menelik proclaimed himself emperor, and he was crowned on Mount Entoto on 3 November 1889.

The Treaty of Wuchale, signed with Italy in 1889, read in the Italian version as a protectorate, while the Amharic text allowed only optional use of Italian diplomatic help. Menelik rejected it in 1891, and Italy invaded in 1895. With an army of over 100,000 he defeated the Italians at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, which secured Ethiopia's independence and full European recognition. Conquests continued until 1900, and he fixed borders by treaty with Britain, France and Italy, began the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway and centralized government through ministries, schools and a state bank.

Menelik suffered strokes in 1906, 1908 and 1909, the last leaving him paralyzed and barely able to speak. Empress Taytu Betul and later Ras Tessema Nadew acted as regents. He died on 12 December 1913. His grandson Iyasu was nominally his successor but was deposed in 1916, and his daughter Zewditu and then Ras Tafari Makonnen, later Haile Selassie, followed.

He is praised as a symbol of African resistance to colonialism and is widely regarded as the founder of modern Ethiopia. Critics among the groups incorporated into his empire accuse him of forced assimilation, land expropriation and cultural suppression, and historians describe the atrocities of his southern conquests, particularly against the Oromo, in severe terms; some regard them as genocide.
menes: The name Menes first appears in the work of Manetho, a priest and historian of the Ptolemaic period, who wrote it in Greek as Menes. The Egyptian form mnj, meaning He who endures, comes from the Turin and Abydos king lists of the Nineteenth Dynasty.

I. E. S. Edwards suggested it may have been a descriptive epithet for a hero of whom little was known, and others have proposed that it conceals the collective identity of the Naqada III rulers Ka, Scorpion II and Narmer, or a leadership role rather than a person.

Menes is almost absent from the archaeological record, whereas Narmer is firmly credited with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. An ivory label from Naqada, found in the tomb of Queen Neithhotep, shows the serekh of Hor-Aha beside a building holding the sign mn, usually taken as Menes. A seal impression from Abydos alternates the serekh of Narmer with the gameboard sign mn.

Flinders Petrie matched Menes with Narmer, and Josep Cervelló-Autuori states the identification categorically, while Stephan Seidlmayer judged it a fairly safe inference that Menes was Hor-Aha. Some scholars read the seal as naming a prince of Narmer called Menes, who would then be his successor Hor-Aha. Opinions still vary, and neither document settles the question.

Menes is missing from the Palermo Stone and the Cairo Stone, but later king lists always place him first among human pharaohs, and some sources have him inherit the throne from Horus. He was regarded as a founding figure through much of Egyptian history, as Romulus was in Rome.

Classical writers gave him many deeds. Herodotus said he founded Memphis as his capital after diverting the Nile with a levee, but a relief found in Sinai in 2012 mentions a visit to Memphis by the earlier ruler Iry-Hor, which suggests the city already existed. Manetho called Menes a native of Thinis and said he led the army across the frontier and won great glory. Diodorus Siculus credited him with the worship of the gods, sacrifice and a more luxurious way of living, and Plutarch mentions a pillar at Thebes inscribed with a curse on Menes for introducing luxury.

Diodorus also records a story of the priests of Sobek that Menes, attacked by his own dogs, fled across Lake Moeris on a crocodile and founded Crocodilopolis. Edwards called the legend devoid of historical value. Manetho says that Menes reigned for 30, 60 or 62 years and was killed by a hippopotamus.
menkaure: Menkaure is known in Greek as Mykerinos, Latinized Mycerinus, and to Manetho as Menkheres. Manetho names Bikheris as his predecessor, but the archaeological evidence points almost certainly to Khafre. A flint knife from his mortuary temple mentions a king's mother, Khamerernebty I, which suggests that she and Khafre were his parents. His brothers Nebemakhet, Duaenre, Nikaure and Iunmin served as viziers during his reign. Queen Khamerernebty II was the mother of a king's son, Khuenre, who probably died before his father, and the throne passed to Shepseskaf, a younger son.

The length of the reign is uncertain. Manetho gives 63 years, which is surely an exaggeration. The Turin King List is damaged where the total should stand, and Egyptologists generally accept that 18 years was meant. A workmen's graffito mentions the year after the 11th cattle count; if the count was held every second year, he might have ruled for 22 years. In 2013 a fragment of a sphinx of Menkaure was found at Tel Hazor.

His pyramid at Giza, called Netjer-er-Menkaure, meaning Menkaure is Divine, measures 103.4 metres at the base and 65.5 metres in height, the smallest of the three main pyramids there. Three subsidiary pyramids stand beside it. His valley temple, mainly of brick, yielded the statues for which he is best known: greywacke triads showing the king with the goddess Hathor and the deities of different nomes, and a double statue of the king with a queen, probably Khamerernebty II.

In 1837 Richard William Howard Vyse and John Shae Perring entered the pyramid and found a basalt sarcophagus in the burial chamber, undecorated by hieroglyphs, beside wooden coffin fragments bearing the king's name and a partial skeleton. The ship carrying the sarcophagus to London was lost after leaving Malta in October 1838. The coffin is now thought to be a replacement made during the Saite period, and radiocarbon dating placed the bones in the Coptic period.

Herodotus, writing long afterwards, made Menkaure a pious son of Khufu whose only daughter died before him and whom an oracle at Buto doomed to a short life. He is said to have turned night into day by revelling, to double his remaining six years. This is a late tradition, not contemporary evidence.
mennonites: The Mennonites trace their roots to the Radical Reformation in the German and Dutch-speaking regions of central Europe. Their persecutors called the forerunners of the movement Täufer or Wiedertäufer, re-baptizers. Their most distinguishing feature was the rejection of infant baptism, an act with political as well as religious meaning, since almost every infant born in western Europe was baptized in the Roman Catholic Church. Their views also developed in opposition to those of Protestant reformers such as Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli.

Menno Simons, a Frisian cleric who lived from 1496 to 1561, became a prominent leader of the wider movement and formalized the teachings of earlier Swiss Anabaptist founders. Anabaptists of Dutch and North German background took their name from him, and the Swiss and South German group later adopted it too. A third group, organized by Jakob Hutter, became the Hutterites.

In the 16th century the Mennonites and other Anabaptists were relentlessly persecuted. Martyrs Mirror, published in 1660, records much of it, including accounts of over 4,000 burnings, and numerous stonings, imprisonments and live burials. Persecution continued in parts of Switzerland until 1710. Rather than resist by arms, most early followers survived by fleeing to neighbouring states whose ruling families tolerated believer's baptism.

Beliefs were set out in the Schleitheim Confession of 24 February 1527, which covered the ban, communion, separation from the world, believer's baptism, pastors, renunciation of the sword and renunciation of the oath. The Dordrecht Confession of Faith, adopted by Dutch Mennonites on 21 April 1632, was later taken up by Alsatian and North American Mennonites.

Persecution and the search for employment drove Mennonites from the Netherlands eastward to Germany in the 17th century. Others settled around Danzig and in West Prussia from about 1530, and from 1791 they founded colonies in the south-west of the Russian Empire. In 1683 families from Krefeld settled at Germantown, Pennsylvania, the first permanent Mennonite settlement in the American colonies, and in 1688 four of them signed the first formal protest against slavery in the United States.

Mennonites are known as one of the historic peace churches because of their pacifism. Congregations range from Old Order Mennonites, who live without certain elements of modern technology, to mainline Mennonites who dress like the general population. There is no single world authority, and the Mennonite World Conference, founded at Basel in 1925, coordinates shared causes without making binding decisions. The Mennonite Central Committee, founded in Chicago on 27 September 1920, provides disaster relief and development work around the world.
menorca: Menorca takes its name from the Latin Insula Minor, the smaller island, in contrast to nearby Mallorca. Its capital is Mahón, at the eastern end of the island, and Ciutadella de Menorca and Mahón are the main ports and largest towns. Its highest point, El Toro, rises to 358 metres. The island is known for its megalithic monuments, including navetes, taules and talaiots, which indicate very early prehistoric human activity.

The end of the Punic Wars brought an increase in piracy in the western Mediterranean, and the pirates used Menorca and Mallorca as bases. The Romans invaded in response, and by 123 BCE both islands were fully under Roman control. The Vandals conquered Menorca in the 5th century and the Byzantine Empire recovered it in 534. In 903 it was annexed to the Caliphate of Córdoba and many Muslims emigrated there. The Arabic name Manûrqa was used until the rule of the last Muslim ra'îs, Abû 'Umar ibn Sa'îd, ended in 1287.

After Christian forces took Mallorca in 1231, Menorca chose to become an independent Islamic state that paid tribute to King James I of Aragon. A Catalan-Aragonese invasion under Alfonso III landed on 17 January 1287, and its anniversary is now Menorca's national day. Most of the Muslim inhabitants were enslaved and sold in the markets of Eivissa, Valencia and Barcelona, while others became Christians. The island was part of the Crown of Aragon, was briefly ceded to the Kingdom of Mallorca, and was retaken by Aragon in 1343.

Anglo-Dutch forces captured Menorca in 1708 during the War of the Spanish Succession, and Spain ceded it to Great Britain in the Peace of Utrecht of 1713. Under British rule the capital moved to Mahón and a Royal Navy base was established in its harbour. French forces captured the island in 1756, Britain regained it in 1763, and Franco-Spanish forces took it in 1782. The British captured it once more in 1798 and ceded it to Spain in the Treaty of Amiens of 1802.

Menorca belongs to Spain and forms a political union with the other Balearic Islands, though it is not a province. It had 102,477 inhabitants in 2025. During the Spanish Civil War it stayed loyal to the Second Spanish Republic, and after the Nationalist victory in February 1939 the Royal Navy assisted in a peaceful transfer of power. UNESCO designated the island a biosphere reserve in October 1993.
mensheviks: The Mensheviks were a faction of the Marxist Russian Social Democratic Labour Party that split with Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks at the Second Party Congress in August 1903. Julius Martov and Lenin disagreed over the editorial committee of the party newspaper Iskra and over the definition of a party member. Lenin's formulation required membership of one of the party's organisations, while Martov's required only work under the guidance of one. Lenin argued for a small party of professional revolutionaries, Martov for a large party of activists with broad representation.

Martov's definition was accepted by 28 votes to 23. But seven delegates then left, five of them representatives of the Jewish Bund who protested the defeat of their own federalist proposal, and Lenin's supporters gained a slight majority, which decided the names of the factions.
