The 4th Congress of 1906 formally reunited the party, with the Mensheviks in the majority, yet Lenin's definition of a party member replaced Martov's. The two factions kept separate structures. Both held that Russia was too undeveloped for socialism, so that the revolution against the tsarist regime would be bourgeois-democratic. After 1905 the Mensheviks were more inclined to work with liberal parties such as the Constitutional Democrats, and argued for legal methods and trade union work, while the Bolsheviks favoured armed violence and alliances with peasant representatives.

Georgi Plekhanov's position that a period of capitalism had to come before a socialist revolution was associated with the Mensheviks. Alexander Potresov called for the party to suspend illegal work, and in 1908 Lenin called Mensheviks who left for legal organisations liquidationists. Leaders included Martov and Pavel Axelrod. The party split formally in 1912. The Menshevik faction split further in 1917: most opposed the war, but a vocal minority supported it as national defence.
menton: Menton lies on the Mediterranean at the Franco-Italian border, just across from the Ligurian town of Ventimiglia. It has always been a frontier town: since the end of the 14th century it has stood on the border between the County of Nice, held by the Duke of Savoy, and the Republic of Genoa. The mild climate favours groves of lemons, oranges, mandarins and clementines, and the lemon is one of the town's symbols.

The first major settlement came in the 11th century, when the count of Ventimiglia built the Château de Puypin. In the 13th century the Vento family of Genoa built a new castle along the Roman road, around which the present town grew. The first mention of Menton is in the peace treaty between Charles of Anjou and Genoa, dated 21 July 1262. In 1346 Charles Grimaldi, Lord of Monaco, acquired it, and the princes of Monaco ruled it until the French Revolution.

In 1848, partly because of a tax on lemon exports, Menton and its neighbour Roquebrune seceded from Monaco and proclaimed the Free Cities of Menton and Roquebrune, hoping to join the Kingdom of Sardinia. Two years later they placed themselves under its protection and were administered by the House of Savoy for ten years.

The Treaty of Turin of 24 March 1860 provided for the annexation of the County of Nice to France, subject to a plebiscite. It was held on 15 and 16 April 1860, and Menton and Roquebrune voted 833 to 54 in favour. Napoleon III paid 4 million francs in compensation to the prince of Monaco, who renounced his rights on 2 February 1861.

James Henry Bennett's book Winter and Spring on the Shores of the Mediterranean (1861) made Menton a destination for sufferers of tuberculosis, and by the end of the 19th century tourism was an important part of its growth. British and Russian aristocrats built many of the hotels, villas and palaces that remain. In June 1940 Menton was the only sizable settlement captured by Italy in its invasion of France, and Italy annexed two thirds of the commune until 8 September 1943. American and Canadian troops of the First Special Service Force liberated it on 8 September 1944. It is nicknamed the Pearl of France and is known for its gardens.
mentuhotep-ii: Mentuhotep II succeeded his father Intef III on the throne at Thebes and ruled for 51 years according to the Turin Canon. He inherited the lands his predecessors had conquered from the first cataract in the south to Abydos in the north. The rival 10th Dynasty ruled Lower Egypt from Herakleopolis. His first fourteen years seem peaceful. In his fourteenth year, named the Year of the crime of Thinis, the Herakleopolitan kings apparently desecrated the ancient royal necropolis at Abydos, and he sent his armies north. At Deir el-Bahari a tomb held the linen-wrapped bodies of 60 soldiers killed in battle, their shrouds bearing his cartouche, and it is believed to be that of men who died in this conflict.

Reunification probably came shortly before his 39th regnal year, when he changed his titulary to Sematawy, 'He who unifies the two lands'. The process took time: commoners were buried with weapons, and an expedition to Punt sent by his successor some twenty years later still had to clear the Wadi Hammamat of rebels loyal to the fallen Herakleopolitan rulers. In his 29th and 31st years his vizier Khety led campaigns into Nubia, the first attested appearance of the term Kush in Egyptian records, and a garrison was posted at Elephantine.

After unification he reversed the decentralisation that had marked the First Intermediate Period. Nomarchs, whose offices had become hereditary in the 6th Dynasty, lost some of their power. He created the posts of Governor of Upper Egypt and Governor of Lower Egypt over them and sent officials from the capital to travel the country and supervise regional leaders. Nomarchs who had supported the 10th Dynasty, such as the governor of Asyut, certainly lost their power. His viziers were Bebi and Dagi, and the treasurer Meketre is among his officials.

His titularies show a return to Old Kingdom tradition and a programme of self-deification. His subjects regarded him as divine or half divine, and stelae of Senusret III and Amenemhat III, some 200 years later, record ceremonies performed on his statues.

Mentuhotep II was buried at Deir el-Bahari. His terraced mortuary temple, Akh-sut Nebhepetre, broke with the Old Kingdom pyramid complex and was the earliest mortuary temple where the king himself enacts ceremonies for the gods and is identified with Osiris. It inspired the temples of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III, built about 550 years later. Lord Dufferin began excavating it in 1859, Howard Carter found the black seated Ka statue of the king in 1898, and Naville, Winlock and Dieter Arnold followed.
meppen: Meppen lies in the central part of the Emsland, at the mouth of the Hase where it meets the Ems, between Lingen and Papenburg and about 20 kilometres from the Dutch border. The Nordradde and the Dortmund–Ems Canal also meet there. The name is said to stem from the word Mappe, meaning delta. Since the district reforms of 1977 it has been the administrative seat of the Emsland district.

The first documented mention dates from 834, in a deed of donation by the Frankish emperor Louis the Pious that transferred a missionary establishment of that name to the abbey of Corvey. Otto the Great granted the settlement coin minting and toll rights in 945 and market rights in 946. In 1252 Countess Jutta von Vechta-Ravensberg sold her possessions to the Bishop of Münster, which brought Meppen into the Lower Prince-Bishopric of Münster. Bishop Adolf granted town rights and permission to build fortifications in 1360. They were extended until 1660 and demolished during the Seven Years War.

After the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 1803 Meppen became the capital of the Duchy of Arenberg under Louis Engelbert. It was incorporated into the First French Empire in 1811 and occupied by Prussia in 1813 and 1814, and the Congress of Vienna awarded it with the Duchy of Arenberg to the Kingdom of Hanover. When Hanover was annexed by Prussia in 1866 Meppen followed, and in 1871 it became part of the German Empire.

In November 1938 local Nazi police and SA members destroyed the town synagogue and plundered Jewish property. In 1939 Stalag VI-B was set up at Meppen-Versen for Polish, French, Belgian, Soviet and Italian prisoners of war. In 1944 it became a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp, where over 1,700 forced labourers were held under severe conditions and over 20 percent died. Canadian forces liberated the town on 8 April 1945.

The centre has few historic buildings. The town hall was built in 1408 from glacial erratics and enlarged between 1601 and 1605. The Priory Church of St. Vitus, a late Gothic hall church, dates from about 1461–62, on the site of a stone building of the 9th century. The Koppelschleuse locks of 1826 to 1830 survive from the old Ems–Hase Canal.
merano: Merano, in German Meran, is a municipality in South Tyrol, northern Italy, and the second-largest city of South Tyrol after Bolzano. It lies in a basin at the entrance to the Passeier Valley and the Vinschgau, surrounded by mountains that rise to 3,335 metres. Both the Italian and German names are official, and an early form, Mairania, is recorded from 857.

The area has been inhabited since the third millennium BCE, and the history of the town proper begins in 15 BCE, when the Romans founded a road station there, Statio Maiensis. In the 13th century the Counts at Castle Tyrol raised it to the status of a city and made it capital of their County of Tyrol. The county passed to the Habsburg dynasty in 1363, and in 1420 Duke Friedrich IV of Austria moved the court to Innsbruck. Merano stayed the official capital until 1848 but lost almost all its importance as a trading point on the roads between Italy and Germany.

In 1809 a peasants' army won a victory over French and Bavarian forces on the Küchelberg above the city. In the 19th century its mild Alpine climate made Meran a spa town within Austria-Hungary, visited by Franz Kafka and Empress Elisabeth. After the First World War, under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye, it became part of Italy.

Merano combines Austrian and Italian cultural heritage. Its medieval city gates survive, as do the Gothic St Nicholas' Church and the Princely Castle, which was a residence of Archduke Sigismund of Austria. The spa years left the Kurhaus, the Stadttheater, the Empress Elisabeth Park and arched promenades along the Passer. Tirol Castle stands close by, and vineyards extend into the city.
mercantilism: Mercantilism became the dominant school of economic thought in Europe through the late Renaissance and the early modern period, before the rise of classical liberalism. Mercantilist practices appeared early in Venice, Genoa and Pisa, in their control of the Mediterranean trade in bullion. The Italian economist Antonio Serra wrote one of the first treatises on political economy in 1613. The term was first used only by critics such as Mirabeau and Adam Smith, and the older English term was the mercantile system. Smith saw the English merchant Thomas Mun as a major creator of the system through Treasure by Foreign Trade, published after his death in 1664.

In its simplest form mercantilism is bullionism, the view that a nation's wealth is measured by the gold and silver it holds. Its writers were concerned with the movement of money more than with hoarding. The aim was to maximise exports and minimise imports and to build state power at the expense of rivals. Policies included high tariffs, banning the export of gold and silver, and the Navigation Acts, which forbade trade to be carried in foreign ships.

In France it is closely tied to Jean-Baptiste Colbert, finance minister for 22 years in the 17th century, so that French mercantilism is sometimes called Colbertism. Under him industries were organised into guilds and monopolies, foreign artisans were brought in, and roads and canals were built. French industrial output grew considerably, but Britain and the Dutch Republic stayed supreme in trade.

Mercantilism fed imperial expansion, as European states conquered colonies as sources of gold or sugar and as exclusive markets, often through chartered monopolies such as the Dutch East India Company. If trade is seen as fixed, one state can increase its trade only by taking it from another, and the Anglo-Dutch Wars can be linked to such theories.

In the 18th century critics undermined it. In 1690 John Locke argued that prices vary in proportion to the quantity of money, and David Hume showed that a constant surplus of trade cannot last. Smith criticised the doctrine as a system serving traders, though he praised the Navigation Acts for their effect on British shipping.
mercator-projection: The Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical map projection first presented by the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. Earlier charts did not use it. The 13th-century portolan charts of the Mediterranean, the earliest to survive, are generally not believed to rest on any deliberate projection. They carried networks of windrose lines that helped set a ship's bearing, and over so small a region a course of constant bearing was approximately straight on the chart. Joseph Needham suggested that some Song dynasty star charts used the Mercator projection, but he gave no evidence, and the historian Kazuhiko Miyajima concluded from measurement that they used an equirectangular projection.

The projection can be pictured as wrapping a cylinder around a sphere, touching it along the equator, and unfolding the sphere onto the cylinder so that angles between intersecting curves are kept. Scale is exact along the equator and grows with distance from it, as the secant of the latitude: about 1.15 at 30 degrees, 2 at 60 degrees and over 11 at 85 degrees. Areas therefore swell towards the poles. Greenland appears about the size of Africa, though Africa is 14 times as large.

Its purpose was navigation. Any course of constant bearing, called a rhumb or loxodrome, appears as a straight segment, so a ship can keep one compass direction rather than making error-prone corrections. Mercator observed that on such a course a ship would not arrive by the shortest route but would surely arrive. He understood the difference between rhumb distance and great-circle distance, and advised that rhumb measurements suit short or moderate courses, especially at low latitudes.

In the 18th century it became the standard projection for navigation, and practically every printed marine chart is based on it. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was perhaps the commonest projection for world maps, until atlases largely abandoned it for such maps in the 1940s. Critics such as George Kellaway and Irving Fisher judged it unsuitable for general world maps. It has been conjectured that it made people think of countries near the equator as less important, but later perception studies have failed to find such an effect. Mercator himself used the equal-area sinusoidal projection to show relative areas. Variants remain in use, including Web Mercator for online maps and the transverse Mercator behind most national grid systems.
mercedes-sosa: Haydée Mercedes Sosa was born on 9 July 1935 in San Miguel de Tucumán, in the north-western Argentine province of Tucumán, of mestizo ancestry: French, Spanish and Diaguita. Her nickname la Negra, common in Argentina for people with a darker complexion, refers to her indigenous heritage. She began her career singing for the Peronist Party in Tucumán under the name Gladys Osorio. In 1950, at fifteen, she won a singing competition run by a local radio station. She recorded her first album, La voz de la zafra, in 1959.

A performance at the Cosquín National Folklore Festival in 1965, where fellow singer Jorge Cafrune brought her on stage from the audience, drew her to the attention of the Argentine public. She toured the United States and Europe in 1967 and widened her repertoire to include material from across Latin America. In the early 1970s she made two concept albums with the composer Ariel Ramírez and the lyricist Félix Luna, Cantata sudamericana and Mujeres argentinas, and in 1971 a tribute to the Chilean musician Violeta Parra that included Gracias a la vida, one of her signature songs. She also popularised songs by Milton Nascimento of Brazil and by Pablo Milanés and Silvio Rodríguez of Cuba.

After the military junta of Jorge Videla came to power in 1976, Sosa faced death threats against herself and her family but for many years refused to leave. At a concert in La Plata in 1979 she was searched and arrested on stage together with those attending, and they were released through international intervention. She was officially barred from performing and moved to Paris and then Madrid. She returned to Argentina in February 1982, several months before the military regime collapsed, and gave concerts at the Teatro Ópera in Buenos Aires, recorded as Mercedes Sosa en Argentina.

She played the Sistine Chapel in 1994 and in 2002 sold out both Carnegie Hall in New York and the Colosseum in Rome. Sosa disliked being called a protest singer; she held that an artist's constituency is the public and that it is the poetry that matters most. She served as a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador for Latin America and the Caribbean. She won Latin Grammy awards, including a lifetime achievement award in 2004.

Sosa was hospitalised in Buenos Aires on 18 September 2009 and died on 4 October 2009 of multiple organ failure, aged 74. Her body lay in the National Congress building, and three days of national mourning were ordered.
mercenary: A mercenary, also called a soldier of fortune, is a private individual who joins an armed conflict for personal profit, is otherwise an outsider to the conflict and is not a member of any other official military. Mercenaries fight for money or other forms of payment rather than for political interests. Whether a person counts as a mercenary may be a matter of degree, since financial and political interests can overlap.

Article 47 of the 1977 Protocol Additional to the Geneva Conventions gives the most widely accepted international definition. It lists conditions such as being specially recruited to fight, taking a direct part in hostilities, being motivated essentially by private gain, and being neither a national of a party to the conflict nor a member of its armed forces. A mercenary has no right to be a combatant or a prisoner of war.

Hired soldiers appear in the earliest records. Ramesses II of Egypt is said to have used 11,000 mercenaries in his battles in the thirteenth century BCE, and Egypt long recruited foreign corps such as the Medjay from Nubia. In 401 BCE Cyrus the Younger hired a large army of Greek mercenaries, the Ten Thousand, to seize the Persian throne from his brother Artaxerxes II. After Cyrus died at the Battle of Cunaxa, Xenophon helped lead the survivors north to the Black Sea, as he recounts in the Anabasis. Carthage was unusual in relying primarily on mercenaries.

Kingdoms of the Warring States period in China regularly employed them, and the Tang dynasty hired Tibetan and Uyghur soldiers against the Göktürks. In Japan the Saika group of Kii Province impeded the forces of Oda Nobunaga during the Siege of Ishiyama Hongan-ji between 1570 and 1580. In Nicaragua in 1855 the American William Walker, hired by the Liberals, defeated the Conservatives at the Battle of La Virgen and became the country's de facto ruler. By 1807 Muhammad Ali of Egypt had imported about 400 French mercenaries to train his army.

From the twentieth century mercenaries came to be seen as less entitled to protection under the rules of war. Foreign nationals who serve in a state's regular forces, such as the Gurkha units of the British and Indian armies and the French Foreign Legion, are not classed as mercenaries under Article 47, because they belong to its armed forces.
mercosur: Mercosur, called Mercosul in Portuguese, has roots in discussions of a Latin American regional market that go back to the treaty of 1960 establishing the Latin American Free Trade Association. In December 1985 the Brazilian president José Sarney and the Argentine president Raúl Alfonsín signed the Iguaçu Declaration, the basis for economic integration of the Southern Cone. Both countries had just come out of dictatorships and needed to turn their economies outwards. The Integration, Cooperation and Development Treaty of 1988 set the goal of a common market that others could join.

On 6 July 1990 Fernando Collor of Brazil and Carlos Menem of Argentina signed the Buenos Aires Act, aiming at full customs integration by 31 December 1994. Paraguay and Uruguay then showed strong interest in the process.

The four countries signed the Treaty of Asunción in 1991, setting the rules for a free trade zone, and the Protocol of Ouro Preto of 1994 completed its institutions. In 2001, on the tenth anniversary, the Mercosur flag was hoisted for the first time at its headquarters in Montevideo. Trade among the members, excluding Venezuela, grew from 10 billion US dollars in 1991 to 88 billion in 2010, though in 2010 this was only 16 percent of the four countries' total trade, comparable in importance to trade with the European Union.

Membership changed over time. Venezuela became an associate in 2004 and was admitted as a full member on 31 July 2012, after Paraguay was suspended following the removal of Fernando Lugo. Bolivia signed the protocol of accession in 2015 and became a full member in July 2024.

The Common Market Council is the highest body. It is made up of the ministers of foreign affairs and the economy of the members, who preside over it in rotating alphabetical order for six-month periods, and it decides by consensus. The Common Market Group is the executive body, coordinated by the foreign ministries, and work subgroups study matters such as customs, technical standards, transport and agricultural policy.

Mercosur promotes free trade within the zone and the movement of goods, people and currency, and now confines itself to a customs union with free internal trade and a common trade policy. Portuguese and Spanish are its working languages, and Guaraní is a recognised language.
merida-spain: Mérida lies 217 metres above sea level in the western-central part of the Iberian Peninsula, crossed by the Guadiana and Albarregas rivers, in the Province of Badajoz. The name comes from the Latin Emerita, 'retired' or 'veteran', and is part of the name Augusta Emerita given to the Roman colony. A hoard of gold jewellery excavated from a girl's grave in 1870, now in the British Museum, shows that the site was inhabited in prehistory.

Augustus ordered the town founded in 25 BCE to settle discharged soldiers of the V Alaudae and X Gemina. It guarded a strategic pass and the bridge over the Guadiana, and quickly became one of the most important cities of Roman Hispania. It was the capital of Lusitania and in the fourth century of the Diocese of Hispania, and a terminus of the Vía de la Plata, the Roman road linking the gold mines near Asturica Augusta with the south. In 409 it became capital of the short-lived Kingdom of the Alans under Attaces, who died in battle against the Visigoths in 418; the city was absorbed into the neighbouring Vandal kingdom and taken by the Visigoths in 469.

The Umayyad commander Musa ibn Nusayr conquered Mérida in 713, and it became capital of the Cora of Mérida. The Arabs reused and expanded Roman buildings, and the emir Abd ar-Rahman II built the Alcazaba in 835 on the Roman walls.

In the ninth century the Mozarabs of Mérida rebelled often against the caliphate, which contributed to the city's gradual decline, and during the Fitna of al-Andalus it became part of the Taifa of Badajoz. Its metropolitan seat passed to Santiago de Compostela in 1119. Alfonso IX of León reconquered the city in 1230 and gave it to the Order of Santiago. Recovery began in the fifteenth century. Monuments were damaged in the Napoleonic Wars, and Nationalist forces took the city on 10 August 1936 during the Spanish Civil War.

Mérida is the capital of the autonomous community of Extremadura, a status it received in 1983, and had 60,119 inhabitants in 2017. It preserves more major Roman monuments than any other city in Spain, among them the Roman theatre and amphitheatre, the remains of a circus and the Puente Romano, the longest surviving Roman bridge. Its archaeological site was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and the National Museum of Roman Art was designed by Rafael Moneo.
merida-yucatan: Mérida lies slightly inland from the north-west corner of the Yucatán Peninsula, about 35 kilometres from the Gulf of Mexico. The land is very flat, only 9 metres above sea level, and almost no surface water exists, though several cenotes give access to underground water. Many Maya sites lie in the area, among them Chichen Itza, Uxmal, Oxkintok, Sayil and Kabah. The historic centre follows the colonial Spanish pattern, with odd-numbered streets running east to west and even-numbered ones north to south, and with Calles 60 and 61 bounding the Plaza Grande.

The Spanish conquistadors, among them Francisco de Montejo the Younger and Juan de la Cámara, founded Mérida in 1542 and named it after Mérida in Extremadura, whose Roman ruins the Maya ruins reminded them of. The city stands on the Maya city of Ti'ho, also called Ichkanzihóo, "City of Five Hills", for its pyramids. Carved stones from the ruins went into the early Spanish buildings, and are visible in the cathedral, built in the late 16th century.

From colonial times to the middle of the 19th century Mérida was a walled city, intended to protect the peninsulares and criollos from periodic revolts by the Maya. Nahua troops who had accompanied Montejo settled in the districts of San Cristóbal, Santiago and San Román and were exempt from taxes for their military help.

The city is called La Ciudad Blanca, the White City, perhaps for the white limestone of its colonial façades. A folk story says it was named because only white Europeans were allowed to live inside it, but the first arches at its entrances were commissioned only in 1690, almost 150 years after its foundation.

In the late 19th century the surrounding area prospered by growing henequen, whose fibre was made into rope and twine and also into a traditional drink. By the early 20th century factories made tobacco, molasses, rum, soap and leather goods. Korean immigration to Mexico began in 1905, when more than a thousand people arrived in Yucatán from Jemulpo and settled around Mérida to work on henequen plantations.

Mérida is the capital and largest city of the Mexican state of Yucatán, with 921,770 people in 2020, and the cultural and financial centre of the peninsula. The Cathedral of Mérida is said to be the oldest cathedral on the mainland of the Americas. The city's heritage is a blend of Maya and Spanish culture formed in the colonial era.
merneptah: Merneptah was probably the fourth child of Ramesses II and Isetnofret and his thirteenth son. He came to power only because all his older brothers had died, and he was the first royal-born king since Tutankhamun. He appears as a prince on family stelae from Aswan and Silsila, dated to the thirtieth and thirty-third or thirty-fourth years of Ramesses II, alongside his parents, his sister Bintanath and his brothers Ramesses and Khaemwaset.

Little else is known of him before the fortieth year of his father's reign, when he became Overseer of the Army. After the death of his brother Khaemwaset in the fifty-fifth year, he was proclaimed crown prince and served as prince regent for the last twelve years of the old king's life. Mummy studies suggest that he was over fifty when he took the throne. His Great Royal Wife was Isetnofret II, probably his full sister or his niece.

Merneptah moved the administrative centre from Pi-Ramesses, his father's capital, back to Memphis, where he built a palace beside the temple of Ptah. He ruled for almost ten years, from 13 August 1213 BCE until his death on 2 May 1203 BCE.

In his fifth year Libyans threatened Egypt from the west, helped by the Sea Peoples, whom the texts name as the Ekwesh, Teresh, Lukka, Sherden and Shekelesh. The Libyan chief Meryre, son of Ded, had reached the fields of Perire, probably on the western edge of the Delta. Merneptah's account, inscribed beside the sixth pylon at Karnak and on the Athribis Stele, tells of a victorious battle of six hours in which the invaders threw down their weapons and fled. He claims to have killed 6,000 soldiers and taken 9,000 prisoners.

The same events appear in a poem on the Merneptah Stele, also called the Israel Stele. It also mentions the suppression of revolts in Canaan and says that 'Israel has been wiped out... its seed is no more', the first known ancient Egyptian record of Israel, named as a people rather than a country or city.

Merneptah died on 2 May 1203 BCE after a reign of almost ten years. He was buried in tomb KV8 in the Valley of the Kings, but his mummy was moved in ancient times and was found in 1898 among those in the tomb of Amenhotep II. It showed that he had suffered from arthritis and atherosclerosis and was about 1.71 metres tall. His son Seti II succeeded him, though not without challenge from a rival king, Amenmesse, who seized Upper Egypt and Kush during Seti's reign.
meroe: Meroë stood on the east bank of the Nile, about 35 kilometres north-east of Shendi and about 200 kilometres north-east of Khartoum. It lay on the edge of Butana, the region the ancients called the Island of Meroë. The Kushite rulers are said to have chosen the site, between the Fifth and Sixth Cataracts, because it lay on the fringe of the summer rainfall belt, was rich in iron ore and hardwood for ironworking, and gave access to trade routes to the Red Sea.

The Kingdom of Kush spanned about 800 BCE to about 350 CE, and its main capital was at first farther north at Napata. King Aspelta moved the capital to Meroë, possibly about 591 BCE, just after the pharaoh Psamtik II sacked Napata. From the reign of Arakamani, around 280 BCE, the royal burial ground also moved to Meroë. Herodotus described it as a great city said to be the mother city of the other Ethiopians.

In 23 BCE the Roman governor Publius Petronius invaded Nubia in answer to raids on southern Egypt and sacked Napata the next year. A peace treaty of 22 BCE was signed between Augustus and the Kushite queen Amanirenas. Meroë faded as a power from the 1st or 2nd century CE, weakened by the war with Roman Egypt and the decline of traditional industries. A Greek inscription of an Aksumite king, thought to be Ezana, was found at the site. Some authorities read it as proof that Aksum destroyed Kush, while others point to archaeological evidence of decline around 300.

The site is marked by more than two hundred pyramids in three groups, many in ruins, with the proportions of Nubian pyramids. Frédéric Cailliaud brought the ruins to European notice in 1821, and excavations followed under C. R. Lepsius in 1844, E. A. Wallis Budge in 1902 and 1905 and Garstang from 1910. The Archeological Sites of Meroë were listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites in 2011.
merovech: Merovech is the ancestor of the Merovingian dynasty and the grandfather of its founder Clovis I, reportedly a king of the Salian Franks, but records of his existence are mixed with legend and myth. Gregory of Tours names him only once, as the father of Childeric I, and remains vague about his relationship to Chlodio, a roughly contemporary Frankish warlord who pushed from the Silva Carbonaria as far south as the Somme. The Chronicle of Fredegar recounts that Merovech was born after Chlodio's wife met a sea creature while bathing, and leaves unclear whether the creature or Chlodio was his father. Another theory takes this legend as a mythological past created to support the rising Frankish rule in Western Europe.

Chlodio is said to have been defeated by Flavius Aëtius at Vicus Helena in Artois in 448, and Ian S. Wood would therefore place Merovech, his apparent son, in the second half of the fifth century. Merovech may have been one of several barbarian kings who joined the Roman general Aëtius against the Huns under Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451. The Salian Franks, bound by a treaty with Rome, probably fought there, but the sources do not say who led them.

The Roman historian Priscus described a fair-haired youth in Rome whom Aëtius had adopted, and said Attila's pretext for war on the Franks was the death of their king and a quarrel among his sons over the succession. Historians are divided on whether Merovech figures in this account. Erich Zöllner thinks the prince was a Ripuarian Frank, Émilienne Demougeot sees Merovech as the king who died, and Christian Settipani takes Merovech to be the son allied with Rome.

Some historians, such as Georg Waitz, suggest Merovech may be a mythological figure, a son of the sea revered before the Franks conversion. Étienne Renard suggests he may be an eponymous founder of the lineage, whose name is linked to no act of war or event. An Austrasian genealogy made between 629 and 639 lists Chloio, Glodobode, Mereveo, Hilbricco and Childeric among the Salian kings, and its order is debated. The legend of his conception was taken up in the 1982 book The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail, whose claim of descent from Jesus has no evidence behind it.
merovingian-dynasty: The Merovingians first appear as kings of the Franks in the Roman army of northern Gaul. The dynastic name means sons of Merovech, a Salian king who was the father of Childeric I, the first well-known Merovingian king. The Chronicle of Fredegar, written in the 7th century, implies that the family descended from a sea-beast like a quinotaur. Today the tale is usually seen as an attempt to explain the name Merovech, meaning sea-bull. Unlike the Anglo-Saxon royal genealogies, the Merovingians never claimed descent from a god.

Their long hair distinguished them from other Franks, who commonly cut theirs short. A Merovingian whose hair was cut could not rule, and a rival could be removed from the succession by being tonsured and sent to a monastery.

In 486 Clovis I defeated Syagrius, a Roman military leader who competed with the Merovingians for power in northern Gaul. According to Gregory of Tours, he adopted his wife Clotilda's Nicene Christian faith when other Germanic tribes were largely Arian. In 507 he defeated the Visigoths at the Battle of Vouillé. The kingdom was treated as a single yet divisible patrimony, so Clovis's four sons divided it, and it stayed divided, with brief exceptions, until 679. The main divisions were Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy and Aquitaine. The Franks conquered Burgundy in 534. In 613 Clotaire II reunited the entire realm.

His son Dagobert I, who died in 639, is commonly seen as the last powerful Merovingian king. Later kings are called rois fainéants, do-nothing kings, and real power passed to the mayors of the palace. Pepin the Middle triumphed at the Battle of Tertry in 687, and his son Charles Martel defeated the Moors at the Battle of Tours in 732. Charles's son Pepin the Short deposed the last king, Childeric III, in 751, with the blessing of Pope Zachary.

On a king's death his property was divided among his heirs as if private. Kings appointed counts to defend, administer and judge, and the counts raised armies, which acclaimed a new king by raising him on their shields. Law depended on a man's origin: the Salian Franks had the Lex Salica, first tentatively codified in 511. Theudebert I was the first to issue distinctly Merovingian coinage. Kings and queens used the church to their advantage, awarding monasteries and bishoprics to supporters, and the most characteristic Merovingian literature is the lives of saints. The main sources are Gregory of Tours, the Chronicle of Fredegar and the Liber Historiae Francorum.
merseburg: Merseburg stands on the river Saale in southern Saxony-Anhalt, about 14 kilometres south of Halle and 30 kilometres west of Leipzig. It is the capital of the Saalekreis district. The town was first mentioned in 850.

King Henry the Fowler built a royal palace at Merseburg, and in the vicinity in 933 he won his great victory over the Hungarians at the Battle of Riade. From 968 until the Protestant Reformation the town was the seat of the Bishop of Merseburg, and it was a favourite residence of the German kings in the 10th, 11th and 12th centuries. Fifteen diets were held there during the Middle Ages, and its fairs had an importance that later passed to those of Leipzig. After the death of Ekkehard on 3 April 1002, Bolesław I Chrobry took Merseburg and Meissen with the help of the local Slavic population.

From 1657 to 1738 it was the residence of the Dukes of Saxe-Merseburg, and in 1815, after the Napoleonic Wars, it became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony. The Merseburg Incantations were rediscovered there in 1841. Written in Old High German, they are the only preserved German documents with a heathen theme: one is a charm to release warriors caught in battle, the other a charm to heal a horse's sprained foot. From 1909 to 1913 Carl Bosch and Friedrich Bergius laid the scientific foundations of high-pressure ammonia synthesis, and Merseburg became an industrial town. In 23 air raids of World War II the historic centre was almost destroyed.

The Merseburg Cathedral of St John the Baptist, founded in 1015 and rebuilt in the 13th and 16th centuries, stands beside the episcopal palace of the 15th century. The town also has the German Museum of Chemistry. Among its natives are the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg and the biologist Ernst Haeckel.
mersin: The coast has been inhabited since the 9th millennium BCE. John Garstang's excavations of the hill of Yumuktepe revealed 23 levels of occupation, with fortifications put up around 4500 BCE. In ancient times the place was ruled by many states, including the Hittites, Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids and Lagids. Under the Greeks it was called Zephyrion, and it profited from its natural harbour, its position on the trade routes of southern Anatolia and trade in molybdenum, or white lead, from nearby mines. It also minted its own coins.

In the Wars of the Diadochi, Ptolemy I Soter established himself there with a fleet. In Roman times the area was part of the province of Cilicia, whose capital was Tarsus, and Mersin was the major port. It was renamed Hadrianopolis in honour of the emperor Hadrian. It was also an episcopal see, and its bishops attended councils from the First Council of Constantinople in 381 to the Council in Trullo in 692.

The Arabs conquered Cilicia in the early 7th century, when Mersin appears to have been a deserted site. The Byzantines held the region between 965 and about 1080, followed by the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. From 1362 to 1513 the Ramadanid Emirate governed it, first under the Mamluk Sultanate and later under the Ottoman Empire. Sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluks in 1517 and annexed Cilicia.

Mersin remained a modest coastal village for much of the Ottoman period. It was only towards the middle of the 19th century that it began to flourish as the port of the Çukurova region. During the American Civil War the region became a major supplier of cotton, and in 1866 railways were extended to link the cotton-growing areas with Mersin. In 1909 its port received 645 steamships and 797,433 tons of goods. French and British troops occupied the city in 1918, and the Turkish army recovered it in 1921 at the end of the Franco-Turkish War.

Mersin is the capital of Mersin Province, formerly İçel, and is made up of four district municipalities: Akdeniz, Mezitli, Toroslar and Yenişehir. Its name comes from the myrtle plant Myrsine, which grows abundantly there. The city has a Mediterranean climate and the longest seashore in Turkey. Its port is an international hub, and the Mersin Free Zone, set up in 1986, was the first in Turkey. Nearby are the ruins of Soli Pompeiiopolis, where two colonnades of the 2nd or 3rd century remain.
merv: Merv, also called the Merv Oasis, lay on the Murghab River, whose canals irrigate cereals, melons, rice and cotton. Archaeological surveys show village life on the site from the 3rd millennium BCE. Under the Achaemenid Empire the city, named Margu in the Behistun inscriptions of about 515 BCE, belonged to a satrapy of Darius the Great. The Seleucid ruler Antiochus I Soter renamed it Antiochia Margiana and rebuilt it at the site now known as Gyaur Gala.

After the Sasanian king Ardashir I took the city, its coins document almost four centuries of direct Sasanian rule. Zoroastrians, Buddhists, Manichaeans and Christians of the Church of the East lived there, and from the 5th to the 11th century it was the seat of an East Syrian metropolitan province. After the Arab conquest it became the capital of the Umayyad province of Khorasan. In 671 Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan sent 50,000 Arab troops there as a garrison, and Qutayba ibn Muslim used it as a base from 705 to 715 to subdue Balkh, Bukhara and Fergana.

The Seljuk leader Tughril took Merv peacefully in 1037, and from 1118 it was the capital of the whole Seljuk empire. Geographers called it the capital of the eastern Islamic world, and Omar Khayyam spent years working at its observatory. In 1221 it opened its gates to Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan; Ibn al-Athir's account of the massacre that followed gives about 700,000 dead. Merv never regained its prosperity. In 1788 and 1789 Shah Murad of Bukhara razed it and broke its dams, and by the late 19th century the oasis was abandoned.

The ruins stand near Baýramaly in Turkmenistan, about 30 kilometres east of the city of Mary, and are preserved as the State Historical and Cultural Park Ancient Merv, established in 1987. UNESCO lists the site as a World Heritage Site. Merv is several walled cities built beside one another in different eras: Erk Gala of the Achaemenid period, Gyaur Gala of the Hellenistic and Sasanian city, the large city of the Abbasid and Seljuk periods, and the small Timurid city. The Tomb of Ahmad Sanjar still stands. Turkmen and British archaeologists have worked there since 1992.
mesa-verde: Mesa Verde, Spanish for green table, lies near the Four Corners region of the American Southwest. Streams eroded the hard sandstone to cut its canyons, and elevations range from about 1,829 to 2,613 metres. The land slants to the south, which contributed to the formation of the alcoves that have preserved its cliff dwellings. Domínguez and Escalante, seeking a route from Santa Fe to California, named the region in 1776 for its tree-covered heights, but never got close enough to see the stone villages.

Nomadic Paleo-Indians were in the wider region by about 9500 BCE and used the mesa in increasing numbers from about 7500 BCE. Archaic people followed, and by 1000 BCE corn had arrived and the Basketmaker culture emerged. The Ancestral Puebloans developed from it by 750 CE, living by hunting, gathering and farming corn, beans and squash. In the Pueblo I period they built interconnected year-round houses and used the old pit-houses mainly for community ceremonies.

By the end of the 12th century they were building the large cliff dwellings. Cliff Palace, in the largest alcove, has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas and housed some 125 people, probably as part of a community of sixty nearby pueblos. Long House was built around 1200 and occupied until 1280, and Spruce Tree House, with 130 rooms, was built between 1211 and 1278. A log at Balcony House was dated to 1278. Severe and prolonged droughts brought social and environmental instability, and by 1285 the people had moved south to Arizona and New Mexico, including the Rio Chama, the Albuquerque Basin and the Pajarito Plateau.

The Wetherill family, ranchers who were friendly with the Ute, learned of the cliff dwellings from a Ute man named Acowitz, who called the largest a sacred place. In 1891 the mineralogist Gustaf Nordenskiöld, a guest of the Wetherills, recorded and photographed the sites and sent many artefacts to Sweden; his 1893 book, The Cliff Dwellers of the Mesa Verde, and the shipment raised concern for protection. Congress and President Theodore Roosevelt established the national park in 1906, and in 1911 the Ute reluctantly traded 10,000 acres on Chapin Mesa for land on Ute Mountain. The park, in Montezuma County, Colorado, preserves more than 600 cliff dwellings and became a World Heritage Site in 1978, the only one in Colorado.
meskhetian-turks: The Meskhetian Turks, also called Ahiska Turks, speak the Kars dialect of Turkish and belong to the Hanafi school of Sunni Islam. They historically lived in Meskheti, the region of Georgia along the Turkish border. Turkic tribes settled there as early as the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the Turkish presence began with the Ottoman expedition of 1578. By the Peace of Amasya in 1555 Meskheti had been divided between the Safavids and the Ottomans, and by the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 all of it fell under Ottoman control. Most Meskhetian Turks see themselves as descended from Ottoman settlers.

Pro-Georgian historiography has argued that they are Turkified Meskhetians, a Georgian ethnographic subgroup converted to Islam under Ottoman rule. The anthropologist Anatoly Khazanov has argued that this oversimplifies the matter, because their traditional culture, though it held some Georgian elements, was close to the Turkish one. Soviet documents of 1944 called them simply Turks, and the term Meskhetian came into use only in the late 1950s. Most call themselves Turks or Ahiskan Turks.

On 15 November 1944 the Soviet government under Joseph Stalin ordered the deportation of the Meskhetian Turks from Georgia. They were secretly driven from their homes and loaded onto rail cars, and as many as 30,000 to 50,000 died of hunger, thirst and cold. They had been accused of smuggling, banditry and espionage with their kin across the border. The Soviet Union was preparing a pressure campaign against Turkey, and in June 1945 Vyacheslav Molotov demanded the cession of Kars, Ardahan and Artvin. Stalin wanted the strategic border region cleared of people likely to be hostile to Soviet intentions. The deportation was officially acknowledged only in 1968.

Unlike other deported Muslim groups, the Meskhetians were not rehabilitated or permitted to return. In 1970 the leaders of their national movement asked the Turkish embassy in Moscow to let them emigrate to Turkey, and the Soviet government answered by arresting them. In 1989 riots broke out in the Fergana Valley between Meskhetian Turks and Uzbeks. Hundreds were killed or injured and nearly 1,000 properties were destroyed. About 70,000 went to Azerbaijan, and others to Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Ukraine.

The Soviet census of 1989 counted 207,502 Turks in the Soviet Union, but many Meskhetian Turks had been recorded as Azeri, Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek, so the official figures understate them. They remain dispersed across the former Soviet Union and live also in Turkey and the United States. Only a few hundred have been able to return to Georgia.
mesoamerica: Mesoamerica lies on the isthmus joining North and South America, between about 10° and 22° north. It covers central and southern Mexico, all of Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, western Honduras and the Greater Nicoya region of Nicaragua and Costa Rica, although its extent varied through time. Its lowlands, below 1,000 metres, are mostly tropical, while the highlands between 1,000 and 2,000 metres are generally temperate. The northern Yucatán Peninsula has almost no rivers and no lakes, and its water comes from aquifers reached through natural openings called cenotes.

Cultivation began as early as 7000 BCE with squash and chili, and maize, beans, tomato and avocado followed. By 2000 BCE maize was the staple crop. No single society was self-sufficient, so regions specialised in local resources and traded them, long-distance trade being mostly in luxuries such as obsidian, jade, cacao and Spondylus shells. The Olmec of the Gulf Coast built the first complex civilisation, at San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán, La Venta and Tres Zapotes, occupied from roughly 1200 to 400 BCE.

In the Preclassic period Maya centres such as El Mirador and Tikal arose, and the Zapotec founded Monte Albán. The first true Mesoamerican writing systems appeared among the Epi-Olmec and Zapotec, and the tradition reached its height in the Classic Maya logosyllabic script. Counting was vigesimal, with bars worth five and dots worth one. In the Classic period Teotihuacan and Tikal were the dominant cities, and Teotihuacan took part in a far-reaching network of exchange, its talud-tablero architecture being copied at distant sites.

After Teotihuacan collapsed around 600 CE, Xochicalco and Cholula competed in central Mexico, and Nahua peoples moved south into the region. In the Postclassic period the Toltec dominated central Mexico and the Mixtec Oaxaca, while Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán led the Maya north. The Aztecs built a tributary empire over most of central Mesoamerica. The Spanish conquest of the 16th century ended the tradition, and Eurasian diseases such as smallpox and measles killed upwards of 90% of the indigenous people. Many descendants still speak their ancestral languages.
mesopotamia: Mesopotamia lies within the Tigris–Euphrates river system, in the northern part of the Fertile Crescent, and corresponds roughly to the territory of modern Iraq. In the broader sense it also includes parts of present-day southwestern Iran, southeastern Turkey, northeastern Syria and Kuwait. The climate is semi-arid, with a vast desert expanse in the north that gives way in the south to a region of marshes, lagoons, mudflats and reed banks of about 15,000 square kilometres. In the south the two rivers unite and empty into the Persian Gulf. The name comes from the Greek for land between rivers.

Mesopotamia is the site of the earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution, from around 10,000 BCE. Writing emerged there in a pictographic script, proto-cuneiform, in the Uruk IV period, in the late 4th millennium BCE, and the documented record of events begins in the early third millennium BCE with cuneiform records of early dynastic kings. The Sumerians and Akkadians dominated the region from the beginning of recorded history, around 3100 BCE, to the fall of Babylon in 539 BCE. The rise of empires began with Sargon of Akkad around 2350 BCE.

In the early second millennium BCE Mesopotamian society divided into Assyria in the north and Babylonia in the south. From 900 to 612 BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire controlled much of the ancient Near East. The Babylonians, long overshadowed by Assyria, then seized power and dominated the region for a century as the final independent Mesopotamian realm until the modern era. In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great conquered Mesopotamia for the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander the Great took it in 332 BCE; among his successors the Seleucids emerged victorious.

Around 150 BCE the region was under the Parthian Empire and became a battleground between Romans and Parthians. In 226 CE the eastern regions fell to the Sassanid Persians under Ardashir I, and the division of the region between the Roman and Sassanid empires lasted until the Muslim conquest of the 7th century CE, after which it came to be known as Iraq.

The earliest language written in Mesopotamia was Sumerian. Akkadian became dominant under the Akkadian and Assyrian empires, but Sumerian was kept for administrative, religious, literary and scientific purposes. Mesopotamian mathematics used a base-60 numeral system, the source of the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle, and Babylonian astronomers could predict eclipses and solstices.

Mesopotamia corresponds roughly to modern Iraq. Modern Assyrians remain descendants of the native Mesopotamians, and the Marsh Iraqis are genetically and culturally the closest modern people to the ancient Sumerians.
mesrop-mashtots: Mesrop Mashtots was born in the village of Hatsekats in the canton of Taron. His father was named Vardan; scholars have taken him for a priest, a nobleman, a member of the Mamikonian clan or a peasant. His pupil and biographer Koriun says he received a Greek education, and he also knew Middle Persian and Syriac. In the late 380s he moved to the Armenian capital, Vagharshapat, and worked at the royal court, where sources give him posts including royal chancellor. Around 394 he became a monk and a hermit, then gathered 40 disciples and, with the blessing of the Catholicos Sahak Partev, began missionary work among Armenians, many of whom were still pagan.

Armenia had lost its independence in 387 and was divided between the Byzantine Empire and Persia. Armenians read Christian texts in Greek, Persian and Syriac, which suited the sounds of their language poorly, so scripture and liturgy were largely unintelligible to the faithful. Mashtots, helped by Sahak and King Vramshapuh, and after consulting the bishop Daniel and the monk Rufinus, created an alphabet of thirty-six letters around 405; two more were added in the twelfth century. He founded schools to teach it and sent pupils to Edessa, Constantinople and other centres to study Greek and bring back texts.

The Bible was translated, the version in use being completed about 434, and the decrees of the first three ecumenical councils and many works of the Greek Fathers followed. Medieval Armenian sources also credit him with the Georgian and Caucasian Albanian alphabets; this is disputed, and most scholars link the Georgian script to the conversion of Iberia.

Mashtots survived Sahak by about six months and died on 17 February 440. He is buried at a chapel in Oshakan. The Armenian Apostolic Church keeps two feasts for him, and pilgrims visit his grave. Armenian writers treat him as the founder of Armenian literature and education and a symbol of the language, church and school system; Koriun compared his return after inventing the alphabet to Moses descending from Mount Sinai. Soviet historians presented him as a secular figure, and the Catholicos Karekin I objected in 1991 that his work was described in purely political terms.
messiah-handel: George Frideric Handel had lived in London since 1712 and was known chiefly for Italian opera. He turned to English oratorio in the 1730s in response to changes in public taste, and Messiah was his sixth work in the genre. Its text was compiled by Charles Jennens from the King James Bible and the Psalms of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer. Jennens was a wealthy landowner who had helped to finance the publication of Handel's scores since 1725 and who received Handel at his estate at Gopsall.

Handel received the text some time after 10 July 1741 and began work on 22 August. He finished Part I in outline by 28 August, Part II by 6 September and Part III by 12 September, and completed the work on 14 September, 24 days in all. Jennens regarded this speed as careless negligence, and the two men remained on strained terms because Handel refused the improvements Jennens urged.

The work is not in dramatic form: its singers play no characters and there is almost no direct speech. Jennens meant it as a reflection on Jesus as the Messiah, not a dramatisation of his life. Part I moves from the prophecies of Isaiah and others to the annunciation to the shepherds. Part II treats the Passion and ends with the Hallelujah chorus. Part III covers Paul's teaching on the resurrection of the dead and the glorification of Christ in heaven.

Handel scored it for two trumpets, timpani, two oboes, two violins, viola and basso continuo. The musicologist Percy M. Young notes its orchestral restraint. The trumpets, introduced in Part I in the chorus Glory to God, are heard afterwards only in The trumpet shall sound, in Hallelujah and in the final chorus, Worthy is the Lamb. Several movements borrow from Handel's Italian cantatas, among them For unto us a child is born.

Handel was invited to Dublin by the Duke of Devonshire, the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and gave subscription concerts there in the winter of 1741 to 1742. The Dublin reception was warm, but the London premiere at Covent Garden on 23 March 1743 was not. Critics argued that so exalted a subject did not belong in a theatre or with secular singer-actresses, and Handel billed it as a New Sacred Oratorio.

During the 1750s it was performed increasingly at festivals and cathedrals. A fashion for large forces began in 1784, when the Westminster Abbey concerts used 525 performers, and a Great Handel Festival at the Crystal Palace in 1857 used a chorus of 2,000. Mozart's reorchestration, Der Messias, began efforts to update the scoring. From the late 20th century performance has moved towards Handel's original intentions, though large productions continue. The autograph manuscript is in the British Library.
messina: Messina stands in the north-eastern corner of Sicily, on the western shore of the Strait of Messina, and is an important access point to Calabria on the mainland, at Villa San Giovanni and Reggio Calabria. Its municipal area of about 213.75 square kilometres stretches along 56 kilometres of coast, which makes it the longest and most maritime city in Italy. The climate is subtropical Mediterranean, with long hot summers and a wet, mild winter.

The early name of the city was Zancle, which Thucydides derived from a Siculian word meaning scythe, because of the shape of its natural harbour. At the beginning of the 5th century BCE Anaxilas of Rhegium settled refugees from Messenia there and renamed it Messene. It was Messana in the Roman age and became Messina in the Byzantine period. It was a major Roman city, contracted under Byzantine and Arab rule, and rose sharply in importance in the Norman era. Between the late Middle Ages and the mid-17th century it competed with Palermo to be the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily.

After an anti-Spanish revolt Messina was put to fire and sword in 1678, and its ruling class was annihilated. An earthquake seriously damaged it in 1783, and in 1908 another destroyed it almost entirely and killed about half the population. Rebuilding began in 1912, largely in the Liberty style. Allied bombers heavily attacked the city in 1943 during the landing in Sicily, in some 2,800 air raids, and it received the Gold Medal of Military Valor.

Messina is the capital of its metropolitan city and the third largest city on Sicily. Its port, for thousands of years one of the main commercial crossroads of the Mediterranean, is the first in Italy by number of passengers in transit, with ferries to Villa San Giovanni. The University of Messina was founded in 1548 by Pope Paul III, and the city has been an archdiocese since the same year. The Museo Regionale holds paintings by Caravaggio and by the Renaissance painter Antonello da Messina. The Good Friday procession of the Barette goes back to 1610.
mestizo: The Spanish word mestizo comes from the Latin mixticius, meaning mixed. It is documented as early as 1275, when it referred to the offspring of an Egyptian and a Canaanite Jew, and was first recorded in English in 1582. In the Spanish colonial period it became one of the labels of the castas, the mixed groups of the colonies. It was a formal label in censuses, parish registers and Inquisition trials, and priests and royal officials could classify persons as mestizos, though individuals also used the word of themselves.

The Spanish colonies developed a complex set of racial terms, often called the sistema de castas. Archival research shows that the labels were not fixed through a person's life, and that in colonial Mexico the category was used flexibly to register births in parishes, without a strict genealogical pattern. The casta paintings made mainly in eighteenth-century Mexico, showing racial types in hierarchical groups, have shaped how modern scholars picture the system.

The term is used chiefly for people whose identity derives mostly from mixing between Spanish and Native heritage. It can also refer to other mixed peoples of partial Spanish descent, such as Filipino Mestizos, and in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands it meant people of mixed Chamorro or Filipino and Spanish ancestry. In Central America, Ladino is a colonial-era term for Spanish speakers who were neither colonial elites nor Indigenous.

With the Bourbon reforms and the independence of the Americas the caste system disappeared and the term lost popularity. The noun mestizaje, for racial mixing, came into use only in the twentieth century. In Mexico the figure of the mestizo became central to a new independent identity, neither wholly Spanish nor wholly Indigenous, and after the Mexican Revolution the government promoted the mestizaje ideology to build a unified identity without racial distinctions. The 1930 census used the word for all Mexicans who did not speak an Indigenous language.

In modern Latin America mestizo is more a cultural term, and indio is kept for those who maintain a separate Indigenous identity. The 1940 census of Peru, the last to use racial categories, grouped mestizos with whites, and together they were more than 53 percent of the population.
methodism: Methodism began as a revival movement within the Church of England, led by John Wesley (1703–1791), his younger brother Charles Wesley (1707–1788) and George Whitefield. The brothers founded the Holy Club at the University of Oxford, whose members took Communion weekly, fasted, avoided most amusements and visited the sick, the poor and prisoners. Fellow students branded them Methodists for the way they used rule and method in their religious affairs. In 1735 both brothers went to North America at the invitation of General James Oglethorpe, founder of the Georgia Colony, as ministers to the colonists and missionaries to the Native Americans, but they were unsuccessful and returned conscious of their lack of genuine faith.

Wesleyan theology centres on sanctification and the transforming effect of the Holy Spirit on a Christian's character. Methodists hold the Arminian view that Christ died for all people and that salvation is open to all, against Calvinist predestination, although Whitefield and several other early leaders were Calvinistic Methodists. Scripture is the primary authority, read with Christian tradition and the historic creeds, and most Methodists recognise two sacraments, baptism and Holy Communion.

Worship combines the liturgy of the Book of Common Prayer with the preaching service, extempore prayer, hymns, many written by Charles Wesley, the quarterly lovefeast and the watchnight service. Members joined class meetings for encouragement. Early Methodists dressed plainly, fasted weekly and condemned gambling, theatre and dancing.

Early Methodism drew followers from all levels of society, and its preachers took the message to outcasts such as criminals. It gave women authority in church leadership, but their role diminished sharply after 1790 as the churches became more structured and male-dominated. In the United States it became the religion of many enslaved people, who later formed black churches in the Methodist tradition.

Methodism became a separate denomination after Wesley's death and spread through the British Empire and the United States by missionary work: to the Caribbean from 1760, to Newfoundland in 1763 and to China in 1847. It is widespread in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. There is no single Methodist church with universal authority; Methodists belong to many independent denominations, called connexions.
metz: Metz lies on the banks of the Moselle and the Seille, 43 km from the Schengen tripoint where the borders of France, Germany and Luxembourg meet. Several branches of the Moselle form islands there, which the urban plan has taken in. In ancient times the town was known as the city of the Mediomatrici, then as Divodurum Mediomatricum, meaning Holy Village or Holy Fortress of the Mediomatrici. During the 5th century the name evolved to Mettis, from which the present spelling comes.

Before the conquest of Gaul in 52 BCE Metz was the oppidum of the Celtic Mediomatrici. Under Roman rule it quickly became one of the principal towns of Gaul, with a population of 40,000, until its transfer to the Franks about the end of the 5th century. Between the 6th and 8th centuries it was the residence of the Merovingian kings of Austrasia. After the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it became the capital of the Kingdom of Lotharingia, and was in the end integrated into the Holy Roman Empire with semi-independent status. In the 12th century it became a republic, which stood until the 15th century.

Gregorian chant was created in Metz in the 8th century as a fusion of Gallican and ancient Roman repertory, and was then called Messin chant. The bishops of Metz, notably Saint Chrodegang, promoted its use for the Roman liturgy in Gallic lands. The city was also a centre of Carolingian manuscript illumination, producing the Drogo Sacramentary.

Metz is the prefecture of the Moselle department. Its Gothic Saint Stephen's Cathedral, built during the 13th century, has the largest expanse of stained-glass windows in the world, and the Germans' Gate of the 13th century is the last medieval bridge castle in France. The Basilica of Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains is described as the oldest church in France. The city is on France's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List. Since 1919 a local law, running parallel to French law, has preserved rules applied before 1870 and enacted by Germany between 1871 and 1918.
meurthe-et-moselle: The department is part of the Grand Est region and of the traditional region of Lorraine, and takes its name from two rivers, the Meurthe and the Moselle. It borders the departments of Meuse to the west, Vosges to the south, and Moselle and Bas-Rhin to the east. To the north it reaches the Belgian province of Luxembourg and the country of Luxembourg, by a salient formed by the arrondissement of Val-de-Briey. It is one of two French departments that border Luxembourg.

It extends for 130 km from north to south and is between 7 and 103 km wide. Its chief rivers are the Moselle, the Meurthe, the Chiers and the Vezouze, and part of it lies within the Lorraine Regional Natural Park.

The department was created in 1871, at the end of the Franco-Prussian War, from the parts of the former departments of Moselle and Meurthe that remained French territory. Its boundary with Moselle was the frontier between France and Germany from 1871 to 1919 and again between 1940 and 1944. Only one change has been made since. In 1997 the small commune of Han-devant-Pierrepont, previously in the Meuse department, was incorporated into Meurthe-et-Moselle for administrative reasons.

Nancy is the prefecture and the largest city. The department had 732,236 inhabitants in 2023, and its people are known as Meurthe-et-Mosellans. The area around Nancy is highly urbanised, whereas the Saintois in the south remains rural.

The economy depended heavily on mining until the 1960s, with iron, salt and lime extraction sites. Around Nancy it now rests largely on services, research and higher education. Air services are provided by Metz–Nancy–Lorraine Airport, and residents also use the airports of Luxembourg and Strasbourg.
meuse: The Meuse rises at Pouilly-en-Bassigny, in the commune of Le Châtelet-sur-Meuse on the Langres plateau, and flows north past Sedan, the head of navigation, and Charleville-Mézières into Belgium. At Namur it is joined by the Sambre. Beyond Namur it winds east, passes Liège and turns north, forming part of the Belgian-Dutch border. In the Netherlands it passes Venlo and turns west to join the delta it shares with the Rhine and the Scheldt.
The name comes from the Latin Mosa, which derives from a Celtic or Proto-Celtic name probably related to the English word maze, a reference to the river's twists and turns.

From 1301 the upper Meuse roughly marked the western border of the Holy Roman Empire with the Kingdom of France, after Count Henry III of Bar had to receive the western part of the County of Bar as a French fief from King Philip IV. In 1408 a Burgundian army led by John the Fearless helped John III against the citizens of Liège, who were in revolt. After defeating them, John ordered the drowning in the Meuse of burghers and nobles whose loyalties he suspected.

The border stayed relatively stable until King Henry II annexed the Three Bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun in 1552, and until the occupation of the Duchy of Lorraine by the forces of King Louis XIII in 1633. The lower Belgian, Walloon, stretch of the valley, part of the sillon industriel, was the first fully industrialised area on the European continent.

In the Netherlands, a flood in the late Middle Ages connected the Maas with the Merwede at Woudrichem. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the connection with the Rhine was closed off and the Maas was given a new artificial mouth, the Bergse Maas, which reduced the risk of flooding. This was regarded as the main achievement of Dutch hydraulic engineering before the Zuiderzee Works and Delta Works. The Meuse and its crossings were a key objective in the Battle of France and the Battle of Sedan, and again in the Battle of the Bulge in December 1944 and January 1945.

The river is about 925 km long and is navigable over a substantial part of its length, linking the ports of Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Antwerp with industrial areas upstream as far as Liège and Namur. The river's basin of about 36,000 km2 lies mostly in Wallonia, France and the Netherlands. As a major communication route the Meuse gave its name to Mosan art, and Joachim Patinir painted its landscape.
mexican-american-war: Mexico became independent from Spain with the Treaty of Córdoba in 1821 and a republic in 1824. Its governments were unstable, and the north was poorly controlled and open to raids by Comanche, Apache and Navajo. The secession of Texas in 1836 was followed by the Treaties of Velasco, which Mexico refused to recognise. The United States annexed Texas in 1845, and the border was disputed: the United States and Texas claimed the Rio Grande, while Mexico claimed the more northerly Nueces River.

James K. Polk was elected in 1844 on a platform of expanding to Oregon, California and Texas. His mission to Mexico offered $25 million for the disputed land, California and everything in between, and was refused. Mexican forces repelled a group of US soldiers on 25 April 1846, and Polk used the clash to persuade Congress to declare war.

Stephen W. Kearny's Army of the West occupied New Mexico, while the Pacific Squadron blockaded the Pacific coast. Zachary Taylor won at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma and then took Monterrey after hard fighting. Polk then sent a second army under General Winfield Scott, who carried out the first major amphibious landing in US history at Veracruz on 9 March 1847 with about 12,000 men.

Scott took Puebla on 1 May and advanced on Mexico City on 7 August. After an armistice failed on 6 September 1847, the battles of Molino del Rey and Chapultepec and the storming of the city gates delivered the capital. Guerrilla warfare followed, and desertion was a major problem for both armies.

Nicholas Trist, though recalled by Polk, concluded the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848. Mexico accepted the Rio Grande as the border and ceded California, Nevada, Utah, most of New Mexico, Arizona and Colorado, and parts of other present-day states. The United States paid $15 million and assumed $3.25 million of Mexican debts to its citizens. A further 30,000 square miles went to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase of 1853.

In the United States most Whigs opposed the war and most Democrats supported it, and the question of slavery in the new territories sharpened sectional division. Some scholars see the war as leading to the American Civil War, in which many officers who had served in Mexico held command. In Mexico the war deepened political turmoil and undermined public finances.
mexican-revolution: Porfirio Díaz came to the presidency in 1876 and, but for the term of his ally Manuel González from 1880 to 1884, stayed in power until 1911 in the era called the Porfiriato. The constitution was amended in 1887 and 1890 to allow unlimited re-election, and regular elections were widely seen as shams.

By 1910 the ageing Díaz had found no orderly way to settle the succession, which set elites and the middle classes against each other during a period of labour unrest, shown in the strikes at Cananea and Río Blanco. The northern landowner Francisco I. Madero challenged him in the 1910 election, and Díaz had him jailed. On 5 October 1910 Madero issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí, calling for a rising from 20 November.

Rebellions broke out first in Morelos and then in northern Mexico. The Federal Army could not put them down, and Díaz resigned in May 1911 and went into exile. Madero became president in November 1911 but, an inexperienced democrat, he dismissed the forces that had brought him to power and faced a revolt by Emiliano Zapata in Morelos, where peasants demanded agrarian reform. In February 1913 generals of the old regime staged a coup in Mexico City, and Madero and Vice President Pino Suárez were assassinated on the orders of the new president, Victoriano Huerta.

Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, led the Constitutionalist Army against Huerta, while Zapata continued his rising. Huerta's regime fell in July 1914 and the Federal Army was dissolved. The victors then fought one another, and by the summer of 1915 Carranza's faction had defeated Pancho Villa's army. Zapata was killed in 1919 by an agent of Carranza.

A new constitution was promulgated in February 1917. It established universal male suffrage and promoted secularism, workers' rights, economic nationalism and land reform, and strengthened the federal government. Carranza served as president until 1920, when northern generals rose against his attempt to impose a civilian successor; he fled Mexico City and was killed.

Revolutionary generals held the presidency from 1920 to 1940, and the army came under civilian control. The party they founded in 1929 became the Institutional Revolutionary Party and ruled Mexico until the election of 2000. Foreign powers, above all the United States, influenced the outcome, and most of the dead were non-combatants.
mexican-war-of-independence: Mexican independence was not an inevitable outcome of the relationship between the Spanish Empire and its American-born Spaniards, the criollos. The Bourbon Reforms of the mid-eighteenth century aimed to strengthen the Spanish state, weaken the Catholic Church and place peninsular-born officials in office, and many historians see them as hastening the breakdown of imperial unity. An unofficial racial hierarchy kept criollos out of the highest offices, though most did not wish to overturn the social order entirely.

The immediate trigger was Napoleon Bonaparte's invasion of Spain in 1808, which deposed Charles IV and put Joseph Bonaparte on the throne. In Mexico City the city council promoted autonomy for New Spain, but on the night of 15 September 1808 a group led by the landowner Gabriel de Yermo overthrew the viceroy José de Iturrigaray, fearing he might make himself head of a new state.

The first phase began on 16 September 1810, when the priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the Cry of Dolores. He drew tens of thousands of ordinary men, but did not organise them into a disciplined force. Hidalgo was captured, defrocked and executed in July 1811. The insurgency had already spread south, where the priest José María Morelos led a second phase, organising his forces, using guerrilla tactics and producing a written statement of aims, the Sentimientos de la Nación of 1813. Morelos was captured and executed in December 1815.

After that, Vicente Guerrero became the most important leader, and from 1815 to 1821 most of the fighting was guerrilla warfare in the hot country of the south. From 1816 to 1820 the war was a stalemate: the royal army held the major cities, but whole stretches of countryside were not pacified.

The decisive change came from Spain. In 1820 a military coup there forced Ferdinand VII to restore the liberal Constitution of 1812. Conservative royalists in New Spain, seeing it as a threat, came to regard independence as a way of keeping their position. The royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide allied with Guerrero under the Plan of Iguala, and many royalist commanders and soldiers changed sides. On 24 August 1821 Iturbide and the new viceroy Juan O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba, which the Spanish government refused to accept.

The Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821, and independence was proclaimed the next day. A First Mexican Empire under Iturbide gave way in 1823 to a federal republic. Spain recognised Mexican independence on 28 December 1836, making Mexico the first former colony it recognised. Mexicans later marked both 16 September, for Hidalgo's call, and 27 September, for actual independence.
mexico: Mexico covers 1,972,550 square kilometres, the thirteenth-largest country in the world, with coastlines on the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. The central and northern territories lie at high altitudes. The highest elevations are in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, which includes Pico de Orizaba at 5,700 metres and Popocatépetl at 5,462 metres, and the Sierra Madre Oriental and Sierra Madre Occidental cross the country from north to south. The Chicxulub crater lies on the Yucatán peninsula, and much of the land mass is unsuited to agriculture because of aridity, soil or terrain.

Human presence dates back to at least 11,500 BCE, although dates as old as 28,000 BCE have been proposed for less securely dated sites. Mexico is the site of the domestication of maize, tomato and beans, which allowed sedentary agricultural villages to begin around 5000 BCE.

The Olmec culture, the earliest complex civilization, flourished on the Gulf Coast from around 1500 BCE, and the Maya and Zapotec civilizations later developed complex centres. Teotihuacán, with a population of more than 150,000, formed a military and commercial empire, and after its collapse around 600 CE other centres competed. Toward the end of the post-Classic period the Aztecs established an empire based in Tenochtitlan.

Spanish colonization began in 1521 with an indigenous alliance that defeated the Aztec Empire, establishing the colony of New Spain. The Mexican War of Independence of 1810 to 1821 ended Peninsular rule. In 1848 Mexico lost nearly half its territory in the Mexican–American War. Liberal reforms in the Constitution of 1857 led to civil war and French intervention, and the Second Mexican Empire under Emperor Maximilian I of Habsburg was overthrown by Republican forces led by Benito Juárez. The long rule of Porfirio Díaz ended with the Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920, which brought the Constitution of 1917, the current one.

Mexico has about 131 million inhabitants, and Mexico City is the capital and largest city. It is a federal republic with a presidential system and 32 states, with a bicameral Congress of the Union of 500 deputies and 128 senators. The Constitution gives Spanish legal equality with 68 indigenous languages.
mexico-city: Mexico City lies in the Valley of Mexico, also called the Basin of Mexico, in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt on the high plateaus of south-central Mexico. Its lowest point is about 2,200 metres above sea level, and mountains and volcanoes of over 5,000 metres surround it. The valley has no natural drainage outlet for the water that runs down from the slopes, so the city has long been open to flooding.

The Mexica founded Mexico-Tenochtitlan in 1325 or 1327 on an island in the lake system, which it shared with a smaller city-state, Tlatelolco. According to legend, the god Huitzilopochtli showed them the site by presenting a golden eagle perched on a prickly pear and devouring a rattlesnake. Between 1325 and 1521 the city came to dominate the other city-states round Lake Texcoco, and the Aztec Empire reached both the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific.
