Hernán Cortés, with the aid of many other native peoples, reached Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519 and was greeted by the ruler Moctezuma II, whom he then placed under house arrest. After the siege of 1521 the city was nearly destroyed and was rebuilt to Spanish urban standards. The municipality of México Tenochtitlán was established in 1524, and from 1585 the city was officially Ciudad de México. It was a major political, administrative and financial centre of the colonial period.

After independence, the Federal Constitution of 4 October 1824 let Congress choose the seat of the federal government. Mexico City was preferred to Querétaro, largely through the persuasion of Servando Teresa de Mier, as the centre of the country's population and history. The choice was made official on 18 November 1824, and a surface of two leagues square centred on the Zocalo was separated from the State of Mexico as the Federal District. Residents won the right to elect their head of government in 1997, and on 29 January 2016 the district was renamed Ciudad de México.

Mexico City is the capital and largest city of Mexico, divided into 16 boroughs, or alcaldías. The 2020 census gave the city proper 9,209,944 people, and Greater Mexico City 21,804,515. Its historic centre and the muralist works of José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros and Diego Rivera, at the National Palace and the Palacio de Bellas Artes among other buildings, belong to the heritage of the Mexican capital.
miao-people: Miao is a Chinese term for many groups with their own names for themselves, such as Hmong, Hmu, Xong and A-Hmao. Most speak Hmongic languages, a subfamily of the Hmong–Mien family, but the languages of the four main groups are mutually unintelligible. Historically the term was applied inconsistently to various non-Han peoples. It reappeared under the Ming dynasty with the sense of barbarian, and Ming writers distinguished raw and cooked Miao by their assimilation and political cooperation. Some scholars hold that Miao existed only as an outsiders' name until the Qing, and others that Miao identity emerged during the rebellions of the 18th and 19th centuries. The term gained official status in 1949 as the name of a nationality.

According to a Tang dynasty legend, the Miao descended from the Jiuli tribe led by Chiyou, who were defeated at the Battle of Zhuolu by Huang Di and Yan Di. Chinese records mention a San Miao kingdom around Dongting Lake, said to have been defeated by Yu the Great.

The Miao are not mentioned again until the Tang dynasty. In the following centuries they migrated across southern China and Southeast Asia, generally living in mountainous or marginal lands and farming by slash-and-burn cultivation. During the Miao rebellions of the Ming dynasty thousands were killed by imperial forces, and mass castrations of Miao boys took place.

Under the Qing the Miao fought three wars against the empire. A rebellion at Weining in Guizhou was suppressed in 1725, and the Yongzheng emperor sent Ortai as Viceroy to the provinces with large Miao populations. In 1735 the Miao of Guizhou rose against forced assimilation, and eight counties with 1,224 villages fought until 1738. A second war, in Guizhou and Hunan, lasted from 1795 to 1806. The largest, from 1854 to 1873, was led in Guizhou by Zhang Xiu-mei until his capture and death at Changsha. It affected over a million people, and by its end, according to Professor Wu of Xiangtan University, only 30 percent of the Miao remained in their home regions. It drove many Hmong to migrate into Laos and Vietnam.

Chinese tradition classes the Miao by the colour of women's clothing: Red Miao (Xong) in west Hunan, Black Miao (Hmu) in south-east Guizhou, Big Flowery Miao (A-Hmao) in west Guizhou and north-east Yunnan, and the Hmong in Yunnan, Sichuan and west Guizhou. Miao women are known for embroidery, weaving, batik and silver jewellery, which symbolises family wealth and is worn at weddings, funerals and spring celebrations. Marriage within one clan name is taboo, and inheritance descends to the youngest son, who stays with and cares for the aging parents.
micaela-bastidas: Micaela Bastidas was born on 23 June 1744, the natural daughter of Josefa Puyucahua Sisa and Manuel Bastidas, who died in 1746. Virtually nothing is known of her father, who was perhaps a priest or of African descent; some documents call her a zamba, the colonial term for a person of mixed African and indigenous ancestry, while her marriage certificate lists both parents as Spaniards, a label that may have been a sign of respectability. As an illegitimate child she was marginalised in the overwhelmingly indigenous highlands. She spoke Quechua better than Spanish, was a devout Catholic and had little formal schooling.

She married on 25 May 1760, before her sixteenth birthday, in the church of Our Lady of Purification in Surimana. Her husband, a descendant of the Inca Túpac Amaru I, was named cacique of Pampamarca, Tungasuca and Surimana in 1764 and traded across a wide network with 350 mules. They lived in Tinta and had three sons, Hipólito, Mariano and Fernando. Letters exchanged early in the rebellion show endearments and concern for each other's safety.

The rebellion opened on 4 November 1780, when the local Spanish commander Antonio de Arriaga was taken prisoner; he was later hanged. The rebels made their headquarters at Tungasuca and defeated the Spanish at Sangarará on 18 November. Because indigenous people were forbidden firearms, obtaining weapons was among the hardest of her tasks. She also issued safe-conducts, took charge of the rearguard, guarded against espionage and organised a service of mounted chasquis that carried messages across rebel territory.

Local rulers called her Señora Gobernadora, La Coya or La Reina, and one description calls her a superior strategist to her husband and certainly more daring. He held off from Cuzco, which allowed the Spaniards to bring in reinforcements. By March 1781 the rebel army numbered seven thousand men and women.

On 18 May 1781 the prisoners were taken to be executed. Hipólito had his tongue cut out and was hanged. Micaela Bastidas fought her executioners until they subdued her and cut off her tongue. A hand-cranked garrote made for the occasion could not be used because her neck was so slender, and she was strangled with a rope, beaten with a club and kicked to death, in front of her husband, who was then killed. Their bodies were dismembered and the parts sent to towns of the region for display. The involvement of women in such risings shocked the Spanish authorities, who gave them the same penalties as men.
micah-prophet: According to the Hebrew Bible, Micah, called the Morashtite, was a prophet of Yahweh, traditionally regarded as the author of the Book of Micah and one of the Twelve Minor Prophets. He is shown as a contemporary of Isaiah, Amos and Hosea. He came from Moresheth, also called Moresheth-Gath, a small town in southwest Judah, and the text gives him no father's name. This has led to the view that he was of common descent, since his message was aimed at the privileged classes. He lived in a rural area and often rebuked the corruption of city life.

He prophesied under the kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah, from about 740 to 698 BCE by one reckoning. He was active before the fall of Israel in 722 BCE and lived through Sennacherib's invasion of Judah in 701 BCE. The name means 'Who is like Yah(weh)?', a rhetorical question implying that no one is like God. Jeremiah, who prophesied about thirty years later, recalls Micah of Moresheth as a prophet in the reign of Hezekiah.

Micah's messages were directed chiefly at Jerusalem and mix denunciation with promise. In his early prophecies he foretold the destruction of both Samaria and Jerusalem. Samaria was rebuked for idol worship, and Jerusalem was doomed because its beautification was financed by dishonest business that impoverished its citizens. He also accused the prophets of his day of accepting money for their oracles. He anticipated the destruction of the Judean state and promised its restoration, with an era of universal peace. He is described as the first prophet to predict the downfall of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah 26 repeats his words that Zion will be plowed like a field.

He told the people what God requires of them: 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God' (Micah 6:8). The Talmud praises him for distilling the Torah into three principles, justice, loving-kindness and humility. The formation of the Book of Micah is debated, with a consensus that its final stage came in the Persian or Hellenistic period. Christians read Micah 5:2 as a prophecy that Bethlehem would be the birthplace of the Messiah, a passage recalled in Matthew 2:6. Several churches commemorate him as a saint, the Roman Catholic Church on 31 July, and the Eastern Orthodox Church on 14 August.
michael-faraday: Michael Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 in Newington Butts, Surrey, now part of the London Borough of Southwark, the third of four children. His family was not well off, and his father, James, was a member of the Glasite sect of Christianity. He had only the most basic schooling and had to educate himself.

At 14 he became an apprentice to George Riebau, a bookbinder and bookseller, and during the seven years read widely, including Jane Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry. In 1812 he heard lectures by Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution and sent Davy a 300-page book based on his notes. When Davy damaged his eyesight in an accident with nitrogen trichloride, he hired Faraday, who was appointed Chemical Assistant on 1 March 1813.

Faraday was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1824 and in 1825 became Director of the Laboratory of the Royal Institution. In 1833 he became its first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry, for life and without the obligation to lecture. He founded the Friday Evening Discourses and was the main popularizer of the Christmas Lecture Series. He also did public work: with Charles Lyell he wrote a report on a colliery explosion at Haswell in 1846 that killed 95 miners, which indicated for the first time that coal dust worsened explosions. He refused to advise on chemical weapons for the Crimean War, declined a knighthood on religious grounds, and twice refused the presidency of the Royal Society.

In chemistry Faraday discovered benzene and tetrachloroethylene, liquefied several gases and found the laws of electrolysis. He popularised the terms anode, cathode, electrode and ion, which William Whewell largely proposed. In 1821 he built two devices producing what he called electromagnetic rotation, one of them the homopolar motor, a foundation of electric motor technology.

In 1845 he discovered diamagnetism and found that a magnetic field can rotate the plane of polarised light, now called the Faraday effect. His ice pail experiment showed that charge sits on the outside of a conductor, the principle of the Faraday cage. His mathematics went no further than simple algebra, and James Clerk Maxwell, who took up his work, wrote that Faraday's lines of force showed him to have been a mathematician of a very high order.
michael-i-of-romania: Michael was born on 25 October 1921 at Foișor Castle in Sinaia, the son of Crown Prince Carol and the grandson of King Ferdinand I of Romania. In December 1925 Carol eloped with his mistress Elena Magda Lupescu and renounced his rights to the throne, and Michael became heir apparent. When Ferdinand died in July 1927 Michael became king before his sixth birthday, with a regency of his uncle Prince Nicolae, Patriarch Miron Cristea and the Chief Justice. In 1930 politicians dissatisfied with the regency invited Carol back, and parliament proclaimed him Carol II.

Carol II was forced to abdicate in 1940 and Michael returned to the throne on 6 September 1940, while Romania was aligned with Nazi Germany under Ion Antonescu. On 23 August 1944 Michael joined pro-Allies politicians and army officers in a coup, and ordered Antonescu's arrest. He appointed Constantin Sănătescu prime minister, announced a ceasefire, accepted the armistice and declared war on Germany. This did not prevent a rapid Soviet occupation, and about 130,000 Romanian soldiers were captured and taken to the Soviet Union, where many died in camps.

In March 1945 political pressure forced him to appoint a pro-Soviet government under Petru Groza. From August 1945 to January 1946 he refused to sign its decrees in the royal strike, but it failed. On 30 December 1947 Groza compelled him to abdicate and the monarchy was abolished.

Michael married Princess Anne of Bourbon-Parma in June 1948, and the couple had five daughters. The communist authorities stripped him of citizenship that year, and from 1956 the couple lived near Versoix in Switzerland. After the fall of Nicolae Ceaușescu he landed in Romania on 25 December 1990 but was made to leave. In 1992 a speech from a hotel window in Bucharest drew an estimated one million people. His citizenship was restored in 1997, and properties such as Peleș Castle were later returned to his family. He died in Switzerland on 5 December 2017, aged 96.
michael-of-russia: Michael, in Russian Mikhail Fyodorovich Romanov, was born on 22 July 1596 (O.S. 12 July), the son of Feodor Nikitich Romanov, later Patriarch Filaret, and Xenia Shestova. He was a first cousin once removed of Feodor I, the last tsar of the Rurik dynasty. In 1600 Tsar Boris Godunov falsely accused his father of treason, and Michael and his mother were exiled to Beloozero.

After the Poles were expelled during the Time of Troubles, a patriotic mood swept the Russian elite. Michael was chosen partly because of his father's martyr-like captivity in Poland and partly because his youth made him seem easily manipulated. On 21 February 1613 some 700 delegates of the Zemsky Sobor agreed on him as a compromise candidate. They did not find him and his mother at the Ipatiev Monastery near Kostroma until 24 March, and he was crowned on 21 July 1613, his seventeenth birthday.

The Treaty of Stolbovo of 17 February 1617 ended the war with Sweden: Russia gave up Ingria and parts of Karelia, and Sweden recognised Michael as its ruler. The Truce of Deulino of 1 December 1618 ended the war with Poland and cost Smolensk, but brought back Filaret, who became Patriarch of Moscow and the effective ruler of Russia until his death in 1633. In the Treaty of Polyanovka in 1634 Władysław IV Vasa gave up his claim to the Russian throne. Meanwhile Cossacks, financed by the Stroganov merchant family, continued the conquest of Siberia, and Russian explorers reached the Pacific before the reign ended.

Michael married three times. His first betrothed, Maria Khlopova, was deported to Siberia after falling ill, and his second wife died four months after the wedding in 1625. His third wife, Eudoxia Streshneva, whom he married in 1626, bore ten children, four of whom reached adulthood, including his successor Alexis. A horse accident early in his life left him with a leg injury that kept him from walking toward the end. He fell ill in April 1645 and died on 23 July 1645. He was a gentle and pious prince who effaced himself behind his counsellors, and the first tsar of the House of Romanov.
michael-psellos: Psellos's family came from Nicomedia and, by his own testimony, counted members of the consular and patrician elite among its ancestors. His baptismal name was Constantine; Michael was the monastic name he took on entering a monastery later. Psellos, meaning the stammerer, was probably a personal by-name referring to a speech defect. At about ten he was sent to work outside the capital as secretary to a provincial judge, to help raise a dowry for his sister. When she died he returned to Constantinople to study under John Mauropus, where he met the later patriarchs Constantine Leichoudes and John Xiphilinos and the later emperor Constantine X Doukas.

After a further spell as a provincial judge, he returned to Constantinople before 1042 as a junior secretary in the imperial chancellery and rose quickly. He became an influential adviser to Constantine IX Monomachos, who reigned from 1042 to 1055, and the leading professor at the University of Constantinople, with the title Chief of the Philosophers. Under political pressure he entered the Olympus monastery in Bithynia in 1054, and Empress Theodora recalled him to court after Monomachos died.

He remained an adviser to successive emperors and played a decisive part in the transfers of power from Michael VI to Isaac I Komnenos in 1057, from Isaac to Constantine X Doukas in 1059 and from Romanos IV Diogenes to Michael VII Doukas in 1071. He had taught Michael, but after the mid-1070s nothing is recorded of his role at court, and some scholars think he withdrew again to a monastery.

The Chronographia, his best-known work, is a series of biographies of fourteen emperors and empresses. It stresses character over political and military detail, gives most weight to the periods when Psellos was himself in politics and has the character of a political memoir. The second part is more apologetic and largely praises the Doukas emperors. He also wrote a shorter world chronicle, the Historia syntomos, treatises on philosophy, theology, astronomy, medicine, music and law, a treatise on demons, didactic poems, funeral orations, speeches and several hundred letters.

He prided himself on reviving serious study of Plato and ancient philosophy in Byzantium, and he read Homer and Plato as precursors of Christian doctrine. His fondness for pagan and Neoplatonic thinkers led some contemporaries to doubt his orthodoxy: in 1054 John Xiphilinos accused him of forsaking Christ to follow Plato, and he made a public profession of faith. Modern commentators have called him vain and opportunistic, while others find in his work an ironic undercurrent critical of the emperors he describes.
michael-somare: Michael Thomas Somare was born on 9 April 1936 at Rabaul, in a village called Rapikid, where his father Ludwig Somare Sana, a policeman who rose to sergeant, was stationed. He was the eldest of his father's six children. He grew up in the family village of Karau in the Murik Lakes district of East Sepik Province, and his first schooling was at a Japanese-run primary school there during the Second World War. From 1946 he attended Boram Primary School, the Dregerhafen Education Centre and Sogeri High School, and in 1957 he gained a Leaving Certificate that served as a teaching qualification.

Somare stressed his Sepik identity, wearing a lap-lap rather than trousers, and held the title of Sana in his father's line, which marks descent from the clan's founder and the role of peacemaker. He married Veronica in 1965, and they had five children.

Somare entered politics in 1968, sitting in the House of Assembly and then in the national parliament for the East Sepik seat. He was a founding member of the Pangu Party, which led Papua New Guinea to independence in 1975. He was the first chief minister at the end of colonial rule and the first prime minister after independence. He held the office from 1975 to 1980, from 1982 to 1985 and from 2002 to 2011, seventeen years in all.

He was also minister of foreign affairs, leader of the opposition on several occasions and governor of East Sepik Province. As prime minister he declared friends with everybody and enemies of none as the principle of his foreign relations, and he opened relations with China soon after independence. In March 2011, while he was in hospital in Singapore, parliament declared the post vacant and Peter O'Neill became prime minister, a change that led to a constitutional crisis.

Somare died of pancreatic cancer at Port Moresby on 25 February 2021, aged 84. He is widely called the father of the nation. He received honorary doctorates, beginning with one from the University of the Philippines in 1976, and was appointed to the Privy Council in 1977. He was made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1990.
michael-the-brave: Michael was born in 1558 as Mihai Pătrașcu. He claimed to be the illegitimate son of the Wallachian prince Pătrașcu cel Bun, though some historians think he invented this descent and that his real father was most likely a Greek merchant. His mother was Theodora Kantakouzene. He rose quickly, becoming Ban of Craiova in 1593, but a conflict with Prince Alexandru cel Rău forced him to flee that year. In Constantinople he secured Ottoman support, helped by a loan of 200,000 florins, and Sultan Murad III invested him as prince in September 1593.

Michael soon turned against the Ottomans. In 1594 he joined the Christian alliance formed by Pope Clement VIII and took several citadels near the Danube. In August 1595 an Ottoman army under Sinan Pasha crossed the Danube. Outnumbered, Michael gave battle on marshy ground near Călugăreni and defeated it, but had too few troops to follow up and withdrew. The war went on until he made peace on 26 June 1599, lacking support from his allies. His rule rested on the Oltenian lords, and he passed a law binding serfs to aristocrats' land.

When Andrew Báthory demanded that Michael give up his throne, Michael marched into Transylvania and defeated him at Șelimbăr on 18 October 1599, then entered Gyulafehérvár as imperial governor under Emperor Rudolf II. In April 1600 his troops entered Moldavia and reached Iași on 6 May, and he had a seal showing the three principalities. The Transylvanian Hungarian nobility rose against him with the help of General Giorgio Basta, while Polish forces drove his troops from Moldavia and Wallachia.

Michael visited Prague in 1601 and received 100,000 florins from Rudolf II. Allied with Basta, he defeated the Hungarian army at Guruslău. A few days later, on 9 August 1601, Basta, who wished to control Transylvania himself, had him killed near Câmpia Turzii, on the emperor's order. From the middle of the nineteenth century he was seen as a unifier and precursor of a modern Romania, though the historian A. D. Xenopol held that there was no national element in his politics.
michael-viii-palaiologos: Michael VIII Palaiologos was the son of the megas domestikos Andronikos Doukas Komnenos Palaiologos and Theodora Angelina Palaiologina, whose ancestry, according to Deno John Geanakoplos, went back to all three imperial houses that ruled before the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204. He governed the Thracian towns of Melnik and Serres under his father. In 1253 he was accused of plotting against Emperor John III Vatatzes and escaped trial by ordeal with a clever reply, though he remained mistrusted. He served the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from late 1256 to 1258 before Theodore II Laskaris recalled him. After Theodore's death in 1258 Michael seized the guardianship of the eight-year-old John IV Laskaris from George Mouzalon and was proclaimed emperor at Nymphaion on 1 January 1259.

In 1259 Michael defeated William of Villehardouin and Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus at the Battle of Pelagonia. A treaty with Genoa followed in 1261, though Genoese help proved unneeded when his general Alexios Strategopoulos captured Constantinople from Baldwin II through treachery on 25 July 1261. Michael entered the city on 15 August. He abolished Latin customs, restored Byzantine ceremonies and repopulated the capital, which grew from about 35,000 people to 70,000 by the end of his reign. In December 1261 he had John IV blinded and sent to a monastery, and Patriarch Arsenios excommunicated him for it until 1268.

From 1266 Michael's main opponent was Charles of Anjou, who in 1267 concluded the Treaty of Viterbo to restore the Latin Empire. To restrain him Michael negotiated union of the churches, which was formally proclaimed at the Second Council of Lyon in 1274. Many Greeks bitterly opposed it, and Michael punished anti-unionists, some by blinding or exile. On 30 March 1282 the Sicilian Vespers rebellion broke out before Charles could sail against Constantinople. Pope Martin IV excommunicated Michael, whom many saw as instigator, though Geanakoplos holds that he had nothing to do with the incident at the church of Santo Spirito.

Michael died at Pachomios village in Thrace on 11 December 1282. He was denied burial in Constantinople because of his persecution of the Church in support of union with Rome. In restoring the empire he kept the old administration without correcting its failures. His focus on Constantinople and the Balkans left the Anatolian frontier stripped of troops, which led to its gradual collapse as Turkish bands infiltrated. The Palaiologan dynasty he founded ruled for almost two centuries, longer than any other in Roman history.
michel-aflaq: Michel Aflaq was born on 9 January 1910 to an Orthodox Christian family in Damascus, where his father Joseph worked as a grain merchant. He was educated in the Westernised schools of the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon. In 1929 he went to the Sorbonne to study philosophy, where Henri Bergson's works influenced him and he met his long-term collaborator Salah al-Din al-Bitar. He founded an Arab Student Union there and discovered the writings of Karl Marx. Back in Syria in 1932 he became active in communist politics, but he left the movement when France's Popular Front government under Léon Blum kept up the old colonial policies and the Syrian-Lebanese Communist Party backed it.

Aflaq and al-Bitar taught at the Tajhiz secondary school in Damascus, Aflaq history and al-Bitar mathematics and physics. In 1940 they founded the Arab Ihya Movement, renamed the Arab Ba'ath Movement in 1942. The name led Zaki al-Arsuzi, leader of a group with the same name, to accuse them of taking it, and the two men became bitter rivals. At the first congress of the Arab Ba'ath Party at Damascus in 1947, which merged the two groups, Aflaq became Amid, the party's leader, with responsibility for ideology.

The party merged with Akram al-Hawrani's Arab Socialist Party in 1952, and Aflaq was elected its Secretary General in 1954. When Nasser pressed for the union of Egypt and Syria, Aflaq dissolved the party without consulting its members. He was forced to resign as leader in 1965 in a struggle with the party's Military Committee. A coup on 23 February 1966, led by Salah Jadid and Hafez al-Assad, overthrew the Syrian government and the party leadership and exiled him. He escaped to Beirut and later to Brazil. In 1968 he was elected Secretary General of the Iraqi-led Ba'ath Party, but he held no de facto power. The Syrian-led party sentenced him to death in absentia in 1971.

Aflaq's books include The Road to Renaissance, The Battle for One Destiny and The Struggle Against Distorting the Movement of Arab Revolution. He held that the Arab world must be unified into one Arab nation to achieve development, and that freedom would come to the Arabs through unity. He criticised capitalism and communism alike and held that Arab socialism was not part of the international socialist movement. He favoured separating state and religion, and opposed atheism. He argued that Islam was the most sublime expression of Arabism, a view that drew criticism from devout Muslims and from some Christians. He died in Paris on 23 June 1989 and was given a state funeral.
michel-ney: Michel Ney was born on 10 January 1769 in Sarrelouis, in Lorraine on the French-German border, the second son of a master cooper, Pierre Ney, a veteran of the Seven Years' War. The town was a French enclave in a predominantly German region and Ney grew up bilingual. After schooling until 1782 he worked as a notary's clerk and then in mines and forges. Civil life did not suit him, and in 1787 he enlisted in the Colonel-General Hussar Regiment. Under the Bourbons the officer corps was closed to those without noble ancestry, but he rose quickly through the non-commissioned ranks.

Ney fought at Valmy in 1792 and was commissioned that October. He was wounded at the Siege of Mainz in 1793, and as a cavalry commander was captured at Neuwied on 17 April 1797 and exchanged on 8 May. He became a general of division in March 1799 and fought at Hohenlinden in December 1800. On 19 May 1804 he received his marshal's baton. He commanded VI Corps in 1805, took Innsbruck, fought at Jena and Eylau, and was made Duke of Elchingen on 6 June 1808. In 1810 he invaded Portugal with Marshal André Masséna, and after bitter complaints about the campaign he was removed for insubordination.

In Russia in 1812 Ney led III Corps, was wounded at Smolensk, fought at Borodino and commanded the rearguard on the retreat from Moscow. Cut off at Krasnoi, he escaped across the Dnieper over fragile ice with heavy losses and rejoined the army at Orsha. Napoleon called him the bravest of the brave, and he was made Prince de la Moskowa on 25 March 1813. At Fontainebleau on 4 April 1814 he spoke for the marshals demanding Napoleon's abdication, then served Louis XVIII, who made him a Peer of France.

When Napoleon returned, Ney set out to stop him but joined him at Lons-le-Saulnier on 14 March 1815 with about 6,000 men. At Quatre Bras on 16 June he was criticised for attacking slowly, and at Waterloo on 18 June he ordered a mass cavalry charge that failed to break the infantry squares; five horses were killed under him. Arrested on 3 August, he was tried before the Chamber of Peers after the court-martial declared itself not competent. The Peers voted 137 for death, and he was shot near the Luxembourg Gardens on 7 December 1815. Accounts of his last words differ. He is buried at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris.
michelangelo: Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was born on 6 March 1475 in Caprese, near Arezzo in Tuscany, where his father Ludovico was the town's judicial administrator. The family had for generations been small-scale bankers in Florence, but the bank failed. Several months after his birth they returned to Florence. After his mother's death in 1481 he lived with a nanny and her husband, a stonecutter, in Settignano, where his father owned a marble quarry and a small farm. He later said he received the knack of handling chisel and hammer with the milk of his nurse.

Michelangelo achieved fame early, and two of his best-known works, the Pietà and David, were sculpted before he was 30. Born in the Republic of Florence, he was mostly active in Rome from his thirties onward. Although he did not consider himself a painter, he created the scenes from Genesis on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and The Last Judgment on its altar wall, two of the most influential frescoes in Western art.

His design of the Laurentian Library pioneered Mannerist architecture. At 71 he succeeded Antonio da Sangallo the Younger as architect of St. Peter's Basilica, and he changed the plan so that the western end was finished to his design, as was the dome, with some modification after his death on 18 February 1564. He was the first Western artist whose biography was published in his lifetime: Giorgio Vasari's Lives of 1550 called him divino, and Ascanio Condivi's Life of 1553 was prepared with his participation.

The Madonna of the Stairs is his earliest known work in marble, carved in shallow relief. His Bacchus, a commission with a set subject, has the traditional wine cup, vine wreath and fawn, but shows the god with bleary eyes and an unsteady stance. In the Madonna of Bruges the Christ Child, held by his mother's hand, is about to step off into the world. His contemporaries admired his terribilità, the ability to instil awe in those who saw his art.

He wrote more than three hundred sonnets and madrigals. He was a devout Catholic whose faith deepened at the end of his life. Attempts by later artists to imitate the expressive physicality of his style helped bring about Mannerism. The dome of St. Peter's influenced church building for centuries, including St Paul's Cathedral in London, and his unfinished giants for the tomb of Pope Julius II had a deep effect on sculptors such as Rodin and Henry Moore.
michelin: In 1889 the brothers Édouard and André Michelin took over Barbier-Daubrée, a struggling farm implement business of Clermont-Ferrand founded in 1832, which made rubber parts such as valves, gaskets, balls and brake pads. According to the company's story, a cyclist came in with a pneumatic tyre glued to its rim, which took over three hours to remove and repair and then had to dry overnight. When Édouard tested the repaired tyre the next day it failed after a few hundred metres. He and his brother set out to make a tyre that did not need to be glued. The firm was reincorporated and renamed Michelin on 28 May 1889.

In 1891 Michelin took out its first patent for a removable pneumatic tyre, and it was used by Charles Terront to win the first Paris–Brest–Paris cycle race. Four years later the company made pneumatic tyres for an automobile, a car called L'Eclair that raced in the Paris–Bordeaux–Paris of 1895. In the 1920s and 1930s it operated large rubber plantations in Vietnam, where conditions led to the labour movement known as Phú Riềng Đỏ. In the 1930s Michelin bought the bankrupt Citroën.

In 1934 it introduced a tyre that ran on a foam lining if punctured, the ancestor of the run-flat tyre, and in 1946 it patented the radial tyre, first sold as the X and developed with the Citroën Traction Avant and 2CV in mind. Radials spread through Europe and Asia, while in the United States bias-ply tyres still had 87 per cent of the market in 1967. Michelin opened its first North American sales office in 1968, the year Consumer Reports acknowledged the radial's superiority, and in 1989 it bought the tyre businesses of B.F. Goodrich and Uniroyal.

Michelin's inventions include the removable tyre, the automobile pneumatic tyre, twin truck tyres, the asymmetric XAS of 1964 and the green low-resistance tyre unveiled in 1992. It published the Red Guides to hotels and restaurants and the Green Guides for tourists, along with road maps. Its roadmaps were reproduced in England for the Allied invasion in the Second World War, and in 1940 the Germans reproduced the 1938 edition for theirs.

The company supplied tyres for the winner of the first 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1923, and it competed in Formula One from 1977 to 1984 and again from 2001 to 2006. Its Red Guide's stars for restaurants and its mascot Bibendum, the Michelin Man, are widely known.
michiel-de-ruyter: Michiel de Ruyter was born on 24 March 1607 in Vlissingen in Zeeland, the son of a seaman who became a member of the guild of beer porters. He worked for a time at a ropewalk and was sent to sea as a boatswain's apprentice at eleven, the usual age for Zeeland boys. In 1622 he fought as a cannoneer under Maurice of Nassau at the relief of Bergen-op-Zoom. He then rose through the merchant fleet to become a ship's master at thirty. He had little formal education but spoke fluent English and tolerable French. The name De Ruyter was probably a nickname, perhaps from the verb ruyten, 'to raid', in reference to his privateering.

In the First Anglo-Dutch War he joined the fleet as a commandeur under Maarten Tromp, after first refusing the post as others were better qualified, and commanded a Zeelandic squadron that convoyed merchant ships through the English Channel. In 1655 he sailed to the Mediterranean with 55 merchantmen to protect Dutch trade and ransom enslaved Christians in Algiers. He took part in the Second Northern War on the Danish side, and was knighted by Frederick III of Denmark after liberating Nyborg in 1659.

As lieutenant admiral in the Second Anglo-Dutch War he retook the Dutch West African posts in 1664, but his raid on Barbados in 1665 had less success. In 1672 an Anglo-French fleet under James, Duke of York, and the Comte d'Estrées faced his fleet of 75 ships. At Solebay he aimed to damage the English ships so heavily they needed long repairs, and later he used the shoals as shelter and detached small squadrons to keep the reluctant French out of the main action. He thus prevented a landing. In 1674 his expedition to Martinique failed with 143 killed and 318 wounded.

In 1676 a cannonball struck him in the leg during the Battle of Augusta, and he died a week later at Syracuse. His embalmed body went to Amsterdam, and on 18 March 1677 he received a state funeral and was buried in the Nieuwe Kerk, where a monument by Rombout Verhulst was completed in 1681. His sailors called him bestevaêr, 'grandfather', for his disregard for hierarchy and bold undertakings. He is credited with a part in founding the Netherlands Marine Corps, established on 10 December 1665, and six ships of the Royal Netherlands Navy have borne his name.
michoacan: Michoacán lies in west-central Mexico, in the extreme south-west of the central highlands, with a coastline of 217 km on the Pacific Ocean. It borders Colima and Jalisco, Guanajuato, Querétaro, the State of México and Guerrero. Its name comes from Nahuatl Michhuahcan, 'place of the fishermen', which refers to those who fish on Lake Pátzcuaro. Vegetation changes with altitude, from conifer forests above 2,600 metres to tropical forests lower down, and the state holds the main wintering ground of the monarch butterflies, which the Purépecha take to be the spirits of the dead.

The first settlers were hunter-gatherers of the Palaeoindian period, known from fluted projectile points found with the bones of mammoths and bison. The Preclassic population lived in agricultural villages at El Opeño in the west and in the Balsas basin in the south, and for a long time the region held various local cultures. By about 900 CE populations had moved to defensible places in the Cuitzeo and Zacapu basins and along the Lerma and Balsas rivers.

The Purépecha, said to descend from late Chichimeca arrivals from the north, began their state in the thirteenth century at Uayameo, today Santa Fé de la Laguna, and by the fifteenth century dominated the Lake Pátzcuaro area. Between 1401 and 1450 they conquered neighbouring peoples, and by the late fifteenth century their state rivalled that of the Aztecs and reached into parts of Colima, Nayarit, Querétaro, Guanajuato, Guerrero and Jalisco. The Aztecs attacked and were repelled, and the Purépecha later refused them aid against the Spanish. They were also skilled in metallurgy, especially in copper.

The ruler Zuanga died of smallpox before any Spaniard arrived, and Tanganxoan II succeeded him. The first Spaniard to reach the area was Cristóbal de Olid. After the Spanish destroyed Tenochtitlan, Tanganxoan agreed to submit, on a promise that he would remain ruler, but Nuño de Guzmán went back on the agreement and killed him in 1530. The empire became a separate province that grew smaller over the colonial period. The state and its people played a major part in the Mexican War of Independence.

Michoacán is one of the 31 states of Mexico, divided into 113 municipalities, with its capital at Morelia, formerly Valladolid, named after the independence hero José María Morelos, who was born there. Morelia's colonial centre, pink stone cathedral and aqueduct were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Many Purépecha still live in the state, and its Day of the Dead celebrations at Janitzio and Pátzcuaro are among the best known in Mexico.
micronesia: Micronesia is a subregion of Oceania in the north-western Pacific, with about 2,100 islands and a total land area of only 2,700 square kilometres spread over some 7,400,000 square kilometres of ocean. The largest island is Guam, at 582 square kilometres. There are four main island groups: the Caroline Islands, the Gilbert Islands, the Mariana Islands and the Marshall Islands, with Nauru and a few other islands separate. Most of the islands are coral atolls, formed as coral grew on the slopes of a central volcano that later sank.

The shared name is a modern grouping. Louis Domeny de Rienzi used it a year before Jules Dumont d'Urville, who is usually credited. The set does not correspond to any geological, archaeological, linguistic or cultural unity.

The Northern Mariana Islands were the first islands in Oceania settled by Austronesian peoples, voyagers who sailed east from the Philippines around 1500 BCE. Later groups moved south and east and became the ancestors of the Polynesian people. The earliest known European contact came in 1521, when Ferdinand Magellan's Spanish expedition reached the Marianas, as Antonio Pigafetta recorded. The Chamorro people he met seem to have had no knowledge of people beyond their own islands.

In the early 17th century Spain colonised Guam, the Northern Marianas and the Caroline Islands, governing them from the Philippines. After the Spanish–American War the United States took Guam in 1898 and Wake Island on 17 January 1899, and Spain sold its remaining islands to Germany in 1899. Germany also held Nauru and the British Empire took the Gilbert Islands. Germany lost its colonies in World War I, and the Northern Mariana Islands became a League of Nations Mandate with Japan as mandatory. After World War II they were placed in the United Nations Trust Territory system under the United States.

Micronesia is divided among six sovereign nations and some territories: Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru and the Marshall Islands, with Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands affiliated with the United States. The Northern Mariana Islands entered a covenant with the United States in 1976 under which they became a commonwealth and their residents received United States citizenship. Wake Island is under United States administration, though the Marshall Islands also claim it. Fishing rights sold to foreign fleets, and grants, mostly from the United States, are the chief sources of income.
microscope: Objects resembling lenses date back 4,000 years, and the earliest known use of simple microscopes, or magnifying glasses, dates to the widespread use of lenses in eyeglasses in the thirteenth century. Several claims for the compound microscope revolve around the spectacle-making centres of the Netherlands, naming Hans Lippershey, who applied for the first telescope patent in 1608, and the expatriate Cornelis Drebbel, who was noted to have a version in London in 1619.

Galileo Galilei seems to have found after 1610 that he could focus his telescope closely to view small objects. After seeing a compound microscope built by Drebbel exhibited in Rome in 1624, he built his own improved version. Giovanni Faber coined the name microscopio in 1625 for the instrument Galileo submitted to the Accademia dei Lincei.

The first detailed account of the microscopic anatomy of organic tissue, Giambattista Odierna's The Fly's Eye, appeared in 1644. Marcello Malpighi began his analysis of biological structures with the lungs. Robert Hooke's Micrographia, published in 1665, had a large impact, largely because of its illustrations. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek achieved up to 300 times magnification with a simple single-lens instrument, rediscovered red blood cells and spermatozoa, and helped popularise the use of microscopes for biological microstructure.

In 1893 August Köhler developed Köhler illumination, which is central to reaching the theoretical limits of resolution. Phase contrast, discovered by Frits Zernike in 1953, and differential interference contrast, by Georges Nomarski in 1955, allowed unstained, transparent samples to be imaged.

In 1931 Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll developed the first prototype electron microscope, which uses electrons in place of light, giving much higher resolution. Knoll developed the scanning electron microscope in 1935, and the first commercial one, the Stereoscan, was marketed in 1965. From 1981 to 1983 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in Zürich created the scanning probe microscope, and in 1986 the atomic force microscope was invented. Stefan Hell shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the STED technique.
midas: Several kings named Midas ruled Phrygia, and later tradition merged them. The oldest, who belongs to myth, was said to be the son of Gordias and the goddess Cybele, or in Arrian's account the son of Gordios, a poor peasant. Arrian tells that the Phrygians, torn by civil discord, were told by an oracle that a wagon would bring them a king.

Midas arrived in a wagon with his parents, was made king and dedicated the wagon in the citadel to Zeus, giving rise to the saying that whoever loosened its knot would rule Asia. Legends place this Midas before the Trojan War, though Homer does not mention him. A second Midas of the late 8th century BCE is the historical figure, and Herodotus names a third, of the 6th century BCE, grandfather of Adrastus.

The Midas of the late 8th century BCE ruled Phrygia until the sack of Gordium by the Cimmerians. Most historians identify him with Mita, king of the Mushki, who according to Assyrian tablets of the reign of Sargon II attacked Assyria's eastern Anatolian provinces. Some historians think he was called king of the Mushki because he had subjected that people and taken them into his army.

Greek sources say that he married Damodice, daughter of Agamemnon of Cyme, and traded extensively with the Greeks. Herodotus records that a Midas son of Gordias gave a royal throne to the oracle at Delphi and was the only foreigner to give an offering there before Gyges of Lydia. Some historians believe that this was the 8th-century king.

Greek writers, among them Strabo, say that Midas killed himself by drinking bull's blood during the Cimmerian attack, which Eusebius dated to about 695 BCE and Julius Africanus to about 676 BCE. Excavation has confirmed that Gordium was destroyed and burned at about that time. In 1957 Rodney Young opened a royal burial in the Great Tumulus at Gordion, with timbers cut around 740 BCE, a collection of Iron Age drinking vessels and inlaid tables. It was named Tumulus MM, for Midas Mound, and is now generally thought to cover his father.

Myth gave Midas the golden touch, granted by Dionysus in thanks for his kindness to Silenus and lifted when he washed in the river Pactolus, whose sands turned to gold. In another story Apollo gave him donkey's ears when he preferred Pan's music, and his barber's whispered secret grew into reeds that repeated it.
middle-ages: The term Middle Ages first appears in Latin in 1469 as media tempestas, middle season. Other early variants were medium aevum, first recorded in 1604, and media saecula, first recorded in 1625. Medieval writers divided history into periods such as the Six Ages or the Four Empires and considered their own time the last before the end of the world. In the 1330s the Italian humanist Petrarch called the post-Roman centuries dark compared with the light of classical antiquity. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use a tripartite periodisation, in 1442, and it became standard after the 17th-century German historian Christoph Cellarius divided history into ancient, medieval and modern.

In the history of Europe the Middle Ages lasted approximately from the 5th to the late 15th centuries and are divided into the Early, High and Late Middle Ages. They began with the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Between the 5th and 8th centuries peoples such as the Ostrogoths under Theoderic the Great, the Burgundians and the Franks filled the political void. The break with classical antiquity was incomplete: the new kingdoms kept Roman institutions, and the Byzantine Empire survived in the Eastern Mediterranean.

In the High Middle Ages, which began after 1000, the population of Europe grew from an estimated 35 to 80 million between 1000 and 1347. Manorialism and feudalism organised society, the East–West Schism came in 1054, and the Crusades were first preached in 1095. The Late Middle Ages brought the Great Famine of 1315–1317 and, from 1347 to 1350, the Black Death, which killed probably about 35 million people, around one-third of Europeans.

The medieval period is often caricatured as a time of ignorance and superstition. The caricature descends from the Renaissance, whose scholars saw the Middle Ages as a decline from the Classical world, and from the Enlightenment, whose scholars saw reason as superior to faith. Others argue that reason was held in high regard in the period.

It is untrue that everyone in the Middle Ages believed the Earth was flat. Lecturers in medieval universities commonly argued that the evidence showed the Earth to be a sphere, and Lindberg and Numbers state that scarcely a Christian scholar of the period failed to acknowledge its sphericity.
middle-atlas: The Middle Atlas is the northernmost and second highest of the three main Atlas chains of Morocco. To the south, the Moulouya and Oum Er-Rbia rivers separate it from the High Atlas. To the north, across the Sebou River, lie the Rif mountains, an extension of the Baetic System, which includes the Sierra Nevada in the south of Spain. The range forms the westernmost end of a large plateaued basin that reaches east into Algeria, bounded by the Tell Atlas to the north and the Saharan Atlas to the south.

It is a solid mountain mass about 350 km long, made primarily of limestone. Tabled rock in the west runs to elevations of 800 to 1,000 metres, while folded rock toward the north-east exceeds 3,000 metres. The highest point is Jbel Bou Naceur at 3,340 metres, and the summits of Moussa ou Sabel (3,172 metres) and Jbel Bou Iblane (3,081 metres) also stand high. Volcanic plateaus lie among the limestone, and Jbel Hebri is a cone volcano.

Extensive forests of cedar, holm oak and cork oak cover the slopes, cut by deep valleys, and small lakes rich in fish lie among the volcanic plateaus. The range borders the Plaine du Saïs and the cities of Fes, Meknes and Beni Mellal. Its upper reaches are the stronghold of Berber tribes who speak Tamazight and live at very low population densities. The Barbary macaque, an endangered primate that once ranged more widely across northern Morocco, is native here, and wild boar and polecat also live in the range.

Snow lies in winter and can fall from 600 metres above sea level, and the town of Ifrane has enough of it to serve as a ski resort. The range feeds four major river basins: the Sebou, the Oum Er-Rbia and the Bou Regreg, which drain to the Atlantic, and the Moulouya, which drains to the Mediterranean. One of the principal roads to the south of Morocco crosses it, linking Fes with Tafilalet. Tazekka National Park lies at its eastern end and Ifrane National Park between Khenifra and Ifrane.
middle-east: The Middle East is a geopolitical region generally defined as all of Egypt and all of West Asia except the Caucasus. It roughly corresponds with what Western Europe historically called the Near East, set against the Far East. Its main features are the Arabian Peninsula, Anatolia, the Levant and Mesopotamia, which together make up the Fertile Crescent, and the Iranian plateau. Most of it is hot and arid, but rivers such as the Nile, the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Jordan irrigate farmland.

The term may have originated with the India Office of the United Kingdom in the 1850s. It became widely known after the American naval strategist Alfred Thayer Mahan used it in 1902 for the area between Arabia and India, in an article on the Persian Gulf. Until the Second World War the area centred on Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean was usually called the Near East.

The Middle East was the first region outside Africa to be settled by modern humans and the first in which writing systems developed. Agriculture was independently developed there and spread during the Neolithic to Europe, the Indus Valley and eastern Africa. The earliest civilisations, Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia in Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt, arose in the Fertile Crescent and the Nile Valley. They were followed by the Hittite, Greek, Hurrian and Urartian civilisations of Asia Minor, Elam, Persia and Media in Iran, and the Levantine civilisations of Ebla, Mari, Ugarit, Canaan, Phoenicia and Israel.

The Near East was first largely unified under the Neo Assyrian Empire, then under the Achaemenid Empire, followed by the Macedonian Empire and, to some degree, by the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire. The Romans stationed five or six legions in the region to defend it from Sasanian and Bedouin raids and invasions. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all originated in the region and have their holiest sites there, as do Manichaeism, Yezidi, the Druze faith and Mandeanism.

Arabs are the largest ethnic group, followed by Iranian and Turkic peoples, with Kurds, Jews, Assyrians and many others. The six languages with most speakers are Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Kurdish, Modern Hebrew and Greek. The Gulf Arab states hold vast reserves of petroleum.
middle-francia: Middle Francia was created in 843 by the Treaty of Verdun, which ended nearly three years of civil war among the surviving sons of Louis the Pious and divided the Carolingian Empire into three kingdoms. It was allotted to the eldest son, Lothair I. It lay between East and West Francia and took in the Frankish lands between the Rhine and the Scheldt, the Frisian coast, the former Kingdom of Burgundy except a western portion, Provence and northern Italy as far as the Veneto, an area of about 300,000 to 350,000 square kilometres. Its long borders were hard to defend, and it shared frontiers with few other states, which limited its trade.

In 855, on his deathbed at Prüm Abbey, Lothair I divided the kingdom among his three sons by the Treaty of Prüm. Louis II received northern Italy and the imperial title, Charles received Burgundy and Provence, and Lothair II received the northern lands, which became known as Lotharingia. Charles died without sons in 863, and his brothers divided his realm, Lothair II taking the western Lower Burgundian parts and Louis II Provence.

When Lothair II died in 869 his only son, Hugh, born to his mistress Waldrada, was declared illegitimate. His heir was Louis II, who was campaigning against the Emirate of Bari, and by the Treaty of Meerssen in 870 Charles the Bald and Louis the German divided Lotharingia between them. When Louis II died in 875 Charles the Bald took his realm in Italy with the backing of Pope John VIII. Charles the Fat was crowned emperor in 881 and reunited the whole Carolingian Empire in 884, which lasted only until his overthrow in 887.

None of Lothair I's three sons left a legitimate male heir, so the territories of Middle Francia were redistributed step by step, which allowed West Francia and East Francia to claim them. Its eventual disappearance should not be taken to mean that it lacked geographical or cultural cohesion.
middle-kingdom-of-egypt: The Middle Kingdom, also called the Period of Reunification, followed the First Intermediate Period, when Old Kingdom power had collapsed and the country was decentralised. Towards the end of that period two rival dynasties, the Tenth at Herakleopolis ruling Lower Egypt and the Theban Eleventh ruling the south from the First Cataract to the Tenth Nome of Upper Egypt, fought for control.

Mentuhotep II took the Theban throne in 2055 BCE and in his fourteenth regnal year used a revolt in the Thinite Nome to attack Herakleopolis, which put up little resistance. He finished consolidating the country by his 39th year, and is regarded as the founder of the period.

Mentuhotep II campaigned as far south as the Second Cataract, in Nubia, restored Egyptian hegemony over Sinai and depicted himself as a god in his lifetime, wearing the headdresses of Amun and Min. He reigned 51 years. The Eleventh Dynasty ruled from Thebes. The Twelfth, whose kings ruled from el-Lisht, began with Amenemhat I, who had to campaign in the Delta, built the Walls of the Ruler in the east Delta and founded a new northern capital, Amenemhet It Tawy.

The Prophecy of Neferty, dating from about this time, presents a king arising from the far south to restore the kingdom. From the Twelfth Dynasty pharaohs kept standing armies with Nubian contingents, but the kingdom's strategy was defensive, with fortresses at the First Cataract, in the Delta and across the Sinai Isthmus.

After the death of Sobekneferu came a series of short-lived kings, the first of the Thirteenth Dynasty, whose members were mostly unrelated and are attested on few monuments. The period was followed by the Second Intermediate Period, in which the Hyksos of West Asia ruled Lower Egypt.

The Eleventh Dynasty rebuilt a centralised administration under a vizier, sometimes divided between north and south, with the Overseer of Sealed Goods as treasurer and the Overseer of the Estate as chief steward. Provinces stayed in the hands of nomarchs from powerful families. High Nile floods, averaging 19 metres above non-flood levels, accompanied the most prosperous years, under Amenemhat III.

Royal pyramids were built of mud brick with a casing of Tura limestone, and statuary and sarcophagi reached a peak of quality. Literature written for entertainment and reflection appeared in the early Twelfth Dynasty, among it the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor, the Story of Sinuhe and the Dispute between a man and his Ba, which later Egyptians counted as classic.
middle-persian: Middle Persian, whose own name for it was Pārsīg, is a Western Middle Iranian language. The Middle period of the Iranian languages runs from the fall of the Achaemenid Empire in the fourth century BCE to the fall of the Sasanian Empire in the seventh century CE. Middle Persian descended from Old Persian and became the literary language of the Sasanian Empire. During the Sassanid period (224 to 651 CE) it was also called Ērānīg, belonging to Iran, and its use in official inscriptions shows that the Sassanids defined themselves as ethnically and culturally Iranian.

The most important change was from the synthetic structure of Old Persian and Avestan to an analytic one: nouns, pronouns and adjectives lost almost all their case endings, and prepositions marked the roles of words. Stress fell on the last syllable, because the syllables after the stress in Old Persian had been dropped: Old Persian pati became Middle Persian pad.

Middle Persian was written in several scripts. The Pahlavi script is notable for its many Aramaeograms, Aramaic words written but pronounced as Iranian ones. The word for father, pidar, was written with a form that was originally the Aramaic for my father. Few words were actually borrowed from Aramaic. The Manichaean script was more straightforward. Early inscriptions of the 3rd and 4th centuries still had a minimal case system, a direct case and an oblique case, and the usual word order was subject, object, verb.

Texts survive in Sasanian inscriptions, Egyptian papyri, coins and seals, fragments of Manichaean writings and Zoroastrian literature. Zoroastrianism was the state religion of Sasanian Iran until the Muslim conquest, and Pahlavi Middle Persian carries a large body of literature on its traditions. The earliest Zoroastrian texts were probably written down in the 6th and 7th centuries, though they codify earlier oral tradition. Most date from the 9th to the 11th century, when Middle Persian had long ceased to be spoken, and the surviving manuscripts are usually 14th-century copies.

Manichaean Middle Persian was used for religious writings, and the Middle Persian of the Church of the East is attested in the Pahlavi Psalter of the 7th century. Both were used across Central Asia, including Turpan, until the beginning of the second millennium. Middle Persian texts were still intelligible to speakers of Early New Persian in the 10th and 11th centuries, and New Persian, Achomi and Luri are its descendants.
middlesex: The boundary of Middlesex follows the Thames in the south, the Lea to the east and the Colne to the west, with a line of hills marking its northern edge with Hertfordshire. The county lay in the London Basin and was largely low-lying, with clay in the north and alluvium on gravel in the south. In the north, a hedge about 20 kilometres long, of great antiquity, marks the boundary between the Colne and Barnet Gate Wood. It is the second smallest of the historic counties of England, after Rutland.

The county grew from the homeland of the Middle Saxons. Their province occupied at least the area of the later county and much of Hertfordshire, and it is recorded only as part of the Kingdom of Essex, though charters show it was not part of the East Saxon core and it was probably independent at some point. The Diocese of London, re-established in 604 as the East Saxon see, kept boundaries based on Essex until the nineteenth century. It is not known exactly when Middlesex became a county, possibly in the early tenth century. The Domesday Book of 1086 records six hundreds: Edmonton, Elthorne, Gore, Hounslow, Ossulstone and Spelthorne.

The City of London became a self-governing county corporate, while Westminster, dominated by Westminster Abbey until the Dissolution of the Monasteries, was separate from it. In the south-east the Tower Division, or Tower Hamlets, was a county within a county with its own Lord Lieutenant. As London grew, the East End reached the Essex boundary and the Tower Division passed a population of one million, while railways spread the north-western suburbs. The Metropolitan Police served areas near London from 1829 and the whole county from 1840.

In 1889 about twenty per cent of the area and a third of the population became part of the new administrative County of London, and the remainder came under Middlesex County Council. The county never had a single established county town; assizes met at the Old Bailey and quarter sessions at Clerkenwell. Suburban growth after the interwar years led to the creation of Greater London in 1965, which took in almost all of the county.

Middlesex lies almost entirely within the ceremonial county of Greater London, with smaller parts in Hertfordshire and Surrey. Middlesex Day is observed on 16 May, recalling the 57th (West Middlesex) Regiment at the Battle of Albuera in 1811, whose commander, Lieutenant-Colonel William Inglis, urged his men to Die hard. The county's coat of arms shows three seaxes, attributed to the Kingdom of Essex. Middlesex County Cricket Club, founded in 1864, remains active.
midwestern-united-states: The Midwestern United States, also called the Heartland or the Middle West, is one of the four census regions defined by the United States Census Bureau, which called it the North Central Region until 1984. It lies between the Northeastern and Western United States, with Canada to the north and the Southern United States to the south. The region generally lies on the broad Interior Plain between the Appalachian and Rocky Mountains. Its major rivers include the Ohio River, the upper Mississippi River and the Missouri River.

The earliest Native American cultures in the Great Plains and Great Lakes areas date from about 12,000 to about 8,000 BCE. They were followed by the Archaic period, the Woodland Tradition and, from 900 to 1500 CE, the Mississippian period, whose traits probably began in the area of St. Louis, Missouri. During the colonial period the French settled the upper Mississippi watershed and called it the Illinois Country. French control ended in 1763, and Napoleon sold Louisiana to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 created the Northwest Territory, bounded by the Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, and was the first large region of the United States to prohibit slavery. Large-scale settlement became possible only after the defeat of Native American tribes at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794. By the time of the Civil War European immigrants were settling directly in the interior: German immigrants in Ohio, Wisconsin, Minnesota and other states, and Irish immigrants in Great Lakes ports such as Cleveland and Chicago. The Republican Party originated in the Midwest in the 1850s.

The Census Bureau's definition covers 12 states: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota and Wisconsin. Chicago is the most populous city and the largest economic and financial centre. The economy mixes heavy industry and agriculture, with extensive areas forming part of the Corn Belt.
mie-prefecture: Mie forms the eastern part of the Kii Peninsula, about 170 km from north to south and 80 km from east to west, with a coastline of 1,094.9 km. Bordering Aichi, Gifu, Shiga, Kyoto, Nara and Wakayama prefectures, it is counted as part of both the Kansai and Tokai regions, and Kansai dialect is spoken there. It has five geographical areas: the Suzuka Mountains in the north-west, the Ise Plain along the coast of Ise Bay, where most of the population lives, the Shima Peninsula, the Iga Basin on the border with Nara, and the Nunobiki Mountainous Region in the south. Forest covers about 65 per cent of the land.

Evidence of human habitation in Mie goes back more than 10,000 years, and agricultural communities formed along the rivers and coasts in the Jomon and Yayoi periods. In the seventh century the Saiku Imperial Residence was built in what is now Meiwa to serve as the home and administrative centre of the Saio, an imperial princess who was high priestess of Ise Shrine.

In the Edo period the area was divided among several feudal domains. Port towns such as Ohminato, Kuwana and Anotsu and castle towns flourished along the Tokaido and Ise Roads, and pilgrimages to Ise Shrine became very popular. After the Meiji Restoration the old provinces were reorganised repeatedly: in 1871 the area from the Kiso Three Rivers to Tsu became Anotsu Prefecture and the area south of it Watarai Prefecture. In 1872 the Anotsu seat moved to Yokkaichi and the prefecture was renamed Mie, but the seat returned to Tsu in 1873, and Mie took its present form in 1876, when it merged with Watarai. In 1959 the Ise-wan Typhoon devastated parts of the prefecture and killed many people.

Tsu is the capital and Yokkaichi the largest city. The prefecture contains some of the oldest and holiest sites of Shinto, among them the Ise Grand Shrine and the Tsubaki Grand Shrine, and the Kumano Kodo, an old pilgrimage road in the south that is a World Heritage Site. Northern Mie has manufacturing, mainly of vehicles, ships and heavy chemicals, and Honda has run a factory at Suzuka since 1960. The poet Matsuo Basho was born in Mie, and so were the scholar Norinaga Motoori and the writer Edogawa Ranpo.
mieszko-i: Nothing certain is known of Mieszko's life before he took control of his lands. Only the Lesser Poland Chronicle gives a birth date, which modern researchers do not treat as reliable, and historians propose dates between 922 and 945. He took power after his father's death, probably about 960, and inherited the lands of the Polans and Goplans, the Sieradz-Łęczyca region and Kuyavia, and perhaps Masovia and Gdańsk Pomerania. The territory was mixed and joined chiefly by tribal structures. Around 966 the traveller Abraham ben Jacob, at the court of Boleslaus I the Cruel in Prague, described Mieszko as one of four Slavic kings, with a large and highly regarded army.

In 965 Mieszko married Dobrawa, daughter of Boleslaus I, Duke of Bohemia, in an alliance he probably sought himself, and he was baptised in 966. Most historians see this as a political decision that brought him closer to the Czechs and lowered the risk of attack by German margraves, and it may have helped him to remove a pagan priestly class that blocked centralised rule. On 21 September 967 Polish and Bohemian troops defeated the Wolinians under Wichmann the Younger, giving him control of the mouth of the Oder. In 972 Margrave Odo I of the Saxon Ostmark attacked Poland.

Mieszko allied with Sweden against Denmark, probably in the early 980s, and the Danes were defeated about 991. A war with Bohemia in 990 left Poland holding Silesia, and Lesser Poland came under his rule at about this time. Around 991 to 992 he issued with his wife Oda and their sons the document called Dagome iudex, placing his lands under the protection of the pope and describing their borders. Only a later summary survives.

Mieszko died on 25 May 992 of a fever in old age, according to Thietmar of Merseburg. He was probably buried in Poznań Cathedral, but his remains have never been found. Thietmar says he divided his state among several princes, probably his sons. He is credited with uniting the Polish lands in the first state that can be called Poland, and his acceptance of Western Christianity brought Poland into the structures of Catholic Europe. Gniezno Cathedral was built during his rule. He left his sons a territory at least twice the size of his inheritance, with Silesia, Western Pomerania and probably Lesser Poland added.
mieszko-ii-lambert: Mieszko II was the second son of Bolesław I the Brave but the eldest born to his third wife, Emnilda of Lusatia. He could read and write and knew Greek and Latin, which was unusual for the period. His father named him successor and used him in dealings with Germany. About 1013 he married Richeza, daughter of Count Palatine Ezzo of Lotharingia and niece of Emperor Otto III, and received Kraków to rule, with Wawel as his residence.

In 1014 he was sent as an envoy to Duke Oldřich of Bohemia and was imprisoned there. He then led Polish troops in the war against Emperor Henry II that ended in the Peace of Bautzen of 30 January 1018, on terms very favourable to Poland.

Bolesław died on 17 June 1025, and Mieszko was crowned king on Christmas Day by Archbishop Hipolit in Gniezno Cathedral. He inherited Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, Silesia, Gdańsk Pomerania, Lusatia, Red Ruthenia and the territory of present-day Slovakia. His half-brother Bezprym and his full brother Otto received nothing, since Bolesław did not wish to divide the kingdom, and according to some chroniclers Mieszko expelled them.

Opponents of Emperor Conrad II sought his help, and in 1028 Polish troops invaded Saxony and devastated it. With Hungary as an ally he invaded again in 1030, while the Hungarians briefly occupied Vienna. Yaroslav I the Wise conquered Red Ruthenia, and in 1031 Conrad besieged Milsko, forcing Mieszko to give up lands. That year a Kievan army installed Bezprym, and Mieszko fled to Bohemia, where Oldřich imprisoned him again.

Bezprym lost his authority amid unrest and was murdered in 1032. At Merseburg on 7 July 1032 Conrad II divided Poland between Mieszko, Otto and a cousin named Dytryk. Otto was killed in 1033, Dytryk was probably expelled, and Mieszko reunited the country, though he still faced the nobility. He died suddenly on 10 or 11 May 1034, probably in Poznań, and was buried in the cathedral of St Peter and St Paul.

After his death peasants revolted in what is called the pagan reaction, and his son Casimir I the Restorer was expelled or driven out. Some modern historians think economic grievances, such as new taxes for the Church, counted for more than religion. The Czechs invaded Silesia and Greater Poland in 1039, and the capital moved to Kraków. He is called Mieszko II Gnuśny, the Lazy, which the sources attached to the way his reign ended.
miguel-angel-asturias: Miguel Ángel Asturias was born in Guatemala City on 19 October 1899, the first child of Ernesto Asturias Girón, a lawyer and judge, and María Rosales de Asturias, a schoolteacher. In 1905 the family moved to the house of his grandparents. He lived in Paris in the 1920s, where he studied ethnology at the Sorbonne with Georges Raynaud, an expert on the Quiché Maya, and finished a translation of the Popol Vuh in 1926. He also associated with the Surrealists, and some scholars credit him with bringing features of modernist style, such as magical realism, into Latin American writing.

Asturias was involved in politics throughout his career, opposed the dictatorship of Manuel Estrada Cabrera and served as ambassador in several Latin American countries. He supported the government of Jacobo Árbenz, whose policies ran against the interests of the United Fruit Company. When Árbenz fell in 1954, Carlos Castillo Armas expelled Asturias and stripped him of his citizenship. He spent eight years in Buenos Aires and Chile and then moved to Europe, where he lived in Genoa. In 1966 he won the Soviet Union's Lenin Peace Prize, and in 1967 the Nobel Prize in Literature, which some critics thought was awarded to a writer little known outside Latin America. He spent his last years in Madrid and died there on 9 June 1974.

His first book, Leyendas de Guatemala (1930), retells Maya myths. El Señor Presidente, completed in 1933 and privately published in Mexico in 1946, denounces the dictator Estrada Cabrera, and has been called a study of fear. Hombres de maíz (Men of Maize, 1949) tells of an indigenous community whose land is threatened by planters and sets the Maya belief that the first humans were made of maize against the modernising society around them. The banana trilogy, Viento fuerte (1950), El Papa Verde (1954) and Los ojos de los enterrados (1960), is a fictional account of foreign control of the banana industry and the exploitation of native workers, and it earned him the Lenin Peace Prize. Mulata de tal followed in 1963.

Asturias, himself a mestizo, proposed a hybrid national identity for Guatemala, ladino in language and Maya in mythology. His prose, rhythmic and rich in repetition and onomatopoeia, has been called tropical baroque. The Miguel Ángel Asturias National Prize in Literature, the country's most distinguished literary prize, is named after him.
miguel-de-cervantes: Many details of Cervantes's life remain uncertain, including his name, background and appearance. He signed his name as Cerbantes, but his printers used Cervantes, which became the common form. In later life he used Saavedra, the name of a distant relative, rather than Cortinas, after his mother. It is generally accepted that he was born around 29 September 1547 in Alcalá de Henares, the second son of the barber-surgeon Rodrigo de Cervantes and Leonor de Cortinas.

Rodrigo was often in debt or looking for work, and the family moved constantly. When he was imprisoned for debt from October 1553 to April 1554, Leonor supported the family alone. They lived in Córdoba until 1556, when his grandfather died. It has been suggested that one or both parents were New Christians, Catholics of Jewish ancestry, but the view has no wide following. No authenticated portrait of Cervantes is known to exist.

In 1569 Cervantes was forced to leave Spain and went to Rome, where he worked in a cardinal's household. In 1570 he enlisted in a Spanish Navy infantry regiment. He was badly wounded at the Battle of Lepanto in October 1571. Captured by Barbary pirates in 1575 while serving as a soldier, he was ransomed after five years and returned to Madrid.

He claimed to have written more than 20 plays, such as El trato de Argel, based on his captivity, but such works were short-lived. His first significant novel, the pastoral romance La Galatea, appeared in 1585 and received little notice. He worked as a purchasing agent and later as a government tax collector. By 1605 he had not been published for 20 years.

Don Quixote, first published in January 1605, set out explicitly to undermine vain and empty chivalric romances. Its portrayal of real life and its everyday speech were considered innovative, and it was instantly popular: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza appeared in masquerades celebrating the birth of Philip IV on 8 April 1605. An unauthorised sequel under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda came out in 1614, and Cervantes published his own second part in 1615. The first part is more comic, the second more sophisticated, with greater depth of characterisation.

His other works include the twelve Novelas ejemplares of 1613, the allegorical poem Viaje del Parnaso, eight short farces, and Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda, published after his death in 1617. English writers rediscovered him in the mid-18th century, and John Bowle published an annotated edition of Don Quixote in 1781. It has been translated into all major languages.
miguel-hidalgo-y-costilla: Hidalgo was born on 8 May 1753, the second child of criollo parents; his father managed a hacienda near Valladolid in Michoacán. He studied with the Jesuits and then at the Colegio de San Nicolás, and took his degree in philosophy and theology at the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico in 1773. He learned Nahuatl, Otomi and Purépecha as well as French, which let him read Enlightenment works forbidden by the Church. He was ordained in 1778 and taught at the Colegio de San Nicolás in Valladolid, becoming its dean in 1790. Authorities ousted him in 1792 for revising traditional teaching and for irregular handling of funds.

He later became parish priest at Dolores, Guanajuato, where he set up brick and pottery works, trained indigenous people in leatherwork and promoted beekeeping, until Spanish mercantile policy ordered him to stop.

After the discovery of the Conspiracy of Querétaro, Hidalgo rang the parish bells on the night of 15 to 16 September 1810 and called the people to arms. His exact words are unknown, and accounts differ on whether they invoked King Ferdinand VII. Hidalgo and Ignacio Allende left Dolores with about 800 men and took San Miguel and Celaya with little resistance. At Guanajuato the insurgents overwhelmed the fortified Alhóndiga de Granaditas and killed an estimated 400 to 600 people. The Inquisition condemned Hidalgo as a seditionist and heretic, and Bishop Manuel Abad y Queipo excommunicated him.

After the Battle of Monte de las Cruces on 30 October 1810 his forces stood close to Mexico City, but Hidalgo turned back, a decision historians still debate. At Guadalajara he formed a government and on 6 December 1810 decreed the abolition of slavery and of tribute. Royalist forces under Félix Calleja defeated his army at the Calderón Bridge in January 1811, and the other leaders took military command from him on 25 January. Ignacio Elizondo betrayed and captured the leaders at the Wells of Baján on 21 March 1811.

Hidalgo was defrocked at Durango on 27 July 1811 and executed, most probably by firing squad, on 30 July at Chihuahua. His head and those of Allende, Aldama and Mariano Jiménez were displayed at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas for ten years. His movement passed to José María Morelos, his former student. Though Agustín de Iturbide became first head of state in 1821, later liberal movements favoured Hidalgo, and 16 September 1810 became recognised as the day of independence. The town of Dolores was renamed Dolores Hidalgo, and the state of Hidalgo was created in 1869. His remains lie in the Angel of Independence in Mexico City.
miguel-lopez-de-legazpi: Miguel López de Legazpi was born in Zumarraga in the Basque province of Guipúzcoa. His family was wealthy and held military and municipal offices, and his father, Juan de Legazpi, was a soldier who had served in the Italian Wars. His education is unknown, but his later posts suggest legal training. After his father's death in 1527 his older brother inherited the family wealth.

Around 1528 he settled in New Spain. He served as clerk of the mint, secretary of the municipal council and, in 1559, alcalde mayor of Mexico City, and he took part in several inquisitorial processes between 1536 and 1543.
