In 1532 he married Isabel Garcés, with whom he had nine children. Two grandsons, Felipe and Juan de Salcedo, later sailed with him.

In 1564 the viceroy Luís de Velasco commissioned him, on the order of King Philip II, to lead an expedition across the Pacific. Five ships and about 500 soldiers sailed from Barra de Navidad in November 1564, with the friar Andrés de Urdaneta as navigator and spiritual adviser. After 93 days they reached the Mariana Islands, where they fought the Chamorro. In the Philippines Legazpi made blood compacts with local chiefs, including Datu Sikatuna on 16 March 1565, and landed at Cebu on 27 April 1565, where he overcame Rajah Tupas and founded a settlement.

A Portuguese blockade of Cebu in 1568 failed. In 1569 food shortages led him to move to Panay. In 1570 he sent Martín de Goiti to Luzon, and Goiti's force defeated a fleet led by Bambalito at the Bangkusay Channel. Legazpi followed, made a pact with the local rulers Rajah Sulayman and Lakan Dula, and established a settlement at Manila on 24 June 1571. He ordered the walled city of Intramuros built and proclaimed Manila the capital.

Legazpi governed the islands for about a year. He died of a stroke in Manila on 20 August 1572, bankrupt after spending most of his fortune on the conquest, and was buried in San Agustin Church in Intramuros. His letters to Philip II on the expedition are kept in the General Archive of the Indies in Seville.

His expedition with Urdaneta effectively created the Manila galleon trade, in which silver mined in Mexico and Potosí was exchanged for Chinese silk, porcelain, spices and other goods. The Philippines remained a Spanish possession until the Treaty of Paris of 10 December 1898, apart from the British occupation of Manila and Cavite in 1762 to 1764. The capital of Albay province bears his name.
miguel-primo-de-rivera: Miguel Primo de Rivera was born on 8 January 1870 into a landowning military family of Jerez de la Frontera, the son of a retired colonel. His uncle Fernando was Captain General in Madrid. He graduated from the General Military Academy in Toledo in 1884 and served as a junior officer in the colonial wars in Morocco, Cuba and the Philippines. He watched Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War in 1898. After fighting the Berbers of the Rif he became convinced that Spain probably could not hold its North African colony and should withdraw if it could not dominate it. He was promoted to brigadier general in 1911 and later commanded the military regions of Valencia, Madrid and Barcelona.

Spain's army suffered a heavy defeat at the Battle of Annual in 1921, and by 1923 deputies of the Cortes were calling for an investigation into the responsibility of King Alfonso XIII and the army. On 13 September 1923 Primo de Rivera, as Captain General in Barcelona, led a military coup. The king named him prime minister. He suspended the constitution, dissolved the Cortes and set up a directorate of eight military men, and on 3 December 1925 replaced it with a civilian directory. His Patriotic Union, meant to be an apolitical party, failed to attract many members.

He withdrew Spanish forces in Morocco, and when Moroccans attacked the French sector, French and Spanish united to crush the rebellion in 1925, with victory in 1927. His regime built dams and railways, and the Barcelona Metro opened in 1924. It organised 27 committees to mediate between employers and workers, and unemployment largely disappeared. It also censored the press, closed the Ateneo club and banned the CNT trade union. To suppress Catalan separatism it made the use of Catalan in church services illegal.

The economic boom ended; the peseta fell and inflation rose. He lost the support of the armed forces after he began to inject politics into promotions in the artillery corps, and the king drew away. On 26 January 1930 he asked the military leaders whether he still had their backing. Their cool answers persuaded him to resign two days later, and he died in Paris on 16 March 1930.

The king, discredited by his support for the dictatorship, went into exile on 14 April 1931 after republican candidates won in 41 provincial capitals, and the Second Republic followed. Primo de Rivera's son José Antonio later founded the Falange.
mikhail-bakunin: Mikhail Alexandrovich Bakunin was born on 30 May 1814 (18 May in the old style) into the Russian nobility. His family's Priamukhino estate in the Tver region had over 500 serfs. His father, Alexander Mikhailovich Bakunin, a diplomat who had served in Italy, raised ten children on the Rousseauan model, and Mikhail was the third child and eldest son.

He trained as a military officer, deserted in 1835 and was discharged. In Moscow he joined the circle of Nikolai Stankevich, read German philosophy and produced the first Russian translation of Hegel. Alexander Herzen funded his studies at the University of Berlin from 1840, where he drew towards the Young Hegelians. His first original publication, The Reaction in Germany, appeared in 1842 and marked his shift from philosophy to revolutionary rhetoric.

Bakunin left for Zürich in 1843, and when he defied Russian orders to return, the Russian Senate stripped him of his noble rights and sentenced him in absentia to penal labour in Siberia. In Paris he befriended Pierre-Joseph Proudhon and met Karl Marx. A speech to Polish emigrants in 1847 led to his deportation from France. He took part in the Prague Slavic Congress and its insurrection in 1848, and in the Dresden uprising of 1849.

Imprisoned, sentenced to death and extradited several times, he was held in solitary confinement in the Peter and Paul Fortress in 1851. Exiled to Siberia in 1857, he escaped in 1861 via Japan and the United States and reached London, where he worked with Herzen on the journal Kolokol.

He joined the International Workingmen's Association in 1868. At the 1872 Hague Congress, which he could not reach, Marx's side prevailed and Bakunin was expelled, after which he founded the Anti-Authoritarian International. He took part in the Lyon insurrection of 1870, wrote Statism and Anarchy in 1873, and planned an unsuccessful insurrection at Bologna in 1874. He died in Bern on 1 July 1876.

Bakunin wrote prolifically but fragmentarily, and was not a systematic thinker; much of his work was published after his death. He first called himself an anarchist in 1867. He wished to replace the state and hierarchical religious, social and economic institutions with free federations of communes and voluntary associations of producers, organised from below upward. God and the State, published in 1882 from a fragment, became his most widely translated work.

He rejected Marx's idea of a dictatorship of the proletariat, warning that a Marxist state would rule over the workers rather than be ruled by them. His split with Marx divided the socialist movement from the anarchist one.
mikhail-frunze: Mikhail Vasilyevich Frunze was born on 2 February 1885 in Pishpek, now Bishkek, then a small Russian garrison town in Russian Turkestan. His father was a Bessarabian Romanian paramedic and his mother was Russian. He began higher studies at Verniy, now Almaty, and in 1904 entered the Saint Petersburg Polytechnical University. In the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party he sided at eighteen with Lenin's Bolsheviks. In the 1905 Revolution he led striking textile workers in Shuya and Ivanovo. Arrested in 1907, he was sentenced to death, spent months on death row, and had the sentence commuted to life at hard labour. After ten years in Siberian prisons he escaped to Chita and edited a Bolshevik weekly.

In 1917 Frunze headed the Minsk civilian militia and was elected president of the Byelorussian Soviet, then led an armed force of workers in Moscow. In March 1919 he took command of the Southern Army Group of the Eastern Front. After his troops defeated Admiral Alexander Kolchak at Omsk, Leon Trotsky gave him overall command of the Eastern Front on 19 July 1919. He drove Basmachi insurgents and White troops from Turkestan and captured Khiva in February 1920 and Bukhara in September 1920. In November 1920 his army took the Crimea and pushed Pyotr Wrangel out of Russia, and he also led the destruction of Nestor Makhno's anarchist movement in Ukraine.

In December 1921 Frunze visited Ankara as an ambassador of the Ukrainian SSR and established Turkish-Soviet relations. His diary of the visit records massacres of Greeks and Armenians that he saw in the Pontus region. He was elected to the Central Committee in 1921, became a candidate member of the Politburo on 2 June 1924 and in January 1925 was named chairman of the Revolutionary Military Council.

Frunze had a chronic ulcer and favoured conservative treatment, but Stalin and Anastas Mikoyan urged an operation. He died during surgery on 31 October 1925, and a number of historians attribute his death to chloroform poisoning. Rumours have held that Stalin arranged it; the claim rests on the accounts of authors such as Roman Brackman and Vadim Rogovin. He was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. Pishpek was renamed Frunze in 1926 and took back its name Bishkek in 1991. The Frunze Military Academy in Moscow and many streets and Metro stations were named after him, and some remember him for his military doctrine.
mikhail-gorbachev: Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev was born on 2 March 1931 in Privolnoye, in North Caucasus Krai, into a poor peasant family of Russian and Ukrainian heritage. His parents named him Viktor, but at his mother's insistence he was secretly baptised Mikhail. At three he moved to the collective farm that his maternal grandfather, a Communist Party member since 1928, chaired. He studied at Moscow State University, married fellow student Raisa Titarenko in 1953 and took his law degree in 1955. In Stavropol he worked for the Komsomol and supported Khrushchev's de-Stalinization. He became first party secretary of the Stavropol Regional Committee in 1970, and in 1978 returned to Moscow as a secretary of the Central Committee.

On 11 March 1985 the Politburo elected Gorbachev general secretary after the death of Konstantin Chernenko. He wished to preserve the Soviet state and its Marxist-Leninist principles but held that significant reform was needed. His glasnost, or openness, widened freedom of speech and the press, and perestroika, restructuring, sought to decentralise economic decision-making. He withdrew troops from the Soviet-Afghan War and met United States president Ronald Reagan at the Reykjavik Summit to discuss limiting nuclear weapons and ending the Cold War.

The elected Congress of People's Deputies that he formed undermined the party's supremacy. When Warsaw Pact countries abandoned Marxist-Leninist rule in 1989 he declined to intervene militarily, and in November East Germany opened the Berlin Wall, a decision he praised. German reunification followed in 1990, and many observers then declared the Cold War over. He received the Nobel Peace Prize that year.

Growing nationalism in the republics threatened to break up the Soviet Union, and in August 1991 hardliners launched an unsuccessful coup against him. In its wake the union dissolved, against his wishes. Out of office he launched the Gorbachev Foundation in 1992 and Green Cross International in 1993. He died in Moscow on 30 August 2022, aged 91. Many, particularly in Western countries, praise his role in ending the Cold War and tolerating the fall of Marxist-Leninist governments in central and eastern Europe, while critics hold that he weakened Russia's global influence and precipitated an economic collapse.
mikhail-kalinin: Kalinin was born on 19 November 1875 into a peasant family in the village of Verkhnyaya Troitsa in Tver Governorate. He worked on the land with his father until he was 13, and a local landowning family later took him to Saint Petersburg as a footman. At 18 he became a lathe operator at the Putilov works.

He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1898. He was arrested the following year, imprisoned for ten months and exiled to the Caucasus, where in Tbilisi he met Sergei Alliluyev and came to know Stalin through the Alliluyev family. Further arrests followed, and in 1906 he joined the Bolshevik faction and married Ekaterina Lorberg, an ethnic Estonian.

At the 1912 Bolshevik conference in Prague Kalinin was elected an alternate member of the Central Committee but not a full member, because he was suspected of being an agent of the Okhrana; the real agent was Roman Malinovsky. In April 1917 he favoured conditional support for the Provisional Government, a position at odds with Lenin's. He was chosen mayor of Petrograd in the autumn city elections and administered it during and after the revolution of 7 November.

When Yakov Sverdlov died in March 1919, Kalinin replaced him as head of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee, the titular head of state. The post was renamed in 1922 and again in 1938, and he held it without a break until 1946. He became a full member of the Politburo in January 1926 and remained one until his death.

The official press called Kalinin the All-Union Elder, a title that stressed his peasant origins, but by the 1930s his part in decisions was nominal. Khrushchev later said that under Stalin Kalinin was the nominal signatory of all decrees. On 5 March 1940 he was one of six Politburo members who signed the order to execute 25,700 Polish prisoners, which led to the Katyn massacre. His wife Ekaterina, arrested on 25 October 1938 as a Trotskyist, was sentenced in 1939 to fifteen years in a labour camp; she was released shortly before he died.

He retired in 1946 and died of cancer in Moscow on 3 June that year. He was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis after a state funeral. The city of Königsberg, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1945, was renamed Kaliningrad after him in 1946, and Tver was called Kalinin until its historic name was restored in 1990.
mikhail-tukhachevsky: Mikhail Nikolayevich Tukhachevsky was born on 16 February 1893 (4 February in the old style) at Alexandrovskoye, near Smolensk, into a family of impoverished hereditary nobles. He attended the Cadet Corps and graduated from the Aleksandrovskoye Military School in 1914, joining the Semyenovsky Guards Regiment as a second lieutenant. Captured by the German forces in February 1915, he escaped four times from prison camps and was held as an incorrigible escapee in the fortress of Ingolstadt, where he shared a cell with Captain Charles de Gaulle. His fifth escape succeeded and he returned to Russia in September 1917, after which he joined the Bolsheviks despite his noble birth.

In the Russian Civil War he was made responsible for defending Moscow, and in 1919 Leon Trotsky gave him command of the Fifth Army, which retook Siberia from Aleksandr Kolchak's forces. In 1920 he completed the defeat of Anton Denikin, and in March 1921 he commanded the 7th Army in the suppression of the Kronstadt rebellion.

In 1920 he commanded the Western Front in the Polish–Soviet War and pushed back the Polish and Ukrainian forces that had taken Kiev in May, but he was beaten by Piłsudski at the Battle of Warsaw. He and Joseph Stalin blamed each other for the failure.

He served as Chief of Staff of the Red Army from 1925 to 1928, became First Deputy Commissar for defence under Kliment Voroshilov, who disliked him. After Stalin accepted the need for an industrialised military in 1931, Tukhachevsky had a leading role in reform and pressed for tanks, aircraft and airborne forces. He was made a Marshal of the Soviet Union on 20 November 1935. He is often credited with the theory of deep operations, though his exact role is disputed for want of firsthand sources.

He was arrested on 22 May 1937. The NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov supervised his interrogation and torture, and he confessed to treason. A military tribunal tried him and eight generals on 11 June 1937, found them guilty that night, and he was shot within the hour.

His wife and two brothers were shot, three sisters were sent to the Gulag, and his daughter Svetlana was raised in an orphanage and the Gulag. In 1956 Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech ended the official view of him as a fascist, and on 31 January 1957 he and his co-defendants were rehabilitated.
miklos-horthy: Miklós Horthy de Nagybánya was born on 18 June 1868 at Kenderes, the fourth of eight children of an untitled Hungarian noble family raised in the Reformed Church. His father, István Horthy de Nagybánya, sat in the House of Magnates and held an estate of 610 hectares. At 14 Horthy entered the Imperial and Royal Naval Academy in Fiume, where teaching was in German, so that he spoke Hungarian with a slight Austro-German accent for the rest of his life.

He became a sub-lieutenant in 1896, served as aide-de-camp to Emperor Franz Josef from November 1909, and fought in the Battle of the Strait of Otranto. In February 1918 Emperor Karl I made him rear admiral and the last commander in chief of the fleet, ahead of eleven other admirals.

Hungary lost two thirds of its territory and a third of its Hungarian speakers in the settlement ratified as the Treaty of Trianon in 1920, and the Communist leader Béla Kun seized power in Budapest in March 1919. Horthy returned to the capital with the National Army. On 1 March 1920 the National Assembly re-established the kingdom, and with National Army officers controlling the parliament building it voted him regent over Count Albert Apponyi by 131 votes to 7. Former king Charles IV tried twice to return and was escorted into exile in 1921.

His first decade was spent stabilising the economy and the political system with his prime minister, István Bethlen, with British support. Historians describe the regime as national conservative and aimed at revising Trianon; some critics point to anti-Jewish laws passed from 1920.

Hungary became in effect a member of the Axis in April 1941 and declared war on the Soviet Union on 27 June 1941. In 1944 Horthy's government made approaches to the Allies, and Hitler summoned him to Klessheim, where he allowed the deportation of a large number of Jews, generally put at 100,000, but refused to go further. In August he installed a new government under Géza Lakatos and halted the mass deportations. After his arrest by the Germans he was held until the end of the war, interviewed at Nuremberg and lived in Portugal until his death on 9 February 1957. His memoirs appeared in 1953.

His body was returned to Kenderes in 1993. Hungarians still dispute whether he was a conservative who allied with Germany to recover lost land or a ruler whose policies led to collaboration in the Holocaust.
mikmaq: Miꞌkmaq, singular Miꞌkmaw, comes from a word meaning my friends, and they also call themselves Lꞌnuk, the people. Their territory, Miꞌkmaꞌki, is one of the five confederated Wabanaki countries and was traditionally divided into seven districts, eight if Ktaqmkuk in Newfoundland is counted. Each had its own government, with a district chief and a council of band chiefs, elders and other leaders, which made laws, administered justice, apportioned hunting and fishing grounds and made war and peace. The Grand Council, Santeꞌ Mawioꞌmi, was the senior body. The 1876 Indian Act disrupted its authority by requiring elected governments on the Canadian model.

The Miꞌkmaq speak Miꞌkmawi'simk, an Eastern Algonquian language. A hieroglyphic writing was created in 1677 by the French missionary Chrestien Le Clerq, who noted that children memorised prayers by counting marks, and the language is now written mainly in Latin letters. Traditions were passed down orally in religious narratives, legends and folklore, the best known being those of Glooscap, a creator and culture hero. Some Miꞌkmaq follow the Catholic faith, some only traditional beliefs, and many both. Chapel Island in Bras d'Or Lake, the gathering place of the Grand Council, is a pilgrimage site.

Archaeological evidence in south-western Nova Scotia traces land use to at least 4,000 years ago. The pre-contact population is estimated at 3,000 to 30,000. In 1616 Father Biard believed it to exceed 3,000, but he remarked that European diseases had caused large losses during the 16th century. Smallpox, other infectious diseases, wars and alcoholism brought a further decline to a low point in the middle of the 17th century. After King Philip's War in southern New England the Miꞌkmaq joined the Wabanaki Confederacy, with the Abenaki, Penobscot, Passamaquoddy and Maliseet, which was allied with the Acadian people.

The Miꞌkmaq, Maliseet and Passamaquoddy signed a series of Peace and Friendship Treaties with the British Crown through the 18th century, the first in 1725 and the last in 1779. The Miꞌkmaq maintain that they did not cede their land title through them. The Shubenacadie Indian Residential School was the only such school in the region and operated from 1930 to 1967.

On 17 September 1999 the Supreme Court of Canada, in R v Marshall, upheld a treaty right of the Miꞌkmaq to hunt, fish and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood, a right already set out in the Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1752. The case began with fishing charges laid in 1993 against Donald Marshall Jr. In 2005 the Miꞌkmaw Nora Bernard led a class action for survivors of the residential schools, which the Government of Canada settled. The first school run by the Miꞌkmaq in Nova Scotia, Miꞌkmaq Kina' matnewey, was established in 1982.
mikulov: Mikulov is a town of about 7,600 inhabitants in Břeclav District, South Moravia, on the border with Austria, about 18 km north-west of Břeclav and 42 km south of Brno. Most of its territory lies in the Pálava Protected Landscape Area. The name comes from Mikul, a short form of Mikuláš, the Czech form of Nicholas; the German name Nikolsburg prevailed in the earliest times, and Mikulov has been used since the 19th century.

A deed mentioning Mikulov in 1173 is a hoax of the 14th century. The first trustworthy mention is from 1249, when the Přemyslid margrave Ottokar II granted a castle and its surroundings to the Austrian noble Henry I of Liechtenstein. In 1572 Emperor Maximilian II granted the fief to Adam of Dietrichstein, and from 1575 until the 20th century the town belonged to the Dietrichstein family and its Mensdorff-Pouilly successors. Under Cardinal Franz von Dietrichstein it became one of the most important towns in Moravia, and in 1621 he signed the Treaty of Nikolsburg with the Transylvanian prince Gabriel Bethlen at the castle. After a fire in 1719 the family rebuilt the castle to its present appearance.

Jewish settlement began in 1421, when Albert II of Austria expelled Jews from Vienna and Lower Austria, and more came after 1454. In the first half of the 16th century Nikolsburg became the seat of the regional rabbi of Moravia. Judah Loew ben Bezalel officiated there for twenty years between 1553 and 1573. A census of 1754 counted some 620 Jewish families, about 3,000 people and half the town. In 1938 there were 472 Jewish residents; only 110 emigrated in time, and 327 did not survive the Holocaust. The German population, 98 per cent in 1890 and 82 per cent in 1930, was expelled after the Second World War.

Mikulov Castle, built in the Romanesque style and rebuilt in the Renaissance and Baroque styles, houses the Regional Museum. The synagogue, originally of the 16th century, is the only preserved synagogue of the Polish type in Moravia. The Jewish cemetery, founded in the mid-15th century, has around 4,000 tombs, the oldest readable one from 1605. The town is the centre of the Mikulovská wine region.
milan: Milan lies in the north-western part of the Po Valley, roughly halfway between the river Po to the south and the foothills of the Alps, with the lakes Como, Maggiore and Lugano to the north, the Ticino to the west and the Adda to the east. The land is flat, and the highest point is 122 m above sea level. The Celtic name Medhelanon, later Latinized as Mediolanum, is usually explained as a settlement in the midst of the plain, or between watercourses, given the Olona, Lambro and Seveso rivers.

According to the account of Livy, the Gaulish king Ambicatus sent his nephew Bellovesus into northern Italy, and Bellovesus is said to have founded the settlement in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus. Around 590 BCE a Celtic tribe of the Insubres, belonging to the Golasecca culture, settled the site as Medhelanon, around a sanctuary in the shape of an ellipse with axes of 443 m and 323 m, near the present Piazza della Scala. The Romans conquered the city in 222 BCE. From 284 to 402 CE it was capital of the western part of the Roman Empire.

In the late fourth century Saint Ambrose, as bishop of Milan, reshaped the centre and built the great basilicas at the city gates: Sant'Ambrogio, San Nazaro in Brolo, San Simpliciano and Sant'Eustorgio, which still stand. In the Late Middle Ages the wealthy Duchy of Milan was one of the great forces behind the Renaissance, and the Visconti family, major patrons of the arts, made the city a centre of Gothic art. Work on the cathedral began in 1386 and ended in 1877. Leonardo da Vinci worked in Milan from 1482 until 1499 and painted the Virgin of the Rocks and The Last Supper there.

In the early modern period Milan was a major centre of the Italian Enlightenment, and its cultural and political struggle against Austrian domination was crucial in the reunification of the Kingdom of Italy. From the 19th century the city led the industrial and financial development of Italy. After the Second World War its population grew with migration, first from poorer and rural parts of Italy and later from abroad, and it peaked at 1,743,427 in 1973.

Milan is the capital of Lombardy and the second-largest city in Italy after Rome, with a population of 1,362,863. It is regarded as the country's industrial and financial centre and is a world centre of fashion. The Cathedral, the largest church in Italy, the Pinacoteca di Brera and the Castello Sforzesco, which holds Michelangelo's last sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà, are among its principal monuments. Of the Roman city, few remains survive, notably the Colonne di San Lorenzo.
milan-cathedral: The cathedral stands on what was the most central site in Roman Mediolanum, that of the public basilica facing the forum. The first cathedral, the new basilica dedicated to St Thecla, was completed by 355, and the old octagonal baptistery, dating to 335, can be visited under the present building. A fire damaged the cathedral and its adjoining basilica in 1075, and they were rebuilt as the Duomo.

In 1386 Archbishop Antonio da Saluzzo began construction of the present cathedral, at the time Gian Galeazzo Visconti took power in Milan. The work was regulated by the Fabbrica del Duomo, which had 300 employees. In 1389 the French engineer Nicolas de Bonaventure was appointed and added Rayonnant Gothic, and Gian Galeazzo gave the Fabbrica exclusive use of the marble of the Candoglia quarry.

The plan is a nave with four side aisles, crossed by a transept and followed by a choir and apse. The nave is about 45 metres high, with the highest Gothic vaults in a completed church. The building is of brick faced with marble, and the roof is known for its forest of openwork pinnacles and spires. In 1762 the spire bearing the Madonnina statue was erected at a height of 108.5 metres. The best-known statue inside is Saint Bartholomew Flayed, of 1562, by Marco d'Agrate.

Construction stalled almost completely after 1402, when about half of the cathedral was complete, and resumed in earnest only after 1480. In 1488 Leonardo da Vinci and Donato Bramante made models for the central cupola. Carlo Borromeo consecrated the whole building in 1577. On 20 May 1805 Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the façade to be finished, and it was completed within seven years. The last portal was inaugurated on 6 January 1965.

Opinions have been divided. John Ruskin called the cathedral a theft from every style, while Henry James found it grandly curious and superbly rich. Mark Twain gave a chapter of The Innocents Abroad to it.
milan-kundera: Milan Kundera was born on 1 April 1929 in Královo Pole, a district of Brno, Czechoslovakia, to a middle-class family. His father, Ludvík Kundera, was a Czech musicologist and pianist who headed the Janáček Music Academy in Brno from 1948 to 1961. He learned the piano from his father and studied musicology and composition, and musical references appear throughout his work. In 1947, at eighteen, he joined the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia. He studied film at the Film and TV School of the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague, and in 1952 became a lecturer in world literature there.

Kundera was expelled from the party in 1950, readmitted in 1956 and expelled again in 1970. His first expulsion inspired the main theme of his first novel, The Joke (1967), a satire of the ruling party. He was peripherally involved in the Prague Spring, which the Warsaw Pact invasion crushed in August 1968. He lost his teaching post, and his books were banned.

On a first visit to Paris in 1968 he befriended the publisher Claude Gallimard, who later smuggled the manuscript of Life Is Elsewhere out of Czechoslovakia and encouraged him to emigrate. Kundera moved to France in 1975. His Czechoslovak citizenship was revoked in 1979, and he became a French citizen in 1981. From 1985 he made a conscious transition from Czech to French, and his first work written in French, Slowness, appeared in 1995.

His early poetry was staunchly pro-communist, but his novels escape ideological classification, and he insisted that he was a novelist rather than a politically motivated writer. The Book of Laughter and Forgetting appeared in 1979 and mixed novel, stories and the author's reflections. The Unbearable Lightness of Being, published in 1984, is his best-known work. It deals with the fragility of an individual fate and the idea of eternal return, and follows a Czech surgeon from Prague to Zurich and back. A film of it appeared in 1988. A Czech edition by an expatriate in Canada was published in 1985, and an official one in Czechoslovakia only in 2006.

His fiction mingles philosophical digression with narrative and drew on Robert Musil. Recurring themes include exile, identity and history as a continual return. He lived quietly and rarely spoke to the media. He received the Jerusalem Prize in 1985 and the Herder Prize in 2000, and died on 11 July 2023.
milan-rastislav-stefanik: Milan Rastislav Štefánik was born on 21 July 1880 at Košariská, then in the Kingdom of Hungary, one of twelve children of a Lutheran pastor, Pavol Štefánik, and Albertína Jurenková. He studied engineering in Prague from 1898 and then astronomy, physics and philosophy at Charles University, where Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk's lectures inspired him with the idea of cooperation between Czechs and Slovaks. He took part in the Slovak student association Detvan. He graduated in 1904 with a doctorate, writing on the supernova of 1572 in the constellation Cassiopeia.

In 1904 Štefánik went to Paris, where Pierre Janssen gave him work at the Paris-Meudon Observatory. He observed from Mont Blanc and joined a French expedition to observe a solar eclipse in Spain, and in 1907 he received the Prix Jules Janssen of the Société astronomique de France. From 1908 he undertook scientific and political missions for the French authorities on several continents, building an observatory in Tahiti, and in 1912 he led a Bureau des Longitudes eclipse mission to Brazil. He became a French citizen in 1912 and patented a design for colour photography in 1911.

In the First World War he joined the French army and trained as an aviator, flying missions over the Serbian Front in 1915. In 1916 he, Masaryk and Edvard Beneš founded the Czechoslovak National Council, and he organised Czechoslovak legions in France and Italy and travelled to Russia in 1917 and Siberia in 1918. His diplomacy helped lead the Entente to recognise the Council as a de facto government. He became Czechoslovakia's Minister of War.

On 4 May 1919 Štefánik was flying home from Italy in a Caproni Ca.3 when the plane crashed near Ivanka pri Dunaji, close to Bratislava, and he died with its three crew. Rumours held that it was shot down, but an Italian eyewitness said an engine exploded during a second landing attempt. His tomb, designed by Dušan Jurkovič, was built on Bradlo Hill in 1927 and 1928. Bratislava Airport, the Slovak armed forces academy and the minor planet 3571 Milanštefánik bear his name.
milas: Milas lies on a fertile plain at the foot of Mount Sodra in south-western Turkey, about 20 kilometres from the coast, and has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate. Large quarries of white marble on and around the mountain have been used since very ancient times. The district has 150 kilometres of coastline on the Gulf of Güllük and the Gulf of Gökova. The ancient name, Mylasa, with its old Anatolian ending in -asa, points to a very early foundation.

The earliest historical mention is from the beginning of the 7th century BCE, when Arselis, a Carian leader from Mylasa, helped Gyges of Lydia in his contest for the Lydian throne. Under Achaemenid rule Mylasa was the chief city of Caria. The Lygdamid dynasty ruled it in the 5th century BCE, and between 460 and 450 BCE it belonged to the Delian League. The Hecatomnids, satraps of the Persian Empire who were Greek in language and culture, made it their capital. Under Mausolus, who ruled from 377 to 352 BCE, the capital moved to Halicarnassus, but Mylasa kept its importance.

In 40 BCE it suffered great damage when Labienus took it in the Roman Civil War. An inscription from Mylasa gives one of the few certain facts about the life of Tacitus, showing that he governed Asia in 112-13.

Saint Ephrem, in the fifth century, was one of its bishops. Turks under Menteşe Bey took the region in the late thirteenth century, and his beylik made the city its capital. Its rulers' administrative centre was the more defensible castle of Beçin, 5 kilometres away. The Ottomans took the beylik in 1390. Timur restored it to the Menteşe beys after the Battle of Ankara, and Sultan Mehmed I brought it back under Ottoman rule in 1420. One of the first acts of the Ottomans was to move the regional seat to Muğla. In 1923 the Greeks of Milas, some 2,900 of 9,000 inhabitants in 1912, were exchanged with Turks from Greece.

Milas is a district of Muğla Province, with twenty-seven archaeological sites of note. Among the sights are the Mausoleum of Hecatomnus, the Roman Baltalıkapı gate, the tomb called Gümüşkesen, and the Orhan Bey Mosque of 1330 and the Great Mosque of 1378, both from the Menteşe period. The ancient cult centre of Labranda lies 14 kilometres away. Milas carpets and rugs of wool have been known internationally for centuries.
milford-connecticut: Milford lies on the coast between New Haven and Bridgeport, and includes the village of Devon and the borough of Woodmont. When the English first came, the Paugussett, an Algonquian-speaking people, predominated in the territory. The small river that runs through the town gave the area its early English name, Wepawaug.

English colonists affiliated with the New Haven Colony bought the land of present-day Milford, Orange and West Haven on 1 February 1639 from Ansantawae, chief of the local Paugusset. They built a grist mill by the Wepawaug River in 1640. During the Revolutionary War the Milford section of the Boston Post Road, a vital route linking Boston, New York and other coastal cities, was blockaded by Continental forces, and Fort Trumbull was built to protect the town. The Liberty Rock monument marks the site of the blockade.

Milford gave rise to several towns. Woodbridge was formed in 1784, partly from New Haven, and Orange, originally North Milford, was chartered in 1822 by residents of the northern and eastern sections. West Haven was created from Orange in 1921. The remaining town was known for shipbuilding, farming and oystering, and in the later 19th century it became a beach resort for people from New Haven and Bridgeport. The Memorial Bridge, a stone bridge and tower commemorating the founders, replaced the last mill over the Wepawaug in 1899. Woodmont was incorporated as a borough in 1903, and in 1959 the town, with Woodmont, became the City of Milford.

One curiosity dates from 1902, when boxes of Quaker Oats held a coupon for the legal deed to a tiny lot, sometimes ten feet by ten, in a subdivision called Liberty Park that was never built. The lots caused paperwork for tax collectors, who often could not find the owners, until the town ended them in the mid-1970s by a general foreclosure.

The 2020 census counted 50,558 people. In the post-World War II period Milford suburbanised, and the Milford section of Interstate 95 was completed in 1958. The Connecticut Post Mall was built in the 1960s and 1970s, and a firm called SCELBI Computer Consulting, which many credit as the world's first personal-computer maker, was on the Boston Post Road in the 1970s. The Milford Oyster Festival has been held each August since 1975. The shoreline includes Silver Sands State Park, where a sandbar at low tide leads to Charles Island, a protected bird nesting ground.
military-industrial-complex: The expression military–industrial complex describes the relationship between a country's military and the defence industry that supplies it, seen together as a vested interest that influences public policy. Both sides benefit, one by obtaining weapons and the other by being paid to supply them. The concept is generally treated as unique to the United States, and its use for other countries is ambiguous. President Dwight D. Eisenhower used the term in his Farewell Address to the Nation on 17 January 1961, saying that the conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry was new in American experience, and that government must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence by the complex.

The speech was written by Ralph E. Williams and Malcolm Moos, and how far Eisenhower and his brother Milton shaped it is unclear from the surviving documents. Eisenhower was neither the first to use the phrase nor the first to warn of the danger. The first known use was by Winfield W. Riefler in 1947, who used it of the economic potentials of the states at war. C. Wright Mills's 1956 book The Power Elite, which described a powerful elite of military and corporate chiefs set against a powerless mass society, served as a framework for the debate of the 1960s and 1970s.

In its later meanings the phrase moved from Eisenhower's warning of a future danger to a claim that the complex already shaped policy. During the Vietnam War, opponents used it, partly because Eisenhower's conservative reputation protected them from charges of disloyalty, as John Kenneth Galbraith said. The Port Huron Statement used it closer to Mills's sense of a power elite. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke in a 1963 sermon of millions of citizens disturbed that the military-industrial complex too often shaped national policy. Dow Chemical became linked with the war after 1966 through its contract to make napalm, and protesters picketed its offices and disrupted shareholder meetings, among them Honeywell's in 1970.

Congress passed the Mansfield Amendment of 1969 to restrict military-sponsored university research, and Stanford and MIT spun off such work into SRI International and Draper Laboratory. Senator William Proxmire became the chief advocate of the view of the complex as an unaccountable bureaucracy, and in 1968 he named 23 defence contractors in a press conference. The economist Seymour Melman argued for converting arms industries to civilian work, while Murray Weidenbaum held that dependence on government contracts harms the contractors themselves. The phrase is often used as a pejorative, and some scholars say it suggests a conspiracy.
millau: Millau stands at the confluence of the Tarn and Dourbie rivers, in a large depression at about 340 metres, on the southern edge of the Massif Central. Its territory lies in the Grands Causses, limestone plateaus known for sheep farming and for cheese, including Roquefort, and is cut by gorges and ravines. The town is a subprefecture of the Aveyron department, in the former province of Rouergue, where people spoke Rouergat, a dialect of Occitan.

The town dates back nearly 3,000 years, when it stood on the Granède hills above the present town. In the second or first century BCE it moved to the plain on the left bank of the Tarn, and took its Gallic name, Condatomagus, from words for confluence and market. Close by was La Graufesenque, one of the major earthenware centres of the Roman Empire, where luxury ceramics such as red terra sigillata were made. By the second century CE trade had collapsed under competition, and barbarian invasions of the 4th and 5th centuries sent the town to the other bank, where it was called Amiliavum.

By the 9th century Millau was a seat of viguerie and a centre of lambskin glove production, with ramparts around it. In 1112 it passed to Béranger III, father of the future king of Aragon, and in 1187 a consular charter gave it communal freedom and consuls to raise taxes and apply justice. In 1271 it passed to the crown of France.

It came under English rule in 1361, during the Hundred Years War, and Louis XI attached it to the crown in 1476. The medieval bridge over the Tarn had 17 arches, and after one collapsed in the 18th century only a single arch remained. Gloves became a major industry in the 19th century, and in the first half of the 20th more than half the townspeople lived from leather. A six-month general strike in the winter of 1934 to 1935 followed a wage cut of 25 to 30 per cent, and the glove industry began to decline in the 1960s.

Millau has 11 listed historical monuments, among them the archaeological site of La Graufesenque, the church of Notre-Dame de l'Espinasse, a 12th-century belfry and the Pégayrolles mansion of 1738, which holds the town museum with its pottery, tannery and glove collections. A few workshops still make gloves for fashion and luxury brands. The Millau Viaduct, a cable-stayed road bridge carrying the A75 motorway across the Tarn valley, opened in 2004 and took traffic out of the town centre. The surrounding Causses and Cévennes have been a World Heritage Site since 2011.
millet: Millets are a varied group of small-seeded grasses grown as a staple cereal and used as fodder for livestock and as food for humans. Most belong to the tribe Paniceae, but the species are not all closely related. Common kinds include pearl millet, the most widely grown, proso, foxtail and finger millet, and fonio. Sorghum is sometimes called great millet. Millets tolerate drought and extreme weather and give a crop in a short season under hot, dry conditions, and their nutrition is comparable to wheat and rice.

Millets may have been eaten for about 7,000 years. In China proso and foxtail millet were important from the Early Neolithic, and the earliest evidence is at Cishan, where proso millet remains in storage pits date to roughly 10,300 to 8,700 years ago. Millet was farmed in Korea from about 3500 BCE. Little millet and kodo millet were domesticated in the Indian subcontinent by about 3000 and 3700 BCE.

Finger millet is native to the highlands of East Africa, and pearl millet was domesticated in the Sahel of West Africa, with early finds at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania and in the Tilemsi valley in Mali. Proso millet reached Italy around 1500 BCE and northern Germany from 1200 BCE. Hesiod and Theophrastus mention it in Greece.

Millet is a staple of the Sahel, making up much of the cereal eaten in Burkina Faso, Chad and the Gambia, and it can be ground and mixed with milk to make fura and brukina. In Namibia pearl millet, there called mahangu, is the dominant food staple. In Ukraine it was a common food of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, as a porridge called kulish.
In India it is usually eaten as a flour, and in the Himalayas it is fermented into drinks such as tongba and raksi. It is also a forage crop, on which lambs gain weight faster than on forage sorghum.
milovan-djilas: Milovan Djilas was born on 12 June 1911 at Podbišće near Mojkovac in the Kingdom of Montenegro, the fourth of nine children in a peasant family. His father Nikola had served in the Montenegrin Army and opposed the incorporation of Montenegro into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Djilas began studying literature at the University of Belgrade in 1929, already a committed communist. In March 1932 he was jailed for eight days for an anti-government demonstration. Arrested again eleven months later, he was tortured and sentenced to three years in Sremska Mitrovica Prison, where he met senior party members and became a committed Stalinist.

After his release in 1936 he gave up study for the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, sided with Josip Broz Tito against Stalin's attempts to control it, and entered the Central Committee in 1938 and the politburo the next year.

After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia in April 1941, Djilas helped Tito establish the Partisan resistance. The party resolved to begin an uprising on 4 July, and he was sent to Montenegro to organise it. In November 1941 Tito dismissed him from command there for his errors, including what were called leftist errors, and made him editor of the party paper Borba. In March 1944 he went on a mission to the Soviet Union and met Stalin. After the war he became vice-president in Tito's government, and in 1948 he was sent to Moscow in an attempt to bridge the gap between Moscow and Belgrade. As the break came, he became one of the leading critics of Stalin's efforts to control Yugoslavia.

Djilas was widely seen as Tito's possible successor, and he held the post of President of the Federal People's Assembly from 25 December 1953 to 28 January 1954. In his Borba articles of that winter he criticised bureaucratic Stalinism and went on to argue against the one-party state itself. He was expelled from the Central Committee in January 1954 and resigned from the League of Communists in March.

He was sentenced in 1956 for backing the Hungarian Revolution, and in 1957 for The New Class, published abroad, which argued that communism was creating a new class of privileged party bureaucrats. It was translated into more than 40 languages. Conversations with Stalin brought a further sentence in 1962. In prison he wrote a biography of Njegoš and translated Paradise Lost into Serbo-Croatian. He was freed by amnesty on 31 December 1966.

Djilas stayed in Belgrade as a dissident. He opposed the breakup of Yugoslavia, though he predicted in the 1980s that it would come on lines of bureaucratic nationalism after Tito. He died on 20 April 1995.
miltiades: Miltiades was a well-born Athenian of the prominent Philaid clan, son of Cimon Coalemos, who won the Olympic chariot race three times in succession. He came of age under the tyranny of the Peisistratids and was named after his father's maternal half-brother, Miltiades the Elder, who had founded a semi-autonomous tyranny on the Thracian Chersonese around 555 BCE. Miltiades the Younger held the eponymous archonship under the tyrant Hippias in 524/23 BCE. When Stesagoras, who had inherited the Chersonese, was killed by an axe in 516 BCE, Hippias sent him to claim the lands. He feigned mourning and imprisoned the men of rank who came to console him, kept 500 troops and made an alliance with King Olorus of Thrace by marrying his daughter Hegesipyle.

Around 513 BCE Darius I of Persia forced the Chersonese into submission and made Miltiades his vassal. Miltiades joined the Scythian expedition and was left with other Greek officers to guard the bridge over the Danube. He later claimed that he urged them to destroy it, a claim some historians doubt. He took part in the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE and captured Lemnos and Imbros, which he ceded to Athens. When the revolt collapsed in 494 BCE, he and his family fled to Athens in five ships in 493 BCE. He was put on trial as a former tyrant, but presented himself as a defender of Greek freedom against Persian despotism and was acquitted.

Elected one of the ten generals for 490 BCE, he insisted, as the general with most experience of the Persians, that they be fought at once at Marathon, and the polemarch Callimachus gave the deciding vote for attack when the generals were split five to five. He is often credited with the tactics that won the battle, among them a thinner centre of four ranks against eight on the flanks, and a run at the Persian line across the range of their archers.

In 489 BCE Miltiades led seventy ships against Paros, which he held a grudge against, and failed to take it. A grievous leg wound left him incapacitated. His rivals exploited the failure, he was charged with treason and sentenced to death, and the sentence was converted to a fine of fifty talents. He died in prison, probably of gangrene from the wound, and his son Cimon paid the debt. The Athenians refused to let him write his name on the Stoa Poikile but had him painted in the front rank of a battle painting there. Pheidias later made a statue of Nemesis at Rhamnus in his honour, said to have been cut from marble Datis had brought for a memorial to Persian victory.
milton-friedman: Milton Friedman was born on 31 July 1912, the youngest of four children and the only son of Jewish working-class immigrants from Beregszász in the Kingdom of Hungary, now Berehove in Ukraine. His parents worked as dry goods merchants, and the family moved soon after his birth to Rahway, New Jersey. Unable to find academic work, he followed his friend W. Allen Wallis to Washington, D.C., in 1935, where the New Deal gave many young economists employment. From 1937 he worked for the National Bureau of Economic Research, where he assisted Simon Kuznets.

From 1943 Friedman worked at the Division of War Research at Columbia University as a mathematical statistician, on weapons design and tactics. His work there produced sequential sampling, later described as the standard analysis of quality control inspection. In 1946 he began teaching economic theory at the University of Chicago, where he stayed for thirty years and helped build the Chicago school. He wrote a weekly column for Newsweek from 1966 to 1984. After retiring in 1977 he was affiliated with the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, and from 1981 he served on President Ronald Reagan's Economic Policy Advisory Board.

Friedman revived interest in the money supply as a determinant of the nominal value of output and is largely responsible for the modern form of monetarism. In 1968 he argued that a government producing greater inflation cannot permanently lower unemployment, which in the long run is set by frictions in the labour market. His book A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957) set out consumption smoothing and the permanent income hypothesis. In Capitalism and Freedom he argued for a volunteer military, freely floating exchange rates, a negative income tax and school vouchers.

His 1976 Nobel prize was controversial, mainly because of his association with the Chilean military ruler Augusto Pinochet; in 1975 Friedman had spent seven days in Chile giving lectures. He died in San Francisco on 16 November 2006, aged 94.
milton-obote: Apollo Milton Obote was born on 28 December 1925 in the village of Akokoro in northern Uganda, the third of nine children of a chief of the Oyima clan of the Lango people. He studied at Busoga College Mwiri and Makerere University, where he took a general arts course because law was not taught, and left without a degree. He worked in Buganda and then in Kenya, where he was involved in the independence movement. After returning to Uganda in 1956 he joined the Uganda National Congress and was elected to the colonial legislative council in 1957. In 1959 he led a faction into the Uganda People's Congress.

Before independence Obote formed a coalition with the Buganda royalist party Kabaka Yekka, and he became prime minister on 25 April 1962; Mutesa II, the Kabaka of Buganda, became ceremonial president. In January 1964 the army mutinied at Jinja, and a settlement gave soldiers large pay rises and rapid promotions, among them Idi Amin. Obote was later implicated in a gold-smuggling plot with Amin. When Parliament demanded an investigation, he suspended the constitution in March 1966 and declared himself president, and an attack on Mutesa's palace sent Mutesa into exile. A new constitution in 1967 abolished the federal structure and created an executive presidency.

After an assassination attempt on 19 December 1969 all opposition parties were banned. His Common Man's Charter set out his Move to the Left, and in 1970 the state took a 60 percent share in major companies and banks. His secret police, the General Service Unit, was held responsible for many cruelties. The army under Amin overthrew him in January 1971 while he attended a Commonwealth conference in Singapore.

Obote went into exile in Tanzania, where President Julius Nyerere supported him, and a rebel invasion of Uganda in 1972 failed. After Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles ousted Amin in 1979, his party won the elections of 1980, which its opponents believed were rigged, and a guerrilla war began under Yoweri Museveni. In 1983 Operation Bonanza killed tens of thousands of people. Estimates of the deaths in the fighting range from 100,000 to 500,000. Army commanders deposed Obote on 27 July 1985, and he lived in Kenya and Zambia. He died of kidney failure in Johannesburg on 10 October 2005, aged 79, and was given a state funeral in Kampala.
mimar-sinan: Sinan was born in Ağırnas, a small town near Kayseri in Anatolia. His origins are disputed. He is often thought to have been of Armenian or Cappadocian Greek origin, and less popular theories make him Albanian, Jewish, Bulgarian or Christian Turkish. In 1512 he was conscripted under the devshirme system, sent to Constantinople to train as an officer of the Janissary Corps, and converted to Islam. He learned carpentry and mathematics and assisted leading architects. He served on campaigns under Suleiman I, including the Battle of Mohács, and on campaign he built fortifications, roads and bridges.

At about the age of fifty Sinan was appointed chief royal architect, a post he held for almost fifty years, overseeing all construction for the empire with a large team of architects and master builders. His army training gave him an empirical rather than theoretical approach. Sources disagree on how many buildings he built or supervised, with counts from more than 300 to 476, and he relied on his office rather than designing every one. They included mosques, schools, mausoleums, hospitals, aqueducts, bridges and baths. Suleiman ordered the Süleymaniye Mosque with its complex of colleges, soup kitchen, hospital and caravanserai, and Sinan finished it in seven years.

Sinan described the Şehzade Mosque as the work of his apprenticeship, the Süleymaniye as that of his qualification and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne as that of his mastery. In his autobiography he named the Selimiye his masterpiece. Its octagonal central dome is 31.28 metres wide and rests on eight piers, and its four minarets are 83 metres high. He claimed its dome surpassed that of the Hagia Sophia, though the diameter is only about half a metre greater. He sought the largest volume under a single dome and a unified interior. His assistants included Sedefkar Mehmed Agha, architect of the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, and Mimar Hayruddin, architect of the Stari Most at Mostar.
mimnermus: Almost no reliable biographical details of Mimnermus have been recorded. The Byzantine encyclopaedia Suda calls him the son of Ligyrtyades, from Colophon, Smyrna or Astypalaea, and says he flourished in the 37th Olympiad, 632 to 629 BCE. Smyrna seems the most likely home, and the Astypalaea suggestion is unsupported. Smyrna's disappearance for three hundred years after its last siege by Alyattes of Lydia may be why Colophon was able to claim him. He may have been alive at that siege and possibly died with the town.

Elegy was accompanied by the aulos, a wind instrument, so its performance needed a singer and a player. Ancient accounts associate Mimnermus with an aulos player named Nanno, and one makes her his lover. Strabo describes him as both a pipe-player and an elegiac poet.

His work was collected by Alexandrian scholars in two books, of which only small fragments survive. Modern scholars think they were the Nanno, a collection of short poems on varied themes, and the Smyrneis, a quasi-epic on Smyrna's conflict with the Lydians. Fragment 1 asks what life is without golden Aphrodite and wishes for death when love and its gifts no longer matter. It goes on to a bleak picture of old age. He also wrote in a patriotic vein: a quotation in Strabo is the earliest surviving account of the Ionian migration from Pylos, and another describes a Greek warrior's deeds against the cavalry of the Lydian king Gyges.

Mimnermus reworked myth to his own needs. Aelian records that he gave Niobe twenty children, where Homer gave her twelve. He was strongly influenced by Homer, whose vocabulary, formulas and similes recur in his verse. The scholar David A. Campbell describes the result as distinctive poetry of easy grace and pleasing rhythm.

Solon, addressing him as Ligyaistades, objected to a couplet in which Mimnermus wished to die at sixty, and urged him to change it to eighty. Plutarch also criticised his self-indulgence. Callimachus praised the sweetness of one of his books, and Hellenistic poets such as Callimachus drew on his work. Propertius preferred his verses to Homer's on love, and Horace cited him as holding that nothing is pleasant without love and jests. Later poets regarded him chiefly as a love poet, though the fragments suggest a sturdier character than that.
minamoto-no-yoritomo: Yoritomo was the third son of Minamoto no Yoshitomo and Yura Gozen, daughter of Fujiwara no Suenori, High Priest of Atsuta Shrine. He was born at the family villa beside Atsuta Shrine in Owari Province, and was a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. His childhood name was Onitakemaru. In the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156 his father sided with the winning party of Emperor Go-Shirakawa and Taira no Kiyomori and had his own father executed.

In December 1159 Yoshitomo joined Fujiwara no Nobuyori in the Heiji rebellion, attacked Sanjō Palace and seized the emperor and the retired emperor while Kiyomori was away. Kiyomori returned and defeated the Minamoto at Rokuhara, and Yoshitomo was betrayed and executed. Yoritomo and his younger brothers were spared because of their age and sent to temples as monks. He grew up in exile and married Hōjō Masako, daughter of Hōjō Tokimasa.

In 1180 Prince Mochihito called the Minamoto clan throughout Japan to arms against the Taira, and Yoritomo took part. He set up his base at Kamakura in the east. His uncle Minamoto no Yukiie and his cousin Minamoto no Yoshinaka plotted against him. He lost his first major battle, at Ishibashiyama in September 1180, and spent the next six months raising a new army. His brothers Minamoto no Yoshitsune and Minamoto no Noriyori defeated the Taira in several battles, though Yoshinaka entered Kyoto in 1183. From 1181 to 1184 a truce with the Taira-dominated court gave Yoritomo time to build an administration of his own at Kamakura.

In the summer of 1189 he invaded the northern provinces of Mutsu and Dewa and razed Hiraizumi, the capital of the northern Fujiwara. Go-Shirakawa died in spring 1192, and Yoritomo took the title of Sei-i Tai Shōgun, which formally placed the feudal lords, the jitō and the shugo under his control. Kyoto was left with national ceremony and ritual.

During the great hunt at Fuji in May 1193 the brothers Soga Sukenari and Soga Tokimune killed Kudō Suketsune, the killer of their father, and Tokimune then raided Yoritomo's mansion before being stopped. Yoritomo was ordained a Buddhist monk in 1199 and died two days later, aged 51.

After his death his wife's family, the Hōjō, held power at Kamakura as regents, under the title of shikken, until 1333. The historian George Bailey Sansom wrote that Yoritomo was a truly great man, with foresight and practical good sense in building machinery to match his growing power. A stone pagoda beside Shirahata Shrine is traditionally believed to be his grave.
minangkabau-people: The Minangkabau language belongs to the Malayic subgroup of the Austronesian family and is closest to Malay, though when the two split from a common ancestor is not known. The highlands suit settlement, with fresh water, fertile soil and a cool climate, and until the twentieth century most of Sumatra's population lived there. Wet rice cultivation probably developed there long before it appeared elsewhere on the island.

Minangkabau tradition, passed down orally, says that the first Minangkabau arrived by ship and landed on Mount Marapi when it was no bigger than an egg. They then spread over the slopes and valleys of the region called the darek, made up of three luhak: Tanah Datar, Agam and Limapuluh Koto. Before Islam spread into the area in the sixteenth century, Buddhism was popular; the Padang Roco Inscription of 1286 records that an image of Avalokiteśvara was brought from Java to Dharmasraya.

The Minangkabau are regarded as the largest matrilineal society in the world. Property, family name and land pass from mother to daughter, while religious and political affairs are the responsibility of men, though some women also play important roles. The ideal is that married sisters stay in the parental home, their husbands having a visiting status, although in the 1990s the anthropologist Evelyn Blackwood found that only about 22 per cent of households in a conservative village were of this kind.

The traditional home is the rumah gadang, or big house, owned by the women of the family. Its roof curves upward in multi-tiered gables, said to imitate the horns of the water buffalo. Clan chiefs, the panghulu, give ceremonial speeches at weddings and funerals, and storytellers recite folktales called kaba to the rebab. Randai, a folk theatre combining music, dance, drama and the martial art silat, took shape early in the twentieth century.

The highlands were the seat of the Pagaruyung Kingdom and the scene of the Padri War of 1821 to 1837. Wandering abroad, called rantau, is seen by many Minangkabau as the way to maturity and success, and over half of them can be counted as living outside the homeland. They form the majority of the population of Negeri Sembilan in Malaysia and have a reputation as merchants. Overseas Minangkabau shaped language, food, music and martial arts in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. Mohammad Hatta, a co-founder of the Republic of Indonesia, Yusof Ishak, the first President of Singapore, and Tuanku Abdul Rahman, the first Yang di-Pertuan Agong of Malaysia, were all Minangkabau.
minaret-of-jam: The Ghurids controlled what is now Afghanistan in the 12th and 13th centuries, together with parts of eastern Iran, Central Asia, northern India and Pakistan. The Minaret of Jam probably stands at the site of their capital, Firozkoh. Its Arabic dating inscription is unclear, but a Kufic inscription on the north face gives the year five hundred ninety, equivalent to 27 December 1193 to 16 December 1194. The British archaeologist Ralph Pinder-Wilson believed it commemorated the victory of Mu'izz ad-Din, Ghiyath ud-Din's brother, over Prithviraj Chauhan, which opened the northern Indian subcontinent to Islam.

The minaret belongs to a group of about 60 minarets and towers built between the 11th and 13th centuries in Central Asia, Iran and Afghanistan. Some are thought to have been symbols of Islam's victory. Its architect, Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Naysaburi, is named in an inscription.

The circular tower rests on an octagonal base. It had two wooden balconies and was topped by a lantern. It is built of baked brick, stucco, terracotta and turquoise glazed tiles, and its outer face is decorated with floral and geometric designs, with bands of Kufic and Naskhi calligraphy and intersecting rhomboidal knots. Inside, a central pillar carries double spiral staircases of 159 steps each, leading up to the balconies, and above them six vaulted brick platforms.

The inscriptions include the Muslim confession of faith in the uppermost band, a verse from the surah al-Saff promising help from God and present victory, the names and titles of the Ghurid sultan Ghiyath ad-Din Muhammad bin Sam, and interlaced bands of the surah Maryam. Its form resembles the Ghazni minarets built by Masud III, and it is thought to have inspired the Qutub Minar in Delhi.

The minaret was assumed to be attached to the Friday Mosque of Firozkoh, which the chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani says was washed away in a flash flood before the Mongol sieges of the early 13th century. Juzjani says the Mongols destroyed Firuzkuh in 1222. Sir Thomas Holdich reported the minaret in 1886 while working for the Afghan Boundary Commission, but it did not come to wide attention until 1957, through the work of the French archaeologists André Maricq and Gaston Wiet. The landscape around it holds the ruins of a palace, fortifications, a pottery kiln and a Jewish cemetery. The site was nominated in 2002 as Afghanistan's first World Heritage site.
minas-gerais: Minas Gerais, literally General Mines, lies in Brazil's Southeast Region and takes its name from the mines found across the territory. Its terrain is rugged: more than 90 per cent lies above 300 metres, and the highest point, Pico da Bandeira, reaches 2,891 metres. The state is the source of several of Brazil's main rivers, among them the São Francisco, Grande, Doce and Jequitinhonha.

The region was inhabited by Indigenous peoples as long as 11,400 to 12,000 years ago. The first European expedition crossed the north between 1553 and 1555. From the late 16th century bandeirantes from São Paulo travelled through the territory in search of gold, precious stones and Indigenous people to enslave. The discovery of gold in the late 17th century brought a large migration and wealth to the captaincy, but gold soon became scarce and many people left. Beginning in the early 1700s along the Jequitinhonha River, Minas Gerais was for about 150 years the world's major supplier of gem diamonds.

The republic was proclaimed in 1889 and Minas Gerais became a state, passing through 14 administrative periods in its first 19 months; coffee growers rose to considerable influence in state politics. Benedito Valadares governed the state from 1933 to 1945, and the Manifesto dos Mineiros of 24 October 1943 called for the democratisation of the country.

Minas Gerais is one of Brazil's 27 federative units, with Belo Horizonte as capital and largest city. Its heritage of colonial architecture and art is preserved in towns such as Ouro Preto, Diamantina, São João del-Rei, Mariana, Tiradentes and Congonhas. The Estrada Real, a tourist circuit, follows the old roads used to carry gold from the mines to Rio de Janeiro and Parati.
mindanao: Mindanao covers 97,530 square kilometres and is mountainous; Mount Apo is its highest peak and the highest in the Philippines. Four seas surround it: the Sulu Sea to the west, the Philippine Sea to the east, the Celebes Sea to the south and the Mindanao Sea to the north. The upland plateaus of Bukidnon and Lanao del Sur hold Lake Lanao, the largest lake on the island, and two large lowlands lie in the valleys of the Agusan River and the Rio Grande de Mindanao. The name comes from the Maguindanao language: min, a past-tense prefix, and danao, 'lake'.

Archaeological finds show human activity about ten thousand years ago, and Austronesian peoples spread through the Philippines around 1500 BCE. Caves in the Zamboanga Peninsula held burial jars, celadons of the Yuan and Ming periods and gold ornaments, which point to long trade between the Subanon and the Chinese. From about 900 CE the people of Mindanao were strongly influenced by Hindu and Buddhist belief from Indonesia and Malaysia, and the island has yielded a golden kinnara and a Ganesha pendant.

Islam spread in the Philippines from the 14th century through merchants from the western Malay Archipelago, and the first mosque in the country was built in the mid-14th century at Simunul. About the 16th century the sultanates of Sulu, Lanao and Maguindanao grew out of earlier Hindu-Buddhist rajahnates. In 1521 Antonio Pigafetta, who sailed with Magellan, wrote of reaching the island. In 1898 Spain sold the archipelago to the United States for 20 million dollars. Settlers from Luzon and the Visayas were encouraged to move to Mindanao in the early 1900s, and settlement displaced the Blaan and Tboli. Japanese forces invaded in April 1942 and burned many towns.

Mindanao is divided into six administrative regions, and its largest cities include Davao City, Zamboanga City, Cagayan de Oro and General Santos. Dozens of languages are spoken, of which Cebuano has the most speakers. Most residents are Christian, and Muslims form the largest minority. The island is a major supplier of pineapples and bananas.
mindaugas: Little is known of Mindaugas's origins or rise to power. Contemporary sources are scarce, and the main ones, the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle and the Hypatian Codex, were produced by enemies of Lithuania and lack dates and places even for major events. A treaty with Galicia-Volhynia in 1219 lists Mindaugas and his brother Dausprungas among the elder dukes of Lithuania, and the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle describes him as ruler of all Lithuania in 1236.

Ruthenian chronicles say he murdered or expelled several dukes, including relatives. The historian S. C. Rowell described his rise as taking place through marriage, murder and military conquest. During the 1230s and 1240s he extended his power over Black Ruthenia and the Principality of Polotsk and made his seat at Navahrudak.

In 1249 war broke out when Mindaugas tried to seize the lands of his nephews Tautvilas and Edivydas and of Duke Vykintas of Samogitia, who allied with the Livonian Order and Daniel of Galicia. Mindaugas bribed the Order's Master, Andreas von Stierland, and agreed to be baptised as a Catholic and to give up some western lands, in return for Pope Innocent IV's recognition as king. He and his wife Morta were crowned in the summer of 1253.

About eight years of relative peace followed. Mindaugas made peace with Galicia-Volhynia, began a court, an administration and a diplomatic service, issued silver coins and sponsored a cathedral in Vilnius. Lithuanian rule in the west stayed weak, and the Livonian Order's government of Samogitian lands was seen as oppressive. In 1261 Mindaugas broke the peace with the Order and may have returned to paganism, though the accounts of this come from enemies.

After Morta died, Mindaugas took her sister, who was already married to Duke Daumantas of Pskov. In retaliation Daumantas and Mindaugas's nephew Treniota killed him and two of his sons in the autumn of 1263. Lithuania fell into disorder, and three of his successors were assassinated within seven years. Stability returned under Traidenis, grand duke from about 1270.

Mindaugas's standing was uncertain until the Lithuanian national revival of the 19th century. He is now generally considered the founder of the Lithuanian state. In the 1990s Edvardas Gudavičius argued for an exact coronation date, 6 July 1253. It is disputed, but it is now Statehood Day, a national holiday.
mindelheim: Mindelheim lies on the river Mindel, about 90 kilometres (56 miles) west of Munich, and is the capital of the Unterallgäu district. Memmingen and the spa towns of Bad Grönenbach, Ottobeuren and Bad Wörishofen are nearby. At various points in its history it was the chief settlement of a state of its own.

In 1365 the Dukes of Teck-Owen came into possession of Mindelheim. The last of that line, Louis of Teck, Patriarch of Aquileia from 1412, died in 1439. An Elector of Bavaria bought the town in the sixteenth century, and in 1704 it was confiscated from Elector Maximilian II Emanuel for his treachery and effectively occupied after the Battle of Blenheim.

On 18 November 1705 Emperor Joseph I made John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, Prince of Mindelheim, and Marlborough was invested at an Imperial Diet in Innsbruck on 24 May 1706. The principality lay south of the Danube, 45 km south-west of Augsburg, and covered about 15 square miles (39 km2), with an income of £2,000. Marlborough's investiture cost was reduced to £4,500 from the usual £12–15,000, and he avoided the wartime imperial tax of £6,000.

The King of Prussia, through the prince of Anhalt-Dessau, proposed that the title pass to all of Marlborough's heirs, but the princes opposed it, and no special remainder was provided. Marlborough visited in late May 1713 and received princely honours. The principality's fate depended on the peace, and under the Treaty of Utrecht Mindelheim was lost in 1714 to the Elector of Bavaria.

The town centre keeps the plan of a medieval settlement, with the town hall and churches around a central market square and parts of the old wall and gates still standing. The castle Mindelburg, with its donjon, is used for festivals and markets. The town has a museum of historic tower clocks and a museum of ethnic art.
minden: The town centre lies on a plateau on the western side of the Weser, 5 kilometres north of the Porta Westfalica gap between the Weser Hills and the Wiehen Hills, where the river leaves the Weser Uplands and flows into the North German Plain. The small Bastau stream joins the Weser from the west near the centre, and the edge of the plateau divides the upper town from the lower town. Routes from the south converged at the gap and met a west to east way and a ford across the river.

The name Minda first appears in the Royal Frankish Annals, in a record of an army assembly held by Charlemagne in 798. A permanent Frankish camp and a royal estate are supposed to have stood close by. The bishopric, founded around 800, was one of seven diocesan foundations of Charlemagne's rule. After the dissolution of the Duchy of Saxony in 1180 the bishop became sovereign of the Prince-Bishopric of Minden, which remained a territory of the Holy Roman Empire until 1648.

The Lutheran Reformation was introduced in 1529, during a vacancy after the death of Bishop Francis of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and the buildings of the dissolved Dominican convent became the first Protestant Gymnasium in Westphalia. Minden kept fortifications from the 15th century to the late 19th, and the fortress was dissolved in 1873. French troops occupied the town on 13 November 1806, and when they left on 3 November 1813 they blew up some arches of the Weser bridge. A Jewish community has existed since 1270. Between 1603 and 1684 there were 128 prosecutions for witchcraft, almost all of the accused women.

Minden is the capital of the district of Minden-Lübbecke in North Rhine-Westphalia. Its cathedral dates to the 11th century, with a Romanesque westwerk and an early Gothic nave of the 13th century; it was badly damaged by bombing in the Second World War and rebuilt by 1957. The town has been the terminus of one of the oldest German railway trunks since 1847, and the Mittelland Canal crosses the Weser here on an aqueduct.
mindoro: Mindoro has a land area of 10,571 square kilometres and lies off the south-western coast of Luzon and north-east of Palawan. It is divided into the provinces of Occidental Mindoro and Oriental Mindoro, and Calapan is its only city. The Mindoro Mountain Range runs 200 km north to south, and Mount Halcon in Oriental Mindoro is the highest point. During the Pleistocene, when lower sea levels joined most Philippine islands, the deeper channels around Mindoro kept it isolated, and the island has a large number of species found nowhere else in the archipelago, including the Mindoro dwarf buffalo, the tamaraw.

The name probably comes from Minolo, the native name recorded by Domingo Navarette in 1676, though the Spaniards also called the island Mina de Oro, gold mine. Han Chinese traders knew it as Ma-i or Mait. According to the historian William Henry Scott, the official history of the Song dynasty for the year 972 mentions Ma-i as a state that traded with China, and later Chinese records refer to it. Its traders exchanged beeswax, cotton, true pearls, tortoiseshell and betel nuts for Chinese porcelain, gold, iron pots, lead, copper, glass beads and iron needles. The Mangyans are the indigenous peoples.

The Sultanate of Brunei conquered the island and there were Moro settlements before the Spanish arrived and converted the population to Christianity. Wars between the Spaniards and Moros from Mindanao, who sought to enslave the converted people, then depopulated the island. Most of the population fled to nearby Batangas, and the once-rich towns fell into ruin. Mindoro joined the Philippine Revolution in 1898 and was the site of a battle in the Second World War. It was a single province from 1920 to 1950, when a referendum split it into its present two.

About 1.4 million people live on the island. Tagalog is the principal language, and indigenous Mangyan languages such as Iraya, Buhid, Tawbuid and Hanuno'o are also spoken. Christianity is the main religion, while the Mangyans are animists. The economy rests chiefly on farming, and only about 5 per cent of the original forest remains. Puerto Galera is its best-known tourist destination.
minerva: Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom, justice, law, victory and the sponsor of arts, trade and strategy. Her Etruscan form is Menrva, and it is disputed whether the Romans borrowed her from the Etruscans or the reverse. Varro attributed Sabine origins to her. She may have taken her place in the Capitoline Triad, with Jupiter and Juno, under Etruscan influence, since the Etruscans had a similar group of Tinia, Uni and Menrva. From the second century BCE the Romans equated her with Athena.

Excavations at a sanctuary in Lavinium found terracotta statues of Minerva from the 4th century BCE, with votive figures of girls and veiled women, swaddled infants and anatomical offerings. The archaeologist Fritz Graf concludes that she guarded young women in the passage to marriage and motherhood.

Minerva is a virgin goddess whose domain includes medicine, wisdom, commerce, weaving and the crafts. She is also a goddess of war, but of strategy rather than the violence of Mars. She is usually shown tall and armed, with a spear, and her sacred creature is the owl. Roman myth gives her the stories of Athena. She was born fully armed from the head of Jupiter, whom Vulcan split with a hammer. She made the olive tree in her contest with Neptune over the naming of Athens, and she turned the weaver Arachne into a spider after a contest. She is thought to have invented the flute, which she threw away because it puffed out her cheeks.

Her festival, the Quinquatria, ran from 19 to 23 March and was a holiday for artisans. According to Ovid the first day was her birthday, with no blood shed, and the next four days had games with drawn swords. A smaller festival of the flute-players was held on the Ides of June. According to Livy the annual nail marking the year was driven into her temple because she was thought to have invented numbers.
