In Roman Britain carpenters owned tools decorated with her image for protection. At Bath she was equated with the Celtic goddess Sulis, and the two names were used together or interchangeably for the deity of the hot springs, whose healing was thought to cure ailments such as rheumatism.
ming-empire: The Mongol-led Yuan dynasty ruled before the Ming. Explanations for its decline include discrimination against the Han people, overtaxation of areas hit by inflation, and massive flooding of the Yellow River after irrigation projects were abandoned. Rebellion broke out among the peasants called up to repair the levees, and a number of Han groups revolted, among them the Red Turbans in 1351. Zhu Yuanzhang, a penniless peasant and Buddhist monk, joined the Red Turbans in 1352, and in 1356 his force captured Nanjing, which he later made the capital. As the Hongwu Emperor (r. 1368–1398) he kept a standing army of over one million troops.

The Jianwen Emperor (r. 1398–1402) came to the throne after the Hongwu Emperor's death, and when he moved against his uncle Zhu Di a three-year civil war followed. The palace at Nanjing was burned, and Zhu Di took the throne as the Yongle Emperor (r. 1402–1424). He made Beijing a capital, built the Forbidden City, and sent the eunuch Zheng He on seven voyages into the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and eastern Africa.

In July 1449 the Oirat leader Esen Tayisi invaded and captured the Zhengtong Emperor on 8 September, an event known as the Tumu Crisis. The navy was then allowed to fall into disrepair, while forced labour fortified the Great Wall into its modern form. In the 16th century European trade, restricted to islands near Guangzhou such as Macau, brought maize, potatoes and chili peppers and a large influx of South American silver, which re-monetised an economy whose paper money was no longer trusted.

A slowdown in agriculture during the Little Ice Age, a rise in the value of silver, crop failure, floods and an epidemic undermined the dynasty. Meanwhile Nurhaci, a Ming vassal, united the Jurchen clans into a Manchu identity and in 1618 renounced Ming overlordship. The dynasty collapsed in 1644 when the rebel Li Zicheng entered Beijing. His Shun dynasty was defeated shortly afterwards by the Manchu-led armies of the Qing dynasty, with the help of the defecting Ming general Wu Sangui, and remnant regimes called the Southern Ming lasted until 1662.
minho-river: The Minho, or Miño in Spanish and Galician, is the longest river in Galicia, with a length of 340 km. By discharge it is the fourth largest river of the Iberian Peninsula after the Douro, Ebro and Tagus. It rises at Pedregal de Irimia in the Sierra de Meira, north of Lugo, about 695 metres above sea level. The lagoon Fonminhá was historically, and wrongly, regarded as its source. After about 73 km it passes just south of the walls of the Roman city of Lugo and flows south through canyons until the valley widens north of Ourense.

The name is recorded as Minius and Mineus and is thought to derive from an Indo-European root meaning to walk or go. The river receives its main tributary, the Sil, at Os Peares, about 20 km north of Ourense. After 260 km through Galicia it forms part of the border between Spain and Portugal for about 80 km, running mainly west. It reaches the Atlantic between A Guarda in Galicia and Caminha in Portugal.

The river has been dammed for hydroelectric power in a series of reservoirs from Portomarín to Frieira, and it also waters vineyards and farmland. Its lower valley is lush and green, producing corn, potatoes, cabbage and even kiwi fruit, with vines along the field edges. These vines yield the light, slightly sparkling Vinho Verde and the Ribeiro wine, and the best wine of the area, Alvarinho or Albariño, comes from around Monção, Arbo and Melgaço.

The medieval towns of Melgaço and Monção stand on the Portuguese bank. The Spanish town of Tui and the Portuguese Valença do Minho face each other across the river and guarded an important bridge for road and rail, and both preserve fortifications that are national monuments. The upper course has been declared a Biosphere Reserve. Oral tradition tells of mythological beings living in the basin, such as witches in the river and fish-men.
minnesota: Minnesota is the northernmost contiguous state, since the isolated Northwest Angle in Lake of the Woods County is the only part of the 48 contiguous states north of the 49th parallel. It borders Manitoba and Ontario to the north, Wisconsin to the east, Iowa to the south and North Dakota and South Dakota to the west. It is known as the Land of 10,000 Lakes, with 14,420 bodies of fresh water of at least ten acres each. About a third of the state is forested, and much of the rest is prairie and farmland.

The name comes from the Dakota name for the Minnesota River, either mní sóta, clear blue water, or Mníssota, cloudy water. The state seal carries the phrase Mni Sóta Makoce, the land where the water reflects the skies.

Native Americans have lived in Minnesota since the Woodland period of the 11th century BCE. The Upper Mississippian culture, made up of the Oneota and other Siouan speakers, emerged around 1000 CE and lasted until Europeans arrived in the 17th century. The Dakota lived in what is now Minnesota when French voyageurs and fur traders arrived, using the Grand Portage to reach trapping areas. The Anishinaabe, also called Ojibwe or Chippewa, were migrating in and formed an alliance with the Dakota. European powers destabilised the region, the alliance collapsed, and the Dakota-Ojibwe War followed.

The region was part of Spanish Louisiana from 1762 to 1802. The part east of the Mississippi became part of the United States at the end of the American Revolutionary War, and the part to the west came with the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Territory of Minnesota was formed in 1849, with Saint Paul as its capital, and Minnesota was admitted as the 32nd state in 1858. Its motto, L'Étoile du Nord, The Star of the North, is the only state motto in French.

Settlers came from across the country, and growth was based first on timber, agriculture and railroad construction. Into the early 20th century European immigrants arrived in large numbers, particularly from Scandinavia, Germany and Central Europe. The state was at the forefront of labour rights, women's suffrage and political reform.

Saint Paul is the capital and Minneapolis the most populous city, and the two form the Twin Cities, where more than half the state's people live. Minnesota has 11 federally recognised Native American reservations, seven Ojibwe and four Dakota, and its culture reflects Scandinavian and German influence.
minoan-civilisation: The Minoan civilisation was centred on Crete, with further settlements around the Aegean, and is often regarded as the first civilisation in Europe. It developed from the local Neolithic culture, whose oldest farming remains date to about 7000 BCE, and Early Minoan society shifted gradually from clan-based villages towards a more urban and stratified society. Crete lies on the sea routes between Europe, Africa and the Middle East and is poor in metals, which is believed to have encouraged overseas trade.

The name is a modern coinage from the mythical King Minos, whom the Greeks believed ruled Knossos, and was popularised by Arthur Evans. The people's own name for themselves is unknown, and the Egyptians called them the Keftiu.

The first palaces were built in the Middle Minoan period, in the decades after about 1925 BCE, at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, on sites used for communal ceremonies since the Neolithic. Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A developed in the following period, which ended in mass destructions usually attributed to earthquakes. Knossos, the largest site, had an estimated 18,000 people around 2000 BCE. The Late Minoan period produced many of the best-known objects, such as the snake goddess figurines and the La Parisienne fresco.

After about 1450 BCE the Minoans came under the cultural and perhaps political domination of the Mycenaean Greeks, forming a hybrid culture that lasted until about 1100 BCE. The civilisation was largely forgotten after the Late Bronze Age collapse and was rediscovered in the early twentieth century through excavation.

Little is known of Minoan society, and it is unclear whether there was ever a unified state. The buildings Evans called palaces are now thought to have served religious and economic purposes more than as royal residences. Minoan art shows no recognisable kings, and before about 1450 BCE a group of elite families may have controlled government and religion. Religion centred on peak sanctuaries and sacred caves, with symbols such as the bull, the double axe and the serpent.

The Minoans raised cattle, sheep, pigs and goats, grew wheat, barley and chickpeas, and cultivated grapes, figs and olives. They traded with Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, Anatolia and mainland Greece. Neither Linear A nor Cretan hieroglyphic has been deciphered, so the Minoan language is unknown.
minos: In Greek tradition Minos and his brothers Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon were sons of Zeus and Europa, adopted and raised by King Asterion of Crete. When Asterion died, Minos claimed the throne, and according to some sources he banished his brothers. To justify his rule he prayed to Poseidon for a sign, and Poseidon sent a giant white bull from the sea. Minos was bound to sacrifice it but substituted another bull, and in rage Poseidon cursed his wife Pasiphaë with a mad passion for the animal. She bore the Minotaur, which Minos shut in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus.

Later poets and mythographers, among them Diodorus Siculus and Plutarch, reconciled the contradictions in his character by assuming two kings of that name: a good Minos I, son of Zeus, and a harsher grandson, Minos II, the Minos of the myths of Theseus, Pasiphaë and Daedalus. There is no evidence that Minos was a real person.

Homer shows Minos conversing with Zeus every nine years, and in Plato's reading of the Odyssey he took his laws from the god. Thucydides says he was the first known king to build a navy, which he used against piracy to secure his revenue, and that he reigned over Crete and the Aegean islands three generations before the Trojan War.

His son Androgeus was killed after winning the Panathenaic Games, by the bull at Marathon in one account and by jealous rivals in another. Minos made war on Athens, and the plague and hunger sent on the city ended when it agreed to send seven boys and seven girls to Crete every nine years to be fed to the Minotaur. The hero Theseus killed the Minotaur with the help of Minos's daughter Ariadne.

In the tale of his death Minos pursued Daedalus from city to city with a riddle about stringing a spiral shell, and learned where he was when King Cocalus at Camicus in Sicily had it solved. Cocalus's daughters and Daedalus then scalded Minos to death in a bath.

After death Minos became a judge of the dead alongside his brother Rhadamanthys and half-brother Aeacus, and held the deciding vote. Dante sets him at the entrance to the second circle of Hell, where he coils his tail to indicate each soul's circle. Arthur Evans named the Minoan civilisation after him.
minotaur: The Minotaur, also called Asterion or Asterius, is a mythical creature shown in classical antiquity with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man. The name means Bull of Minos. According to the myth, Minos prayed to Poseidon for a snow-white bull as a sign of his favour, and then kept the bull instead of sacrificing it. To punish him, Poseidon arranged with Aphrodite for Minos's wife Pasiphaë to fall in love with the bull. She had the craftsman Daedalus make a hollow wooden cow and bore the Minotaur.
He grew ferocious and devoured humans, and on the advice of the oracle at Delphi Minos had Daedalus build the Labyrinth to hold him. The palace at Knossos has been found, but the Labyrinth never was.

All the stories agree that Androgeus, son of Minos, died through the fault of the Athenians. The common tradition holds that Minos waged a war of revenge and won, and that Athens then had to send seven young men and seven young women into the Labyrinth every nine years as victims. Pausanias says Minos simply harassed the Athenians until they agreed.

When the third sacrifice approached, the Athenian prince Theseus volunteered to kill the Minotaur. Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with him and in most accounts gave him a ball of thread to retrace his path. Classical sources say he killed the Minotaur with his sword, a club or his bare hands. On the way home he abandoned Ariadne on Naxos, and the crew forgot to change the black sail for the white one promised to his father Aegeus, who saw the black sail, presumed his son dead and leapt into the sea since named after him.

The contest of Theseus and the Minotaur was frequently shown in Greek art, and a didrachm of Knossos shows the Labyrinth on one side and the Minotaur among small balls, probably stars, on the other. Some nineteenth-century mythologists saw the Minotaur as a personification of the sun. In the Middle Ages some versions showed a man's head on a bull's body, the reverse of the classical form.

Dante places the Minotaur as guardian of the seventh circle in the Inferno. Pablo Picasso made etchings of the Minotaur, and Jorge Luis Borges told the story from the monster's perspective in The House of Asterion.
minsk: Minsk stands on the southeastern slope of the Minsk Hills, on the Svislach River and the now subterranean Nyamiha, at an average altitude of 220 metres. The Svislach flows through an ancient river valley formed by meltwater at the end of the last Ice Age, and six smaller rivers lie within the city limits. The city was first built on the hills, which allowed defensive fortifications, and its western parts are still the most hilly. Pine and mixed forests border its north and east, and the Zaslawskaye reservoir, built in 1956 and known as the Minsk sea, lies five kilometres from its north-western edge.

The Svislach valley was the boundary between two early East Slavic tribes, the Krivichs and the Dregoviches, and by 980 it was part of the Principality of Polotsk. The Primary Chronicle mentions the settlement as Měneskъ for the year 1067, in connection with the Battle on the River Nemiga. That year is now widely accepted as the founding date, and city authorities give 3 March 1067, though the town already had wooden walls and must have existed for some time. Kiev annexed the Principality of Minsk in 1129, the Polotsk dynasty regained it in 1146, and by 1150 Minsk rivalled Polotsk as the major city of the former principality.

The city was later annexed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and received town privileges in 1499. From 1569 it was the capital of Minsk Voivodeship in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Polish rule brought a massive migration of Jews to Belarusian lands. Minsk passed to the Russian Empire in 1793 after the Second Partition of Poland. In 1897 Jews were the largest religious group, 47,562 of 90,912 residents. From 1919 to 1991 it was the capital of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, a republic of the Soviet Union from 1922.

Minsk is the capital and largest city of Belarus, with a special administrative status and a population of about two million. Since 1991 it has been the capital of the independent Republic of Belarus. The city is divided into nine districts. Among its historic churches are the Orthodox Cathedral of the Holy Spirit, a former Bernardine convent church, and the Cathedral of Saint Mary, built by the Jesuits. Its first theatres and libraries date from the middle of the 19th century.
minturnae: Minturnae was one of three towns of the Ausones that made war against Rome in 314 BCE, during the Second Samnite War, the others being Ausona, the modern Sessa Aurunca, and Vescia. A Roman settlement was founded there as a fort, Castrum Minturnae, about 296 BCE. The early town grew around the square fort, with polygonal stone walls along the river and the Appian Way as a military road, and in the 3rd century BCE it expanded with new tufa walls and towers. A Capitolium in the Italic style was built after 191 BCE next to the Appian Way and was probably an affirmation of Roman loyalty and identity.

The city was transformed when it became a colonia under Augustus. The stretch of the Appian Way through the town was given porticos, temples to Augustus and Julius Caesar were built, and the theatre was rebuilt. Under Hadrian it received thermal baths, a macellum, a nymphaeum and an aqueduct. The town was destroyed by the Langobards in 590 and was probably destroyed again by Saracens in 883. Its low site was increasingly abandoned for the hill town of Minturno, which until the 19th century was known as Traetto.

Many of the main buildings of the ancient city can be seen outside the modern town, mostly dating from the time of Hadrian. They include a theatre and an aqueduct in opus reticulatum, thermal baths with a large pool, two fora, a republican forum and an imperial one, the Appian Way with a colonnade, the macellum and the Capitolium.

The aqueduct was more than 11 km long from the springs of Capodacqua, and its distribution basin formed part of the central pier of the city gate. An amphitheatre is now almost entirely demolished. About 2 km away, near the river mouth, lay the sacred grove of the Italic goddess Marica, and a nearby sanctuary of Marica with a temple of tuff was built about 500 BCE.
mir-osman-ali-khan: Mir Osman Ali Khan was born on 5 or 6 April 1886 at Purani Haveli, the second son of Mahboob Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, and Amat-uz-Zahra Begum. He was educated privately and reportedly became fluent in Urdu, Persian, Arabic and English; from early 1899 Brian Egerton served for two years as his English tutor. His father died on 29 August 1911, and he was proclaimed Nizam the same day; the coronation was held at the Chowmahalla Palace on 18 September 1911. He lived at King Kothi Palace from the age of 13 until his death.

Hyderabad was the largest of the princely states of colonial India, and its ruler was one of only five princes entitled to a 21-gun salute. For his financial contribution to the British war effort in the First World War, amounting to nearly £25 million, King George V raised his style in 1918 to His Exalted Highness, and he was named Faithful Ally of the British Government. After the Great Musi Flood of 1908 he had two reservoirs, Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar, built on the advice of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. In 1919 he formed an Executive Council, and in 1941 the Hyderabad State Bank, which managed the state's own currency.

When the British withdrew in 1947 the Nizam ruled more than 16 million people. He refused to sign the instrument of accession, preferring a separate kingdom within the British Commonwealth, and signed a one-year standstill agreement instead. He negotiated openly with India and covertly with Pakistan, while his power was weakened by the Telangana Rebellion and by the Razakars, a Muslim militia he could not put down. In 1948 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Polo, under Major General Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri, and the annexation was over in 109 hours. The Nizam kept his personal wealth and title.

He served as Rajpramukh of Hyderabad State from 26 January 1950 to 31 October 1956, after which the state was partitioned. He gave 14,000 acres of his estate to the Bhoodan movement of Vinoba Bhave for distribution among landless farmers. He died on 24 February 1967 and was buried the next day, as his will asked, in the Masjid-e Judi, where his mother lay; the chief curator of the Nizam's Museum, D. Bhaskara Rao, put the funeral procession at an estimated one million people. His grandson Mukarram Jah succeeded him as titular Nizam.
mirabai: Mirabai was born into a Rathore Rajput royal family at Kudki, in the present Beawar district of Rajasthan, and spent her childhood at Merta. She was the daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore and the granddaughter of Rao Dudaji of Merta, which made her a great-granddaughter of Rao Jodha. In 1516 she had an arranged marriage to Bhoj Raj, the crown prince of Mewar.

He was wounded in a war with the Delhi Sultanate in 1518 and died of his wounds in 1521. Both her father and her father-in-law Rana Sanga died a few days after their defeat by Babur at the Battle of Khanwa. After Rana Sanga, Vikram Singh became ruler of Mewar.

Her poems, often sung as bhajans, are lyrical padas in the Rajasthani language and describe love for Krishna, separation from him and dissatisfaction with the world. She often calls him Girdhar, the mountain lifter, and speaks of him as her only true husband. In poems of separation she sometimes portrays him as a detached yogi who leaves lovers in agony, and she presents herself as a yogini.

The earliest datable reference to her is a poem of praise in Nabhadas's Bhaktamal, composed about 1600. Millions of hymns are attributed to her in the Indian tradition, but scholars think only a few hundred authentic, and only two poems have been found in manuscripts older than the early 18th century. Poets who admired her probably composed many of the rest.
Poems attributed to her also appear in a copy of the Adi Granth made in 1604, which the Sikh gurus did not include in the standard edition, and in the Prem Ambodh Pothi of 1693.

The legends of her life vary widely. In the best known, her in-laws tried to kill her with poison sent as nectar and with a basket holding a snake, and she was saved by Krishna. Scholars doubt a story that Akbar and Tansen visited her, because Tansen joined Akbar's court 15 years after her death. The three oldest records that mention her all date from the 17th century.

Nancy Martin-Kershaw suggests that any persecution she met was likelier to come from political chaos and conflict between the Rajput kingdom and the Mughal Empire than from religious or social convention. Tradition holds that she spent her last years at Dwarka or Vrindavan and disappeared into an idol of Krishna in 1547 after being poisoned by her brother-in-law, which scholars contest for lack of evidence.
miri: Miri is a coastal city in north-eastern Sarawak, on the island of Borneo, near the border of Brunei. It lies on the alluvial plain of the Miri River. Beach drift has built up Peninsula Road as a barrier beach between the river and the shore, so that the river runs parallel to the coast before breaking through into the South China Sea. The climate is tropical rainforest, with a dry southwest monsoon from April to September and a wet northeast monsoon from October to March. The town takes its name from a small ethnic group, the Jati Miriek, among the earliest settlers of the region; Europeans who came for oil mispronounced the name as Miri.

The first foragers visited the West Mouth of Niah Cave, about 110 kilometres southwest of Miri, 50,000 years ago. A modern human skull nicknamed the Deep Skull, found by Tom Harrisson in 1958, is the oldest in Southeast Asia and probably belongs to an adolescent girl.

In 1883 the Sultan of Brunei ceded the Baram region, including Miri, to Charles Brooke, Rajah of Sarawak. Miri was then a fishing village of about 20 scattered houses, a few Chinese shops and a lone Arab trader, and Claudetown, now Marudi, was the administrative centre. Miri was founded in 1910 when Royal Dutch Shell drilled the first oil well, and by 1929 it was the administrative centre of northern Sarawak.

As war approached, British forces withdrew to Singapore in 1941, and the Brooke government adopted a denial scheme to destroy the oil installations at Miri and Lutong, since the 48-kilometre coastline was impossible to defend. Miri was the first landing point of Japanese troops in Borneo. The occupation made it a target for Allied air raids, which destroyed refinery facilities. Oil exploration moved offshore from the 1950s, and Petronas, formed in 1974, began production-sharing contracts with Shell in 1976.

Miri is the second largest city in Sarawak, with a population of 356,900 in 2020, and the capital of Miri District. It received city status in 2005. It is the birthplace of the Malaysian petroleum industry, and timber, oil palm and tourism also matter. It is the gateway to Gunung Mulu National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and to the national parks of Niah, Lambir Hills and Loagan Bunut. The population includes Iban, Malay, Chinese, Melanau and many other groups, and the languages include Malay, Malaysian Mandarin and Iban.
miriam-makeba: Zenzile Miriam Makeba was born on 4 March 1932 in the Black township of Prospect near Johannesburg. Her Xhosa father, Caswell Makeba, was a teacher who died when she was six. Her Swazi mother, Christina, was a domestic worker. The name Zenzile comes from the Xhosa words her grandmother muttered after a difficult birth, which mean 'you brought this on yourself'.

Makeba began with the Cuban Brothers, a close-harmony group, and at 21 joined the Manhattan Brothers, the only woman among them. With them she recorded her first hit in 1953. In 1956 she joined the all-woman Skylarks, who blended jazz with traditional South African melodies, though she received no royalties from this work. These groups performed mbube, a style of vocal harmony drawing on jazz, ragtime, Anglican hymns and indigenous music.

She and Harry Belafonte received a Grammy Award for Best Folk Recording for An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba (1965). After she married Stokely Carmichael in March 1968, her popularity in the United States fell sharply and the government took an interest in her. While she was in the Bahamas she was refused a visa to return, and the couple moved to Guinea; she did not go back to the United States until 1987. Her daughter Bongi died in 1985, and Makeba moved to Brussels. In 1986 she joined Paul Simon's Graceland tour, which caused controversy because the album had been recorded in South Africa, in breach of a cultural boycott that she herself endorsed.

After Nelson Mandela's release in February 1990, Makeba entered South Africa on a six-day visa on 10 June 1990. In 1991 she recorded Eyes on Tomorrow with Dizzy Gillespie and Nina Simone, and in 1992 she played the mother in the film Sarafina! She died of a heart attack during a concert in Italy on 9 November 2008.

Makeba released more than 30 albums and was among the first African musicians to gain worldwide recognition. She said that what she sang was not politics but the truth, and she sang at independence ceremonies in Kenya, Angola, Zambia, Tanganyika and Mozambique. On her death Mandela said that her music inspired a powerful sense of hope in all of us.
miroslav-krleza: Miroslav Krleža was born in Zagreb on 7 July 1893, the son of a constable. He enrolled in a preparatory military school in Pécs and then in the Ludoviceum military academy at Budapest, both within Austria-Hungary. He defected to Serbia but was dismissed as a suspected spy. On his return to Croatia he was demoted in the Austro-Hungarian army and sent as a common soldier to the Eastern front in the First World War. After the war he established himself as a major Modernist writer and as a politically controversial figure in the newly created Yugoslavia.

Krleža was the driving force behind the leftist reviews Plamen (1919), Književna republika (1923–1927), Danas (1934) and Pečat (1939–1940). He joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia in 1918 but was expelled in 1939 because of his unorthodox views on art, his opposition to socialist realism and his unwillingness to support the Great Purge openly. This followed a long polemic known as the Conflict on the Literary Left; the commissar sent to mediate was Josip Broz Tito. When the Independent State of Croatia was set up under Ante Pavelić he refused to join Tito's Partisans, and after 1945 he faced a brief period of social stigma before being rehabilitated.

In 1947 he became vice-president of the Yugoslav Academy of Science and Arts in Zagreb, and in 1950, with Tito's support, he founded the Yugoslav Institute for Lexicography, which he headed until his death. He was president of the Yugoslav Writers' Union from 1958 to 1961. His speech at the 1952 Congress of Yugoslav Writers signalled a new era of comparative freedom in Yugoslav literature.

Krleža's main interest was drama. He began with experimental expressionist plays such as Adam i Eva and Michelangelo Buonarroti, then turned to naturalist plays; the best known, Gospoda Glembajevi, is a cycle on the decay of a bourgeois family. His chief poetic work is Balade Petrice Kerempuha, centred on a plebeian prophet, a Croatian Till Eulenspiegel. The short story collection Hrvatski bog Mars (1922) is anti-war and follows Croatian soldiers sent to the battlefields.

His four novels are The Return of Philip Latinowicz, On the Edge of Reason, The Banquet in Blitva and The Banners, a multi-volume view of Croatian and Central European society before, during and after the First World War, which won the NIN Award in 1962. He died in Zagreb on 29 December 1981 and was given a state funeral.
mirza-ghalib: Mirza Ghalib was born in Kala Mahal, Agra, into a family of Mughals that had moved to Samarkand. His paternal grandfather, Mirza Qoqan Baig, a Seljuq Turk, came to India from Samarkand, worked in Lahore, Delhi and Jaipur and finally settled in Agra. His father, Mirza Abdullah Baig, married Izzat-ut-Nisa Begum, an ethnic Kashmiri, and served the Nawab of Lucknow and then the Nizam of Hyderabad; he died in a battle in 1803 at Alwar when Ghalib was a little over five. His uncle Mirza Nasrullah Baig Khan raised him, but died in 1806 after falling from an elephant.

Urdu was his first language, though Persian and Turkish were also spoken at home. He began composing poetry at eleven. At fourteen he met Abdus Samad, a newly converted Muslim from Iran who had been a Zoroastrian named Hormuzd, and who stayed with him for two years teaching him Persian, Arabic, philosophy and logic.

Until 1827 Ghalib received a monthly share of his uncle's government pension, and he travelled to Calcutta to petition the Governor-General to keep it. In 1850 the Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar gave him the title of Dabir-ul-Mulk, secretary of state, with the addition of Najm-ud-daula, star of the state, and the title Mirza Nosha, which marked his incorporation into the nobility of Delhi. In 1854 he became the emperor's poet tutor, and he was also tutor to the emperor's eldest son, Prince Fakhr-ud Din Mirza, and royal historian of the Mughal court.

Ghalib wrote in Urdu and Persian. His Persian Divan is at least five times longer than his Urdu one, but his fame rests on his Urdu poetry. Before him the ghazal was chiefly an expression of anguished love; Ghalib took up philosophy and the travails and mysteries of life, widening its scope. His first pen name was Asad, from his given name Asadullah Khan, and he later took Ghalib, meaning all-conquering.

He was also a gifted letter writer. Before him Urdu letters were highly ornamental, and he made his talk like conversation, sometimes writing just the name of the person addressed. His letters gave a foundation to easy and popular Urdu prose, and Ralph Russell translated them in The Oxford Ghalib. He followed Shia theology and wrote verses in praise of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he placed more weight on seeking God than on ritual. A large part of his poetry consists of naʽats, poems in praise of Muhammad, among them the Persian Abr-i gauharbar.
misiones-province: Misiones is one of the 23 provinces of Argentina, in the north-eastern corner of the country, in the region called Mesopotamia. Paraguay lies to the north-west, Brazil to the north, east and south and Corrientes Province to the south-west. It is the second-smallest province, after Tucumán. The Paraná, Uruguay and Iguazú rivers embrace it, and the Iguazú Falls are in its north-western corner, shared with the Brazilian state of Paraná. The soil of the Misiones plateau is reddish from iron in the rocks, and the native forest, the Selva Misionera, survives in Iguazú National Park.

Indigenous peoples lived in the area for thousands of years; at the time of European contact the Kaingang and Xokleng were there, later followed by the Guaraní. Sebastian Cabot reached Apipé Falls in December 1527, and Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca reached the Iguazú Falls in 1541. From 1609 the Jesuits, led at first by Diego de Torres Bello, founded a string of reductions, of which San Ignacio, founded in 1610, was the most notable. They soon had 30 mission villages and taught the Guaraní western-style agriculture and crafts. When the missions were abandoned, their trade vanished, and colonists imposed a brutal plantation economy that forced the Guaraní to work as slaves.

The territory was claimed by several countries and in practice governed itself. In 1830 Argentine forces from Corrientes took control, and in 1838 Paraguay occupied it. Paraguayan troops invaded again in 1865 in the War of the Triple Alliance, and after Paraguay's defeat it gave up its claim in a peace agreement signed in 1876. Academics tend to date Argentine possession from that war. On 22 December 1881 the national government detached the National Territory of Misiones from Corrientes. European colonists arrived under the Immigration and Colonization Law, many by way of southern Brazil, among them Poles, Ukrainians and Swedes, and the city of Eldorado was founded in 1919. The territory became a province on 10 December 1953.

Misiones has 1,280,960 people, according to the 2022 census. Yerba mate has long been its chief crop, and tea, citrus fruit and timber are also produced. In 1984 UNESCO designated the ruins of four mission sites in Argentina as World Heritage Sites. The Yacyretá dam, begun after a 1973 agreement, raised the Paraná along the province's shores in the 1990s.
mississippi-river: The Mississippi rises at its traditional source, Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, and flows generally south for 2,340 miles (3,770 km) to the Mississippi River Delta in the Gulf of Mexico. Its main stem lies entirely within the United States, and its watershed drains all or parts of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces. It is divided into the Upper Mississippi, from the headwaters to the Missouri at St. Louis; the Middle Mississippi, to the Ohio at Cairo, Illinois; and the Lower Mississippi, from there to the Gulf.

The name comes from Misi zipi, the French rendering of the Anishinaabe name Misi-ziibi, meaning Great River. The Laurentide Ice Sheet of the last Ice Age left sediment that made the valley flat and fertile. In March 1876 the river suddenly changed channel near Reverie, Tennessee, so that the state line still follows the old channel.

The basin was first settled by hunting and gathering peoples and is considered one of the few independent centres of plant domestication in human history. Early cultivation of sunflower and an indigenous squash dates to the 4th millennium BCE, and the Mound Builders formed agricultural and urban societies. Alonso Álvarez de Pineda was the first recorded European to reach the river, in 1519, and Hernando de Soto reached it on 8 May 1541. The French explorers Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette began exploring it in the 17th century. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 made it the border between the British and Spanish empires.

Steamboat commerce ran from about 1830 to 1870, and Mark Twain described it in Life on the Mississippi. In the American Civil War control of the river was a strategic objective of both sides: Union forces cleared Island Number 10 and Memphis and captured New Orleans in 1862, and the Siege of Vicksburg ended on 4 July 1863 with a Union victory. In the spring of 1927 the river broke out of its banks in 145 places and flooded 27,000 square miles.
missolonghi: Missolonghi lies between the Achelous and Evinos rivers, with a port on the Gulf of Patras and the Missolonghi-Aitoliko lagoons to the west. It is the capital of the Aetolia-Acarnania regional unit, and its municipality bears the title Sacred Town of Missolonghi. The town was first mentioned by a Venetian called Paruta, describing the naval Battle of Lepanto, fought nearby. Its name probably comes from the Italian mezzo and laghi, meaning in the middle of lakes. Remains of the ancient town of Pleuron, mentioned in Homer, lie to the north-west.

The settlement grew as a fishing and trading hub. The Venetians captured it in 1684 and held it through the Morean War, but it returned to the Ottoman Empire after the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699. It joined the Orlov Revolt in 1770, which was quickly put down.

When the Greek War of Independence began, Missolonghi was the first place in western Greece to join, on 20 May 1821, led by town notables. Protected by islands and its lagoon on the sea side and by a wall and marshes on the land side, it lay close to the Peloponnese and the Ionian Islands. Alexandros Mavrokordatos landed in July and on 4 November 1821 convened an assembly that set up the Senate of Western Continental Greece.

The defences were at first a shallow ditch and a low wall with fourteen guns. An Ottoman army of 7,000 to 8,000 besieged the town from 25 October 1822, but a garrison of about 500 held out until Greek ships brought reinforcements, and the siege was lifted on 31 December. A second attack in September 1823 was abandoned on 17 November. The third siege began on 15 April 1825 under Reşid Mehmed Pasha, with an army of 30,000, later reinforced by 10,000 under Ibrahim Pasha. After a year, facing starvation, the 10,500 people inside, 3,500 of them armed, left in a sortie on the night of 10 April 1826. Few survived after the plan was betrayed.

For its resistance and the massacre that followed, the town received the title Hiera Polis, the Sacred City. Lord Byron, who died there in 1824, is commemorated by a cenotaph holding his heart. The Entrance Gate and part of the fortification survive, and the Garden of Heroes holds graves of fighters of the sortie. The Exodus is remembered each year on Palm Sunday.
mitanni: Mitanni, also written Mittani, was known by other names to its neighbours. Babylonian texts called it Ḫabigalbat, the Assyrians Ḫanigalbat, the Egyptians Naharin and the Hittites Ḫurri. The Hurrians were in the region by the late 3rd millennium BCE, and the group that became Mitanni moved gradually south into Mesopotamia before the 17th century BCE. No histories, royal annals or chronicles have been found in its excavated sites, so knowledge of Mitanni depends largely on what its neighbours wrote.

At its maximum extent Mitanni reached west to Kizzuwatna by the Taurus Mountains, south to Tunip, east to Arraphe and north to Lake Van. Shaushtatar sacked the Assyrian capital Assur and carried its palace doors to Washukanni, and Assyria may have paid tribute to Mitanni for generations afterwards.

Egypt and Mitanni first fought over the Levant and later became allies. The daughter of King Artatama I married Thutmose IV, Gilukhipa, daughter of Shuttarna II, married Amenhotep III, and Tadukhipa, daughter of Tushratta, was also sent to Egypt. Mitanni was especially interested in Egyptian gold. Tushratta's son Shattiwaza later became a vassal of the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I. The Assyrian king Adad-nirari I took Washukanni and other cities, and Shalmaneser I defeated a rebellion by Shattuara II of Hanigalbat around 1250 BCE. Hanigalbat then came under direct Assyrian control.

The kingdom's organisation is poorly understood, even at its peak. Succession generally passed from father to son. Members of the royal family bore Hurrian names, and kings took an Indo-Aryan throne name. Its military power rested on a warrior elite, the maryannu, who specialised in the battle chariot, held the highest position in society and often owned large estates.

Indo-Aryan influence appears in names, in the technical terms of the horse-training text of Kikkuli, and in the gods Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya, invoked in treaties found at Hattusa. The pottery most characteristic of the kingdom is Painted Nuzi Ware, found from about 1550 BCE.
mithridates-i-of-parthia: Mithridates was the son of Priapatius and the great-nephew of the first Arsacid king, Arsaces I. His name is the Greek form of the Iranian Mihrdāt, meaning given by Mithra. Parthian custom required a ruler to be succeeded by his own son, but his elder brother Phraates I broke the custom and named Mithridates as successor. The Roman historian Justin says Phraates had noticed his competence.

The kingdom he inherited was one of several medium-sized powers that had arisen as the Seleucid Empire declined. It covered present-day Khorasan Province, Hyrcania, northern Iran and the south of present-day Turkmenistan.

Mithridates first attacked the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, weakened by wars with its neighbours. Between 163 and 155 BCE he took Aria, Margiana and western Bactria from Eucratides I, and Merv became a Parthian stronghold. Turning west, he occupied Ecbatana in 148 or 147 BCE and conquered Media Atropatene. In 141 BCE he captured Babylonia, minted coins at Seleucia and held an investiture ceremony there. Elymais and Characene became vassals, and Parthian authority reached the Indus.

In about 140 BCE, while he fought the Saka in the east, the Seleucid king Demetrius II Nicator tried to retake Babylonia. He was captured in 138 BCE and sent to a palace in Hyrcania, where Mithridates treated him hospitably and married him to his daughter Rhodogune. Mithridates then punished Elymais for helping the Seleucids and made Persis a vassal.

He was the first Parthian king to take the Achaemenid title King of Kings. His later coins show a Hellenistic diadem and the title Philhellene, friend of the Greeks, aimed at his new Greek subjects. He renamed Nisa as Mithradatkert, and Ctesiphon was founded in his time.

Mithridates died in about 132 BCE and was succeeded by his son Phraates II. Historians such as Klaus Schippmann argue that his campaigns were more than raids for plunder and aimed at reaching Syria and the Mediterranean. Homa Katouzian has compared him with Cyrus the Great.
mithridates-ii-of-parthia: Mithridates II was crowned after the abrupt death of Artabanus I and inherited an empire under pressure from the east and the west, after humiliating defeats by eastern nomads. His parentage is uncertain. The Roman historian Justin makes him a son of Artabanus I, but a cuneiform tablet of 119 BCE calls the dead Artabanus his brother. Vesta Sarkhosh Curtis argues that he was a son of Priapatius, while Marek Jan Olbrycht holds that he was Artabanus's son and a middle-aged man at his accession.

In Mesopotamia he won the allegiance of Hyspaosines of Characene and then invaded Elymais, captured Susa and defeated its king Pittit. About 120 BCE he invaded Armenia and made King Artavasdes I accept Parthian suzerainty, taking Tigranes as a hostage. Iberia, and possibly Caucasian Albania, probably became vassal states too. In 114 or 113 BCE he captured Dura-Europos from the Seleucids. About 95 BCE Tigranes was released and made king of Armenia, and Adiabene, Gordyene and Osrhoene were conquered, moving the western border to the Euphrates.

In the east he reconquered western Bactria, avenging the nomads who had killed his predecessors. Sakastan, the land of the Saka, was recovered by a general of the House of Suren, who received it as a fiefdom, and the empire reached Arachosia. At the Euphrates the Parthians met the Romans for the first time: in 96 BCE Mithridates sent an official named Orobazus to Sulla, who apparently gained the upper hand in the talks. A Chinese delegation is attested at his court in 120 BCE, and the Silk Road opened to trade the following year.

Mithridates II used the title King of Kings regularly from about 109 BCE, and he stressed the dynasty's link to the Achaemenid Empire. His coins show him in an Iranian tiara instead of the Hellenistic diadem, and the omphalos on the reverse gives way to a high-backed Achaemenid throne. Justin says his achievements earned him the surname Great.

His son Gotarzes, who had served as satrap of satraps under him, was proclaimed king at Babylon after his death in 91 BCE. The period that followed, known as the Parthian Dark Age, is poorly documented, and political instability brought territorial losses, including land that Tigranes of Armenia seized. The crisis ended with the accession of Sinatruces.
mithridates-vi-of-pontus: Mithridates was born in Sinope on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, the first son of Mithridates V Euergetes and the Seleucid princess Laodice VI. His name is the Greek form of the Iranian Mihrdāt, given by Mithra, and he claimed descent from Cyrus the Great and Darius the Great on his father's side and from Antigonus I Monophthalmus and Seleucus I Nicator on his mother's. His father was poisoned at a banquet in about 120 BCE. Laodice VI held power as regent and favoured the younger son, Mithridates Chrestus, and Mithridates escaped her plots and went into hiding. In 113 BCE he overthrew his mother and ruled alone.

Mithridates meant to make Pontus the dominant power of the Black Sea and Anatolia. He subjugated Colchis, and Tauric Chersonesus and the Bosporan Kingdom gave up their independence in return for protection against the Scythians. In Anatolia he divided Paphlagonia and Galatia with Nicomedes III of Bithynia, then fell out with him over Cappadocia. After Rome intervened twice for Nicomedes, from 95 to 92 BCE, he resolved to expel the Romans from Asia.

In 89 BCE Nicomedes IV of Bithynia, urged on by Roman advisers, invaded Pontus, and Mithridates defeated him while Rome was occupied with the Social War. In 88 BCE he ordered a massacre of Roman and Italian settlers in cities including Pergamon and Tralles, in which as many as 80,000 people are said to have died, an episode known as the Asiatic Vespers. He presented himself as protector of Greek culture against Rome and won over much of mainland Greece, including Athens. Sulla won a string of victories in the first of the Mithridatic Wars but offered a generous peace. The second war began in 83 BCE, and the third in 73 BCE.

After Pompey defeated him at the Battle of the Lycus in 66 BCE, Mithridates fled north of the Black Sea, hoping to raise a new army and invade Italy by way of the Danube. His preparations burdened the local nobles and people, who rebelled, and his son Pharnaces rose against him. He retreated to Panticapaeum and killed himself. According to Appian, after a failed attempt with poison he asked his Gallic bodyguard Bituitus to kill him with a sword.

He was said to have made himself immune to poison by taking small doses, and a universal antidote, mithridate, was named after him. Pliny the Elder reports that he spoke the languages of the twenty-two nations he ruled, and his name later gave titles to works on comparative linguistics.
mito-ibaraki: Mito lies in the centre of Ibaraki Prefecture in the northern Kantō region, about ten kilometres inland from the Pacific Ocean, near the Naka River. Immediately to the south is Lake Senba, a recreational area. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cold winters with light snowfall.

The Yamato people settled in Mito around the 4th century CE. Near the end of the Heian period Baba Sukemoto, a warlord of the Heike clan, built a castle there. Mito Castle changed hands several times and passed to the Satake clan in the Sengoku period, but the Satake had to surrender it to Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1603 after the Battle of Sekigahara. Ieyasu gave it to his son Tokugawa Yorifusa, who became head of one of the three gosanke branches of the Tokugawa family, qualified to provide a new shōgun if the main line failed. The Tokugawa ruled Mito until the Meiji Restoration.

Mito was the seat of the Mito School, nativist scholars of Confucian persuasion led by Aizawa Seishisai, who advocated Western learning as a way to develop Japan's technology and strength and to prove Japanese uniqueness among nations. The Kōdōkan was the largest of the domain schools. In 1842 Tokugawa Nariaki laid out the garden of Kairaku-en, known for its ume trees and counted among the Three Great Gardens of Japan.

The city of Mito was created on 1 April 1889, with 25,000 people, one of the first 31 cities in Japan, and was made capital of Ibaraki Prefecture. By 1900 the Jōban Line linked it with Tokyo. More than three-quarters of Mito burned in the air raid of 2 August 1945, shortly before the end of World War II. It is mainly a regional administrative and commercial centre, since most of Ibaraki's industry lies around Tsukuba and Hitachi. Visitors come mostly to Kairaku-en, Mito Castle, the Kōdōkan school and museums of the Tokugawa family.
mixtecs: The name Mixtec comes from the Nahuatl word mixtecah, meaning cloud people. The Mixtecs call themselves by several names, such as ñuù savi, all of which can be translated as the land of the rain. Their historic homeland, La Mixteca, covers roughly the western half of the state of Oaxaca and parts of Puebla and Guerrero. It is divided into the Mixteca Alta, the highlands, the drier Mixteca Baja and the humid Mixteca Costa on the Pacific coast.

The Mixteca Alta has been studied most by archaeologists, with evidence of settlement from the Archaic and Early Formative periods, and the first urbanised sites emerged there. For most of Mixtec history it was the dominant political force, with the capitals in the central highlands. The Mixtec culture is held to have lasted from around 1500 BCE until the Spanish conquest. Before it, the Mixtecs numbered around 1.5 million.

Mixtec kingdoms competed and allied with each other and with Zapotec kingdoms in the Central Valleys, and the Valley of Oaxaca was often a disputed border region. Important centres included Tilantongo, Achiutla, Cuilapan, Tlaxiaco and Tututepec, and the Mixtecs also made major constructions at Monte Albán, a city of Zapotec origin that they came to control. The Costa came under Mixtec control through the campaigns of the cultural hero Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, who set out from Tilantongo, conquered kingdoms on the way and established the capital of Tututepec in the lower Río Verde valley.

The Aztecs moved into Oaxaca in the 1450s and defeated the Mixtecs in 1458. In 1486 they founded a fort on the hill of Huaxyácac, now El Fortín, which let them collect tribute from Mixtecs and Zapotecs, though not every Mixtec town became a vassal. The Mixtecs were later subdued by the Spanish and their central Mexican allies in the 16th century.

The Mixtecs wrote their histories and genealogies in painted fold-books on deerskin. The best-known story is that of Lord Eight Deer, told in several codices including the Codex Bodley and the Codex Zouche-Nuttall. They were goldsmiths said to be the foremost of Mesoamerica, practising lost-wax casting, and their gold work formed part of the tribute they paid the Aztecs. Turquoise mosaic masks were given as gifts to seal alliances, worn by those impersonating a god, and fixed to funerary bundles seen as oracles.
The Mixtec languages form a major branch of the Oto-Manguean family. About 800,000 Mixtec people live in Mexico today, and many have migrated within Mexico and to the United States.
miyagi-prefecture: Miyagi lies in the central part of the Tōhoku region, on Japan's eastern Pacific coast. It borders Iwate Prefecture to the north, Akita to the northwest, Yamagata to the west and Fukushima to the south. The Ōu Mountains, the longest range in Japan, bound it on the west, and there are also high mountains along the northeast coast, but the central plain around Sendai is fairly large. The Oshika Peninsula projects from the northern coastline. Miyagi was formerly part of the province of Mutsu.

Matsushima, a bay of about 260 small islands covered in pine groves, is counted among the Three Views of Japan. About 24 per cent of the prefecture's land is designated as natural parks, among them the Sanriku Fukkō National Park and the Kurikoma and Zaō Quasi-National Parks.

Sendai, the capital and the largest city in Tōhoku, was the castle town of the daimyō Date Masamune, and the remains of Sendai Castle stand on a hill above it. Rice and livestock were produced in the countryside, and the coast supported fishing. In the 20th century the prefecture's population grew most between 1940 and 1950 and continued to grow into the 21st century, with manufacturing, notably electronics, appliances and food processing, concentrating around Sendai.

Miyagi lies in a part of Japan that is prone to earthquakes, with large ones frequent offshore. On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0 earthquake and a tsunami about 10 metres high struck the prefecture and caused major damage; Miyagi suffered the most damage of any prefecture in the country. A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck off its coast on 7 April 2011.

The prefecture is home to many universities, among them Tohoku University in Sendai. Its festivals include the Sendai Tanabata Festival in August, the Aoba Festival in May and the Shiogama Port Festival in July. The Tōhoku Shinkansen and expressways link it with Tokyo, and Sendai has a port and an airport.
miyamoto-musashi: The details of Musashi's early life are difficult to verify. In The Book of Five Rings he says he was born in the village of Miyamoto, and an early biography, the Niten Ki, gives the year as 1584. His father, Shinmen Munisai, was an accomplished martial artist, a master of the sword and the jutte, and his mother, Omasa, died giving birth to him. He gives his full name as Shinmen Musashi-no-Kami Fujiwara no Harunobu, and he was also called Shinmen Takezō and Niten Dōraku, his Buddhist name. Accounts say he never took a wife, cut his hair or entered a bath.

By his own account his first duel took place at the age of 12 or 13, against Arima Kihei, and he won. At 16 he beat Tadashima Akiyama, and in 1599 he left his village. At 21 he defeated several students of a sword school in Kyoto.

In 1600 Musashi probably served in the army of Kuroda Yoshitaka on the Eastern side. A popular theory put him with the Western Army at Sekigahara, but recent research suggests that he and his father were on the Eastern side, although whether he fought at Sekigahara or at the battle of Ishigakihara in Kyūshū is still debated. In 1608 he met the Tokugawa general Mizuno Katsunari and taught him the secrets of his sword style. He is said to have served in the Tokugawa army at the Siege of Osaka in 1614 and in the suppression of the Shimabara Rebellion in 1638.

His best-known duel was with Sasaki Kojirō on Ganryū Island, arranged through Hosokawa Tadaoki. Musashi, it is said, deliberately arrived late and had carved an oar into a wooden sword, and he killed Kojirō with one vertical stroke. From 1633 he stayed with Hosokawa Tadatoshi at Kumamoto Castle, and in 1640 he became a retainer of the Hosokawa lords.

In 1641 Musashi wrote the Hyōhō Sanjūgo, the "Thirty-five Instructions on Strategy", for Tadatoshi, which became the basis of The Book of Five Rings. In 1643 he retired to the cave Reigandō and wrote that book, finishing it in the second month of 1645. A week before his death he gave it, with the Dokkōdō, "The Path of Aloneness", to his student Terao Magonojō. He died around 13 June 1645, and sources disagree on whether it was in the cave or at a house in Kumamoto. He developed the two-sword technique Niten Ichi-ryū, and left calligraphy and ink paintings, recognised as masterpieces, in the style called sumi-e.
mizoram: Mizoram is a landlocked state of North East India. It borders Bangladesh to the west and Myanmar to the east and south, and the Indian states of Assam, Manipur and Tripura to the north and west. It covers 21,081 square kilometres, most of it forested, and the Tropic of Cancer runs through its middle. The name means land of the Mizos, from Mizo, the native inhabitants, and ram, land or forest. Excavations at Vangchhia, a large necropolis, have found human remains, ornaments and pottery dating from 600 BCE to 1750 CE.

Tibeto-Burman-speaking peoples migrated south from the Chin Hills in present-day Myanmar and formed autonomous chiefdoms, each village behaving like a small state under a hereditary chief called a Lal. Chiefdoms lived mainly by slash-and-burn jhum farming and by trade on routes linking Yunnan to the Bay of Bengal, using the sial, a tame bison, as a unit of wealth. By the eighteenth century the Sailo dynasty dominated much of the region. After the Lushai Expedition of 1870–71, the British conducted further expeditions and annexed the area in 1895 as the Lushai Hills District of Assam. Missionaries wrote the first script for Mizo about 1895 and opened the first primary school in 1898 at Aijal, and Christianity gradually replaced the Sakhua practices.

On 15 August 1947 no Indian flags were hoisted in the Lushai Hills, because of opposition from rival factions of the Mizo Union. The district stayed within Assam, and discontent over the state's handling of the mautam famine fuelled an uprising in 1966, led by the Mizo National Front. Mizoram became a union territory on 21 January 1972, although the Front continued its armed struggle for complete independence. In 1973 the central government expelled foreign missionaries, which unintentionally led to a revival of Mizo culture, including the festival Chapchar Kut. Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and the Front's leader Laldenga signed the Mizoram Peace Accord on 30 June 1986, and on 20 February 1987 Mizoram became India's 23rd state.

Aizawl is the capital and largest city. Mizo and English are the official languages, and about 87 per cent of the people are Christian, mostly Presbyterian and Baptist; the largest religious minority is Theravada Buddhist, mainly Chakma. The census of 2011 counted 1,091,014 people, nearly 95 per cent of them members of Scheduled Tribes, the highest share in India. Literacy reached 92 per cent in 2011. The bamboo that covers much of the state flowers about every fifty years, an event called mautam that sets off an explosion of rats; the plague of 1958–59 preceded the uprising of 1966.
mljet: Mljet is the southernmost and easternmost of the larger Adriatic islands of Dalmatia. It lies south of the Pelješac peninsula, from which the Mljet Channel divides it, and is 37 km long with an average breadth of 3.2 km. Its area is about 98 square kilometres, and over 84 per cent of it is forest. The island is of volcanic origin, with chasms and gorges, and the limestone and dolomite form ridges and slopes. The north-west includes an inland lake with a small island in it, within the Mljet National Park, which was established on 12 November 1960.

Ancient geographers knew the island as Melite or Melita. It is described in the Periplus attributed to Scylax of Caryanda, and Appian reports that its people, islanders accused of piracy, revolted against Rome and were punished harshly in the Illyrian campaigns of Octavian, with the young men executed and the rest enslaved. The Roman emperor Septimius Severus is said to have banished Agesilaus, the father of the poet Oppian, to the island. Around 950 the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitos listed it in De Administrando Imperio among the islands held by the Narentines. A tradition first set out in the 10th century by Constantine VII holds that Mljet was the Melita where Paul the Apostle was shipwrecked, though the wreck is generally placed on Malta.

The Benedictines of Pulsano in Apulia became the feudal lords of the island in 1151. Between 1187 and 1198 Desa, Grand Prince of Serbia, built and gave them the Church and Monastery of Saint Mary on the islet in the Big Lake, and Pope Innocent III consecrated the church in 1198. The Benedictines gave up their rule in 1345, keeping a third of the land, and the island received a statute and a municipality at Babino Polje. It later came under the Republic of Ragusa.

In the 16th century the monastery was the centre of the Mljet Congregation of Benedictine houses in the territory of the Republic of Ragusa, and its abbots included the poets Mavro Vetranović and Ignjat Đurđević. The monastery was disbanded in 1809 under Napoleon.

Mljet is part of Croatia and had 1,062 residents in 2021 in fourteen settlements, the largest being Babino Polje. It has no airport and is reached by ferry from the Pelješac peninsula and from Dubrovnik. Small Indian mongooses, introduced in the early 20th century to control the venomous snake, ate most of the island's birds.
moamoria-rebellion: The followers of the Mayamara Satra were predominantly Morans, the mainstay of the Ahom militia, joined by Sonowal Kacharis, Chutias, professional castes such as potters, weavers and fishermen, and some Ahom nobles and officers. The Ahom state rested on the Paik system, under which any able-bodied man who was not a Brahmin or a noble could be called up for labour, service or the army. The satras gave refuge to those seeking to escape it, and the loss of manpower brought them into growing conflict with the kingdom. The Mayamara Satra belonged to the non-conformist Kala-samhati sect, which competed with the royalist satras.

On 15 September 1769 Raghav Moran, a leading disciple of the satra, was flogged by Ahom officials for not supplying the required number of elephants. The Morans gathered an army of about seven thousand, and on 21 November 1769 they occupied the capital, imprisoned King Sunyeophaa and placed Ramakanta, son of the rebel leader Naharkhora, on the throne. After four months, when the peasant soldiers had gone home for the spring festival, nobles in disguise killed Raghav Moran on 14 April 1770 and retook the capital.

In April 1782 the Moamorias attacked the convoy of the newly crowned King Suhitpangphaa and briefly held Rangpur; the royalists who drove them out killed several thousand people. A third rising began in 1786. The rebels surrounded Rangpur in January 1788, the king left for Guwahati, and the continuous fighting in Upper Assam brought a famine described as the severest in the history of Assam. The rebels struck coins in the names of their leaders Bharat and Sarbananda but set up no central administration. A British contingent under Captain Welsh captured Rangpur in March 1794, but it was recalled and the rebels took the city again.

After the king's death Purnananda Burhagohain became the effective ruler and raised a standing army of paid sepoys in place of the paik militia. In 1805 his forces fought those of Sarbananda in the Bengmara region. Both sides recognised a stalemate, and Sarbananda accepted peace: he received the title of Barsenapati and autonomous command of the region, which came to be called the Matak rajya and paid annual tribute to the Ahom kingdom.

The population fell to about half of what it had been and economic life was disrupted. The paik and khel systems broke down, compelling the state to move towards a money economy. The weakened kingdom later fell to a Burmese invasion, which ultimately led to British colonisation.
mobile-phone: A handheld radio telephone was imagined early in radio engineering. In 1917 the Finnish inventor Eric Tigerstedt filed a patent for a pocket-size folding telephone with a very thin carbon microphone. Early predecessors of cellular phones included analog radio communications from ships and trains. The race to build truly portable telephones began after the Second World War, and advances are traced in successive generations, starting with the zeroth-generation services such as the Bell System's Mobile Telephone Service. These systems were not cellular, supported only a few simultaneous calls and were very expensive.

A mobile phone connects over a radio link to the switching systems of an operator, which gives access to the public switched telephone network. The advantage of modern cellular networks over earlier systems is frequency reuse, which lets thousands of subscribers talk at once in an area. Feature phones have limited capabilities, while smartphones have advanced computing power and a full operating system. The first SIM card was made in 1991 by the Munich smart card maker Giesecke & Devrient for the Finnish operator Radiolinja.

The first SMS was sent from a computer to a mobile phone in the UK in 1992, and the first person-to-person message from phone to phone was sent in Finland in 1993. In 1998 Radiolinja sold ringtones, one of the first examples of selling media content through the phone. Apple's App Store, opened in July 2008, popularized manufacturer-hosted distribution of third-party applications. In Kenya the operator Safaricom's M-PESA lets customers hold cash balances recorded on their SIM cards and transfer money from person to person. In the UK the number of mobile phones overtook the number of houses in 1999.
mobutu-sese-seko: Mobutu, born Joseph-Désiré Mobutu on 14 October 1930 at Lisala in the Belgian Congo, belonged to the Ngbandi ethnic group. His mother, Marie Madeleine Yemo, was a hotel maid, and her husband, Albéric Gbemani, was a cook for a Belgian judge. Gbemani died when Mobutu was eight, and an uncle and a grandfather raised him.

He found discipline and a father figure in the colonial army, in Sergeant Louis Bobozo, and read European newspapers and books whenever he could, among them the writings of Charles de Gaulle, Winston Churchill and Niccolò Machiavelli. In 1956 he left the army and became a journalist in Léopoldville, writing for the daily L'Avenir. He later joined the Congolese National Movement of Patrice Lumumba and became his personal aide. Several accounts say he was also an informer for Belgian intelligence and for the Americans.

After the mutiny of the Force Publique on 5 July 1960 Mobutu helped negotiate the release of officers and their families. During the Congo Crisis, as Chief of Staff of the army, he deposed Lumumba's government with American and Belgian support. He installed a government that arranged for Lumumba's execution in 1961, and he continued to lead the armed forces.

In March 1965 parliament twice refused to confirm the prime minister-designate Évariste Kimba, and the government was in near-paralysis. On 24 November 1965 Mobutu took power in a bloodless coup. He assumed almost absolute powers under a state of exception, and in March 1966 his government permanently suspended parliament. In 1967 he made the Popular Movement of the Revolution the only legal party.

Mobutu pursued a campaign of cultural change called authenticité. From 1 June 1966 he renamed cities, so that Léopoldville became Kinshasa and Stanleyville Kisangani, and in October 1971 he renamed the country Zaire. People were ordered to take African names, Western dress was banned, and men wore the Mao-style abacost. He also put rivals to death: Kimba and three ministers were hanged on 30 May 1966 before an audience of 50,000. His rule involved a cult of personality, widespread corruption and the expropriation of foreign-held businesses under Zairianisation.

His opposition to communism won support from the United States, France and Belgium. In May 1990 he gave up the party's monopoly, and troops killed at least 290 students at Lubumbashi on 12 May, after which Western countries ended non-humanitarian aid. After the Rwandan genocide of 1994, Hutu refugees and fighters based in eastern Zaire destabilised the region. In May 1997 rebels under Laurent-Désiré Kabila overran the country. Mobutu left on 23 May, lived in Rabat, and died of prostate cancer on 7 September 1997.
moctezuma-ii: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin, called Moctezuma II in European sources because the Aztecs used no regnal numbers, was a son of the emperor Axayácatl and a daughter of Nezahualcóyotl of Texcoco. Two of his uncles, Tízoc and Ahuizotl, were the emperors before him. His name is interpreted as meaning he frowns like a lord. Most historians place his coronation in 1502, though some argue for 1503, a date that appears on the Stone of the Five Suns.

After his coronation Moctezuma set up thirty-eight more provincial divisions and sent out bureaucrats with military garrisons to collect tax, uphold the laws and act as local judges. His reign began with a drought in 1505 that lasted three years. He and the rulers of Texcoco and Tlacopan used the food supplies to feed the population and raised tribute for one year. Through warfare he extended the empire south to Xoconosco in Chiapas and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and brought the Zapotec and Yopi peoples into it.

He widened the divide between the pipiltin, or nobles, and the macehualtin, or commoners, by barring commoners from working in the royal palaces. He also fought Huejotzingo and Tlaxcala, sometimes in flower wars, which were arranged by the parties to capture warriors for sacrifice. Many of his dominions around Tlaxcala were reluctant to fight their former allies, so his support there was limited.

In 1518 Moctezuma learned of the landing at San Juan de Ulúa of the expedition of Juan de Grijalva and ordered extra watchtowers on the coast. After the arrival of Hernán Cortés he became a prisoner in his own house; the sources do not make clear why. During the fighting after Cortés returned he was killed, probably on 29 June 1520, and accounts differ on how and by whom. The Spaniards fled the city and made a treaty with Tlaxcala to conquer Tenochtitlan.

Portraits of him are divided. Spanish writers called him weak-willed and superstitious, and the historian James Lockhart suggests that he serves as a scapegoat for the defeat. Indigenous accounts of omens before the Spanish arrival are seen by many ethnohistorians as explanations made after the conquest. His name was later invoked in indigenous rebellions against Spanish rule, including in Chiapas in 1721.
modena: Modena lies on the south side of the Po Valley, between the rivers Secchia and Panaro, both tributaries of the Po. The Apennines begin about ten kilometres to the south. The territory was inhabited by the Villanovans in the Iron Age and later by Ligurian tribes, Etruscans and the Gaulish Boii. The Etruscan name was Mutna and the Latin Mutina. The settlement existed by the 3rd century BCE: in 218 BCE, during Hannibal's invasion of Italy, the Boii revolted and besieged it, and Livy described it as a fortified citadel where Roman magistrates took shelter.

Mutina was refounded as a Roman colony in 183 BCE as a military base for Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. The Ligurians sacked it in 177 BCE, but it was rebuilt and became the most important centre of Cisalpine Gaul, standing at the crossing of the Via Aemilia and the road to Verona. It was besieged in 78 BCE by Pompey and in 44 BCE by Mark Antony, when Octavian relieved it in the Battle of Mutina. It declined with the Empire and, according to tradition, a fog sent by its patron Saint Geminianus hid it from Attila, but a great flood buried it in the 7th century and it was abandoned.

Modena became a free comune from the 12th century. The Este were lords from 1288, when Obizzo d'Este held power, and the comune briefly reasserted itself after 1308, but by 1336 the Este were permanently in power. Borso d'Este made it a duchy. When Ferrara fell to the Pope in 1598, Modena became the primary ducal residence. Francesco I d'Este built the citadel and began the palace, and Francesco II embellished it. Napoleon made it part of the Cispadane Republic, and Francis IV received back the Este estates in 1814. Francis V was expelled in the Revolutions of 1848, restored by Austrian troops, and driven out again when Piedmontese forces annexed Modena to the Kingdom of Italy on 20 August 1859.

The Cathedral of Modena, the Torre della Ghirlandina and Piazza Grande have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. The University of Modena was founded in 1175 and expanded by Francesco II d'Este in 1686, and the Military Academy is partly housed in the Baroque Ducal Palace. The Biblioteca Estense holds 3,000 manuscripts. The city has 184,361 inhabitants and is known for its car industry and for balsamic vinegar.
modest-mussorgsky: Mussorgsky was born on 21 March 1839 in Karevo, in the Pskov Governorate, about 400 kilometres south of Saint Petersburg, into a wealthy landowning noble family. His mother, Julia Chirikova, a trained pianist, taught him from the age of six. At ten he and his brother were taken to Saint Petersburg to study at the Petrischule, and at thirteen he entered the Cadet School of the Guards. In 1856 he graduated and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment. That year he met Alexander Borodin and Alexander Dargomyzhsky, and he soon came to know Vladimir Stasov, César Cui and Mily Balakirev, who taught him musical form.

In 1858 he resigned his commission to devote himself to music. The emancipation of the serfs soon afterwards deprived his family of half its estate, and he spent much time in Karevo trying in vain to stave off its impoverishment.

In the 1860s Mussorgsky embraced artistic realism, depicting life as it is lived and the lower strata of society and rejecting repeating, symmetrical musical forms. His first realistic songs, including Hopak and Darling Savishna, date from 1866. In 1867 he finished the original orchestral version of Night on Bald Mountain, which Balakirev refused to conduct, so that it was never performed in his lifetime. Influenced by Dargomyzhsky's The Stone Guest, he set the first scenes of Gogol's Marriage in 1868, trying to render natural speech in music.

He then wrote Boris Godunov, shaping a text from Pushkin's play and Karamzin's history. The theatre rejected it in 1871, and he produced a revised and enlarged version, from which three excerpts were staged at the Mariinsky Theatre in 1873. The first production, in February 1874, was far from a critical success, but popular reaction in its favour made it the peak of his career. His other works of 1874 include the song cycle Sunless and the piano suite Pictures at an Exhibition, written in memory of his friend Viktor Hartmann. The cycle Songs and Dances of Death dates from 1877.

Mussorgsky's alcoholism worsened through the 1870s and he was dismissed from government service in 1880. Khovanshchina and The Fair at Sorochyntsi were left unfinished. After four seizures in early 1881, he died on 28 March 1881, a week after his 42nd birthday, and was buried at the Tikhvin Cemetery of the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov completed Khovanshchina, which premiered in 1886, and re-orchestrated Boris Godunov in 1896, so that for many years his works were known mainly in revised versions. Maurice Ravel's orchestration made Pictures at an Exhibition widely known. Western views of him changed after the European premiere of Boris Godunov in 1908.
modibo-keita: Modibo Keïta was born in Bamako-Coura, a neighbourhood of Bamako, then the capital of French Sudan, in 1915. His Muslim family claimed direct descent from the Keita dynasty that founded the medieval Mali Empire. He was educated in Bamako and at the école normale William-Ponty in Dakar, where he was top of his class. From 1936 he worked as a teacher in Bamako, Sikasso and Tombouctou. In 1937 he coordinated an art and theatre group, and with Ouezzin Coulibaly he helped found the Union of French West African Teachers.

In 1943 he founded L'oeil de Kénédougou, a magazine critical of colonial rule, which led to three weeks' imprisonment in Paris in 1946. In 1945 he and Mamadou Konaté founded the Bloc soudanais, which developed into the Sudanese Union. When the African Democratic Rally was created at Bamako in October 1946, Keïta became its Secretary-General in French Sudan and head of its Sudanese affiliate, the US-RDA.

In 1948 Keïta was elected general councillor of French Sudan, and in 1956 mayor of Bamako and a member of the French National Assembly. He twice served as a secretary of state in French governments. In 1959 he became premier of the Mali Federation, made up of French Sudan and Senegal; on 20 July 1960 he was elected president of its constituent assembly. After the federation collapsed, the Sudanese Republic proclaimed full independence as the Republic of Mali, and Keïta became its first president.

He soon declared the US-RDA the only legal party and pursued socialist policies based on extensive nationalisation, including the state company SOMIEX, which held a monopoly on exports and many imports. The Malian franc, created in 1962, brought severe inflation and discontent among peasants and businessmen. Keïta left the French Community and kept close ties with the Eastern bloc, while also seeking good relations with Washington and meeting President John F. Kennedy in 1961. He imprisoned opponents such as Fily Dabo Sissoko. The economy kept deteriorating, and Mali rejoined the Franc Zone in 1967. In August 1967 he began the revolution active and suspended the constitution, and the militia of the US-RDA caused unrest.

A committed Pan-Africanist, Keïta helped draft the charter of the Organization of African Unity in 1963. That year he invited the king of Morocco and the president of Algeria to Bamako and, with Emperor Haile Selassie, negotiated the Bamako Accords, which ended the Sand War. He received the Lenin Peace Prize.

On 19 November 1968 General Moussa Traoré overthrew him and sent him to prison at Kidal. He was moved back to Bamako in February 1977 and died there as a prisoner on 16 May 1977. His reputation was rehabilitated in 1992, after Traoré's fall, and a monument to him was dedicated in Bamako in 1999.
modu-chanyu: According to the account of Sima Qian in the Shiji, Modu was a gifted child whose father Touman wanted the son of another wife to succeed him. Touman sent Modu to the Yuezhi as a hostage and then attacked them, hoping they would kill him, but Modu stole a fast horse and escaped, and was made commander of 10,000 horsemen.

He trained his followers with a whistling arrow, having them shoot at whatever it flew toward, and tested their loyalty by ordering them to shoot his favourite horse and then a favourite wife, executing those who hesitated. In 209 BCE he had them shoot his father on a hunting trip and proclaimed himself chanyu. He then executed his rival half-brother, his stepmother and officials who refused to support him.

The Qin invasion of the Ordos Plateau in 215 BCE had come as the Xiongnu confederation faced a leadership crisis, and Modu used the resulting militarisation to build a centralised political structure. By 208 BCE he had defeated the Donghu, whose remnants split into the Xianbei and Wuhuan, and he went on to subdue the Dingling and defeat the Yuezhi in 203 BCE. His empire reached from the Liao River in the east to the Pamir Mountains in the west and Lake Baikal in the north.

In 200 BCE Emperor Gaozu of Han led an army north and advanced to Pingcheng with 40,000 men, where Modu surrounded him with 40,000 cavalry. The Xiongnu withdrew some of their men, and Gaozu broke out. He then made peace through heqin, a marriage alliance with gifts of silk, wine and food. In 192 BCE Modu proposed marriage to Empress Dowager Lü Zhi, in a letter meant to intimidate and mock her. She refused humbly, and kept up the heqin policy and tribute.

Modu died in 174 BCE and was succeeded by his son Laoshang. Historians note that Han weakness gave Modu and his successors a steady flow of luxury and staple tribute to pass down to the aristocracy that supported them. Christopher Beckwith has pointed out that the story of his youth resembles a widespread class of folk tales of an abandoned young hero who proves his worth and becomes king.
