In Turkic languages Modu is known as Mete Khan, and the Turkish Land Forces take 209 BCE as their symbolic founding date.
moesia: Moesia was bounded to the south by the Haemus (Balkan Mountains) and Scardus (Šar) ranges, to the west by the river Drinus (Drina), to the north by the Danube and to the east by the Black Sea. It was later divided into Moesia Superior and Moesia Inferior, with the river Ciabrus (the modern Tsibritsa) as the boundary between them. The name itself is thought to have been a Roman invention of the age of Augustus: the Moesi are not mentioned in sources before his death in 14 CE and only by Ovid, Strabo and Livy, and the ethnonym was carried over from the Mysians of Asia Minor to replace that of the Dardani.

Before Roman rule the land was inhabited chiefly by Thracian, Dacian, Illyrian and Thraco-Illyrian peoples. The Dardani had their own kingdom in what became Moesia Superior, and the Dacian king Burebista ruled part of the region between 82 and 44 BCE. Augustus took up Julius Caesar's plan to advance the frontier to the Danube. Marcus Licinius Crassus, proconsul of Macedonia from 29 BCE, defeated the Moesi, drove back the Bastarnae and killed their king Deldo in single combat. Augustus proclaimed the victory in 27 BCE.

The region was not organised as a province until the last years of Augustus, and a governor, Caecina Severus, is mentioned in 6 CE. In 15 CE Tiberius placed Macedonia and Achaea under the governor of Moesia. After the Dacian king Duras attacked, Emperor Domitian reorganised it into Moesia Superior and Moesia Inferior, each under an imperial consular legate. Trajan's Dacian Wars of 101 to 102 and 105 to 106 were triggered by the constant Dacian threat to Moesia.

From the 3rd century the province was raided by the Carpi and the Goths. In the Gothic War of 248 to 253 the Gothic king Cniva defeated the Romans at the Battle of Abrittus, where Emperor Decius was killed. Diocletian divided Moesia Superior into Moesia Prima and Dardania, and Moesia Inferior into Moesia Secunda and Scythia Minor. In 376 the Goths, pressed by the Huns, settled in Moesia with the permission of Emperor Valens; these Moeso-Goths received the Gothic Bible of Ulfilas. Slavs allied with the Avars destroyed much of the region in 583 to 587 and settled it in the 7th century. Bulgars conquered Lower Moesia by its end, and the area returned to Byzantine control under Basil II in 1018.
mogao-caves: Dunhuang was founded as a frontier garrison by the Han emperor Wudi in 111 BCE to guard against the Xiongnu, and became a gateway to the West on the Silk Road. The Mogao Caves began, according to a book from the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, in 366 CE, when the monk Le Zun had a vision of a thousand Buddhas bathed in golden light at the site and decided to build a cave there. A second monk, Faliang, joined him, and a community of monks formed by the time of the Northern Liang. The caves first served hermit monks for meditation. Caves continued to be cut until the 14th century.

The cliff stretches nearly two kilometres. At its height under the Tang, more than a thousand caves existed, and 735 survive. The 487 in the southern section, which are decorated, were places of pilgrimage and worship, while 248 in the north were living quarters, meditation chambers and burial sites for monks. The murals cover about 46,000 square metres, from the 5th to the 14th century, and their quality peaked in the Tang period. About 2,400 clay sculptures survive. The largest, a Maitreya in cave 96, 35.5 metres high, was built in 695 under the orders of Empress Wu Zetian.

Early murals show strong Indian and Central Asian influence, and a distinct Dunhuang style emerged under the Northern Wei. Local rich clans built several caves as family caves, which show their devotion and social standing.

On 25 June 1900 Wang Yuanlu, a Taoist abbot who had made himself guardian of some of the temples, found a walled-up small cave, Cave 17, packed with manuscripts. It had been sealed in the 11th century and may originally have been a memorial cave for the monk Hongbian, who died in 862. It held up to 50,000 manuscripts dating from the 5th to the early 11th century, mostly Chinese and Buddhist but also in Tibetan, Uighur, Sanskrit, Sogdian and Khotanese. They include the Diamond Sutra of 868, the earliest dated printed book. The manuscripts were later scattered, with the largest collections now in Beijing, London, Paris and Berlin.
mogilev: The city stands on the Dnieper, about 76 kilometres from the border with Russia's Smolensk Oblast, and was first mentioned in historical records in 1267. Its name may derive from the Russian mogila, grave, and lev, lion. According to folk legend it was named after the grave of a young peasant, known as the Tomb of the Lion, around which a fortress was built. Its founding has also been linked to the Galician prince Leo I.

From the 14th century Mogilev belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and after the Union of Lublin of 1569 to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, where it was known as Mohylew. In the 16th and 17th centuries it was one of the main nodes of the east–west and north–south trade routes.

In 1654, during the Russo-Polish War, the townsmen agreed to surrender to the Russians if the Jews were expelled and their property divided. Tsar Aleksei Mikhailovitch accepted, but Russian troops led the Jews to the outskirts of the town and massacred them. Lithuanian forces besieged the city in 1655 and 1660. Peter the Great's forces set it afire in 1708, during the Great Northern War.

In 1897 the Russian census counted 21,500 Jews among 41,100 inhabitants, over half the total. In 1919 Soviet Russia incorporated the city into the Byelorussian SSR. In 1938 the Belarusian leadership decided to move the capital here from Minsk, which lay too close to the Polish border, and a government building was raised in 1938–1940. German forces took the city on 26 July 1941 and held it until 28 June 1944. The Jews were confined in a ghetto and systematically murdered by police and SS personnel, and Heinrich Himmler witnessed the shooting of 279 Jews on 23 October 1941. A plan for a death camp was dropped in favour of Maly Trostenets.

Mogilev is the administrative centre of Mogilev Region and the third-largest city in Belarus. After World War II it became a large metallurgical centre with steel mills and factories making cranes, cars and tractors, and it has an inland port on the Dnieper. Its convent of St. Nicholas has a cathedral built in 1668, with the original iconostasis, bell tower, walls and gates.
mohamed-amin-didi: Mohamed Amin Didi was born on 20 July 1910, the son of Athireegey Ahmed Dhoshimeynaa Kilegefaan and Roanugey Aishath Didi, and through his father a descendant of the Huraa dynasty. In 1920 he was sent to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to study at Saint Joseph's College in Colombo, and in 1928 he went to India for further studies at Aligarh Muslim University, returning to the Maldives a year later. He married Fathimath Saeed; their only child was a daughter, Annabeela Ameena Mohamed Amin.

In 1931 he was appointed to the Constituent Assembly convened by Sultan Muhammad Shamsuddeen III to draft the country's first written constitution. He went on to hold many posts: chief officer of customs, head of the post office, minister of trade, minister of education from 1933 to 1936 and from 1944 to 1952, minister of finance from 1942 to 1952 and minister of foreign affairs from 1944 to 1953. He sat in the first Maldivian parliament and was principal of Majeedhiyya School from 1946 to 1953.

He was appointed prime minister on 1 January 1947, at a time when the country was suffering widespread famine and exhausted resources after the Second World War. He led the first political party in the Maldives, the Rayyithunge Muthagaddim Party. His programme included the advancement of women and a ban on tobacco smoking. As prime minister he also wrote a booklet for foreigners, Ladies and Gentlemen: The Maldive Islands, on the life, culture and economy of the country.

According to a report in the newspaper Mihaaru, the revolt of 1953 was staged by Ibrahim Zaki, Mohamed Zaki and Ibrahim Nasir, who invited the vice-president, Ibrahim Muhammad Didi, to join; he agreed out of distaste for Amin's handling of state funds. A special assembly passed a vote of no confidence that handed all powers temporarily to Ibrahim Didi. Amin, in Sri Lanka, learned of events by letter but not of his removal. He returned by way of RAF Gan to Malé, was taken to Dhoonidhoo, where he was beaten by the army, and was then banished to Vihamanaafushi, where he died of health complications on 19 January 1954.

In September 2021 a member of parliament, Ibrahim Rasheed, lodged a case with the Office of the Ombudsperson for Transitional Justice seeking justice for his death and the overturning of his conviction as a traitor. The office's mandate expired on 19 November 2023.
mohamed-morsi: Mohamed Morsi was born on 8 August 1951 in the village of El Adwah in the Sharqia Governorate, north of Cairo, during the last years of the Egyptian monarchy. His father was a farmer. He studied engineering at Cairo University, graduating in 1975, and a government scholarship took him to the University of Southern California, where he received a doctorate in materials science in 1982. He taught at California State University, Northridge, until 1985, then returned to Egypt and taught engineering at Zagazig University.

Morsi sat in parliament from 2000 to 2005 as an officially independent member, since the Muslim Brotherhood was barred from fielding candidates under President Hosni Mubarak. In 2011 the Brotherhood chose him as first president of its new Freedom and Justice Party. When Khairat El-Shater was disqualified from the 2012 presidential election, Morsi became the Brotherhood's candidate. He narrowly defeated Ahmed Shafik, a former prime minister under Mubarak, and was sworn in on 30 June 2012, ending six decades of military rule.

In November 2012 he issued a declaration freeing his decisions from judicial review. He aimed to stop judges appointed under Mubarak from dissolving the constituent assembly. Critics called the move an Islamist coup, and protests followed; he rescinded the decrees as part of a compromise. A new constitution was approved by about two thirds of voters in a referendum with a turnout below a third of the electorate.

On 30 June 2013 protests across Egypt called for Morsi's resignation. The armed forces issued an ultimatum on 1 July, Morsi rejected it, and on 3 July General Abdel Fattah el-Sisi deposed him and suspended the constitution. Demonstrations by his supporters were crushed, with over 800 deaths. Morsi faced charges including inciting the killing of protesters and espionage. On 17 June 2019 he collapsed in court during a hearing and died; he was buried in Cairo.
mohammad-daoud-khan: Mohammad Daoud Khan was born in Kabul on 18 July 1909 into a Mohammadzai Pashtun family. His father, Prince Mohammad Aziz Khan, was assassinated in 1933 in Berlin while serving as Afghan ambassador to Germany. Daoud and his brother Naim Khan then came under the guidance of their uncle Mohammad Hashim Khan. Educated in France, Daoud served as governor of the Eastern Province and of Kandahar Province between 1934 and 1939. In 1939 he became Commander of the Central Forces and led forces against the Safi in the tribal revolts of 1944-1947, which brought him national attention. He was Defense Minister from 1946 to 1948 and Interior Minister from 1949 to 1951.

Daoud became prime minister in September 1953 through an intra-family transfer of power. His decade in office saw a turn toward the Soviet Union, the completion of the Helmand Valley project and tentative steps toward the emancipation of women. He rejected the Durand Line and supported the reunification of Pakistan's Pashtuns with Afghanistan, which worried the Hazara, Tajik and Uzbek populations. Afghan incursions into Bajaur in 1960 and 1961 failed, and in 1961 Pakistan closed its border, which deepened dependence on the Soviet Union. Daoud asked King Zahir Shah to approve a one-party constitution. When it was rejected, he resigned in March 1963, and the border reopened in May.

After planning for more than a year, Daoud seized power on 17 July 1973 in a bloodless coup backed by army officers. For the first time in Afghan history he did not proclaim himself shah but established a republic with himself as president. The parliament was disbanded and replaced by a largely nominated loya jirga. Pro-communist Parchamite officers had taken part in the coup, but over time he removed communist influence from his cabinet. In 1977 a loya jirga approved a constitution creating a presidential one-party system under his National Revolutionary Party.

After the funeral of the Parchamite ideologue Mir Akbar Khyber on 19 April 1978, he ordered the arrest of leaders of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan, but acted too slowly. A coup began on 27 April, and Daoud and most of his family were shot in the Arg palace on 28 April. Their remains were found in mass graves in 2008, and he was given a state funeral in 2009.
mohammad-hatta: Hatta was born Athar on 12 August 1902 in Fort De Kock, now Bukittinggi, into a prominent and strongly Islamic family. His grandfather, Sheikh Abdurrahman, was a respected Naqshbandi-Khalidi murshid. His father died when he was eight months old, and in keeping with Minangkabau matrilineal custom he was raised in his mother's wealthy family. He studied Dutch and completed the Qur'an after school.

He attended the Dutch elementary school in Padang and then, from 1919, the HBS in Batavia, finishing with distinction in 1921. He went on to study economics in Rotterdam and earned a doctorandus degree in 1932. He completed the requirements for a doctorate but never finished his thesis, because politics had taken over his life.

In the Netherlands Hatta joined the Indies' Association, which became the Perhimpoenan Indonesia. He was its treasurer from 1922 to 1925 and its chairman from 1926 to 1930, and edited its magazine Indonesia Merdeka. In his inaugural speech he supported non-cooperation with the Dutch colonial government. Returning home in 1932, he became chairman of the New PNI, which concentrated on cadre training. He was imprisoned in the Boven Digoel camp for his activism.

On 16 August 1945 young activists took Hatta and Sukarno to Rengasdengklok to press them to declare independence. They returned to Jakarta that night and drafted the proclamation at Maeda's house. It was issued on 17 August 1945 in a short statement signed by both men. The next day Hatta was chosen first vice president.

In the early republic Hatta issued three decisions: giving the KNIP legislative powers, authorising political parties and transferring the role of head of government to a prime minister. He became prime minister and defence minister himself, and in August 1948 had to demobilise some soldiers. In December 1948 he stayed in Yogyakarta, was arrested by the Dutch and sent to Bangka. In 1948 he gave the speech Rowing Between Two Rocks, the origin of the Independent and Active foreign policy doctrine.

He announced his retirement from the vice presidency in 1955 and afterwards criticised Sukarno, whose Guided Democracy he called a form of dictatorship in his 1960 book Our Democracy. He died on 14 March 1980 in Jakarta, and was named a proclaiming hero in 1986. Soekarno-Hatta International Airport carries his name.
mohammad-mosaddegh: Mohammad Mosaddegh was born on 16 June 1882 in Ahmadabad, near Tehran, into a family of high officials. His father was finance minister under the Qajar dynasty, and his mother was a descendant of the reformist prince Abbas Mirza. In 1909 he went to Paris to study at Sciences Po, and in June 1913 he received a doctorate in law from the University of Neuchâtel, becoming the first Iranian to earn a doctorate in law from a European university.

His political career began in the Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1907, when at 24 he was elected to the Majlis from Isfahan but could not take his seat because he was under the legal age of 30. He later served as minister of justice, finance minister, foreign minister and governor of Fars and Azerbaijan, and was re-elected to the Majlis in 1923.

On 28 April 1951 the Shah confirmed Mosaddegh as prime minister after the Majlis elected him by 79 votes to 12. His government nationalised the Iranian oil industry, which had been run since 1913 by the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, and the clash with Britain became known as the Abadan Crisis.

On 16 July 1952 he resigned after the Shah refused to let him name the minister of war and the chief of staff. Ahmad Qavam was appointed in his place, but strikes and demonstrations in which over 250 demonstrators were killed or seriously injured brought Mosaddegh back. Parliament gave him emergency powers on 3 August 1952, and he cut the Shah's budget and transferred royal lands to the state. In October 1952 he cut diplomatic relations with Britain.

Britain, which had lost control of Iranian oil, looked to the United States for help. In March 1953 Secretary of State John Foster Dulles directed the CIA to draft plans to overthrow Mosaddegh, and on 4 April Allen Dulles approved $1 million for the purpose. Kermit Roosevelt Jr., chief of the CIA's Near East and Africa division, arrived in Tehran to direct the plot, known as Operation Ajax. The coup of August 1953 ended his government.

On 21 December 1953 Mosaddegh was sentenced to three years of solitary confinement in a military prison, well short of the death sentence the prosecutors asked for. He was then held under house arrest at Ahmadabad until his death from cancer on 5 March 1967. He was denied a funeral and was buried in his own living room. He remains one of the most popular figures in Iranian history. Some argue that the loss of support from the cleric Ayatollah Abol-Ghasem Kashani was fatal to his cause. The overthrow became a rallying point in anti-American protests in the 1979 revolution.
mohammad-nadir-shah: Nadir Khan was born in Dehradun, British India, on 9 April 1883, into the Musahiban branch of the ruling family, of the Mohammadzai section of the Barakzai Pashtuns. His ancestors had been exiled to British India by Emir Abdur Rahman Khan, who distrusted their ambitions. Nadir helped the Afghan government defeat the Khost rebellion in 1912, became a general under King Amanullah Khan, and led the Royal Afghan Army in the Third Anglo-Afghan War. He then served as Minister of War and, from early 1924 to 1926, as ambassador to France.

Disagreements with Amanullah led to Nadir's exile shortly after Habibullah Kalakani's rebellion against the monarchy. When Kalakani overthrew Amanullah, Nadir returned with an army of Mangal, Mahsud and Wazir tribesmen, with British support, and took most of the country. His forces captured Kabul by 13 October 1929 and sacked it, and he arrived on the 15th. Kalakani was shot on 1 November 1929 with his brother and nine of his circle.

As king, Nadir quickly abolished most of Amanullah's reforms. The army remained weak while religious and tribal leaders grew strong, and he faced many revolts, among them the Koh Daman revolt, the Shinwari rebellion of February 1930 and the Darre Khel revolt of November 1932. Most had been subdued by the end of 1931. A loya jirga of 286 members confirmed his accession in September 1930, and in 1931 he promulgated a constitution that, despite its constitutional appearance, in effect set up a royal oligarchy.

Nadir modernised more quietly than Amanullah. He improved roads, notably the Great North Road through the Hindu Kush, and helped establish Kabul University in 1931. He forged commercial links with foreign powers, began a banking system and long-range economic planning, and by 1933 had built a military force of 40,000.

On 8 November 1933 he was shot dead by Abdul Khaliq Hazara at a school graduation ceremony in Kabul. The assassin was executed along with most of his relatives, and the government used the occasion to arrest other rivals. Nadir was buried on Maranjan Hill, and Muhammad Iqbal wrote an elegy for him. His son Mohammad Zahir Shah succeeded him.
mohammad-najibullah: Mohammad Najibullah Ahmadzai was born on 6 August 1947 in Gardez, in Paktia Province, into the Ahmadzai clan of the Ghilji Pashtuns. He studied at Habibia High School in Kabul and at Kabul University, where he completed a medical degree in 1975 but never practised. In 1965 he joined the Parcham faction of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA), was twice imprisoned for political activity and served as a close associate and bodyguard of Babrak Karmal. After the Saur Revolution of 1978 the rival Khalq faction gained the upper hand, and he was briefly ambassador to Iran before going into exile in Europe until the Soviet intervention of 1979.

In 1980 Najibullah became head of the KHAD, the Afghan counterpart of the KGB, after lobbying by Soviet officials including Yuri Andropov. Its staff grew from 120 to between 25,000 and 30,000, and it reported directly to the KGB. He joined the PDPA Politburo in June 1981. Mikhail Gorbachev wanted Karmal to resign and supported Najibullah, who became General Secretary on 4 May 1986, although a Soviet military intelligence report had warned that he was a Pashtun nationalist.

In September 1986 he created a National Compromise Commission for his policy of National Reconciliation, calling a six-month ceasefire and offering talks that would lead to a coalition government. The programme failed, but some mujahideen commanders defected with their followers. He moved away from socialism towards Afghan nationalism, and the 1990 constitution made Islam the state religion and removed references to communism. On 18 February 1989, four days after the Soviet withdrawal, he declared a state of emergency, and 1,700 intellectuals were arrested that month.

With the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, Najibullah lost his foreign aid, and the defection of General Abdul Rashid Dostum to Ahmad Shah Massoud brought his government down. He resigned in April 1992. Dostum's troops blocked his flight to the airport, and he lived in the United Nations compound in Kabul, where he translated Peter Hopkirk's The Great Game into Pashto. The Taliban tortured and killed him on 27 September 1996, when they took Kabul. Supporters praise his efforts at reconciliation, while critics cite the abuses of the KHAD and alleged corruption under his government.
mohammad-reza-pahlavi: Mohammad Reza was born in Tehran on 26 October 1919, the son of Reza Khan, a brigadier general in the Persian Cossack Brigade, later Reza Shah, and his second wife, Tadj ol-Molouk. In 1931 he was sent to Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland, the first Iranian heir apparent educated abroad. On 15 March 1939 he married Princess Fawzia of Egypt in Cairo; the marriage ended in divorce on 17 November 1948.

After the Anglo-Soviet invasion of 1941 Reza Shah resigned, and on 17 September 1941 his son took the oath as shah. Iran became a main route for British and later American aid to the Soviet Union. On 11 December 1946 the army, led by the Shah in person, entered Iranian Azerbaijan, and the Soviet-sponsored government of Ja'far Pishevari collapsed with little resistance.

Mohammad Mosaddegh became prime minister in 1951 and nationalised the oil industry controlled by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. He was overthrown in the 1953 coup, carried out by pro-monarchy forces with British and American involvement. In 1963 the Shah launched the White Revolution, whose referendum let women vote. Clerics objected, and demonstrations in 1963 and 1964, centred on Qom, killed at least 200 people; Ruhollah Khomeini was exiled to Iraq in October 1965. On 26 October 1967 the Shah took the title Shahanshah at a coronation in Tehran, and in October 1971 he marked 2,500 years of Persian monarchy since Cyrus the Great.

Protests began after a newspaper article attacking Khomeini appeared on 7 January 1978. On 8 September 1978 troops shot dead at least 64 people in Jaleh Square. Shapour Bakhtiar became prime minister on 6 January 1979, and on 16 January the Shah left Iran. The monarchy collapsed within a month and Khomeini became supreme leader of the new Islamic republic. The Shah travelled through Egypt, Morocco, the Bahamas and Mexico, and died in exile in Egypt on 27 July 1980. Historians remain divided on his rule, some stressing repression and autocracy, others economic growth and modernisation.
mohammad-shah-qajar: Mohammad Mirza was born in Tabriz on 5 January 1808, the eldest son of the crown prince Abbas Mirza. He was a quiet and shy boy who became a skilled calligrapher and painter. A turning point came when the dervish Haji Mirza Aqasi was appointed his chief tutor and made him a devotee of Sufi teachings. In the Second Russo-Iranian War he led an army to protect Ganja and was defeated, but was praised and nicknamed Gazi.

After Abbas Mirza died in 1833, Mohammad became crown prince at Nowruz of 1834 and governor of Azarbaijan. Under the influence of his tutor Abol-Qasem Qa'em-Maqam, he imprisoned four brothers and later blinded them to remove their claims to the throne.

After Fath-Ali Shah died in 1834, claimants such as Hossein Ali Mirza rose against Mohammad, who suppressed them. He made Qa'em-Maqam his grand vizier, then arrested him on 22 June 1835 and had him executed four days later, and appointed Aqasi in his place. His chief aim was to bring the rebellious city of Herat back under Iranian rule. In 1837 he marched there and besieged it without success, withdrawing when the British government threatened to invade Iran.

He also put down a revolt in Isfahan, led by the cleric Mohammad Bagher Shafti, who had declared a man named Ramazan Shah and struck coins in his name. Through British and Russian mediation he concluded the Second Treaty of Erzurum with the Ottoman Empire, after negotiations that ran four years from 1843. Pressed by the British envoy Justin Sheil, he refused to abolish the slave trade in the Persian Gulf, saying it would contradict Islamic tradition. He was the last Qajar king to attend a foreign war in person.

Mohammad suffered from gout and refused European doctors on Aqasi's advice, and in his last years he lost the will to rule and handed the government to Aqasi. He died on 4 September 1848 of gout and erysipelas and was buried at the Fatima Masumeh Shrine in Qom, and his son Naser al-Din Shah succeeded him.

He patronised Sufis, and the ulama became his firmest rivals. He refused to persecute the followers of the Báb despite a fatwa from Shiite clerics. He sent students to Europe, including the future grand vizier Mirza Hosein Khan Sepahsalar, and in 1837 ordered the first Iranian newspaper published in Tehran. Historians describe his reign as an interregnum between Fath-Ali Shah and Naser al-Din Shah, with Aqasi governing in his name and costly wars and maladministration.
mohammad-zahir-shah: Mohammad Zahir Shah was born on 15 October 1914 in Kabul, into the Musahiban branch of the Mohammadzai clan of the Barakzai Pashtuns. His father, Mohammad Nadir Shah, had been Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Afghan Army under King Amanullah Khan. Zahir was educated at schools in Kabul where subjects were taught in English and French, and then in France, at the Pasteur Institute and the University of Montpellier. On his return he helped his father and uncles restore order, and served as deputy war minister and minister of education.

He was proclaimed king on 8 November 1933, at the age of 19, after the assassination of his father. For his first twenty years he did not effectively rule, leaving power to his paternal uncles Mohammad Hashim Khan and Shah Mahmud Khan, who both served as prime minister. In 1934 Afghanistan joined the League of Nations and was recognised by the United States. Despite close relations with the Axis powers, the country stayed neutral in the Second World War, and from 1944 to 1947 it saw a series of tribal revolts.

After the war Zahir Shah recruited foreign advisers, and Afghanistan's first modern university was founded. He sought aid from both the United States and the Soviet Union, and the country was one of the few to receive it from both.

A new constitution promulgated in 1964 at his behest introduced free elections, a parliament, civil and political rights, women's rights and universal suffrage. His rule has been characterised as a lengthy era of peace. In July 1973 his cousin Mohammad Daoud Khan, a former prime minister whom Zahir had forced to resign a decade earlier, overthrew him in a coup while he was undergoing medical treatment in Italy. In August 1973 Zahir Shah sent a letter from Rome declaring his abdication.

He spent 29 years in exile near Rome. In 1983, during the Soviet-Afghan War, he was involved in plans for a government in exile, but they failed when he could not reach agreement with the Islamist factions. In 1991 he survived an attack by a knife-wielding man posing as a journalist. He returned to Kabul on 18 April 2002, after the end of Taliban rule, and was welcomed by Afghans of all ethnic groups.

Of the Loya Jirga he said he would accept the duties of head of state if it asked, but had no intention to restore the monarchy. Afterwards Hamid Karzai gave him the title Father of the Nation, which ended with his death. He died in the Arg, the old palace in Kabul, on 23 July 2007, at the age of 92, and was buried in the royal mausoleum on Maranjan Hill.
mohammed-v-of-morocco: Muhammad bin Yusef was born in Fes on 10 August 1909, the third and youngest son of Sultan Yusef and Lalla Yacout. In March 1912 the Treaty of Fes made Morocco a French protectorate, and the French enthroned his father in September of that year. He studied the Quran in the palace at Fes and, after the court moved to Rabat, with private teachers there, until he became a hafiz. He also studied French. He was enthroned on 18 November 1927, at the age of 17, after his father's death.

In May 1930 the young sultan signed the Berber Dahir, which changed the legal system in the areas where Berber languages were mainly spoken. Moroccan nationalists criticised it sharply, and it gave rise to the Moroccan nationalist movement. During the Second World War he took part in the Anfa Conference at Casablanca and met Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill on 22 January 1943. Most scholars stress his benevolence towards Moroccan Jews under Vichy, since he reportedly refused to approve measures to deport them, though he did sign two decrees barring Jews from certain schools and positions. The historian Michel Abitol holds that his role has been exaggerated.

After the war he became a central figure of the independence cause. In speeches at Tangier on 9 and 10 April 1947 he appealed for independence and stressed Morocco's ties with the Arab world. Relations with the French worsened, and on 20 August 1953 the French authorities deposed him and sent him to Corsica, later moving him to Madagascar. They installed Muhammad Ben Aarafa, a cousin, in his place. The deposition sparked active opposition, and he returned on 16 November 1955. In 1956 he negotiated Moroccan independence with France and Spain, and in 1957 he took the title of king.

Muhammad V died on 26 February 1961, aged 51, of cardiac arrest after an operation on his nasal septum. His son Moulay Hassan, who succeeded him as Hassan II, announced his death on national radio, and a seven-day period of mourning followed. A mausoleum for his remains was built in 1971. Many streets, schools, an airport and a university in Morocco bear his name, and historians often describe him as a moderate and conciliatory ruler.
moheli: Mohéli, also called Mwali, lies in the Indian Ocean off the coast of Africa and is the smallest of the four major Comoro Islands. Its capital and largest city is Fomboni, where about 19,000 of the island's roughly 38,000 people lived at a count of 2006. Its main ethnic group, as on the other Comoro islands, is the Comorian people, a synthesis of Bantu, Arab, Malay and Malagasy culture, and its main religion is Sunni Islam.

Until 1830 Mohéli was part of the Ndzuwani Sultanate, which also controlled the neighbouring island of Anjouan. In 1830 migrants from Madagascar led by Ramanetaka, who later changed his name to Abderemane, took over the island and established the sultanate of Mwali. Its ruler in the mid-nineteenth century was Queen Jumbe-Souli. In 1886 France made the island a protectorate. Mwali kept its own French resident until 1889, when it was placed under the residency of Anjouan, and the sultanate was dismantled in 1909 after the French annexation of the island.

In 1975 Mohéli agreed to join the Comoros, together with Grande Comore and Anjouan. Political, economic and social turmoil followed. On 11 August 1997 Mohéli seceded, a week after Anjouan, under the leaders Said Mohamed Soefu, who became president, and Soidri Ahmed, who became prime minister. It rejoined the Comoros in 1998. In 2002 it ratified a new Comorian constitution that provided for a less centralized federal government and more power to the island governments, which helped to settle the turmoil.

Mohéli Marine Park, gazetted on 19 April 2001, was the first protected area in the Comoros. It came out of an arrangement negotiated between the government and the communities of the ten villages around its boundaries. It was redesignated Mohéli National Park in 2010 and in 2015 was enlarged to cover about three-quarters of the island's land area. A tract of 6,268 hectares in the western highlands, including Mount Mlédjélé, is an Important Bird Area for species such as the Comoro olive pigeon and the Moheli scops owl. The island's only airport lies between Fomboni and Djoièzi on the north coast.
mohenjo-daro: Mohenjo-daro lies off the right bank of the lower Indus in Larkana District, on a Pleistocene ridge in the river's flood plain, about 28 kilometres from the town of Larkana. The modern name, in Sindhi, means 'Mound of the Dead Men'. The city's original name is unknown; Iravatham Mahadevan, from a seal, speculated that it could have been Kukkuṭārma, 'the city of the cockerel'. At its height the Indus Civilisation spread from the Iranian border to Gujarat, with other great centres at Harappa, Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi.

The city was divided into the Citadel, a mud-brick mound around 12 metres high, and the Lower City. The Citadel held public baths, a large residential structure for about 5,000 people and two large assembly halls. In 1950 Mortimer Wheeler identified a Great Granary, but Jonathan Mark Kenoyer pointed to the complete lack of evidence for grain and suggested a Great Hall of uncertain function. Repeated flooding led the builders to raise platforms of mud brick. Wheeler proposed that the city had been flooded and silted over perhaps six times and rebuilt each time on the same spot, while Gregory Possehl argued for frequent small floods combined with land worn out by crops and pasture.

The ruins were undocumented for around 3,700 years until R. D. Banerji of the Archaeological Survey of India visited in 1919 to 1920 and, finding a flint scraper, concluded that the site was ancient. Kashinath Dikshit excavated in 1924 to 1925 and John Marshall in 1925 to 1926, with later campaigns in the 1930s, in 1945 under Mortimer Wheeler and in 1964 and 1965 under George Dales. Excavation was banned after 1965 because exposed structures were weathering.

Finds include seated and standing figures, carved seals, balance-scales and weights, gold and jasper jewellery, and copper tablets bearing the undeciphered Indus script. Pakistan and India divided some 12,000 objects at independence; Pakistan received the Priest-king, and India kept the Dancing Girl, a bronze statuette 10.5 centimetres high found in 1926. The site is a World Heritage Site and is threatened by erosion and improper restoration.
moldova: Moldova is a landlocked country of 33,843 km2 between the Prut river on the west, which separates it from Romania, and the Dniester on the east. Most of it is hilly, with elevations that never exceed 430 metres, the highest point being the Bălănești Hill, and exceptionally rich Chernozem soil covers around three-quarters of the land. About 88% of the area lies in the Bessarabia region, and a narrow strip on the east bank of the Dniester is in the unrecognised breakaway state of Transnistria.

In 1999 Moldova acquired from Ukraine a 0.45 kilometre frontage on the Danube, which turned the village of Giurgiulești into a river port. The name comes from the Moldova River; a legend recounted by the chroniclers Dimitrie Cantemir and Grigore Ureche says that Prince Dragoș named it after his hound Molda, which drowned there.

In antiquity the area was a crossroads for invasions by the Scythians, Goths, Huns and other tribes, followed by periods of Roman and Byzantine control. The Principality of Moldavia emerged in the 1350s, reached prominence under rulers such as Stephen the Great, and was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire from 1538. In 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the eastern half to the Russian Empire, which called it Bessarabia. Southern Bessarabia was returned to Moldavia in 1856, three years before Moldavia united with Wallachia to form Romania, but Russia restored its rule over the entire region in 1878.

Bessarabia declared independence in February 1918 and joined Romania later that year after a vote of its assembly, a decision disputed by Soviet Russia. In 1940, as a consequence of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, Romania was compelled to cede Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union, which created the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. It declared independence on 27 August 1991 and took the name Moldova, and the Transnistria War of 1992 left the breakaway region de facto independent.

Moldova adopted its constitution in 1994 and is a parliamentary republic with a 101-seat unicameral parliament. It was granted European Union candidate status in June 2022. The population was an estimated 2,423,300, and ethnic Moldovans were almost 77% of it in the census.
molepolole: Molepolole is a large village in Kweneng District, Botswana, about 50 kilometres west of the national capital Gaborone, and serves as a gateway for exploring the Kalahari Desert. It is named after the Molepolole River. Its people are the Bakwena, one of the eight major tribes of Botswana, and it is the capital of the Bakwena. It has a large traditional kgotla, the assembly place of a community, and the Scottish Livingstone Hospital.

The Bakwena capital moved several times in the 19th century. Dimawe was settled in August 1851 and attacked by Boers in August 1852. Kolobeng, where Livingstone had a house and workshop and designed a square house for the chief Sechele I, was the capital until 1853. Livingstone arrived at Dithubaruba, the next Kwena capital, in 1853. A cave about 3 kilometres from Molepolole is linked with Livingstone and Sechele.

Ntsweng, a few kilometres south-east of Molepolole, was first occupied by the Bakwena under Sechele I in 1864. Visible house foundations of stones set on edge survive there, together with the ruins of the office of Sebele II, which stands beside the old royal kraal, now a royal cemetery. Analyses of the layout suggest that cattle were kept at the centre of each ward, as in the central cattle pattern of southern Bantu settlements. The chief Sebele I was one of three chiefs who went to England to seek British protection.

Molepolole is one of the largest traditional villages in Africa, with a population of over 74,674 at the 2022 count. It has a college of education, an institute of health sciences and eight government junior secondary schools. Nearby are rock paintings, iron smelting sites and caves in the Kopong hills, and the burial cairns of Sechele I, Sebele I and Sebele II.
moliere: Molière was born in Paris and baptised as Jean Poquelin on 15 January 1622, the first son of Jean Poquelin and Marie Cressé, from a prosperous bourgeois family. He lost his mother at 10. His father bought the post of valet of the King's chamber and keeper of carpets and upholstery in 1631, and the son took it over in 1641. He studied at the Jesuit Collège de Clermont and around 1642 as a provincial lawyer, though it is not documented that he qualified. In June 1643 he left his social class for the stage, joined the actress Madeleine Béjart, and founded the Illustre Théâtre.

Thirteen years as an itinerant actor refined his comic skill, and he began to write, combining commedia dell'arte elements with the more refined French comedy. Through aristocratic patrons, including Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, brother of Louis XIV, he gained a command performance before the King at the Louvre. He was granted the grande salle of the Petit-Bourbon and later the theatre in the Palais-Royal, where plays such as The Affected Ladies, The School for Husbands and The School for Wives succeeded. His troupe received a royal pension and the title Troupe du Roi.

His satires drew criticism. The Catholic Church in France denounced Tartuffe, a study of religious hypocrisy, and the Parlement banned it, while Don Juan was withdrawn and never restaged by Molière. His other plays include The Misanthrope, The Miser and The Learned Ladies. His health suffered from the work, and by 1667 he had to take a break from the stage.

Molière suffered from pulmonary tuberculosis. On 17 February 1673, while playing Argan in his last play, The Imaginary Invalid, he collapsed in a fit of coughing and haemorrhage. He finished the performance, collapsed again, and died at home a few hours later without the last rites: two priests refused to come and a third arrived too late. As actors could not then be buried in consecrated ground, his widow Armande asked the King for a normal funeral at night, and he was buried in the part of the cemetery reserved for unbaptised infants. In 1817 his remains were moved to Père Lachaise Cemetery.

He is considered the creator of modern French comedy. A tartuffe is a hypocrite, and a harpagon, after the miser of The Miser, is an obsessively greedy man. His works were translated into English prose by John Ozell in 1714, and the first complete English version, by Baker and Miller, appeared in 1739.
molise: Molise covers 4,460.65 square kilometres, making it the second smallest region of Italy after the Aosta Valley. It is bordered by Abruzzo to the north, Apulia to the east, Lazio to the west and Campania to the south, and has 35 kilometres of sandy coastline on the Adriatic Sea. The countryside is mostly mountainous, with 55 percent covered by mountains and most of the rest by hills. The Volturno, the longest river of southern Italy, rises there. The name first appears in the High Middle Ages as that of a Norman county, taken from the name of the ruling family, the de' Moulins.

Evidence from the site of Isernia La Pineta shows that Molise was inhabited in the Paleolithic, with traces of human presence up to 700 000 years old. Before the Romans arrived it formed part of Samnium. The Pentri settled around Isernia and Campobasso from about the 7th century BCE. Roman expansion from the 4th century BCE brought the Samnite Wars. Isernia and Bojano, the Pentri capital, were captured, but the Samnites were completely defeated only after Sulla won the Social War.

The region declined in late antiquity, and the Lombards found it thinly populated. Around 667 Grimoald I, King of the Lombards, created the gastaldate of Bojano and gave it to the Bulgar commander Alzeco. In 1045 Rudolf of Moulins conquered what became the County of Bojano, which broke up into smaller fiefs after the family lost power at the end of the 11th century. In 1806 Joseph Bonaparte extended the French provincial model to the Kingdom of Naples, and by 1811 the Province of Molise had roughly its present area.

Molise has a population of 285,940 and its capital and largest city is Campobasso. Its two provinces are Campobasso and Isernia. It was formed in 1963 by separation from Abruzzo, with which it had been joined as Abruzzi e Molise. Emigration in 1951–71 emptied many small towns. Its two minorities are the Molisan Croats, who speak an old Dalmatian dialect of Croatian, and speakers of Arbëresh, a dialect of Albanian. Its sights include the Italic theatre at Pietrabbondante and the Roman site of Saepinum at Altilia.
molokai: Molokaʻi is the fifth most populated of the eight major islands of the Hawaiian archipelago. It measures 38 by 10 miles (61 by 16 km) in length and width and lies south-east of Oʻahu across the 25-mile-wide Kaʻiwi Channel, and north of Lānaʻi. The island grew from two shield volcanoes, East Molokaʻi and the much smaller West Molokaʻi. The northern half of East Molokaʻi collapsed about 1.5 million years ago, and what remains of the volcano includes the highest sea cliffs in the world. The highest point is Kamakou, at 4,970 feet (1,510 m). The largest town is Kaunakakai.

It was long thought that Molokaʻi was first settled around 650 CE by people from the Marquesas Islands. A 2010 study using revised radiocarbon dating placed the settlement of the Marquesas much later, and later migrants likely came from Tahiti and other islands of the south Pacific. Captain James Cook sighted Molokaʻi in 1778, and the first European sailor to visit was Captain George Dixon of the Royal Navy in 1786. A Protestant mission was founded at Kaluaʻaha in 1832.

Rudolph Wilhelm Meyer, an immigrant from Germany who arrived in 1850, was the first to grow and mill sugar and coffee commercially on the island, and he built its only sugar mill in 1878. Ranching began in the first half of the 19th century, when King Kamehameha V set up a country estate that Meyer managed and that became the Molokai Ranch.

Leprosy reached the Hawaiian Islands with traders, sailors and workers from places where it was common, and sugar planters, worried for their labour force, pressed the government to act. A law required people with the disease to be quarantined, and settlements at Kalawao and then Kalaupapa served as a colony from 1866 to 1969. More than 8,500 people were sent there and declared legally dead. Father Damien, a Belgian priest, served the sufferers for 16 years and died at Kalaupapa in 1889; Mother Marianne Cope and her Sisters also worked there.

Molokaʻi is part of Maui County, except for the Kalaupapa Peninsula, which forms Kalawao County. The forced quarantine laws were abolished in 1969, and the Kalaupapa National Historical Park now preserves the former settlement. Molokaʻi is believed to be the birthplace of the hula, which is marked at the annual Molokaʻi Ka Hula Piko festival.
molotov-ribbentrop-pact: Talks between the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and France broke down after the Soviet Union was excluded from the Munich Agreement of September 1938. Britain and France had judged Soviet participation in the conference dangerous and useless, partly because of Hitler's anti-Soviet rhetoric, while the Soviet leadership believed that the West wanted to encourage German aggression in the East. Rapprochement between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany began in early 1939. In May Stalin replaced his foreign minister Maxim Litvinov, who had advocated rapprochement with the West, with Vyacheslav Molotov. Contacts at first went through economic negotiations, and in early August the two sides began to discuss a political agreement, finding common ground in their opposition to the capitalist democracies.

The Treaty of Non-Aggression between Germany and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was dated 23 August 1939 and signed by Molotov and the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop. It ran for ten years and provided for consultation, arbitration of disagreements, neutrality if either party went to war with a third power, and no membership of any group aimed at the other.

The Secret Additional Protocol provided for the partition of Poland. Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Bessarabia were allotted to the Soviet sphere, and Lithuania, apart from the Vilnius region, to the German one. The existence of the protocol was rumoured in the West and was proved only when it was made public at the Nuremberg trials. The agreement stunned governments, the press, Germany's allies such as Japan and foreign Communist parties.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. On 17 September, stating concern for ethnic Ukrainians and Belarusians there, Stalin ordered the Soviet invasion. The German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty of 28 September then drew a new border on former Polish territory and moved Lithuania into the Soviet sphere. After the Soviet Union attacked Finland on 30 November in the Winter War, Finland ceded parts of Karelia, Kuusamo and Salla, and Hanko was leased as a naval base. About 422,000 Finns, 12 per cent of the population, lost their homes.

In mid-June 1940 Soviet NKVD troops raided border posts in Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia. Their state administrations were replaced by Soviet cadres, who deported or killed 34,250 Latvians, 75,000 Lithuanians and almost 60,000 Estonians. Elections with a single pro-Soviet candidate for many positions produced assemblies that asked for admission to the Soviet Union, which was granted. Parts of Romania, among them Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina, were also annexed. The pact ended on 22 June 1941 with Operation Barbarossa. Ribbentrop was convicted at Nuremberg and executed in 1946.
mon-people: The Mon descend from Proto-Austroasiatic people, who are believed to have migrated from the Yangtze valley in southern China to Southeast Asia between 3,000 and 2,000 BCE along the Mekong, Salween, Sittaung, Irrawaddy and Ping rivers, bringing riverine agriculture and wet rice. Their language belongs to the Monic branch of the Austroasiatic family and is close to Nyah Kur, spoken in northeastern Thailand.

The Mon were among the earliest peoples of mainland Southeast Asia and founded some of its earliest civilisations: Dvaravati in central Thailand, Sri Gotapura in central Laos, the Hariphunchai Kingdom in northern Thailand and the Thaton Kingdom in Lower Myanmar. They were the first to receive Theravada Buddhist missionaries from Sri Lanka, and they adopted the Pallava script; the oldest Mon inscription, found in a cave at Saraburi, dates to about 550 CE.

When the Pagan Kingdom collapsed in 1287, Wareru, born to a Mon mother and a Tai father, made himself king of the Mon at Martaban and later moved the capital to Pegu. His Hanthawaddy kingdom lasted from 1287 to 1539. Binnya U defended it against Lan Na in the mid-14th century, and his son Razadarit, who reigned from 1384 to 1421, repelled invasions from Ava and made contributions to the Shwedagon Pagoda.

In 1539 King Tabinshwehti of Taungoo took Hanthawaddy after a siege of Pegu lasting four years. Many Mon refugees fled to Ayutthaya, where the Mon aristocracy joined the court. The fall of Martaban in 1541 was accompanied by massacre and pillage on a large scale. In 1740 Mon rebels, joined by the Gwe Shan, restored a Hanthawaddy kingdom with French support, but King Alaungpaya conquered it in 1757. Tens of thousands of Mon civilians were killed, among them over 3,000 monks in the capital alone.

Under the Konbaung dynasty further rebellions, including one in 1814, were put down harshly, and large numbers of Mon migrated to Siam. The British took control of the Mon territories after the Second Anglo-Burmese War in 1852, but never restored the Mon kingdom.

Today the Mon are a major ethnic group in Myanmar and a minor one in Thailand, and the two Mon dialects are mutually intelligible. The Tai Tham and Burmese alphabets are adaptations of the Mon script, and Burmese has borrowed vocabulary from Mon, especially for administration, architecture, cloth, cuisine and flowers. Cities including Yangon and Lamphun were founded by Mon people or Mon rulers. Their symbol is the hongsa, a mythological water bird. Mon National Day, set up in 1947, commemorates the founding of Hanthawaddy.
monemvasia: Monemvasia stands on a tied island off the east coast of the Peloponnese, connected to the mainland by a sandy isthmus about 400 metres long. An earthquake in 375 CE separated the rock from the mainland. Most of the rock is a plateau about 100 metres above the sea. The upper town stood on the plateau, with a rectangular acropolis with four towers built in the sixth century, and the lower town lies on the southern slope. There are no natural springs, so the town depended on cisterns.

The name comes from two Greek words, moni, 'single', and emvasis, 'approach', meaning the city of the single entrance. Its Italian form, Malvasia, gave its name to malmsey wine, which was not grown locally but reached Europe through the town's extensive trade, mostly from the Peloponnese and the Cyclades, especially Tinos.

Monemvasia was founded in the sixth century by settlers from Sparta, then called Lacedaemon. A later local chronicle says that the city's inhabitants fled a Slav raid in 587 to 588, but archaeology does not support this, since the first level of the church of Christ Elkomenos dates from Justinian's reign, some decades earlier. While other settlements in the Peloponnese declined from the seventh century, Monemvasia grew into a commercial and cultural centre on sea routes such as the one to Sicily.

After Mehmed II took most of the Peloponnese in 1460 and 1461, Monemvasia fell to the Venetians by the end of 1463. In the Sixth Ottoman-Venetian War Francesco Morosini failed to take it in 1687 and 1689, but Girolamo Corner entered it on 12 August 1690. In the Greek War of Independence the fortress was besieged from 15 March 1821 and surrendered to the Greeks on 23 July after four months. The war left it nearly ruined, and the census of 1828 counted only 659 inhabitants.

The upper town has been uninhabited since the second Venetian occupation, but its Byzantine church of Hagia Sophia, built on a cross-in-square plan in the style of the twelfth century, survives, with parts of frescoes. A former mosque in Elkomenos square has housed the town's archaeological collection since 1999. From the 1970s Monemvasia revived as a tourist destination, as visitors bought and restored houses, and a bridge linked it to the road network in 1971.
mongke: Möngke was born on 11 January 1209, the eldest son of Genghis Khan's son Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki. A shaman, Teb Tengri Khokhcuu, claimed to see a great future for the child in the stars and gave him the name Möngke, meaning eternal. He was raised at the camp of his uncle Ögedei Khan's queen Angqui. In 1224 Genghis Khan performed the hunting ceremony on him and his brother Kublai near the Ili River, and in 1230 he went to war for the first time, against the Jin dynasty. Tolui died in 1232.

On his mother's advice Möngke went to Batu of the Golden Horde, who backed his election. A first kurultai at Ala Qamaq approved him, though its attendance was limited and its validity was questionable, and a second, organized by Sorghaghtani and Berke, proclaimed him Great Khan on 1 July 1251. He was the first khagan from the Toluid line. He drafted his own decrees, limited costly gifts to princes by turning them into salaries, taxed merchants and punished commanders whose troops plundered civilians. He also paid the merchants' drafts issued under his predecessor Güyük, and favoured officials of Muslim, Chinese and Uyghur origin. He exempted clergy of all faiths from tax.

His conquests were aimed at East Asia and the Middle East. Goryeo was ravaged by the Mongol army, which took 206,800 captives in 1254. Kublai took the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan in 1253 to 1254 and outflanked the Song, and in 1257 Uriyangkhadai sacked Thăng Long but withdrew after a Vietnamese counter-attack. In 1252 Möngke gave his brother Hülegü the conquest of Western Asia, with the Nizari Ismailis and the Abbasid Caliphate as priorities, and the Ismaili resistance in Iran was crushed by the end of 1256. In 1254 he received the envoy William of Rubruck at Karakorum.

In October 1257 Möngke set out against the Song, leaving Ariq Böke in charge at Karakorum. He took Paoning in 1258 and was last seen at the siege of Diaoyucheng near Chongqing, where he is generally agreed to have died on 11 August 1259. Sources disagree on the cause. Chinese accounts and Bar Hebraeus say a crossbow bolt killed him, the History of Yuan a stone projectile, and Persian accounts dysentery or cholera. He was buried at Burkhan Khaldun near Genghis and Tolui.

He left no designated successor. His brothers Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke fought the four-year Toluid Civil War, and that war and the later Kaidu–Kublai war led to the permanent division of the Mongol Empire.
mongkut: Mongkut, whose name means crown, was born on 18 October 1804, the second son of Prince Itsarasunthon, who was crowned Rama II in 1809, and Princess Bunrot. In 1824 he became a Buddhist monk, as Siamese custom asked of young men, and in the same year his father died. The nobility passed him over for the older and more experienced Prince Chetsadabodin, known as Nangklao, and Mongkut stayed in the monastery. In 1835 he began a reform movement that became the Dhammayut sect.

In 1836 he became first abbot of Wat Bowonniwet, where he studied Latin, English and astronomy with missionaries and sailors and became friends with Vicar Pallegoix. In 1829 at Phetchaburi he had met the monk Buddhawangso, who followed the vinaya, the monastic discipline, strictly.

Dit Bunnag, the most powerful noble of the previous reign, and British merchants backed Mongkut, who left the monkhood and took the throne in 1851 at the age of 47. He took the name Phra Chom Klao and crowned his brother Isaret as second king, Pinklao. The Bunnag family was at its height under him. He ordered nobles to wear shirts at court, ended the practice of sending envoys to the Qing court, banned forced marriages and the sale of wives to pay debts, and released many royal concubines. He had 32 wives and 82 children. He hired missionaries to teach English to the princes and urged a European-style education. Siamese forces failed to take Kengtung in 1855 after a siege of 21 days.

John Bowring came to Siam in 1854 to negotiate a treaty. It abolished the Royal Storage, which had held the monopoly on foreign trade since Ayutthaya, and limited import tax to 3 per cent, collected once. Trade, rice growing, milling and sugar production expanded, and coinage was introduced in 1860. The treaty also gave British subjects extraterritoriality, and more treaties with other powers followed, undermining national revenue and legal rights. In 1862 the court hired Anna Leonowens, whose memoir became the source of The King and I.

Mongkut studied indigenous astrology and Western astronomy and predicted the total solar eclipse of 18 August 1868. He invited European and Siamese officials to watch it at Wakor, south of Hua Hin, and his calculations proved accurate. He and his son Prince Chulalongkorn caught malaria on the expedition, and the king died six weeks later, on 1 October 1868. Chulalongkorn, who survived, succeeded him, and in 1902 gave the Thammayut sect royal recognition, making it one of the two major Buddhist denominations of modern Thailand.
mongol-empire: The ancestors of the Mongols are first recorded in the late tenth century, migrating from eastern Manchuria onto the Mongolian Plateau and settling south-east of Lake Baikal. In the twelfth century their khans raided the Chinese Jin dynasty, but the killing of the khans Qutula and Ambaghai in the 1160s ended this first confederation. At a kurultai, an assembly, in 1206 the shaman Teb Tenggeri proclaimed Temüjin khan of the Great Mongol Nation, and he took the title Genghis Khan. He redistributed the tribal peoples into units of tens, hundreds and thousands, which the historian Timothy May calls a social revolution.

Genghis Khan died on 18 August 1227, when the empire ruled from the Pacific to the Caspian Sea, twice the size of the Roman Empire or the Umayyad Caliphate at their height. His son Ögedei was elected in 1229. After Ögedei's death in 1241 a stalemate over the succession lasted more than four years. In 1251 a kurultai proclaimed Möngke great khan, moving power from the Ögedeid to the Toluid line. In 1260 the Mamluks defeated the Mongol force under Kitbuqa at the Battle of Ain Jalut, the western limit of Mongol advance in the Middle East.

After Möngke died in 1259, rival councils elected his brothers Ariq Böke and Kublai Khan, who fought the Toluid Civil War from 1260 to 1264. Kublai prevailed but never regained control of the Chagatayid and Ögedeid families. On 18 December 1271 he issued an edict giving his regime the dynastic name Great Yuan. By his death in 1294 the empire had split into four: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty. The Ilkhanate disintegrated between 1335 and 1353, and the Yuan lost China in 1368, when Ming forces took Dadu.

Every adult Mongol man was a soldier, and returned to pastoralism when not called up. Most were horse-archers, taking five or six horses on campaign. Genghis Khan imposed strict discipline, with officers responsible for training and equipment, and failure was often punished by execution.

Genghis Khan set up complete religious freedom, though he was himself a shamanist, and exempted religious leaders from taxation. A relay mail system, the Yam, had stations about 40 kilometres apart, and riders regularly covered 200 kilometres a day. Trade routes formed across the empire, and the Mongols supported merchants. The Secret History of the Mongols, the oldest surviving literary work in Mongolian, was written for the royal family after 1227.
mongol-invasion-of-kievan-rus: In 1207 Genghis Khan sent his eldest son Jochi to subdue the tribes north of the Selenga River and in the Irtysh valley, lands that included Eastern Europe in the Jochi Ulus. In 1222 to 1224 Subutai and Jebe led a force of 30,000 through Transcaucasia and south-eastern Europe, traditionally regarded as a reconnaissance. On 31 May 1223 they defeated a united Rus' army, together with the remnants of the Cumans, at the Battle of the Kalka River, and then withdrew. A kurultai of 1235 renewed the plan, and Batu, a son of Jochi, led the army that gathered in the Caspian steppes in the autumn of 1236.

The army first conquered Volga Bulgaria, which fell by the spring of 1237, and then defeated the Cumans and Alans. In November 1237 Batu sent envoys to Yuri II of Vladimir demanding submission. Yuri sent gifts but avoided open conflict. The Mongols attacked from several directions. Ryazan fell after three days, and a chronicler records that the Mongols killed its prince and princess and many of its people. They burned Kolomna and Moscow, besieged Vladimir on 4 February 1238 and took and burned it three days later. On 4 March the army Yuri had raised was destroyed at the Battle of the Sit River.

Batu then divided his force and ransacked fourteen cities of the north-east, among them Rostov, Yaroslavl, Tver and Torzhok. Kozelsk resisted for seven weeks. Novgorod was spared by an early decision to surrender. In the winter of 1239 Batu sacked Chernigov and Pereyaslavl. His army stormed Kyiv in December 1240 after many days of siege and pillaged it, although the Cathedral of Saint Sophia survived. The Mongols then moved into Hungary and Poland and took Esztergom on Christmas Day 1241.

The siege of Kyiv is generally held to mark the end of the state of Kievan Rus', which had already been fragmenting. The principalities became part of the Jochid appanage, the Golden Horde, whose capital Sarai lay on the lower Volga. Tribute demands continued until about 1480, though a Russian army defeated the Mongols at Kulikovo in 1380. Colin McEvedy estimates that the population fell from 7.5 million to seven million, and many cities took over a century to recover.

Moscow rose under Mongol rule. After the prince of Tver led an uprising in 1327, Ivan I of Moscow joined the Mongols in crushing it and received the title of Grand Prince. Most historians hold that the invasion accelerated a fragmentation already under way.
mongol-invasions-of-japan: After a series of Mongol invasions between 1231 and 1281, the Korean kingdom of Goryeo signed a treaty favouring the Mongols and became a vassal state. Kublai Khan was declared Khagan in 1260 and made Khanbaliq, now Beijing, his capital in 1264. Japan was then ruled by the Hōjō regents of the Kamakura shogunate. Between 1266 and 1273 Mongol and Korean diplomatic missions went to Japan six times to demand submission, and the Japanese ignored every demand.

In 1274 the invasion fleet left Hoppo, now Masan, on 2 November. It landed on Tsushima two days later and attacked Iki Island on 13 November, where the governor Taira no Kagetaka made a spirited defence before killing himself with his family. The fleet landed in Hakata Bay on 19 November, and the Battle of Bun'ei followed the next day. The Japanese were unused to Mongol tactics, and the invaders advanced behind shields and threw paper and iron casing bombs that frightened the Japanese horses. By morning most Yuan ships had gone. A storm is recorded, though it is uncertain whether it struck at Hakata Bay or on the way back, and of the 30,000-strong force 13,500 did not return.

The shogunate prepared for a second attempt, building a two-metre wall around Hakata Bay in 1276. Two sets of Yuan envoys, five in 1275 and five in 1279, were beheaded. In 1281 two fleets, one from Korea and one from southern China, sailed with a reported 142,000 soldiers and sailors. The Eastern Route army attacked Tsushima on 9 June and Iki on 14 June, then landed at Hakata, but could not get past the wall. Japanese night raids in small boats harassed the fleet. On 15 August a great typhoon, the kamikaze, struck the fleet at anchor, and the Japanese killed the survivors they found, except southern Chinese, who they believed had been coerced.

Thomas Conlan argues that the force of 1281 was exaggerated by an order of magnitude; Morris Rossabi suggests about 70,000. The defeated Mongol Empire lost most of its naval power, and Korea, which had built the ships, cut down much of its timber. Japan won no new land, so the Kamakura shogunate could not reward its gokenin, and its authority declined. Later Ming discussions of invading Japan were never carried out. The invasions are an early case of gunpowder warfare outside China, and bomb shells packed with gunpowder and scrap iron have been found in a wreck off Japan. The word kamikaze, divine wind, was first used for the typhoons, and the belief that Japan would never be invaded lasted into the twentieth century.
mongolia: Mongolia is a landlocked country between Russia to the north and China to the south, with an area of 1,564,116 square kilometres. Its landscape is grassy steppe, mountains in the north and west, and the Gobi Desert in the south, and the whole country is part of the Mongolian Plateau. The highest point is Khüiten Peak, at 4,374 metres. The climate is high, cold and windy, with long winters, and Ulaanbaatar is the world's coldest capital city. The country is subject to harsh conditions known as zud, in which large numbers of livestock die from starvation or freezing.

The Khoit Tsenkher Cave holds paintings dated to 20,000 years ago, and Neolithic agricultural settlements from about 5500 to 3500 BCE predate horse-riding nomadism, which became the dominant culture. The territory was ruled by nomadic empires, among them the Xiongnu, the Xianbei, the Rouran Khaganate, the First Turkic Khaganate, the Second Turkic Khaganate and the Uyghur Khaganate. In 1206 Genghis Khan founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history. His grandson Kublai Khan conquered China proper and established the Yuan dynasty. After the Yuan collapsed, the Mongols retreated to Mongolia and resumed factional conflict, except in the era of Dayan Khan and Tumen Zasagt Khan.

Tibetan Buddhism spread to Mongolia in the 16th century, and by the early 20th century almost one-third of adult men were Buddhist monks. The Qing dynasty absorbed the country in the 17th century. Mongolia declared independence after the Qing collapsed in 1911 and achieved actual independence from the Republic of China in 1921, shortly after which it became a satellite state of the Soviet Union. The Mongolian People's Republic was founded as a socialist state in 1924.

After the anti-communist revolutions of 1989, Mongolia carried out its own peaceful democratic revolution in 1990, which led to a multi-party system, a new constitution in 1992 and a market economy. It is a semi-presidential democratic republic with a unicameral legislature, the State Great Khural, of 126 seats. The 2024 population was 3,544,835, and roughly half live in Ulaanbaatar.
About 30 per cent of the population is nomadic or semi-nomadic, and horse culture remains integral. Mahayana Buddhism is the majority religion, at 51.7 per cent. The traditional dwelling is the ger.
monmouthshire: The centre of the county is the plain of Gwent, formed by the basin of the River Usk, with hilly land to the west. In the east the border with England largely follows the River Wye and its tributary the River Monnow, and the Wye Valley is a designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. The southern border is the Severn Estuary. The Gwent Levels along it are an almost entirely man-made landscape, reclaimed from the sea since Roman times and long vulnerable to flooding: the Bristol Channel floods of 1607 drowned some 2,000 people, many on this coast.

Remains from the Mesolithic period have been found across the county. In the Iron Age south-east Wales was held by the Silures, whom Tacitus called exceptionally stubborn. After the Roman conquest of Britain began in 43 CE they resisted under Caratacus, who was defeated in 50 CE, but the whole of south-east Wales was not subdued until about 75 CE. The ruins of Venta Silurum at Caerwent mark Roman rule. After the Romans left, the Kingdom of Gwent arose, with Caerwent as its capital.

From the late 1060s the Norman invasion destroyed the kingdom and replaced it with five Marcher lordships, based at Striguil (Chepstow), Monmouth, Abergavenny, Usk and Caerleon. Their castles began as earth and timber and were later built in stone, Chepstow's being begun by William FitzOsbern as early as 1067. The county's status was long disputed. A Laws in Wales Act formed the county from the Marches, but a later act of 1542 listed the counties of Wales and omitted Monmouthshire, which began a centuries-long dispute over whether it was Welsh or English.

The Local Government Act 1972 took effect in April 1974, abolished the historic county and created Gwent, confirming the area as part of Wales. The present county of Monmouthshire was re-created on 1 April 1996 with only the eastern three-fifths of the historic area. Its largest town is Abergavenny and its administrative centre is Usk. It has a fine collection of castles, among them Chepstow and Raglan, and Tintern Abbey became a focus of the Wye Tour in the late eighteenth century.
monothelitism: Monothelitism grew out of earlier disputes over the nature of Christ. The Council of Chalcedon defined Christ as having two natures in one hypostasis, while the non-Chalcedonians held that he had one nature. Since one nature seemed to imply one will, Eastern Roman rulers in the seventh century hoped a doctrine of one will would unite the quarrelling parties. Many provinces later lost to the Umayyad Caliphate were non-Chalcedonian: in Egypt about 30,000 Chalcedonian Greeks faced some five million Coptic non-Chalcedonians.

The first attempt was monoenergism, the teaching of one energy. Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople promoted it with Emperor Heraclius, who by 622 had written of Christ's single energy. By 630 three of the five patriarchates taught one theandric energy. A monk named Sophronius opposed it, became Patriarch of Jerusalem in 634 and attacked it as a disguised form of monophysitism. Support faded and Sergius and Heraclius dropped it.

Sergius then devised a new formula, which Heraclius issued as the Ecthesis in 638. It banned talk of one or two energies and declared that Christ had two natures but a single will, which could never oppose the divine will. The eastern patriarchs accepted it, but Pope Severinus and Pope John IV rejected it, producing a schism between Rome and Constantinople. Heraclius, old and ill, said on his deathbed that Sergius had pressured him into approving it.

Maximus the Confessor led the opposition in Africa. Constans II, who succeeded Heraclius, issued the Type of Constans, which forbade any discussion of one or two wills. Pope Martin I, at the Lateran Council of 649, condemned both the Ecthesis and the Type. The exarch Theodore I Calliopas seized Martin and took him to Constantinople, where he was imprisoned, tortured and banished to Chersonesus, where he soon died. Maximus lost his tongue and right hand.

After Constans died in 668, his son Constantine IV left the question to a church council. Pope Agatho held a synod at Rome in 680, and synods in the West condemned the doctrine. The Third Council of Constantinople, meeting in 680 and 681, condemned monothelitism and affirmed that Christ had two natural wills and two natural energies. It also anathematised Pope Honorius I, a point later debated in discussions of papal infallibility; Leo II's letter read the censure as aimed at his silence rather than at error of belief. The Oriental Orthodox deny that they ever held the doctrine.
monpazier: Monpazier, in Occitan Montpasièr, is a commune in the Dordogne department in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, in south-west France, 40 kilometres from Bergerac Airport. It belongs to the association Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, and in 2019 it received the designation Ville et Métiers d'Art because of the many artisans working in the village. From 1790 to 2015 it was the capital of the canton of Monpazier. Its inhabitants are called Monpaziérois in French.

Monpazier is a 13th-century bastide town founded by King Edward I of England. It was created by an act of paréage: the lord of Biron supplied the land and Edward the authority and permission, and any profits from taxes or commercial activity were split between the two. Like other bastides it was laid out on a grid pattern, with a square at its centre, one end of which contains an open market hall. It is one of the best preserved of its kind and keeps many original features.

The parish church of St. Dominique was built between the 13th and 16th centuries in a rectangular plot that adjoins a corner of the marketplace. Its apse was added in the fifteenth century and its choir is believed to have been completed in 1506.

The bastide draws visitors, among them guests of the four-star Hôtel Edward Premier, named after its founder. In summer the town holds a cycle race around the bastide, usually at the start of August, a medieval day, a kermesse and several specialist markets. Each July the Chorale of Monpazier gives a concert in the church. The actor Julien Guiomar (1928-2010) spent his last years in Monpazier.
monrovia: Monrovia lies along the Cape Mesurado peninsula, between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mesurado River, whose mouth forms a large natural harbour. The Saint Paul River lies directly north of the city and forms the northern boundary of Bushrod Island. The historic downtown, centred on Broad Street, is at the very end of the peninsula, and the market district of Waterside faces the harbour. The harbour was significantly expanded by United States forces during the Second World War.

Before 1816 the area around Cape Mesurado was called Ducor, a long-established crossroads of trade inhabited by fishing, trading and farming communities including the Dey, Kru, Bassa, Gola and Vai. The French cartographer and slave trader Chevalier des Marchais visited it in 1723. The American Colonization Society's representatives negotiated the purchase of land at Cape Mesurado from local leaders in December 1821, an agreement valued at about $300 in trade goods whose circumstances historians continue to debate.

On 7 January 1822 a ship took African American settlers to Dazoe Island, now Providence Island, and they went ashore at Cape Mesurado and founded Christopolis. In 1824 it was renamed Monrovia after President James Monroe, a supporter of the Society. A constitutional convention met there in 1845, and its document was adopted two years later as the constitution of the independent Republic of Liberia. At the start of the 20th century 2,500 of Monrovia's 4,000 residents were Americo-Liberian, living in houses reminiscent of the southern United States, while Krutown was inhabited mainly by Kru. By 1937 the population had grown to 10,000.

Monrovia is the capital and largest city of Liberia and the seat of its government, and the Freeport of Monrovia is the country's main port. Its name is one of only two world capitals taken from an American president, the other being Washington, D.C. The 2022 census counted 1,761,032 residents in the city. Capitol Hill holds the Temple of Justice and the Executive Mansion.
monsoon: The English word monsoon came from Portuguese monção, ultimately from Arabic mawsim, 'season', although partly by way of early modern Dutch monson; its etymology is not wholly certain. It was first used in English in British India and neighbouring countries for the big seasonal winds that blew from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea in the southwest and brought heavy rainfall. The word is usually applied to the rainy phase of a seasonal pattern, although technically there is also a dry phase.

Monsoons were once explained as a large-scale sea breeze caused by land being warmer than the sea, but this is no longer considered the cause. The monsoon is now seen as a planetary-scale phenomenon tied to the annual migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which varies with the contrast in heating between land and sea. The major systems are the West African, South Asian–Australian, North American and South American monsoons.

The southwest summer monsoon of South Asia occurs from June to September. The Thar Desert and neighbouring areas heat up and create a low-pressure area, and moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean rush in. The Himalayas block them and force them to rise, cool and release rain; some areas receive up to 10,000 mm a year. It is generally expected to begin between the end of May and the beginning of June and to fade between the end of September and the start of October.

The strengthening of the Asian monsoon has been linked to the uplift of the Tibetan Plateau after the collision of the Indian subcontinent with Asia some 50 million years ago. Records from the Arabian Sea and wind-blown dust on China's Loess Plateau led many geologists to think the monsoon first became strong around 8 million years ago, while plant fossils in China and sediment records from the South China Sea suggest a start 15 to 20 million years ago.

Its strength has since varied with global climate, especially the Pleistocene ice ages. A study of the past million years found that South Asian monsoon rainfall was significantly lower during glacial periods than in interglacials.
