The East Asian summer monsoon intensified in the Middle Holocene, about 6,000 years ago, and began to wane from about 5,000 to 4,500 years ago.
mont-saint-michel: The island lies about a kilometre off the north-western coast of France, at the mouth of the Couesnon River near Avranches. It is a granite outcrop with a circumference of about 960 metres and a highest point 92 metres above sea level. Tides vary by roughly 14 metres, and medieval pilgrims crossing the flats nicknamed it St. Michael in peril of the sea. It was accessible to pilgrims at low tide, and defensible because the incoming tide could strand, drive off or drown attackers on foot.

Before the first monastic establishment of the 8th century the island was called Mont Tombe. According to a legend, the archangel Michael appeared in 708 to Aubert, bishop of Avranches, and told him to build a church on the rock. In 933 William I Longsword annexed the Cotentin Peninsula from the weakened Duchy of Brittany, which made the mount definitively part of Normandy. The Bayeux Tapestry shows it. In 1067 the monastery supported William the Conqueror's claim to the English throne, and he rewarded it with English properties, including St Michael's Mount in Cornwall.

In the 11th century Richard II, Duke of Normandy, chose William of Volpiano as builder. He designed the Romanesque abbey church with its transept crossing at the top of the mount, and many underground crypts and chapels were built to carry the weight. In 1204 Guy of Thouars besieged the mount, burned the village and massacred its people, and the fire spread to the abbey. Philip Augustus then offered Abbot Jordan a grant to rebuild in the new Gothic style. Abbot Pierre le Roy, from 1386 to 1410, added fortifications. English forces besieged the island unsuccessfully from 1423 and again from 1433, under Thomas Scales, 7th Baron Scales.

The abbey's prestige as a pilgrimage centre declined after the Reformation, and by the French Revolution scarcely any monks remained. It became a prison, first for clerical opponents of the republic and then for political prisoners. A campaign including Victor Hugo for its restoration began by 1836. The prison closed in 1863, the abbey was classified a historic monument in 1874, and the architect Édouard Corroyer spent fifteen years restoring the part known as la Merveille. German soldiers occupied the island in the Second World War, and it was liberated on 1 August 1944.

The mount and its bay were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1979, and over 60 buildings in the commune are protected as historical monuments. A community of the Monastic Fraternities of Jerusalem has lived there since 2001.
mont-ventoux: Mont Ventoux lies about 20 km north-east of Carpentras in Vaucluse, and its north side borders the department of Drôme. It is nicknamed the Beast of Provence, the Giant of Provence and the Bald Mountain. Geologically part of the Alps, it is often treated as separate because no mountains of similar height stand nearby. It rises alone north of the Luberon range, just east of the Dentelles de Montmirail, its foothills. The summit is bare limestone without trees, so from a distance it looks snow-capped all year, though snow lies only from December to April.

The name comes from the French venteux, windy: in the 10th century the forms Mons Ventosus and Mons Ventorius were used interchangeably. The mistral has produced wind speeds as high as 320 km/h at the summit, and the road is often closed by wind, especially at the col des tempêtes just below the top.

People have probably climbed the mountain since prehistory. The first recorded ascent was by the scholastic philosopher Jean Buridan, before 1334, on his way to the papal court at Avignon, to make meteorological observations. Petrarch wrote a possibly fictional account of climbing it with his brother on 26 April 1336. A chapel dedicated to the Holy Cross was built on the top in the 15th century, and a meteorological station was built there in 1882, planned in 1879 together with a carriage road. A 50-metre telecommunications mast followed in the 1960s, and a hill climb for cars and motorcycles ran on its roads from 1902 to 1976.

The mountain was originally forested, but from the 12th century trees were systematically cut for the shipbuilders of the naval port of Toulon. Some areas have been replanted since 1860 with hardwoods such as holm oak and beech and with conifers such as Atlas cedar and larch.

The mountain marks the boundary between the flora and fauna of northern and southern France, and some spiders and butterflies are found only there. UNESCO created the Réserve de Biosphère du Mont Ventoux in 1990, protecting an area of 810 square kilometres. Two small ski stations, Mont Serein on the north side and Chalet Reynard on the south, operate when the wind allows.

The Tour de France first climbed it in 1951. The British cyclist Tom Simpson died on the slope on 13 July 1967, from heat exhaustion made worse by dehydration, amphetamines and alcohol, and a memorial near the summit is visited by cyclists. Charly Gaul in 1958 and Eddy Merckx in 1970 won stages at the summit.
montalcino: Montalcino sits on a high hill in the Val d'Orcia, west of Pienza, about 42 kilometres from Siena and 110 from Florence. Its height gives views over the valleys of the Asso, Ombrone and Arbia, and the lower slopes are covered with vines and olive orchards. The town takes its name from a variety of oak that once covered the terrain, and the hill has probably been settled since Etruscan times.

The first mention in documents dates from 814, suggesting a church there in the 9th century, most likely built by monks of the nearby Abbey of Sant'Antimo. The population grew suddenly in the middle of the 10th century, when people fleeing the town of Roselle settled there. In the Middle Ages it was known for its tanneries and leather goods, and as an independent commune on the Via Francigena, the main road between France and Rome. It came increasingly under the sway of Siena and was a satellite of that city after the Battle of Montaperti in 1260, drawn into its wars with Florence and into the conflict between Ghibellines and Guelphs.

The first walls were built in the 13th century, and in 1361 the Sienese architects Mino Foresi and Domenico di Feo built a pentagonal fortress on the highest point. After Florence under the Medici conquered Siena in 1555, Montalcino held out for almost four years before it fell. It stayed under Florentine control until the Grand Duchy of Tuscany became part of a united Italy in 1861.

The fortress, the Romanesque church of Sant'Agostino, the cathedral of San Salvatore and the old town hall mark the medieval town, and the Musei Riuniti hold Sienese paintings, among them works attributed to Ambrogio Lorenzetti and Simone Martini. The town is divided into four quarters, Borghetto, Travaglio, Pianello and Ruga. Brunello di Montalcino, made from sangiovese grosso grapes, was the first wine to be awarded DOCG status, and its producers grew from eleven in the 1960s to more than two hundred.
montana: Montana is a landlocked state in the Mountain West of the western United States, with an area of 147,040 square miles. It is the fourth-largest state and the only one to border three Canadian provinces: British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The Continental Divide splits much of the state into distinct eastern and western regions. Most of its hundred or more named mountain ranges lie in the western half, which is part of the northern Rocky Mountains, while about 60 per cent of the state is prairie.

For thousands of years various indigenous peoples have lived in what is now Montana. Tribes met by Europeans and settlers from the United States included the Crow in the south-central area, the Cheyenne and Lakota in the southeast, the Blackfeet, Assiniboine and Gros Ventres in the central and north-central area, and the Kootenai and Salish in the west. Early Spanish explorers called the whole mountainous region of the west Montaña del Norte, from which the name derives.

Most of Montana came under American sovereignty with the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 and was explored by the Lewis and Clark Expedition soon after. Fur trappers followed and were the main economic activity until gold was discovered in 1858. The gold rush and the Homestead Acts of 1862 brought large numbers of American settlers. When Montana Territory was proposed in 1864, a representative objected that the name was a misnomer for a largely non-mountainous territory and that a Native American name would be better; the House Committee on Territories kept Montana.

Rapid growth led to statehood on 8 November 1889. Mining, particularly around Butte and Helena, remained the state's main economic engine through the mid-twentieth century. Montana granted women the vote in 1914, and in 1916 it became the first state to elect a woman to Congress, Jeannette Rankin.

Montana's capital is Helena and its most populous city is Billings. The state has no official nickname, but is known as Big Sky Country and the Treasure State. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture, with mining, oil, gas, coal and lumber also important. Glacier National Park and the site of the Battle of Little Bighorn are among its sights.
monte-carlo: The name means Mount Charles. Strictly it belongs to one ward of Monaco, Monte Carlo/Spélugues, but it is also used for a larger district, the Monte Carlo Quarter, which corresponds to the former municipality and includes the wards of La Rousse/Saint Roman, Larvotto/Bas Moulins and Saint Michel. Monaco has four traditional quarters: Fontvieille, the newest, Monaco-Ville, the oldest, La Condamine and Monte Carlo. The ward covers only 28.14 hectares, on a prominent escarpment at the base of the Maritime Alps, facing the Mediterranean. At its eastern border one crosses into the French town of Beausoleil.

In 1856 Charles III of Monaco granted a concession to Napoleon Langlois and Albert Aubert to set up a sea-bathing facility for the treatment of various diseases and to build a German-style casino. The first casino opened in La Condamine and did not succeed. It moved several times before reaching its present site in the area called Les Spélugues, the Caves. Success came slowly, largely because Monaco was inaccessible from much of Europe, and the railway of 1868 brought an influx of visitors and growing wealth. Charles III also established the Hôtel de Paris in 1864, and the church of Saint-Charles was completed in 1883.

The Salle Garnier, the casino's theatre and home of the Opéra de Monte-Carlo, was designed by Charles Garnier, who also designed the Paris opera house. It was inaugurated on 25 January 1879 with a performance by Sarah Bernhardt dressed as a nymph, and the first opera performed there was Robert Planquette's Le Chevalier Gaston on 8 February 1879. Tramways served the quarter from 1898 to 1931. In 1911 the constitution divided the principality into three municipalities, one of them Monte Carlo. They were merged in 1917, after accusations that the government used them to divide and conquer, and have been wards since.

Monte Carlo centres on the Place du Casino, with the casino, the Hôtel de Paris, the Café de Paris and the Salle Garnier. In the east, Larvotto has Monaco's only public beach and the Grimaldi Forum convention centre. Much of the Circuit de Monaco, on which the Monaco Grand Prix is run, lies within the quarter. The Monte Carlo Rally is run mostly on French roads, and the Monte Carlo Masters tennis tournament is held in the neighbouring French commune of Roquebrune-Cap-Martin.
monte-cassino: The abbey stands on a rocky hill about 130 kilometres south-east of Rome, in the Latin Valley, on the site of the ancient Roman town of Casinum. The Volsci first settled the nearby town of Cassino in the fifth century BCE and built a citadel on the summit. The Romans defeated them in 312 BCE and built a temple to Apollo there. Casinum became a bishopric in the fifth century CE, but it lacked strong defences and was later abandoned and neglected. The hill overlooks Highway 6 and has always been of strategic importance.

According to Pope Gregory I's Life of Saint Benedict, Benedict smashed the idol of Apollo, overturned the altar and dedicated one chapel to Saint Martin and another to Saint John the Baptist. Excavations after 1944 found traces of both oratories. At Monte Cassino Benedict wrote the Rule that became the foundation of Western monasticism and received a visit from Totila, king of the Ostrogoths, and he died there. After the Lombards sacked the first monastery, the monks fled to Rome. Petronax of Brescia re-established it in 718.

In 744 a donation from Gisulf II of Benevento created the Terra Sancti Benedicti, secular lands answerable only to the abbot and the pope. Saracens sacked and burned the abbey in the ninth century, and the monks lived at Teano and then Capua until it was rebuilt in 949.

The abbey reached its height in the 11th century under Abbot Desiderius, later Pope Victor III. He brought Byzantine mosaicists from Constantinople, and the abbey church was consecrated by Pope Alexander II in 1071. The library, the scriptorium and the school of illuminators became widely known, and the Beneventan script flourished. Three popes came from the abbey: Stephen IX, Victor III and Gelasius II. An earthquake damaged it in 1349, French troops sacked it in 1799, and the Italian state dissolved it in 1866 and made it a national monument.

During the Battle of Monte Cassino in 1944 the abbey lay on the German Gustav Line. On 15 February 1944 Allied air raids nearly destroyed it, on reports that German troops occupied it. None were present, and the only people killed in the monastery were 230 Italian civilians sheltering there. German paratroopers then occupied the ruins. The abbey was rebuilt after the war with the support of President Luigi Einaudi, and Pope Paul VI consecrated the rebuilt basilica on 24 October 1964. It remains a Benedictine monastery.
monte-titano: Monte Titano, meaning Mount Titan, is a mountain of the Apennines and the highest point of San Marino. Its peak lies within the municipal limits of the capital, San Marino, immediately east of the urbanized area. Italians often call it Monte Brugola, because from the Po Plain its shape resembles a hex key. The rocky outcrop is about 200 metres high at most and has three peaks, each crowned by one of the Three Towers of San Marino: Guaita, Cesta and Montale. The towers appear on the coat of arms in the centre of the national flag.

In the Tertiary era the area lay under the sea. Earthquakes lifted a mass of rock about 80 km away, which slid slowly toward the Adriatic and gave rise to several mountains, Monte Titano among them. Fossils of fish, especially shark teeth dated to the Miocene, have been found on its slopes, and a fossil whale is preserved in the Bologna Archaeological Museum. Chestnuts, oaks, cypress and fir grow on the mountain, and Ephedra nebrodensis, a plant typical of Sicily and Sardinia, is found on its cliffs. Roe deer, wild boar, foxes and badgers are among its animals.

The city of San Marino stands on the ridge of the mountain, and its history dates from the early 4th century. According to legend a small monastery existed on the summit during the 8th century. The mountain's isolated location gave San Marino the seclusion that let it survive as a republic over many centuries. Saint Marinus is always represented holding Monte Titano in his hands.

In 2008 UNESCO inscribed the site under the combined title San Marino Historic Centre and Mount Titano, covering 55 hectares with a buffer zone of 167 hectares. The committee cited the continuity of a free republic since the Middle Ages. The site includes the fortification towers, walls, gates and bastions, the nineteenth-century Basilica di San Marino, convents of the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, the eighteenth-century Teatro Titano and the nineteenth-century Palazzo Pubblico. An urban network of roads links the fortresses, and the capital lies on the western side of the mountain.
montego-bay: Montego Bay lies on the north-west coast of Jamaica, in the parish of St. James. A broad valley runs down to the Caribbean Sea from the Bogue, Kempshot and Salem limestone hills, and the coastal plain is narrow. White sand beaches lie on the east side of the bay, with coral reefs to the north and south and mangrove swamps where the reefs give shelter. Christopher Columbus named the bay Golfo de Buen Tiempo, the Fair Weather Gulf. The name Montego Bay is believed to come from the Spanish word manteca, lard, because lard, leather and beef were exported from the port in the Spanish period.

Jamaica was a Spanish colony from 1511 until 1655, when Oliver Cromwell's Western Design expedition drove the Spanish out. The British then created the parish of St. James, and Montego Bay became the island's largest producer of sugar cane. From the mid-17th century until 1834 the town functioned mainly as a sugar port, and it remained one well into the 20th century.

The Christmas Rebellion, or Baptist War, of 1831 to 1832, the island's last major slave revolt, took place in and around the town. It set estates and plantations on fire and began a broader political push towards emancipation. The British took retribution and many were hanged, among them the leader Samuel Sharpe, who was hanged there in 1832. Sharpe was proclaimed a national hero of Jamaica in 1975, and the main square was renamed in his honour.

Emancipation began on 1 August 1834, with an apprenticeship system that lasted four years, and the town's sugar industry took a hit. It then expanded into exporting bananas and coffee. The town had lost any city status it held in the colonial period and was proclaimed a city again by act of parliament in 1980, though it remains part of the parish of St. James.

Montego Bay has a cruise terminal and free port, and Sangster International Airport lies within the city limits. Many resorts stand along the nearby coast, some on the grounds of old sugar plantations where original buildings and mills remain, such as Rose Hall. Part of the bay, almost sixteen square kilometres including Bogue Island, is set aside as the Montego Bay Marine Park. Most residents are of African descent, with minorities of East Indian and Chinese descent whose ancestors came as indentured servants in the 19th century.
montereau-fault-yonne: Montereau-Fault-Yonne, often called simply Montereau, stands on the confluence of the Yonne and the Seine, at the far south-east of the Île-de-France region, 70 km south-east of Paris. It lies about midway between Melun and Sens. The name describes its position: fault, also spelled faut, comes from the verb faillir in its old sense of to fall, since the Yonne falls into the Seine here. Until 1992 the name was written Montereau-Faut-Yonne. The rivers split the town in three, with the old town centre in the ville basse on the southern shore and Surville on the hill to the north.

In 1359 Charles II of Navarre, who held the town through his Champagne inheritance, lost it to the regent of France, the future Charles V. In September 1419 John the Fearless was killed on the town's bridge by Tanneguy du Chastel and the sire de Barbazan during a conference with the dauphin, who became Charles VII in 1422. An inscription on the bridge recalls the event. In 1420 Philip the Good, John's son, seized the town, which stayed for eight years in the hands of the Anglo-Burgundian coalition until Charles VII, helped by Jacques de Chabannes and Jean de Dunois, retook it after a long siege.

In 1567, during the Wars of Religion, Condé briefly seized it. In 1587 the inhabitants sided with the Catholic League, but in 1590 they accepted Henry IV as king. The Hôtel de Ville was commissioned in the mid-18th century, and on 14 February 1814 the town was the scene of one of Napoleon's last victories.

Surville is largely a group of high-rise buildings put up after World War II, and the old château park there is now the site of a school. The port and an industrial park lie on the east side between the two rivers, and the town has a strong industrial history. Its inhabitants are called Monterelais, and it is twinned with the British town of Otley. The collegiate church of Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Loup holds a sword long said to be John the Fearless's, though it is certainly more recent.
monterey-california: Monterey lies on the southern edge of Monterey Bay, in Monterey County on the Central Coast. The area was inhabited long before the Spanish by the Rumsen Ohlone, one of seven linguistically distinct Ohlone groups, who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering on the Monterey Peninsula. Sebastián Vizcaíno anchored in the bay on 16 December 1602 and named it Puerto de Monterrey, in honour of the Conde de Monterrey, then viceroy of New Spain. Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo had earlier called it the Bay of the Pines.

Despite these voyages and Spain's trade between Asia and Mexico, the Spanish did not make the bay a permanent harbour until the 18th century, since the harbour was too exposed to rough currents and winds. It was known for tall pines used to repair masts. The Spanish founded the Presidio of Monterey and a mission church. In 1777 Monterey became capital of the Province of the Californias, the administrative and military headquarters of Alta California and Baja California and their only official port of entry, and it stayed capital of the Mexican Department of the Californias after Mexican independence.

On 24 November 1818 the Argentine corsair Hippolyte Bouchard landed about 7 kilometres from the Presidio, under a letter of marque from the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. After Mexico became independent in 1821 the institutions of Alta California stayed much the same until the 1830s, when the secularisation of the missions turned mission pasture lands into private ranchos. In 1834 Agustín V. Zamorano brought a printing press to Monterey and founded the first print shop in California.

American forces seized the city in the Battle of Monterey in 1846 during the Mexican-American War, and it remained the capital of the American interim government of California until 1849. In 1849 Colton Hall, built by Walter Colton, hosted the first constitutional convention, where American and Californio delegates drafted California's first constitution in English and Spanish.

Monterey had 30,218 inhabitants at the 2020 census. In the late 19th century the town and its surroundings drew artists and writers, and an art colony formed. John Steinbeck's friends there included the marine biologist Ed Ricketts. The Monterey Jazz Festival began in 1958. Cannery Row and the Monterey Bay Aquarium stand on the north side of the Presidio, and the Defense Language Institute and the Naval Postgraduate School are in the city. California's First Theater, an adobe building begun in 1847, survives and is now closed.
monterrey: Monterrey stands 540 metres above sea level at the foothills of the Sierra Madre Oriental, in the northeastern state of Nuevo León. The Santa Catarina River, dry on the surface for most of the year, crosses the city from east to west. The city is named after Gaspar de Zúñiga, 5th Count of Monterrey, viceroy of New Spain from 1595 to 1603. Before the European foundation the area was home to nomadic indigenous groups, among them the Azalapas, Huachichiles, Coahuiltecos and Borrados.

The first expeditions, led by Alberto del Canto, named the place Santa Lucia, but the Spanish were attacked by the native people and fled. Luis Carvajal y de la Cueva negotiated with Philip II of Spain for a territory to be called Nuevo León, the New Kingdom of León, arrived in 1580 and in 1582 established a settlement called San Luis Rey de Francia within present-day Monterrey. Nuevo León was then abandoned for eight years, until a third expedition of 13 families led by Diego de Montemayor founded the Ciudad Metropolitana de Nuestra Señora de Monterrey in 1596.

After Mexican independence the city became a key economic centre, thanks to its ties with Europe through Tampico, with the United States through San Antonio and with the capital through Saltillo. In 1824 the New Kingdom of León became the State of Nuevo León, with Monterrey as its capital. The city was linked by railroad in the late 19th century, and a steel-producing company founded in 1900 accelerated its industrialisation.

Monterrey is the capital and largest city of Nuevo León, and its metropolitan area has more than five million inhabitants. It holds a leading place in steel, cement, glass, auto parts and brewing, and its economy has been tied closely to the United States border. It is home to the Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Education. In 1986 it hosted games of the FIFA World Cup, and in 2002 the United Nations Conference on Financing for Development adopted the Monterrey Consensus there.
montesquieu: Charles Louis de Secondat was born on 18 January 1689 at the Château de la Brède, 25 kilometres south of Bordeaux. His mother, an heiress who brought the Barony of La Brède to the family, died when he was seven. He attended the Catholic College of Juilly from 1700 to 1711, and in 1714 became a counsellor of the Bordeaux Parlement. In 1715 he married the Protestant Jeanne de Lartigue, and when his uncle, the Baron de Montesquieu, died in 1716 he inherited the title, the fortune and the office of président à mortier, which he held for twelve years.

The Persian Letters of 1721, a satire on contemporary French society as seen by two Persian visitors to Paris, was an instant success and was pirated at once. He went to Paris in 1722, sold his office in 1726 and was elected to the Académie Française in January 1728. He then toured Europe and stayed in England from the end of October 1729 until spring 1731, where he met Viscount Bolingbroke. In 1734 he published Considerations on the Causes of the Greatness of the Romans and their Decline.

The Spirit of Law appeared anonymously in 1748, and Thomas Nugent's English translation followed in 1750. It was received enthusiastically by many in France, but was denounced by the Sorbonne and, in 1751, placed on the Index of Prohibited Books by the Catholic Church. It was praised in Britain and the American colonies, where it influenced the Founding Fathers in drafting the United States Constitution.

In The Spirit of Law Montesquieu identifies three forms of government, each supported by a principle: monarchies rely on honour, republics on virtue and despotisms on fear. He held that in every state there are legislative, executive and judicial powers and that freedom is lost when the same person or body combines the legislative with the executive, or the power to judge with either. He also argued that climate and geography significantly influence individuals and laws, and called slavery inherently wrong because all humans are born equal. He died of a fever on 10 February 1755 and was buried in the Église Saint-Sulpice.
montevideo: Montevideo lies on the north shore of the Río de la Plata, the arm of the Atlantic Ocean that separates the south coast of Uruguay from the north coast of Argentina; Buenos Aires is 230 kilometres to the west on the Argentine side. The Bay of Montevideo forms a natural harbour, the largest in the country. The city's highest point is the peak of the Cerro de Montevideo, at 134 metres, crowned by a fortress. The name comes from this hill, though explanations of the second part differ: one holds that a sailor of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition cried out in Portuguese that he had seen a mount.

Portugal founded Colonia do Sacramento across the bay from Buenos Aires between 1680 and 1683, and met no resistance from the Spanish until 1723, when they began to fortify the heights around Montevideo Bay. On 22 November 1723 the Portuguese Field Marshal Manuel de Freitas da Fonseca built a fort there. Bruno Mauricio de Zabala, the Spanish governor of Buenos Aires, sent an expedition that forced the Portuguese to leave in 1724, and families from Buenos Aires and the Canary Islands settled. A census of 1724 counted more than 100 families of Galician and Canary Islands origin, more than 1,000 indigenous people, mostly Guaraní, and some enslaved people of Bantu origin.

No official document establishes the foundation, but Zabala's diary gives the date as 24 December 1726. The city won full independence from Buenos Aires only on 1 January 1730. It was briefly under British rule in 1807 before Spanish criollos, who had defeated the British invasions of the River Plate, retook it. From 1828 it belonged to Uruguay. By 1880 its population had quadrupled, mainly through European immigration.

Montevideo is the capital and largest city of Uruguay, with 1,287,452 people in the city proper in the 2023 census, about 36.8 per cent of the country's population. It is the country's chief port and its centre of commerce and higher education, and its University of the Republic was founded on 18 July 1849. It hosted every match of the first FIFA World Cup in 1930. Uruguayan tango originated in its neighbourhoods towards the end of the 1800s.
montgomery-alabama: Montgomery stands beside the Alabama River on the Gulf Coastal Plain, on rolling terrain about 220 feet above sea level. Downtown lies along the southern bank of the river, about 6 miles downstream from the confluence of the Coosa and Tallapoosa rivers. The city was named for Richard Montgomery, a major-general of the Continental Army. The Alabama State Capitol stands on a hill at one end of Dexter Avenue, on which also lies the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, where Martin Luther King Jr. was pastor. Both are National Historic Landmarks.

Before European colonisation the east bank of the Alabama River was inhabited by the Alibamu, who with the Coushatta on the west side were descended from the Mississippian culture. Both spoke closely related Muskogean languages. The present city stands on the site of two Alibamu towns: Ikanatchati, meaning red earth, and Towassa, built on a bluff. Hernando de Soto and his expedition passed through Ikanatchati in 1540 and camped for a week at Towassa.

Montgomery was incorporated in 1819 as a merger of two towns on the river. In 1846 it replaced Tuscaloosa as the state capital, a change that reflected the shift of power to south-central Alabama as cotton grew in the Black Belt and Mobile rose as a port. In 1840 Montgomery County led the state in cotton production, and by 1911 the city processed 160,000 to 200,000 bales a year. In February 1861 Montgomery was chosen the first capital of the Confederate States of America, until the seat of government moved to Richmond, Virginia, in May. In the middle of the 20th century it was a major centre of the civil rights movement, including the Montgomery bus boycott and the Selma to Montgomery marches.

Montgomery is the capital of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County, with a population of 200,603 at the 2020 census. The governor's office, the Alabama Legislature and the Alabama Supreme Court are located there. Maxwell Air Force Base gives it a large military presence. Its civil rights history is commemorated at the Legacy Museum, the Civil Rights Memorial and the National Memorial for Peace and Justice.
montmartre: Montmartre is a hill 130 metres high in the 18th arrondissement of Paris, on the Right Bank. Its name may come from Mons Martis, the Mount of Mars, where temples of Mars and Mercury are said to have stood, or from Mons Martyrum, the Mount of the Martyrs, a reinterpretation recorded by the abbot Hilduin. There is no consensus, and both explanations are considered valid. The hill was occupied from at least Gallo-Roman times, and the remains of Roman baths from the 2nd century were found in the 17th century.

Hilduin's Miracles of Saint-Denis, written before 885, told how Saint Denis was beheaded on the hilltop in 250 for preaching the Christian faith. In 1134 King Louis VI bought the Merovingian chapel, built the church of Saint-Pierre de Montmartre and founded the Royal Abbey of Montmartre, a Benedictine house whose lands covered most of the hill. The abbey was destroyed in 1790, and its last abbess was guillotined in 1794. Mills were built on the western slope from 1529, and gypsum was mined on the hill from Roman times until 1860, leaving tunnels beneath it that required a foundation 40 metres deep for the Sacré-Cœur. Montmartre was annexed to Paris on 1 January 1860.

In the Franco-Prussian War the French army stored cannons on the summit. On 18 March 1871 soldiers who tried to remove them were blocked by the Paris National Guard, who captured and killed two generals and set up a revolutionary government, the Paris Commune, that lasted two months. The army retook the heights at the end of May in the Semaine Sanglante, or Bloody Week. The Basilica of the Sacré-Cœur, built from 1876 to 1919 and paid for by public subscription, was meant as an act of expiation for the suffering of France in that war.

The cabarets Le Chat Noir, founded in 1881, and the Moulin Rouge, founded in 1889, drew crowds to the hill, and between 1872 and 1914 Renoir, Picasso, Modigliani, van Gogh and many others lived and worked there for its low rents. Picasso painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in the Bateau-Lavoir, and most of the artists left for Montparnasse after the First World War. Montmartre is now an officially designated historic district of 60 hectares with limited development, and it keeps a small vineyard. The Musée de Montmartre and the Espace Dalí are among its museums.
montreal: Montreal lies in the southwest of the province of Quebec. The city covers most of the Island of Montreal, at the confluence of the Saint Lawrence and Ottawa Rivers, between the Saint Lawrence to the south and the Rivière des Prairies to the north. It is 196 km east of Ottawa and 258 km southwest of Quebec City. Its port lies at one end of the Saint Lawrence Seaway, the river gateway that stretches from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic. The most prominent feature of the island is Mount Royal, a mountain with three heads that rises 232 metres above sea level.

Archaeological evidence shows that First Nations peoples occupied the island as early as 4,000 years ago. By the year 1000 they had begun to cultivate maize, and within a few hundred years they had built fortified villages. The Saint Lawrence Iroquoians, a group distinct from the Haudenosaunee of present-day New York, established the village of Hochelaga at the foot of Mount Royal two centuries before the French arrived. The French explorer Jacques Cartier visited Hochelaga on 2 October 1535 and estimated its people at over a thousand. In the Mohawk language the land is called Tiohtià:ke, loosely where the group divided; in Ojibwe it is Mooniyaang, the first stopping place in the Ojibwe migration story.

Settlers from La Flèche in the Loire Valley founded the town in 1642 as Ville Marie, named for the Virgin Mary. The present name is generally thought to derive from Mount Royal, since réal and royal were used interchangeably in 16th-century French. Another explanation points to the Venetian geographer Giovanni Battista Ramusio, who wrote Monte Real on his 1556 map, but the Commission de toponymie du Québec disputes it. For over a century and a half Montreal was the industrial and financial centre of Canada, and Toronto surpassed it in population and economic strength in the 1970s.

French is the official language of Montreal, which is the largest primarily French speaking city in the Americas and one of the most bilingual in Canada. The city is divided into 19 boroughs, many of which were independent cities until a municipal reorganization in January 2002. It holds 50 National Historic Sites of Canada, more than any other city, many of them factories, warehouses and mills from its industrial past. Montreal hosted the 1967 International and Universal Exposition and the 1976 Summer Olympics, and is the headquarters of the International Civil Aviation Organization.
montu: Montu was a falcon war god of the ancient Egyptian religion, an embodiment of the conquering vitality of the pharaoh, worshipped particularly in Upper Egypt and the district of Thebes. His name, transcribed as mntw, means nomad, and is also rendered Mont, Month, Monthu or Menthu. A very ancient god, he was originally a manifestation of the scorching effect of the sun god Ra and often appeared as Montu-Ra. The destructiveness of that trait gave him the character of a warrior, and he became a widely revered god of war. The Egyptians thought he attacked the enemies of Maat, the cosmic order, while inspiring glorious warlike exploits.

In art Montu appears as a falcon-headed or bull-headed man whose head is surmounted by the solar disk, with one or two uraei and two feathers. He may carry a curved sword, a spear, a bow and arrows or knives. Raging bulls were associated with strength and war, and Montu was believed to manifest himself as the white, black-snouted bull Buchis, a living animal revered at Armant with dozens of servants. His consorts included the Theban goddesses Tjenenyet and Iunit and Raet-Tawy, a female form of Ra. The Greeks associated him with Ares, though he was also assimilated to Apollo.

The kings of the 11th Dynasty chose Montu as protective and dynastic deity, and four of them were called Mentuhotep, 'Montu is satisfied'. Their conquests reunified Egypt around 2055 BCE and ended the First Intermediate Period. In the Middle Kingdom Montu assumed the role of supreme god, before Amun of Thebes gradually surpassed him. Later rulers claimed his strength. Thutmose III was described as a a valiant Montu on the battlefield, and Ramesses II called himself Montu of the Two Lands and was said to have raged at the enemy at Kadesh like Montu, Lord of Thebes.

Temples to him stood at Medamud, where Senusret III built a complex that housed the living Buchis bull, and at Armant, where Mentuhotep II is the first known builder. The Armant temple was enlarged under later dynasties and was demolished in 1861 to supply material for a sugar factory. Amenhotep III built a sacred enclosure to Montu at Karnak.
monza: Monza lies on the Lambro river, about 15 kilometres north-north-east of Milan, in the central part of the Po Valley. Its Latin name was Modoetia. Medieval tradition explains it with a legend: the Lombard queen Theodelinda, resting by the Lambro, dreamt of a dove, a symbol of the Holy Spirit, that said modo, here, and she replied etiam, yes, accepting the sign to found a church on the site.

The area was inhabited from at least the Bronze Age. The Roman conquest of the Insubrian territory took place in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. After 476 northern Italy passed to Odoacer and then, in 493, to the Ostrogoths under Theodoric the Great. Monza gained documented political and religious importance under the Lombards. In 589 the Bavarian princess Theodelinda, daughter of Duke Garibald I, married the Lombard king Authari, and after his death in 590 she married Agilulf, duke of Turin, who was elected king. The couple used Milan as one of the principal centres of the kingdom and made Monza a royal residence.

In the Carolingian and later centuries Monza remained linked to the institutions of kingship in Italy, and its cathedral chapter, treasury and school gave it symbolic importance beyond its size. From the 11th century it was drawn into the orbit of Milan, and after the Visconti defeated the Della Torre at the Battle of Desio in 1277 the city became progressively subject to Milan. The Treaties of Utrecht in 1713 and Rastatt in 1714 confirmed the passage of the Duchy of Milan from Spanish to Austrian Habsburg control. Monza was part of the Cisalpine Republic and later of Napoleonic Italy, returned to Austrian rule in 1815 and was granted the title of city in 1816.

After Italian unification textile manufacturing, mechanical engineering and electrical production grew alongside traditional crafts. On 29 July 1900 the anarchist Gaetano Bresci shot King Umberto I of Italy at close range after a public event organised by the sports society Forti e Liberi; the king died shortly afterwards at the Royal Villa.

Monza is the capital of the Province of Monza and Brianza, with a population of 123,672. The cathedral houses the Iron Crown of Lombardy, a medieval relic traditionally associated with the coronation of the kings of Italy, among them Charlemagne. The Royal Villa adjoins Monza Park, one of the largest enclosed urban parks in Europe, and the Monza Circuit has long hosted the Italian Grand Prix.
monzon: Monzón lies at the confluence of the Cinca and Sosa rivers, in the Cinca Medio comarca of the province of Huesca. The earliest evidence of continuous human occupation comes from Neolithic remains at the Sosiles Altos and Peña Lucas sites, and most traces of settlement date from the Bronze Age, when the Ilergetes are believed to have lived between the Cinca, Sosa and Clamor. After the defeat of the Ilergetes in the 3rd century BCE the area was brought under Roman rule from the 2nd century BCE, and Monzón became a junction connecting Caesaraugusta and Osca with Italy.

Under Muslim rule Monzón was disputed between the Banu Sabrit of Huesca and the Banu Qasi of Zaragoza, and in the 11th century it passed to the Banu Hud. El Cid took it in 1083. The Christian kingdoms wanted it in order to cut communications between the taifa kingdoms of Zaragoza and Lleida. Sancho Ramírez created a so-called Kingdom of Monzón for his son Peter before Peter came to the throne of Aragon. Control was lost and regained several times between 1126 and 1141, and in 1143 the town came under the Knights Templar.

The Knights Templar made Monzón a major stronghold between the Segre and Cinca valleys, and the Teutonic Knights kept a commandery there from 1222. After Peter II of Aragon died at the Battle of Muret in 1213, the Knights Templar of Monzón acted as guardians and tutors to the young James I. When Pope Clement V dissolved the order, Monzón resisted, but the castle fell in 1309 and passed to the Knights Hospitaller in 1317. In 1109 Urraca of Castile married Alfonso I of Aragon at Monzón.

In 1626 Cardinal Richelieu and the Count-Duke of Olivares signed the Treaty of Monzón, which ended the conflict over the Valtellina. During the Catalan Revolt Franco-Catalan forces took the town in 1642 and Castilian troops retook it the following year. The castle was again held by the French in the Peninsular War and was recaptured by Spanish forces under General Copons in 1814.

Monzón had 17,176 inhabitants in 2014. Industry began in the early 20th century with a sugar factory, and further factories arrived after the Spanish Civil War. The Aragon and Catalonia Canal, which crosses the Sosa on the viaduct known as the Siphon of the Sosa, supplies irrigation, and road and rail links join the town to Zaragoza, Lleida and Barcelona. Places of interest include the castle of the Knights Templar, the Romanesque Cathedral of Santa María del Romeral and the 17th-century Shrine of the Virgin of Joy. Among its natives are the writer Ignacio de Luzán and the intellectual Joaquín Costa.
moorea: Moʼorea lies 17 kilometres northwest of Tahiti and is about 16 kilometres across. Tahiti and Moʼorea are the largest of the Windward Islands in the Society Islands. The name means 'yellow lizard' in Tahitian, and an older name is ʼAimeho. It formed as a shield volcano 1.5 to 2.5 million years ago from the hotspot responsible for all the Society Islands, and a coral reef now encircles it, forming a lagoon. Two nearly symmetrical bays cut the north shore, Cook's Bay, also called Pao Pao Bay, and Ōpūnohu Bay. Charles Darwin, looking at the island from a peak on Tahiti, found in the encircling barrier reef inspiration for his theory of how coral atolls form, calling it a 'picture in a frame'.

The Society Islands were probably settled from Samoa and Tonga around 200 CE. On Moʼorea nine tribal principalities emerged in the enclosed valleys, each divided into clans, with an elite that combined political and religious power. Its leading families stayed linked by marriage and kinship with those of Tahiti for centuries, which brought alliances and at times bloody conflicts. Research in the Ōpūnohu Valley, begun by Kenneth P. Emory in the 1920s and continued by Roger C. Green in the 1960s, traces the change: little stratification before 1000 CE, terraces and a hierarchical society in the Atiroʼo period (1000–1650), then the Marama period (1650–1788), when the Marama chiefs united the valley's clans and built large step-pyramid marae.

Pedro Fernandes de Queirós sighted the island in 1606, and Domingo de Bonechea named it Santo Domingo in 1774. James Cook arrived in October 1777, and the first contact with Europeans there is said to have begun when one of his goats was stolen. After negotiations failed, two armed parties went ashore to burn houses and boats, and the goat was returned. Cook first landed in Ōpūnohu Bay, and Cook's Bay was later named after him. Near Afareaitu, the Marae Umarea, built around 900 CE, is the oldest worship platform.

The island forms the commune of Moʼorea-Maiʼao, with ʼĀfareaitu as its main village, and had 17,718 inhabitants in 2017. Most of the population is Christian. Tourism has been the main income since the 1960s, after an American company built the first luxury hotel in 1961. The University of California, Berkeley, runs the Richard B. Gump research station on Cook's Bay, and a French research centre works at Ōpūnohu Bay on coral reefs. Tahiti is reached by ferry to Vaiʼare or by a flight of about five minutes.
morava-river: The Morava rises on the slope of the Králický Sněžník mountain at an elevation of 1,371 m, close to the border with Poland. Its total length is 352 km, of which 269.4 km lie in the Czech Republic, and it carries an average of 110 cubic metres of water a second from a drainage area of 26,658 square kilometres. It is a lowland river and, unusually for Europe, a blackwater river. Its valley forms the Upper Morava Valley and the Lower Morava Valley in Moravia, the Marchfeld in Lower Austria and the Záhorie Lowland in Slovakia, which together make up a large part of the Vienna Basin.

Olomouc, Kroměříž, Otrokovice, Uherské Hradiště, Veselí nad Moravou and Hodonín stand on the river, and Brno lies within its basin. The Thaya, its longest tributary, joins it at the tripoint of the Czech Republic, Austria and Slovakia. The river enters the Danube just below Devín Castle on the outskirts of Bratislava.

The root of the name, mor-, comes from a Proto-Indo-European word for water or marsh. The river was first recorded as Maraha in a deed of 892, while the oldest record of the land of Moravia, from 822, is older than that of the river. The German name March derives from the Slavic one.

People have lived on the banks for a very long time: Stillfried, on the Austrian side, had a settlement 30,000 years ago, and farming began in the valley about 7,000 years ago. Below the confluence with the Thaya the river is one of the oldest national boundaries still in use in continental Europe. Around 800 it was the eastern boundary of the Carolingian Empire with the Avar Khaganate, and from the 10th century it divided the imperial marcha orientalis, later the Duchy of Austria, from the Kingdom of Hungary. In the Cold War it formed part of the Iron Curtain between Austria and Czechoslovakia.

The river links the Danube valley with the plains of northern Europe. Its gentle slope makes it meander and flood, and its floodplains are among the most biologically diverse in Europe, with some 12,000 species recorded. Much of the river, especially downstream from Litovel, was regulated in the 20th century, with the loss of floodplain. The central part has kept much of its natural character.
moravia: Moravia is one of the three historical Czech lands, with Bohemia and Czech Silesia, and takes its name from the Morava river. Its largest city and historical capital is Brno. Olomouc served as the capital until the Swedish army sacked it in the Thirty Years' War, and it is still the seat of an archdiocese. The depression between the Bohemian Massif and the Outer Western Carpathians gives an easy link between the Danubian and Polish regions, in a Central Europe where highlands otherwise make north-south movement difficult.

Human presence goes back more than 600,000 years at Stránská skála, and the Venus of Dolní Věstonice is the oldest ceramic figure in the world. Around 60 BCE the Celtic Volcae withdrew and were succeeded by the Germanic Quadi. Slavs established themselves in the 6th century, and a Moravian Principality became Great Moravia in 833 through the conquest of the Principality of Nitra. Rastislav, who ruled from 846 to 870, asked the Byzantine emperor Michael for missionaries, and the result was the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius, who translated liturgical books into Slavonic. Great Moravia reached its largest extent in the 890s under Svatopluk I and ended when the Magyars overran it in 907.

After 955 Boleslaus I of Bohemia took control of Moravia, and in 1055 Bretislaus decreed that Bohemia and Moravia would be inherited together. After 1526 Ferdinand I of Austria ruled it as part of the Crown of Bohemia, and tension grew between the Habsburg rulers and the Protestant Moravian nobility. After 1918 it belonged to Czechoslovakia, and in 1928 it was merged with Czech Silesia. The Munich Agreement of 1938 gave German-speaking border areas to Nazi Germany, and Moravia as a land was dissolved in 1948.

Moravia lies in the east of the Czech Republic and has about 3.0 million of its inhabitants. It holds 94 per cent of the country's vineyards. Until the expulsions after 1945, significant parts of Moravia were German-speaking.
moravian-church: The Moravian Church traces its heritage to 1457 and the Lands of the Bohemian Crown, which included Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia. Its roots lie in the Hussite movement begun by Jan Hus in early 15th-century Bohemia. Hus objected to some practices and doctrines of the Roman Catholic Church: he wanted the liturgy in Czech, priests allowed to marry, and indulgences and the idea of Purgatory done away with. Because these actions predate the Protestant Reformation by a century, some historians claim the Moravian Church was the first Protestant church.

Under the Habsburg rulers the Counter-Reformation pressed on the Protestants of the Bohemian lands. The Jesuits were invited to found Roman Catholic schools, among them the university in the Moravian capital of Olomouc, and in 1582 they forced the closure of local Protestant schools.

In 1722 a small group of the Bohemian Brethren, called the Hidden Seed, arrived at the Berthelsdorf estate of Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf in present-day Saxony. They had lived in northern Moravia for nearly a hundred years as an illegal underground remnant in the Catholic setting of the Habsburg Empire. Their leader, the itinerant carpenter Christian David, asked that they be allowed to settle on Zinzendorf's lands in Upper Lusatia. Zinzendorf, a nobleman raised in the traditions of Pietistic Lutheranism, agreed out of a personal commitment to helping the poor and needy. The community they founded was Herrnhut, which gave the church its German name, Herrnhuter Brüdergemeine.

The church soon became a missionary movement. Together with the Royal Danish Mission College, its missionaries formed the first large-scale Protestant missionary effort, and the first were sent out when Herrnhut had only 300 inhabitants. Within thirty years hundreds had gone to the Caribbean, North and South America, the Arctic, Africa and the Far East. The Moravians were the first to send lay people as missionaries and the first Protestant denomination to minister to slaves, though some of their communities also owned slaves.

The church teaches the necessity of the New Birth, a personal conversion to Christ, together with piety, evangelism and good works. Its emblem is the Lamb of God with the flag of victory, and its motto runs: In essentials, unity; in nonessentials, liberty; and in all things, love. Bishops serve as spiritual leaders rather than administrators, and the church holds that it has preserved apostolic succession.
morbihan: Morbihan is one of the original 83 departments created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution. It was formed from part of the Province of Brittany and takes its name from the Morbihan, the enclosed 'small sea' in Breton that is the principal feature of its coastline. The Carnac stones, the megalithic alignments of Carnac, stand in the department and are noted as older and more extensive than Stonehenge in Wiltshire.

In 1945 cadets of the École Spéciale Militaire de Saint-Cyr, France's foremost military academy for officers, were relocated to Camp Coëtquidan at Guer. The camp was later developed to include the École militaire interarmes, for non-commissioned officers, and the École Militaire du Corps Technique et Administratif, so that three major military educational facilities now stand at Guer.

The department lies in the northwest of France and is bounded by Finistère, Côtes-d'Armor, Ille-et-Vilaine and Loire-Atlantique, with the Atlantic Ocean to the southwest. The Gulf of Morbihan holds many islands, 365 according to legend, though in fact there are between 30 and 40 depending on how they are counted, as well as islets too small for any development. All but two of them, l'Île-aux-Moines and l'Île-d'Arz, are privately owned.

Outside the gulf the department has four further inhabited islands: Belle Île, Groix, Houat and Hoëdic. Meaban, just outside the Port du Crouesty, is an ornithological reserve that visitors may not enter. The most populous commune is Lorient, and the prefecture, Vannes, is the second.

Many residents support the maintenance and use of the Breton language, and there are numerous advocates of bilingual education. The painter Raymond Wintz (1884–1956) depicted places around the Gulf of Morbihan.
mordvins: Mordvins is the official term used in Russia and the Soviet Union since 1928 for both the Erzya and the Moksha. The Mordvins do not use it as a self-designation, and when they speak of themselves as a whole they say Erzya and Moksha. The name is thought to come from an Iranian word, mard, meaning man. Possible early mentions include the Mordens in Jordanes' Getica and a land called Mordia in the De Administrando Imperio of Constantine VII, and the Russian Primary Chronicle names the Mordva in the 11th century.

Researchers distinguish the ancestors of the Erzya and the Moksha from the mid-1st century CE by the orientation of burials, costume and bronze jewellery. The two peoples did not intermarry before their conversion to Christianity.

The ancient Mordvins met the Bulgars around the 7th century and later paid tribute to Volga Bulgaria. In the 13th century the Mongols conquered the region and incorporated the Mordvins into the Golden Horde. In the late 14th century the Principality of Moscow took much of the western Mordvin lands, while the east was held by the Kazan Khanate. When Russia conquered the Kazan Khanate in 1552, all Mordvins became Russian subjects.

Under Russian rule the Mordvins suffered forced conversion to Christianity, displacement, migration and an influx of Russian settlers, which made them a minority in their own area. In the 17th century the Mordvins, Chuvash and Mari rose against Russian rule. After the revolt was suppressed many Mordvins fled east beyond the Volga, and those who stayed became serfs. Assimilation to Russian culture was rapid until a Mordvin nationalism appeared in the late 19th century. The Mordvins received an autonomous territory in the Soviet Union in 1928, but Russification intensified in the 1930s, and by the 1950s knowledge of their languages was declining rapidly.

The two Mordvinic languages, Erzya and Moksha, belong to the Uralic family and have about 275,000 native speakers together. They are not mutually intelligible, so Russian is often used between the groups. Their literary forms were standardised in 1922 and 1923, and both are written in the Russian alphabet. Both are official languages of Mordovia alongside Russian.

The Erzya and Moksha have no common mythology. In Erzya belief the gods hatched from an egg, with Ange Patiai as the mother of gods and the sun god Chipaz after her. In Moksha belief the supreme god is Viarde Skai. Many Mordvins also live outside Mordovia, in the Volga region and Siberia. The Erzya now practise Christianity and a native religion, and the Mordvins are known as skilled beekeepers.
morelos: Morelos is landlocked and borders Mexico City to the north, the State of México to the northeast and northwest, Puebla to the east and Guerrero to the southwest. It is the second-smallest state of Mexico after Tlaxcala and has 36 municipalities. The region is a basin into which abundant water flows, and most of it has a warm climate year-round, suited to sugar cane and other crops. Visitors from the Valley of Mexico have come to it since Aztec times.

The first known inhabitants, from about 6000 BCE, were nomadic hunters and gatherers. After the Spanish arrived, agriculture shifted from maize and cotton to sugar cane and its refining in nearby mills, a system that remained largely intact until the Mexican Revolution. Conditions on the sugar plantations made Miguel Hidalgo's call to arms welcome, and rebellions began in 1811. José María Morelos y Pavón took over after Hidalgo's execution. In 1812 he and his men held Cuautla for 58 days under royalist siege, an early vital success; he was captured and executed in 1815. In 1869 President Benito Juárez separated the territory from the State of México and named it in his honour.

The state was ready for the Mexican Revolution. Emiliano Zapata, born at Anenecuilco, led its best-known movement. His victory in the Battle of Cuautla, 11 to 19 May 1911, brought about the abdication of Porfirio Díaz. After Francisco Madero's election, Zapata, feeling betrayed, called with his followers for agrarian reform in the Plan de Ayala. The motto Tierra y Libertad was first used by Ricardo Flores Magón in 1910.

Cuernavaca, about 90 km south of Mexico City, is the capital and is called the City of the Eternal Spring. It has the Palacio de Cortés, which now holds Diego Rivera's mural History of Morelos, Conquest and Revolution. The state is also home to Xochicalco and to the Monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl, a World Heritage Site.
morioka: Morioka lies in the Kitakami Basin in central Iwate Prefecture, at the confluence of the Kitakami, the Shizukuishi and the Nakatsu. The Kitakami is the longest river in the Tōhoku region and the second largest on the Pacific side of Japan, after the Tone. It runs through the city from north to south. The active volcano Mount Iwate dominates the view to the north-west, and Mount Himekami lies to the north. The climate is cold and humid, with warm, short summers and long winters with heavy snowfall.

The area has been inhabited continuously since the Japanese Paleolithic, and tombs and remains of the Jōmon, Yayoi and Kofun periods have been found. The Emishi lived there into the Heian period. In 803 Sakanoue no Tamuramaro was ordered to Shiwa Castle, a military centre meant to extend imperial rule over Mutsu Province. The area was later ruled by the Abe clan until its destruction in the Former Nine Years War by the Minamoto and Kiyohara clans, and then by the Ōshū Fujiwara of Hiraizumi, until Minamoto no Yoritomo destroyed them at the start of the Kamakura period.

Several samurai clans disputed the region until the Nanbu clan, based at Sannohe to the north, expanded its territory in the Sengoku period and built Kozukata Castle. After the Battle of Sekigahara and the formal recognition of Morioka Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate, the castle was renamed Morioka Castle, and the town's name was rewritten from 森岡 to 盛岡, both read Morioka. During the Boshin War the domain was a key member of the pro-Tokugawa Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei.

The domain became Morioka Prefecture in 1870 and part of Iwate Prefecture in 1872. The city was established as the prefectural capital on 1 April 1889, and a railway joined it to Tokyo in 1890. It came through the Second World War with little damage, having suffered only two minor air raids.

The city had a population of 283,981 in August 2023. The site of Morioka Castle and the ruins of Shiwa Castle are National Historic Site, and the Bank of Iwate Red Brick Building is an Important Cultural Property. The Rock-Breaking Cherry Tree is a natural monument. Hōon-ji, a Sōtō Zen temple moved to Morioka by the Nanbu lords, holds statues of the 500 Rakan, among them figures of Kublai Khan and Marco Polo. Local dishes include jajamen, reimen and wanko soba.
moriscos: Muslims had lived in Spain since the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in the eighth century. By the end of the fifteenth century the Muslim population was estimated at 500,000 to 600,000 out of a Spanish population of 7 to 8 million, about half of them in the former Emirate of Granada, which surrendered to Catholic forces in 1492. The Treaty of Granada first guaranteed the Muslims their rights, but efforts at conversion, first by Archbishop Hernando de Talavera and then more forcefully by Cardinal Cisneros, led Granada's Muslims to rebel in 1499. The revolt lasted until early 1501, and the treaty's protections were abandoned.

In 1502 the Catholic Monarchs outlawed the practice of Islam, and Muslims in Castile had to accept baptism or go into exile. In Valencia, a revolt of Christian brotherhoods in the 1520s forced Muslims to become Christians, and King Charles V upheld those conversions and ordered the rest of the Muslims to convert. The label morisco appeared in texts in the first half of the sixteenth century. In their own texts the Moriscos more often called themselves simply Muslims.

Moriscos were a majority in some places, such as Hornachos, but elsewhere they lived among Old Christians. They made up about 20 per cent of the population of Aragon, where they did not speak Arabic and were allowed by their lords to practise their faith relatively openly. Many Moriscos became devout Christians, while others held on to Islam in secret. A legal opinion known as the Oran fatwa allowed them to conform outwardly to Christianity when necessary for survival while keeping their faith inwardly.

The Spanish crown mistrusted the Moriscos and feared they would support invasions from the Ottoman Empire. At the urging of the Duke of Lerma and Archbishop Juan de Ribera, Philip III expelled them between 1609, from Aragon, and 1614, from Castile, ordering them to leave on pain of death and to take nothing but what they could carry. Contemporary accounts give between 270,000 and 300,000 expelled, about 4 per cent of the Spanish population, most of them from the Crown of Aragon and above all from Valencia.

Most of the expelled settled on the western edge of the Ottoman Empire and in Morocco. The Hornacheros, who left Castile armed, founded the Corsair Republic of Bou Regreg and Salé in Morocco. Morisco mercenaries in the service of the Moroccan sultan, armed with arquebuses, crossed the Sahara and conquered Timbuktu in 1591, and their descendants formed the Arma. Historians agree that many more Moriscos avoided expulsion than was once thought, though the numbers are not known. The last mass prosecution of Moriscos for secret Islamic practice took place at Granada in 1727.
morocco: Morocco has coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, and covers about 446,300 km2. The Atlas Mountains run along the centre and south, the Rif Mountains lie in the north, and both ranges are mainly inhabited by Berber people. Most of the southeast lies in the Sahara Desert and is sparsely populated. The capital is Rabat, beside the Oued Bou Regreg River, and the largest city is the port of Casablanca. The English name Morocco comes from the Spanish Marruecos, itself derived from the name of Marrakesh, the capital of the Almoravid dynasty, the Almohad Caliphate and the Saadian dynasty.

People have lived in the region since the Paleolithic. Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud were dated to roughly 315,000 years ago. At Oued Beht a Neolithic farming society of 3400–2900 BCE formed the largest known agricultural complex in Africa outside the Nile Valley at that time. Phoenicians later established trading colonies, the most substantial being Chellah, Lixus and Mogador.

The Moroccan state traces its origins to the Idrisid dynasty founded by Idris I in 788. It reached its height as a regional power in the 11th and 12th centuries under the Berber Almoravid and Almohad dynasties, which controlled the southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula and the Maghreb. In the 15th and 16th centuries Portugal seized some territory, but the Marinid and Saadi dynasties resisted foreign domination, and Morocco was the only North African nation to escape Ottoman rule. The Alawi dynasty, which still reigns, seized power in 1631. France and Spain established protectorates in 1912, and Morocco regained independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V.

Morocco is a unitary semi-constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament of two chambers, and the 2011 constitutional reforms reduced the king's executive powers and enlarged the prime minister's. The king remains Commander of the Faithful and holds wide powers over the military, foreign policy and religious affairs. The population was about 37 million in the 2024 census. Arabic and Tamazight are the official languages, and Islam is the official religion.
morogoro: Morogoro lies in eastern Tanzania, about 196 kilometres west of Dar es Salaam, and is the capital of the Morogoro Region. The city stands at the foothills of the Uluguru Mountains and is a significant agricultural centre, with many sisal plantations around it. Its climate is warm and tropical, with hot days and cool nights. Informally it is sometimes called Mji kasoro bahari, which translates as the city short of an ocean or port.

The Mindu Dam on the Ngerengere River, begun in 1978, supplies about 80 per cent of the city's water. It has been controversial: the reservoir has raised rates of bilharzia infection, mining runoff has polluted the water with mercury, and deforestation nearby has increased sedimentation and reduced the dam's capacity.

Morogoro has many educational institutions. The Sokoine University of Agriculture is based there, together with the Muslim University of Morogoro, St. Joseph University College, Jordan University College, the Ardhi Institute, a teachers college and the Livestock Training Institute. Kilakala Girls High School, formerly Marian College, is one of the oldest secondary schools in the country, and the Morogoro International School, teaching in English, was established in 1975.

The city has a musical heritage. The Morogoro Jazz Band was established in 1944, and Salim Abdullah, founder of the Cuban Marimba Band, came from Morogoro. From the mid-1960s to the 1970s it was the home of Mbaraka Mwinshehe, a highly influential lead guitarist and singer-songwriter. The football club Mtibwa Sugar represents it in the Tanzanian Premier League. Local transport includes buses called dala dalas, motorcycles known as boda bodas and three-wheeled Bajaj vehicles. On 10 August 2019 a fuel tanker exploded in the town, killing 100 people.
morse-code: Early in the 19th century, European experimenters made progress with electrical signalling, using static electricity and Voltaic piles. The simple on-or-off nature of the signals made it desirable to find a way of sending natural language with only electrical pulses and the silence between them. Samuel Morse's first proposal for a telegraph code was replaced by an alphabet-based code developed by Alfred Vail, which was used for commercial telegraphy in North America.

Friedrich Gerke's 1848 proposal, the Hamburg alphabet, did away with the different-length dashes and spaces of American Morse, leaving two elements, the dot and the dash. It was first used between Hamburg and Cuxhaven. Gerke changed nearly half the alphabet and all of the numerals.

In International Morse, a dah lasts three times as long as a dit. The space between elements equals one dit, between letters three dits and between words seven. Vail designed his code so that the length of each symbol was roughly the inverse of the frequency of its letter in English, which is why E is a single dit. International Morse was standardised by the International Telegraph Convention in Paris on 17 May 1865, which formed the International Telegraph Union. Vail's version, known as American Morse or railroad code, remained in use only for land-line telegraphy in the United States and Canada.

In the original telegraph the receiver's armature clicked as it marked a paper tape. Operators soon learned to translate the clicks directly into dots and dashes, which made the tape unnecessary. In the 1890s Morse began to be used extensively for early radio, before voice could be transmitted, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries most high-speed international communication used it on telegraph lines, undersea cables and radio circuits. Radiotelegraphy was vital in the Second World War.

The final commercial Morse transmission in the United States took place on 12 July 1999, signing off with Morse's 1844 message, What hath God wrought. Radio amateurs still use it, and radio navigation aids broadcast their identities in it.
moruroa: Moruroa, also spelled Mururoa, is an atoll in the Tuamotu Archipelago of French Polynesia, about 1,250 kilometres south-east of Tahiti, and is part of the commune of Tureia. The first recorded visit was by Commander Philip Carteret on HMS Swallow in 1767, who named it Bishop of Osnaburgh Island. The British whaler Matilda was wrecked there in 1792. The atoll was not continuously inhabited: Frederick William Beechey found it empty in 1826, and a visiting ship in 1834 killed all but three of the inhabitants it found. Copra workers lived there briefly in the late nineteenth century and again in 1942 to 1943 and 1950 to 1952.

France established the atoll as a nuclear test site on 21 September 1962, and construction began in May 1963, with the atoll of Hao as a support base. The first test, Aldebaran, a plutonium fission bomb exploded in the lagoon, took place on 2 July 1966 despite objections from about 30 members of the Polynesian Territorial Assembly. President Charles de Gaulle was present for a test on 10 September 1966. Forty-one atmospheric tests were conducted between 1966 and 1974, after which France moved underground amid intense world pressure, to which New Zealand contributed by sending two frigates in July 1973.

The underground tests cracked the atoll and raised fears that radioactive material would escape. On 25 July 1979 a device stuck halfway down its 800-metre shaft was detonated at half the usual depth, causing a large submarine landslide, a tsunami and a crack two kilometres long. New tests on 5 September and 2 October 1995 caused worldwide protests, an embargo of French wine and riots in Polynesia. The last test at Moruroa took place on 27 December 1995, and the site was dismantled afterwards. In all 181 explosions took place there, though nuclear scientists working at the site claim 175.

The atoll has had no permanent inhabitants since 1952. In February 2021 the French National Institute of Health and Medical Research published a report on the health consequences of the atmospheric tests in French Polynesia for the general population and for civilian and military workers.
mosbach: Mosbach lies in the north of Baden-Württemberg, about 35 km east of Heidelberg, at the confluence of the Neckar and the Elz, south of the Odenwald mountains, at a height of 134 to 354 metres. It is the seat of the Neckar-Odenwald district and has about 25,000 inhabitants, spread over six boroughs: Mosbach Town, Lohrbach, Neckarelz, Diedesheim, Sattelbach and Reichenbuch.

The settlement developed around the Benedictine monastery of Mosbach Abbey, called Monasterium Mosabach, whose first written record dates from the 9th century. In 1241 Mosbach was granted the rights and privileges of an Imperial free city, which it lost in 1362 when it became part of the Electorate of the Palatinate. When the lands of King Rupert were divided in 1410, Mosbach became the capital of a small principality, Palatinate-Mosbach, the inheritance of his son Otto I. After the death of his brother John, Count Palatine of Neumarkt, in 1443, Palatinate-Neumarkt was added in a personal union, creating Palatinate-Mosbach-Neumarkt. The principality was dissolved with the death of Count Palatine Otto II in 1499.

The town and its territory reverted to the Electorate of the Palatinate, and Mosbach became the capital of the administrative district of Oberamt Mosbach. In 1806 it was made part of the Grand Duchy of Baden. In World War II the Mosbach area was the location of an underground Daimler-Benz factory for aircraft engines, codenamed Goldfisch. The 289th Combat Engineer Battalion occupied it in the immediate postwar period.

The historic town centre has a pedestrian area and timber-framed houses. Among them are the Palm House, built in 1610 and the town's emblem, and the Salzhaus, the oldest timber-framed house. The old town hall has a tower. The former collegiate church is now a parish church, its nave used by Protestants and its chancel by Roman Catholics. In the borough of Neckarelz stands the Tempelhaus, which has the character of both a castle and a church. Mosbach lies on two heritage routes, the Burgenstraße or Castle Road and the Deutsche Fachwerkstraße or German Half-timbered Road.
moscow: Moscow lies on the Moskva River, which flows for about 500 kilometres through the East European Plain in Central Russia, and 49 bridges span the river and its canals within the city. The city's name is thought to derive from the river's. The best-grounded theory traces it to a Proto-Balto-Slavic root meaning 'wet', so that Moskva would mean a river at a marsh. A Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, 'Black River'.

The site has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and around 950 CE two Slavic tribes, the Vyatichi and Krivichi, settled there. Chronicles first mention Moscow in 1147, as a minor town on the western border of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal and a meeting place for Yuri Dolgorukiy and Sviatoslav Olgovich. It was fortified in the 1150s, when the first walls of the Kremlin were built, and was sacked during the Mongol invasions of 1237–1238 after the destruction of Ryazan.

The Grand Principality of Moscow led the unification of Russian lands in the 15th century, and the Kremlin was rebuilt then, with towers and churches by Italian architects. After the Tsardom of Russia was proclaimed in 1547, Moscow remained its political and economic centre until Peter the Great moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg in 1712. The capital returned to Moscow in 1918, after the establishment of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.

Moscow had 13,010,112 residents in the 2021 census, up from 11,503,501 in 2010. It is a federal city, divided into 12 administrative okrugs and 125 districts. Its road system radiates from the Kremlin and crosses circular roads that began as lines of fortification, among them the Boulevard Ring, on the line of the 16th-century wall of Bely Gorod, and the Garden Ring.

The Moscow Metro opened in 1935, and its original stations were decorated to impress and instruct the population. The city also holds Lomonosov Moscow State University, founded in 1755, and the Tretyakov Gallery, which has works by the icon painter Andrei Rublev.
moscow-kremlin: The Kremlin comprises five palaces, four cathedrals and an enclosing wall with numerous towers. It overlooks the Moskva River to the south, Red Square to the east and Alexander Garden to the west. In Russian, kreml' means a fortress within a city, but the Moscow Kremlin has also become a metonym for the Russian government; during the Cold War the term meant the government of the Soviet Union.

The site was inhabited by the Meryans from the 2nd century BCE, and Slavs held part of Borovitsky Hill by the 11th century. The word Kremlin was first recorded in 1331. The Mongols destroyed the fortress in 1237, and Ivan I Kalita rebuilt it in oak in 1339. Dmitri Donskoi replaced the palisade with a white limestone citadel in 1366 to 1368, which withstood a siege by Khan Tokhtamysh. Ivan III invited Italian architects, among them Pietro Antonio Solari, who designed the wall and towers, built between 1485 and 1495.

Polish forces held the Kremlin from 1610 to 1612, and its liberation paved the way for the election of Mikhail Romanov as tsar. Peter abandoned it for Saint Petersburg in 1703. French forces occupied it from 2 September to 11 October 1812, and Napoleon on retreating ordered it blown up; rain damaged the fuses and the damage was less than intended.

The Soviet government moved to Moscow on 12 March 1918, and Lenin chose the Senate building as his residence. In all 28 of the 54 historic buildings in the Kremlin were destroyed during Soviet rule, among them the Chudov Monastery and the Ascension Convent.

The Grand Kremlin Palace, built in 1839 to 1849, is the residence of the president of the Russian Federation. The complex was closed to tourists until 1955, the Kremlin Museums were established in 1961, and it was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1990.
moscow-peace-treaty: The Winter War began on 30 November 1939 with the Soviet invasion of Finland. On 29 January 1940 the Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov dropped the puppet Terijoki Government and recognised the Ryti–Tanner government as the legal government of Finland, saying the Soviet Union was willing to negotiate. The first tentative conditions reached Finland through Stockholm two days later and were larger than the claims made before the war. They demanded the Karelian Isthmus, including the city of Viipuri, and Finland's shore of Lake Ladoga, with the Hanko Peninsula leased for 30 years. Finland rejected them and appealed to Sweden, France and the United Kingdom for troops.

In February 1940 the commander-in-chief, Marshal Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim, expressed pessimism about the military situation, and the government began peace talks on 29 February, the day the Red Army began an attack on Viipuri.

A Finnish delegation led by Prime Minister Risto Ryti travelled to Moscow on 6 March, while the Red Army was close to surrounding Viipuri. President Kyösti Kallio resisted giving up any territory but agreed to sign, and is said to have exclaimed: Let the hand wither that signs this monstrous treaty! The treaty was signed on the evening of 12 March, Moscow time, for the Soviet Union by Molotov, Andrei Zhdanov and Aleksandr Vasilevsky and for Finland by Ryti, Juho Kusti Paasikivi, Rudolf Walden and Väinö Voionmaa.

Finland ceded approximately half of Finnish Karelia, more than the Soviets had demanded before the war. The area included Viipuri, Käkisalmi, Sortavala, Suojärvi and the whole of Viipuri Bay, along with a part of the Salla area, the Finnish part of the Rybachi Peninsula and several islands in the Gulf of Finland.
