In 666 Emperor Gaozong of Tang held the sacrifices, attended by representatives from Japan, India, Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla, the Turks, Khotan, the Khmer and the Umayyad Caliphate. A total of 72 emperors are recorded as visiting the mountain. Writers also climbed it for inspiration, leaving stone inscriptions and tablets, and the mountain played an important role in the development of both Buddhism and Taoism.

Mount Tai was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. The Dai Temple at its foot, first built under the Qin and modelled since the Han on an imperial palace, covers 96,000 square metres and holds a mural of 1009 showing the god of the mountain on a journey. The Shrine of the Blue Dawn near the top honours the goddess Bixia Yuanjun. About 6,660 stone steps lead from the red gate at the foot to the South Heaven Gate at the top, and the mountain carries many temples, stone tablets and cliff inscriptions.
mount-tambora: Mount Tambora, also called Tomboro, is an active stratovolcano in the northern part of Sumbawa, in the Lesser Sunda Islands. It forms its own peninsula, the Sanggar peninsula, between the Flores Sea to the north and Saleh Bay to the south. Its volcanism results from the Australian Plate moving beneath the Sunda Plate, and estimates for its onset range from 57 to 43 thousand years ago. Before 1815 it was a high cone with a single central vent and a base 60 kilometres across.

After lying dormant for several centuries, the volcano began to rumble in 1812. A moderate eruption on 5 April 1815 was followed by thunderous detonations heard in Ternate, 1,400 kilometres away. The climax came days later, and the explosions were heard on Sumatra, more than 2,600 kilometres away, and possibly in Thailand and Laos.

Ash fell as far away as Borneo, Sulawesi, Java and the Maluku Islands, and the mountain's height dropped from about 4,300 to 2,850 metres. The eruption ejected up to 150 cubic kilometres of material, rated VEI-7, and killed at least 71,000 people, though estimates vary.

The eruption cooled the global climate, and 1816 became known as the Year Without a Summer in North America and Europe, where crops failed, livestock died and the worst famine of the century followed.

In 2004 a team led by Haraldur Sigurðsson found a village buried about 25 kilometres west of the caldera, with a house holding the remains of two adults, bronze bowls, ceramic pots and iron tools. The finds suggested well-off traders, and the site was called the Pompeii of the East. The Tambora language was lost; remaining word lists suggest it was not Austronesian, but possibly a language isolate or related to the Papuan languages far to the east. Local folklore explained the disaster as divine punishment of a ruler who had killed a hajji.

The Swiss botanist Heinrich Zollinger reached the summit in 1847, the first to do so after the eruption, and found smoking sulphur and some regrown vegetation. Resettlement began in 1907, and a coffee plantation was set up in the 1930s at Pekat. A dense rain forest of Duabanga moluccana trees covers up to 80,000 hectares of the slopes. The Directorate of Volcanology monitors the mountain from a post at Doro Peti village.
mouseion: The word mouseion originally meant any place dedicated to the Muses, often connected with the study of music or poetry, and later it came to be associated with sites of learning such as Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum. According to Johannes Tzetzes, the Mouseion of Alexandria was founded by Ptolemy I Soter, though it more probably took shape under Ptolemy II Philadelphus. It arguably included the Library of Alexandria. The Ptolemies reputedly set out to bring together some of the best scholars of the Hellenistic world and to collect all the books then known.

The Mouseion was a community gathered under the protection of the Muses, supported by the patronage of the Ptolemies and later of the Roman emperors. It held no collection of sculpture and painting, unlike the one that their rival Attalus assembled at the Library of Pergamum. It was rather an institution of learning, compared by Germain Bazin to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. Reports are few, but scholars and staff appear to have been salaried by the state and to have paid no taxes; according to Strabo they also received free room and board and free servants.

Strabo, in the first century CE, described it as part of the Brucheion, the palace complex, with a lobby, a columned hall and a large dining hall for the common table of its members, under a priest once appointed by the kings and now by Caesar. Scholars there evidently pursued literary criticism, and translated some foreign texts from Egyptian, Assyrian, Persian, Jewish and other languages. Many editions of the Greek canon, from Homer and Hesiod onwards, rest on texts collated and corrected by scholars presumably linked to it.

Under Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, in a time of political turmoil, most intellectuals were killed or expelled from the city, among them the last recorded head librarian, Aristarchus of Samothrace, who is said to have resigned in 145 BCE. The Mouseion continued under Roman rule but never regained its former standing, and its membership came to include politicians and athletes rewarded for service to the state. The Brucheion was probably destroyed by fire on the orders of Emperor Aurelian in 272 CE.

Its members included Callimachus, who produced the first comprehensive book catalogue, the Pinakes, Zenodotos, the first head librarian, Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the Argonautica, and Eratosthenes of Cyrene, who measured the Earth's circumference. Through their work the writings of Homer and the tragedians survive. The word mouseion is the root of the modern museum.
moynaq: Moynaq, also spelled Muynak, is a city in northern Karakalpakstan, an autonomous republic in Uzbekistan, and the seat of the Moynaq district. It was formerly a seaport on the Aral Sea and now lies about 150 km from the water, in the Aralkum Desert. Its population was 13,000 in 1991 and 18,196 in 2012. Most inhabitants are Karakalpaks, with many Uzbeks and Kazakhs and smaller groups of Tatars and Turkmens. Uzbek and Karakalpak have official status, and Russian serves as a language of interethnic communication.

Moynaq was a bustling fishing community, once Uzbekistan's only port city, with tens of thousands of residents. Fishing had always been part of the regional economy, and the town became a centre of industrial fishing and canning. In the 1960s the Soviet government diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate a regional monoculture of cotton, which starved the Aral Sea of its inflows. Agricultural chemical runoff caused severe pollution, the sea evaporated, and the remaining water became highly saline and toxic. The shoreline receded dozens of kilometres from the town and the economy collapsed.

Dust storms from the dried and polluted seabed cause chronic and acute illnesses among the few residents who remained, and weather no longer moderated by the sea brings hotter summers and colder winters.

The town's main attractions are the rusting hulks of its former fishing fleet, which stand beside the Aral Sea Memorial at its northern end, and a one-room museum with paintings and photographs of its more prosperous days, including fur farming and rush mat manufacture. Saiga antelope still live wild around Moynaq, and about 230 species of birds are recorded in the region, around half of which breed in the Sudochye Wetland. The Stihia electronic music festival has been held among the ships since 2018 to draw attention to the Aral Sea disaster. Water transport has ceased, and the port is not functioning.
mozaffar-ad-din-shah-qajar: Mozaffar ad-Din was born on 23 March 1853 in Tehran, the fourth son of Naser al-Din Shah Qajar. His mother was Shokouh al-Saltaneh, a daughter of Fathollah Mirza and a granddaughter of the second Qajar shah, Fath-Ali Shah. He was named crown prince and sent as governor to the northern province of Azerbaijan in 1861.

He spent some 35 years as crown prince, in the pursuit of pleasure. His relations with his father were frequently strained, and he was not consulted in important matters of state, so that when he came to the throne in May 1896 he was unprepared for the burdens of office.

Iran faced a financial crisis at his accession, with annual government expenditure far above revenue. Mozaffar ad-Din attempted some reforms of the central treasury, but the debts to England and Russia incurred by the Qajar court undermined them. He borrowed further from Britain, France and Russia, and the later loans went to pay off earlier ones rather than to fund economic development. To meet the costs of the state and of his own extravagant life he also signed concessions that gave foreigners monopoly control over various industries and markets.

Like his father he visited Europe three times. On the urging of his chancellor Amin-os-Soltan he borrowed from Nicholas II of Russia to pay for the journeys. In Paris he saw the cinematographe and ordered his photographer to bring the equipment to Tehran, which began Persian cinema. On his visit to the United Kingdom in August 1902 he hoped for the Order of the Garter, but King Edward VII refused it to a non-Christian; in 1903 the king gave way and the shah was appointed a member.

Fear among the aristocracy, the educated elite and the religious leaders of foreign control led to protests in 1906. The shah then agreed to the creation of a Majles, a National Consultative Assembly, granting a constitution and a parliament that curtailed the monarch's power. He died of a heart attack 40 days after granting the constitution, on 8 January 1907, and was buried in the Imam Husayn Shrine in Kerbala.

Contemporaries judged his character in varied terms. The historian Abbas Amanat describes a man of gentle disposition with an earnest wish to open the country to social and educational reforms, who lacked his father's panache and political skill in playing the European powers against each other. The British diplomat Mortimer Durand, who knew both shahs, wrote that he was more amiable than his father but weak and easily misled. He suffered ill health from youth, including a weak heart and a chronic kidney infection, yet enjoyed riding, hunting and shooting. He is often credited with the Persian Constitution of 1906.
mozambique: Mozambique lies on the southeast coast of Africa, bordered by the Indian Ocean, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini and South Africa. The Zambezi River divides it into two topographical regions. North of the river a narrow coastal strip gives way to inland hills, low plateaus and rugged highlands covered with miombo woodlands. South of it the lowlands are broader. The climate is tropical, with a wet season from October to March and a dry season from April to September.

The country was named Moçambique by the Portuguese after the Island of Mozambique. The island's name is derived from Musa ibn Bique, an Arab trader who first visited it, later lived there and was its ruler when Vasco da Gama called in 1498. The island-town was the capital of the Portuguese colony until 1898, when the capital moved south to Lourenço Marques, now Maputo.

Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into Southeast Africa as early as the 4th century BCE. Between the 1st and 5th centuries CE waves of migration passed through the Zambezi valley into the plateau and coastal areas. They established agricultural communities and herding societies and brought the technology of iron smelting and smithing. From the late first millennium CE, Indian Ocean trade networks reached as far south as the port town of Chibuene. From the 9th century, port towns grew along the East African coast and shared in an incipient Swahili culture. Islam was often adopted by urban elites, which facilitated trade.

Sofala, Angoche and Mozambique Island were regional powers by the 15th century. Inland states such as the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa Empire supplied gold and ivory, which were exchanged up the coast to larger ports such as Kilwa and Mombasa. Vasco da Gama's voyage of 1498 marked the Portuguese entry into the region. They gained control of the Island of Mozambique and of Sofala in the early 16th century, and by the 1530s traders and prospectors seeking gold had set up garrisons and trading posts at Sena and Tete on the Zambezi. Portuguese posts and forts displaced Arab commercial and military dominance.

Mozambique is the Republic of Mozambique, a presidential republic with its capital and largest city at Maputo. It became independent in 1975 after more than four centuries of Portuguese rule, and a civil war followed from 1977 to 1992. Portuguese is the only official language, alongside local languages such as Tsonga, Makhuwa and Sena. The Makonde are known for their wood carving and masks, and the Chopi for their marimba music and dance.
mozambique-island: The Island of Mozambique lies between the Mozambique Channel and Mossuril Bay and belongs to Nampula Province. It is about 3 kilometres long and between 200 and 500 metres wide. Most of the historic buildings stand at the northern end, in what is now called Stone Town, while most residents live in reed houses in Makuti Town at the southern end. The island is entirely urbanised, and since the 1960s a bridge of 3 kilometres has joined it to the mainland. The country takes its name from the island.

Pottery shows that the town was founded no later than the fourteenth century, and tradition says its first Swahili population came from Kilwa. By the fifteenth century its rulers had links with those of Angoche and Quelimane. In 1514 Duarte Barbosa noted that its people were Muslim and spoke the same Swahili dialect as Angoche. The name Moçambique derives from Ali Musa Mbiki, called Mussa Bin Bique, the sultan of the island at the time of Vasco da Gama.
The Portuguese established a port and naval base in 1507 and built the Chapel of Nossa Senhora de Baluarte in 1522, now considered the oldest European building in the Southern Hemisphere.

In the 16th century they built Fort São Sebastião, and their settlement became the capital of Portuguese East Africa and an important missionary centre. The island withstood Dutch attacks in 1607 and 1608 in a defence led by the captain-general Dom Estêvão de Ataíde. It was a major post on Portuguese voyages to India and a place where slaves, spices and gold were traded. The opening of the Suez Canal reduced its fortunes, the capital moved to Lourenço Marques, now Maputo, in 1898, and by the middle of the 20th century the new harbour of Nacala took most of the remaining business.

The island is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with a permanent population of about 14,000. Besides the old fortifications, its buildings include the Palace and Chapel of São Paulo, built in 1640 as a Jesuit college and later the governor's residence, now a museum. The Museum of Sacred Art, in the Church of the Misericórdia, displays a Makonde crucifix. A neo-classical hospital of 1877 survives, and the island also has mosques and a Hindu temple.
mozarabs: The name Mozarab comes from the Arabic musta'rab, meaning Arabized. It is first documented in Christian sources from the 11th century, and Muslims did not use it for Christians; Arabic sources called them Nazarenes or described them by their legal status as people of the covenant. More precisely they were Andalusi Christians, the Christians of the territories of Iberia under Muslim rule after the Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom. Most were descendants of local Christians who spoke Romance varieties, together with members of the former Visigothic ruling elite who neither converted nor emigrated north.

As dhimmi, Christians paid the jizya, a personal tax, and kept their own judges, tribunals and Roman-derived civil law. Some held high office: Recemundus, a palace official, wrote the Calendar of Córdoba for Abd ar-Rahman III, and in 1064 the emir of Zaragoza sent the Mozarabic bishop Paternus of Tortosa as an envoy to Ferdinand I of León. Their guarantees, at first fairly broad, steadily diminished. The building of new churches and the ringing of church bells were eventually forbidden. An estimated 50 per cent had converted to Islam by 951.

Mozarabs took Arabic names and learned Arabic, and Petrus Alvarus of Córdoba lamented the decline of spoken Latin among them. Latin remained the language of the liturgy and of culture. Their Romance dialects, today called the Mozarabic language, are first written down in the kharjas, the closing choruses of Arabic and Hebrew muwashshah poems, and passed many words of Andalusi Arabic origin into Portuguese, Spanish and Catalan.

Between 850 and 859 a movement in Córdoba brought Christians to seek martyrdom by insulting Muhammad and criticizing Islam. Eulogius of Córdoba, beheaded in 859, recorded their deaths and opposed the Arabization of the Christians, while Albarus of Córdoba defended the martyrs in his Indiculus luminosus. Kenneth Baxter Wolf concludes that Eulogius was a hagiographer rather than the instigator, and records further executions in Córdoba in 860, in 888–912, in 913–920.

Mozarabs migrated north to the Christian kingdoms, and this northward movement explains Arabic place names in areas where Muslim rule did not last long. Many who lived under Christian rule kept their distinctive rite until the 14th century. How many Christians lived in al-Andalus is debated: one scholar puts them at about 75,000, roughly 15 per cent of the population of Islamic Iberia, at the end of the 11th century.
mozdok: Mozdok stands on the left shore of the Terek River in North Ossetia–Alania, 92 kilometres north of Vladikavkaz, and is the administrative centre of Mozdoksky District. Its name comes from a Kabardian phrase, mez degu, meaning the deaf forest.

The Russians established the fort in 1763 on the site of a Kabardian village founded four years earlier, and settled families of Volga Cossacks in stanitsas around it. In 1764 one of the first Ossetian schools opened there, and the Kabardian leaders' request that the fortress be destroyed went unanswered. The Kabardians later tried to besiege the town but were compelled to retreat. Russian authorities encouraged Ossetians, Georgians, Armenians and other Christians to settle, and the town became a key military outpost linked to Kizlyar by a fortified line and a centre of trade. A census of 1777 counted 674 Georgians, 565 Armenians, 180 Kabardians, 95 Ossetians and 21 Greeks.

Mozdok was the northern end of the Georgian Military Road to Tbilisi until Vladikavkaz, founded in 1784, took its place. Ossetian settlement grew in the 1820s when the Russian commander Yermolov began removing Kabardians from the area of the road and settling Ossetians there. Muslim Ossetian families from Digoria also settled early in the 19th century. The brothers Dubinin built the first oil-refining apparatus in the world there in 1823. German troops took the town on 23 August 1942 during Case Blue, and the Red Army recaptured it on 3 January 1943.

Under the Russian Empire Mozdok was the seat of the Mozdoksky Otdel of the Terek Oblast. The census of 2002 recorded 62.7 per cent Russians, 7.7 per cent Ossetians and 6.1 per cent Armenians. From 1961 to 1998 the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, flying Tupolev Tu-95s, was based at the nearby airbase.
mozhaysk: Mozhaysk lies 110 kilometres west of Moscow on the historic road leading to Smolensk and then to Poland. It is the administrative centre of Mozhaysky District. One theory holds that its name comes from the Mozhay river, whose name may be of Baltic origin, compared with the Lithuanian mažoji, small, in contrast to the larger Moskva river nearby. The town was frequently the last major obstacle on the way to the capital, and gave rise to the Russian expression to push beyond Mozhay, meaning to crush an enemy completely and drive them far away. It is said to have originated when the Polish army retreated to Mozhaysk after the Battle of Moscow in 1612.

Mozhaysk is first mentioned in 1231 as an appanage of Chernigov. It became an important stronghold of the Smolensk dynasty and in the 13th century was ruled by Duke Theodore the Black, later a saint. The Muscovites seized it in 1303, but during the following century they had serious trouble defending it against Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1345 to 1377. A younger brother of the ruling Grand Duke of Moscow usually held the Principality of Mozhaysk. In 1562 Denmark and Russia signed the Treaty of Mozhaysk there during the Livonian War, and in 1708 the administration of Peter the Great granted the town its status.

The town helped defend the western approaches to Moscow in the 19th and 20th centuries. During the French invasion of 1812 the Battle of Borodino was fought 12 kilometres away. German forces took Mozhaysk on 18 October 1941 and the Red Army recaptured it on 20 January 1942.

A first fortified settlement existed in the 12th century. After the great fire of 1541 Ivan the Terrible ordered it rebuilt, and a brick kremlin replaced the stone fortress in 1624 to 1626. The Cathedral of St. Nicholas, in Gothic Revival style by Aleksei Bakarev, was begun in 1802, ransacked by the retreating French in 1812 and consecrated in 1814. The Luzhetsky Monastery was founded in 1408 by Saint Ferapont and rebuilt in brick in the 16th century. The 2010 census counted 31,363 inhabitants.
mpla: The movement grew out of two organizations: the Party of the United Struggle for Africans in Angola, founded in 1953 by Viriato da Cruz and Matias Miguéis, and the Angolan Communist Party, founded in December 1955 as a Luanda cell of the Portuguese Communist Party. Viriato da Cruz belonged to both and arranged their merger into a broad nationalist front. On 10 December 1956, at the house of Ilídio Machado in Luanda, Machado, da Cruz and Mário Pinto de Andrade wrote the Manifesto of 1956 calling for a broad Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola. Machado was the first president until his arrest in 1959, and part of the leadership moved to exile in Paris and Frankfurt from 1957.

The MPLA took up arms against the Portuguese in 1961. In the early 1970s its guerrilla activity declined under Portuguese counter-insurgency, and internal conflict split it for a time into three factions. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 the Angolan independence coalition broke down, and on 11 November 1975 Agostinho Neto, holding Luanda and the oil fields of the Atlantic coast, declared the People's Republic of Angola. UNITA and the FNLA declared independence separately at Huambo. South Africa and Zaire intervened for the FNLA and UNITA, Cuba intervened for the MPLA, and the Soviet Union aided Cuba and the MPLA.

At its first congress in 1977 the MPLA adopted Marxism-Leninism and added Partido do Trabalho to its name. After Nito Alves's attempted coup that year, Neto ordered the killing of suspected followers of orthodox communism; estimates of the dead range from 2,000 to 70,000, with some placing the toll at 18,000. In December 1990 the party declared social democracy its ideology. After it won the 1992 election, fighting resumed, and tens of thousands of UNITA and FNLA sympathizers were killed in what is called the Halloween Massacre. The war ended in 2002 with the death of Jonas Savimbi and a ceasefire; more than 500,000 civilians died in it.

The MPLA's core base is the Ambundu ethnic group and the educated intelligentsia of Luanda. Its armed wing, the People's Armed Forces for the Liberation of Angola (FAPLA), became the national armed forces from 1975 to 1991. Its mass organizations include the Angolan Women's Organization, the National Union of Angolan Workers, the Agostinho Neto Pioneer Organization and the Youth of the MPLA.
mpumalanga: The name means East, or literally the place where the sun rises, in the Nguni languages. The province borders Limpopo to the north, Gauteng to the west, the Free State to the south-west and KwaZulu-Natal to the south, and takes up 6.3 percent of South Africa's land. The Drakensberg escarpment divides it into a western half of high-altitude grassland, the Highveld, and an eastern half of low-altitude subtropical Lowveld, mostly savanna, where the southern half of Kruger National Park lies. Some of the oldest rocks on earth have been found in the Barberton area.

Archaeological sites show human settlement going back 1.7 million years, and the Lion Cavern at Ngwenya on the Eswatini border shows iron ore being mined at least 28,000 years ago. The Lydenburg Heads, from about 500 CE, are the oldest Iron Age artworks south of the equator. Stone-walled Mbayi sites on the Highveld point to a large agropastoral society between about 1500 and 1820, connected to the Portuguese trading post in Maputo Bay. The groups that became the Swazi, Pedi, Ndebele and Tsonga peoples settled in the area.

The first Dutch-speaking settlers arrived in 1845 in the Great Trek, and in 1852 the Boers established the South African Republic. The Pedi, Swazi and Zulu kingdoms offered significant resistance, and the Pedi fought the Boers in the Sekhukhune Wars of 1876. Gold was first found near Barberton in 1883, and the region became a thoroughfare for trade between Johannesburg and Delagoa Bay. Under a system known as Inboekstelsel, Boers raided to capture children and force them into indentured labour. Kruger National Park was established in 1898.

After 1948 apartheid policy moved Black South Africans by forced removals into homelands, among them KaNgwane, KwaNdebele, Lebowa and Gazankulu. In 1959 the town of Bethal was the centre of a consumer potato boycott against conditions on local farms. In 1986 a disaster at Kinross Mine killed 177 mine workers. The province was formed on 27 April 1994, the day of South Africa's first democratic elections, from the Eastern Transvaal and the former homelands, and was renamed Mpumalanga on 24 August 1995.

The capital is Mbombela. The province is home to Swazi, Ndebele, Afrikaans, Tsonga, Zulu, Mapulana, Portuguese and Pedi communities, and the Ndebele Cultural Village at Botshabelo displays Ndebele house painting. At the 2011 census it had about four million people, 30 percent of whom spoke siSwati.
mtskheta: Mtskheta lies on a lowland surrounded by mountains, at the confluence of the Kura, called the Mtkvari in Georgian, and the Aragvi. The Greater Caucasus rise to the north and the Lesser Caucasus to the south. Archaeology traces settlement in the area from the 2nd millennium BCE to the early 1st millennium CE, and numerous Bronze Age burials show that it was already a significant settlement at the start of the 1st millennium BCE.

The Georgian Chronicles say that Mtskheta was founded by Mtskhetos, son of Kartlos, the eponymous ancestor of the Georgians. Historians more readily accept another account, that the Meschian tribes founded it in the 5th century BCE. It was the capital of the early Georgian Kingdom of Iberia from the 3rd century BCE. The chronicles have Alexander the Great conquering it, which some historians do not accept. The first Georgian king, Parnavaz, built a new wall around it at the start of the 3rd century BCE, and his son Saurmag strengthened it. The city was strongly fortified, with the citadel of Armazi on Mount Bagineti and forts at Tsitsamuri and Sarkine.

Mtskheta was a site of early Christian activity, and in 337 Christianity was proclaimed the state religion of Iberia. A small wooden church built in the centre of the city soon after the conversion became Svetitskhoveli Cathedral, and in the 5th century Vakhtang Gorgasali built a large basilica on the site. The first katolikos was elected in the 5th century and resided in Mtskheta. Vakhtang's successor, King Dachi, moved the capital to the more defensible Tbilisi in the early 6th century, following his father's will. Mtskheta nevertheless remained the coronation and burial place of most Georgian kings until the end of Georgian political independence in the 19th century.

The city was heavily damaged during the Umayyad defeat of the Khazars between 736 and 739. It regained its standing under King George I and Katolikos Melchizedek I, who oversaw the building of the present Svetitskhoveli and Samtavro cathedrals. Timur burned the city in the 15th century, and Alexander I rebuilt Svetitskhoveli in 1425. Further attacks, including one in 1625, reduced it so that by 1801, when Georgia became part of Russia, it was little more than a village.

Mtskheta remains the seat of the Georgian Orthodox Church. Svetitskhoveli Cathedral, the Samtavro Monastery and the Jvari Monastery are among the most significant monuments of Georgian Christian architecture, and their early inscriptions are a valuable reference for the origins of the Georgian alphabet. The Historical Monuments of Mtskheta became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. Nearby lie the ruins of the Armaztsikhe fortress.
muammar-gaddafi: Muammar Gaddafi was born about 1942 near Qasr Abu Hadi, outside Sirte in Tripolitania, during Italian colonial rule. His family belonged to a small, relatively uninfluential tribe, the Qadhadhfa. As a boy he saw the Arab–Israeli War of 1948, the Egyptian Revolution of 1952 and the Suez Crisis of 1956, and he became an Arab nationalist at school in Sabha. In October 1961 he led a demonstration there against Syria's secession from the United Arab Republic, and the authorities expelled him and his family from the town. He later enrolled in the Royal Military Academy in Benghazi.

Gaddafi founded a revolutionary group, the Free Officers, which deposed the Senussi monarchy of King Idris in the coup of 1969. Its central committee became the Revolutionary Command Council, with Gaddafi as chairman and de facto head of state. Ruling by decree, he deported Libya's Italian population and ejected Western military bases. He nationalised the oil industry and used the revenue to build up the military, fund foreign revolutionaries and expand housing, healthcare and education.

On 2 March 1977 the General People's Congress established the Jamahiriya, a state of the masses. Gaddafi gave up his formal post in 1979 and took the title Leader of the Revolution, remaining commander-in-chief and head of the Revolutionary Committees that policed and suppressed dissent. Border conflicts with Egypt and Chad, support for foreign militants and alleged responsibility for the Pan Am Flight 103 bombing isolated Libya, and the United States bombed it in 1986, followed by United Nations sanctions. After 1999 he turned from pan-Arabism to pan-Africanism and chaired the African Union from 2009 to 2010.

Protests against corruption and unemployment began on 17 February 2011, during the Arab Spring, and became a civil war in which NATO intervened on the side of the National Transitional Council. After the fall of Tripoli in August 2011, Gaddafi retreated to Sirte, where he was captured, tortured and killed by militants of the Council on 20 October 2011.

He dominated Libyan politics for four decades. Supporters praise improvements in housing, education and free healthcare. Critics point to human rights abuses, persecution of Berbers, Jews, migrants and foreign workers, and the financing of terrorism.
muawiya-i: Early Islamic sources give Mu'awiya's year of birth as 597, 603 or 605. His father, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, was a prominent Meccan merchant who led trade caravans to Byzantine Syria and became leader of the Banu Abd Shams clan of the Quraysh. Mu'awiya and his father opposed Muhammad until Muhammad captured Mecca in 630, after which Mu'awiya became one of his scribes. Caliph Abu Bakr appointed him a deputy commander in the conquest of Syria, and he rose through the caliphate of Umar until Uthman made him governor of Syria. There he allied with the Banu Kalb tribe, marrying a daughter of its ruling house about 650. He also launched the first Muslim naval campaigns against Byzantium, with Uthman's permission, beginning with Cyprus.

After Uthman was killed in 656, Mu'awiya took up the cause of avenging him and withheld allegiance from Ali. Their armies met at Siffin in 657 and reached a stalemate, and arbitration talks failed. In April or May 658 the Syrians pledged allegiance to Mu'awiya as caliph, and his ally Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt from Ali's governor.

After Ali was killed in 661, Mu'awiya marched on Kufa, where Hasan, Ali's son, abdicated in return for a financial settlement. Mu'awiya entered the city in July or September 661, and early sources call that year the year of unity.

He made Damascus his capital and moved the treasury there from Kufa. He relied on a Syrian tribal army of about 100,000 men and ruled the provinces indirectly through governors with full civil and military authority, preferring agreements and bribes to confrontation. Armenia became a tributary of the Caliphate, and almost every year his troops raided Byzantine territory across the Anatolian frontier. In 670 the commander Uqba ibn Nafi began the conquest of Ifriqiya. In an unprecedented move he nominated his son Yazid as his successor, making the caliphate hereditary.

Mu'awiya died of an illness in Damascus in April or May 680, at about the age of 80, and was buried by the Bab al-Saghir gate. The surviving Muslim histories come from Abbasid-era Iraq and are mostly hostile to the Umayyads, yet they portray him in a relatively balanced way, stressing his hilm, meaning mildness and the skilful management of people. Sunnis do not count him among the rightly-guided caliphs, since he gained the caliphate through civil war and made it hereditary, but they honour him as a companion of Muhammad and a scribe of the revelation. In Shia Islam he is reviled for opposing Ali.
mudbrick: A mudbrick, also called an unfired brick, is an air-dried brick made from a mixture of mud containing loam, clay, sand and water with a binding material such as rice husks or straw. From around 5000–4000 BCE mudbricks evolved into fired bricks, which are stronger and more durable. In some warm regions with little timber to fuel a kiln, mudbricks stayed in use, and they remain the standard of vernacular architecture in parts of Africa and western Asia. In the 20th century the compressed earth block was developed, using high pressure to make a cheap non-fired brick stronger than the simpler air-dried kind.

Mudbrick production in the southern Levant goes back to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, as at Jericho, where dwellings of about 9000 BCE were built of mudbricks set in mud. Mixtures of sand, clay and water, often tempered with chopped straw and chaff, were the most common material for earthen buildings across the ancient Near East for millennia. Well-preserved bricks from Tel Tsaf in the Jordan Valley date to 5200 BCE, and their composition stayed stable for at least 500 years. The people of Mehrgarh in South Asia lived in mudbrick houses between 7000 and 3300 BCE, and more than 15 sites of the Indus Valley civilization in the 3rd millennium BCE used them, though the Mature Harappan phase used fired bricks.

Mesopotamians built cities of sun-dried bricks, typically flat below and curved on top, called plano-convex, and some walls had a few courses of fired brick at the base to protect them from splashing. Sun-dried bricks were found in Neolithic Knossos. They were the most common building material in pharaonic Egypt, where workers trampled Nile mud with straw in a pit; because the bricks were chemically suitable as fertilizer, many ruins such as Edfu were destroyed, while Amarna is a well-preserved site. Greeks used mudbrick for walls and citadels, including Troy II.

In areas of Spanish influence the technique is called adobe. The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali, the world's largest mudbrick structure, is built of banco, a fermented mixture of mud and grain husks whose plaster must be reapplied annually.
mughal-empire: The empire is conventionally said to have been founded in 1526 by Babur, a Timurid prince from the Fergana Valley. He descended from Timur on his father's side and from Genghis Khan on his mother's. Driven from Central Asia, he established himself in Kabul and pushed south through the Khyber Pass. At the First Battle of Panipat he defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, with firearms and cannon despite being outnumbered, using a formation taught by the Ottoman expert Ustad Ali Quli. The Battle of Khanwa against Rana Sanga of Mewar in 1527 was a second decisive victory, and the centre of Mughal power shifted to Agra.

Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605, first under the regent Bairam Khan. Through a series of wars he controlled almost the whole subcontinent north of the Godavari River and set up the centralised administration. He allowed freedom of religion at his court and tried to bridge differences by founding a new religion, Din-i Ilahi. The empire reached its maximum extent under Aurangzeb, and historians date its imperial structure from about 1600 to 1720.

After Aurangzeb's son Bahadur Shah I died in 1712 the dynasty sank into feuds, and in 1719 alone four emperors came to the throne as figureheads under the Sayyid brothers. Historians cite weak rulers, succession wars and imperial overstretch. The empire was reduced to the region around Old Delhi by 1760 and formally dissolved by the British Raj after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

Below the emperor stood four ministries: finance under the diwan, the military under the mir bakhshi, law and religious patronage under the sadr as-sudr, and the imperial household under the mir saman. The empire was divided into subahs under governors. The capitals were Agra, Delhi, Lahore and Fatehpur Sikri. Agricultural taxes, which amounted to well over half a cultivator's output, were paid in a regulated silver currency. Persian became the official and courtly language, and Hindustani developed in Delhi in the late Mughal era. Mughal monuments listed as World Heritage Sites include Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, the Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Lahore Fort and the Taj Mahal.
muhammad: The early sources for Muhammad's life are Muslim authors of the 8th and 9th centuries CE, and scholars dispute how far they can be trusted because of the gap between his life and their writing. Western historians describe the early biographies as written largely to convey a message rather than to record history exactly. What follows is the traditional account.

According to it, Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh, the leading tribe of western Arabia. His father Abdullah died around the time of his birth and his mother Amina when he was six, and his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then his uncle Abu Talib brought him up. At 25 he married Khadija, a wealthy woman of 40. He would withdraw for nights of prayer to a mountain cave named Hira, where, at about 40, around 610, he reported that the angel Gabriel gave him his first revelation from God.

In 613 Muhammad began to preach publicly that God is One and that complete submission, Islam, to God is the right way of life. His followers were few and were persecuted by Meccan polytheists for 13 years. In 622 he and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, then called Yathrib. This migration, the Hijrah, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina he united the tribes under the Constitution of Medina.

After years of intermittent fighting with Meccan tribes, he marched on Mecca in 630 with 10,000 converts and seized the city with minimal casualties. He declared an amnesty for past offences, except for ten men and women, and had the statues of Arabian gods in and around the Kaaba destroyed. By his death most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam.

Muhammad fell ill in June 632 and died on 8 June in the house of his wife Aisha, where he was buried. A dispute over succession followed. Umar ibn al-Khattab nominated Abu Bakr, who was confirmed as the first caliph, while some companions held that Muhammad had designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib. Within a decade Muslims conquered Mesopotamia, Byzantine Syria and Egypt and large parts of Persia. Muslims hold that he was the last prophet sent by God and that his revelations form the Quran. His sayings and practices, preserved in the hadith, make up the sunnah, which supplies many details of prayer, fasting and pilgrimage not found in the Quran.
muhammad-abduh: Muhammad Abduh was born in 1849 in the Nile Delta, to a father of Turkish ancestry and an Egyptian mother; his family belonged to the Ottoman Egyptian elite. He was educated at a private school in Tanta and at the Ahmadi mosque, and in these years studied under his Sufi uncle Darwish, a member of the reformist Madaniyya order, which stressed adherence to foundational teachings and shunned taqlid, the imitation of earlier authorities. In 1866 he entered al-Azhar in Cairo, where he criticised the traditional curriculum and chose Jamal al-Din al-Afghani as his guide. Their relationship lasted eight years, and al-Afghani gave his mysticism a philosophical basis and drew him towards a rationalist reading of Islam.

Abduh received the degree of alim in 1877 and began teaching logic, theology and ethics at al-Azhar. In 1878 he became professor of history at the teachers' training college Dar al-Ulum and also taught Arabic. In 1880 he became editor-in-chief of the official gazette, the official gazette, which he used to spread anti-colonial ideas and calls for social and religious reform. British forces exiled him in 1882 for six years for supporting the Urabi revolt. He spent several years in Ottoman Lebanon, helping to establish an Islamic educational system, and in 1884 joined al-Afghani in Paris to publish al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.

After returning to Egypt in 1888 he served as a judge in the Courts of First Instance of the Native Tribunals and became a consultative member of the Court of Appeal in 1891. As Grand Mufti from 1899, he was involved in decisions considered liberal, such as allowing meat butchered by non-Muslims and accepting loan interest. This endeared him to Lord Cromer but caused a rift with the khedive Abbas Hilmi and the nationalist leader Mustafa Kamil Pasha. He proposed reforms to al-Azhar's examinations, curriculum and working conditions, and in 1900 founded the Society for the Revival of Arabic Literature. He died of renal cell carcinoma in Alexandria on 11 July 1905.

Abduh wrote the Risalat al-Tawhid, a commentary on the Quran, and articles in al-Manar and al-Ahram. He argued that Islam reproved slavish imitation of tradition and gave humans independence of will and thought, and he held that education, religious and scientific, was the best means of reform. He opposed polygamy where it led to injustice between wives and criticised superstition and the veneration of saints, while remaining sympathetic to Sufism. He urged friendship among the schools of thought within Islam and between Muslims, Christians and Jews. Opponents accused him of being an unbeliever; followers regarded him as a reviver of Islam.
muhammad-ahmad: Muhammad Ahmad was born on Labab Island, Dongola, in northern Sudan, into a notable religious Arabized Nubian family from the Danagla tribe, who traced their descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hassan. His father was a boat-builder. While his brothers joined the trade, he turned to religious study and in 1861 sought out Sheikh Muhammad Sharif Nur al-Dai'm of the Samaniyya Sufi order. After seven years he was recognised for his piety and given the title of sheikh. In 1870 he settled on Aba Island, built a mosque and taught the Quran. In 1878 his teacher expelled him from the order, and when Sheikh al-Qurashi wad al-Zayn died on 25 July 1878 his followers recognised Muhammad Ahmad as their leader.

On 29 June 1881 he claimed to be the Mahdi, the redeemer who would prepare the way for the second coming of Jesus. The Samaniyya already expected a Mahdi from its own line. He said that a prophetic assembly, a hadra, had appointed him, and he called his followers Ansār, after the people of Medina who welcomed Muhammad, in place of darwish. Some scholars loyal to the Ottoman Sultan rejected his claim. When the governor general sent a party to arrest him, it was overwhelmed on 11 August 1881. Late in 1883 his forces, armed with spears and swords, overwhelmed a 4,000-man Egyptian force near El Obeid, and then defeated the 8,000-man force of William Hicks at the Battle of Shaykan.

General Charles George Gordon reached Khartoum in February 1884, and the Ansār besieged the city from April. A British relief force arrived on 28 January 1885 to find that Khartoum had fallen two days earlier. The garrison was killed, the male population massacred, and women and children enslaved. Gordon was killed at the palace.

Muhammad Ahmad died of typhus a few months after Khartoum and was buried at Omdurman. He had chosen three deputies, and Abdallahi ibn Muhammad succeeded him. After the British under Kitchener defeated the Khalifa in 1898, his tomb was destroyed and his bones thrown into the Nile, to stop it from becoming a rallying point; it was later rebuilt.

His posthumous son Abd al-Rahman al-Mahdi led the neo-Mahdist movement and sponsored the Umma Party before Sudan's independence in 1956. Some Sudanese regard the Mahdi as a precursor of Sudanese nationalism. His collected works, about 1,000 letters, proclamations, sermons, prayers and rulings written between 1881 and 1885, were published in 1993.
muhammad-al-amin-bey: Born on 4 September 1881, he married Lalla Jeneïna Beya, the daughter of a Tripolitanian merchant of Tunis, in 1902. On 25 June 1942 Moncef Bey named him Bey al-Mahalla, the heir apparent. A month later he warned Moncef that the court counsellor General M'hammed Belkhodja was urging the French Resident General Jean-Pierre Esteva to depose him.

In May 1943 General Alphonse Juin came to Tunis with orders to remove Moncef Bey for alleged attempts to collaborate with the Axis forces. Juin found no grounds for condemning him. Lamine at first refused to promise that he would accept the throne and agreed largely because of the benefits to his family. Juin installed him at the Bardo palace on 15 May 1943. Moncef abdicated only on 6 July.

For most Tunisians he remained a usurper, the Bey of the French. The other Husainid princes boycotted him. The death of Moncef Bey in exile on 1 September 1948 removed the possibility of a restoration, and his subjects began to regard him as their legitimate ruler.

He then worked clandestinely with Habib Bourguiba and Salah Ben Youssef for self-government. In 1952 the Resident General Jean de Hauteclocque imprisoned Bourguiba and had the Bey's ministers arrested; the Bey refused to sign decrees, bringing government to a standstill, and gave way after the trade union leader Farhat Hached was assassinated in December 1952. In 1954 he accepted a reform package negotiated by Muhammad Salah Mzali while Bourguiba was still confined. After the French Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France announced internal autonomy on 31 July 1954, France dealt with the Neo Destour alone.

As king he signed without protest the decree of 31 May 1956 that abolished the privileges of the ruling family. On 15 July 1957 the Tunisian army replaced the Royal Guard around the palace, and on 25 July the Constituent Assembly voted by a show of hands to abolish the monarchy.

He was taken with members of his family to an abandoned palace in Manouba without water or electricity; two of his sons and his son-in-law were imprisoned. In October 1958 he and his wife were moved to a small villa in La Soukra, still under house arrest. She died two days after three days of interrogation about the family jewels, and his confinement was then lifted. He died in Tunis on 30 September 1962 and was buried beside her in the cemetery of Sidi Abdelaziz in La Marsa, not in the dynasty's mausoleum of Tourbet el Bey.
muhammad-al-idrisi: Al-Idrisi came from the Hammudid dynasty of North Africa and Al-Andalus, which claimed descent from Muhammad through the Idrisid dynasty. He is believed to have been born in Ceuta in 1100, at that time held by the Almoravids, where his great-grandfather had been forced to settle after Hammudid Málaga fell to the Zirids of Granada. He spent much of his youth travelling through North Africa and Al-Andalus and acquired detailed information on both regions. He visited Anatolia when he was barely sixteen and studied at the university in Córdoba. His travels also took him to Portugal, the Pyrenees, the French Atlantic coast, Hungary and Jórvík, now York.

Because of conflict and instability in Al-Andalus, al-Idrisi joined contemporaries such as Abu al-Salt in Sicily, where the Normans had overthrown Arabs who had been loyal to the Fatimids. He drew the Tabula Rogeriana in 1154 for King Roger II after a stay of eighteen years at the court, during which he worked on the commentaries and illustrations of the map. Its legends are in Arabic. It shows the Eurasian continent in its entirety but only the northern part of Africa, and it lacks detail for the Horn of Africa and Southeast Asia. For Roger the map was also inscribed on a massive disc of solid silver two metres in diameter.

Al-Idrisi combined knowledge of Africa, the Indian Ocean and the Far East gathered by Islamic merchants and explorers, recorded on Islamic maps, with the information brought by Norman voyagers. The map illustrates his Kitab nuzhat al-mushtaq, which may be translated A Diversion for the Man Longing to Travel to Far-Off Places. It survives in nine manuscripts, seven of them with maps. In its introduction he names Ptolemy and an astronomer, probably Ishaq ibn al-Hasan al-Zayyat, as sources for geographical coordinates and says he cross-checked oral reports from different informants. It records Chinese trade, mentioning the glassware of Hangzhou and the silk of Quanzhou. He also compiled a medical dictionary listing drugs and plants with their names in as many as twelve languages.

His work influenced Islamic scholars including Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi, Hafiz-i Abru and Ibn Khaldun, but it was unknown in Western Europe and had little effect on Renaissance cartography. An abridged Arabic text was printed in Rome in 1592, one of the first Arabic books ever printed. An abridged Latin translation appeared in Paris in 1619, and a complete French translation by Pierre Amédée Jaubert in the middle of the 19th century.
muhammad-ali-jinnah: Jinnah was born Mahomedali Jinnahbhai, probably on 25 December 1876, at Wazir Mansion near Karachi, then in the Bombay Presidency. His family came from Gujarat and had followed the Nizari Isma'ili branch of Shia Islam; he later followed Twelver Shia teachings, and after his death relatives and other witnesses claimed that he had turned to Sunni Islam. In 1892 a business associate of his father offered him an apprenticeship in London. He accepted despite his mother's opposition, and before he left she had him marry a cousin, Emibai. Both women died while he was in England, where he trained as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn.

Jinnah began practice in Bombay at the age of 20, the only Muslim barrister in the city. His first three years brought few briefs, but he later earned large fees. He also took an interest in labour causes: he was elected president of the All India Postal Staff Union in 1925 and helped to pass the Trade Union Act of 1926. In politics he rose in the Indian National Congress and worked to bring Congress and the Muslim League together. As president of the League in 1916 he signed the Lucknow Pact, which set quotas for Muslim and Hindu representation in the provinces, and Sarojini Naidu called him an ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity.

In 1920 he left Congress, which had agreed to a campaign of satyagraha that he regarded as political anarchy. In 1923 he was elected Muslim member for Bombay in the Central Legislative Assembly, and in 1925 he declined a knighthood from Lord Reading, saying he preferred to be plain Mr Jinnah. In the early 1930s Muslims urged him to resume leadership of the inactive League. Muhammad Iqbal, with whom he corresponded in 1936 and 1937, urged Muslims to strengthen his hands, and Jinnah later called Iqbal his mentor.

Until the late 1930s most Muslims of British India expected to belong to a single state after independence. After the Second World War began, the British increasingly treated Jinnah and the League as the representatives of India's Muslims, and the League passed the Lahore Resolution in 1940. Talks between Congress and the League failed to find a formula that would keep British India united, and the parties agreed instead to the independence of a Hindu-majority India and of Pakistan.

As first Governor-General, Jinnah worked to set up the new government and personally supervised refugee camps for the millions of Muslims who migrated to Pakistan. He fixed his salary at 1 rupee a month. He died on 11 September 1948, aged 71. He is revered in Pakistan as Quaid-e-Azam and Baba-e-Qaum, universities and public buildings bear his name, and his birthday is a national holiday.
muhammad-ali-of-egypt: Muhammad Ali was born on 4 March 1769 in a village in Albania, to ethnic Albanian parents from the Korça region. His family moved to Kavala, where his father Ibrahim Agha, a tobacco and shipping merchant, commanded a small Ottoman unit. After his father died, his uncle raised him and made him a collector of taxes. He then became second-in-command of the Kavala contingent of Albanian mercenaries sent in 1801 to retake Egypt from the French after the withdrawal of Napoleon Bonaparte.

Between 1801 and 1805 he worked with both the Ottomans and the Mamluks, allied himself with the Egyptian leader Umar Makram, and won the support of the public. In 1805 a group of prominent Egyptians led by the ulama demanded that Governor Hurshid Pasha be replaced by Muhammad Ali, and the Ottomans yielded. His aim was an Egypt ruled by his own hereditary dynasty, which required a reorganised society, a streamlined economy, a professional bureaucracy and a modern army. Recruits were housed in barracks under close surveillance, and each soldier was given a number identifying his unit and role.
He sent the first educational mission of Egyptian students to Europe in the 1820s, and the Bulaq Press, the first indigenous press in the Arab world, was founded in 1819 or 1821.

His first campaign was in Arabia, where his son Tusun led an expedition in 1811 and Hejaz was retaken in 1812; his son Ibrahim then crushed the Saudis, and their leader Abdullah ibn Saud was sent to Constantinople and executed. In 1820 an army of 5,000 under his son Ismail marched into Sudan, which he valued for territory, gold and slaves. In 1821 Sultan Mahmud II offered him Crete in return for help against the Greek rebels. Ibrahim led 16,000 soldiers to Greece, and on 20 October 1827 the entire Egyptian navy was sunk at Navarino by a fleet of Britain, France and Russia. On 31 October 1831 Ibrahim invaded Syria, beginning the First Turko-Egyptian War.

In his last years Muhammad Ali grew paranoid, and whether the cause was senility or the silver nitrate he had once been given for dysentery remains debated. He governed until 1848 and died on 2 August 1849. The prevailing view calls him the Father of Modern Egypt, the first ruler since the Ottoman conquest of 1517 to remove the sultan's power there for good. His central bureaucracy, schools and cotton economy lasted, and his descendants ruled Egypt and Sudan for nearly 150 years. Others see him as a conqueror: he was of Albanian origin, his court used Ottoman Turkish, and critics argue that he took Egyptian manpower for his own ends. Sudan remembers his rule there as brutal.
muhammad-bin-tughluq: Muhammad was the eldest son of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, and was known as Fakhr Malik Jauna Khan before he became sultan. In 1321 his father sent him to the Deccan to campaign against the Kakatiya dynasty, and in 1323 he besieged and took their capital Warangal, ending the dynasty and defeating King Prataparudra. He was skilled in Persian, Hindavi, Arabic, Sanskrit and Turkic and had an interest in medicine.

He ascended the throne on 4 February 1325, three days after his father's death. In his reign the sultanate took Warangal, Ma'abar and Madurai and reached the south of present-day Karnataka. In 1327 he ordered the capital moved from Delhi to Daulatabad, a more central site, and many who made the journey died of hunger and exhaustion on the road. In 1334 a rebellion in Mabar led by Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan founded the Madurai Sultanate. Plague struck his army at Bidar, and Mabar and Dwarsamudra broke away, followed by a revolt in Bengal. In 1335 he moved the capital back to Delhi.

In 1330 he issued token currency of brass and copper, with the value of gold and silver coins. Forgeries multiplied and the coins lost their value, and the experiment had ended by 1333. His expedition to Kumaon in 1333 ended in the near-destruction of his army, and his own generals rebelled. One of them, Hasan Gangu, went on to found the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan.

Muhammad died in 1351 on the way to Thatta in Sindh, while campaigning against the Taghi. During his reign the sultanate lost ground in Rajputana, and Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara Empire in the south.

Medieval writers such as Ziauddin Barani and Ibn Battuta, who visited his court, say Delhi was emptied by the move, though modern historians regard this as exaggeration. Historians disagree on his religious policy: some sources report intolerance, while Peter Jackson notes that he took part in Hindu festivities, and Jain writers record cordial relations with Jain scholars. Later historians called him the Wisest Fool.
muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab was born in 1703 into the Banu Tamim clan in Uyayna, a village in Najd in central Arabia. His father was the Hanbali jurisconsult of Najd and his grandfather a judge of Hanbali law. He left Uyayna around the age of twenty, in circumstances that are unclear, made the pilgrimage to Mecca and spent time in Medina, where he studied under Abdallah ibn Ibrahim ibn Sayf and Muhammad Hayat al-Sindi, who taught him to reject practices associated with saints and their tombs and to reject rigid imitation of medieval legal commentaries.

He then studied in Basra for four years, where his preaching against such practices brought a strong backlash and he was driven out of the town. He went on to Baghdad, where he married a wealthy woman, and travelled on before settling in Huraymila, where his father was judge. There he wrote the Kitab al-Tawhid, the Book of Oneness,.

Ibn Abd al-Wahhab taught that the primary doctrine of Islam was the oneness of God, tawhid. He judged much of the folk religion of Najd, including visits to the tombs of Companions, sacred trees and sacrifices before a blind sage, to be polytheism, shirk, resembling the pre-Islamic age. He called for a return to the Quran and hadith, opposed taqlid, the imitation of established opinion, and urged ijtihad, independent legal reasoning, by qualified scholars. His followers called themselves al-Muwahhidun, the Unitarians, and opponents named them Wahhabis after his father's name, a label many adherents reject. Some of his contemporaries, including Hanbali scholars, rejected his views.

Driven from Uyayna, he was invited to Diriyah by its ruler Muhammad ibn Saud. After some time in Diriyah the two agreed to bring the Arabs of the peninsula back to what they saw as the true principles of Islam. The alliance gave the Al Saud a religious mission and drove the expansion of the first Saudi state. A war with the chieftain of Riyadh lasted nearly thirty years until Abd al-Aziz conquered the town in 1773. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab then left government to Abd al-Aziz and devoted himself to teaching, preaching and worship. In 1787 he called on the people to swear allegiance to Saud, Abd al-Aziz's son, as heir. He died in 1792.
muhammad-ibn-qasim: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Thaqafi belonged to the Banu Thaqif, an Arab tribe centred on the city of Taif in western Arabia. His first assignment was in the province of Fars, where he subdued a group of Kurds and was appointed governor, probably succeeding his uncle Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi.

Umayyad interest in Sindh was stirred by pirates, among them the Meds, who preyed on shipping from bases at Kutch, Debal and Kathiawar. Muslim sources say that the kidnapping of Muslim women travelling from Sri Lanka by the Meds of Debal gave the pretext, and that Raja Dahir, the ruler, refused to release prisoners or pay compensation, saying that he had no control over the raiders.

Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the governor in Iraq, sent Muhammad against Sindh in 711, when he was in his teens, after two earlier commanders had failed. The army that left Shiraz held 6,000 Syrian cavalry and detachments of mawali, joined by camel cavalry and by reinforcements and catapults sent by sea to Debal, at the mouth of the Indus. Towns were given the choice of submitting peacefully or being attacked. Where they were taken by force, fighting men were executed and surviving dependants enslaved.

As governor of Sindh from 712 until his death he asked for acceptance of Muslim rule in return for non-interference in religious practice, so long as taxes and tribute were paid. Villages kept their headmen and their own laws, non-Muslims paid the jizya and Hindus and Buddhists were taken into the administration.

Al-Hajjaj died in 714 and Caliph al-Walid I a year later. The new caliph, Sulayman, took revenge on the generals close to al-Hajjaj. Muhammad was put in chains and died in Mosul on 18 July 715. Al-Baladhuri says that he was tortured to death by officials who had a grievance against al-Hajjaj's family; some sources place his burial in Makran. Dahir's son soon recaptured Brahmanabad.

Historians disagree about the conquest. Stanley Lane-Poole called it liberal, while early historians such as Elliot and Majumdar held that the conversion of Sindh was coercive. Others, among them Thomas W. Arnold, argue that it was largely peaceful. Conversion was in fact slow, and most of the population stayed Hindu. Port Qasim is named after him.
muhammad-iqbal: Iqbal came from a Punjabi family of Kashmiri ancestry and studied at Government College in Lahore, where he took his Master of Arts in 1899. He taught Arabic at the Oriental College, Lahore, and then philosophy at Government College. Encouraged by his teacher Sir Thomas Arnold, he went to England in 1905, took a second Bachelor of Arts at Trinity College, Cambridge, and was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn. In Germany he studied under Friedrich Hommel, and his thesis, The Development of Metaphysics in Persia, was published in London in 1908.

On his return he practised before the Chief Court of Lahore, where more than 100 reported judgements bear his name, but he gave most of his time to writing. He joined the Punjab Muslim League as one of its first joint secretaries, was elected to the Punjab Legislative Council in 1927 and criticised the Indian National Congress as dominated by Hindus. He became convinced that Muhammad Ali Jinnah alone could keep the League united, and corresponded with him.

Of his roughly 12,000 verses, about 7,000 are in Persian. Asrar-i-Khudi (Secrets of the Self, 1915) sets out his idea of khudi, the self, whose aim is self-realisation and which passes through stages toward becoming a vice-regent of God. Reynold Alleyne Nicholson's translation introduced his writing to Western readers. His first Urdu collection, Bang-e-Dara (1924), has three phases: patriotic and nature poems to 1905, poems on European society written in Europe, and poems on the heritage of the Muslim community, addressed to the Ummah.

His six English lectures, delivered at Madras, Hyderabad and Aligarh, appeared in 1930 as The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam. In the same year, in the Allahabad Address to the Muslim League, he outlined a political framework for the Muslim-majority regions of northwestern India. In the late 1930s he debated nationalism with Hussain Ahmad Madani, who defended a culturally plural India while Iqbal looked first to a Muslim community in Muslim-majority lands.

After a throat illness that began in 1933, Iqbal stopped practising law in 1934 and received a pension from the Nawab of Bhopal. He died in Lahore on 21 April 1938 and is buried in Hazuri Bagh, between the Badshahi Mosque and the Lahore Fort.

In Pakistan he is honoured as national poet, and 9 November, his birthday, is a public holiday. Many institutions bear his name, among them Allama Iqbal Open University and Allama Iqbal International Airport in Lahore. In Iran he is known as Iqbal of Lahore, and the Indonesian president Sukarno was among his admirers.
muhammad-naguib: Muhammad Naguib was born on 19 February 1901 in Khartoum, in Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, the eldest of nine children. His father was a ranking officer of the Egyptian Armed Forces, and his mother came from an Egyptian military family living in Omdurman. He attended secondary and military schools at Gordon Memorial College in Khartoum, graduating in 1918, and joined the Egyptian Royal Guard in 1923. In 1927 he became the first Egyptian military officer to obtain a law licence, and he took postgraduate degrees in political economy in 1929 and in civil law in 1931.

Naguib was promoted to captain in December 1931 and to major on 6 May 1938. In 1937 he founded a newspaper for the Egyptian Armed Forces in Khartoum. He became regional governor of the Sinai Peninsula in 1944 and a brigadier general in 1948. In the 1948 Arab-Israeli War he was wounded seven times and received the first military star of Fuad and the title of Bey. He was then made director of the Egyptian Military Academy, where Abdel Hakim Amer introduced him to the Free Officers.

Gamal Abdel Nasser had led the movement and felt it needed an older officer of distinguished record in order to be taken seriously. Naguib was invited to lead it. Historians note that he saw himself as its true leader, while the younger officers regarded him as a figurehead who would yield to their collective decisions. When the coup began on 23 July 1952 he was appointed Commander in Chief of the Army. On 26 July Ali Maher presented King Farouk with Naguib's ultimatum to abdicate, and Farouk sailed from Egypt the next day. Naguib became prime minister in September 1952, and when the republic was declared on 18 June 1953 he was sworn in as its first president.

He began to show independence from Nasser by distancing himself from the land reform decrees and drawing closer to the Wafd Party and the Muslim Brotherhood. In late 1953 Nasser accused him of supporting the outlawed Brotherhood and of dictatorial ambitions. Nasser won the struggle that followed and forced Naguib to resign in November 1954, then placed him under informal house arrest in a suburban Cairo villa. President Anwar Sadat released him in 1971.

Naguib died in Cairo on 28 August 1984 of liver cirrhosis, at the age of 83, and was given a military funeral attended by President Hosni Mubarak. Shortly before his death he published memoirs, which appeared in English as Egypt's Destiny. A Cairo Metro station and a major road in the Al Amarat district of Khartoum are named after him.
muhammad-of-ghor: Muhammad of Ghor, also called Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad ibn Sam, was born in Ghur in what is now west-central Afghanistan, the son of the Ghurid ruler Baha al-Din Sam I, who died in 1149. His birth year, about 1144, is worked out from the writings of Juzjani, who makes him three years and a few months younger than his brother Ghiyath al-Din, born in 1140. Their uncle Ala al-Din Husayn imprisoned both brothers, suspecting their loyalty, until his son freed them after his death in 1161. The brothers then ruled as a dyarchy. Ghiyath al-Din governed the west from Firozkoh and was engaged against the Khwarazmians, while Muhammad extended Ghurid rule eastwards from Ghazni.

Muhammad crossed the Indus in 1175 and took Multan from the Qarmatians. Near Mount Abu he was wounded and routed by a coalition of Rajput chiefs led by the Chaulukya king Mularaja, so he changed his route. He expelled the Ghaznavids by 1186, taking the upper Indus plain and most of Punjab, and secured the Khyber Pass.

In 1191 he was wounded at the first Battle of Tarain, defeated by the Rajput Confederacy under Prithviraj Chauhan, and returned to Khurasan. A year later he came back with a large army of mounted archers and won the second battle at the same place, and he executed Prithviraj shortly afterwards. In 1194 he defeated the Gahadavala king Jayachandra at Chandawar, and Varanasi was looted and Kanauj annexed in 1198. Most operations in India were left to slave commanders such as Qutb ud-Din Aibak, who pushed the frontier as far as Bengal and Bihar.

After Ghiyath al-Din died on 13 March 1203, Muhammad became supreme sultan. He suffered a heavy defeat at Andkhud against the Khwarazmians, who were aided by the Qara Khitai, and lost most of Khurasan.

While Muhammad was planning to avenge Andkhud, a rebellion by the Khokhars drew him to the Salt Range, where he crushed it. On 15 March 1206 he was assassinated at Dhamiak while at evening prayers. Sources name the Khokhars or Isma'ili emissaries. His only child, a daughter, had died before him, and his slaves and the Ghurid elite quarrelled over the succession. Muhammad II of Khwarazm annexed the Ghurid lands west of the Indus by 1215, but the conquests east of the Indus became the Delhi Sultanate under Aibak. At their height the Ghurids ruled a territory 3,000 km across, from Gorgan to Lakhnauti.
muhammad-shaybani: Muhammad Shaybani was a Shaybanid, a descendant of Shiban, son of Jochi Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan. His father was Budaq Sultan, one of the eleven sons of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, ruler of the Uzbek ulus, and his mother was Aq Quzi Begum. According to the historian Kamal ad-Din Binai, his father nicknamed him Shibägh, wormwood. Budaq Sultan was an educated man who had Persian works translated into Turkic, and Shaybani was fluent in both languages. He was fond of history in his youth, and in 1475 was presented with the Alexander Romance of Nizami Ganjavi.

He first appears leading 3,000 men in the army of the Timurid ruler of Samarkand, Sultan Ahmed Mirza. When Ahmed went to war with Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan over Tashkent, Shaybani secretly agreed with the Moghul khan to betray and plunder Ahmed's army, which he did at the Battle of the Chirciq River in 1488. Mahmud Khan rewarded him with Turkistan. There he oppressed the local Kazakhs, which led to a war between Moghulistan and the Kazakh Khanate that Moghulistan lost, while Shaybani's standing among the Uzbeks grew.

He ousted the Timurids from Samarkand in 1500, retook it in 1501, conquered Bukhara the same year and founded the Shaybanid dynasty of the Khanate of Bukhara. He fought successfully against Babur, later founder of the Mughal Empire, and married Babur's sister Khanzada Begum; Babur's freedom to leave Samarkand depended on his consent. He aligned himself with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II against the Shia Safavids. He patronised the Yemeni religious figure known as Mir-i Arab and wrote religious and philosophical works in Chagatai, among them the Bahr ul-Khudo of 1508. Raids on Kazakh lands in 1508–09 ended in a major defeat by Kasym Khan in 1510.

In 1510 Ismail I invaded western Khorasan. Shaybani had lost most of his cavalry in a campaign against the Hazaras, so he withdrew behind the walls of Merv. Ismail besieged the city for a month without result and then feigned a retreat. According to some sources the khan's emirs advised waiting for reinforcements, but his wife Aisha Sultan Khanum shamed the council into fighting. His army was surrounded by Ismail's 17,000 men and destroyed, and Shaybani was killed trying to escape, on 2 December 1510. Shaybani was succeeded by an uncle, a cousin and a brother, whose descendants ruled Bukhara until 1598 and Khwarezm until 1687.
muhammad-zia-ul-haq: Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq was born on 12 August 1924 in Jullundur, Punjab, into an Arain family. His father worked at the Army General Headquarters in Delhi and was noted for his religiousness. Zia studied history at St. Stephen's College in Delhi, graduating in 1943, and was commissioned into the British Indian Army, serving in a tank unit, the 13th Lancers, in the Burma campaign. After the Partition of India in 1947 he joined the army of Pakistan. He took part in the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965 as a tank commander, and from 1967 to 1970 headed a Pakistani training mission in Jordan.

In 1975 Zia commanded the II Corps at Multan, and on 1 March 1976 Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto made him Chief of Army Staff, choosing the most junior of eight lieutenant generals. Following civil disorder after the 1977 general election, Zia carried out a coup on 5 July 1977, codenamed Operation Fair Play, and Bhutto and his cabinet were arrested. Zia promised elections within 90 days, but they were postponed. The Supreme Court upheld the coup under the doctrine of necessity. Bhutto was arrested again on 3 September 1977 for authorising the murder of a political opponent, and on 18 March 1978 he was sentenced to death. Zia declared himself president on 16 September 1978.

In 1979 he banned all political parties and disbanded parliament, and at the end of 1981 set up a nominated consultative council, the Majlis-e-Shoora. After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan on 25 December 1979 he decided to support the Afghan mujahideen with American help, and Pakistan became the main base of the war against the Soviet forces. He lifted martial law in 1985, after non-partisan elections, but kept wide presidential powers through the Eighth Amendment, and in 1988 dismissed the government of Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo.

On 17 August 1988 Zia left Bahawalpur, where he had watched a tank demonstration, in a C-130B Hercules. Soon after take-off contact was lost, and witnesses said the plane flew erratically before it crashed. Twenty-nine others died, among them General Akhtar Abdur Rahman and the American ambassador Arnold Lewis Raphel. The cause has given rise to many conspiracy theories. Zia remains a polarising figure: some credit him with checking Soviet advance towards Pakistan, while critics hold that he weakened democratic institutions and passed laws that encouraged religious intolerance.
muharram: Muharram, meaning sacred, is the first month of the Islamic calendar, with at most thirty days. Warfare in it was forbidden before the advent of Islam. The word is short for Muharram Safar, the sacred Safar, which in the ancient Arab calendar distinguished Safar I, which was sacred, from Safar II, which was not. Over time the adjective itself became the name of the first month of the year.

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and months begin when the first crescent of a new moon is sighted. Because the lunar year is eleven or twelve days shorter than the solar year, Muharram falls on different days in successive solar years.

The tenth day of Muharram is Ashura. For Sunni Muslims it marks the parting of the Red Sea by Moses and the salvation of the Israelites, and tradition also places on this day Noah's disembarking from the Ark, God's forgiveness of Adam and the release of Joseph from prison. It is observed by voluntary fasting and other pious acts. Some Sunni communities hold carnivals, bonfires and special dishes, though some Sunni scholars have criticised such practices.

For Shia Muslims Ashura is a day of mourning for Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and the third imam. Husayn refused on moral grounds to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya and was killed, with most of his male relatives and his small retinue, by the Umayyad army at the Battle of Karbala on Ashura in 61 AH (680 CE). Sunnis also regard the killing of Husayn as a tragic event, and Husayn and his companions are widely regarded as martyrs by all Muslims.

The events of Karbala are remembered day by day. Husayn arrived there on 2 Muharram and was forced to camp in the desert; on 7 Muharram the Umayyad army cut off his access to the Euphrates; on 9 Muharram, called Tasu'a, negotiations failed and the commander Umar ibn Sa'd was persuaded to delay the attack until the next day. After the battle the women and children of the camp were taken prisoner and marched to Damascus.

Most Shia mourning takes place in the first ten days, ending with processions in major Shia cities on the tenth. Practices include gatherings in mosques and husayniyyas where scholars and maddahs recount Karbala, the recitation of elegies, charitable distribution of food and water, reenactments, and ritual chest-beating, called latmiyya or sīnah-zanī. Among the Shia, mourning for Husayn is viewed as protest against oppression and as a struggle for God.
muhlhausen: Mühlhausen lies in the northwest of Thuringia on the Unstrut river, on the eastern edge of the Hainich hills, in the flat and fertile Thuringian Basin at about 215 metres above sea level. It is 50 km north-west of Erfurt and 5 km north of Niederdorla, the geographical centre of Germany. Archaeological finds near St. George's Church show a large settlement of the Thuringii and Francia period, from the 6th to the early 10th century, which is seen as the origin of the town. After 1815 Mühlhausen belonged to the Prussian Province of Saxony, and industrialisation reached it late, around 1870, with the railway.

The town was first mentioned in 967, in a territory given by Otto II to his wife Theophanu. It belonged to the imperial estate, and emperors from Otto III to Henry III visited its Kaiserpfalz in the 10th and 11th centuries. The election of Philip of Swabia in 1198 ended with a homage there. Mühlhausen became a Freie Reichsstadt, an independent and self-ruled member of the Holy Roman Empire that controlled about 220 square kilometres and 19 villages, and with its long-distance trade it was prosperous, with some 10,000 inhabitants around 1500.

The Reformation brought disturbances. The monk Heinrich Pfeiffer preached at St. Mary's in 1523, and Thomas Müntzer in August 1524. They made political demands as well as religious ones, aimed at the privileges and oligarchic rule of the magistrates, and the council was replaced by an Eternal Council. During the German Peasants' War of 1524 and 1525 the monasteries were looted and churches stripped. After the imperial army defeated the uprising, Müntzer and Pfeiffer were executed, Müntzer on 27 May 1525 just outside the city. The city paid a fine of 40,000 guilders and lost part of its independence. The Reformation was introduced by force in 1542.

Because it was spared later destruction, Mühlhausen has one of the largest medieval city centres remaining in Germany, with eleven Gothic churches and an almost completely preserved fortification. St. Blaise's, first mentioned in 1227, is a major 13th-century church where Johann Sebastian Bach was organist in 1707 and 1708. St. Mary's, from the early 14th century, has the highest steeple in Thuringia and now houses a Müntzer memorial, opened in 1975. John A. Roebling, who built the Brooklyn Bridge, was born in the town.
muhu: Muhu is an island of Estonia in the West Estonian archipelago of the Baltic Sea. It has an area of 208 square kilometres and is the third largest island of Estonia, after Saaremaa and Hiiumaa.
