The Big Strait divides it from the mainland and the Little Strait from Saaremaa. The German and Swedish name for the island is Moon, and the waters to its north are called the Sea of Straits, or Moon Sound. With four neighbouring islets, Muhu forms a rural municipality in Saare County, whose main settlements are Kuivastu, Liiva and Koguva. Muhu is linked to Saaremaa by the Väinatamm causeway, opened in 1896.

In January 1227 an army of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, with Letts, Germans of Riga and native Livonians, 20,000 men commanded by William of Modena, crossed on sea ice from the mainland and attacked Saaremaa, the last holdout of the pagan Estonians. The Estonians surrendered on Muhu at a circular stronghold called Mona, whose earthworks are still preserved near the causeway between the islands. This ended the Estonian Crusade.

The Battle of Karuse, also called the Battle on the Ice, was fought on 16 February 1270 on the frozen Baltic Sea between Muhu and the mainland. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania won a decisive victory over the Livonian Order, in what was the fifth-largest defeat of the Livonian or Teutonic Orders in the 13th century. The same waters saw the Battle of Moon Sound between Russian and German naval forces in September and October 1917, during the First World War.

The island has a medieval Lutheran church, St. Catherine's, and the traditional village of Koguva, where the Muhu Museum stands. Muhu is known for having the only traditional windmills in Estonia that are still operational and for its traditional knitted stockings.
mukachevo: Mukachevo lies in the valley of the Latorica River in Zakarpattia Oblast, close to the borders of Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania. It is a rail terminus and highway junction. The name most probably derives from the Hungarian surname Muncas, from munkás, worker, though another theory points to a Proto-Slavic root meaning flour. Ukraine's parliament officially renamed the city from Mukacheve to Mukachevo in 2017, after it emerged that the former spelling, in use since 1947, had come about by a mistake.

Excavations have found a Celtic oppidum of the 3rd to 1st century BCE and an Iron Age Thracian fort in the area. Slavs settled it in the 6th century, and Hungarian tribes entered the Carpathian Basin in 895. In 1397 Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor, granted the town to the exiled prince of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania Fyodor Koriatovych, who settled many Ruthenians there; other sources say he bought it in 1396. It became a Hungarian royal free city in 1445 and later part of the Principality of Transylvania. Imre Thököly's revolt against the Habsburgs started from Munkács in 1678, and Palanok Castle was important in Ferenc II Rákóczi's war of independence.

After 1711 the city came under Austrian control. In 1726 the Habsburgs gave the castle and town to the Schönborn family, who settled many Germans there. The castle served as a prison from 1796 to 1897 and held the Greek leader Alexander Ypsilanti from 1821 to 1823.

Mukachevo became part of Czechoslovakia on 4 June 1920, was re-annexed by Hungary in 1938 by the First Vienna Award, passed to the Soviet Ukraine in 1945 and is now in Ukraine. Jews made up about half the town's population before the Second World War, and it was known for its Hasidic community under Chief Rabbi Chaim Elazar Spira, who led it from 1913 until his death in 1937. The remaining Jews, nearly 15,000 in the spring of 1944, were deported to Auschwitz. A new synagogue was dedicated in 2006. Palanok Castle dates from the 14th century.
mukalla: Mukalla lies on the Gulf of Aden, on the shores of the Arabian Sea, about 480 kilometres east of Aden, and is the most important port of the Hadhramaut region. It is not far from Qana, the ancient principal Hadrami trading post between India and Africa, with incense-producing areas in its hinterland. The name comes from the Arabic verb kala, to preserve or nurture, reflecting its role as a sheltered harbour. Earlier names include Al-Kheesa, meaning bay or cove, Bandar Yaqoub, after the saint Yaqoub bin Yusuf, who settled there about the 12th century, and Bandar Al-Naqeeb, after Captain Salah bin Hamad Al-Kassadi of the dynasty that governed the town in the 18th century.

Mukalla was founded in 1035 as a fishing settlement. In the 19th and 20th centuries the Kathiri and Qu'aiti sultanates struggled for control of it, and it became the capital of the Qu'aiti State of Hadhramaut. The Qu'aiti Sultanate belonged to the Eastern Aden Protectorate, and a British Resident Advisor was stationed in the town. The sultanates' other major cities were Ash-Shihr and Shibam.

Captain Haines, a British officer who surveyed Yemen in the 1830s, described Mukalla as a town of 4,500 inhabitants with a significant trade in slaves. Theodore Bent and Mabel Bent used it several times in the 1890s to enter and leave the Wadi Hadhramaut, and Theodore Bent called it the only spot between Aden and Maskat with any claim to the name of port.

In 1967 Mukalla lost its status as capital of the Qu'aiti Sultanate when it became part of the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen. After Yemeni unification in 1990 it became part of the present state of Yemen.

Mukalla is the capital city district of Hadhramaut, Yemen's largest governorate. The port lies east of the town, with an oil pipeline for tankers and a cement factory of an Omani-Yemeni company, and the main market souq is a commercial hub. The old town has the sultan's royal palace and guard towers that once served as outposts, and the Hadhramaut Mountains, such as Husn Ghuraf, lie nearby. The College of Medicine of Hadhramout University is in the city, and Riyan International Airport serves it.
mukden-incident: Japan's economic and political interest in Manchuria had grown since the end of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. The Treaty of Portsmouth gave Japan the lease of the South Manchuria Railway, and Japanese railway guards were stationed along it, though they often carried out manoeuvres outside the railway zone. Meanwhile the newly formed Chinese government sought to reassert its authority and challenged treaties with Japan. The Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin was assassinated by the Kwantung Army, and his son Zhang Xueliang joined the Nanjing government of Chiang Kai-shek. In 1929 the Soviet Red Army defeated Zhang Xueliang's forces in a conflict over the Chinese Eastern Railway, which revealed Chinese military weakness to Kwantung Army officers.

Colonel Seishirō Itagaki and Lieutenant Colonel Kanji Ishiwara planned to provoke an incident in order to prompt Japan to invade Manchuria. When the Minister of War sent Major General Yoshitsugu Tatekawa to curb the army's insubordination, they decided to stage the incident themselves. They chose a spot near Liutiao Lake, only eight hundred metres from the Chinese garrison at Beidaying. At about 10:20 p.m. on 18 September 1931, Lieutenant Suemori Kawamoto of the unit guarding the railway set off explosives beside the track. The blast damaged only a 1.5 metre section of one rail, and a train passed over it within minutes.

The army blamed Chinese dissidents and on 19 September opened fire on the Chinese garrison near Mukden. Five hundred Japanese troops attacked a garrison of around seven thousand, and by evening Mukden was occupied at the cost of five hundred Chinese lives and only two Japanese dead. General Shigeru Honjō, the commander of the Kwantung Army, at first objected that the plan had been carried out without his permission but then approved it. Zhang Xueliang had ordered his men not to resist. Within five months the Japanese army had overrun all the major towns of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang.

China appealed to the League of Nations, which on 24 October demanded Japanese withdrawal, but Japan refused. In March 1932 Japan established the puppet state of Manchukuo, with Puyi as head of state. The Lytton Report of 2 October 1932 rejected the claim that the invasion was self-defence, but did not say that the Japanese had set off the explosion. The League refused to recognise Manchukuo, and Japan left it in March 1933.

Strong evidence points to young Kwantung Army officers having plotted the blast, with or without orders from Tokyo. Historians differ over whether the Tokyo leadership shared their aims, the historian James Crowley arguing that the officers and the civilian leaders held the same overall intentions.
mukunda-deva: Mukunda Deva, also called Mukunda Harichandana, traced his descent from the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, and the traditions of Odisha call him Telinga Mukundadeva. His Bhimeswara temple inscription names his father as Saravaraju and his grandfather as Singaraju. He took the throne at Kataka in 1559 after killing Raghuram Raya Chotaraya, the last ruler of the Bhoi dynasty, and is counted as the founder and only monarch of a Chalukya dynasty of Odisha.

As king he tried to revive the power of Odisha. He laid out two streets from the Lion's Gateway to the Gundicha Temple and made the road smooth by filling its pits and holes. On the outer side of the southern walls he raised a swing arch, the Dola Mandap, on which the deities are swung during the Dola festival in the last five days of the month of Falguna. He also built a chain of forts at Raibania, in the present Balasore district.

His foreign relations were shaped by two powers: the Sultan of Bengal, his enemy, and the Mughal emperor Akbar, his ally. In 1560 Sultan Ghiyasuddin Jalal Shah of Bengal invaded and marched as far as Jajpur, and Mukunda Deva defeated him and drove him out.

In 1567, while Akbar was occupied with the invasion of Chittorgarh, the Karrani sultan of Bengal invaded. Mukunda Deva was defeated and took shelter in the fort of Kotsima, and the Bengal army under the general Kalapahada made a devastating attack on the capital, Cuttack. In the king's absence Ramachandra Bhanja, a feudatory of Sarangagarh, declared himself king. Mukunda Deva hurried back and met him in battle at Gohiratikiri, near Jajpur, where Mukunda Deva was killed.

Ramachandra Bhanja was himself later executed by the sultan's forces. Afterwards Ramachandra Deva I of the Bhoi dynasty, son of Danai Vidyadhara, allied himself with Akbar to avoid an Afghan invasion and continued to rule as a subordinate king of Odisha.
mullah-mohammad-omar: Mohammad Omar was born into a poor Pashtun farming family in Kandahar Province, in a year that is uncertain: sources give a date between 1950 and 1962. He came from a line of Islamic scholars; his father, a poor, landless itinerant teacher of the Quran, died when Omar was a small child, and his uncles raised him. After the Soviet invasion of 1979 he joined the mujahideen and fought in the districts of Maiwand, Zhari, Panjwai and Dand, and was wounded four times. He lost his right eye to shrapnel.

With the country in chaos as factions fought for control, Omar began a movement in 1994 with fewer than 50 armed madrasa students, who were known simply as the Taliban, Pashto for students. They fought warlord rule and corruption and were at first welcomed by Afghans weary of it. On 4 April 1996 his supporters gave him the title Amir al-Mu'minin, Commander of the Faithful. The Taliban formed a Sunni Islamic theocracy, the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, which strictly enforced Sharia. It was widely condemned for massacres of civilians, discrimination against minorities, and banning women from school and most employment.

In July 1999 Omar issued a decree in favour of preserving the Buddhas of Bamiyan, but in March 2001 an edict from him ordered that all the statues in Afghanistan be destroyed, and they were. In July 2000 he declared the growing of poppies un-Islamic, and opium cultivation in Taliban areas fell by 99 per cent. After the September 11 attacks of 2001, he refused to hand over Osama bin Laden. The American-led invasion began in October 2001, and on 5 December 2001 he handed the leadership to Mullah Obaidullah and two days later left Kandahar for Zabul Province.

Omar was the subject of an international manhunt, and the United States offered a reward of US$10 million. Research published in 2019 by the journalist Bette Dam indicates that he spent the rest of his life in Zabul Province. He died of tuberculosis on 23 April 2013, a fact first announced officially in July 2015 by Afghanistan's National Directorate of Security and confirmed by the Taliban the next day.

Little was publicly known of him; he made only one public speech and refused to meet foreigners, and only one confirmed photograph existed before his death. Taliban members regard him as a freedom fighter who defended Afghanistan's Islamic principles, while others criticise his method of governing and his religious dogmatism.
multan: Multan lies on the eastern bank of the Chenab River in the Punjab province of Pakistan and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Asia. The region holds archaeological sites of the early Harappan period of the Indus Valley Civilisation, dated between 3000 and 2800 BCE. Hindu texts say the sage Kashyapa founded it and that it was the capital of the Trigarta Kingdom during the Kurukshetra War of the Mahabharata. In the time of Alexander the Great the city stood on an island in the Ravi River, which has since shifted course many times. The origin of its name is unclear; an ancient name was Malli-istan, after the Malli tribe.

Multan is believed to have been the Malli capital that Alexander besieged in 326 BCE. During the siege of the citadel Alexander was wounded by an arrow that penetrated his lung. A Muslim army first invaded after the reign of the caliph Ali, in 664, but the expedition seems to have been one of exploration. Muhammad ibn Qasim took the city in 712 after a two-month siege, and its subjects remained mostly non-Muslim for some decades under the Umayyad Caliphate.

The Banu Munabbih came to rule Multan by the mid-800s, and in 855 it became capital of the Emirate of Multan. Multan attracted many Sufi mystics in the 11th and 12th centuries and is called the City of Saints. In 1445 it became capital of the Langah Sultanate. Akbar made it the headquarters of the Multan Subah, one of the Mughal Empire's largest provinces, and Mughal rule was re-established there in 1557.

Ahmad Shah Durrani captured Multan in 1752, and after repeated invasions following the collapse of the Mughal Empire the city declined from an important early-modern commercial centre to a regional trading town. The Sikh Empire ruled it from 1818 to 1849. By December 1848 the British had taken parts of the outskirts and destroyed the Multan Fort in bombardment; on 22 January 1849 they breached its walls and Diwan Mulraj surrendered. Between the 1890s and 1920s the British laid a vast network of canals across the region.

Multan is the administrative headquarters of its division and district, and a major cultural, religious and economic centre of the Punjab. With nearby Uch it is known for its large number of Sufi shrines, many dating from the medieval period. The old city, like other ancient cities in South Asia, had a walled town and a royal citadel, but Multan lost its citadel, largely destroyed by the British in 1848.
multatuli: Eduard Douwes Dekker was born in Amsterdam on 2 March 1820, the fourth of five children of a Mennonite family. His father, Engel Douwes Dekker, was a sea captain from the Zaan district, and his mother, Sietske Eeltjes Klein, was born on Ameland. He attended the Latin school on the Singel, and his father at first intended him to become a minister. He worked for a time as a clerk at a textile firm, and in 1838 sailed on one of his father's ships to Batavia, where he held colonial posts over the next two decades, starting in the accounting department, work he disliked.

In 1842 he became comptroller of the troubled district of Natal on Sumatra. A deficit in the funds, partly older than his time in office, brought a serious reprimand from General Andreas Victor Michiels and a temporary suspension. He refunded the deficit himself and was transferred, acknowledging that he was not well suited to administration. He married Everdine Hubertina van Wijnbergen on 10 April 1846.

In 1848 he became secretary to the Resident of Menado, Reinier Scherius, who shared his sense of fair play towards the indigenous population. He was promoted to Assistant Resident of Ambon at the end of 1851 but soon went on health leave to the Netherlands, where he stayed from 1852 to May 1855, gambling and running up debts. As Assistant Resident of Lebak on Java he protested openly against colonial abuses and was threatened with dismissal; he resigned and returned to the Netherlands.

Max Havelaar appeared in 1860 under the pen name Multatuli, Latin for "I have suffered much". His friend Jacob van Lennep had identifiable place names changed, yet the book caused great controversy. Defenders of colonialism accused him of exaggeration, and he was unsuccessfully pressed to withdraw it. It was read across Europe.

He followed it with Minnebrieven (1861), a satire in the form of a fictitious correspondence, and seven volumes of Ideën between 1862 and 1877, which first printed his novel Woutertje Pieterse. His play Vorstenschool was staged three years after publication, for fear of offending the king. He stopped writing in 1877, having settled about ten years earlier at Ingelheim am Rhein. In 2002 the Society of Dutch Literature named him the most important Dutch writer of all time.
mumbai: Mumbai lies on the Konkan coast of western India, on a narrow peninsula of Salsette Island bounded by the Arabian Sea, Thane Creek and Vasai Creek, at the mouth of the Ulhas River. It has a deep natural harbour. The city grew from an archipelago of seven islands: the Isle of Bombay, Parel, Mazagaon, Mahim, Colaba, Worli and Old Woman's Island, also called Little Colaba. Greater Mumbai covers 603 square kilometres in two districts, Mumbai City, the southern Island City, and Mumbai Suburban.

The islands were inhabited since the South Asian Stone Age. They became part of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, followed by the Satavahana dynasty in the 2nd century BCE, and Ptolemy mentioned them in 150 CE. The Koli fishing community, whose goddess Mumbadevi is believed to have given the city its name, settled the region around the beginning of the Common Era. The Delhi Sultanate and then the Gujarat Sultanate ruled them in the Middle Ages. The islands were ceded to the Portuguese in 1535 and in 1661 passed to the British Crown, which leased them to the East India Company in 1668.

Under British rule Bombay became the capital of the Bombay Presidency and a major trading and administrative centre. The Hornby Vellard project, begun in 1782 and completed in 1845, reclaimed land between the seven islands from the Arabian Sea and unified them. With new roads and railways and the cotton boom of the 19th century, it made the city a major seaport. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation was established in 1888. The city played a major part in the Indian independence movement. After 1947 it became the capital of Bombay State, and after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement the capital of Maharashtra in 1960.

Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra and the financial and commercial capital of India. Its population was 12,442,373 at the 2011 census, with more than 18 million in the metropolitan region. Its buildings from the British period, such as Victoria Terminus, are largely in the Gothic Revival style, while the Gateway of India is Indo-Saracenic and Marine Drive has many Art Deco buildings. The city is also the centre of Bollywood, the Hindi film industry, whose name blends Bombay and Hollywood.
munger: Munger lies on the south bank of the Ganges in Bihar, about 180 km east of Patna and 480 km west of Kolkata. It forms a twin city with Jamalpur and is the headquarters of Munger district and division. Historically it sat at a strategic bottleneck on the main route into Bengal from the west: steep hills blocked travel to the south, and the many tributaries of the Ganges were the obstacle to the north.

The town is said to have been founded by the Guptas in the fourth century CE. In the classical period it was called Guptagadh or Guptagarh, and an inscription on a rock at the kasta-harani ghat, near the north-western side of the present fort, names it as founded by Chandragupta Vikramaditya. In early medieval times it was Mudgagiri, from the Sanskrit mudga, the mung bean, and giri, hill. It was a royal residence of the Pala Empire, and a significant battle between the Palas and the Pratiharas was fought there as part of a Pratihara invasion of Bengal.

It was later mentioned as the residence of the Pala ruler Ramapala. In the twelfth century it seems to have been under Sena rule, and in April 1146 the Gahadavala ruler Govindachandra advanced as far as Mudgagiri and bathed in the Ganges, probably on an unsuccessful expedition to Bengal.

At the end of the twelfth century Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Munger and Patna. The region was a province of Bengal until 1330, when Muhammad Tughlaq annexed it, and from 1397 it belonged to the Jaunpur Sultanate until Sikander Lodi overran Bihar before 1499. In 1521 Nusrat Shah annexed a few of its forts, and it later fell to Sher Shah Suri. From 1545 the Karrani dynasty held it until Akbar's invasion of Bengal.

In 1763 the Nawab of Bengal Mir Qasim made Munger his capital and built an arsenal and several palaces. The British, who took Bihar in the 1760s, made it a municipality in 1864 and set up the railway workshops at Jamalpur in 1862.

The fort covers about 222 acres and holds the tomb of the Muslim saint Shah Mushk Nafā, who died in 1497. Munger is also known for the Bihar School of Yoga, founded in 1964, and for the Sitacharan temple on a boulder in the Ganges, a centre of the Chhath festival.
munich: Munich lies on the elevated plains of Upper Bavaria, in the Northern Alpine Foreland, about 50 kilometres north of the Alps and about 520 metres above sea level. The rivers Isar and Würm flow through the city. The northern part of the plateau is a fertile flint area, the southern part is covered with morainic hills, and between them lie outwash plains where groundwater rising through the gravel has formed marshes in the north.
The name goes back to a tiny monastic settlement of the 10th century called zu den Munchen, 'to the monks'; the Old High German Munche is the base of the modern München.

The Isar was a prehistoric trade route, and in the Bronze Age Munich was among the largest raft ports in Europe; settlements up to four thousand years old have been found, along with Celtic settlements of the Iron Age. The Roman road Via Julia, linking Augsburg and Salzburg, crossed the Isar south of the city. From the 6th century the Baiuvarii settled the area, and the first known Christian church was built in Fröttmanning around 815. Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, founded the town to control the salt trade after burning down Föhring and its bridges over the Isar; historians date this to about 1158.

Munich remained Catholic during the Reformation and became the capital of the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. Its population, only 24,000 in 1700, doubled about every 30 years: 100,000 in 1852, 250,000 in 1883 and 500,000 in 1901. The House of Wittelsbach ruled until 1918, when the German revolution of 1918–1919 ended its reign and brought the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic. In the 1920s the city became a centre of political movements, including the rise of the Nazi Party, and it was known as the Capital of the Movement. Munich was heavily bombed in the Second World War, though much of its historic architecture has since been restored. It passed one million inhabitants in 1957 and hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

Munich is the capital of Bavaria and the third-largest city in Germany, with about 1.5 million inhabitants. It is the seat of the Bavarian Landtag and of institutions such as the Federal Finance Court and the European Patent Office. The old town centres on the Marienplatz, with the Old Town Hall and the New Town Hall, and includes the Frauenkirche, the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising, and the Michaelskirche. Nymphenburg Palace was begun in 1664, the Englischer Garten was laid out between 1789 and 1807, and the city is known for the annual Oktoberfest.
munich-agreement: Czechoslovakia was created in 1918 after the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Its population included more than three million Germans, 22.95 percent of the total, who lived mostly in the border regions that came to be called the Sudetenland. They had not been consulted on becoming citizens, and although the constitution promised equality they remained underrepresented in the government and the army. By 1936 60 percent of the unemployed in Czechoslovakia were Germans.

Britain and France wished to avoid war. The French government followed the British government of Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, who considered the Sudeten German grievances justified. Both advised Czechoslovakia to give way to German demands. President Beneš resisted and ordered a partial mobilisation on 19 May 1938. Hitler later signed a secret directive for war against Czechoslovakia to begin no later than 1 October.

Chamberlain asked Hitler for a personal meeting and flew to Germany on 15 September. At Berchtesgaden Hitler insisted that the Sudeten Germans be allowed national self-determination and union with Germany. On 17 September Germany began a low-intensity undeclared war on Czechoslovakia, and on 20 September Britain and France formally asked Czechoslovakia to cede the Sudetenland. Poland and Hungary made territorial demands on 21 and 22 September.

The emergency meeting of the main European powers took place in Munich on 29 and 30 September. Czechoslovak representatives were in the town but were not admitted. A deal was reached on 29 September, and at about 1:30 a.m. on 30 September 1938 Hitler, Chamberlain, Benito Mussolini and Édouard Daladier signed the agreement. The German army was to complete the occupation of the Sudetenland by 10 October, and an international commission would decide the future of other disputed areas. Britain and France told Czechoslovakia it could resist Germany alone or submit, and on 30 September its government reluctantly capitulated.

Many Czechs and Slovaks call the agreement the Munich Diktat or the Munich Betrayal. Czechoslovakia lost its defensible border and fortifications, 70 percent of its iron and steel industry and 3.5 million citizens. On 2 November the First Vienna Award gave southern Slovakia and southern Subcarpathian Rus' to Hungary, and on 30 November Poland received small areas in Spiš and Orava. In March 1939 the First Slovak Republic declared independence as a German puppet state, and Hitler broke his promise to respect the country's integrity by occupying the rest and creating the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.

Much of Europe welcomed the agreement as a way of preventing a major war. Later it came to be regarded as a failed act of appeasement. Chamberlain was attacked as one of the Men of Munich in the 1940 book Guilty Men,.
muqaddimah: Ibn Khaldun wrote the first version of the Muqaddimah in Qalʿat ibn Salama, where he secluded himself for almost four years after withdrawing from political life. It was the first of three parts of a project on which he worked for almost thirty years, the Kitab al-ʿIbar, or Book of Lessons, a universal history that fills seventeen volumes of 500 pages each in its modern edition. A draft of the Muqaddimah was completed in 1377. Manuscripts copied in his lifetime survive, some with his own marginal notes, and already in his lifetime it came to be regarded as a work in its own right.

Ibn Khaldun begins with a criticism of the errors his fellow historians regularly commit. He lists seven, among them partisanship towards a creed or opinion, over-confidence in sources, failure to place an event in its context, the wish to flatter the powerful, and, most important, ignorance of the laws governing the transformation of human society. Against this seventh point he sets out his theory of society.

Its best known concept is ʿasabiyyah, group feeling or social cohesion. As it declines, a more compelling ʿasabiyyah may take its place, so that civilisations rise and fall. Ruling houses tend to emerge on the peripheries of great empires and use the unity found there to bring about a change of leadership. Once settled at the centre, the rulers grow lax and concerned with their lifestyles, and a new dynasty emerges at the periphery to begin the cycle again. His framework contrasts nomadic life with sedentary life. The book also discusses economics, political theory, theology, law, and alchemy, which he refutes on social, scientific, philosophical and religious grounds.

The Muqaddimah is held to be a foundational work for historiography, cultural history and the philosophy of history. Ibn Khaldun criticised idle superstition and uncritical acceptance of historical data, and called his approach a new science. He treated the past as strange and in need of interpretation, and he questioned the sizes of armies in earlier accounts by considering military logistics, including those given by the historian al-Masudi.

Some modern thinkers view it as the first work to deal with sociology, demography and cultural history. Dawood described it as the earliest attempt by any historian to discover a pattern in changes in political and social organisation. Its attention to systemic bias in the making of history is said not to have been matched, apart from al-Maqrizi, until Hegel, Marx and Nietzsche in nineteenth-century Germany.
murad-i: Murad I was the son of Orhan Gazi and Nilüfer Hatun, a slave concubine of ethnic Greek descent. He took the nickname Hüdavendigâr, from a Persian word meaning sovereign. He came to the throne after the death of his elder half-brother Süleyman Pasha. Ottoman sources give him many titles, among them Bey, Great Emir, Ghazi, Khan, Padishah and Sultan of sultans, while Bulgarian and Serbian sources call him Tsar and a Genoese document names him master lord of the Turks.

Murad conquered Adrianople in the 1360s and made it the Ottoman capital. He then brought most of the Balkans under Ottoman rule and forced the princes of Serbia, the emperor of Bulgaria and the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos to pay him tribute. He divided his realm administratively into two provinces, Anatolia and Rumelia, the Balkans. He fought the beylik of Karaman in Anatolia, and in Europe the Serbs, Albanians, Bulgarians and Hungarians.

On 26 September 1371 a Serbian expedition to drive the Turks from Adrianople, led by King Vukašin and Despot Uglješa, was defeated by Murad's lieutenant Lala Şâhin Paşa, the first governor of Rumeli. Sofia fell to the Ottomans in 1385. In 1386 Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović beat an Ottoman force at the Battle of Pločnik, where the Ottomans suffered heavy casualties and could not take Niš on the way back. In 1378 he married his daughter to the ruler of Karaman in an unsuccessful attempt to stop the war with it.

Murad's army met the Serbian army and its allies under Lazar at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, and both Lazar and the sultan died there. Accounts of how Murad was killed were recorded decades later, in the 15th century and after. Some name the Serbian knight Miloš Obilić, who stabbed him, either early in the battle or, in most Ottoman chronicles, while he inspected the field after it had ended. His son Bayezid I, who commanded the left wing, took charge and had his brother Yakub strangled, so that he alone claimed the throne.

Murad's internal organs were buried on the battlefield, at a place called Meshed-i Hudavendigar, and the rest of his remains were taken to Bursa, to a tomb in the complex built in his name. Ottoman sources describe a charitable, just ruler devoted to holy war, while Byzantine sources remember a man who spoke little but eloquently, was fond of hunting, was merciful to Christians and was always successful against his enemies.
murad-ii: Murad was born in June 1404 to Mehmed I. The identity of his mother is disputed: a 15th-century historian called her a concubine, a 20th-century writer named Şahzade Hatun, daughter of Divitdar Ahmed Pasha, and the most widely accepted view is that she was Emine Hatun of the Dulkadirid Beylik. He spent his early childhood in Amasya, came to the capital Edirne with his father in 1410, and was made governor of the Amasya Sanjak after Mehmed became sultan. When Mehmed I died in 1421 Murad was recognised as sultan at 16 and girded with the Sword of Osman at Bursa.

His reign was troubled by insurrection from the start. The Byzantine Emperor Manuel II released a pretender, Düzmece Mustafa, who defeated Murad's general Bayazid Pasha and declared himself Sultan of Adrianople. Murad out-manoeuvred him, his troops defected, and with help from a Genoese commander named Adorno he besieged and stormed Gallipoli, where Mustafa was taken and put to death. Murad then formed a new army, the Azeb, and besieged Constantinople, but had to abandon the siege when the Byzantines, in league with Anatolian states, sent his 13-year-old brother Küçük Mustafa to rebel and besiege Bursa. Murad executed him and annexed the Aydinid, Germiyanid, Menteshe and Teke states.

He defeated the Karamanids in 1428, and Venice withdrew in 1432 after Murad took Thessalonica in 1430. In the 1430s he captured large territories in the Balkans and annexed Serbia in 1439. He won the Crusade of Varna against John Hunyadi in 1444, and at Varna, according to the chronicles, he dismounted to pray as the Hungarians gained ground, and Władysław III of Poland, King of Hungary, was killed in a charge. Exhausted by war and by the death of his son Shehzade Alaedin, he signed the Peace of Szeged and abdicated in favour of his son Mehmed II, then 12. A rebellion at Edirne in 1446, probably sparked by debasement of the akçe, brought about Murad's return to the throne.

He presented himself as a ghazi sultan, modelling his conduct on the caliph of the epic Battalname, and a collection of his campaigns was given the title The Ghazas of Sultan Murad. His reign saw an increase in trade and the growth of cities; in 1432 the traveller Bertrandon de la Broquière noted that Ottoman annual revenue had risen to 2,500,000 ducats.
murad-iii: Murad was born in Manisa on 4 July 1546 to Şehzade Selim and his powerful consort Nurbanu Sultan, and was a grandson of Suleiman I and Hürrem Sultan. He learned Arabic and Persian, and after his ceremonial circumcision in 1557 Suleiman appointed him governor of Akşehir in 1558. In 1564 he became governor of Saruhan with Manisa as his seat, and he remained there during his father's reign, continuing his education under the historian Hoca Sadeddin Efendi. Contemporary accounts describe him there as highly educated, talented and deeply religious.

Murad succeeded Selim II in December 1574. His authority was increasingly influenced by the imperial harem, above all by his mother and later by his favourite consort Safiye Sultan, often at the expense of the Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, who served until his assassination in October 1579. In 1576 Abd al-Malik and Ramazan Pasha set out from Algiers with an army of about 10,000, mostly Ottoman Turks, and restored Abd al-Malik to the Moroccan throne as an Ottoman client. His brother Ahmad al-Mansur at first recognised Ottoman suzerainty but declared full independence in 1582.

The Ottomans had been at peace with the Safavids since the Treaty of Amasya of 1555. In 1577 Murad declared war to take advantage of the disorder at the Safavid court after the death of Shah Tahmasp I, influenced by the viziers Lala Kara Mustafa Pasha and Sinan Pasha and against the counsel of Sokollu. The Ottoman–Safavid War of 1578 to 1590 ended with the Treaty of Constantinople, which brought temporary significant gains. Admiral Mir Ali Beg established Ottoman supremacy in cities on the Swahili coast between Mogadishu and Kilwa, and Ottoman suzerainty was recognised in Mogadishu in 1585.

By 1580 an influx of silver from the New World had caused high inflation and unrest, especially among the Janissaries and officials paid in debased currency. Ottoman and Habsburg sources accuse Murad himself of taking large bribes. He exchanged letters and envoys with Elizabeth I, and England exported tin, lead and ammunition to the Ottomans. Like his father, Murad never went on campaign; in his last years he did not leave Topkapı Palace, and the historians Mustafa Âlî and Mustafa Selaniki disapproved of his sedentary life. He commissioned the Siyer-i-Nebi and other illustrated manuscripts.
murano: Murano is made up of seven islands in the Venetian Lagoon, linked by bridges over eight channels. It measures about 1.5 kilometres across. It was once an independent comune but is now a frazione of the comune of Venice. Its countryside was known for orchards and vegetable gardens until the nineteenth century, when more housing was built.

Murano was first settled by the Romans and, from the sixth century, by people from Altinum and Oderzo. At first it prospered as a fishing port and through the production of salt. From the eleventh century it began to decline as islanders moved to Dorsoduro. It had a Grand Council like that of Venice, but from the thirteenth century it was governed by a podestà from Venice. Unlike the other islands of the lagoon, Murano minted its own coins.

Early in the second millennium hermits of the Camaldolese Order founded the Monastery of St Michael, which became a great centre of learning and printing. The cartographer Fra Mauro, whose maps were important to European exploration, was a monk there. French forces under Napoleon suppressed it in 1810 and the grounds became Venice's major cemetery.

In 1291 all the glassmakers of Venice were required to move to Murano, since the Republic feared fire among the city's mostly wooden buildings. Exports began in the following century, at first of glass beads and mirrors. Aventurine glass was invented on the island, and for a while Murano was the main producer of glass in Europe.

By the fourteenth century glassmakers were allowed to wear swords, were immune from prosecution by the Venetian state, and saw their daughters marry into Venice's wealthiest families, but they were forbidden to leave the Republic. Many took the risk and set up furnaces in other cities, sometimes in England and the Netherlands.

Murano held a monopoly on high-quality glass for centuries and developed or refined optically clear glass, enamelled glass, aventurine, multicoloured millefiori, milk glass called lattimo and imitation gemstones. The Republic partly lost its monopoly at the end of the sixteenth century, when some glassmakers let the secrets be known in other European countries. Decline set in during the eighteenth century, yet glassmaking is still the island's main industry. The Murano Glass Museum is housed in the Palazzo Giustinian.
murasaki-shikibu: Murasaki Shikibu is a descriptive name, and her personal name is unknown, though she may have been the Fujiwara no Kaoruko mentioned in a court diary of 1007. She was born in Heian-kyō around 973 into the northern Fujiwara clan. Her branch of the family had declined from the top tier of the aristocracy by the time of her birth. Her father, Fujiwara no Tametoki, was a respected scholar of Chinese classics and poetry who entered public service around 968 and held a governorship from 996 to about 1018.

Heian women were excluded from learning Chinese, the written language of government, but Murasaki, raised in her father's household, showed an aptitude for the Chinese classics and acquired fluency. In 996 she went with her father to his governorship in Echizen Province. She returned to Kyoto probably in 998 to marry Fujiwara no Nobutaka, a much older second cousin. Her husband died after two years of marriage.

It is uncertain when she began The Tale of Genji, but it was probably while she was married or soon after she was widowed. About 1005 Fujiwara no Michinaga invited her to serve as a lady-in-waiting to his daughter, Empress Shōshi, probably because of her reputation as a writer. She continued to write at court, adding scenes of court life to her work. Michinaga probably wanted Shōshi to surround herself with skilled women such as Murasaki to build a rival salon.

Murasaki taught Shōshi classical Chinese in secret, since written Chinese was regarded as the language of men; the scholar Richard Bowring calls it almost subversive. A lady-in-waiting who disliked her nicknamed her The Lady of the Chronicles after chapters of Genji were read aloud to the Emperor and one courtier remarked on the author's learning. When Emperor Ichijō died in 1011, Shōshi retired to a Fujiwara mansion near Lake Biwa, and Murasaki most likely went with her. Most scholars date her death to 1014, while others suggest she lived with Shōshi until about 1025.

Three works are attributed to her: The Tale of Genji, The Diary of Lady Murasaki and Poetic Memoirs, a collection of 128 poems. Her work reflects the shift of Japanese from an unwritten vernacular to a written language, after the development of the kana script in the mid-to-late 9th century. Within a decade of its completion Genji was circulating in the provinces, and within a century it was recognised as a classic of Japanese literature. Since the 13th century Japanese artists have illustrated her works.
murcia: Murcia lies on the Segura River in the south-east of the Iberian Peninsula, near the centre of a low-lying fertile plain known as the huerta, the orchard of Murcia. The river has flooded the city many times, in 1651, 1879, 1946 and 1948 among other years, and a levee was built. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with mild winters and very hot summers. Because of its long agricultural tradition and its fruit, vegetables and flowers, the city is called Europe's orchard.

The city on its present site was founded in 825 as Madinat Mursiyah by Abd ar-Rahman II, then emir of Córdoba. Umayyad planners used the course of the Segura to create a complex network of irrigation channels that made the town's agriculture prosperous. The name is widely thought to come from the Latin myrtea, land of the myrtle.

After the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031 Murcia became the capital of its own kingdom under Ibn Tahir. Ibn Mardanis made it the capital of a new independent kingdom after the fall of the Almoravid empire. It was famed for ceramics exported to Italian towns and for silk and paper industries, and the mystic Ibn Arabi (1165-1240) was born there. The Almohades conquered it in 1172.

By the Treaty of Alcaraz in 1243 Ferdinand III of Castile made Murcia a protectorate. Christians became the majority as immigrants arrived, while Muslims were confined to the suburb of Arrixaca. A Muslim revolt in 1264 was put down by James I of Aragon in 1266. In 1304 the Treaty of Torrellas incorporated the city finally into Castile. Murcia flourished after the conquest of Granada in 1492 and again in the 18th century, with a boom in silk. Napoleonic troops looted it in 1810, and an earthquake in 1829 killed an estimated 6,000 people across the province.

Murcia is the capital of the autonomous community of the Region of Murcia, created in 1982, and is mainly a services city and a university town. Its main sights are the Cathedral of Murcia, baroque buildings and the works of the sculptor Francisco Salzillo. The Holy Week procession and the Fiestas de Primavera are its main festivals.
mures-river: The Mureș rises in the Hășmașu Mare Range, close to the headwaters of the river Olt, and joins the Tisza at Szeged in south-eastern Hungary. Its drainage basin covers about 30,332 square kilometres. It flows through the Romanian counties of Harghita, Mureș, Alba, Hunedoara, Arad and Timiș and the Hungarian county of Csongrád. Its largest cities are Târgu Mureș, Alba Iulia, Deva and Arad in Romania and Makó and Szeged in Hungary. For 73 kilometres in its Hungarian reach it forms the state border, and part of the northern bank there belongs to the Körös-Maros National Park.

Since ancient times the Mureș has been a heavily used waterway for trade and for military purposes, a kind of highway for the area north of the Danube. Herodotus is the first to mention it, as Maris, Strabo calls it Marisos, and a document of the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII from 948 calls it Morisis. It was known in German as the Mieresch, because of the Transylvanian Saxon settlements and Habsburg rule, and in Turkish as the Maroş under the Ottomans.

From the Dacian-Roman wars onward control of the river was a key aim of the Roman army against the defences of the Dacian Kingdom. In the opening operations of Trajan's Second Dacian War a force from Pannonia Inferior under Aelius Hadrianus, the later Emperor Hadrian, is thought to have advanced into Dacia by the Mureș valley, probably using the river fleet, the Classis Flavia Pannonica. Gold, iron, salt and wood went by water to Rome and the western provinces. Apulum, where the river route met the main imperial road of the province, was the most important civilian river port of Roman Dacia. In medieval times salt was still traded down the river on large rafts.
murom: Murom lies on the Oka River in Vladimir Oblast, close to the border with Nizhny Novgorod Oblast and 137 kilometres from the oblast's administrative centre, Vladimir. Its name comes from the Muroma, a Finnic tribe that lived in the area. In the 9th century it was the easternmost settlement of the East Slavs in the land of the Muroma.

The Primary Chronicle mentions Murom as early as 862, which makes it one of the oldest cities in Russia. Around 900 it was an important trading post on the route from Volga Bulgaria to the Baltic Sea. Between 1010 and 1392 it was the capital of a separate principality. Its rulers included Gleb, who was assassinated in 1015 and canonized in 1071, Konstantin the Blessed, and Peter and Fevronia of Murom, who are the subjects of an opera by Rimsky-Korsakov. The town was also believed to be the home of the epic hero Ilya Muromets.

With the Principality of Ryazan, Murom bore the brunt of attacks from the east, since it formed the south-eastern border of Russia, and as a result it became dependent on the other Russian principalities. Vasily I of Moscow received the patent for the throne of Murom in 1392, and the principality was incorporated into the Grand Principality of Moscow.

Murom keeps many marks of antiquity. The Transfiguration Monastery, one of the oldest in Russia, was first chronicled in 1096, when Oleg of Chernigov besieged it and killed Vladimir Monomakh's son Izyaslav, who is buried there. Ivan the Terrible visited it in 1552 and commissioned a stone cathedral. The Trinity Convent displays the relics of Saints Peter and Fevronia and has a cathedral of 1642 to 1643. The tent-like church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, built in 1565 on the bank of the Oka, commemorates the Russian conquest of Kazan. A statue of Ilya Muromets shows him holding his sword's hilt in one hand and a cross in the other.
murshidabad: Murshidabad lies on the eastern bank of the Bhagirathi River in West Bengal and is the headquarters of the Lalbag subdivision of Murshidabad district. The area was part of the Gauda Kingdom and the Vanga Kingdom in ancient Bengal. The Riyaz-us-Salatin credits the initial development of the town to a merchant named Makhsus Khan. In the 17th century the area was well known for sericulture, and in 1621 English agents reported large quantities of silk available there.

In the early 18th century Murshid Quli Khan, prime minister of the Bengal Subah, had a bitter rivalry with Prince Azim-ush-Shan, the viceroy of Bengal, who even tried to have him killed. With the Mughal court in Delhi losing authority, Emperor Farrukhsiyar promoted Khan to the status of a princely Nawab. He moved the capital of Bengal from Dhaka, which had lost its strategic importance after the expulsion of the Arakanese and Portuguese from Chittagong, and founded Murshidabad. It became the centre of political, economic and cultural life, and the Nawab's jurisdiction covered Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The capital of the Bengal Subah stayed there for seventy years.

The princely court, the Mughal Army, artisans and merchants of many origins brought wealth. The Murshidabad mint became the largest in Bengal. Murshid Quli Khan built a palace and a caravanserai with a grand mosque, the Katra Masjid, and the third Nawab, Shuja-ud-Din Muhammad Khan, built a compound called Farrabagh with a revenue office, a durbar hall and a treasury. Siraj-ud-Daulah built a palace near the Motijhil. Jain traders, Armenian financiers and the banking family of the Jagat Seth family settled in the city, and the French, Dutch, Danish and British East India Companies and the Ostend Company operated factories nearby.

Siraj-ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab, was defeated at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, betrayed by his commander Mir Jafar. The British installed Mir Jafar's family as a puppet dynasty and reduced the Nawab to a zamindar. Warren Hastings moved the supreme civil and criminal courts to Calcutta in 1772, and in 1790 Lord Cornwallis moved the whole revenue and judicial staff there. The Hazarduari Palace was built in 1837.
The Hazarduari Palace and its associated sites in the Kila Nizamat area, with the Katra Masjid, the Fauti Mosque, the Jama Masjid and the Motijhil, are the town's main attractions.
murska-sobota: Murska Sobota lies near the Mura river in north-eastern Slovenia and is the regional capital of Prekmurje and the centre of its own municipality. Inhabitants usually call it simply Sobota, while people from other parts of Slovenia say Murska. Its German name is Olsnitz, derived from an old Slovene name, Olšnica. The modern Slovene name translates the Hungarian Muraszombat, the official name until 1919; szombat means Saturday and refers to the weekly fairs held on that day. The settlement is first attested in writing in 1297 as Belmura, and later as Murazombatha in 1348 and Murazumbota in 1366.

The town was part of the Balatin Sanjak under Ottoman rule, which belonged first to the Budin Eyalet and later to the Kanije Eyalet, until the Treaty of Karlowitz. In the Kingdom of Hungary it was a district town of Vas County until 1918. In 1919 a republic of Prekmurje was declared here, and the town was its capital. Murska Sobota later stood as the northernmost town of Yugoslavia, and its borders shifted repeatedly between Slovenia, Yugoslavia and Hungary. Hungary annexed most of Prekmurje from 1941 to 1944, German forces occupied it in 1944 and 1945, and Soviet troops captured the town in May 1945.

The town had a significant Jewish community. Its synagogue, built by Lipót Baumhorn, was consecrated on 31 August 1908. On 26 April 1944 all the Jews of the town were ordered to gather there with hand luggage only and were locked in overnight without food or water. The next morning they were sent to Čakovec and then to Nagykanizsa, the main camp before Auschwitz, where the last rabbi, Lazar Roth, was murdered. The community was destroyed, and the local communist authorities, having bought the building from the decimated congregation, demolished the synagogue in 1954.

Hungarians still form a minority of about 3,000 in the town. Its economy rests on regional administration, light industry, commerce and spa tourism. In April 2006 it became the seat of the newly created Roman Catholic Diocese of Murska Sobota, a suffragan of the archdiocese of Maribor. A memorial to the Jews of Prekmurje, the first Holocaust memorial in Slovenia, was unveiled at its railway station on 29 January 2010.
murzuq: Murzuq, also spelled Murzuk, is an oasis town and the capital of the Murzuq District in the Fezzan region of south-western Libya. It lies on the northern edge of the Murzuq Desert, an extremely arid region of ergs, or great sand dunes, that forms part of the Sahara.

The town developed around an oasis that served as a stop on the north-south trade route across the Sahara. From the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE the area was home to the Garamantian Empire, a city state that operated the trans-Saharan routes between the Carthaginians, and later the Roman Empire, and the states of West and Central Africa. By 1300 the Arab Banu Sulaym tribe ruled the area. By 1400 it was ruled by the Bornu Empire, whose legacy survives in street names in the Kanembu and Kanuri languages, and in the later 15th century it became a tributary of the Hafsid dynasty of Tunis.

Early in the 16th century Muhammad al-Fasi founded the Awlad Muhammad dynasty, which held power in the city until 1812. Tradition holds him to be a Moroccan sharif. His dynasty reinvigorated pilgrim traffic and the slave trade, and Murzuq became part of a slaving network reaching into present-day Chad and the Central African Republic. By the late 16th century it was more important than Ghat and Ghadames.

Under Ottoman rule, from 1574 to 1912, Murzuq was at times the capital of Fezzan and enjoyed a long period of prosperity. It had a major fort and was termed the Paris of the Sahara. An Ottoman garrison was usually kept there, but local control stayed with the Sultan of Fezzan.

In the early nineteenth century Murzuq was the jumping-off point for British expeditions in search of Lake Chad and Timbuktu. The expedition of Denham, Oudney and Clapperton travelled there from Tripoli in 1822. Many British explorers thought the town unhealthy: James Richardson, in 1846, reported that three quarters of the Europeans who came there fell ill with what was called Mourzuk fever.

The town declined as modern transport replaced the caravan routes. The Ottomans ceded Fezzan to the Italians in 1912, though the town was not occupied until 1914. On 11 January 1941 about 70 men of the British Long Range Desert Group and a few Free French soldiers from Chad raided the town and its small Italian airbase, and the Italian garrison in the old fort eventually surrendered.
mus: Muş is one of the principal cities of the predominantly Kurdish-inhabited region of eastern Anatolia. It is the seat of Muş Province and Muş District. The town and the surrounding plain are often covered in fog in the mornings, and the name is sometimes linked to the Armenian word mshush, meaning fog. The 17th-century traveller Evliya Çelebi tells of a giant mouse, created by Nimrod, that destroyed the city, which was then called Muş, the Persian word for mouse. Others connect the name with the Mushki or the Mysians.

The date of foundation is unknown, but a settlement is believed to have existed by the time of Menua, king of Urartu, around 800 BCE, whose cuneiform inscription was found near the city. An inscription of the Urartian king Argisti I, who reigned from 785 to 765 BCE, was found near Kepenek Castle. In the Middle Ages the city was the centre of the Taron region of Armenia and is first mentioned as a city in Armenian manuscripts of the 9th and 10th centuries.

Taron came under the Bagratid dynasty in the late 8th century and was annexed to the Byzantine Empire in 969. After the Seljuk victory at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 it passed to the Ahlatshahs, and later to the Ayyubids, Ilkhanids and Kara Koyunlu. Between the 10th and 13th centuries Muş grew into a major city of an estimated 20 to 25 thousand people. Timur apparently took it without a battle in 1387. The Safavids held it before the Ottoman sultan Selim I took the town and region in the early 16th century, and it kept a large Armenian population under Ottoman rule.

At the turn of the twentieth century the city had around 20,000 inhabitants, of which 11,000 were Muslims and 9,000 were Christian Armenians. In June and July 1915, during the Armenian genocide, over 140,000 Armenians of the Muş sanjak, in 234 villages and towns, were targeted; the city's Armenians were killed only after the surrounding villages had been destroyed. Russian forces captured the town in February 1916, and the Second Army under Mustafa Kemal Pasha retook it in 1917.

The municipality had about 120,699 inhabitants in 2022, a majority of them Kurds, with Arabs and Hidden Armenians among them. Sights include the Murat Bridge, Muş Castle, Kepenek Castle and mosques showing Seljuk influence, among them the Ulu Mosque of the 14th century, once an Armenian church. Medieval Armenian monasteries and churches near the city, such as Arakelots and Surb Karapet, are mostly ruins; Arakelots was dynamited by local officials in the 1960s.
muscat: Muscat lies in northeast Oman on the Gulf of Oman, near the Strait of Hormuz, with the Hajar Mountains rising behind it. The water along its coast is deep, forming two natural harbours, at Muttrah and at Muscat itself. Muttrah, with its corniche and harbour, lies at the northeastern edge of the city. The climate is hot and arid, with about 10 centimetres of rain a year.

Ptolemy knew Muscat as a port in the 1st century CE, calling it Cryptus Portus, the Hidden Port, and Pliny the Elder called it Amithoscuta. It fell to a Sassanid invasion in the 3rd century under Shapur I, and conversion to Islam came in the 7th century. Coastal ports such as Muscat prospered from maritime trade and ties with the Indian subcontinent.

The Portuguese admiral Afonso de Albuquerque sailed to Muscat in 1507 to establish trade, but his ships were fired on as he approached, and he decided to conquer it. Most of the city burned. The Portuguese held it for over a century, despite a bombardment by the Ottoman Turks in 1546, and the Turks captured it twice, in 1552 and in 1581–88. The election of Nasir bin Murshid Al-Ya'rubi as Imam in 1624 shifted power to local Omanis. On 23 January 1650 the Imam's troops forced a Portuguese surrender.

A civil war and repeated incursions by the Persian king Nader Shah in the 18th century left a power vacuum, from which the Al Bu Sa'id dynasty emerged, and it has ruled Oman ever since. In 1793 the capital was transferred from Rustaq to Muscat. Said bin Sultan, who restored its naval strength in the 19th century, moved his capital to Zanzibar in 1840. On 23 July 1970 Qaboos bin Said took power in a bloodless coup, and Muscat then developed rapidly.

Muscat is the capital and most populous city of Oman, and the seat of the Governorate of Muscat, which has six wilayat. Arabic is the predominant language, and Islam, mostly Ibadi, is the main religion. The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque is among its many mosques, and Old Muscat and the Old Palace, with the forts, hold its past.
muscogee: The Muscogee, or Mvskoke, are a group of related Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands. Their historical homelands lie in what is now southern Tennessee, much of Alabama, western Georgia and parts of northern Florida. Their ancestors were part of the Mississippian cultures, which between 800 and 1600 CE built complex cities with earthwork mounds, surrounded by satellite towns and farmsteads. The Muscogee are associated with mound sites such as Ocmulgee, Etowah and Moundville.

Spanish explorers met their ancestors in the mid-16th century. The Spanish expedition brought epidemics of smallpox and measles, and the Indian slave trade conducted by colonists in the 17th and 18th centuries added to the losses. As survivors and their descendants regrouped, the Muscogee Creek Confederacy arose as a loose alliance of Muskogee-speaking peoples.

The English founded Charles Town in 1670, and traders from Carolina visited Muscogee towns to exchange firearms, gunpowder, axes, glass beads, cloth and rum for deerskins and Indian slaves. Spain built missions, while the British and French preferred trade to conversion. In the American Revolutionary War the Muscogee leaned towards the British, but, divided by factions, generally avoided sustained fighting. Many leaders of the period, among them Alexander McGillivray and William McIntosh, bore British names through intermarriage.

In 1811 the Shawnee leader Tecumseh visited Tuckabatchee, telling the Muscogee that a comet signalled his coming. Upper Towns, inspired by him and by their own religious leaders, resisted American encroachment. The result was the Red Stick War, or Creek War, of 1813-1814, which began as a civil war and became entangled with the War of 1812. General Andrew Jackson put down the rebellion with the help of Southern Muscogee, and the nation was forced to sign the Treaty of Fort Jackson on 9 August 1814, ceding land even from those who had fought beside him.

Under Jackson's presidency from 1829 the government pursued the removal of all tribes east of the Mississippi River to Oklahoma. In the 1830s most of the Muscogee were forcibly relocated to Indian Territory. A small group remained in Alabama, and others had earlier moved into Florida, where they helped form the Seminole.

The Muscogee are matrilineal: each person belongs to the clan of their mother, and inheritance and property pass through the maternal line. Hereditary chiefs were born into certain clans. Town networks were laid out around plazas, ballparks and square ceremonial dance grounds. The Stomp Dance and the Green Corn Ceremony remain revered gatherings, and stickball games, festivals and language classes continue to sustain a tribal identity.

The Muscogee language belongs to the Eastern Muskogean branch of the Muskogean family. Today the Muscogee (Creek) Nation is headquartered at Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and the Poarch Band of Creek Indians is federally recognised in Alabama.
muses: The earliest known records of the Muses come from Boeotia, and some ancient authorities regarded them as Thracian in origin. Their number and names differed by region. Pausanias reports three original Muses worshipped on Mount Helicon: Aoide, Melete and Mneme, 'song', 'practice' and 'memory'. At Delphi three were worshipped as Nete, Mese and Hypate, the names of the chords of the lyre.

From the Classical period the number was standardised at nine, the daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne in Hesiod's Theogony, from about 700 BCE. Diodorus Siculus noted that writers disagreed whether there were three or nine, and that nine prevailed on the authority of Homer and Hesiod. Alcman and Mimnermus made them children of Uranus and Gaia. They were also seen as water nymphs of the springs of Helicon and Pieris.

Not until Hellenistic times were functions assigned systematically: Calliope to epic poetry, Clio to history, Polyhymnia to hymn and mime, Euterpe to song and elegiac poetry, Terpsichore to chorus and dance, Erato to lyric choral poetry, Melpomene to tragedy, Thalia to light verse and comedy, and Urania to astronomy. Classical writers made Apollo their leader, and their cult was commonly connected with his.

In myth, Thamyris boasted that he could beat them in song; they defeated him and took away his gift of song and his sight. The Pierides, nine daughters of Pierus of Macedon, challenged them and, in Ovid's Metamorphoses, were turned into magpies. The Muses also gathered the body of Orpheus, the son of Calliope, and buried it in Leibethra.

The Greek word mousa meant 'art' or 'poetry', and mousike, source of the word music, was only one of the arts of the Muses, which also covered science, mathematics and philosophy. Before books were widely available this included nearly all learning. Alexandrian editors divided the Histories of Herodotus into nine books named after the Muses, and Solon called them the key to the good life.

Ancient poets invoked the Muse near the start of a work, as Homer does in the Odyssey. In Renaissance art, emblem books such as Cesare Ripa's Iconologia of 1593 standardised their props: a writing tablet for Calliope, a tragic mask for Melpomene and compasses and a globe for Urania.
musket: The musket was a muzzle-loaded long gun that fired black powder and appeared as a smoothbore weapon in the early 16th century, at first as a heavier variant of the arquebus capable of penetrating plate armour. The word is first recorded in Europe in 1499, but evidence of the musket as a type of firearm dates from 1521, when it described an arquebus so heavy that it had to be rested on a forked stick. The historian David A. Parrot thinks the musket as a genuine innovation uncertain, perhaps only a change of name. The heavy type went out of use by the mid-16th century as heavy armour declined, but the word remained the general term for smoothbore shoulder arms into the 19th century.

Musketeers were the first infantry to give up armour entirely. They took cover behind walls or in sunken lanes and sometimes acted as skirmishers, and their numbers rose relative to pikemen because they were more mobile. Matchlock firearms were used in India by 1500, in Đại Việt by 1516 and in Southeast Asia by 1540. In Sri Lanka the kingdoms of Sitawaka and Kandy made hundreds of muskets with a bifurcated stock, a longer barrel and a smaller calibre.

Slow reloading made volley fire important, with each row firing and reloading in turn. Matchlock volley fire was first used in 1526 when the Ottoman Janissaries fired in volleys at the Battle of Mohács, and appeared next in China under Qi Jiguang and in late 16th-century Japan. In China and Japan matchlocks stayed in use until percussion locks arrived in the 19th century.

Smoothbore muskets remained the main firearm of most armies until the mid-19th century, because rifles, known in Europe by the late 15th century, fouled quickly and loaded slowly. In New Zealand, between 1805 and 1843, at least 500 conflicts took place among Māori groups that often used trade muskets alongside traditional weapons. The Minié ball, invented by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, brought the rifled musket into wide use, and breech-loading weapons, the Henry rifle of 1860 and its descendant the Winchester ended the era of the musket.
muslim-brotherhood: Hassan al-Banna founded the Society in the city of Ismailia in March 1928 with six workers of the Suez Canal Company. They appointed him their leader and vowed to work for Islam through jihad, taking the pledge that its members would be soldiers in the call to Islam. The Brothers regard their movement as the practical extension of the pan-Islamist movement of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, and al-Banna was seen as its builder. He described the movement as a Salafiyya message, a Sunni way, a Sufi truth, a political organization, an athletic group, a cultural-educational union, an economic company and a social idea.

After the Second World War the Brotherhood established a Palestinian branch in October 1945, and a small branch appeared in Jordan around the turn of 1946. Governments in Egypt have cracked down on it repeatedly since 1948. Al-Banna led it until 1949, followed by Hassan al-Hudaybi until 1972 and Umar al-Tilmisani until 1986. The group remained on the fringe of Arab politics until the Six-Day War of 1967, when Islamism replaced secular Arab nationalism as a popular current after the Arab defeat. Under Hosni Mubarak it was the largest opposition group in Egypt and had built a wide network of support through Islamic charities working among poor Egyptians.

The movement spread beyond Egypt. It reached Algeria in the last years of French rule, where Ahmad Sahnoun led it in 1953–1954 and its members took part in the uprising of 1954–1962, but it was marginalised under the one-party rule of the FLN after independence in 1962. In Europe, the first members arrived from the Middle East in the late 1950s and early 1960s, among them leaders who had fled Gamal Abdel Nasser's rule. Student groups grew into organisations, and mosques were run as community centres.

After the fall of Mubarak in 2011 the Egyptian Brotherhood was legalised. On 30 April 2011 it launched the Freedom and Justice Party, which won 235 of the 498 seats in that year's parliamentary elections, and in 2012 its candidate Mohamed Morsi won the presidency. Morsi was overthrown in 2013 and the group was banned in Egypt.

The Brotherhood's best-known slogan is Islam is the Solution. Its English-language website lists among its principles the Islamic Sharia as the basis for controlling the affairs of state and society and the unity of Islamic countries. Views of the group differ. Authors in Foreign Affairs wrote that it has at times used or supported violence but, since the 1970s, has disavowed it and sought to take part in Egyptian politics, while others question the sincerity of its statements. Many Islamist movements and parties have drawn on al-Banna's teachings.
muslim-conquest-of-persia: In the early 7th century the Sasanian Empire was under strain. The Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 had exhausted its army, and after the execution of the shah Khosrow II in 628 ten claimants were enthroned within four years. A civil war, the Sasanian Interregnum, left the government decentralized by 632. Yazdegerd III came to the throne aged about eight and did not rebuild the army. The empire was in effect a confederation with Parthian families, some of whom wished to withdraw, and the northern and eastern houses later made peace with the Arabs rather than fight beside the Sasanians.

Muhammad died in June 632 and Abu Bakr became caliph at Medina. The Ridda Wars kept the caliphate occupied until March 633, after which the Arab chief al-Muthanna ibn Haritha raided Sasanian towns in Mesopotamia with light cavalry, and his success led Abu Bakr to consider expansion.

Under Caliph Umar the Muslims lost ground in Mesopotamia after Khalid ibn al-Walid left for Syria with half his army, and the Persians defeated Abu Ubaid al-Thaqafi in the Battle of the Bridge. Al-Muthanna won at Buwayb, and in 635 Yazdegerd III sought an alliance with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius. By 638 the Tigris and Euphrates valleys were under Muslim control, with the Persians withdrawn east of the Zagros. In Khuzestan the Persian chief Hormuzan signed and broke two treaties before he was defeated and captured at Tuster.

Umar was wary of attacking what remained of the empire, but a new offensive followed, and the Battle of Nahavand in 642 proved the key to Persia. Yazdegerd fled to raise another army with limited success. Isfahan fell after a siege of a few months, Fars was taken in stages, and expeditions went to Kerman, Sakastan, Azerbaijan and Armenia. In 651 Ahnaf ibn Qais took Nishapur, Herat and Merv, where Yazdegerd had held court; the remainder of his army was beaten at the Battle of Oxus River and retreated across the Oxus. Umar was assassinated in November 644 by an Iranian slave, Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz.

The conquerors settled in garrison towns. Non-Muslim subjects were tolerated as dhimmi and paid the jizya, and mass conversion was neither wanted nor allowed in the first centuries. Conversion was slow and incomplete, stretching over many centuries, with a majority of Persians still following Zoroastrianism at the turn of the millennium. Middle Persian stayed the official language under the Rashidun, but Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf later changed the administrative language of Iraq to Arabic. Persian survived as New Persian, with many Arabic words and the Arabic alphabet.

Historians have long relied on Arabic accounts written well after the events and on the Armenian bishop Sebeos. Parvaneh Pourshariati, in a 2008 study, questions the traditional narrative, including its timeline and specific dates.
mustafa-kemal-ataturk: Shortly after graduating from military school he was arrested for activities against the regime of Sultan Abdul Hamid II, and he was released after months only with the support of his former school director. He was posted to the Fifth Army in Damascus as a staff captain, joined a small secret society of reformist officers called Vatan ve Hürriyet, and later joined the Committee of Union and Progress, though he became known for his criticism of its leaders.

He took part in the suppression of a tribal rebellion in Tripolitania in 1908 and in the suppression of the counter-revolution of April 1909, the 31 March Incident, which ended with the deposition of Abdul Hamid II. He fought in the Italo-Turkish and Balkan Wars and rose to prominence in the Defence of Gallipoli during the First World War. After the Ottoman defeat he directed the Turkish National Movement against the partition of the country by the victorious powers, set up the provisional Ankara government and won the war against Greece, Armenia, France and the United Kingdom, a result confirmed in the Treaty of Lausanne.

During and after the war the ethnic cleansing of Armenians and Greeks from Anatolia outside Istanbul was largely completed through massacres, flight, expulsions and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. His government abolished the Ottoman sultanate in 1922 and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey in 1923, with Atatürk as its first president until his death on 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, aged 57. He was succeeded by İsmet İnönü.

As president he sought complete independence, which he defined as economic, financial, juridical, military and cultural. He led reforms to build a republican and secular nation-state with a Western facing society. The Ottoman Caliphate was abolished, a fully secular civil code replaced the semi-secular Mecelle, the fez was banned, thousands of schools were opened and a Latin-based Turkish alphabet was introduced. State-owned enterprises were set up and the first five-year plan was begun. Turkish women received equal civil and political rights.
mutapa-empire: The Mutapa Empire lay on the northern Zimbabwean Plateau, between the Zambezi and Limpopo valleys. The Portuguese term Monomotapa transliterates the royal title Mwenemutapa, from mwene, lord, and mutapa, conquered land; the title came to name the kingdom itself. Shona tradition links its beginnings to Great Zimbabwe: some Karanga migrated north, perhaps after a salt shortage, and an elephant hunter named Mutota became prominent, took an interest in Zambezi trade and found salt in Dande.

Early in the fifteenth century Angoche traders had opened a route along the Zambezi to the goldfields near Khami, and the Karanga intermarried with the Tonga and Tavara and influenced their succession disputes. Mutota led the militaristic Nzou Samanyanga clan to conquer Dande, built a stone enclosure, called a zimbabwe, as capital at Chitako-Changonya Hill and gave land and posts to his allies.

After Mutota and his successor Matope, a son named Nyahuma Mukombero conquered Uteve, valuable because Kilwa and Sofala traded with the interior through it. Tradition says Changamire I, governor of the southern province of Guruuswa, helped him. The Tonga of the Lower Zambezi rebelled from about 1550. Portugal sent Francisco Barreto to conquer the gold, but his army reached Sena by 1571 and returned empty-handed, and his successor Vasco Homem's force was destroyed at Chikova.

After Mwenemutapa Gatsi Rusere died, his son Nyambo Kapararidze killed a Portuguese ambassador and declared war on the Portuguese. A Portuguese army, mostly of African soldiers, defeated him at Masapa in 1629 and placed Mavhura on the throne. Mavhura accepted terms of vassalage, including the Portuguese king's suzerainty, the expulsion of Muslims and open mines, and was baptised. In the 1680s Changamire Dombo, who had used the royal cattle to gain followers, defeated the Portuguese and Mukombwe's forces and went south to conquer Butua. Later reigns saw civil war and a capital in Chidima, in present-day Mozambique.

The ruler, the mambo, took the title Mwenemutapa and held court in a zimbabwe, a walled stone enclosure; later courts were of mud and wood. His wives, hundreds in number, were daughters of vassals, divided into nine houses. The economy rested on farming and cattle, lent out under the kuronzera system, which acted as vassalage. Religion centred on spirits and ancestors: mhondoro mediums, said to have begun with Matope, were consulted on war, succession and rain.
mutare: Mutare lies near the border with Mozambique, about 290 kilometres from the Mozambican port of Beira, which has earned it the title Zimbabwe's Gateway to the Sea. The town lies north of the Bvumba Mountains and south of the Imbeza Valley, and it is also called the Gateway to the Eastern Highlands. Christmas Pass, a winding road with views of the highlands, leads into the city from the west and was named by colonial pioneers who camped at its foot on Christmas Day 1890. Many Zimbabweans call the city Kumakomoyo, place of many mountains.

The region had a long history of trading caravans passing through on the way between Indian Ocean ports such as Sofala and inland settlements such as Great Zimbabwe. The British archaeologist E. M. Andrews found a large hoard of soapstone carvings, jewellery, weapons and other objects near Mutare early in the twentieth century; they were donated to the British Museum in 1905. The area was the site of Chief Mutasa's kraal. In 1890 A. R. Coquhoun was given concessionary rights and Fort Umtali was established between the Tsambe and Mutare Rivers. The name Mutare is said to derive from utare, meaning iron or possibly gold, probably given to the river after gold was found in the Penhalonga valley.

In 1891 the settlement was moved to a site now known as Old Mutare, about 14 kilometres north of the city centre. The construction of the railway between Beira and Bulawayo led to a third move, closer to the line, and the British South Africa Company paid compensation to the townspeople for the cost. A tramway carried passengers from the railway station up to the Umtali Club from 26 January 1897 until 23 May 1921. The town was proclaimed a municipality on 11 June 1914 and was granted city status in 1971. The name was officially changed from Umtali to Mutare in 1982. The population was 46,000 in 1965, 69,621 in 1982 and 131,367 in 1992.

Mutare is the capital of Manicaland Province, a centre of trade on the Beira-Bulawayo railway, with road and pipeline links between the coast and the interior. The population is predominantly Shona, most of them speaking the Manyika dialect. Industries include timber, forestry, farming and food processing, and gold is mined in the area. Its attractions include the Mutare Museum, the National Gallery of Zimbabwe and Murahwa Hill, known for its rock paintings and an Iron Age village.
mutsamudu: Mutsamudu, also written Moutsamoudou, was likely founded in 1482. It grew into a prosperous Swahili port that funnelled traffic between the Swahili ports of Mozambique and Madagascar. Later, Arab, Persian, Indian, Somali and Malagasy sailors and traders settled in the town. By the 1700s it was the most prosperous town in the Comoros archipelago.

In 1773 the commissioner Frederick Holtzappel visited it during an expedition along the Swahili Coast and recorded his admiration. He noted that the houses were built of stone, whitewashed inside and out, with painted plank ceilings and roofs thatched with coconut leaves. He saw several two-storey houses belonging to the elite, whom he called Turkified. There were numerous public baths in the town, and every elite household had its own. The men wore white linen gowns and turbans, as well as silk clothing and daggers with silver sheaths. The citadel was built in 1786 with British help to protect the town from Malagasy slave raisers, and it was badly damaged in 1950 at the landfall of a cyclone.
